shelves.title: Hormone therapy and stroke: the WHI verdict
shelves.question: Observational studies said hormone therapy protected women’s hearts. What did the randomized trials find — above all, about stroke?
shelves.balance: The observational claim that “hormones protect the heart” was refuted by randomization. HERS warned first, in 1998: no protection for women who already had coronary disease, more venous clots, and a pattern of early coronary harm. The Women’s Health Initiative then answered in healthy postmenopausal women — twice. Estrogen plus progestin increased stroke (HR 1.41) alongside coronary events, pulmonary embolism, and breast cancer, against fewer colorectal cancers and hip fractures, for a global index of net harm; and estrogen alone increased stroke too (HR 1.39), with no coronary benefit to set against it. Two randomized trials, two hormone regimens, one direction on stroke: up. The benefits that are real — hip fracture on both WHI cards, colorectal cancer on the combined card — are on the cards, at full weight. (Panel positions: Endocrine Society and NAMS statements — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: WHI Estrogen + Progestin 2002: stopped early — stroke HR 1.41, CHD 1.29, pulmonary embolism 2.13, breast cancer 1.26; the global index said net harm.
cards.summary: WHI 2002 — the estrogen-plus-progestin trial was stopped after a mean 5.2 years, because the breast-cancer statistic crossed its stopping boundary and the global index supported risks exceeding benefits. Hazard ratios vs placebo: CHD 1.29 , stroke 1.41 , pulmonary embolism 2.13 , invasive breast cancer 1.26 — against colorectal cancer 0.63 and hip fracture 0.66 — with the global index at 1.15 in 16,608 healthy postmenopausal women. Absolute excess risk of global-index events: 19 more per 10,000 person-years.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Women’s Health Initiative), JAMA 2002
cards.people: 16,608 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 years with an intact uterus, recruited by 40 US clinical centers in 1993–1998. Conjugated equine estrogens 0.625 mg/d plus medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg/d in one tablet (8,506 women) or placebo (8,102). Planned duration 8.5 years; on May 31, 2002, after a mean of 5.2 years of follow-up, the data and safety monitoring board recommended stopping the trial
cards.result: Estimated hazard ratios (nominal 95% CIs): CHD 1.29 (1.02–1.63; 286 cases); invasive breast cancer 1.26 (1.00–1.59; 290 cases); stroke 1.41 (1.07–1.85; 212 cases); pulmonary embolism 2.13 (1.39–3.25; 101 cases); colorectal cancer 0.63 (0.43–0.92; 112 cases); endometrial cancer 0.83 (0.47–1.47); hip fracture 0.66 (0.45–0.98; 106 cases); total mortality 0.98 (0.82–1.18); and the global index 1.15 (1.03–1.28) — overall health risks exceeded benefits. In absolute terms, per 10,000 person-years, estrogen plus progestin caused 7 more CHD events, 8 more strokes, 8 more pulmonary emboli, and 8 more invasive breast cancers, against 6 fewer colorectal cancers and 5 fewer hip fractures. The authors’ conclusion: the regimen should not be initiated or continued for primary prevention of CHD
cards.watchOut: The women were 50–79 and, on average, well past menopause — so the later “timing hypothesis” (that starting near menopause might differ) is a subgroup story this trial was not designed to test, and no trial designed to test it has confirmed a cardiac benefit. The benefits on this card are real and filed at full weight: fewer hip fractures and fewer colorectal cancers. They did not outweigh the harms in the trial’s own prespecified accounting — which is exactly what the global index was built to say
cards.source: Rossouw JE, Anderson GL, Prentice RL, et al; Writing Group for the Women’s Health Initiative Investigators. Risks and benefits of estrogen plus progestin in healthy postmenopausal women: principal results from the Women’s Health Initiative randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002;288(3):321–333. DOI 10.1001/jama.288.3.321. PMID 12117397.
cards.search: whi women's health initiative estrogen plus progestin rossouw stroke coronary heart disease pulmonary embolism breast cancer colorectal hip fracture global index jama 2002 pmid 12117397 doi 10.1001/jama.288.3.321

cards.headline: WHI Estrogen-Alone 2004: stroke HR 1.39 again — no coronary benefit (HR 0.91, not significant), hip fractures down (0.61). Stopped early too.
cards.summary: WHI Estrogen-Alone 2004 — in 10,739 postmenopausal women with prior hysterectomy, conjugated equine estrogen increased stroke (HR 1.39 , 95% CI 1.10–1.77 — an absolute excess of 12 additional strokes per 10,000 person-years), did not affect CHD incidence (HR 0.91 , not significant), and reduced hip fracture (HR 0.61 ); breast cancer’s direction was favorable but not significant (0.77). The NIH ended the intervention early, after an average follow-up of 6.8 years; the global index was 1.01 — no overall benefit.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Women’s Health Initiative), JAMA 2004
cards.people: 10,739 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 years with prior hysterectomy, enrolled at 40 US clinical centers beginning in 1993, randomised to conjugated equine estrogen 0.625 mg/d or placebo. In February 2004 the National Institutes of Health decided to end the intervention phase of the trial early; average follow-up 6.8 years
cards.result: Estimated hazard ratios (95% CIs) for estrogen vs placebo: CHD 0.91 (0.75–1.12; 376 cases) — no significant effect on the primary outcome; stroke 1.39 (1.10–1.77; 276 cases); pulmonary embolism 1.34 (0.87–2.06; 85 cases); breast cancer 0.77 (0.59–1.01; 218 cases); colorectal cancer 1.08 (0.75–1.55); hip fracture 0.61 (0.41–0.91; 102 cases); total cardiovascular disease 1.12 (1.01–1.24); total fractures 0.70 (0.63–0.79); total mortality 1.04 (0.88–1.22); global index 1.01 (0.91–1.12). For the outcomes significantly affected, the absolute changes were 12 additional strokes and 6 fewer hip fractures per 10,000 person-years. The authors’ conclusion: estrogen increases stroke risk, decreases hip fracture, does not affect CHD — and should not be recommended for chronic disease prevention
cards.watchOut: This card is the shelf’s stroke replication: a different regimen (no progestin) in a different population (prior hysterectomy) produced the same direction and nearly the same size of stroke increase as Card 1 — which is why the developer’s comment on this shelf is written about stroke risk specifically. The breast-cancer figure (0.77) favors estrogen alone, but its interval crosses 1; the authors say a possible reduction requires further investigation, and the card files it as exactly that — possible, unproven
cards.source: Anderson GL, Limacher M, Assaf AR, et al; Women’s Health Initiative Steering Committee. Effects of conjugated equine estrogen in postmenopausal women with hysterectomy: the Women’s Health Initiative randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004;291(14):1701–1712. DOI 10.1001/jama.291.14.1701. PMID 15082697.

cards.headline: HERS 1998: the warning that came first — no protection in women with coronary disease (RH 0.99), more clots (RH 2.89), and NO significant difference in stroke.
cards.summary: HERS 1998 — in 2,763 postmenopausal women with established coronary disease, estrogen plus progestin did not reduce the primary outcome: 172 women in the hormone group and 176 in the placebo group had MI or CHD death (RH 0.99 ) over an average 4.1 years — despite LDL cholesterol 11% lower and HDL 10% higher on hormones. Within the overall null there were more CHD events in year 1 and fewer in years 4 and 5. Venous thromboembolic events: 34 vs 12 (RH 2.89 ); gallbladder disease: 84 vs 62 (RH 1.38 ). And on stroke, stated plainly: there was no significant difference between the groups.
cards.type: Randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled secondary prevention trial (HERS), JAMA 1998
cards.people: 2,763 women with coronary disease, younger than 80 years, postmenopausal with an intact uterus (mean age 66.7 years), at 20 US clinical centers. Conjugated equine estrogens 0.625 mg plus medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg in one tablet daily (1,380 women) or identical placebo (1,383); follow-up averaged 4.1 years
cards.result: Overall, there were no significant differences between the groups in the primary outcome or in any of the secondary cardiovascular outcomes — and the secondary outcomes included stroke or transient ischemic attack. Primary outcome (nonfatal MI or CHD death): 172 women in the hormone group and 176 in the placebo group — relative hazard 0.99 (95% CI 0.80–1.22). The lack of overall effect occurred despite a net 11% lower LDL cholesterol and 10% higher HDL cholesterol in the hormone group (each P<.001). Within the null, a statistically significant time trend: more CHD events in the hormone group in year 1, and fewer in years 4 and 5. More women in the hormone group experienced venous thromboembolic events (34 vs 12; RH 2.89 , 95% CI 1.50–5.58) and gallbladder disease (84 vs 62; RH 1.38 , 95% CI 1.00–1.92). Total mortality: 131 vs 123 deaths (RH 1.08, not significant). The authors did not recommend starting this treatment for the purpose of secondary prevention of CHD
cards.watchOut: The accuracy point of this shelf lives on this card: HERS showed no significant difference in stroke . The increased-stroke verdict belongs to the two WHI trials (Cards 1 and 2), in healthier women; HERS’s demonstrated harms were venous clots, gallbladder disease, and the early coronary pattern. Folding the three trials into “all showed stroke harm” would be exactly the kind of error this library exists to catch. HERS was also explained away for years — secondary prevention, the wrong population — until WHI tested healthier women and found net harm there too
cards.source: Hulley S, Grady D, Bush T, Furberg C, Herrington D, Riggs B, Vittinghoff E; Heart and Estrogen/progestin Replacement Study (HERS) Research Group. Randomized trial of estrogen plus progestin for secondary prevention of coronary heart disease in postmenopausal women. JAMA. 1998;280(7):605–613. DOI 10.1001/jama.280.7.605. PMID 9718051.

shelves.title: Ginger for nausea in pregnancy
shelves.question: Does oral ginger improve nausea or vomiting during pregnancy?
shelves.balance: Ginger eases nausea in pregnancy in the trial evidence; symptom relief is the whole claim — no outcome data beyond it.

cards.headline: Viljoen 2014: ginger for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
cards.summary: Meta-analysis, 12 RCTs, 1,278 pregnant women — nausea mean difference 1.20 (0.56–1.84; P=0.0002) ; vomiting mean difference 0.72 , not significant (P=0.06).
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
cards.people: 12 RCTs with 1,278 pregnant women
cards.result: Compared with placebo, ginger improved nausea scores by a mean difference of 1.20 points (95% CI 0.56–1.84; P=0.0002; I²=0%). Vomiting episodes were not significantly reduced (mean difference 0.72 , 95% CI −0.03 to 1.46; P=0.06; I²=71%)
cards.watchOut: Trials used variable doses and subjective scales, study quality was low, and vomiting did not significantly improve The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.search: viljoen 2014 ginger nausea vomiting pregnancy systematic review meta-analysis randomized trials nutrition journal pmid 24642205

shelves.title: Magnesium before preterm birth: the BEAM trial
shelves.question: Does magnesium sulfate given to a mother before early preterm birth protect her baby’s brain?
shelves.mesh: Cerebral Palsy · Double-Blind Method · Follow-Up Studies · Gestational Age · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Magnesium Sulfate · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Pregnancy · Tocolytic Agents
shelves.balance: The trial the world cites for magnesium missed its primary endpoint. What it found instead — cerebral palsy halved, as a prespecified secondary outcome — is real, is labelled secondary, and is why guidelines recommend it anyway.

cards.headline: BEAM (Rouse 2008): the primary endpoint missed; cerebral palsy was halved as a secondary outcome.
cards.summary: PRIMARY outcome (stillbirth or infant death by 1 year, or moderate/severe cerebral palsy at 2 years): 11.3% magnesium vs 11.7% placebo, RR 0.97 (0.77–1.23) — NOT significant. Prespecified secondary outcome: moderate/severe cerebral palsy 1.9% vs 3.5% , RR 0.55 (0.32–0.95) . Death alone 9.5% vs 8.5% , RR 1.12 (not significant). No life-threatening maternal events.
cards.people: 2,241 women, US Maternal-Fetal Medicine Units Network
cards.result: PRIMARY outcome (stillbirth or infant death by 1 year, or moderate/severe cerebral palsy at 2 years): 11.3% magnesium vs 11.7% placebo, RR 0.97 (0.77–1.23) — NOT significant. Prespecified secondary outcome: moderate/severe cerebral palsy 1.9% vs 3.5% , RR 0.55 (0.32–0.95) . Death alone 9.5% vs 8.5% , RR 1.12 (not significant). No life-threatening maternal events.
cards.watchOut: the famous benefit is a secondary outcome under a null primary — the card leads with that, not with the cerebral palsy figure; single trial, shelved by developer’s exception.
cards.source: Rouse DJ et al., N Engl J Med 2008 (PMID 18753646 · NCT00014989)

shelves.title: Mirabegron for overactive bladder: two trials
shelves.question: Does mirabegron, a β3-adrenoceptor agonist, relieve overactive bladder symptoms better than placebo — and with what side effects?
shelves.mesh: Acetanilides · Adrenergic beta-3 Receptor Agonists · Aged · Australia · Benzhydryl Compounds · Cresols · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists · Phenylpropanolamine · Quality of Life · Receptors, Adrenergic, beta-3 · Single-Blind Method · Surveys and Questionnaires · Thiazoles · Tolterodine Tartrate · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Bladder, Overactive · Urinary Incontinence, Urge · Urination
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 trials agree: mirabegron buys roughly a third to half an incontinence episode and about half a void a day over placebo. Its real advantage is what it is not — the dry mouth of the anticholinergics shows up at placebo rates.

cards.headline: SCORPIO (Khullar 2013): mirabegron beat placebo on leaks and voids — by fractions of an episode a day.
cards.summary: Incontinence episodes per 24h fell −1.57 (50 mg) and −1.46 (100 mg) vs −1.17 on placebo; micturitions per 24h fell −1.93 and −1.77 vs −1.34 (all p<0.05) — real, and modest.
cards.type: randomized, double-blind phase 3 trial (placebo- and tolterodine-controlled), Europe/Australia
cards.people: 1,978 patients randomised, 27 countries
cards.result: Incontinence episodes per 24h fell −1.57 (50 mg) and −1.46 (100 mg) vs −1.17 on placebo; micturitions per 24h fell −1.93 and −1.77 vs −1.34 (all p<0.05); adverse-event rates were similar across groups, and a tolterodine arm ran as active control.
cards.watchOut: 12 weeks only, diary outcomes, and the margin over placebo is a fraction of an episode a day — real, and modest.
cards.source: Khullar V et al., Eur Urol 2013 (PMID 23182126 · NCT00689104)

cards.headline: ARIES (Nitti 2013): the North American trial found the same modest gains — and placebo-level dry mouth.
cards.summary: Incontinence episodes per 24h fell −1.47 (50 mg) and −1.63 (100 mg) vs −1.13 on placebo; micturitions fell −1.66 and −1.75 vs −1.05 (p<0.05); dry mouth 0.5% (50 mg) and 2.1% (100 mg) vs 1.5% on placebo.
cards.type: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, US and Canada
cards.people: adults with overactive bladder, US and Canada
cards.result: Incontinence episodes per 24h fell −1.47 (50 mg) and −1.63 (100 mg) vs −1.13 on placebo; micturitions fell −1.66 and −1.75 vs −1.05 (p<0.05); dry mouth 0.5% (50 mg) and 2.1% (100 mg) vs 1.5% on placebo, with hypertension, UTI, headache and nasopharyngitis similar to placebo.
cards.watchOut: same modest margins as Card 1; the tolerability contrast with anticholinergics — not raw efficacy — is the clinical story.
cards.source: Nitti VW et al., J Urol 2013 (PMID 23079373)

shelves.title: Vaginal estriol for recurrent UTI
shelves.question: Does intravaginal estriol prevent recurrent urinary tract infections in postmenopausal women?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Double-Blind Method · Enterobacteriaceae · Estriol · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lactobacillus · Menopause · Middle Aged · Ointments · Recurrence · Urinary Tract Infections · Vagina
shelves.balance: One small 1993 trial, never repeated at this size, with a ten-fold difference too large to ignore and too old to rest on comfortably — shelved by developer's exception, with its attrition printed on the card.

cards.headline: Raz & Stamm 1993: vaginal estriol cut recurrent UTIs from 5.9 to 0.5 episodes a year.
cards.summary: Urinary tract infection incidence 0.5 vs 5.9 episodes per patient-year (P<0.001); lactobacilli, absent in all women before treatment, reappeared in 61% of the estriol group and none of the placebo group; mean vaginal pH fell from 5.5 to 3.8 on estriol with no significant change on placebo; vaginal colonization with Enterobacteriaceae fell from 67% to 31% on estriol and was virtually unchanged on placebo.
cards.people: 93 women enrolled (50 estriol, 43 placebo); 36 and 24 completed the 8 months.
cards.result: Urinary tract infection incidence 0.5 vs 5.9 episodes per patient-year (P<0.001); lactobacilli, absent in all women before treatment, reappeared in 61% of the estriol group and none of the placebo group; mean vaginal pH fell from 5.5 to 3.8 on estriol with no significant change on placebo; vaginal colonization with Enterobacteriaceae fell from 67% to 31% on estriol and was virtually unchanged on placebo.
cards.watchOut: side effects stopped treatment in 28% of the estriol group and 17% on placebo, and only 60 of 93 women finished — a small, old, single trial, shelved by developer’s exception; low-dose vaginal estrogen is a different question from the systemic hormone therapy convicted on Shelf #109/#137.
cards.source: Raz R, Stamm WE, N Engl J Med 1993 (PMID 8350884; no registry ID — the record carries none)

shelves.title: Aspirin in pregnancy: CLASP’s null and ASPRE’s answer
shelves.question: Does aspirin in pregnancy prevent preeclampsia — and do dose, timing, and risk selection decide the answer?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aspirin · Birth Weight · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Death · Fetal Growth Retardation · Humans · Incidence · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Pre-Eclampsia · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Outcome · Risk · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Sixty milligrams for everyone at risk did nothing measurable in 1994. Twenty-three years later: screen for risk, start 150 mg at night by 14 weeks, stop at 36 — and preterm preeclampsia fell by more than half. Same drug, different trial.

cards.headline: CLASP 1994: 60 mg of aspirin for 9,364 women at risk — no significant protection.
cards.summary: Aspirin was associated with only a 12% relative reduction in proteinuric preeclampsia, which was NOT significant; no significant effect on IUGR or on stillbirth and neonatal death; preterm delivery was lower on aspirin, 19.7% vs 22.2% (absolute reduction 2.5 per 100 women , 2p=0.003), with a significant trend toward greater preeclampsia reductions the more preterm the delivery (p=0.004).
cards.people: 9,364 women (74% entered for preeclampsia prophylaxis, the rest for IUGR prophylaxis or treatment)
cards.result: Aspirin was associated with only a 12% relative reduction in proteinuric preeclampsia, which was NOT significant; no significant effect on IUGR or on stillbirth and neonatal death; preterm delivery was lower on aspirin, 19.7% vs 22.2% (absolute reduction 2.5 per 100 women , 2p=0.003), with a significant trend toward greater preeclampsia reductions the more preterm the delivery (p=0.004).
cards.watchOut: a null headline with a signal inside it — the benefit concentrated in early, severe disease, which is exactly the subgroup Card 2’s trial went and selected for; transfusion after delivery was slightly increased.
cards.source: CLASP Collaborative Group, Lancet 1994 (PMID 7906809; no registry ID — pre-registration era)

cards.headline: ASPRE 2017: screened, high-dose, nighttime aspirin cut preterm preeclampsia by more than half.
cards.summary: Preterm preeclampsia 1.6% (13/798) aspirin vs 4.3% (35/822) placebo, OR 0.38 (0.20–0.74) , P=0.004; results materially unchanged in the sensitivity analysis; adherence of 85% or more of tablets in 79.9% of participants; no significant differences in neonatal adverse outcomes.
cards.people: 1,776 women randomized; 798 aspirin and 822 placebo in the analysis (152 withdrew consent, 4 lost)
cards.result: Preterm preeclampsia 1.6% (13/798) aspirin vs 4.3% (35/822) placebo, OR 0.38 (0.20–0.74) , P=0.004; results materially unchanged in the sensitivity analysis; adherence of 85% or more of tablets in 79.9% of participants; no significant differences in neonatal adverse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: the win is specific — screened high-risk women, 150 mg, at night, started by 14 weeks; it does not rehabilitate low-dose aspirin for unscreened populations (Reference 1), and term preeclampsia was not the endpoint it moved.
cards.source: Rolnik DL et al., N Engl J Med 2017 (PMID 28657417 · ISRCTN13633058)

shelves.title: Multiple micronutrients vs iron–folate in pregnancy: one positive, one null
shelves.question: In pregnancy, do multiple-micronutrient supplements improve fetal and infant outcomes compared with iron–folic acid alone?
shelves.balance: The Indonesian trial found fewer early infant deaths with multiple micronutrients than with iron–folate alone; the equally large Bangladeshi trial found no mortality difference, though babies were less often preterm or low birthweight. One positive against a large null — the mortality claim is a maybe. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence) for infant mortality · POSSIBLE for preterm birth and low birthweight.

cards.headline: SUMMIT: multiple micronutrients cut early infant mortality vs iron–folate in Indonesia (RR 0.82)
cards.summary: Early infant mortality 35.5 vs 43.0 per 1,000 live births (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70–0.95, p=0.010); combined fetal loss and neonatal death RR 0.89 (0.81–1.00).
cards.people: 31,290 pregnant women in Indonesia; multiple micronutrients vs iron–folic acid through routine prenatal care
cards.result: Early infant mortality 35.5 vs 43.0 per 1,000 live births (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.70–0.95, p=0.010); combined fetal loss and neonatal death RR 0.89 (0.81–1.00); benefits larger in mothers undernourished (RR 0.75) or anaemic (RR 0.62) at enrolment.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomized, and the combined fetal-loss/neonatal-death interval touches 1.00. The larger benefits sat in undernourished and anaemic mothers — and Card 2's equally large trial did not reproduce the mortality result.
cards.source: Shankar et al. (SUMMIT). Lancet. 2008;371:215–227. PMID 18207017 · ISRCTN34151616.

shelves.title: Calcium in pregnancy: helps where intake is low
shelves.question: Does calcium supplementation in pregnancy prevent preeclampsia and hypertensive disorders?
shelves.balance: Calcium helps where dietary intake is low — fewer hypertensive disorders in Argentina, and in the WHO trial less severe disease even though preeclampsia itself was not significantly reduced. In a well-nourished US population it did nothing. The benefit follows the deficiency. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE in low-intake populations · the null in replete populations is solid.

cards.headline: Belizán 1991: calcium cut hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in a low-intake Argentine population (OR 0.63)
cards.summary: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy 9.8% vs 14.8% (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.44–0.90).
cards.people: 1,194 nulliparous women in Argentina (low baseline calcium intake); 2 g/day elemental calcium from week 20 vs placebo
cards.result: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy 9.8% vs 14.8% (OR 0.63, 95% CI 0.44–0.90).
cards.watchOut: Baseline intake was low — the population the rest of this shelf identifies as the one that benefits.

shelves.title: Overactive bladder drugs: the anticholinergic head-to-head
shelves.question: Head to head, how do tolterodine and oxybutynin compare for overactive bladder — on symptoms, and on dry mouth?
shelves.mesh: Tolterodine Tartrate · Muscarinic Antagonists · Double-Blind Method · Xerostomia · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: The mirabegron half of this topic is already home on Shelf #149 (SCORPIO and ARIES: modest gains over placebo, dry mouth at placebo rates) and is not re-carded here. This shelf adds the anticholinergic head-to-head, OBJECT — and it cuts against the usual summary: extended-release oxybutynin beat tolterodine on all three of the trial’s main diary outcomes, while dry mouth, the side effect that decides tolerability, was no less common on tolterodine (33.2% vs 28.1%, not significant). For refractory overactive bladder, the named next-step trials are BESIDE (mirabegron added to solifenacin) and ROSETTA (onabotulinumtoxinA vs sacral neuromodulation) — noted here, not carded.

cards.headline: OBJECT (Appell 2001): extended-release oxybutynin beat tolterodine on every main outcome — and dry mouth was no kinder on tolterodine
cards.summary: 378 randomised (315 women, 63 men): oxybutynin ER 10 mg/day beat tolterodine 2 mg twice daily on weekly urge incontinence (P=.03), total incontinence (P=.02) and voiding frequency (P=.02) at 12 weeks; dry mouth 28.1% vs 33.2% (P=.32).
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, parallel-group trial (OBJECT study), 37 US sites
cards.people: 378 randomised and treated (315 women, 63 men) with 7–50 urge-incontinence episodes per week and 10 or more voids per 24 hours; oxybutynin ER 10 mg once daily vs tolterodine 2 mg twice daily for 12 weeks; 332 completed
cards.result: At 12 weeks, adjusted for baseline, oxybutynin ER was significantly more effective on weekly urge incontinence (P=.03), total incontinence (P=.02), and micturition frequency (P=.02); both drugs improved all three measures versus baseline (P<.001). Dry mouth: 28.1% on oxybutynin ER vs 33.2% on tolterodine (P=.32); CNS and other adverse events were low and similar.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week trial with diary outcomes, and the oxybutynin was the extended-release form — the result does not transfer to immediate-release oxybutynin, whose dry-mouth burden is higher. The trial also enrolled men (17%).
cards.source: Appell et al. Mayo Clin Proc. 2001;76:358–363. PMID 11322350 · no registry ID (pre-registration era).

shelves.title: Emergency contraception: the standard changed twice
shelves.question: After unprotected sex, which emergency-contraception pill works best — and how did the standard change twice?
shelves.mesh: Contraceptives, Postcoital, Hormonal · Levonorgestrel · Norpregnadienes · Contraception, Postcoital · Pregnancy · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: Two trials, two changes of standard. In 1998 the WHO Task Force trial showed levonorgestrel alone beat the Yuzpe combined regimen on pregnancies (1.1% vs 3.2%) with far less nausea and vomiting — and levonorgestrel became the standard. In 2010 ulipristal acetate was non-inferior to levonorgestrel within 72 hours (1.8% vs 2.6%), and in the 72–120-hour group every one of the three pregnancies was on levonorgestrel. For both regimens, earlier is better: efficacy fell the longer treatment was delayed.

cards.headline: Glasier 2010: ulipristal matched levonorgestrel within 72 hours — and kept working out to 5 days
cards.summary: Pregnancies within 72 h: 1.8% on ulipristal vs 2.6% on levonorgestrel (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35–1.31) — 2,221 women randomised; between 72 and 120 h, all 3 pregnancies were on levonorgestrel.
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre non-inferiority trial (participants masked; investigators not masked), Lancet 2010
cards.people: 2,221 women with regular menstrual cycles requesting emergency contraception within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse; a single supervised dose of ulipristal acetate 30 mg (1,104) or levonorgestrel 1.5 mg (1,117)
cards.result: In the efficacy-evaluable population treated within 72 hours (n=1,696), pregnancies were 15 ( 1.8% ) on ulipristal vs 22 ( 2.6% ) on levonorgestrel (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35–1.31) — non-inferior. Between 72 and 120 hours (203 women) there were 3 pregnancies, all on levonorgestrel. A meta-analysis with an earlier trial (0–72 h) gave 1.4% vs 2.2% (OR 0.58, 0.33–0.99). Headache was the commonest adverse event (about 19% in both groups).
cards.watchOut: Not a fully double-blind trial — participants were masked, investigators were not. The within-72-hour difference was not significant on its own; the claim is non-inferiority plus the 5-day window.

shelves.title: Ovulation induction in PCOS: letrozole, clomiphene, metformin
shelves.question: For infertility in the polycystic ovary syndrome, which first drug gives the most live births — letrozole, clomiphene, or metformin?
shelves.mesh: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome · Clomiphene · Metformin · Letrozole · Live Birth · Ovulation Induction · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: Metformin alone lost clearly in 2007: live birth 7.2% against 22.5% on clomiphene, and adding metformin to clomiphene (26.8%) was not significantly better than clomiphene alone. In 2014 letrozole then beat clomiphene outright — live births 27.5% vs 19.1%, a higher ovulation rate, and fewer twin pregnancies (3.4% vs 7.4%). The popular drug order is not the order the trials support: on live births, it is letrozole first, clomiphene second, metformin a distant third.

cards.headline: Legro 2014: letrozole beat clomiphene on live births — 27.5% vs 19.1%
cards.summary: Cumulative live births 103/374 (27.5%) on letrozole vs 72/376 (19.1%) on clomiphene (rate ratio 1.44, 95% CI 1.10–1.87; P=0.007) — 750 women with PCOS.
cards.type: Double-blind, multicenter trial, N Engl J Med 2014
cards.people: 750 women aged 18–40 with PCOS (modified Rotterdam criteria), at least one patent fallopian tube and a partner with a sperm concentration of at least 14 million per milliliter; letrozole vs clomiphene for up to five treatment cycles
cards.result: Cumulative live births were 103 of 374 ( 27.5% ) on letrozole vs 72 of 376 ( 19.1% ) on clomiphene (rate ratio 1.44, 95% CI 1.10–1.87; P=0.007). Cumulative ovulation was higher with letrozole (61.7% vs 48.3% of cycles, P<0.001). Pregnancy loss (31.8% vs 29.1%) and congenital anomalies (4 vs 1 major anomalies, P=0.65) did not differ significantly; twin pregnancy was 3.4% vs 7.4%. Hot flushes were commoner on clomiphene; fatigue and dizziness on letrozole.
cards.watchOut: Live birth, not ovulation, was the primary outcome — the endpoint that matters. The anomaly counts (4 vs 1) were small and not significant, and they are printed here rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: Legro et al. N Engl J Med. 2014;371:119–129. PMID 25006718 · NCT00719186.

cards.headline: PPCOS I (Legro 2007): metformin alone was clearly worst — live birth 7.2% vs 22.5% on clomiphene
cards.summary: Live births: clomiphene 22.5% (47/209), metformin 7.2% (15/208), both 26.8% (56/209) — 626 women; the combination was not significantly better than clomiphene alone (P=0.31).

cards.result: Live-birth rates were 22.5% (47/209) on clomiphene, 7.2% (15/208) on metformin, and 26.8% (56/209) on the combination (P<0.001 for metformin vs each clomiphene-containing arm; P=0.31 for clomiphene vs the combination). shelves.title: Endometriosis pain: elagolix, the twin Elaris trials
shelves.question: Does elagolix, an oral GnRH antagonist, reduce endometriosis pain — and what does the estrogen suppression cost?
shelves.mesh: Endometriosis · Dysmenorrhea · Pelvic Pain · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Bone Density · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: The twin Elaris trials agree: both elagolix doses beat placebo on dysmenorrhea and nonmenstrual pelvic pain at 3 months, sustained at 6 months — and the higher dose (200 mg twice daily) roughly doubled the dysmenorrhea response of the lower dose. The cost is printed on both cards: dose-dependent loss of bone mineral density, more hot flushes, and higher serum lipids — the hypoestrogenic price of GnRH blockade, and the reason treatment duration is limited.

cards.headline: Elaris EM-I (Taylor 2017): dysmenorrhea response 46.4% and 75.8% on elagolix vs 19.6% on placebo
cards.summary: At 3 months, response for dysmenorrhea 46.4% (150 mg daily) and 75.8% (200 mg twice daily) vs 19.6% placebo; for nonmenstrual pelvic pain 50.4% and 54.5% vs 36.5% (all P<0.001) — 872 women.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, 6-month phase 3 trial (Elaris Endometriosis I, EM-I), N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 872 women with surgically diagnosed endometriosis and moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain; elagolix 150 mg once daily, elagolix 200 mg twice daily, or placebo
cards.result: At 3 months, the proportion meeting the clinical response criteria for dysmenorrhea was 46.4% on the lower dose and 75.8% on the higher dose vs 19.6% on placebo; for nonmenstrual pelvic pain, 50.4% and 54.5% vs 36.5% (P<0.001 for all comparisons). Responses were sustained at 6 months; 74.9% of women completed the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Bone mineral density fell more on elagolix than on placebo, in a dose-dependent pattern, alongside more hot flushes and higher serum lipids — hypoestrogenic effects that cap how long the drug can be used. Reported in the same paper as Elaris EM-II (Reference 2).

shelves.title: Uterine fibroids: relugolix combination therapy
shelves.question: Does once-daily relugolix combination therapy control fibroid bleeding — without costing bone?
shelves.mesh: Leiomyoma · Uterine Neoplasms · Menorrhagia · Drug Therapy, Combination · Estradiol · Norethindrone Acetate · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: Two replicate trials, one answer: about 7 in 10 women on relugolix combination therapy met the response definition (menstrual blood loss under 80 mL and at least 50% down from baseline) against about 1 in 6 on placebo — with bone mineral density preserved, because the combination’s low-dose estradiol and norethindrone add back what the GnRH blockade takes away. The trial’s own delayed-treatment arm, which spent its first 12 weeks on relugolix alone, lost bone — the internal control that proves the add-back is doing the work. Adverse events overall were similar to placebo.

cards.headline: LIBERTY 1 (Al-Hendy 2021): response 73% on relugolix combination vs 19% on placebo
cards.summary: Response (blood loss <80 mL and ≥50% below baseline): 73% on relugolix combination vs 19% on placebo (P<0.001) — 388 women over 24 weeks; bone density preserved on the combination.
cards.type: Double-blind, 24-week, phase 3 trial (LIBERTY 1), N Engl J Med 2021
cards.people: 388 women with fibroid-associated heavy menstrual bleeding, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, relugolix combination therapy (relugolix 40 mg, estradiol 1 mg, norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg, once daily), or delayed combination therapy (12 weeks of relugolix alone, then 12 weeks of the combination)
cards.result: 73% of the combination group met the primary response definition (blood loss under 80 mL and at least 50% below baseline) vs 19% on placebo (P<0.001). Six of seven key secondary endpoints improved, including amenorrhea, pain, anemia, and uterine volume — but not fibroid volume. Adverse events were similar to placebo; bone mineral density was preserved on the combination and fell on relugolix monotherapy.
cards.watchOut: The response definition is a bleeding endpoint, not a fibroid-shrinkage endpoint: fibroid volume itself did not significantly improve. Reported in the same paper as LIBERTY 2 (Reference 2).
cards.source: Al-Hendy et al. N Engl J Med. 2021;384:630–642. PMID 33596357 · NCT03049735.

cards.headline: LIBERTY 2 (Al-Hendy 2021): the replicate trial — response 71% vs 15%
cards.summary: Response 71% on relugolix combination vs 15% on placebo (P<0.001) — 382 women over 24 weeks, with bone density preserved on the combination, as in LIBERTY 1.
cards.type: Double-blind, 24-week, phase 3 trial (LIBERTY 2), N Engl J Med 2021

cards.result: 71% of the combination group met the primary response definition (blood loss under 80 mL and at least 50% below baseline) vs 15% on placebo (P<0.001), with the same pattern of secondary-endpoint improvements and bone density preserved on the combination, as in LIBERTY 1.

shelves.title: Heavy menstrual bleeding: the IUS, and surgery head-to-head
shelves.question: For heavy menstrual bleeding, what beats what — the hormonal IUS against usual medical therapy, and ablation against hysterectomy?
shelves.mesh: Menorrhagia · Levonorgestrel · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Endometrial Ablation Techniques · Hysterectomy · Quality of Life · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: ECLIPSE, in primary care: the levonorgestrel IUS beat usual medical therapy on bleeding-specific quality of life at 2 years (between-group difference 13.4 points on the Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale), and more women were still using it (64% vs 38%). HEALTH, among women who had reached surgery: laparoscopic supracervical hysterectomy beat endometrial ablation on satisfaction at 15 months (97% vs 87%) and on best-possible quality-of-life scores — bought with a longer operation and a longer recovery, at a similar rate of serious complications. Both trials were open-label and their headline outcomes are patient-reported; the cards carry the label.

cards.headline: ECLIPSE (Gupta 2013): the levonorgestrel IUS beat usual medical therapy on bleeding quality of life at 2 years — open-label
cards.summary: MMAS scores favored the LNG-IUS by 13.4 points (95% CI 9.9–16.9; P<0.001) at 2 years; still on treatment 64% vs 38% — 571 women in primary care.

cards.people: 571 women with menorrhagia presenting to their primary care providers; levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) vs usual medical treatment (tranexamic acid, mefenamic acid, combined estrogen-progestogen, or progesterone alone)
cards.result: Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale (MMAS) scores rose by 32.7 points on the LNG-IUS vs 21.4 on usual treatment by 6 months (P<0.001 for both), and the advantage was maintained at 2 years: mean between-group difference 13.4 points (95% CI 9.9–16.9; P<0.001). All MMAS domains and seven of eight quality-of-life domains favored the LNG-IUS. At 2 years, 64% were still using the LNG-IUS vs 38% still on usual treatment (P<0.001). Surgical intervention and serious adverse events did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a patient-reported primary outcome — women knew which treatment they had. “Usual medical therapy” was a menu of standard drugs, not one comparator.

shelves.title: Stress incontinence surgery: slings, and tape vs colposuspension
shelves.question: For stress incontinence surgery, which sling route — and how does the tension-free tape compare with the older colposuspension?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Incontinence, Stress · Suburethral Slings · Urologic Surgical Procedures · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: TOMUS found the two sling routes equivalent on objective success at 12 months (80.8% retropubic vs 77.7% transobturator, inside the pre-set ±12-point margin) — so the choice is made on complications, which differ: voiding dysfunction needing surgery 2.7% vs 0% with the retropubic route, neurologic symptoms 9.4% vs 4.0% with the transobturator route. Against the older open operation, tension-free vaginal tape at 2 years cured at least as many women (63% vs 51% on the strict count that treats missing data as failure; the authors’ own conclusion was “as effective as”). Both trials were open-label — surgery cannot be blinded — and the cards carry that label.

cards.result: Objectively assessed success was 80.8% with retropubic vs 77.7% with transobturator slings (difference 3.0 percentage points, 95% CI −3.6 to 9.6) — inside the ±12-point equivalence margin. Subjectively assessed success was 62.2% vs 55.8% (difference 6.4, −1.6 to 14.3) — similar, but not within the equivalence margin. Voiding dysfunction requiring surgery: 2.7% vs 0% (P=0.004); neurologic symptoms: 4.0% vs 9.4% (P=0.01). Urge incontinence, satisfaction, and quality of life did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Open-label — unavoidable in a surgical trial, and the subjective endpoint is the one expectations can bend. The equivalence margin was wide (±12 points) by design.

shelves.title: Hot flushes without hormones: fezolinetant
shelves.question: Without hormones, does the neurokinin-3 blocker fezolinetant reduce menopausal hot flushes — and what needs monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Hot Flashes · Menopause · Receptors, Neurokinin-3 · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: The twin SKYLIGHT trials agree: fezolinetant 30 mg and 45 mg cut flush frequency by roughly 2 to 2.5 more flushes a day than placebo at weeks 4 and 12, with severity down as well, benefit visible by week 1 and maintained through the 40-week extension — a real but moderate effect, measured against a large placebo response. Liver monitoring is printed on this shelf as the desk required: enzyme elevations in the trials were uncommon and transient (in SKYLIGHT 2, ALT/AST rises above 3× the upper limit of normal occurred in 6 participants across all groups, with no Hy’s-law cases) — and liver-function monitoring is part of the drug’s labeled use.

cards.headline: SKYLIGHT 1 (Lederman 2023): fezolinetant cut flush frequency by about 2.4–2.6 more per day than placebo at week 12
cards.summary: Vs placebo at week 12: frequency difference −2.39 (30 mg) and −2.55 (45 mg) flushes/day; severity difference −0.24 and −0.20 (all significant) — 522 women treated.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (SKYLIGHT 1), Lancet 2023
cards.people: 527 women aged 40–65 with an average of seven or more moderate-to-severe hot flushes a day, randomised at 97 facilities (522 received at least one dose); placebo, fezolinetant 30 mg, or fezolinetant 45 mg once daily — 12 weeks placebo-controlled, then a 40-week active extension
cards.result: Versus placebo, the difference in change in flush frequency was −1.87 (30 mg) and −2.07 (45 mg) at week 4, and −2.39 and −2.55 at week 12 (P<0.001); severity differences were −0.24 and −0.20 at week 12 (P=0.002 and P=0.007). Improvement was seen by week 1 and maintained over 52 weeks. Treatment-emergent adverse events in the first 12 weeks: 37% (30 mg), 43% (45 mg), 45% (placebo). Liver enzyme elevations were few (placebo 1, 30 mg 2, 45 mg 0), asymptomatic and transient.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase is 12 weeks; the 40-week extension had no placebo arm. Liver monitoring is part of this drug’s labeled use — enzyme rises were rare here, but the trials were not powered for liver injury.

shelves.title: Uncomplicated UTI in women: which short course cures?
shelves.question: For uncomplicated cystitis in women, which short course actually cures — and which convenient option underperforms?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Tract Infections · Cystitis · Fosfomycin · Nitrofurantoin · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Anti-Infective Agents, Urinary · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: Huttner 2018 was the surprise: the single 3 g dose of fosfomycin — the most convenient regimen on this shelf — resolved fewer infections than 5 days of nitrofurantoin (clinical resolution 58% vs 70% through day 28). Gupta 2007 supplies the older comparison: 5 days of nitrofurantoin matched 3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (clinical cure 84% vs 79%) — except where the organism was TMP-SMX-resistant, when TMP-SMX cure fell to 41%. Both trials were open-label. For preventing recurrent UTI rather than treating it, methenamine (ALTAR 2022, non-inferior to daily antibiotic prophylaxis) is noted here without a card; cranberry and vaginal estriol already live on Shelves #50 and #150.

cards.headline: Huttner 2018: single-dose fosfomycin lost to 5-day nitrofurantoin — resolution 58% vs 70% — open-label
cards.summary: Clinical resolution through day 28: 70% (171/244) on nitrofurantoin vs 58% (139/241) on single-dose fosfomycin (difference 12%, 95% CI 4–21%; P=.004) — 513 women.
cards.type: Multinational, open-label, analyst-blinded randomized clinical trial, JAMA 2018
cards.people: 513 nonpregnant women aged 18 or older with symptoms of lower UTI and a positive urine dipstick, recruited in Switzerland, Poland, and Israel; nitrofurantoin 100 mg three times a day for 5 days (255) vs a single 3 g dose of fosfomycin (258)
cards.result: Clinical resolution through day 28 was achieved by 171 of 244 women ( 70% ) on nitrofurantoin vs 139 of 241 ( 58% ) on fosfomycin (difference 12%, 95% CI 4–21%; P=.004). Microbiologic resolution: 74% vs 63% (difference 11%, 1–20%; P=.04). Adverse events were few and mainly gastrointestinal (nausea 3% vs 2%; diarrhea 1% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label — women knew whether they had one dose or five days, and the primary outcome is symptom resolution, which expectations can bend; the microbiologic outcome pointed the same way, which strengthens the finding.

shelves.title: Tdap in pregnancy: antibodies across the placenta, 91% programme effectiveness in the newborn’s first months
shelves.question: Does Tdap vaccination in pregnancy protect the newborn against pertussis?
shelves.mesh: Diphtheria-Tetanus-acellular Pertussis Vaccines · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pertussis Vaccine · Pregnancy · Whooping Cough
shelves.balance: The mechanism is randomised and the outcome is measured where it matters. A small double-blind trial showed Tdap at 30–32 weeks puts high pertussis-antibody concentrations into the newborn (68.8 vs 14.0 EU/mL at birth), still present at two months, with no safety signal in 48 women. England’s national programme then measured the clinical claim: 91% effectiveness [84–95] against confirmed pertussis in infants under 3 months, with cases in that age group falling 78% in the programme’s first year. LIKELY, with the fence printed: the effectiveness is observational (screening method), and the trial’s size proves mechanism, not rare-event safety. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: The randomised trial (Munoz 2014, JAMA): Tdap at 30–32 weeks put pertussis antibodies into the newborn — and found no safety signal in 48 women
cards.summary: A phase 1–2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 48 pregnant women received Tdap (n=33) or placebo (n=15) at 30–32 weeks’ gestation, with crossover vaccination postpartum. No Tdap-associated serious adverse events occurred in women or infants , and infant growth and development were similar. Pertussis-toxin antibody concentrations at delivery were 51.0 EU/mL in women vaccinated in pregnancy vs 9.1 in controls; in their infants, 68.8 EU/mL at birth vs 14.0 (P<.001) and 20.6 vs 5.3 EU/mL at 2 months — the window when pertussis kills and infants are too young for their own series. No pertussis cases occurred in either group (the trial was far too small to see any). After the infants’ own DTaP series, their antibody responses did not differ by maternal group.
cards.type: Phase 1–2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, JAMA 2014. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT00707148.
cards.people: 48 pregnant women aged 18–45 years (33 Tdap, 15 placebo) vaccinated at 30–32 weeks’ gestation, and their infants, followed to 13 months.
cards.result: Significantly higher concentrations of pertussis antibodies were measured at delivery in women who received Tdap during pregnancy vs postpartum (pertussis toxin antibodies: 51.0 EU/mL [95% CI, 37.1–70.1] and 9.1 EU/mL [95% CI, 4.6–17.8]; P<.001) and in their infants at birth (68.8 EU/mL [95% CI, 52.1–90.8] and 14.0 EU/mL [95% CI, 7.3–26.9]; P<.001) and at age 2 months (20.6 EU/mL [95% CI, 14.4–29.6] and 5.3 EU/mL [95% CI, 3.0–9.4]; P<.001). No Tdap-associated serious adverse events occurred in women or infants. The authors concluded that this preliminary assessment did not find an increased risk of adverse events and that maternal immunization resulted in high concentrations of pertussis antibodies in infants during the first 2 months of life.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight women is a proof of mechanism, not a safety database: the trial shows antibodies cross and persist to two months, and it rules out nothing rarer than the very common. The shelf’s effectiveness claim therefore does not rest on this trial — it rests on Card 2’s programme data — and its safety claim must be read as ‘no signal in a small trial, consistent with the surveillance programmes built since’, not as proven safety.

cards.headline: The English programme’s effectiveness (Amirthalingam 2014, The Lancet): 91% effective against pertussis in infants under 3 months
cards.summary: England introduced pertussis vaccination in pregnancy in October 2012, mid-resurgence, and evaluated it from national surveillance. Vaccine effectiveness in infants born into the programme and younger than 3 months at onset was 91% [84–95] ; restricted to infants younger than 2 months, 90% [82–95] . Programme coverage before delivery averaged 64%. In the first nine months of 2013 versus the same period of 2012, confirmed cases in infants under 3 months fell 78% (328 to 72) and hospital admissions 68% (440 to 140) — the only age group whose 2013 cases also fell below pre-resurgence 2011.
cards.type: Observational programme evaluation (screening-method vaccine-effectiveness analysis of national surveillance data), The Lancet 2014. No registry ID — an observational study; none on the record.
cards.people: Infants in England with laboratory-confirmed pertussis from 2008 to September 2013 (effectiveness analysis: 82 confirmed cases in infants under 3 months born after 1 October 2012), with maternal coverage estimated from 26,684 women in the Clinical Practice Research Datalink.
cards.result: Vaccine effectiveness based on 82 confirmed cases in infants born from Oct 1, 2012, and younger than 3 months at onset was 91% (95% CI 84 to 95). Vaccine effectiveness was 90% (95% CI 82 to 95) when the analysis was restricted to cases in children younger than 2 months. The authors concluded that the assessment is consistent with high vaccine effectiveness, probably resulting from protection of infants by both passive antibodies and reduced maternal exposure.
cards.watchOut: The screening method estimates effectiveness from case vaccination status against population coverage — efficient and standard for programme evaluation, but sensitive to coverage misclassification, and the case count is 82. The two mechanisms the authors name (transferred antibody, and fewer infectious mothers) cannot be separated in this design. What disciplines the estimate is its size: a 91% effect with a lower bound of 84% sits far beyond this library’s 0.5 observational floor.

cards.headline: Reading the Tdap evidence together: mechanism randomised, effect measured at programme scale
cards.summary: The division of labour on this shelf is explicit. The randomised trial (n=48) proves the mechanism — vaccine in the third trimester, antibody in the cord blood, protective concentrations still present at two months — and detects no safety signal at its small scale. The programme evaluation supplies the outcome: 91% effectiveness against confirmed pertussis in the under-3-months window the mechanism predicts, corroborated by the sharp, age-specific fall in cases and admissions when the programme started. Neither card alone carries the claim; together they are the standard architecture of maternal-immunisation evidence, and the shelf grades the combination, with the small-trial fence left standing on Card 1.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states the fence.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: 48 pregnant women and their infants in a US randomised trial, and the English national birth cohort under a maternal pertussis programme from October 2012.
cards.result: The evidence establishes that third-trimester Tdap raises infant pertussis antibody concentrations through the highest-risk first two months and that a national programme using it was associated with about 90% effectiveness against infant pertussis. It does not, on these records, quantify rare maternal or fetal harms — that assurance comes from later surveillance programmes not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Cite the 91% as programme effectiveness (observational, screening method), not trial efficacy — and cite the trial for antibody transfer and the absence of an early safety signal, not for protection against disease, which it never measured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 24794369; PMID 25037990).

shelves.title: Treating gum disease in pregnancy to prevent preterm birth — OPT trial
shelves.question: Does treating periodontal (gum) disease during pregnancy, with scaling and root planing, reduce preterm birth or improve birth weight or fetal growth?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Birth Weight · Dental Scaling · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Small for Gestational Age · Periodontal Diseases · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Outcome · Premature Birth
shelves.balance: LIKELY: periodontal treatment in pregnancy improves gum measures and appears safe, but it does not significantly reduce preterm birth. The OPT trial (preterm birth 12.0% treatment vs 12.8% control; hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.37) and the larger MOTOR trial (13.1% vs 11.5%) were both null, and the Cochrane pooled estimate for preterm birth under 37 weeks was relative risk 0.87 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.10). Proposed stamp LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: OPT trial: periodontal treatment improved gums but did not alter preterm birth
cards.summary: OPT (823 women, NEJM 2006): periodontal treatment improved gum measures but preterm birth was 12.0% vs 12.8% (hazard ratio 0.93 [0.63–1.37]); birth weight and small-for-gestational-age were likewise null. Treatment was safe; it did not prevent preterm birth.
cards.people: 823 pregnant women randomized between 13 and 17 weeks of gestation (413 treatment, 410 control); 407 and 405 in the follow-up analysis; women only, by design; abstract does not state mean age
cards.result: Preterm birth before 37 weeks occurred in 49 of 407 women (12.0%) in the treatment group and 52 of 405 women (12.8%) in the control group (P=0.70; hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.37). Birth weight was 3239 g vs 3258 g (P=0.64) and small-for-gestational-age delivery was 12.7% vs 12.3% (odds ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.58). Periodontal measures improved (P<0.001). There were 5 spontaneous abortions or stillbirths in the treatment group versus 14 in the control group (P=0.08).
cards.watchOut: Treatment was scaling and root planing before 21 weeks plus monthly polishing; the null result is for this timing and intensity and for preterm birth, not for treating gum disease for the mother's own oral health.
cards.source: Michalowicz BS et al; OPT Study. N Engl J Med. 2006;355(18):1885-94. PMID 17079762. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00066131, from the record's own databank field.

cards.headline: MOTOR trial: periodontal therapy also did not reduce preterm delivery
cards.summary: MOTOR (1,806 women): preterm delivery 13.1% vs 11.5% — 1.6 points in the wrong direction, not significant; no differences in obstetric or neonatal outcomes. The second large trial agrees with the first.
cards.people: 1,806 pregnant women with periodontal disease randomized at three sites; 1,760 evaluable; women only, by design; abstract does not state mean age
cards.result: Preterm delivery before 37 weeks was 13.1% in the periodontal treatment group versus 11.5% in the delayed-treatment control group (P=.316), an absolute difference of 1.6 percentage points in the direction of more preterm delivery with treatment, not statistically significant. No significant differences in adverse event rate or major obstetric and neonatal outcomes, and no significant difference for delivery before 35 weeks as reported.
cards.watchOut: Control was delayed treatment after delivery, not no care ever; treatment was scaling and root planing early in the second trimester.

cards.headline: Synthesis: LIKELY no preterm-birth reduction from treating gum disease in pregnancy
cards.summary: Two large null RCTs and a null pooled estimate: treating gum disease in pregnancy does not reduce preterm birth — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Treat for the mother’s oral health, not as preterm prevention.
cards.people: Pregnant women with periodontal disease across the cards above; no pooled mean age stated
cards.result: Two large independent RCTs (OPT and MOTOR) and the Cochrane pool all fail to show a significant preterm-birth reduction, with absolute rates close in both arms (OPT 12.0% vs 12.8%; MOTOR 13.1% vs 11.5%). Treatment remains reasonable for maternal oral health and was safe in OPT, but should not be offered as a preterm-birth preventive. Needed evidence: trials of treatment before conception or very early in pregnancy, or in high-risk subgroups, would be a different question; none was verified in the 2024-11-08 to 2026-11-08 sweep.
cards.watchOut: Do not rescue the hypothesis with the Cochrane low-birth-weight signal alone: it is low-quality, high-bias evidence and preterm birth, the prespecified primary outcome in OPT, was null.

shelves.title: Overactive bladder drugs compared: small symptom gains, traded against dry mouth — combination adds a little more
shelves.question: Head to head, how do overactive bladder drugs — antimuscarinics and the beta-3 agonist mirabegron, alone and combined — compare on symptoms and side effects?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Bladder, Overactive · Solifenacin Succinate · Tolterodine Tartrate · Muscarinic Antagonists · Acetanilides · Thiazoles · Drug Therapy, Combination · Urinary Incontinence · Humans
shelves.balance: No overactive-bladder drug is a large-effect drug; the comparison is about small margins and which side effects a patient will accept. In STAR, flexible-dose solifenacin beat tolterodine ER on urgency episodes, incontinence, urge incontinence and pad use — with a dosing asymmetry fenced on its card. In BESIDE, patients still incontinent on solifenacin 5 mg gained more from adding mirabegron 50 mg than from staying on solifenacin 5 mg, and the combination matched solifenacin 10 mg on key endpoints while beating it on micturitions. The 64-trial network meta-analysis (46,666 patients) puts mirabegron 50 mg at efficacy comparable to most antimuscarinics, with significantly less dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention than most comparators, and the solifenacin-plus-mirabegron combination ahead of mirabegron alone on some outcomes. Mirabegron's own placebo-controlled trials live on Shelf #149 and the oxybutynin–tolterodine head-to-head on Shelf #243; this shelf is the comparison layer above them. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: STAR (Chapple 2005, Eur Urol): flexible-dose solifenacin beat tolterodine ER on urgency, incontinence and pad use over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Prospective, double-blind, double-dummy, 12-week trial comparing solifenacin 5/10 mg (dose increase permitted at week 4) with tolterodine extended-release 4 mg in overactive bladder. Solifenacin showed greater efficacy on urgency episodes, incontinence, urge incontinence and pad usage, and increased volume voided per micturition; more solifenacin patients became continent. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate and discontinuations comparably low. The record's abstract prints no event rates or arm sizes, and none are printed here.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group head-to-head trial (STAR), Eur Urol 2005. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: Patients with overactive bladder syndrome treated for 12 weeks. The record's abstract does not print the number randomised, mean age or sex breakdown, and the card does not import them.
cards.result: Solifenacin (flexible 5/10 mg) was superior to tolterodine ER 4 mg on the majority of efficacy variables: urgency episodes, incontinence and urge-incontinence episodes, pad usage and volume voided per micturition all favoured solifenacin; more solifenacin-treated patients became continent and reported improved perception of bladder condition. Numerical effect sizes are not printed in the record's abstract.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is asymmetric by design: only the solifenacin arm could raise its dose at week 4 (tolterodine patients were dummied), so STAR compares a flexible solifenacin regimen against fixed-dose tolterodine — a regimen comparison, not a pure molecule-versus-molecule test at equal dosing freedom.
cards.source: Chapple CR et al. A comparison of the efficacy and tolerability of solifenacin succinate and extended release tolterodine at treating overactive bladder syndrome: results of the STAR trial. Eur Urol. 2005;48(3):464-70. PMID 15990220

cards.headline: BESIDE (Drake 2016, Eur Urol): adding mirabegron to solifenacin beat solifenacin 5 mg and matched 10 mg in patients still incontinent on solifenacin
cards.summary: 2,174 patients who remained incontinent after 4 weeks of solifenacin 5 mg were randomised double-blind to solifenacin 5 mg plus mirabegron (25 mg rising to 50 mg), solifenacin 5 mg, or solifenacin 10 mg for 12 weeks. Combination was superior to solifenacin 5 mg on daily incontinence episodes (P=0.001), daily micturitions (P<0.001) and 3-day-diary incontinence (P=0.014); it was noninferior to solifenacin 10 mg on key secondary endpoints and superior on micturitions. All arms were well tolerated.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre phase 3b trial (BESIDE), Eur Urol 2016. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01908829.
cards.people: 2,174 patients randomised (727 combination, 728 solifenacin 5 mg, 719 solifenacin 10 mg) with overactive bladder and persistent incontinence despite 4 weeks of solifenacin 5 mg. The record's abstract does not print a mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: At end of treatment, combination therapy was superior to solifenacin 5 mg for change in daily incontinence episodes (P=0.001), daily micturitions (P<0.001) and incontinence episodes on a 3-day diary (P=0.014); noninferior to solifenacin 10 mg on key secondary endpoints and superior for micturitions. The record's abstract does not print the absolute episode counts, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: An add-on trial in proven antimuscarinic non-responders — the population in whom combination looks best; it says nothing about starting two drugs in a treatment-naive patient. Its cardiovascular-safety companion report (PMID 28419650) found no synergistic CV signal; that analysis is referenced here, not carded separately.

cards.headline: Kelleher 2018 network meta-analysis (64 trials, 46,666 patients): mirabegron matches most antimuscarinics on symptoms, with significantly less dry mouth
cards.summary: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs (2000–2017) of overactive-bladder drug treatments. Mirabegron 50 mg was significantly more efficacious than placebo on all efficacy endpoints and comparable to most active treatments; solifenacin 10 mg and solifenacin-plus-mirabegron combinations were more efficacious on some or all outcomes. Mirabegron was significantly better tolerated than 21 of 22 active comparators for dry mouth, 9 of 20 for constipation and 7 of 10 for urinary retention.
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials, Eur Urol 2018. The record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 64 studies, 46,666 participants with overactive bladder. The record's abstract does not print a pooled mean age or sex breakdown.
cards.result: Mirabegron 50 mg: significantly better than placebo on micturition frequency, urgency urinary incontinence, dry rate and 50% incontinence reduction; efficacy comparable to most antimuscarinics; dry mouth significantly less frequent than with 21/22 active comparators, constipation 9/20, urinary retention 7/10. Combination solifenacin 5 mg + mirabegron 25 or 50 mg was more efficacious than mirabegron 50 mg alone on the outcomes assessed.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis: most drug-versus-drug contrasts are indirect, built across trials with differing endpoint definitions and populations (the authors' own stated limitation). It ranks classes; it does not replace a head-to-head trial, and its sponsor context is the mirabegron literature — read the ranking as approximate, the dry-mouth gradient as the robust part.
cards.source: Kelleher C et al. Efficacy and Tolerability of Mirabegron Compared with Antimuscarinic Monotherapy or Combination Therapies for Overactive Bladder: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. Eur Urol. 2018;74(3):324-333. PMID 29699858

cards.headline: Synthesis: choose by side-effect profile and by what has already failed — the symptom differences between drugs are fractions of an episode a day
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3, read with Shelf #149 (mirabegron versus placebo: gains of fractions of an episode a day) and Shelf #243 (oxybutynin ER versus tolterodine). Across the comparison record, no monotherapy separates decisively on symptoms; dry mouth and constipation track antimuscarinic dose, mirabegron avoids most of that at comparable efficacy, and adding mirabegron to solifenacin buys a further small gain in non-responders. No card on this shelf addresses long-term anticholinergic cognitive burden — a separate question, not answered by these 12-week trials.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–3 together with the pointer shelves named in the summary.
cards.people: 46,666 participants across the network meta-analysis; 2,174 in BESIDE; STAR's randomised N is not printed in its record.
cards.result: Direction of the record: solifenacin regimen > tolterodine ER (STAR); solifenacin + mirabegron > solifenacin 5 mg and ≈ solifenacin 10 mg (BESIDE); mirabegron 50 mg ≈ most antimuscarinics with significantly less dry mouth (Kelleher NMA).
cards.watchOut: Twelve-week symptom trials cannot settle years-long questions (persistence, cognition, retention in older men with BPH); do not let a dry-mouth advantage or a fractions-of-an-episode advantage masquerade as a long-term outcome.

shelves.title: Stress incontinence: pelvic floor training first, or straight to a midurethral sling?
shelves.question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, how does initial pelvic floor muscle training (physiotherapy) compare with initial midurethral-sling surgery?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Incontinence, Stress · Pelvic Floor · Exercise Therapy · Suburethral Slings · Physical Therapy Modalities · Treatment Outcome · Female · Humans
shelves.balance: This is the rare shelf with a direct randomised answer. Labrie's multicentre trial (460 women) compared initial midurethral-sling surgery with initial physiotherapy, crossover allowed: at 12 months subjective improvement was 90.8% with surgery versus 64.4% with physiotherapy (absolute difference 26.4 percentage points), subjective cure 85.2% versus 53.4%, objective cure 76.5% versus 58.8% — while 49.0% of the physiotherapy group crossed over to surgery (and 11.2% of the surgery group crossed to physiotherapy). The 12-year follow-up (2025) found crossover from physiotherapy had reached 86.9% among responders, and women who had physiotherapy only remained about 50 percentage points behind on improvement — on a 47.7% questionnaire response, fenced on its card. Physiotherapy itself is not placebo: Cochrane's review of PFMT versus no or inactive treatment found women with stress incontinence eight times more likely to report cure (56% vs 6%). The sling-versus-sling and sling-versus-colposuspension record lives on Shelf #249 and is not repeated here. The choice the evidence frames: surgery wins on cure at one year and at twelve; training is non-invasive, helps about half, and half of its starters end up in theatre anyway. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer's review.

cards.headline: Labrie 2013 (NEJM): initial sling surgery beat initial physiotherapy — improvement 90.8% vs 64.4%, cure 85.2% vs 53.4% at 12 months
cards.summary: Multicentre randomised trial of 460 women with stress urinary incontinence assigned to midurethral-sling surgery (230) or physiotherapy with pelvic-floor muscle training (230), crossover permitted. Intention-to-treat at 12 months: subjective improvement 90.8% (surgery) vs 64.4% (physiotherapy), absolute difference 26.4 percentage points [95% CI 18.1–34.5]; subjective cure 85.2% vs 53.4% (difference 31.8 points [22.6–40.3]); objective cure 76.5% vs 58.8% (difference 17.8 points [7.9–27.3]). Crossover: 49.0% of the physiotherapy group and 11.2% of the surgery group switched treatment.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised controlled trial (PORTRET), N Engl J Med 2013. Registry as printed in the record's own text: Dutch Trial Register NTR1248; the record's databank carries no ClinicalTrials.gov ID.
cards.people: 460 women with stress urinary incontinence randomised (230 surgery, 230 physiotherapy) in the Netherlands. The record's abstract does not print a mean age.
cards.result: Subjective improvement at 12 months: 90.8% surgery vs 64.4% physiotherapy (absolute difference 26.4 percentage points; 95% CI 18.1 to 34.5). Subjective cure: 85.2% vs 53.4% (difference 31.8 points; 22.6 to 40.3). Objective cure: 76.5% vs 58.8% (difference 17.8 points; 7.9 to 27.3). Crossover to the alternative treatment: 49.0% (physiotherapy arm) and 11.2% (surgery arm).
cards.watchOut: Open treatment comparison with very heavy crossover — the intention-to-treat gap understates the per-treatment gap (the authors' per-protocol analysis shows crossover patients doing as well as initial-surgery patients), and subjective outcomes in an unblinded trial favour the more invasive arm. The surgical harms side (mesh complications, reoperation) is carried on Shelf #249 and in Card 2's reoperation figure, not in this trial's abstract.
cards.source: Labrie J et al. Surgery versus physiotherapy for stress urinary incontinence. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(12):1124-33. PMID 24047061 · NTR1248

cards.headline: van Oorschot 2025 (BJOG): at 12 years, 86.9% of the physiotherapy group had crossed to surgery — physiotherapy-only women stayed ~50 points behind on improvement
cards.summary: Observational 12-year follow-up of the Labrie PORTRET randomised trial in women with moderate-to-severe stress incontinence: 184 of 386 women (47.7%) returned the questionnaire. Intention-to-treat analysis found no statistically significant differences; crossover from initial physiotherapy to surgery was 86.9%. Post hoc, women who had physiotherapy only reported substantially less improvement than women who had initial surgery (absolute difference 50.6 percentage points [95% CI 28.2–73.1]) or surgery after physiotherapy (49.7 points [25.8–73.7]); subjective cure, severity and impact also favoured the surgery groups. Reoperation was reported by 4.6% of women.
cards.type: Observational long-term follow-up of a randomised trial, BJOG 2025 (found in the 2026-11-08 freshness sweep). The record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 184 of 386 eligible women (47.7%) from the PORTRET trial responded at 12 years; women with moderate-to-severe stress urinary incontinence, Netherlands. The record's abstract does not print a mean age at follow-up.
cards.result: Crossover physiotherapy-to-surgery 86.9%. Post hoc absolute differences in subjective improvement favouring surgery: 50.6 percentage points (95% CI 28.2 to 73.1) for initial surgery versus physiotherapy only, and 49.7 points (25.8 to 73.7) for surgery after physiotherapy versus physiotherapy only. Intention-to-treat comparison: no statistically significant differences. Reoperation reported by 4.6%.
cards.watchOut: Fence this card hard: under half the cohort responded, the headline contrasts are post hoc, and an 86.9% crossover means 'physiotherapy only' at 12 years is a small self-selected residue, not a randomised arm. It corroborates the direction of Card 1 over the long term; it does not re-randomise anyone.

cards.headline: Dumoulin 2018 Cochrane: pelvic floor training versus nothing — women with stress incontinence were 8 times more likely to report cure (56% vs 6%)
cards.summary: Cochrane review of 31 trials (1,817 women) of pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment, placebo, sham or inactive controls. In women with stress incontinence, PFMT groups were eight times more likely to report cure (56% vs 6%; RR 8.38 [95% CI 3.68–19.07]; 4 trials, 165 women; high-quality evidence per the review) and six times more likely to report cure or improvement (74% vs 11%; RR 6.33 [3.88–10.33]; 3 trials, 242 women). Trials were small-to-moderate, follow-up generally under 12 months, many at moderate risk of bias.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018. The record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 31 trials, 1,817 women from 14 countries with stress, urgency or mixed urinary incontinence; the stress-incontinence cure analysis rests on 4 trials, 165 women. Pooled mean age is not printed in the record's abstract.
cards.result: Stress incontinence, cure at end of treatment: 56% PFMT vs 6% control (RR 8.38; 95% CI 3.68 to 19.07; 4 trials, 165 women). Cure or improvement: 74% vs 11% (RR 6.33; 3.88 to 10.33; 3 trials, 242 women). For any incontinence type, cure RR 5.34 (2.78 to 10.26).
cards.watchOut: The RR of 8.38 is a relative effect on a 6% control cure rate — the absolutes (56% vs 6%) are printed beside it, as they must be. This card answers 'training versus nothing', not 'training versus surgery': the head-to-head is Card 1, and conflating the two comparisons is the standard way this literature gets misquoted.
cards.source: Dumoulin C et al. Pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment, or inactive control treatments, for urinary incontinence in women. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;(10):CD005654. PMID 30288727

cards.headline: Synthesis: training is a real treatment that about half its patients leave for surgery; surgery is the more effective first move for moderate-to-severe disease
cards.summary: Synthesis of Cards 1–3. PFMT beats nothing decisively (Cochrane) and loses head-to-head to the sling on improvement and cure at 1 year (Labrie), with 49% crossing over by 12 months and 86.9% by 12 years (van Oorschot, responder-limited). Sling-versus-sling route and tape-versus-colposuspension comparisons are on Shelf #249 and are not duplicated here. What remains untested in these cards: a strategy trial of mandatory training-first versus surgery-first on lifetime reoperation and mesh-harm endpoints — Labrie's crossover design approximates it but was not powered for harms.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study; reads Cards 1–3 together.
cards.people: 460 women randomised head-to-head; 1,817 women across the Cochrane PFMT-versus-control trials; 184 responders at 12 years.
cards.result: Improvement 90.8% vs 64.4% and cure 85.2% vs 53.4% (surgery vs physiotherapy, 12 months); PFMT cure 56% vs 6% versus inactive control; 12-year crossover from physiotherapy 86.9%, reoperation 4.6%.
cards.watchOut: Quote both halves: 'surgery beats training' without the crossover and harm context, or 'training works' without the head-to-head, each misstates this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMID 24047061, PMID 39931871 and PMID 30288727 on this shelf; no additional source.

shelves.title: Treating gestational diabetes
shelves.question: Does treating gestational diabetes (including mild GDM) improve pregnancy and neonatal outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Birth Weight · Blood Glucose/analysis · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Depression, Postpartum/epidemiology · Diabetes, Gestational/complications/diet therapy/therapy · Dystocia/epidemiology/etiology · Fetal Macrosomia/epidemiology/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Treating gestational diabetes reduced serious perinatal complications in ACHOIS (1% vs 4%; adjusted relative risk 0.33, relative) and, in the mild-GDM Landon trial, treatment missed its primary composite (32.4% vs 37.0%, P=0.14) but reduced large-for-gestational-age babies (7.1% vs 14.5%), shoulder dystocia (1.5% vs 4.0%), caesarean delivery (26.9% vs 33.8%) and pre-eclampsia/gestational hypertension (8.6% vs 13.6%). Treatment buys these gains at the price of more inductions and more neonatal-nursery admissions in ACHOIS.

cards.headline: ACHOIS: treating gestational diabetes cut serious perinatal complications from 4% to 1%
cards.summary: ACHOIS: serious perinatal complications 1% vs 4% (adjusted relative risk 0.33 , a relative measure) with treatment of gestational diabetes.
cards.people: 1,000 women between 24 and 34 weeks' gestation with gestational diabetes: 490 assigned to intervention (dietary advice, blood glucose monitoring and insulin as needed) and 510 to routine care; the abstract does not state mean age (all participants were pregnant women).
cards.result: Serious perinatal complications (death, shoulder dystocia, bone fracture and nerve palsy) occurred in 1% of infants in the intervention group versus 4% on routine care (adjusted relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.75; P=0.01 — a relative reduction, with the absolute rates 1% vs 4% beside it). More intervention infants were admitted to the neonatal nursery (71% vs 61%; adjusted relative risk 1.13) and more intervention mothers had labour induced (39% vs 29%; adjusted relative risk 1.36), while caesarean rates were similar (31% vs 32%). At three months postpartum, intervention women had lower rates of depression and better health-status scores.
cards.watchOut: The intervention was a package — diet, monitoring and insulin as needed — so no single component can be credited; the benefit came with more nursery admissions and more inductions.
cards.source: Crowther CA et al. Effect of treatment of gestational diabetes mellitus on pregnancy outcomes. N Engl J Med. 2005 Jun 16;352(24):2477-2486. PMID: 15951574. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.
