cards.headline: Landon (MFMU): treating mild gestational diabetes missed its primary composite, but shrank overgrowth, shoulder dystocia and caesareans
cards.summary: Landon (MFMU): the primary composite did not differ (32.4% vs 37.0%) — but overgrowth, shoulder dystocia and caesarean delivery all fell.
cards.people: 958 women at 24 to 31 weeks' gestation meeting criteria for mild gestational diabetes (abnormal oral glucose-tolerance test with fasting glucose below 95 mg/dL): 485 assigned to treatment (dietary intervention, self-monitoring of blood glucose and insulin if necessary) and 473 to usual prenatal care; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite (stillbirth or perinatal death plus neonatal complications including hyperbilirubinaemia, hypoglycaemia, hyperinsulinaemia and birth trauma) did not differ significantly: 32.4% on treatment versus 37.0% on usual care (P=0.14), and there were no perinatal deaths. Prespecified secondary outcomes favoured treatment: mean birth weight 3302 vs 3408 g, neonatal fat mass 427 vs 464 g, large-for-gestational-age infants 7.1% vs 14.5%, birth weight over 4000 g 5.9% vs 14.3%, shoulder dystocia 1.5% vs 4.0%, caesarean delivery 26.9% vs 33.8%, and combined pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension 8.6% vs 13.6% (P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Lead with the null primary composite: in mild GDM the proven gains are in fetal overgrowth and its consequences, not in the composite the trial was powered on.
cards.source: Landon MB et al. A multicenter, randomized trial of treatment for mild gestational diabetes. N Engl J Med. 2009 Oct 1;361(14):1339-1348. PMID: 19797280. Registry ID: NCT00069576, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treatment works for overgrowth and serious perinatal complications — LIKELY, with more intervention as the price
cards.summary: Treatment works for overgrowth and serious perinatal complications, with more intervention as the price — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ACHOIS (1,000 women with gestational diabetes) and the Landon MFMU trial (958 women with mild gestational diabetes).
cards.result: Two large randomised trials in two GDM severity bands point the same way on the baby-size pathway: ACHOIS found serious perinatal complications at 1% vs 4% (adjusted relative risk 0.33, relative), and Landon found large-for-gestational-age births at 7.1% vs 14.5% with shoulder dystocia at 1.5% vs 4.0%, despite its null primary composite (32.4% vs 37.0%). This shelf is stamped LIKELY: the direction is consistent across both trials, while the Landon primary null and ACHOIS's extra inductions and nursery admissions keep the claim two-handed. This shelf is about treating screening-detected gestational diabetes; metformin in pregnancy for pre-existing diabetes or obesity lives on Shelf #286, and delaying diabetes after GDM lives on Shelf #112 — neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two trials into one claim: ACHOIS's primary was positive and Landon's was null; the shared ground is fetal overgrowth and its downstream events.
cards.source: Synthesis of Crowther CA et al. N Engl J Med. 2005;352(24):2477-2486. PMID: 15951574; Landon MB et al. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(14):1339-1348. PMID: 19797280. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Progesterone for miscarriage: threatened and recurrent
shelves.question: Does progesterone prevent miscarriage in women with early-pregnancy bleeding, or with recurrent miscarriage?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/prevention & control · Administration, Intravaginal · Live Birth · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/diagnostic imaging · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Progesterone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY the overall null; POSSIBLE for the prior-miscarriage subgroup: In women with early-pregnancy bleeding, PRISM found live births at 75% on progesterone vs 72% on placebo (relative rate 1.03, P=0.08) — no significant overall benefit — and in women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, PROMISE found 65.8% vs 63.3% (relative risk 1.04, P=0.45), also null. The signal is confined to a prespecified PRISM subgroup, labelled as such throughout this shelf: among women with bleeding who had had three or more previous miscarriages, live births were 72% vs 57% (relative rate 1.28, relative) — a subgroup finding inside an overall-null trial, in a population PROMISE (recurrent miscarriage without the bleeding criterion) did not reproduce.

cards.headline: PRISM: progesterone for early-pregnancy bleeding did not significantly raise live births overall — 75% vs 72%
cards.summary: PRISM: live births 75% vs 72% (relative rate 1.03; P=0.08) — not significant overall.
cards.people: 4,153 women with vaginal bleeding in early pregnancy, recruited at 48 UK hospitals, randomised to vaginal progesterone 400 mg twice daily (2,079) or matching placebo (2,074) from presentation through 16 weeks of gestation; primary-outcome data were available for 97% (4,038 of 4,153); the NEJM abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Live births after at least 34 weeks of gestation occurred in 75% (1513 of 2025) of the progesterone group and 72% (1459 of 2013) of the placebo group (relative rate 1.03, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.07; P=0.08) — not significant. A sensitivity analysis with imputed missing data gave the same result. Adverse events did not differ significantly between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The overall trial is null; any benefit claim for this shelf must come from the prespecified subgroup card below and be labelled a subgroup finding, not a trial result.
cards.source: Coomarasamy A et al. A Randomized Trial of Progesterone in Women with Bleeding in Early Pregnancy. N Engl J Med. 2019 May 9;380(19):1815-1824. PMID: 31067371. Registry ID: ISRCTN14163439, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PRISM subgroup (prespecified, labelled as such): live births rose with the number of previous miscarriages — 72% vs 57% after three or more
cards.summary: PRISM's prespecified subgroup: benefit rose with previous miscarriages — after three or more, live births 72% vs 57% (interaction P=0.007); with none, nothing. Labelled prespecified on the card.
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis, reported in the trial's own HTA report (same trial as the card above — not separate evidence)
cards.people: The same PRISM population (4,153 women with early-pregnancy bleeding), split by prespecified subgroups of previous miscarriages: none, one or two, and three or more (285 women in the three-or-more stratum: 137 progesterone, 148 placebo).
cards.result: The trial's HTA report records a significant subgroup effect by number of previous miscarriages (interaction test P=0.007): no previous miscarriage — live births 74% on progesterone vs 75% on placebo (relative rate 0.99, P=0.72); one or two previous miscarriages — 76% vs 72% (relative rate 1.05, P=0.07); three or more previous miscarriages — 72% (98 of 137) vs 57% (85 of 148) (relative rate 1.28, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.51; P=0.004 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates 72% vs 57% beside it). A post hoc grouping of women with any previous miscarriage gave 75% vs 70% (relative rate 1.09; P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: This is a subgroup inside an overall-null trial. The gradient is prespecified and biologically ordered, which strengthens it, but it remains one trial's subgroup — and PROMISE (card below), in recurrent miscarriage without required bleeding, found no benefit, so the signal may depend on the bleeding-plus-history combination.
cards.source: Coomarasamy A et al. Progesterone to prevent miscarriage in women with early pregnancy bleeding: the PRISM RCT. Health Technol Assess. 2020 Jun;24(33):1-70. PMID: 32609084. cards.headline: PROMISE: in unexplained recurrent miscarriage, first-trimester progesterone did not improve live births — 65.8% vs 63.3%
cards.summary: PROMISE (unexplained recurrent miscarriage): live births 65.8% vs 63.3% — null again.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (full HTA report)
cards.people: 836 women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage (three or more first-trimester losses), aged 18 to 39 years at randomisation, conceiving naturally, at 36 UK and 9 Netherlands sites: 404 received micronised progesterone 400 mg vaginally twice daily and 432 placebo, from a positive pregnancy test (no later than 6 weeks) until 12 completed weeks; follow-up to the primary outcome was 98.8% (826 of 836).
cards.result: Live birth beyond 24 completed weeks occurred in 65.8% (262 of 398) on progesterone and 63.3% (271 of 428) on placebo (relative risk 1.04, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.15; P=0.45). There was no significant difference for any secondary outcome. The economic analysis suggested a favourable incremental cost-effectiveness ratio but with wide confidence intervals and a high level of uncertainty.
cards.watchOut: PROMISE's population had recurrent miscarriage but was not required to have bleeding in the index pregnancy — the difference from PRISM's positive subgroup is a population difference, and this shelf does not resolve which feature (bleeding, history, or both) carries the signal.
cards.source: Coomarasamy A et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, two overall nulls, one prespecified subgroup signal — the split stamp is the shelf
cards.summary: Two overall nulls (LIKELY) and one prespecified subgroup signal (POSSIBLE) — the split stamp is the shelf.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PRISM (4,153 women with early-pregnancy bleeding, plus its HTA companion report) and PROMISE (836 women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage).
cards.result: Overall, progesterone did not significantly raise live births in either large trial (PRISM 75% vs 72%, relative rate 1.03, P=0.08; PROMISE 65.8% vs 63.3%, relative risk 1.04, P=0.45) — that null is stamped LIKELY. The exception is a prespecified PRISM subgroup, stamped POSSIBLE and labelled a subgroup wherever it appears: women with bleeding and three or more previous miscarriages, at 72% vs 57% (relative rate 1.28, relative). This shelf is deliberately distinct from preterm-birth progesterone: 17-OHPC for recurrent preterm birth lives on Shelf #417 and vaginal progesterone for short cervix on Shelf #418, and no trial from either shelf is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Never quote the 72% vs 57% subgroup figure without the word subgroup and the overall-null result beside it; never quote PROMISE and PRISM as if they studied the same women.

shelves.title: Treating hypertension in pregnancy: targets and thresholds
shelves.question: Should hypertension in pregnancy be treated tightly, and should mild chronic hypertension be treated to under 140/90?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/etiology · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Hypertension, Pregnancy-Induced/drug therapy · Infant, Newborn · Intensive Care, Neonatal/statistics & numerical data · Perinatal Death/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The two trials answer two halves of the question. CHIPS found tight diastolic control (target 85 mm Hg) no better than less-tight control (target 100 mm Hg) on pregnancy loss or high-level neonatal care (30.7% vs 31.4%), but less-tight control produced far more severe hypertension (40.6% vs 27.5%). CHAP then showed that actively treating mild chronic hypertension to under 140/90 lowered its primary composite (30.2% vs 37.0%; adjusted risk ratio 0.82, relative) with no increase in small-for-gestational-age births (11.2% vs 10.4%). Treating to under 140/90 in mild chronic hypertension is the supported strategy; pushing diastolic pressure to 85 rather than 100 added nothing on the baby outcomes CHIPS measured.

cards.headline: CHIPS: tight vs less-tight diastolic control — no difference in pregnancy loss or neonatal care, but severe hypertension was far commoner with less-tight control
cards.summary: CHIPS: the primary composite was 31.4% vs 30.7% (adjusted odds ratio 1.02) for less-tight vs tight control — no difference; severe hypertension was far more common with less-tight control.
cards.people: 987 women analysed (493 less-tight, 488 tight, with outcome data as reported) at 14 weeks 0 days to 33 weeks 6 days of gestation with nonproteinuric preexisting or gestational hypertension and office diastolic pressure 90 to 105 mm Hg (85 to 105 if on antihypertensive medication); 74.6% had preexisting hypertension; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The composite primary outcome (pregnancy loss or high-level neonatal care for more than 48 hours in the first 28 postnatal days) occurred in 31.4% with less-tight control and 30.7% with tight control (adjusted odds ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.35). Serious maternal complications were 3.7% vs 2.0% (adjusted odds ratio 1.74, 95% CI 0.79 to 3.84), despite mean diastolic pressure running 4.6 mm Hg higher in the less-tight group. Severe hypertension (at least 160/110 mm Hg) developed in 40.6% of the less-tight group versus 27.5% of the tight group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: CHIPS compared diastolic targets of 85 vs 100 mm Hg in women already hypertensive — it did not test whether to start treatment at all, which is CHAP's question; its primary outcome is null and the severe-hypertension difference is a secondary outcome.

cards.summary: CHAP: treating mild chronic hypertension to under 140/90 cut the primary composite from 37.0% to 30.2% (adjusted risk ratio 0.82, relative), with no excess of small-for-gestational-age infants.
cards.people: 2,408 pregnant women with mild chronic hypertension (blood pressure under 160/100 mm Hg) and singleton fetuses at under 23 weeks' gestation, assigned to active treatment with pregnancy-recommended antihypertensive medication targeting under 140/90, or to no treatment unless severe hypertension developed; the abstract does not state mean age.

shelves.title: Magnesium sulfate for the mother: preventing and treating eclamptic seizures
shelves.question: Does magnesium sulfate prevent eclampsia in pre-eclampsia, and is it the best drug once seizures occur?
shelves.mesh: Anticonvulsants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure · Fetal Death · Gestational Age · Infant, Newborn · Magnesium Sulfate/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Maternal Mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large trial programmes answer the mother's seizure question directly. For prevention, the Magpie Trial found eclampsia in 0.8% of women with pre-eclampsia given magnesium sulfate versus 1.9% on placebo — a 58% lower risk (95% CI 40 to 71), a relative reduction with the absolute rates beside it — with maternal mortality lower but not significantly (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.14) and no clear difference in baby deaths. For treatment once seizures have occurred, the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial found recurrent convulsions in 13.2% on magnesium versus 27.9% on diazepam, and 5.7% versus 17.1% on phenytoin. Side effects were commoner on magnesium in Magpie (24% vs 5%).

cards.headline: Magpie: magnesium sulfate halved eclampsia in pre-eclampsia — 0.8% vs 1.9%
cards.summary: Magpie: eclampsia 0.8% vs 1.9% (40 vs 96 women) — a 58% relative reduction, 11 fewer cases per 1,000 women treated.
cards.people: 10,141 women with pre-eclampsia (blood pressure at least 140/90 mm Hg and proteinuria 1+ or more) who had not given birth or were within 24 hours postpartum, in 33 countries, randomised to magnesium sulfate (5,071) or placebo (5,070) where there was clinical uncertainty about magnesium; follow-up data were available for 10,110 (99.7%); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Women allocated magnesium sulfate had a 58% lower risk of eclampsia than those allocated placebo (95% CI 40 to 71 — a relative reduction), with absolute rates of 40 women (0.8%) versus 96 (1.9%): 11 fewer women with eclampsia per 1000 women treated. Maternal mortality was also lower on magnesium (relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.14) but not significantly. For women randomised before delivery there was no clear difference in the risk of the baby dying (12.7% vs 12.4%; relative risk 1.02, 99% CI 0.92 to 1.14). Side effects were reported by 24% of women given magnesium versus 5% given placebo, and placental abruption was less frequent on magnesium (relative risk 0.67, 99% CI 0.45 to 0.89).
cards.watchOut: The mortality difference is not significant — the proven outcome is eclampsia prevention. Magpie enrolled only where clinicians were uncertain about magnesium, and its baby outcome is death, not the neuroprotection question shelved elsewhere (see synthesis).
cards.source: Magpie Trial Collaborative Group. Do women with pre-eclampsia, and their babies, benefit from magnesium sulphate? The Magpie Trial: a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2002 Jun 1;359(9321):1877-1890. PMID: 12057549. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Collaborative Eclampsia Trial: once seizures occur, magnesium beat diazepam and phenytoin on recurrent convulsions
cards.summary: Collaborative Eclampsia Trial: recurrent convulsions 13.2% vs 27.9% against diazepam — magnesium is also the treatment drug once seizures occur.
cards.people: 1,687 women with eclampsia recruited into an international multicentre trial comparing standard anticonvulsant regimens; outcome data were available for 1,680 (99.6%): 453 allocated magnesium sulfate versus 452 allocated diazepam, and 388 allocated magnesium sulfate versus 387 allocated phenytoin; 99% received the allocated drug; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Against diazepam, women allocated magnesium sulfate had a 52% lower risk of recurrent convulsions (95% CI 64% to 37% reduction — relative), with absolute rates of 60 (13.2%) versus 126 (27.9%): 14.7 fewer women with recurrent convulsions per 100 women. Against phenytoin, magnesium gave a 67% lower risk of recurrent convulsions (95% CI 79% to 47% reduction — relative), with rates of 22 (5.7%) versus 66 (17.1%): 11.4 fewer per 100 women. Maternal mortality was non-significantly lower on magnesium in both comparisons. Against phenytoin, women on magnesium were also less likely to be ventilated, to develop pneumonia, or to be admitted to intensive care, and their babies were less likely to be intubated at delivery or admitted to a special care nursery.
cards.watchOut: Mortality differences were not significant in either comparison; the decisive outcome is recurrent convulsions. The two comparisons used locally standard regimens, so this is magnesium against each alternative, not a three-way single randomisation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: magnesium sulfate is the mother's seizure drug, for prevention and for treatment — LIKELY
cards.summary: Magnesium sulfate is the mother's seizure drug, for prevention and for treatment — LIKELY. (Its fetal-neuroprotection question lives on its own shelves.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Magpie (10,141 women with pre-eclampsia) and the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial (1,687 women with eclampsia).
cards.result: For prevention in pre-eclampsia, magnesium cut eclampsia from 1.9% to 0.8% (a 58% relative reduction); for treatment of established eclampsia, it cut recurrent convulsions from 27.9% to 13.2% against diazepam and from 17.1% to 5.7% against phenytoin. Maternal mortality pointed the same way in both programmes without reaching significance. This shelf is stamped LIKELY. One-home note: magnesium given before preterm birth to protect the baby's brain is a different indication with different trials, and it lives on Shelves #147, #257 and #413 — none of those fetal-neuroprotection trials is carded here, and nothing on this shelf rules on that question.
cards.watchOut: Do not transfer Magpie's eclampsia-prevention numbers to the fetal-neuroprotection shelves or vice versa: different population, different outcome, different trials.

shelves.title: Vaginal laser treatment for postmenopausal vaginal symptoms
shelves.question: Does fractional CO2 laser improve genitourinary syndrome of menopause symptoms more than sham treatment?
shelves.mesh: Atrophy/radiotherapy · Lasers, Gas/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Low-Level Light Therapy/adverse effects · Postmenopause · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Failure · Vagina/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, on one rigorous sham trial against an earlier positive small-trial pooling): The one large, double-blind, sham-controlled trial with 12-month follow-up (Li 2021, 85 women) found no significant difference between fractional CO2 laser and sham on symptom severity, quality of life, Vaginal Health Index or histology. A 2021 systematic review of the three earlier, much smaller sham-controlled trials (164 women in total) had pooled in laser's favour on symptom, sexual-function and urinary scores. The rigorous trial outranks the small-trial pooling, but with a single such trial the null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Li 2021: fractional CO2 laser was no better than sham at 12 months on symptoms, quality of life, vaginal health or histology
cards.summary: Li 2021: fractional CO2 laser was no better than sham at 12 months on symptoms, quality of life, vaginal health or histology (all differences non-significant).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, sham-controlled trial with 12-month follow-up
cards.people: 85 postmenopausal women with vaginal symptoms substantive enough to seek medical treatment, randomised at a single tertiary hospital in Sydney, Australia, to fractional microablative CO2 laser (43) or sham (42), three treatments 4 to 8 weeks apart; mean age 57 (SD 8) years; 78 women (91.7%) completed 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: From baseline to 12 months there was no significant difference between laser and sham in change in symptom severity: visual analogue scale for overall vaginal symptoms −17.2 vs −26.6 (difference 9.4, 95% CI −28.6 to 47.5), most-severe-symptom VAS −24.5 vs −20.4 (difference −4.1, −32.5 to 24.3), and Vulvovaginal Symptom Questionnaire −3.1 vs −1.6 (difference −1.5, −5.9 to 3.0). There were no significant differences in quality of life (difference 4.8, −3.9 to 13.5), Vaginal Health Index (difference −0.4, −4.3 to 3.6) or histology. Adverse events numbered 16 in the laser group and 17 in the sham group, including vaginal pain/discomfort (44% vs 68%), spotting, discharge and lower urinary tract symptoms; no severe adverse events were reported in either group.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and single-device, with 85 women: it is the most rigorous sham test available, not a definitive class verdict on every laser platform or dosing schedule.
cards.source: Li FG et al. Effect of Fractional Carbon Dioxide Laser vs Sham Treatment on Symptom Severity in Women With Postmenopausal Vaginal Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021 Oct 12;326(14):1381-1389. PMID: 34636862. Registry ID: ACTRN12616001403426 (Australian and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Khamis 2021: pooling the three earlier small sham trials favoured laser — 164 women in total, against Li's null
cards.summary: Khamis 2021: pooling the three earlier small sham trials favoured laser — 164 women in total , against Li's larger null.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Three randomised trials meeting inclusion criteria, totalling 164 postmenopausal women with genitourinary syndrome of menopause, comparing fractional CO2 laser with sham; searches ran to March 2021, so the pooling predates the Li trial carded above; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: CO2 laser was associated with a significant reduction in Vaginal Assessment Scale score versus sham (mean difference −0.49, 95% CI −0.75 to −0.22; P=0.004), a significant improvement in Female Sexual Function Index (mean difference 9.37, 6.59 to 12.14; P<0.001), a significant reduction in Urogenital Distress Inventory-6 score (mean difference −6.95, −13.24 to −0.67; P=0.03), and more satisfied women (risk ratio 1.98, 1.36 to 2.89; P=0.004 — a relative figure). The authors call laser a promising alternative and state that further randomised trials with larger sample sizes are required to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: Three small trials, none larger than a fraction of Li's sample, pooled before Li existed: small-trial pools of device interventions are exactly where sham and reporting effects inflate estimates. The satisfaction risk ratio of 1.98 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own terms as well.
cards.source: Khamis Y et al. Vaginal CO2 laser therapy versus sham for genitourinary syndrome of menopause management: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Menopause. 2021 Aug 9;28(11):1316-1322. PMID: 34374686. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: when a rigorous sham trial arrived, the apparent benefit disappeared — POSSIBLE the null
cards.summary: When a rigorous sham trial arrived, the apparent benefit disappeared — POSSIBLE, leaning to the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Li 2021 (85 postmenopausal women, sham-controlled, 12 months) and Khamis 2021 (3 earlier sham trials, 164 women).
cards.result: The evidence order matters on this shelf: small early sham trials pooled positive (Khamis), then the largest and longest sham-controlled trial found differences of 9.4, −4.1 and −1.5 points on its three symptom scales, all non-significant (Li). That pattern — benefit shrinking to nothing as rigour rises — is why the shelf leans null, and the single-trial ceiling is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. This shelf tests a device for vaginal symptoms only: vaginal oestrogen for recurrent urinary tract infection lives on Shelf #150 and the hot-flush drug fezolinetant on Shelf #250, and neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the Khamis pooling without Li beside it; pre-Li marketing claims for vaginal laser rest on the smaller half of this shelf.

shelves.title: Long-acting reversible contraception: levonorgestrel intrauterine system vs copper IUD
shelves.question: How do the levonorgestrel intrauterine system and copper IUD compare on continuation, bleeding, and satisfaction in head-to-head randomised data?
shelves.mesh: Contraceptive Agents, Female/adverse effects,therapeutic use · HIV Infections/drug therapy,etiology · Intrauterine Devices, Copper/adverse effects · Levonorgestrel/adverse effects,therapeutic use · South Africa
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The one head-to-head randomised trial — 199 women living with HIV in Cape Town, South Africa (median age 31) — found the levonorgestrel intrauterine system did not increase genital or plasma HIV viral load versus the copper IUD over 24 months, while continuation favoured the levonorgestrel system (copper users had significantly more expulsions, 8% vs 1%, and far more elective discontinuations, adjusted hazard ratio 8.75, a relative figure) and haemoglobin rose more with the levonorgestrel system (+0.71 g/dL at 24 months). A single trial in a specific population caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and its continuation and bleeding findings should not be generalised beyond that population without corroboration. A second implant-versus-IUD randomised anchor named in the topic file could not be pinned to a verified head-to-head record at build and was not carded (see summary.md). Emergency contraception lives on Shelf #244 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Todd 2020: in women living with HIV, the LNG-IUS matched the copper IUD on viral-load safety and won on continuation
cards.summary: Todd 2020: in women living with HIV, the LNG-IUS matched the copper IUD on viral-load safety and won on continuation.
cards.type: Double-masked, randomised, noninferiority trial (Cape Town, South Africa)
cards.people: 199 women living with HIV, aged 18–40, not pregnant or desiring pregnancy within 30 months, randomised to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (101) or copper intrauterine device (98) within antiretroviral-therapy (ART) strata (71 non-ART, 134 ART-using women enrolled across the strata as reported); median age 31 years; 95% had one or more prior pregnancies.
cards.result: Proportions with detectable genital tract viral load did not differ between LNG-IUS and copper IUD at 6 months (adjusted odds ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.38) or 24 months (1.03, 0.68 to 1.57); plasma viral load results were likewise non-significant in ART users and non-ART women. Overall intrauterine-contraception continuation was 78%; copper users had significantly higher expulsion (8% vs 1%, p=0.02) and elective discontinuation (adjusted hazard ratio 8.75, 3.08 to 24.8 — a relative figure; p<0.001). Of 39 serious adverse events, 7 were judged directly device-related (3 pelvic inflammatory disease cases and 4 pregnancies with a device in place, with no discernible trend by arm). Mean haemoglobin change favoured LNG-IUS at 6 months (+0.57 g/dL, 0.24 to 0.90) and 24 months (+0.71 g/dL, 0.47 to 0.95).
cards.watchOut: Population-specific by design: women living with HIV in one South African setting, with the non-ART stratum under-recruited after ART guideline changes and 24-month data truncated for 17 women; a viral-load assay change mid-study may have introduced measurement discrepancy. Continuation and satisfaction findings in this population are hypothesis-confirming for, not proof in, the general contraceptive population.
cards.source: Todd CS et al. Safety and continued use of the levonorgestrel intrauterine system as compared with the copper intrauterine device among women living with HIV in South Africa: A randomized controlled trial. PLoS Med. 2020;17(5):e1003110. PMID: 32442189. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01721798, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one rigorous head-to-head trial, in one population — LNG-IUS at least as acceptable, with less blood loss
cards.summary: One rigorous head-to-head trial, in one population — LNG-IUS at least as acceptable, with less blood loss: POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Todd 2020 (199 women living with HIV, Cape Town).
cards.result: Within its population the trial answers the safety worry that motivated it (no viral-load increase with the hormonal device) and adds two practical findings in the LNG-IUS's favour: devices stayed in (continuation 78% overall, with copper users discontinuing electively far more often) and haemoglobin rose instead of falling (+0.71 g/dL by 24 months), consistent with lighter bleeding on the hormonal system. Emergency contraception (Shelf #244) is a different question and stays home there.

shelves.title: Early medical abortion at home and by telemedicine
shelves.question: Is home administration of misoprostol (and telemedicine-supported medical abortion) as effective and safe as clinic-based care?
shelves.mesh: Misoprostol/administration & dosage · Pregnancy · Sweden · Abortion, Induced/methods · Abortifacient Agents, Nonsteroidal/administration & dosage · Mifepristone/administration & dosage · Patient Satisfaction
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — home first misoprostol dose at 12–22 weeks · MAYBE (weak evidence) — telemedicine consultation for early abortion. PRIMA (457 participants, six Swedish hospitals) found taking the first misoprostol dose at home in medical abortion at 12–22 gestational weeks significantly increased day-care completion (71% vs 46%; difference 24.9 percentage points) with adverse events in 22% of the safety population and no signal that home dosing was unsafe — one large open-label trial, so POSSIBLE. The UTAH telemedicine trial was stopped by COVID-19 at about 10% of planned recruitment (125 women): efficacy looked similar (90.5% vs 77.4% complete abortion without surgery) but non-inferiority was formally not demonstrated, so the telemedicine half is MAYBE (weak evidence) — an underpowered pilot, not a verdict.

cards.headline: PRIMA (Rydelius) 2024: first misoprostol dose at home raised day-care completion to 71% vs 46% in abortion at 12–22 weeks
cards.summary: PRIMA (Rydelius) 2024: first misoprostol dose at home raised day-care completion to 71% vs 46% in abortion at 12–22 weeks.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (six hospitals in Sweden)
cards.people: 457 pregnant people aged 18 or older undergoing medical abortion at 85–153 days of pregnancy, assigned to mifepristone in clinic followed by the first 800 µg misoprostol dose at home 2 hours before admission (220 in the intention-to-treat population) or in hospital (215); 444 were in the safety analysis.
cards.result: The primary outcome — abortion completed as a day-care procedure (<9 hours) — occurred in 156 of 220 (71%) in the home group vs 99 of 215 (46%) in the hospital group (difference 24.9%, 95% CI 15.4 to 34.3; p<0.0001). In total, 97 of 444 (22%) participants in the safety analysis had an adverse event; 7 (2%) aborted after mifepristone only, and 2 (1%) of 220 in the home group aborted after the first misoprostol dose before hospital admission. The authors concluded home administration significantly increases day-care procedures in medical abortion after 12 gestational weeks and is a safe and effective alternative to in-clinic protocols.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, in a Swedish hospital system where admission followed the home dose by 2 hours — this tests where the first dose is taken inside an organised care pathway, not unsupervised abortion; gestational range 12–22 weeks, distinct from early medical abortion.

cards.headline: UTAH (Reynolds-Wright) 2023: telemedicine consultation looked effective (90.5% vs 77.4%) but the COVID-stopped trial could not prove non-inferiority
cards.summary: UTAH (Reynolds-Wright) 2023: telemedicine consultation looked effective (90.5% vs 77.4%) but the COVID-stopped trial could not prove non-inferiority.
cards.type: Randomised controlled non-inferiority trial (community abortion service, Edinburgh, UK), stopped early
cards.people: 125 participants randomised (63 telemedicine telephone consultation, 62 in-person consultation) for early medical abortion with mifepristone 200 mg and misoprostol 800 µg — approximately 10% of the planned sample before COVID-19 closed recruitment; primary outcome available for 115.
cards.result: Complete abortion without surgical intervention occurred in 57 of 63 (90.5%) with telemedicine vs 48 of 62 (77.4%) in person; however, non-inferiority was not demonstrated (difference +3.3% in favour of telemedicine, 95% CI −6.6% to +13.3%, whose lower bound crossed the 3% non-inferiority margin as the authors report). Unscheduled contact with care was more frequent in the telemedicine group (19% vs 5%, p=0.01), while total clinical contact time was lower (mean 94 vs 111 minutes, p=0.0005). Most secondary outcomes, including satisfaction and complication rate, did not differ significantly. The authors state the study was underpowered to confirm its conclusion and warrants larger studies.
cards.watchOut: A pilot stopped at a tenth of its sample: absence of demonstrated non-inferiority here is absence of evidence, and the efficacy percentages rest on 115 outcomes. Early abortion by telemedicine consultation is also a different intervention from PRIMA's home first dose at 12–22 weeks — the two halves of this shelf must not be merged.

cards.headline: Synthesis: home dosing within a care pathway is supported; telemedicine consultation is promising but formally unproven in randomised data
cards.summary: Home dosing within a care pathway is supported (POSSIBLE); telemedicine consultation is promising but formally unproven (MAYBE (weak evidence)).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PRIMA (457 participants, 12–22 weeks, home vs hospital first dose) and UTAH (125 participants, early abortion, telemedicine vs in-person consultation).
cards.result: The split stamp is the honest summary: PRIMA's day-care advantage (71% vs 46%) is a large, significant, patient-flow benefit with no safety signal in 444 treated participants — POSSIBLE on one trial. UTAH's point estimates favour telemedicine but its confidence interval (−6.6% to +13.3%) is too wide to claim equivalence, so MAYBE (weak evidence) is the correct label for that half until a full-sized trial reports. Observational telemedicine series exist in large numbers but are not carded: this shelf is the randomised record.
cards.watchOut: Never quote UTAH's 90.5% vs 77.4% without the non-inferiority caveat — the trial's own authors decline to conclude from it.

shelves.title: Preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidy (PGT-A) in IVF
shelves.question: Does PGT-A with single embryo transfer improve live-birth rates per transfer or per started cycle versus morphology-based selection?
shelves.mesh: Aneuploidy · Blastomeres · Chromosome Disorders/diagnosis · Embryo Transfer · Fertilization in Vitro · Genetic Testing · High-Throughput Nucleotide Sequencing
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on live birth per started cycle): In the Yan 2021 trial (1212 subfertile women with at least three good-quality blastocysts), cumulative live birth within a year was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% with conventional IVF — conventional IVF was noninferior (absolute difference −4.6 percentage points, 95% CI −9.2 to −0.0), though clinical pregnancy loss was less frequent with PGT-A (8.7% vs 12.6%). STAR likewise found no overall ongoing-pregnancy advantage per transfer (50% vs 46%) or per intention-to-treat (41.8% vs 43.5%), with a per-transfer subgroup signal at ages 35–40 that disappeared per intention-to-treat. Two concordant randomised trials justify LIKELY that PGT-A does not raise live-birth rates per started cycle in these populations.

cards.headline: Yan 2021: cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% with conventional IVF — conventional IVF noninferior
cards.summary: Yan 2021: cumulative live birth was 77.2% with PGT-A vs 81.8% with conventional IVF — conventional IVF noninferior.
cards.people: 1212 subfertile women aged 20 to 37 years with three or more good-quality blastocysts, assigned to PGT-A (606; three blastocysts screened by next-generation sequencing) or conventional IVF (606; morphology-based selection), with up to three single-embryo transfers within 1 year.
cards.result: Live births occurred in 468 women (77.2%) in the PGT-A group and 496 (81.8%) in the conventional-IVF group (absolute difference −4.6 percentage points, 95% CI −9.2 to −0.0; P<0.001 for noninferiority against the 7-point margin). The cumulative frequency of clinical pregnancy loss was lower with PGT-A (8.7% vs 12.6%; absolute difference −3.9 points, −7.5 to −0.2). Incidences of obstetrical or neonatal complications and other adverse events were similar. The authors concluded conventional IVF resulted in a cumulative live-birth rate noninferior to PGT-A in this population.
cards.watchOut: Women with at least three good-quality blastocysts are a good-prognosis group with embryos to spare; the trial does not test PGT-A where few blastocysts are available, and the miscarriage difference coexists with fewer total live births — both numbers belong in counselling.

cards.headline: STAR (Munné) 2019: no overall ongoing-pregnancy benefit from PGT-A per transfer (50% vs 46%) or per intention-to-treat (41.8% vs 43.5%)
cards.summary: STAR (Munné) 2019: no overall ongoing-pregnancy benefit from PGT-A per transfer (50% vs 46%) or per intention-to-treat (41.8% vs 43.5%).
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (single frozen-thawed embryo transfer)
cards.people: 661 women aged 25–40 years undergoing IVF with at least two blastocysts that could be biopsied (mean age 33.7, SD 3.6 years), randomised to embryo selection by PGT-A euploid status (330) or morphology alone (331).
cards.result: Ongoing pregnancy rate at 20 weeks per embryo transfer was 50% (137 of 274) with PGT-A vs 46% (143 of 313) with morphology — no significant difference — and per intention-to-treat at randomisation 41.8% (138 of 330) vs 43.5% (144 of 331). A post hoc analysis of women aged 35–40 years showed a significant increase in ongoing pregnancy per embryo transfer with PGT-A (51% [62 of 122] vs 37% [54 of 145]) but not per intention-to-treat. The authors concluded PGT-A did not improve overall pregnancy outcomes per transfer or per intention-to-treat.
cards.watchOut: The 35–40 signal is post hoc and per-transfer only: it counts women who reached transfer, excluding those whose embryos were all called aneuploid — precisely the denominator where PGT-A can lose pregnancies. Per-started-cycle (ITT) is the governing analysis for the shelf question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: PGT-A rearranges losses; it does not create more babies per started cycle in good-prognosis patients
cards.summary: PGT-A rearranges losses; it does not create more babies per started cycle in good-prognosis patients — LIKELY the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Yan 2021 (1212 women, cumulative live birth) and STAR (661 women, single frozen transfer).
cards.result: Both trials agree on the outcome patients ultimately ask about: no improvement in live birth (Yan: 77.2% vs 81.8% cumulative) or ongoing pregnancy per intention-to-treat (STAR: 41.8% vs 43.5%). PGT-A's demonstrable effect is fewer clinical pregnancy losses among transfers that occur (Yan: 8.7% vs 12.6%) — a real benefit for some patients' experience of treatment, bought with biopsy cost, embryo discard, and no gain in babies per cycle started. The stamp is LIKELY for that combined statement because two independent trials converge on it.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled poor-prognosis patients (recurrent loss, advanced age with few blastocysts) as its primary population; do not quote this shelf against PGT-A in populations it did not test.

shelves.title: Induction of labour: timing at 39 weeks, and Foley catheter vs prostaglandin
shelves.question: Does elective induction at 39 weeks in low-risk nulliparas change caesarean rates or perinatal outcomes (ARRIVE) — and is a Foley catheter as effective as prostaglandins?
shelves.mesh: Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Gestational Age · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Newborn, Diseases · Labor Pain/classification · Labor, Induced/adverse effects · Parity
shelves.balance: LIKELY: ARRIVE (6106 low-risk nulliparous women) found induction at 39 weeks did not significantly change the composite of perinatal death or severe neonatal complications (4.3% vs 5.4%; relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.00 — non-significant, and no perinatal-mortality benefit is claimed from it) but significantly lowered caesarean delivery (18.6% vs 22.2%; relative risk 0.84). In the PROBAAT programme, a Foley catheter matched vaginal prostaglandin E2 on caesarean rates (23% vs 20%; relative risk 1.13, interval spanning no effect), and oral misoprostol was noninferior to Foley on the composite of asphyxia or postpartum haemorrhage (12.2% vs 11.5%) — so the mechanical and pharmacological routes are equivalent for effectiveness in an unfavourable cervix, with the choice resting on safety profile and logistics.

cards.headline: ARRIVE (Grobman) 2018: induction at 39 weeks lowered caesarean delivery (18.6% vs 22.2%) without significantly changing the perinatal composite
cards.summary: ARRIVE (Grobman) 2018: induction at 39 weeks lowered caesarean delivery ( 18.6% vs 22.2% ) without significantly changing the perinatal composite (relative risk 0.80, CI 0.64 to 1.00 — non-significant; no perinatal benefit is claimed).
cards.people: 6106 low-risk nulliparous women at 38 weeks 0 days to 38 weeks 6 days of gestation, assigned to induction at 39 weeks 0 days to 39 weeks 4 days (3062) or expectant management (3044). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite of perinatal death or severe neonatal complications occurred in 4.3% of neonates in the induction group vs 5.4% with expectant management (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.00) — not statistically significant, and printed here as a non-significant result, not a perinatal benefit. Caesarean delivery was significantly less frequent with induction: 18.6% vs 22.2% (relative risk 0.84, 0.76 to 0.93 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it). The authors concluded induction at 39 weeks did not result in a significantly lower frequency of the adverse perinatal composite but did lower caesarean delivery.
cards.watchOut: Low-risk nulliparas in US centres with a policy of offering induction; expectant management in the trial era often meant induction by 42 weeks. The perinatal composite's interval reaches 1.00 — quoting '20% relative reduction' from this trial would overstate a non-significant result.
cards.source: Grobman WA et al. Labor Induction versus Expectant Management in Low-Risk Nulliparous Women. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(6):513-523. PMID: 30089070. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01990612, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PROBAAT (Jozwiak) 2011: Foley catheter matched prostaglandin E2 gel on caesarean rate (23% vs 20%) with fewer side effects
cards.summary: PROBAAT (Jozwiak) 2011: Foley catheter matched prostaglandin E2 gel on caesarean rate (23% vs 20%) with fewer side effects.
cards.type: Open-label, randomised controlled trial (12 hospitals in the Netherlands), with an accompanying meta-analysis
cards.people: 824 women with a term singleton pregnancy in cephalic presentation, intact membranes, an unfavourable cervix, an indication for induction, and no prior caesarean section, allocated to a 30 mL Foley catheter (412) or vaginal prostaglandin E2 gel (412). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Caesarean section rates were much the same: 23% with Foley vs 20% with prostaglandin E2 (risk ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.47 — a relative figure whose interval spans no effect). A meta-analysis including the trial confirmed a Foley catheter did not reduce caesarean rates. Two serious maternal adverse events were recorded, both in the prostaglandin group (one uterine perforation, one uterine rupture). The authors concluded Foley induction is similar in effectiveness to prostaglandin E2 gel with fewer maternal and neonatal side effects.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable for a device-versus-gel comparison) and in women without a prior caesarean; 'similar' here is a non-significant difference in a trial of 824, not a formal noninferiority proof — PROBAAT-II supplies the noninferiority design for the Foley comparison.

cards.headline: PROBAAT-II (ten Eikelder) 2016: oral misoprostol was noninferior to Foley catheter on safety composite (12.2% vs 11.5%)
cards.summary: PROBAAT-II (ten Eikelder) 2016: oral misoprostol was noninferior to Foley catheter on the safety composite (12.2% vs 11.5%).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised non-inferiority trial (29 hospitals in the Netherlands)
cards.people: 1859 women with a term singleton pregnancy in cephalic presentation, an unfavourable cervix, intact membranes, and no previous caesarean section, assigned to oral misoprostol 50 µg every 4 hours (932) or a 30 mL transcervical Foley catheter (927). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite of asphyxia (pH ≤7.05 or 5-minute Apgar <7) or postpartum haemorrhage (≥1000 mL) occurred in 113 of 924 (12.2%) with misoprostol vs 106 of 921 (11.5%) with Foley (adjusted relative risk 1.06, 90% CI 0.86 to 1.31), meeting the 5% non-inferiority margin. Caesarean section occurred in 155 (16.8%) vs 185 (20.1%) women (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.02; p=0.067). Adverse events numbered 27 vs 25, none directly related to the study procedure. The authors concluded the two methods have similar safety and effectiveness in an unfavourable cervix at term.
cards.watchOut: Open-label noninferiority with a 5% margin on a composite dominated by postpartum haemorrhage; the caesarean difference favouring misoprostol was not significant (p=0.067) and should not be quoted as a win.

cards.headline: Synthesis: induce at 39 weeks for fewer caesareans if the patient wishes; pick the ripening method on safety and logistics, not efficacy
cards.summary: Induce at 39 weeks for fewer caesareans if the patient wishes; pick the ripening method on safety and logistics — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ARRIVE (6106 women, timing) and PROBAAT / PROBAAT-II (824 and 1859 women, ripening method).
cards.result: The timing question and the method question have cleanly different answers. Timing: a policy of 39-week induction in low-risk nulliparas trades nothing measurable in perinatal outcomes (composite non-significant) for a 3.6-point absolute reduction in caesarean delivery. Method: Foley, prostaglandin E2 gel and oral misoprostol are effectiveness-equivalent in an unfavourable cervix (caesarean 23% vs 20%; safety composite 12.2% vs 11.5%, noninferior), so hyperstimulation risk, monitoring burden, cost and patient preference — not efficacy — should drive the choice.
cards.watchOut: All three trials exclude women with a prior caesarean (PROBAAT programme) or enrol only low-risk nulliparas (ARRIVE); neither answer transfers to scarred uteri or high-risk pregnancies.

shelves.title: Oral antihypertensives for severe hypertension in pregnancy
shelves.question: For acute severe hypertension in pregnancy, are oral nifedipine, labetalol, and methyldopa equally effective at reaching target blood pressure without caesarean or adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Hypertension, Pregnancy-Induced/drug therapy · India/epidemiology · Infant, Newborn · Labetalol/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: All three oral drugs controlled severe hypertension in pregnancy in most women in the Easterling trial (894 women, two Indian public hospitals): blood-pressure control within 6 hours without adverse outcomes in 84% on nifedipine retard, 77% on oral labetalol and 76% on methyldopa — nifedipine significantly beat methyldopa (p=0.03) but not labetalol (p=0.05). The smaller Shekhar trial points the same way on speed: oral nifedipine reached target faster than intravenous labetalol (median 40 vs 60 minutes). One large open-label trial plus one small single-centre trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Magnesium for seizure prophylaxis is a different drug and question, home on Shelf #602, and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Easterling 2019: all three oral drugs worked — control within 6 hours in 84% (nifedipine), 77% (labetalol), 76% (methyldopa)
cards.summary: Easterling 2019: all three oral drugs worked — control within 6 hours in 84% (nifedipine), 77% (labetalol), 76% (methyldopa).
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-group, open-label, randomised controlled trial (two public hospitals in Nagpur, India)
cards.people: 894 pregnant women aged at least 18 years, at least 28 weeks' gestation, requiring pharmacological control for severe hypertension (systolic ≥160 or diastolic ≥110 mm Hg) and able to swallow, assigned to oral nifedipine retard 10 mg (298), oral labetalol 200 mg (295) — both hourly with dose escalation if needed — or methyldopa 1000 mg as a single dose (301).
cards.result: The primary outcome (blood pressure 120–150/70–100 mm Hg within 6 hours with no adverse outcomes) was significantly more common with nifedipine than methyldopa: 249 of 298 (84%) vs 230 of 301 (76%) (p=0.03). It did not differ between nifedipine and labetalol (249 [84%] vs 228 of 295 [77%]; p=0.05) or between labetalol and methyldopa (p=0.80). Seven serious adverse events (1% of births) were reported: one intrapartum seizure in the labetalol group and six stillbirths (one nifedipine, two labetalol, three methyldopa); no birth had more than one adverse event. The authors concluded all three oral drugs are viable initial options, with nifedipine retard attaining the primary outcome most often as a single-drug regimen.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with different escalation protocols per arm (methyldopa was a single non-escalated dose — a design asymmetry that handicaps it), in a low-resource setting the authors themselves specify; p=0.05 for the nifedipine–labetalol contrast is borderline and is not claimed as a difference here.
cards.source: Easterling T et al. Oral antihypertensive regimens (nifedipine retard, labetalol, and methyldopa) for management of severe hypertension in pregnancy: an open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2019;394(10203):1011-1021. PMID: 31378394. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01912677 (and Clinical Trials Registry–India ctri/2013/08/003866), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Shekhar 2013: oral nifedipine reached target blood pressure faster than intravenous labetalol (median 40 vs 60 minutes)
cards.summary: Shekhar 2013: oral nifedipine reached target blood pressure faster than intravenous labetalol (median 40 vs 60 minutes).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, controlled trial (single centre, India)
cards.people: 60 pregnant women with sustained systolic blood pressure of 160 mm Hg or higher or diastolic of 110 mm Hg or higher, randomised to oral nifedipine 10 mg tablets (up to five doses) with intravenous placebo, or intravenous labetalol in escalating doses (20, 40, 80, 80, 80 mg) with a placebo tablet, every 20 minutes until target (≤150/100 mm Hg) was reached; crossover was given if the initial treatment failed.
cards.result: Median time to achieve target blood pressure was 40 minutes (IQR 20–60) with oral nifedipine vs 60 minutes (IQR 40–85) with intravenous labetalol (P=0.008); the median number of doses required was two vs three (P=0.008). No serious adverse maternal or perinatal side effects were witnessed in either group. The authors concluded oral nifedipine lowered blood pressure more quickly than intravenous labetalol as administered in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Only 60 women at one centre, and the comparison is oral nifedipine against intravenous labetalol — route and drug are confounded, so it corroborates nifedipine's speed, not oral-versus-intravenous labetalol. Zero serious adverse events in 60 patients excludes nothing uncommon.
cards.source: Shekhar S et al. Oral nifedipine or intravenous labetalol for hypertensive emergency in pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial. Obstet Gynecol. 2013;122(5):1057-1063. PMID: 24104790. Registry ID: Clinical Trials Registry–India CTRI/2013/02/003350, stated in the record's abstract; the record's databank fields carry no registry entry.

cards.headline: Synthesis: oral treatment is a legitimate first line for severe hypertension in pregnancy; nifedipine has the edge on speed and single-drug success
cards.summary: Oral treatment is a legitimate first line for severe hypertension in pregnancy; nifedipine has the edge — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Easterling 2019 (894 women, three oral drugs) and Shekhar 2013 (60 women, oral nifedipine vs intravenous labetalol).
cards.result: The trials answer the shelf's practical question: where intravenous access and monitoring are scarce, oral regimens controlled severe hypertension within 6 hours in roughly three quarters to five sixths of women (84% / 77% / 76%), and nifedipine was the fastest agent in both datasets (attainment advantage over methyldopa, p=0.03; median 40 vs 60 minutes against IV labetalol). Serious adverse events were uncommon in both trials (1% of births in Easterling). Treating hypertension targets and thresholds in pregnancy is a chronic-management question home on Shelf #601, and magnesium for seizures is Shelf #602; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for rare maternal catastrophes (stroke, eclampsia); the evidence supports oral drugs as initial therapy, not as proof of equivalence on the outcomes that matter most.
cards.source: Synthesis of Easterling T et al. Lancet. 2019;394(10203):1011-1021. PMID: 31378394; Shekhar S et al. Obstet Gynecol. 2013;122(5):1057-1063. PMID: 24104790. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth for term breech
shelves.question: For a singleton breech at term, does planned caesarean reduce perinatal death or serious morbidity versus planned vaginal birth (Term Breech Trial) — and can external cephalic version avert the choice?
shelves.mesh: Breech Presentation · Cesarean Section · Gestational Age · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Maternal Age · Maternal Mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: perinatal mortality claim). The Term Breech Trial (2088 women, 121 centres in 26 countries) found the composite of perinatal mortality, neonatal mortality or serious neonatal morbidity was significantly lower with planned caesarean than planned vaginal birth (1.6% vs 5.0%; relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.56 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it), while maternal mortality or serious maternal morbidity did not differ (3.9% vs 3.2%). External cephalic version can avert the choice for some women: the Cochrane review found starting ECV at 34–35 weeks rather than at term reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.81, high-quality evidence) at the cost of more late preterm labour (6.6% vs 4.3%). Because the headline claim includes perinatal death, this shelf is Tier C and its stamp is proposed only.

cards.headline: Term Breech Trial (Hannah) 2000: planned caesarean cut the perinatal death/serious morbidity composite to 1.6% vs 5.0% (relative risk 0.33)
cards.summary: Term Breech Trial (Hannah) 2000: planned caesarean cut the perinatal death/serious morbidity composite to 1.6% vs 5.0% (relative risk 0.33, relative). (Tier C — the composite includes perinatal mortality; PROPOSED pending the developer's verdict.)
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre trial (121 centres in 26 countries)
cards.people: 2088 women with a singleton fetus in frank or complete breech presentation at term, assigned to planned caesarean section (1041) or planned vaginal birth (1042), with data received for 2083; an experienced clinician attended planned vaginal breech births; follow-up to 6 weeks postpartum. Of the planned-caesarean group 90.4% delivered by caesarean; 56.7% of the planned-vaginal group delivered vaginally.
cards.result: Perinatal mortality, neonatal mortality, or serious neonatal morbidity was significantly lower with planned caesarean: 17 of 1039 (1.6%) vs 52 of 1039 (5.0%); relative risk 0.33 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.56; p<0.0001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it). There were no differences in maternal mortality or serious maternal morbidity: 41 of 1041 (3.9%) vs 33 of 1042 (3.2%); relative risk 1.24 (0.79 to 1.95; p=0.35). The authors concluded planned caesarean is better than planned vaginal birth for the term breech fetus, with similar serious maternal complications.
cards.watchOut: A year-2000 trial conducted under selection criteria and with experienced attendants that many units can no longer reproduce; the composite is driven partly by serious neonatal morbidity, and the trial's longer-term child follow-up is not part of this record. The 0.33 relative risk describes a composite including death — which is why this shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Hannah ME et al. Planned caesarean section versus planned vaginal birth for breech presentation at term: a randomised multicentre trial. Term Breech Trial Collaborative Group. Lancet. 2000;356(9239):1375-1383. PMID: 11052579. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Cochrane ECV review (Hutton) 2015: starting external cephalic version at 34–35 weeks reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.81) but raised late preterm labour
cards.summary: Cochrane ECV review (Hutton) 2015: starting external cephalic version at 34–35 weeks reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.81, relative) but raised late preterm birth.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: Five studies including 2187 women with breech presentation, comparing external cephalic version (ECV) begun before term, ECV at term, or no ECV. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Three studies (1906 women) compared ECV started at 34–35 weeks with ECV at 37–38 weeks: early ECV reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (risk ratio 0.81, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.90; high-quality evidence), failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth (0.90, 0.83 to 0.97) and vaginal breech delivery (0.44, 0.25 to 0.78 — relative figures), but the caesarean difference was not statistically significant (0.92, 0.85 to 1.00), and preterm labour was more frequent with early ECV (6.6% vs 4.3%; risk ratio 1.51, 1.03 to 2.21). One study (179 women) of a policy of ECV initiated before term versus none showed fewer non-cephalic presentations (0.59, 0.45 to 0.77); a single small study of completed pre-term ECV versus none found no difference (1.04, 0.64 to 1.69). There was no clear difference in low 5-minute Apgar or perinatal death, both graded low-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: This review is specifically about ECV begun BEFORE term; the at-term ECV evidence base is a separate Cochrane question. The intervention cannot be blinded, and the perinatal-death data within it are low-quality — the review supports ECV as a presentation-changing procedure, not as a proven mortality intervention.
cards.source: Hutton EK et al. External cephalic version for breech presentation before term. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(7):CD000084. PMID: 26222245. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: planned caesarean prevents about 3.4 composite events per 100 term breech births in the trial — and ECV can shrink the number who face the choice (Tier C, proposed)
cards.summary: Planned caesarean prevents about 3.4 composite events per 100 term breech births in the trial — and ECV can shrink the number who face the choice: LIKELY, PROPOSED (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Term Breech Trial (2088 women) and the Cochrane pre-term ECV review (5 studies, 2187 women). PROPOSED stamp pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.result: Put in absolute terms, the Term Breech Trial's composite difference is 1.6% vs 5.0% — about 34 fewer perinatal deaths or seriously morbid neonatal outcomes per 1000 planned caesareans — at no measured increase in serious maternal harm (3.9% vs 3.2%, non-significant). ECV operates upstream: performed from 34–35 weeks it leaves fewer babies breech at birth (relative risk 0.81 for non-cephalic presentation) at a small cost in late preterm labour (6.6% vs 4.3%). The shelf's perinatal-mortality-bearing claim is exactly the class the developer reserves for personal verdict, so the LIKELY stamp on this shelf is proposed only.
cards.watchOut: Practice since 2000 has shifted toward planned caesarean, eroding vaginal breech skills — the trial's planned-vaginal arm may be safer than what many units could now deliver, which strengthens rather than weakens caution about generalising in the other direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hannah ME et al. Lancet. 2000;356(9239):1375-1383. PMID: 11052579; Hutton EK et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(7):CD000084. PMID: 26222245. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Breastfeeding promotion and support (PROBIT)
shelves.question: Does a Baby-Friendly-style breastfeeding promotion intervention increase duration and exclusivity of breastfeeding — and children's later health?
shelves.mesh: Breast Feeding/statistics & numerical data · Eczema/epidemiology · Gastrointestinal Diseases/epidemiology · Health Promotion · Infant Welfare · Infant, Newborn · Republic of Belarus
shelves.balance: LIKELY: PROBIT — a cluster-randomised trial of 17,046 mother–infant pairs in 31 Belarusian maternity hospitals and polyclinics — found a Baby-Friendly-style promotion intervention markedly increased exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months (43.3% vs 6.4%) and 6 months (7.9% vs 0.6%), any breastfeeding at 12 months (19.7% vs 11.4%), and reduced gastrointestinal infection (9.1% vs 13.2%; adjusted odds ratio 0.60, a relative figure) and atopic eczema (3.3% vs 6.3%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54) in the first year, with no reduction in respiratory infection. A smaller home-based peer-counselling trial (130 mothers, Mexico City) was strongly concordant on exclusivity (67% and 50% with six and three visits vs 12% control at 3 months). Promotion works on the behaviour; the infant-health effects carded here are the ones PROBIT actually measured.

cards.headline: PROBIT (Kramer) 2001: Baby-Friendly-style promotion raised exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months from 6.4% to 43.3% and cut gastrointestinal infections
cards.summary: PROBIT (Kramer) 2001: Baby-Friendly-style promotion raised exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months from 6.4% to 43.3% and cut gastrointestinal infections.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial (31 maternity hospitals and affiliated polyclinics, Republic of Belarus)
cards.people: 17,046 mother–infant pairs — full-term singleton infants weighing at least 2500 g and healthy mothers who intended to breastfeed — at 31 sites randomised to the experimental intervention (16 sites) modelled on the WHO/UNICEF Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative or continuing usual practices (15 sites); 16,491 (96.7%) completed 12 months of follow-up.
cards.result: Infants at intervention sites were more likely to be exclusively breastfed at 3 months (43.3% vs 6.4%; P<0.001) and 6 months (7.9% vs 0.6%; P=0.01), and to be breastfed to any degree at 12 months (19.7% vs 11.4%; adjusted odds ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.69 — reported by the authors as the adjusted odds of discontinuation, a relative figure). One or more gastrointestinal tract infections occurred in 9.1% vs 13.2% (adjusted odds ratio 0.60, 0.40 to 0.91) and atopic eczema in 3.3% vs 6.3% (adjusted odds ratio 0.54, 0.31 to 0.95); respiratory tract infection (two or more episodes) did not differ significantly (39.2% vs 39.4%; adjusted odds ratio 0.87, 0.59 to 1.28). The authors concluded the intervention increased breastfeeding duration and exclusivity and reduced gastrointestinal infection and eczema in the first year.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised in 1996–97 Belarus, where baseline exclusive breastfeeding was very low (6.4% at 3 months) — absolute gains will compress where baseline rates are higher. PROBIT's later-life follow-up reports are separate records and are not carded here; this card covers the first-year outcomes only.
cards.source: Kramer MS et al. Promotion of Breastfeeding Intervention Trial (PROBIT): a randomized trial in the Republic of Belarus. JAMA. 2001;285(4):413-420. PMID: 11242425. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Morrow 1999: home-based peer counselling raised exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months to 67% (six visits) vs 12% in controls
cards.summary: Morrow 1999: home-based peer counselling raised exclusive breastfeeding at 3 months to 67% (six visits) vs 12% in controls.
cards.people: 130 pregnant women identified by census who participated (of 170 invited), assigned to six peer-counsellor home visits (44), three visits (52), or no intervention (34); peer counsellors were recruited from the same community and trained by La Leche League; data collected by independent interview. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 3 months postpartum, exclusive breastfeeding (WHO criteria) was practised by 67% of the six-visit group, 50% of the three-visit group and 12% of controls (intervention vs control P<0.001; six vs three visits P=0.02 — a dose response). Duration of breastfeeding was significantly longer in the intervention groups (P=0.02), and fewer intervention infants had an episode of diarrhoea (12% vs 26%, P=0.03). The authors describe this as the first reported community-based randomised trial of breastfeeding promotion.
cards.watchOut: Small (130 mothers) and from the 1990s; the diarrhoea figure is a secondary outcome in a small sample. Its role on this shelf is independent corroboration, in a very different setting, of the direction PROBIT established at scale.
cards.source: Morrow AL et al. Efficacy of home-based peer counselling to promote exclusive breastfeeding: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 1999;353(9160):1226-1231. PMID: 10217083. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Synthesis: structured promotion changes feeding behaviour at scale, and PROBIT's measured infant benefits are gastrointestinal and skin — not respiratory
cards.summary: Structured promotion changes feeding behaviour at scale — LIKELY; PROBIT's measured infant benefits are gastrointestinal and skin, not respiratory.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PROBIT (17,046 pairs, cluster-randomised) and Morrow 1999 (130 mothers, individually randomised).
cards.result: Two designs, two continents, one direction: exclusivity at 3 months rose from a low base to 43.3% (PROBIT, system-level Baby-Friendly practices) and to 50–67% (Morrow, peer home visits, dose-dependent). On infant health, quote only what was measured: gastrointestinal infection 9.1% vs 13.2% and eczema 3.3% vs 6.3% in PROBIT's first year, diarrhoea 12% vs 26% in Morrow — and a clean respiratory null in PROBIT (39.2% vs 39.4%). Claims about later cognition, obesity or allergy beyond these records are not part of this shelf's randomised evidence.
cards.watchOut: Both trials start from low baseline exclusivity; in populations already near Baby-Friendly practice, the same interventions have far less headroom, and effect sizes should be expected to shrink accordingly.

shelves.title: Surgery for pelvic organ prolapse: mesh, graft, or native-tissue repair (PROSPECT)
shelves.question: For primary transvaginal prolapse repair, does mesh or biological graft beat native-tissue repair on symptoms and reoperation?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Cattle · Collagen · Heterografts · Intestinal Mucosa/transplantation · Pelvic Organ Prolapse/surgery · Plastic Surgery Procedures/methods
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — mesh/graft augmentation does not improve patient-reported outcomes (PROSPECT) · POSSIBLE — mesh improves 1-year anatomical success, with more complications (Altman). PROSPECT (1352 women, two parallel trials) found no difference in prolapse symptom scores or prolapse-related quality of life at 1 or 2 years between standard native-tissue repair and repair augmented with synthetic mesh or biological graft, while 12% of mesh-exposed women had a mesh complication within 2 years. Altman 2011 (389 women, anterior compartment only) found a trocar-guided mesh kit beat colporrhaphy on a 1-year composite dominated by anatomical staging (60.8% vs 34.5%) — with longer surgery, more haemorrhage, more new stress incontinence (12.3% vs 6.3%) and 3.2% needing reintervention for mesh exposure. The split is real: anatomy improves, symptoms do not, and the price is mesh-specific harm. Stress-incontinence surgery is Shelf #249 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: PROSPECT (Glazener) 2017: mesh or graft augmentation did not improve symptoms or quality of life at 1–2 years; 12% of mesh-exposed women had a mesh complication
cards.summary: PROSPECT (Glazener) 2017: mesh or graft augmentation did not improve symptoms or quality of life at 1–2 years; 12% of mesh-exposed women had a mesh complication.
cards.type: Two parallel, pragmatic, multicentre, randomised controlled trials (35 UK centres, 65 surgeons)
cards.people: 1352 women undergoing primary transvaginal anterior or posterior compartment prolapse surgery, randomised across the mesh trial (865 women: standard repair alone vs mesh-augmented) and the graft trial (735 women: standard vs biological-graft-augmented), with some standard-arm women counted in both trials by design; 1348 included in the analysis; follow-up 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean Pelvic Organ Prolapse Symptom Score at 1 year did not differ: standard 5.4 (SD 5.5) vs mesh 5.5 (5.1) (mean difference 0.00, 95% CI −0.70 to 0.71; p=0.99); standard 5.5 (5.6) vs graft 5.6 (5.6) (difference −0.15, −0.93 to 0.63; p=0.71). Prolapse-related quality-of-life scores likewise did not differ at 1 year, and POP-SS and quality-of-life results at 2 years were also non-significant in both trials. Serious adverse events other than mesh complications occurred with similar frequency. The cumulative proportion of women with a mesh complication over 2 years among those actually exposed to synthetic mesh was 51 of 434 (12%). The authors concluded augmentation did not improve effectiveness, quality of life or adverse effects in the short term.
cards.watchOut: Primary outcomes were participant-reported symptoms — the outcomes patients feel; anatomical recurrence, where mesh might differ, was not the primary endpoint of PROSPECT (that is the Altman contrast, carded next). Two-year horizon for a problem whose failures accrue over decades.
cards.source: Glazener C et al. Mesh, graft, or standard repair for women having primary transvaginal anterior or posterior compartment prolapse surgery: two parallel-group, multicentre, randomised, controlled trials (PROSPECT). Lancet. 2017;389(10067):381-392. PMID: 28010989. Registry ID: ISRCTN60695184, stated in the record's abstract; the record's databank fields carry no registry entry.

cards.headline: Altman 2011: mesh kit beat colporrhaphy on the 1-year anatomical composite (60.8% vs 34.5%) but with more bleeding, new incontinence and mesh-exposure reoperations
cards.summary: Altman 2011: mesh kit beat colporrhaphy on the 1-year anatomical composite ( 60.8% vs 34.5% ) but with more bleeding, new incontinence and mesh-exposure reoperations.
cards.people: 389 women with anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) randomly assigned to a trocar-guided transvaginal polypropylene-mesh kit (200) or traditional colporrhaphy (189); primary outcome at 12 months was a composite of anatomical stage 0–1 on Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification plus absence of vaginal bulging symptoms.
cards.result: The primary outcome was significantly more common with mesh: 60.8% vs 34.5% (absolute difference 26.3 percentage points, 95% CI 15.6 to 37.0). Surgery lasted longer and intraoperative haemorrhage was higher with mesh (P<0.001 for both). Bladder perforation occurred in 3.5% vs 0.5% (P=0.07), new stress urinary incontinence in 12.3% vs 6.3% (P=0.05), and surgical reintervention for mesh exposure in 3.2% of 186 mesh patients during follow-up. The authors concluded mesh gave higher short-term treatment success with higher surgical complications and postoperative adverse events.
cards.watchOut: One compartment (anterior), one mesh kit, one year — and a composite led by examination findings rather than symptoms, which is why it can favour mesh while PROSPECT's symptom-led outcomes do not.

cards.summary: Mesh wins the examination, ties the patient — split LIKELY (no patient-reported gain) / POSSIBLE (anatomical success, with harms).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PROSPECT (1352 women, symptom-led outcomes) and Altman 2011 (389 women, anatomy-led composite).
cards.result: The apparent contradiction resolves once the endpoints are separated: on anatomical staging at 1 year, mesh is better (60.8% vs 34.5% composite success); on the symptoms and quality of life women actually report, augmentation with mesh or graft adds nothing at 1–2 years (differences 0.00 and −0.15 points); and mesh carries harms native tissue cannot have — 12% complication by 2 years in PROSPECT, 3.2% reoperation for exposure and doubled new stress incontinence in Altman. Native-tissue repair is the evidence-supported default for primary repair on this record; mesh's case would have to be made on long-term reoperation data these trials do not provide.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial reports the long-horizon reoperation outcome that could rehabilitate mesh; absence of that data is itself part of the shelf's message. Sacrocolpopexy (abdominal/laparoscopic mesh) is a different operation and is not judged here.

shelves.title: Non-hormonal drugs for menopausal hot flushes: SSRI/SNRI options
shelves.question: Do low-dose paroxetine or escitalopram reduce hot-flush frequency versus placebo in women who cannot or will not use hormones?
shelves.mesh: Black or African American · Citalopram/therapeutic use · Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Menopause · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · White People
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of different serotonin-reuptake inhibitors converge: escitalopram 10–20 mg reduced hot-flush frequency by 1.41 more flushes per day than placebo at 8 weeks (55% vs 36% achieving at least a 50% reduction), and paroxetine CR 12.5–25 mg reduced daily flush frequency by about 3.3 per day versus 1.8 on placebo at 6 weeks (median reductions 62–65% vs 38%). The effect is real but modest in absolute terms, the trials last only 6–8 weeks, and flushes rebound above placebo levels within weeks of stopping (escitalopram). Fezolinetant specifically is Shelf #250 and hormone-therapy harms are Shelf #109; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: Freeman 2011: escitalopram cut hot flushes by 1.41 more per day than placebo at 8 weeks; 55% vs 36% halved their flushes
cards.summary: Freeman 2011: escitalopram cut hot flushes by 1.41 more per day than placebo at 8 weeks; 55% vs 36% halved their flushes.
cards.type: Multicentre, 8-week, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial
cards.people: 205 healthy menopausal women (95 African American, 102 white, 8 other) receiving escitalopram 10–20 mg/day or matching placebo for 8 weeks; mean baseline hot-flush frequency was 9.78 (SD 5.60) per day. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean hot-flush frequency fell by 4.60 per day (95% CI 3.74 to 5.47) on escitalopram vs 3.20 (2.24 to 4.15) on placebo — a mean difference of 1.41 fewer flushes per day (0.13 to 2.69; P<0.001 as reported). A reduction of at least 50% in flush frequency was reported by 55% on escitalopram vs 36% on placebo (P=0.009). Severity scores also fell more with escitalopram (−0.52 vs −0.30; P<0.001), race did not significantly modify the effect (P=0.62), and discontinuation for adverse events was 4% overall. Three weeks after treatment ended, the escitalopram group reported a mean 1.59 more flushes per day than the placebo group (P=0.02) — a rebound after stopping.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks only, in healthy volunteers; the placebo response alone removed 3.2 flushes a day, so the drug-attributable gain (~1.4/day) is the honest number to quote. The post-treatment rebound means benefit requires continued use.
cards.source: Freeman EW et al. Efficacy of escitalopram for hot flashes in healthy menopausal women: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2011;305(3):267-274. PMID: 21245182. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00894543, from the record's databank fields.
