cards.headline: Stearns 2003: paroxetine CR reduced daily hot-flush frequency by ~3.3 vs 1.8 on placebo at 6 weeks
cards.summary: Stearns 2003: paroxetine CR reduced daily hot-flush frequency by about 3.3 vs 1.8 on placebo at 6 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study (17 US sites)
cards.people: 165 menopausal women experiencing at least 2–3 daily hot flushes, off hormone therapy for at least 6 weeks, assigned after a 1-week placebo run-in to placebo (56), paroxetine CR 12.5 mg/day (51) or 25.0 mg/day (58) for 6 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean daily hot-flush frequency fell from 7.1 to 3.8 (reduction 3.3) on 12.5 mg and from 6.4 to 3.2 (reduction 3.2) on 25 mg, vs from 6.6 to 4.8 (reduction 1.8) on placebo. Placebo-adjusted reductions in the hot-flush composite score (frequency × severity) were −4.7 (95% CI −8.1 to −1.3; P=0.007) for 12.5 mg and −3.6 (−6.8 to −0.4; P=0.03) for 25 mg. Median reductions were 62.2% and 64.6% on paroxetine vs 37.8% on placebo (relative-style percentage reductions, reported beside the absolute frequencies above). The authors concluded paroxetine CR may be an effective, acceptable alternative to hormone replacement.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks, with a placebo run-in that pre-selects against early placebo responders; the two doses performed alike, so there is no dose–response to exploit. Long-term SSRI effects in this population are outside this trial.
cards.source: Stearns V et al. Paroxetine controlled release in the treatment of menopausal hot flashes: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003;289(21):2827-2834. PMID: 12783913. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SSRIs work for flushes — modestly, briefly trialled, and only while taken
cards.summary: SSRIs work for flushes — modestly, briefly trialled, and only while taken: LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Freeman 2011 (205 women, escitalopram) and Stearns 2003 (165 women, paroxetine CR).
cards.result: Two different agents, two placebo-controlled trials, the same shape of result: an extra reduction of roughly 1.4–1.5 flushes per day beyond a large placebo response, with about 55–65% of treated women halving their flush burden versus 36–38% on placebo. That consistency across agents is why the class claim carries LIKELY, while the absolute size of the benefit — and the rebound on stopping — is printed on both cards so the stamp is never quoted without them. Fezolinetant (Shelf #250) and hormone therapy (Shelf #109) are separate shelves with their own evidence and are not compared here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial ran beyond 8 weeks or enrolled women with breast-cancer treatment–induced flushes (e.g. on tamoxifen, where paroxetine has a specific interaction concern outside these records); do not extend this shelf to those populations.

shelves.title: Cervical cerclage for short cervix
shelves.question: In singleton pregnancies with a short cervix, does cerclage prevent preterm birth — in women with and without prior spontaneous preterm birth?
shelves.mesh: Cerclage, Cervical/statistics & numerical data · Cervical Length Measurement/methods · Combined Modality Therapy · Premature Rupture of Fetal Membranes/etiology,prevention & control · Gestational Age · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Second
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for women WITHOUT prior spontaneous preterm birth, the population both of this shelf's anchors study: the individual-patient meta-analysis of five trials (419 women with cervical length <25 mm) found no significant reduction in preterm birth <35 weeks with cerclage (21.9% vs 27.7%; relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.23) and graded the evidence low quality; the 2025 randomised trial of cerclage plus progesterone vs progesterone alone (90 women analysed, stopped early) likewise missed its primary outcome (preterm birth <35 weeks 16.3% vs 23.4%; relative risk 0.70, 0.30 to 1.63) while showing longer latency to delivery. Subgroup signals (cervical length <10 mm in the meta-analysis) are hypothesis-generating only. In women WITH prior spontaneous preterm birth the trial background differs — the 2025 trial's own record notes cerclage is associated with decreased neonatal morbidity/mortality there — but no card on this shelf tests that population, and vaginal progesterone versus pessary for short cervix lives on Shelf #418.

cards.headline: Berghella 2017 (individual-patient meta-analysis): cerclage did not significantly reduce preterm birth <35 weeks in no-prior-preterm-birth short cervix (21.9% vs 27.7%)
cards.summary: Berghella 2017 (individual-patient meta-analysis): cerclage did not significantly reduce preterm birth <35 weeks in no-prior-preterm-birth short cervix ( 21.9% vs 27.7% ).
cards.type: Systematic review and individual patient-level data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: Five randomised trials including 419 asymptomatic singleton pregnancies without prior spontaneous preterm birth, with transvaginal cervical length <25 mm in the second trimester, randomised to cerclage or no cerclage. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Preterm birth <35 weeks occurred in 21.9% with cerclage vs 27.7% without (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.23; I²=0%) — not significant; nor were preterm birth at <34, <32, <28 or <24 weeks, gestational age at delivery, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, or neonatal outcomes. In planned subgroups, preterm birth <35 weeks was lower with cerclage when cervical length was <10 mm (39.5% vs 58.0%; relative risk 0.68, 0.47 to 0.98) and when tocolytics (0.54, 0.31 to 0.93) or antibiotics (0.58, 0.33 to 0.98) accompanied cerclage. The authors graded the overall quality of evidence low (downgraded for imprecision and indirectness) and concluded cerclage does not seem to prevent preterm delivery in this population, with the subgroup findings requiring further study.
cards.watchOut: The headline relative risk sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own, and the significant subgroups are small (126 women for the <10 mm analysis) and multiple — they generate the next trial's question, not this shelf's answer.
cards.source: Berghella V et al. Cerclage for sonographic short cervix in singleton gestations without prior spontaneous preterm birth: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials using individual patient-level data. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol. 2017;50(5):569-577. PMID: 28295722. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a meta-analysis, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Boelig 2025: adding cerclage to progesterone did not significantly reduce preterm birth <35 weeks (16.3% vs 23.4%) in a trial stopped early
cards.summary: Boelig 2025: adding cerclage to progesterone did not significantly reduce preterm birth <35 weeks (16.3% vs 23.4%) in a trial stopped early.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, international randomised controlled trial (4 sites in the US and Italy), halted early for lagging enrolment
cards.people: 93 participants randomised (90 in the intention-to-treat analysis: 43 cerclage plus vaginal progesterone, 47 progesterone alone) — singleton pregnancies without prior spontaneous preterm birth, with transvaginal cervical length ≤25 mm at 18 0/7 to 23 6/7 weeks found on universal screening; planned enrolment had been 206; 40 participants (40.4%) had cervical length ≤15 mm.
cards.result: The primary outcome, preterm birth <35 weeks, did not differ significantly: 16.3% with cerclage plus progesterone vs 23.4% with progesterone alone (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.63 — a relative figure whose interval spans substantial benefit and harm). Latency from randomisation to delivery was significantly longer with cerclage (median difference 13 days, 95% CI 5 to 20; P=0.01) and gestational age at delivery later (median difference 1.0 week, 0.2 to 1.7; P=0.035), in both cervical-length subgroups. The authors state the trial was halted early and its findings should be confirmed in a larger trial or meta-analysis.
cards.watchOut: Less than half the planned sample: the confidence interval cannot exclude the 0.54 relative risk the trial was designed around — this is an underpowered null, which is why the shelf stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a firmer null. Both arms received progesterone, so the trial tests cerclage as an add-on, not cerclage versus nothing.
cards.source: Boelig RC et al. Cerclage in singleton pregnancies with no prior spontaneous preterm birth and short cervix: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Obstet Gynecol MFM. 2025;7(4):101602. PMID: 39880123. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03251729, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in women without prior preterm birth, cerclage for short cervix remains unproven — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: In women without prior preterm birth, cerclage for short cervix remains unproven — MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Berghella 2017 individual-patient meta-analysis (5 trials, 419 women) and Boelig 2025 (90 women analysed, cerclage as add-on to progesterone).
cards.result: Two independent looks at the same population agree on the primary outcome: no significant reduction in preterm birth <35 weeks (relative risk 0.88, CI 0.63 to 1.23; and 0.70, CI 0.30 to 1.63). The residual signals — the <10 mm subgroup, the latency prolongation in 2025 — are exactly the kind of secondary findings that keep a question open rather than settle it, hence MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a null stamp: the meta-analysis graded its own evidence low quality and the newest trial stopped at 44% of target enrolment. The with-prior-preterm-birth population, where cerclage's background evidence is stronger, is not tested by either anchor and is not claimed here; progesterone-versus-pessary management of short cervix is Shelf #418.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the latency result (+13 days) as a preterm-birth benefit: the trial's primary endpoint, preterm birth <35 weeks, was not significantly reduced.

shelves.title: Supplemental MRI screening in extremely dense breasts
shelves.question: Does adding MRI to mammography in women with extremely dense breasts reduce interval cancers (DENSE) — and an abbreviated-MRI versus tomosynthesis comparison (EA1141)?
shelves.mesh: Breast/diagnostic imaging,pathology · Breast Density · Breast Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,epidemiology · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · False Positive Reactions · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Mammography
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the randomised DENSE trial (40,373 women with extremely dense breasts and a normal mammogram), invitation to supplemental MRI halved the interval-cancer rate over a 2-year screening period (2.5 vs 5.0 per 1,000 screenings). The EA1141 comparative-accuracy study (1,444 women with dense breasts, all receiving both tests) found abbreviated MRI detected invasive cancer at 11.8 per 1,000 women vs 4.8 per 1,000 for digital breast tomosynthesis, with lower specificity (86.7% vs 97.4%). Both endpoints are detection and interval cancers — no trial here shows a mortality effect, and none is claimed. Mammography screening itself is a neighbouring question and is not re-carded.

cards.headline: Bakker 2019 (DENSE): inviting women with extremely dense breasts to supplemental MRI halved interval cancers (2.5 vs 5.0 per 1,000 screenings)
cards.summary: Bakker 2019 (DENSE): inviting women with extremely dense breasts to supplemental MRI halved interval cancers ( 2.5 vs 5.0 per 1,000 screenings).
cards.people: 40,373 women between the ages of 50 and 75 years in the Netherlands with extremely dense breast tissue and normal results on screening mammography, assigned in a 1:4 ratio to invitation to supplemental MRI (8,061) or mammography screening only (32,312); the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The interval-cancer rate was 2.5 per 1000 screenings in the MRI-invitation group and 5.0 per 1000 screenings in the mammography-only group, a difference of 2.5 per 1000 screenings (95% CI 1.0 to 3.7; P<0.001). Of the women invited to undergo MRI, 59% accepted the invitation. Of the 20 interval cancers diagnosed in the MRI-invitation group, 4 were diagnosed in women who actually underwent MRI (0.8 per 1000 screenings) and 16 in those who did not accept the invitation (4.9 per 1000 screenings). The MRI cancer-detection rate among women who actually underwent MRI screening was 16.5 per 1000 screenings (95% CI 13.3 to 20.5); the positive predictive value was 17.4% for recall and 26.3% for biopsy; the false positive rate was 79.8 per 1000 screenings. Among women who underwent MRI, 0.1% had either an adverse event or a serious adverse event during or immediately after screening.
cards.watchOut: Invitation-to-screen analysis with 59% uptake, and interval cancer is a surrogate for benefit: the trial does not show fewer deaths, and the false-positive rate (79.8 per 1,000) is the price of the extra detection.
cards.source: Bakker MF et al. Supplemental MRI Screening for Women with Extremely Dense Breast Tissue. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(22):2091-2102. PMID: 31774954. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01315015, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Comstock 2020 (EA1141): abbreviated MRI detected invasive cancer at 11.8 per 1,000 women vs 4.8 per 1,000 for tomosynthesis — at lower specificity
cards.summary: Comstock 2020 (EA1141): abbreviated MRI detected invasive cancer at 11.8 per 1,000 women vs 4.8 per 1,000 for tomosynthesis — at lower specificity.
cards.type: Cross-sectional comparative accuracy study with longitudinal follow-up (both tests in every participant, performed in randomized order and read independently)
cards.people: 1,444 women (1,516 enrolled) aged 40 to 75 years with heterogeneously dense or extremely dense breasts undergoing routine screening at 48 academic, community hospital, and private practice sites in the United States and Germany, all of whom underwent both digital breast tomosynthesis and abbreviated breast MRI in randomized order; median age 54 (range 40-75) years, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The reference standard was positive for invasive cancer with or without DCIS in 17 women and for DCIS alone in another 6; no interval cancers were observed during follow-up. Abbreviated breast MRI detected all 17 women with invasive cancer and 5 of 6 women with DCIS; tomosynthesis detected 7 of 17 and 2 of 6. The invasive cancer detection rate was 11.8 (95% CI 7.4-18.8) per 1000 women for abbreviated MRI vs 4.8 (2.4-10.0) per 1000 women for tomosynthesis (difference 7 per 1000, 2.2-11.6; P=.002). For detection of invasive cancer and DCIS, sensitivity was 95.7% (79.0-99.2) with MRI vs 39.1% (22.2-59.2) with tomosynthesis (P=.001) and specificity was 86.7% (84.8-88.4) vs 97.4% (96.5-98.1) (P<.001). The additional imaging recommendation rate was 7.5% vs 10.1% (P=.02) and the PPV of biopsy 19.6% vs 31.0% (P=.15).
cards.watchOut: A detection-accuracy comparison resting on 23 women with cancer, not a randomised outcomes trial: it says abbreviated MRI finds more cancers than tomosynthesis in the same women, not that finding them changes outcomes.

shelves.title: AI-supported mammography screening (MASAI)
shelves.question: Does AI-supported screen reading match double human reading on interval cancers and workload (the MASAI randomised trial, interim and interval-cancer reports)?
shelves.mesh: Artificial Intelligence · Retrospective Studies · Mammography/methods · Breast Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,epidemiology · Predictive Value of Tests · Mass Screening · Early Detection of Cancer/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial (MASAI, Sweden) with two sequential reports, counted once as evidence. The prespecified clinical safety analysis (80,020 women analysed) found AI-supported reading detected cancer at 6.1 vs 5.1 per 1,000 screened (ratio 1.2, 95% CI 1.0-1.5) with a 44.3% lower screen-reading workload and the same false-positive rate (1.5%). The full screening-performance analysis (105,915 women) found detection of 6.4 vs 5.0 per 1,000 (ratio 1.29, 1.09-1.51), again with 44.2% less reading workload and no significant increase in recall or false-positive rates. A single trial, however large, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the trial's primary endpoint — the interval cancer rate — is a separate later analysis, so no interval-cancer or mortality claim is made here.

cards.headline: Lång 2023 (MASAI safety analysis): AI-supported reading detected 6.1 vs 5.1 cancers per 1,000 and cut screen-reading workload by 44.3%
cards.summary: Lång 2023 (MASAI safety analysis): AI-supported reading detected 6.1 vs 5.1 cancers per 1,000 and cut screen-reading workload by 44.3%.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, population-based, non-inferiority, single-blinded screening accuracy study (prespecified clinical safety analysis)
cards.people: 80,033 women aged 40-80 years eligible for mammography screening at four screening sites in Sweden, randomly assigned to AI-supported screening (40,003) or standard double reading without AI (40,030), with 13 excluded from the analysis; median age 54.0 years (IQR 46.7-63.9); race and ethnicity data were not collected, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: AI-supported screening among 39,996 participants resulted in 244 screen-detected cancers, 861 recalls, and 46,345 screen readings; standard screening among 40,024 participants resulted in 203 cancers, 817 recalls, and 83,231 screen readings. Cancer detection rates were 6.1 (95% CI 5.4-6.9) per 1000 participants in the intervention group and 5.1 (4.4-5.8) per 1000 in the control group — a ratio of 1.2 (95% CI 1.0-1.5; p=0.052), a relative measure. Recall rates were 2.2% (2.0-2.3) in the intervention group and 2.0% (1.9-2.2) in the control group. The false positive rate was 1.5% (1.4-1.7) in both groups. The PPV of recall was 28.3% (25.3-31.5) vs 24.8% (21.9-28.0). In the intervention group, 184 (75%) of 244 cancers detected were invasive and 60 (25%) in situ; in the control group, 165 (81%) of 203 were invasive and 38 (19%) in situ. The screen-reading workload was reduced by 44.3% using AI.
cards.watchOut: A safety analysis of detection performance, not the trial's primary endpoint: interval cancers — the outcome that would show whether extra detection matters — were still in follow-up, and the detection-rate difference was borderline (p=0.052).
cards.source: Lång K et al. Artificial intelligence-supported screen reading versus standard double reading in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI): a clinical safety analysis of a randomised, controlled, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study. Lancet Oncol. 2023;24(8):936-944. PMID: 37541274. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04838756, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Hernström 2025 (MASAI screening performance): AI support raised detection to 6.4 vs 5.0 per 1,000 — more small, node-negative invasive cancers — with 44.2% less reading
cards.summary: Hernström 2025 (MASAI screening performance): AI support raised detection to 6.4 vs 5.0 per 1,000 — the record is the screening-performance analysis, carded as what it is; no interval-cancer claim is made.
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, parallel-group, non-inferiority, single-blinded, screening accuracy study (protocol-defined analysis of secondary outcome measures — same MASAI trial as the card above)
cards.people: 105,934 women recruited within the Swedish national screening programme at four screening sites in southwest Sweden, randomly assigned to AI-supported screening (53,043 analysed) or standard double reading (52,872 analysed), with 19 excluded from the analysis; median age 53.7 years (IQR 46.5-63.2), as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Cancer-detection rates were 6.4 per 1000 (95% CI 5.7-7.1) screened participants in the intervention group and 5.0 per 1000 (4.4-5.6) in the control group, a ratio of 1.29 (95% CI 1.09-1.51; p=0.0021 — a relative measure). AI-supported screening resulted in increased detection of invasive cancers (270 vs 217, a proportion ratio of 1.24 [95% CI 1.04-1.48]), which were mainly small lymph-node negative cancers (58 more T1, 46 more lymph-node negative, and 21 more non-luminal A). It also increased detection of in situ cancers (68 vs 45, a proportion ratio of 1.51 [1.03-2.19]), with about half of the increased detection being high-grade in situ cancer. The recall and false-positive rates were not significantly higher in the intervention group (ratios 1.08 [0.99-1.17; p=0.084] and 1.01 [0.91-1.11; p=0.92]), and the positive predictive value of recall was significantly higher (ratio 1.19 [1.04-1.37; p=0.012]). There were 61,248 screen readings in the intervention group and 109,692 in the control group, a 44.2% reduction in screen-reading workload.
cards.watchOut: Same trial as the card above — a fuller analysis population, not a second trial. Extra detection includes more in-situ cancer, so overdiagnosis is part of the balance until interval-cancer outcomes are reported.
cards.source: Hernström V et al. Lancet Digit Health. 2025;7(3):e175-e183. PMID: 39904652. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04838756, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: HPV self-sampling to reach screening non-attenders
shelves.question: Does offering self-sampling (mailed kits, or choice of self- vs clinician-sampling) raise cervical-screening participation among non-attenders versus repeat invitations?
shelves.mesh: Cervix Uteri/virology · Colposcopy · Early Detection of Cancer · Mass Screening/methods · Netherlands · Papillomavirus Infections/diagnosis · Patient Compliance
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two programmes in two countries agree that offering self-sampling raises participation among screening non-attenders, and that how it is offered matters. The 2025 UK offer-mode trial (Lim) found returning a self-sample in 12.3% of overdue women sent a kit directly, vs 4.8% sent a letter inviting them to order one, vs 1.7% with no systematic offer; opportunistic in-practice offers returned 5.6% vs 1.9%. The Dutch PROHTECT programme (Gök 2010) found compliance of 27.5% (adjusted) with a mailed self-sampling offer vs 16.6% with a recall invitation for conventional cytology, with high-grade lesion yields among responders of 1.3% for CIN II or worse. Participation endpoints only — no cancer-outcome claim is made.

cards.headline: Lim 2025: sending overdue women a self-sampling kit directly beat inviting them to order one — 12.3% returned a sample vs 4.8% (letter) vs 1.7% (no offer)
cards.summary: Lim 2025: sending overdue women a self-sampling kit directly beat inviting them to order one — 12.3% returned a sample vs 4.8% (letter) vs 1.7% (no offer).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (GP practices cluster-randomised for the opportunistic component; women individually randomised for the systematic component)
cards.people: People overdue cervical screening in England: 13 GP practices were randomised (1:1) to flagging women 6 or more months overdue so they could be offered a kit opportunistically (6,080 women) or no opportunistic offer (6,577 women); additionally, 6,400 never-screened women and women overdue by 15 or 27 months were individually randomised (2:1:1) to usual care (no systematic offer), a letter inviting them to order a kit, or being sent a kit; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary outcome was returning a self-sampling kit. In opportunistic-offer practices, 342 (5.6%) returned a self-sample compared with 1.9% (123/6577) in practices not randomised to opportunistic offering (adjusted risk difference 4.4% [95% CI 2.8%-6.0%]); half (234/449) of women offered self-sampling opportunistically returned a sample. Among the 6,400 individually randomised women, 1.7% (54/3197) with no systematic offer, 4.8% (76/1587) with a letter (difference relative to no systematic offer 3.1% [95% CI 2.0-4.2%]) and 12.3% (198/1616) with a kit sent directly (difference 10.5% [95% CI 8.9-12.2%]) returned a self-sample. These differences were maintained in the secondary outcome, any cervical screening. No adverse effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: Absolute returns remain low even in the best arm (12.3%): self-sampling outreach converts a minority of non-attenders, and the trial measures participation, not lesion yield or cancer outcomes.
cards.source: Lim AWW et al. Impact of mode of offer of self-sampling to people overdue cervical screening on screening participation: a randomised controlled trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2025;86:103357. PMID: 40895516. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial Number (ISRCTN) is 23940319.

cards.headline: Gök 2010 (PROHTECT): mailing a self-sampling device to non-attenders raised compliance to 27.5% vs 16.6% for a cytology recall, and found CIN II or worse in 1.3% of responders
cards.summary: Gök 2010 (PROHTECT, pinned at build and Europe-PMC cross-checked): mailing a self-sampling device to non-attenders raised compliance to 27.5% vs 16.6% for a cytology recall.
cards.type: Cohort study within the PROHTECT trial programme (self-sampling offer vs recall control) — labelled as the record labels it
cards.people: 28,073 women in the Noord-Holland and Flevoland regions of the Netherlands who had not responded to two invitations to the regular cervical screening programme: 27,792 women were assigned to the self sampling group and invited to submit a self collected cervicovaginal sample for high-risk HPV testing; 281 were assigned to the recall control group and received a second re-invitation for conventional cytology; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The compliance rate in the self sampling group was significantly higher than in the control group (crude 26.6% vs 16.4%, P<0.001; adjusted 27.5% vs 16.6%, P<0.001). The number of detected CIN II or worse and CIN III or worse lesions in self sampling responders was 99 (1.3%) and 76 (1.0%), respectively. Self sampling responders who had not participated in the previous round of screening (43%) had increased relative risks of CIN II or worse (2.04, 95% CI 1.27 to 3.28) and CIN III or worse (2.28, 1.31 to 3.96) compared with self sampling women who had been screened in the previous round — relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Allocation was extremely unequal (27,792 vs 281) and the record is indexed as a cohort study: it is the PROHTECT programme's participation and yield report, not a balanced two-arm RCT — the randomised corroboration for the participation claim is the Lim trial above.
cards.source: Gök M et al. HPV testing on self collected cervicovaginal lavage specimens as screening method for women who do not attend cervical screening: cohort study. BMJ. 2010;340:c1040. PMID: 20223872. Registry ID: ISRCTN45527158, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: putting a kit in a non-attender's hands raises participation — LIKELY, on participation only
cards.summary: Putting a kit in a non-attender's hands raises participation — LIKELY, on participation only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lim 2025 (randomised offer-mode trial, England) and Gök 2010 (PROHTECT programme, Netherlands).
cards.result: Participation among non-attenders rises when a kit is put in their hands: 27.5% vs 16.6% (PROHTECT, adjusted) and 12.3% vs 1.7% for kit-sent vs no offer (Lim 2025), with a letter inviting women to order a kit in between (4.8%) and in-person offers strongest per person actually offered (half of 449 offered women returned a kit). shelves.title: Gestational diabetes screening: one-step versus two-step
shelves.question: Does the one-step (75-g, IADPSG criteria) screening approach diagnose more GDM and improve outcomes versus the two-step approach — or only label more women (Hillier 2021)?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/analysis · Diabetes, Gestational/blood,diagnosis,epidemiology · Fetal Macrosomia/epidemiology · Glucose Tolerance Test/methods · Hyperglycemia/blood,diagnosis · Incidence · Mass Screening
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on clinical outcomes): One very large pragmatic randomised trial (23,792 women) found the one-step approach nearly doubled the diagnosis rate of gestational diabetes (16.5% vs 8.5%; unadjusted relative risk 1.94, 97.5% CI 1.79-2.11) while every clinical primary outcome was statistically indistinguishable: large-for-gestational-age infants 8.9% vs 9.2% (relative risk 0.95), the perinatal composite outcome 3.1% vs 3.0% (1.04), gestational hypertension or preeclampsia 13.6% vs 13.5% (1.00), and primary cesarean section 24.0% vs 24.6% (0.98) — relative measures with their absolute rates beside them. A single trial, but a very large one with concordant nulls across all primary outcomes, so the null is stamped LIKELY under the library's large-null rule. Treating diagnosed gestational diabetes is home on Shelf #599 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Hillier 2021: one-step screening doubled gestational-diabetes diagnoses (16.5% vs 8.5%) with no difference in any clinical outcome
cards.summary: Hillier 2021: one-step screening doubled gestational-diabetes diagnoses ( 16.5% vs 8.5% ) with no difference in any clinical outcome.
cards.people: A total of 23,792 pregnant women who received care in two health systems underwent randomization to one-step screening (75-g oral glucose tolerance test in the fasting state) or two-step screening (50-g glucose challenge test in the nonfasting state, followed if positive by a 100-g oral glucose tolerance test in the fasting state); 66% of the women in the one-step group and 92% of those in the two-step group adhered to the assigned screening; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Gestational diabetes was diagnosed in 16.5% of the women assigned to the one-step approach and in 8.5% of those assigned to the two-step approach (unadjusted relative risk 1.94; 97.5% CI 1.79 to 2.11). In intention-to-treat analyses, the respective incidences of the other primary outcomes were: large-for-gestational-age infants, 8.9% and 9.2% (relative risk 0.95; 97.5% CI 0.87 to 1.05); perinatal composite outcome (stillbirth, neonatal death, shoulder dystocia, bone fracture, or any arm or hand nerve palsy related to birth injury), 3.1% and 3.0% (relative risk 1.04; 97.5% CI 0.88 to 1.23); gestational hypertension or preeclampsia, 13.6% and 13.5% (relative risk 1.00; 97.5% CI 0.93 to 1.08); and primary cesarean section, 24.0% and 24.6% (relative risk 0.98; 97.5% CI 0.93 to 1.02). The results were materially unchanged in analyses with inverse probability weighting to account for differential adherence to the screening approaches.
cards.watchOut: Differential adherence (66% in the one-step group vs 92% in the two-step group) is the trial's main caveat — addressed by inverse-probability-weighted analyses that did not change the results. The trial compares screening strategies as implemented in two integrated health systems.
cards.source: Hillier TA et al. A Pragmatic, Randomized Clinical Trial of Gestational Diabetes Screening. N Engl J Med. 2021;384(10):895-904. PMID: 33704936. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02266758, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Uterine artery embolization vs surgery for symptomatic fibroids: FEMME and EMMY
shelves.question: For symptomatic uterine fibroids, how does uterine artery embolization compare with myomectomy on quality of life (FEMME) — and with hysterectomy on recovery and reintervention (EMMY)?
shelves.mesh: Hysteroscopy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Intraoperative Complications · Laparoscopy · Leiomyoma/surgery,therapy · Length of Stay · Menorrhagia
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — myomectomy for 2-year quality of life · POSSIBLE — embolization as a hysterectomy-sparing alternative: FEMME (254 women, open-label) found myomectomy ahead on fibroid-related quality of life at 2 years by an adjusted 8.0 points on a 0–100 scale. EMMY (177 women) found embolization spared a hysterectomy in about three quarters of women at 2 years (23.5% had gone on to hysterectomy), with no significant difference in pain or bulk-complaint improvement. These are two different comparisons, each resting on a single unblindable procedural trial — hence POSSIBLE for each half, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: FEMME 2020: myomectomy beat embolization on fibroid-related quality of life at 2 years — 84.6 vs 80.0, adjusted difference 8.0 points
cards.summary: FEMME (2020): myomectomy beat embolization on fibroid-related quality of life at 2 years — 84.6 vs 80.0 , adjusted difference 8.0 points.
cards.people: 254 women with symptomatic uterine fibroids who did not want hysterectomy, recruited at 29 UK hospitals, randomised to myomectomy (127; 105 underwent it) or uterine-artery embolization (127; 98 underwent it); primary-outcome data were available for 206 women (81%). The abstract does not state mean age.

cards.people: 177 patients with uterine fibroids and menorrhagia who were eligible for hysterectomy, recruited at 28 Dutch hospitals, randomised to uterine artery embolization (88) or hysterectomy (89). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Two years after treatment, 23.5% of embolization patients had undergone a hysterectomy. There were no significant differences between the groups in improvement compared with baseline in pain and bulk-related complaints. shelves.title: Relugolix combination therapy for endometriosis pain (SPIRIT 1 and 2)
shelves.question: Does once-daily relugolix combination therapy (GnRH antagonist plus hormonal add-back) reduce dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain in endometriosis versus placebo, without costing bone?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid/therapeutic use · Dysmenorrhea/drug therapy,etiology · Endometriosis/complications,drug therapy · Estradiol/therapeutic use · Pelvic Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Phenylurea Compounds · Pyrimidinones
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two replicate double-blind phase 3 trials (SPIRIT 1 and 2, 1,261 women randomised across the two) agree closely: dysmenorrhoea responder rates of about 75% on relugolix combination therapy vs 27–30% on placebo, and non-menstrual pelvic pain responder rates of 58–66% vs 40–43%. Lumbar-spine bone density fell only slightly on the combination (−0.70% and −0.78% vs +0.21% and +0.02% on placebo) — far less than the −2.0% and −1.9% seen with relugolix alone in the delayed-combination arms. Two concordant blinded trials support LIKELY.

cards.headline: SPIRIT 1 and 2 (2022): relugolix combination therapy roughly doubled-to-tripled pain responder rates vs placebo in both replicate trials
cards.summary: SPIRIT 1 and 2 (2022): relugolix combination therapy roughly doubled-to-tripled pain responder rates vs placebo in both replicate trials — dysmenorrhoea responders 75% vs 27% and 75% vs 30% .
cards.type: Two replicate phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, reported in one paper
cards.people: Women aged 18–50 years with surgically or directly visualised endometriosis (with or without histological confirmation) or histological diagnosis alone, with moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain; 638 patients enrolled in SPIRIT 1 and 623 in SPIRIT 2, randomised 1:1:1 to relugolix combination therapy, placebo, or delayed relugolix combination therapy for 24 weeks, at 219 centres. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Dysmenorrhoea responders at week 24: SPIRIT 1, 158 (75%) of 212 on relugolix combination vs 57 (27%) of 212 on placebo (treatment difference 47.6%, 95% CI 39.3 to 56.0; p<0.0001); SPIRIT 2, 155 (75%) of 206 vs 62 (30%) of 204 (difference 44.9%, 36.2 to 53.5; p<0.0001). Non-menstrual pelvic pain responders: SPIRIT 1, 124 (58%) of 212 vs 84 (40%) (difference 18.9%, 9.5 to 28.2; p<0.0001); SPIRIT 2, 136 (66%) of 206 vs 87 (43%) of 204 (difference 23.4%, 13.9 to 32.8; p<0.0001). The most common adverse events were headache, nasopharyngitis and hot flushes; there were nine reports of suicidal ideation across both studies spread across all arms including placebo, and no deaths. Least-squares mean change in lumbar-spine bone mineral density on combination therapy vs placebo was −0.70% vs 0.21% (SPIRIT 1) and −0.78% vs 0.02% (SPIRIT 2), vs −2.0% and −1.9% in the delayed (relugolix-alone first) arms. Opioid use fell in treated patients compared with placebo.
cards.watchOut: Responder definitions combine pain scores with analgesic use, and the trials ran 24 weeks — long-term bone and durability data come from the open-label extension, not from these blinded comparisons. The delayed-combination arm shows what the add-back is protecting against, not a treatment option.
cards.source: Giudice LC et al. Once daily oral relugolix combination therapy versus placebo in patients with endometriosis-associated pain: two replicate phase 3, randomised, double-blind, studies (SPIRIT 1 and 2). Lancet. 2022;399(10343):2267-2279. PMID: 35717987. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03204318 (SPIRIT 1) and NCT03204331 (SPIRIT 2), from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Mifepristone plus misoprostol for missed miscarriage (MifeMiso)
shelves.question: Does adding mifepristone to misoprostol improve complete expulsion in missed miscarriage versus misoprostol alone — in the blinded MifeMiso trial and in Schreiber's early-pregnancy-loss trial?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Missed/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Mifepristone/therapeutic use · Misoprostol/therapeutic use · Oxytocics/therapeutic use · Abortifacient Agents, Nonsteroidal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Abortifacient Agents, Steroidal/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials agree that mifepristone pretreatment improves medical management of early pregnancy loss: MifeMiso (711 women with missed miscarriage) cut failure to pass the gestational sac within 7 days from 24% to 17% (relative risk 0.73), and Schreiber 2018 (300 women) raised complete expulsion with one misoprostol dose from 67.1% to 83.8% (relative risk 1.25) and halved-plus uterine aspiration (23.5% to 8.8%). Both headline ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band, so the stamp rests on two concordant blinded trials with consistent absolute differences (about 7 and about 17 percentage points), not on any single ratio.

cards.headline: MifeMiso 2020: adding mifepristone cut failure to pass the gestational sac within 7 days from 24% to 17% (relative risk 0.73)
cards.summary: MifeMiso (2020): adding mifepristone cut failure to pass the gestational sac within 7 days from 24% to 17% (risk ratio 0.73).
cards.people: 711 women aged 16 years and older diagnosed with a missed miscarriage by ultrasound in the first 14 weeks of pregnancy who chose medical management, at 28 UK hospitals, randomised to oral mifepristone 200 mg (357) or placebo (354), each followed 2 days later by misoprostol 800 μg. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Failure to spontaneously pass the gestational sac within 7 days: 59 (17%) of 348 women in the mifepristone-plus-misoprostol group vs 82 (24%) of 348 in the placebo-plus-misoprostol group (risk ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.99; p=0.043 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates 17% vs 24% beside it). Surgical intervention to complete the miscarriage: 62 (17%) of 355 vs 87 (25%) of 353 (risk ratio 0.71, 0.53 to 0.95; p=0.021). There was no difference in the incidence of adverse events between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The primary result is statistically fragile (p=0.043, confidence interval reaching 0.99) and the population is missed miscarriage specifically — it should not be read across to every early-pregnancy-loss presentation without the Schreiber card beside it.
cards.source: Chu JJ et al. Mifepristone and misoprostol versus misoprostol alone for the management of missed miscarriage (MifeMiso): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2020;396(10253):770-778. PMID: 32853559. Registry ID: ISRCTN17405024, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Schreiber 2018: mifepristone pretreatment raised complete expulsion from 67.1% to 83.8% (relative risk 1.25) and cut uterine aspiration from 23.5% to 8.8%
cards.summary: Mifepristone pretreatment (2018): complete expulsion rose from 67.1% to 83.8% (relative risk 1.25) and uterine aspiration fell from 23.5% to 8.8%.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment
cards.people: 300 women with an anembryonic gestation or confirmed embryonic or fetal death, randomised to mifepristone 200 mg orally followed by vaginal misoprostol 800 μg, or vaginal misoprostol 800 μg alone. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Complete expulsion after one dose of misoprostol, with no additional intervention within 30 days: 124 of 148 women (83.8%, 95% CI 76.8 to 89.3) in the mifepristone-pretreatment group vs 100 of 149 (67.1%, 59.0 to 74.6) with misoprostol alone (relative risk 1.25, 1.09 to 1.43 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Uterine aspiration was performed in 8.8% vs 23.5% (relative risk 0.37, 0.21 to 0.68). Bleeding resulting in transfusion occurred in 2.0% vs 0.7% (P=0.31); pelvic infection was diagnosed in 1.3% in each group.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than MifeMiso and its population mixes anembryonic gestation with embryonic/fetal death; the transfusion figures (2.0% vs 0.7%) are imprecise and not significant — do not read them as a proven bleeding penalty.
cards.source: Schreiber CA et al. Mifepristone Pretreatment for the Medical Management of Early Pregnancy Loss. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(23):2161-2170. PMID: 29874535. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02012491, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Tubal ectopic pregnancy: systemic methotrexate vs laparoscopic salpingostomy, fertility after treatment, and the GEM3 combination
shelves.question: In haemodynamically stable tubal ectopic pregnancy, does systemic methotrexate resolve the pregnancy as safely as laparoscopic salpingostomy — and what does each cost in subsequent fertility (the Hajenius trial; DEMETER/GEM3-era data)?
shelves.mesh: Chorionic Gonadotropin/blood · Fallopian Tube Patency Tests · Laparoscopy · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy, Tubal/therapy · Salpingostomy/methods
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — methotrexate matches salpingostomy on resolution and later fertility · POSSIBLE the null — adding gefitinib does not help: Hajenius 1997 (100 women) found similar treatment success and identical homolateral tubal patency (55% vs 59%) for systemic methotrexate vs laparoscopic salpingostomy, and DEMETER (406 women) found no significant difference in 2-year intrauterine pregnancy rates between medical treatment and conservative surgery (67% vs 71%). GEM3 (328 women), the one large double-blind trial here, found adding gefitinib to methotrexate did not reduce surgical intervention (30% vs 29%). Each half rests on a small older trial plus one larger trial, or on a single large trial — POSSIBLE for both.

cards.headline: Hajenius 1997: methotrexate and salpingostomy succeeded equally — tubal patency 55% vs 59%, no significant difference
cards.summary: Methotrexate vs salpingostomy (1997): the two succeeded equally — tubal patency 55% vs 59% , no significant difference.
cards.people: 100 haemodynamically stable patients with laparoscopically confirmed unruptured tubal pregnancy and no signs of active bleeding, randomised to systemic methotrexate (51; four 1.0 mg/kg intramuscular doses alternated with oral folinic acid) or laparoscopic salpingostomy (49), 1994–1996. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Of 51 patients allocated methotrexate, 42 (82%) were successfully treated with one course and 2 (4%) needed a second course for persistent trophoblast; surgical intervention was needed in 7 (14%), with salpingectomy in 5 for tubal rupture. Of 49 allocated salpingostomy, 35 (72%) were successfully treated by salpingostomy alone, salpingectomy was needed in 4 (8%), and 10 (20%) needed methotrexate for persistent trophoblast. The tube was preserved in 46 (90%) vs 45 (92%) (rate ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.1). Homolateral tubal patency (assessed in 81 patients) was 23 (55%) of 42 vs 23 (59%) of 39 (rate ratio 0.93, 0.64 to 1.4).
cards.watchOut: A small 1997 trial using a four-dose methotrexate regimen and laparoscopic confirmation before randomisation — modern single-dose practice and ultrasound-based diagnosis differ, and subsequent fertility was explicitly left awaited by the authors.
cards.source: Hajenius PJ et al. Randomised trial of systemic methotrexate versus laparoscopic salpingostomy in tubal pregnancy. Lancet. 1997;350(9080):774-779. PMID: 9297998. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: DEMETER 2013: 2-year intrauterine pregnancy rates did not differ — 67% after methotrexate vs 71% after conservative surgery; 70% vs 64% for conservative vs radical surgery
cards.summary: DEMETER (2013): 2-year intrauterine pregnancy rates did not differ — 67% after methotrexate vs 71% after conservative surgery.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (two randomisations by ectopic-pregnancy activity)
cards.people: 406 women with ultrasound-confirmed ectopic pregnancy at 17 centres in France, 2005–2009: arm 1 (less active ectopic pregnancy, 207 women) randomised to methotrexate alone or conservative surgery with a systematic post-operative methotrexate injection; arm 2 (active ectopic pregnancy, 199 women) randomised to conservative or radical surgery, the conservative procedure including post-operative methotrexate. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Arm 1: cumulative fertility curves were not significantly different between medical treatment and conservative surgery (hazard ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.22; P=0.37); 2-year intrauterine pregnancy rates were 67% after medical treatment and 71% after conservative surgery. Arm 2: no significant difference between conservative and radical surgery (hazard ratio 1.06, 0.69 to 1.63; P=0.78); 2-year rates were 70% after conservative surgery and 64% after radical surgery. Both hazard ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band and are printed as non-significant.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment fell slightly short of plan (especially arm 2, where women were reluctant to be randomised to radical surgery), and every surgical patient in the conservative arms also received methotrexate — this is not a pure drug-vs-surgery fertility comparison.
cards.source: Fernandez H et al. Fertility after ectopic pregnancy: the DEMETER randomized trial. Hum Reprod. 2013;28(5):1247-1253. PMID: 23482340. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00137982, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: GEM3 2023: adding gefitinib to methotrexate did not reduce surgery — 30% vs 29% (adjusted relative risk 1.15) — and added diarrhoea and rash
cards.summary: GEM3 (2023): adding gefitinib to methotrexate did not reduce surgery — 30% vs 29% (adjusted relative risk 1.15) — and added diarrhoea and rash.
cards.people: 328 participants diagnosed with tubal ectopic pregnancy across 50 UK hospitals, all given a single intramuscular methotrexate dose (50 mg/m2) and randomised to 7 days of oral gefitinib 250 mg daily (165) or placebo (163); three placebo-group participants withdrew. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Surgical intervention to resolve the ectopic pregnancy occurred in 50 (30%) of 165 participants in the gefitinib group and 47 (29%) of 160 in the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio 1.15, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.58; adjusted risk difference −0.01, −0.10 to 0.09; p=0.37 — the relative figure sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band and the result is null). Median time to resolution without surgery was 28.0 days in both groups (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.03, 0.75 to 1.40). Serious adverse events occurred in 5 (3%) vs 6 (4%); diarrhoea and rash were more common with gefitinib.
cards.watchOut: GEM3 tests an add-on to methotrexate, not methotrexate itself — its null closes the gefitinib idea but says nothing against methotrexate as a salpingostomy alternative, which rests on the Hajenius and DEMETER cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for stable tubal ectopic pregnancy, methotrexate is a genuine alternative to tube-sparing surgery — and no add-on has improved on it
cards.summary: For stable tubal ectopic pregnancy, methotrexate is a genuine alternative to tube-sparing surgery — and no add-on has improved on it — Split: POSSIBLE · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hajenius 1997 (100 women), DEMETER 2013 (406 women) and GEM3 2023 (328 women).
cards.result: Resolution and tube preservation were equivalent in the head-to-head trial (patency 55% vs 59%), later fertility was equivalent in DEMETER (67% vs 71% at 2 years for medical vs conservative surgical treatment), and the one modern attempt to strengthen methotrexate pharmacologically failed (GEM3: surgery needed in 30% vs 29%). shelves.title: Freeze-all embryo transfer vs fresh transfer in IVF: PCOS and non-PCOS
shelves.question: Does freezing all embryos and transferring later improve live birth versus fresh transfer — in polycystic ovary syndrome (Chen), and in women without PCOS (Vuong)?
shelves.mesh: Cryopreservation · Embryo Culture Techniques · Embryo Transfer · Embryo, Mammalian · Follicle Stimulating Hormone/administration & dosage · Infertility, Female/etiology · Live Birth
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — freeze-all improves live birth in PCOS · POSSIBLE the null — no benefit shown without PCOS: In PCOS, Chen 2016 (1,508 women) found frozen transfer raised live birth after the first transfer (49.3% vs 42.0%, relative rate ratio 1.17) and cut ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (1.3% vs 7.1%), at the cost of more pre-eclampsia (4.4% vs 1.4%). In women without PCOS, Vuong 2018 (782 women) found no significant difference in ongoing pregnancy (36.3% vs 34.5%) or live birth (33.8% vs 31.5%). The discordance by population is the shelf: a positive large trial in PCOS, a null large trial outside it. The PCOS stamp is LIKELY on one very large trial with concordant secondary outcomes; the non-PCOS null is POSSIBLE on a single trial.

cards.headline: Chen 2016 (PCOS): frozen transfer raised live birth to 49.3% vs 42.0% (relative rate ratio 1.17), cut hyperstimulation — and raised pre-eclampsia
cards.summary: Frozen vs fresh transfer in PCOS (2016): live birth 49.3% vs 42.0% (rate ratio 1.17), with less hyperstimulation and more pre-eclampsia.
cards.people: 1,508 infertile women with polycystic ovary syndrome undergoing their first IVF cycle, randomised to fresh-embryo transfer or embryo cryopreservation followed by frozen-embryo transfer (up to two embryos after 3 days of development). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Live birth after the first transfer: 49.3% with frozen-embryo transfer vs 42.0% with fresh (rate ratio 1.17, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.31; P=0.004 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Pregnancy loss was lower with frozen transfer (22.0% vs 32.7%; rate ratio 0.67, 0.54 to 0.83; P<0.001), as was ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (1.3% vs 7.1%; rate ratio 0.19, 0.10 to 0.37; P<0.001), but pre-eclampsia was higher (4.4% vs 1.4%; rate ratio 3.12, 1.26 to 7.73; P=0.009). There were no significant differences in other pregnancy or neonatal complications; there were five neonatal deaths in the frozen-embryo group and none in the fresh group (P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: A PCOS-only, first-cycle population in a Chinese multicentre programme, with day-3 transfers — and the pre-eclampsia excess and the non-significant neonatal-death imbalance (5 vs 0) must travel with the live-birth benefit wherever it is quoted.
cards.source: Chen ZJ et al. Fresh versus Frozen Embryos for Infertility in the Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(6):523-533. PMID: 27509101. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01841528, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Freeze-all is a PCOS answer, not a universal IVF answer — the population decides — Split: LIKELY (PCOS) · POSSIBLE (the null, non-PCOS).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Chen 2016 (1,508 women with PCOS) and Vuong 2018 (782 women without PCOS).
cards.result: The two large trials point in different directions by design population: a 7.3-percentage-point live-birth gain with frozen transfer in PCOS (49.3% vs 42.0%) alongside less hyperstimulation but more pre-eclampsia, and a 1.8-point non-significant difference outside PCOS (36.3% vs 34.5% ongoing pregnancy). shelves.title: Ovulation induction for unexplained infertility: letrozole vs gonadotropins vs clomiphene (AMIGOS)
shelves.question: In unexplained infertility, which stimulation drug gives the most live births with the fewest multiple pregnancies — letrozole, clomiphene, or gonadotropins (AMIGOS)?
shelves.mesh: Clomiphene/therapeutic use · Fertility Agents, Female/therapeutic use · Gonadotropins/therapeutic use · Infertility, Female/drug therapy · Letrozole · Live Birth/epidemiology · Nitriles/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large three-arm trial (AMIGOS, 900 women) ranks the drugs: live birth was highest with gonadotropins (32.2%), then clomiphene (23.3%), then letrozole (18.7%) — but multiple gestation among ongoing pregnancies ran the other way for gonadotropins (32%, including 10 triplet gestations) vs 9% with clomiphene and 13% with letrozole. The older Bhattacharya trial (580 couples) adds the caution that empirical clomiphene did not beat expectant management on live birth (14% vs 17%). One large modern trial plus one older pragmatic trial, with stimulation-plus-IUI practice varying between them, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: AMIGOS 2015: gonadotropins gave the most live births (32.2%) and the most multiples (32% of ongoing pregnancies); letrozole the fewest live births (18.7%)
cards.summary: AMIGOS (2015): gonadotropins gave the most live births ( 32.2% ) and the most multiples (32% of ongoing pregnancies); letrozole the fewest live births (18.7%).
cards.people: 900 ovulatory women aged 18–40 with unexplained infertility and at least one patent fallopian tube, randomised to ovarian stimulation for up to four cycles with gonadotropin (301), clomiphene (300) or letrozole (299).
cards.result: Clinical pregnancies occurred in 35.5% (gonadotropin), 28.3% (clomiphene) and 22.4% (letrozole) of women, and live birth in 32.2%, 23.3% and 18.7% respectively; pregnancy rates with letrozole were significantly lower than with standard therapy (gonadotropin or clomiphene, P=0.003) or gonadotropin alone (P<0.001) but not vs clomiphene alone (P=0.10). Among ongoing pregnancies, the multiple-gestation rate with letrozole (9 of 67, 13%) did not differ significantly from gonadotropin-or-clomiphene combined (42 of 192, 22%; P=0.15) or clomiphene alone (8 of 85, 9%; P=0.44) but was lower than gonadotropin alone (34 of 107, 32%; P=0.006). All multiple gestations with clomiphene and letrozole were twins, whereas gonadotropin produced 24 twin and 10 triplet gestations. There were no significant differences in congenital anomalies or major fetal and neonatal complications.
cards.watchOut: Stimulation was paired with insemination in a US network protocol of up to four cycles; the trial's primary outcome was multiple gestation among pregnancies, so the live-birth ranking is a (large, prespecified) secondary reading, not the powered endpoint.
cards.source: Diamond MP et al. Letrozole, Gonadotropin, or Clomiphene for Unexplained Infertility. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(13):1230-1240. PMID: 26398071. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01044862, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Bhattacharya 2008: empirical clomifene did not beat expectant management on live birth (14% vs 17%; odds ratio 0.79)
cards.summary: Empirical clomifene vs expectant management (2008): no live-birth benefit — 14% vs 17% (odds ratio 0.79).
cards.type: Three-arm, parallel-group, pragmatic randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 580 women with unexplained infertility for over two years, confirmed ovulation, patent fallopian tubes and motile sperm, at four teaching hospitals and a district general hospital in Scotland, randomised for six months to expectant management (193), oral clomifene citrate (194) or unstimulated intrauterine insemination (193). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Live birth rates were 32/193 (17%) with expectant management, 26/192 (14%) with clomifene citrate and 43/191 (23%) with unstimulated intrauterine insemination. Compared with expectant management, the odds ratio for a live birth was 0.79 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.38) after clomifene citrate and 1.46 (0.88 to 2.43) after unstimulated insemination — both relative figures inside the 0.5–2.0 band and both non-significant. More women found clomifene (159/170, 94%) and insemination (155/162, 96%) acceptable than expectant management (123/153, 80%).
cards.watchOut: Unstimulated insemination and expectant management are not AMIGOS-style stimulated cycles — this card bounds the enthusiasm for empirical clomifene, it does not contradict AMIGOS's ranking among stimulated regimens.
cards.source: Bhattacharya S et al. Clomifene citrate or unstimulated intrauterine insemination compared with expectant management for unexplained infertility: pragmatic randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: gonadotropins win on live birth and lose on multiples; letrozole is not the free lunch it was proposed as — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Gonadotropins win on live birth and lose on multiples; letrozole is not the free lunch it was proposed as — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: AMIGOS (900 women) and Bhattacharya 2008 (580 couples).
cards.result: AMIGOS's ordering — live birth 32.2% (gonadotropin) > 23.3% (clomiphene) > 18.7% (letrozole), with multiples concentrated in the gonadotropin arm (32% of ongoing pregnancies, including triplets) — is the best drug ranking available for unexplained infertility, and Bhattacharya warns that doing something empirical (clomifene, 14% live birth) can be no better than expectant management (17%). Ovulation induction for PCOS-related infertility is home on Shelf #245; it is a different diagnosis and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Couples' priorities decide this one: the regimen with the most babies per woman treated also carries the multiple-pregnancy burden, and neither trial was powered for rare fetal or neonatal harm.

shelves.title: Zuranolone for postpartum depression: the oral 14-day course
shelves.question: Does a 14-day oral course of zuranolone relieve postpartum depression versus placebo — in the ROBIN trial and the SKYLARK trial at the 50 mg dose?
shelves.mesh: Depression, Postpartum/drug therapy · Major Depressive Disorder/drug therapy · GABA Modulators/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Postpartum Period · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind phase 3 trials at two doses agree almost exactly on effect size: ROBIN (zuranolone 30 mg, 150 patients in the efficacy set) improved HAMD-17 by −17.8 vs −13.6 on placebo (difference −4.2) at day 15, and SKYLARK (zuranolone 50 mg, 196 patients) by −15.6 vs −11.6 (difference −4.0), with significant differences sustained to day 45 in both. Somnolence, dizziness and sedation are the common costs. Two concordant blinded trials support LIKELY for short-term symptom relief.

cards.headline: ROBIN 2021: zuranolone 30 mg improved HAMD-17 by −17.8 vs −13.6 on placebo at day 15 (difference −4.2), sustained to day 45
cards.summary: ROBIN (2021): zuranolone 30 mg improved HAMD-17 by −17.8 vs −13.6 on placebo at day 15 (difference −4.2), sustained to day 45.
cards.people: 153 randomised patients (efficacy set 150; mean age 28.3 [SD 5.4] years), women aged 18–45, six months or fewer postpartum, with postpartum depression (major depressive episode beginning in the third trimester or within 4 weeks of delivery) and baseline HAMD-17 of 26 or higher, at 27 US sites; 76 randomised to placebo and 77 to zuranolone 30 mg orally each evening for 2 weeks; 148 (98.7%) completed treatment.
cards.result: Day-15 change in HAMD-17: −17.8 with zuranolone vs −13.6 with placebo (difference −4.2, 95% CI −6.9 to −1.5; P=.003). Differences favouring zuranolone were sustained from day 3 (difference −2.7; P=.03) through day 45 (difference −4.1; P=.003). At day 15, HAMD-17 response (odds ratio 2.63, 1.34 to 5.16; P=.005) and remission (odds ratio 2.53, 1.24 to 5.17; P=.01) favoured zuranolone — relative figures. One patient per group had a serious adverse event (confusional state with zuranolone; pancreatitis with placebo), and one zuranolone patient discontinued for an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: A 30 mg dose in a trial run 2017–2018, with follow-up only to day 45: it establishes short-term symptom relief, not relapse prevention, and the marketed-dose evidence is the SKYLARK card.

cards.summary: SKYLARK (2023): zuranolone 50 mg improved HAM-D by −15.6 vs −11.6 at day 15 (difference −4.0).

shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — antenatal massage reduces episiotomy and suturing in first births · POSSIBLE — warm compresses and second-stage massage reduce severe tears: The antenatal-massage Cochrane review (4 trials, 2,497 women) found less trauma requiring suturing (relative risk 0.91) and fewer episiotomies (relative risk 0.84), significant only in women without a previous vaginal birth, and no difference in third/fourth-degree tears. The second-stage Cochrane review (20 trials, 15,181 women) found warm compresses (relative risk 0.46) and perineal massage (relative risk 0.49) reduced third/fourth-degree tears on moderate-quality evidence, while hands-on vs hands-poised made no clear difference to tears and may affect episiotomy rates on low-quality evidence. All headline ratios for the suturing/episiotomy outcomes sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band, and the reviews rest on unblindable, heterogeneous trials — POSSIBLE for both halves.

cards.headline: Beckmann & Stock 2013 (Cochrane): antenatal massage cut trauma requiring suturing (relative risk 0.91) and episiotomy (0.84) — in women without a previous vaginal birth
cards.summary: Antenatal perineal massage (Cochrane, 2013): less trauma requiring suturing (relative risk 0.91 ) and fewer episiotomies (0.84) — in women without a previous vaginal birth.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials
cards.people: Four trials, 2,497 women, comparing digital perineal massage for at least the last four weeks of pregnancy with control; outcome analyses included 2,480 women. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Antenatal digital perineal massage was associated with an overall reduction in trauma requiring suturing (four trials, 2,480 women; risk ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.86 to 0.96; number needed to treat to benefit 15, 10 to 36) and fewer episiotomies (four trials, 2,480 women; risk ratio 0.84, 0.74 to 0.95; NNTB 21, 12 to 75) — both relative figures inside the 0.5–2.0 band. These findings were significant for women without previous vaginal birth only. There were no differences in first- or second-degree tears or in third/fourth-degree trauma. Only women who had previously birthed vaginally reported a significant reduction in pain at three months (one trial, 376 women; risk ratio 0.45, 0.24 to 0.87). No significant differences were observed in instrumental deliveries, sexual satisfaction, or incontinence.
cards.watchOut: Four trials searched to October 2012, with the benefit concentrated in first births and driven substantially by episiotomy practice, which varies by unit and era — the review predates more recent perineal-protection bundles.
cards.source: Beckmann MM, Stock OM. Antenatal perineal massage for reducing perineal trauma. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013;(4):CD005123. PMID: 23633325. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Aasheim 2017 (Cochrane): warm compresses (relative risk 0.46) and second-stage massage (0.49) reduced third/fourth-degree tears; hands-on vs hands-off was unclear
cards.summary: Second-stage techniques (Cochrane, 2017): warm compresses (relative risk 0.46 ) and second-stage massage (0.49) reduced third/fourth-degree tears.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials (update)
cards.people: Twenty-two trials eligible, 20 trials involving 15,181 women providing data, on perineal techniques during the second stage of labour; overall the trials were at moderate-to-high risk of bias, none had adequate blinding, and evidence was downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Warm compresses vs control: fewer third- or fourth-degree tears (average risk ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.79; 1,799 women; four studies; moderate-quality evidence), with no clear effect on intact perineum, suturing, second-degree tears or episiotomy. Massage vs control: more intact perineum (average risk ratio 1.74, 1.11 to 2.73; six studies, 2,618 women; low-quality evidence, substantial heterogeneity) and fewer third/fourth-degree tears (average risk ratio 0.49, 0.25 to 0.94; five studies, 2,477 women; moderate-quality evidence). Hands off (poised) vs hands on: no clear difference in intact perineum (average risk ratio 1.03, 0.95 to 1.12; moderate-quality evidence) or third/fourth-degree tears (average risk ratio 0.68, 0.21 to 2.26; very low-quality evidence, substantial heterogeneity); episiotomy was more frequent in the hands-on group (average risk ratio 0.58, 0.43 to 0.79; low-quality evidence, considerable heterogeneity). All are relative figures.
cards.watchOut: No trial could blind the attendant's hands, heterogeneity is high for several pooled outcomes, and most studies did not report the secondary outcomes women care about (pain, incontinence, sexual function) — the severe-tear signal is the strongest part and still only moderate-quality.
cards.source: Aasheim V et al. Perineal techniques during the second stage of labour for reducing perineal trauma. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;6(6):CD006672. PMID: 28608597. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: massage before birth mainly buys fewer episiotomies in first births; warmth and massage during the second stage are the severe-tear interventions — POSSIBLE for both
cards.summary: Massage before birth mainly buys fewer episiotomies in first births; warmth and massage during the second stage are the severe-tear interventions — Split: POSSIBLE · POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Beckmann & Stock 2013 (4 trials, 2,497 women) and Aasheim 2017 (20 trials, 15,181 women).
cards.result: The two reviews answer two different moments: antenatal massage reduced suturing (relative risk 0.91) and episiotomy (0.84) without touching severe tears, while second-stage warm compresses (0.46) and massage (0.49) reduced third/fourth-degree tears — the outcome with the lasting morbidity. Hands-on vs hands-poised remains genuinely unsettled on these data.
cards.watchOut: Both syntheses are built from unblindable trials with variable technique; local episiotomy culture can swamp effects of this size, so unit-level audit matters more than the pooled ratios.

shelves.title: Ulipristal acetate for uterine fibroids: the PEARL trials, and the liver-safety ending
shelves.question: Does ulipristal acetate control fibroid bleeding and shrink fibroids before surgery versus placebo (PEARL I) — and how does it compare with monthly leuprolide (PEARL II), given the later hepatotoxicity restrictions that ended its use?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anemia/etiology · Intention to Treat Analysis · Leiomyoma/complications,drug therapy,surgery · Menorrhagia/drug therapy,etiology · Norpregnadienes/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Receptors, Progesterone/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for the efficacy the trials tested — a stamp on evidence that no longer translates into an available treatment): PEARL I (242 women) showed bleeding control in 91–92% on ulipristal vs 19% on placebo at 13 weeks, with fibroid shrinkage, and PEARL II (307 women) showed ulipristal non-inferior to leuprolide for bleeding control (90–98% vs 89%) with far fewer moderate-to-severe hot flushes (10–11% vs 40%). Two concordant blinded trials support LIKELY on pre-surgical efficacy. The shelf face also carries the ending: ulipristal's fibroid use was later restricted and effectively ended over drug-induced liver injury, so this is a record of a treatment that worked and was withdrawn for safety — efficacy LIKELY, availability gone.

cards.headline: PEARL I 2012: ulipristal controlled bleeding in 91–92% vs 19% on placebo at 13 weeks, and shrank fibroids (−21%/−12% vs +3%)
cards.summary: PEARL I (2012): ulipristal controlled bleeding in 91–92% vs 19% on placebo at 13 weeks, and shrank fibroids.
cards.people: 242 women with symptomatic fibroids, excessive uterine bleeding (pictorial blood-loss assessment chart score >100) and anaemia (haemoglobin ≤10.2 g/dL), randomised to oral ulipristal acetate 5 mg/day (96), 10 mg/day (98) or placebo (48) for up to 13 weeks; all patients received iron supplementation. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: At 13 weeks, uterine bleeding was controlled (PBAC score <75) in 91% of women receiving 5 mg ulipristal, 92% receiving 10 mg, and 19% receiving placebo (P<0.001 for each dose vs placebo). Amenorrhoea rates were 73%, 82% and 6% respectively, occurring within 10 days in the majority on ulipristal. Median changes in total fibroid volume were −21%, −12% and +3% (P=0.002 for 5 mg vs placebo; P=0.006 for 10 mg vs placebo). Ulipristal induced benign histological endometrial changes that had resolved by 6 months after treatment ended. Serious adverse events occurred in one patient on 10 mg ulipristal (uterine haemorrhage) and one on placebo (fibroid protruding through the cervix); headache and breast tenderness were the most common ulipristal adverse events but were not significantly more frequent than with placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 13-week pre-surgical course in anaemic women — the trial says nothing about long-term or repeated-course safety, which is exactly where the later liver problem emerged; the efficacy figures must never be quoted without the shelf's liver-safety ending.
cards.source: Donnez J et al. Ulipristal acetate versus placebo for fibroid treatment before surgery. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(5):409-420. PMID: 22296075. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00755755, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PEARL II 2012: ulipristal was non-inferior to leuprolide for bleeding control (90%/98% vs 89%) with hot flushes in 10–11% vs 40%
cards.summary: PEARL II (2012): ulipristal was non-inferior to leuprolide for bleeding control ( 90%/98% vs 89% ) with hot flushes in 10–11% vs 40%.
cards.people: 307 patients with symptomatic fibroids and excessive uterine bleeding, randomised to 3 months of daily oral ulipristal acetate 5 mg or 10 mg, or once-monthly intramuscular leuprolide acetate 3.75 mg. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Uterine bleeding was controlled in 90% of patients receiving 5 mg ulipristal, 98% receiving 10 mg, and 89% receiving leuprolide — differences vs leuprolide of 1.2 percentage points (95% CI −9.3 to 11.8) for 5 mg and 8.8 points (0.4 to 18.3) for 10 mg, against a prespecified non-inferiority margin of −20%. Median times to amenorrhoea were 7 days (5 mg), 5 days (10 mg) and 21 days (leuprolide). Moderate-to-severe hot flushes were reported by 11% (5 mg), 10% (10 mg) and 40% (leuprolide) (P<0.001 for each ulipristal dose vs leuprolide).
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority margin (−20 percentage points) was generous, and the comparison is against leuprolide's hypoestrogenic burden over a single 3-month course — not against surgery, embolization (Shelf #830) or relugolix combination therapy (Shelf #247).
cards.source: Donnez J et al. Ulipristal acetate versus leuprolide acetate for uterine fibroids. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(5):421-432. PMID: 22296076. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00740831, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the PEARL programme proved efficacy beyond reasonable doubt — and the drug still left practice over liver injury
cards.summary: The PEARL programme proved efficacy beyond reasonable doubt — and the drug still left practice over liver injury — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PEARL I (242 women, vs placebo) and PEARL II (307 women, vs leuprolide).
cards.result: Bleeding control of 91–92% vs 19% (placebo) and non-inferiority to leuprolide with a tenth to a quarter of its hot-flush rate made ulipristal the best-evidenced oral pre-surgical fibroid treatment of its era. Its fibroid indication was subsequently restricted and effectively ended after cases of serious drug-induced liver injury on repeated courses — a harm that 13-week trials of a few hundred women could not have detected. Relugolix combination therapy (Shelf #247) and embolization vs surgery (Shelf #830) carry the live fibroid questions; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is a historical record with a live lesson — do not present ulipristal as a current fibroid option, and do not cite PEARL efficacy without the withdrawal context.
cards.source: Synthesis of Donnez J et al. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(5):409-420. PMID: 22296075; Donnez J et al. N Engl J Med. 2012;366(5):421-432. PMID: 22296076. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Endometrial scratching before IVF: two large nulls
shelves.question: Does endometrial scratching before IVF improve live birth — the international Lensen trial, and the UK scratch trial in first-time IVF?
shelves.mesh: Embryo Transfer · Endometrium/injuries · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Live Birth · Odds Ratio · Pain Measurement · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null: Two large randomised trials (2,412 women in total) found live-birth rates essentially identical with and without endometrial scratching — 26.1% vs 26.1% (adjusted odds ratio 1.00) in the international Lensen trial, and 38.6% vs 37.1% (absolute difference 1.5%, 95% CI −4.4 to 7.4) in the UK first-cycle trial, whose authors recommend the procedure not be undertaken in that population. Two large concordant nulls justify LIKELY the null, per the library's rule for very large null evidence.

cards.headline: Lensen 2019: live birth was 26.1% in both arms — adjusted odds ratio 1.00 — after endometrial scratching before IVF
cards.summary: Endometrial scratching before IVF (2019): live birth was 26.1% in both arms — adjusted odds ratio 1.00.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled trial
cards.people: 1,364 women undergoing IVF (fresh or frozen embryo transfer) with no recent disruptive intrauterine instrumentation, randomised 1:1 to endometrial scratching by pipelle biopsy (between day 3 of the preceding cycle and day 3 of the transfer cycle) or no intervention. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Live birth occurred in 180 of 690 women (26.1%) in the endometrial-scratch group and 176 of 674 (26.1%) in the control group (adjusted odds ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.27). There were no significant between-group differences in ongoing pregnancy, clinical pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage. The median pain score from scratching was 3.5 (interquartile range 1.9 to 6.0) on a 0–10 scale.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and without a sham procedure — acceptable here because the outcome (live birth) is objective, but the trial's scratch timing window was broad, and proponents' narrower-timing claims are not tested by it.
cards.source: Lensen S et al. A Randomized Trial of Endometrial Scratching before In Vitro Fertilization. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(4):325-334. PMID: 30673547. Registry ID: ACTRN12614000626662 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Metwally 2020/2021: in first-time IVF, scratching gave live birth 38.6% vs 37.1% — difference 1.5% (−4.4 to 7.4), and the authors recommend against it
cards.summary: First-time IVF (2020): scratching gave live birth 38.6% vs 37.1% — difference 1.5 points, CI including zero; the authors recommend against it.
cards.type: Pragmatic, superiority, open-label, multicentre, parallel-group randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 1,048 women aged 18–37 undergoing their first cycle of IVF, with or without ICSI, at 16 UK fertility clinics (July 2016–October 2019), randomised to endometrial scratch in the mid-luteal phase plus treatment as usual (523) or treatment as usual alone (525); 453 (86.6%) of the scratch group received the procedure.
cards.result: Live birth rate was 38.6% (202/523) in the scratch group and 37.1% (195/525) with treatment as usual — an unadjusted absolute difference of 1.5% (95% CI −4.4 to 7.4; P=0.621). There were no statistical differences in secondary outcomes, and adverse events were comparable across groups. The authors state the trial is the largest adequately powered assessment in first-cycle IVF and recommend that endometrial scratching is not undertaken in this population.
cards.watchOut: No sham procedure was used in the control group (the authors argue objective fertility outcomes make this immaterial), and the result is specific to first-cycle IVF — recurrent-implantation-failure populations are a separate, untested-here claim.
cards.source: Metwally M et al. A randomised controlled trial to assess the clinical effectiveness and safety of the endometrial scratch procedure prior to first-time IVF, with or without ICSI. Hum Reprod. 2021;36(7):1841-1853. PMID: 34050362. Registry ID: ISRCTN23800982, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, one identical answer — scratching does not raise live birth; LIKELY the null
cards.summary: Two large trials, one identical answer — scratching does not raise live birth — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lensen 2019 (1,364 women, any IVF cycle) and Metwally 2020/2021 (1,048 women, first IVF cycle).
cards.result: Across 2,412 randomised women the live-birth differences were 0.0 percentage points (26.1% vs 26.1%) and +1.5 points (38.6% vs 37.1%, CI including zero) — an add-on procedure with a median pain score of 3.5/10 and no measurable return. Freeze-all strategy is on Shelf #834 and PGT-A is drafted at #661; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The null is for the populations and timings tested; clinics still marketing scratching for other subgroups carry the burden of proof this shelf does not discharge for them.
