shelves.title: Breast screening with tomosynthesis (TOSYMA)
shelves.question: Does digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detect more invasive cancers than digital mammography alone in population screening — and at what recall and interval-cancer cost (TOSYMA; the TMIST trial in North America)?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,epidemiology · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Mammography/methods · Mass Screening · Breast Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,pathology,epidemiology · Carcinoma, Ductal, Breast/diagnostic imaging,pathology,epidemiology · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/diagnostic imaging,pathology,epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One very large randomised screening trial programme. TOSYMA (99,689 women) found tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detected more invasive cancers than digital mammography alone (7.1 vs 4.8 per 1,000 screened; odds ratio 1.48, a relative figure). Its 24-month follow-up found fewer invasive interval cancers with tomosynthesis (14.2 vs 18.6 per 10,000 screen-negative women), but that second primary endpoint did not reach significance (adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.06; P=0.11). Detection is a surrogate for benefit, there is no mortality endpoint, and a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The North American TMIST trial has published no main-results report, so it cannot be carded.

cards.headline: TOSYMA-1 (Heindel 2022): tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detected more invasive cancers than mammography alone (7.1 vs 4.8 per 1,000; OR 1.48)
cards.summary: TOSYMA-1 (2022): tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography detected more invasive cancers than mammography alone ( 7.1 vs 4.8 per 1,000 women screened).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled superiority trial (population screening)
cards.people: 99,689 women aged 50–69 years invited to a population-wide, quality-controlled mammography screening programme in two German federal states, randomised to digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised two-dimensional mammography (n=49,804) or digital mammography alone (n=49,830); 49,715 and 49,762 women respectively had evaluable primary-endpoint data. The abstract does not state mean age (eligibility was 50–69 years).
cards.result: Invasive breast cancers were detected in 354 of 49,715 women in the tomosynthesis group (detection rate 7.1 cases per 1,000 women screened) and 240 of 49,762 in the digital mammography group (4.8 per 1,000; odds ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.25 to 1.75; P<0.0001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Adverse events and device deficiencies were rare (six adverse events in each group; device deficiencies 23 in the tomosynthesis group vs five with digital mammography) and no serious adverse events were reported. This report covers the detection endpoint only; the interval-cancer endpoint was reserved for the follow-up study carded next.
cards.watchOut: A higher detection rate is not itself proof of benefit: some additionally detected cancers may be overdiagnosed, and this report contains no mortality or stage outcome. Open-label by necessity — radiologists cannot be blinded to the imaging modality.
cards.source: Heindel W et al. Digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography versus digital screening mammography for the detection of invasive breast cancer (TOSYMA): a multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial. Lancet Oncol. 2022;23(5):601-611. PMID: 35427470. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03377036, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TOSYMA-2 (2026): invasive interval cancers were fewer with tomosynthesis (14.2 vs 18.6 per 10,000) but the primary endpoint was not significant (OR 0.76; P=0.11)
cards.summary: TOSYMA-2 (2026): invasive interval cancers were fewer with tomosynthesis ( 14.2 vs 18.6 per 10,000 ) but the primary endpoint was not significant.
cards.type: 24-month follow-up report of the TOSYMA randomised screening trial (second primary endpoint)
cards.people: The TOSYMA cohort followed for 24 months after a negative screen: 49,299 of 49,762 women assigned tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography screened negative, as did 49,456 of 49,796 assigned digital mammography with evaluable data; suspected interval cancers were identified by linkage to cancer registries. Median age 57 years (IQR 53–62); all participants were female.
cards.result: Invasive interval cancers were detected in 70 of 49,299 women in the tomosynthesis group (14.2 cases per 10,000 women screened with a negative result) and 92 of 49,456 in the digital mammography group (18.6 per 10,000; adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.06; P=0.11 — a relative figure whose confidence interval crosses 1). Within 12 months, interval cancers occurred in 22 women in the tomosynthesis group (4.5 per 10,000) and 31 in the digital mammography group (6.3 per 10,000; odds ratio 0.71, 0.52 to 0.97). The authors conclude that about a quarter of the invasive interval cancers occurring with digital mammography over two years might be avoided with tomosynthesis screening, while stating the primary outcome did not reach statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: The headline interval-cancer result is non-significant at 24 months; the significant 12-month figure is a secondary outcome. Interval cancers are still a surrogate for the outcome screening ultimately aims at — breast-cancer mortality — which neither TOSYMA report measures.
cards.source: Weigel S et al. Invasive interval breast cancer rates after digital breast tomosynthesis plus synthesised mammography versus digital mammography screening (TOSYMA): 24-month follow-up of the multicentre, open-label, randomised, controlled, superiority trial. Lancet Oncol. 2026;27(11):1382-1392. PMID: 42854706. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03377036, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: more cancers found, interval cancers probably fewer, benefit on mortality untested — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: More cancers found, interval cancers probably fewer, benefit on mortality untested — POSSIBLE. No TMIST main-results report exists; the shelf rests on TOSYMA, and the gap is disclosed on it.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: one trial programme, TOSYMA (99,689 women screened in Germany), reported at detection (2022) and at 24-month interval-cancer follow-up (2026).
cards.result: TOSYMA-1 and TOSYMA-2 are two endpoints of one trial, not two trials: detection rose by a relative 48% (7.1 vs 4.8 per 1,000) while the 24-month interval-cancer rate fell by a non-significant relative 24% (14.2 vs 18.6 per 10,000). That is a coherent but unproven benefit story, capped at POSSIBLE by the single-programme rule. The TMIST trial in North America (ECOG-ACRIN EA1151) has published design and lead-in reports only — no main-results report exists to card, a gap stated plainly here rather than filled. Mammography screening itself is Shelf #213, supplemental MRI in dense breasts is drafted as Shelf #800 and AI-supported reading as Shelf #803; none is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Recall rates and false-positive burden are not reported in either abstract carded here; a screening decision needs those figures from the programme's own reports, not from this shelf.

shelves.title: Ovarian suppression in premenopausal breast cancer: SOFT and TEXT
shelves.question: In premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer, does adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen — or using exemestane with ovarian suppression — improve disease-free survival, and in whom (SOFT; TEXT)?
shelves.mesh: Androstadienes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antineoplastic Combined Chemotherapy Protocols/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aromatase Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy,radiotherapy,surgery · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Disease-Free Survival
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — exemestane plus ovarian suppression beats tamoxifen plus ovarian suppression for recurrence · POSSIBLE — adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen, where benefit concentrates in women at high enough risk to have had chemotherapy. In the joint TEXT/SOFT primary analysis (4,690 women), five-year disease-free survival was 91.1% with exemestane plus suppression vs 87.3% with tamoxifen plus suppression (hazard ratio 0.72). In SOFT alone, adding suppression to tamoxifen did not significantly improve disease-free survival overall (hazard ratio 0.83, P=0.10 at first report; 15-year breast cancer-free interval hazard ratio 0.82 in the final report), and the 15-year final outcomes confine meaningful survival benefit to high-risk subgroups, with overall survival in the combined HER2-negative analysis at hazard ratio 0.89 (0.74 to 1.06) — no standalone mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: SOFT (Francis 2015): adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen did not significantly improve disease-free survival overall (HR 0.83; P=0.10), but exemestane plus suppression did beat tamoxifen alone
cards.summary: SOFT (2015): adding ovarian suppression to tamoxifen did not significantly improve disease-free survival overall (HR 0.83; P=0.10).
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trial (three arms, five years of endocrine therapy)
cards.people: 3,066 premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer, stratified by prior chemotherapy (46.7% had not received chemotherapy; 53.3% had and remained premenopausal), randomised to five years of tamoxifen, tamoxifen plus ovarian suppression, or exemestane plus ovarian suppression; primary analysis after median follow-up of 67 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Estimated five-year disease-free survival was 86.6% in the tamoxifen–ovarian suppression group and 84.7% in the tamoxifen group (hazard ratio for disease recurrence, second invasive cancer or death 0.83, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.04; P=0.10 — a relative figure whose interval crosses 1). Multivariable adjustment suggested a greater effect (hazard ratio 0.78, 0.62 to 0.98). Most recurrences occurred in patients who had received prior chemotherapy, among whom five-year freedom from breast cancer was 82.5% with tamoxifen plus suppression vs 78.0% with tamoxifen (hazard ratio 0.78, 0.60 to 1.02). At five years, freedom from breast cancer was 85.7% in the exemestane–ovarian suppression group (hazard ratio for recurrence vs tamoxifen 0.65, 0.49 to 0.87).
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison the trial was powered on was not significant in the overall population; the benefit story rests on the prior-chemotherapy (higher-risk) stratum and on the exemestane arm. Suppression was by GnRH agonist, oophorectomy or ovarian irradiation, with the menopausal side-effect burden that implies.
cards.source: Francis PA et al. Adjuvant ovarian suppression in premenopausal breast cancer. N Engl J Med. 2015;372(5):436-446. PMID: 25495490. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00066690, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TEXT/SOFT joint analysis (Pagani 2014): exemestane plus ovarian suppression improved five-year disease-free survival over tamoxifen plus suppression (91.1% vs 87.3%; HR 0.72)
cards.summary: TEXT/SOFT joint analysis (2014): exemestane plus ovarian suppression improved five-year disease-free survival over tamoxifen plus suppression ( 91.1% vs 87.3% ; HR 0.72).
cards.type: Preplanned joint analysis of two randomised phase 3 trials (TEXT and SOFT)
cards.people: 4,690 premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer in the two phase 3 trials TEXT and SOFT, randomised to exemestane plus ovarian suppression or tamoxifen plus ovarian suppression for five years; primary analysis after median follow-up of 68 months. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Disease-free survival at five years was 91.1% in the exemestane–ovarian suppression group and 87.3% in the tamoxifen–ovarian suppression group (hazard ratio for disease recurrence, second invasive cancer or death 0.72, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.85; P<0.001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Freedom from breast cancer at five years was 92.8% vs 88.8% (hazard ratio 0.66, 0.55 to 0.80; P<0.001). With 194 deaths (4.1% of patients), overall survival did not differ significantly between the groups (hazard ratio for death 1.14, 0.86 to 1.51; P=0.37). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events were reported in 30.6% of the exemestane group and 29.4% of the tamoxifen group.
cards.watchOut: A joint analysis of two trials sharing a comparison, not two independent confirmations of it; and at this report overall survival numerically favoured neither arm (hazard ratio 1.14, non-significant) — the claim is about recurrence, not survival.
cards.source: Pagani O et al. Adjuvant exemestane with ovarian suppression in premenopausal breast cancer. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(2):107-118. PMID: 24881463. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00066703 (TEXT) and NCT00066690 (SOFT), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SOFT/TEXT final outcomes (2026): at 15 years the recurrence gradient persisted (BCFI 78.6% vs 75.7% vs 72.1% in SOFT), and survival benefit was confined to high-risk subgroups
cards.summary: SOFT/TEXT final outcomes (2026): at 15 years the recurrence gradient persisted (breast cancer-free interval 78.6% vs 75.7% vs 72.1% in SOFT); the combined survival estimate was non-significant and no mortality claim is made.
cards.type: Final (15-year) outcomes report of the SOFT and TEXT phase 3 trials
cards.people: Final 15-year outcomes of SOFT (3,047 women in the intention-to-treat population) and TEXT (2,660), premenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive early breast cancer randomised to five years of tamoxifen, tamoxifen plus ovarian function suppression, or exemestane plus suppression (SOFT), or tamoxifen vs exemestane, both with suppression (TEXT). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In SOFT, 15-year breast cancer-free interval was 78.6% for exemestane plus suppression, 75.7% for tamoxifen plus suppression and 72.1% for tamoxifen (tamoxifen plus suppression vs tamoxifen: hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.98; P=0.03). In the SOFT no-chemotherapy cohort, suppression reduced breast cancer events at 15 years while distant recurrence-free interval and overall survival remained high regardless of assignment. After prior chemotherapy for HER2-negative tumours (n=1,257), 15-year overall survival in SOFT was 81.0% with exemestane plus suppression, 77.1% with tamoxifen plus suppression and 76.8% with tamoxifen alone; in women under 35 with HER2-negative tumours (n=241) it was 82.5%, 77.9% and 68.1% respectively. In the combined SOFT and TEXT HER2-negative analysis (n=4,035), exemestane plus suppression vs tamoxifen plus suppression reduced distant recurrence (hazard ratio 0.75, 0.63 to 0.90), with a smaller, non-significant reduction in deaths (hazard ratio 0.89, 0.74 to 1.06). The authors conclude meaningful overall-survival benefit is limited to high-risk premenopausal subgroups.
cards.watchOut: The survival gradients by subgroup (prior chemotherapy; age under 35) are subgroup analyses of a follow-up report; the overall combined mortality result is non-significant (hazard ratio 0.89), and this card must not be read as a general survival claim for suppression.
cards.source: Francis PA et al. Final outcomes of the SOFT and TEXT phase III trials in premenopausal hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer. Ann Oncol. 2026;37(10):1367-1385. PMID: 42229584. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the report is a follow-up analysis of trials registered as NCT00066690 (SOFT) and NCT00066703 (TEXT), as carded on the earlier reports.

cards.headline: Synthesis: escalate to exemestane plus suppression when recurrence risk justifies it; suppression added to tamoxifen is the conditional half — split stamp
cards.summary: Escalate to exemestane plus suppression when recurrence risk justifies it; suppression added to tamoxifen is the conditional half — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SOFT (3,066 randomised; 3,047 in final ITT), TEXT, their joint analysis (4,690 women) and the 15-year final outcomes report.
cards.result: Three readouts of one twin-trial programme agree on an ordering: exemestane plus ovarian suppression gives the fewest recurrences (five-year disease-free survival 91.1% vs 87.3% against tamoxifen plus suppression; 15-year breast cancer-free interval 78.6% at the top of SOFT's gradient), tamoxifen plus suppression sits in between, and tamoxifen alone is last — but the middle step was not significant overall at first report and its long-term gains concentrate in women whose risk warranted chemotherapy. Hence LIKELY for the exemestane-plus-suppression comparison and POSSIBLE for adding suppression to tamoxifen. Postmenopausal endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors live on Shelf #365; extending therapy to ten years is Shelf #942. Neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: All three cards describe the same two trials at different maturities — count the evidence as one twin programme, never as three trials.

shelves.title: Extending adjuvant endocrine therapy to ten years: ATLAS and MA.17R
shelves.question: Does extending adjuvant endocrine therapy beyond five years — tamoxifen to ten years (ATLAS), or letrozole after five years of aromatase-inhibitor-based therapy (MA.17R) — reduce recurrence and breast-cancer death enough to justify the extra years of harm?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents, Hormonal/administration & dosage · Breast Neoplasms/chemistry,drug therapy · Chemotherapy, Adjuvant · Receptors, Estrogen/analysis · Tamoxifen/administration & dosage · Aromatase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Breast Neoplasms/drug therapy,epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: ATLAS carries a breast-cancer mortality claim): LIKELY — continuing tamoxifen to ten years reduces recurrence and breast-cancer mortality in ER-positive disease (ATLAS: recurrence 21.4% vs 25.1% and breast-cancer mortality 12.2% vs 15.0% over years 5–14, an absolute mortality reduction of 2.8%, bought with more endometrial cancer, 3.1% vs 1.6%, and more pulmonary embolism) · POSSIBLE — extending an aromatase inhibitor with five more years of letrozole (MA.17R: disease-free survival hazard ratio 0.66 and fewer contralateral cancers, but overall survival 93% vs 94%, hazard ratio 0.97, and more bone pain, fractures and new osteoporosis).

cards.headline: ATLAS (Davies 2013): continuing tamoxifen to 10 years cut recurrence (21.4% vs 25.1%) and breast-cancer mortality (12.2% vs 15.0%) in ER-positive disease
cards.summary: ATLAS (2013): continuing tamoxifen to 10 years cut recurrence ( 21.4% vs 25.1% ) and breast-cancer mortality (12.2% vs 15.0%) in ER-positive disease.
cards.type: Randomised trial (open-label; continue tamoxifen to 10 years vs stop at 5 years)
cards.people: 12,894 women with early breast cancer who had completed five years of tamoxifen, randomised worldwide (1996–2005) to continue tamoxifen to ten years or stop at five years (open control); breast-cancer outcomes are reported among the 6,846 women with oestrogen-receptor-positive disease (3,428 continue, 3,418 control) and side-effects among all 12,894. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Among women with ER-positive disease, continuing tamoxifen reduced recurrence (617 recurrences in 3,428 women vs 711 in 3,418 controls; P=0.002), breast-cancer mortality (331 vs 397 deaths; P=0.01) and overall mortality (639 vs 722 deaths; P=0.01). Benefits were larger after year ten (recurrence rate ratio 0.90 [95% CI 0.79 to 1.02] during years 5–9 and 0.75 [0.62 to 0.90] later; breast-cancer mortality rate ratio 0.97 [0.79 to 1.18] then 0.71 [0.58 to 0.88] — relative figures). Cumulative recurrence risk during years 5–14 was 21.4% (continue) vs 25.1% (control); breast-cancer mortality was 12.2% vs 15.0% (absolute mortality reduction 2.8%). Harms among all women: pulmonary embolus rate ratio 1.87 (1.13 to 3.07; P=0.01), endometrial cancer 1.74 (1.30 to 2.34; P=0.0002) with cumulative endometrial-cancer risk 3.1% vs 1.6% during years 5–14 (mortality 0.4% vs 0.2%); stroke 1.06 (0.83 to 1.36) and ischaemic heart disease 0.76 (0.60 to 0.95). There was no apparent effect in ER-negative disease.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with yearly follow-up forms, recruited 1996–2005 — an era before aromatase inhibitors were standard, so the comparison is against stopping endocrine therapy altogether. The mortality benefit emerges mainly after year ten, so it accrues to women who live long enough on treatment to reach it, against a doubled endometrial-cancer risk.
cards.source: Davies C et al. Long-term effects of continuing adjuvant tamoxifen to 10 years versus stopping at 5 years after diagnosis of oestrogen receptor-positive breast cancer: ATLAS, a randomised trial. Lancet. 2013;381(9869):805-816. PMID: 23219286. Registry ID: ISRCTN19652633, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: MA.17R (Goss 2016): five more years of letrozole improved disease-free survival (HR 0.66) but not overall survival (93% vs 94%), with more bone harm
cards.summary: MA.17R (2016): five more years of letrozole improved disease-free survival (HR 0.66 ) but not overall survival (93% vs 94%), with more bone events.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (extended letrozole vs placebo)
cards.people: 1,918 postmenopausal women who had received aromatase-inhibitor-based adjuvant therapy (as up-front monotherapy or after tamoxifen), randomised double-blind to letrozole or placebo for a further five years; median follow-up 6.3 years. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: There were 165 events of disease recurrence or contralateral breast cancer (67 with letrozole, 98 with placebo). Five-year disease-free survival was 95% (95% CI 93 to 96) with letrozole and 91% (89 to 93) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.66; P=0.01 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Five-year overall survival was 93% (92 to 95) with letrozole and 94% (92 to 95) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.97; P=0.83), with 200 deaths (100 in each group). The annual incidence of contralateral breast cancer was 0.21% (0.10 to 0.32) with letrozole vs 0.49% (0.32 to 0.67) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.42; P=0.007). Bone-related toxic effects were more frequent with letrozole, including more bone pain, bone fractures and new-onset osteoporosis; most quality-of-life subscales did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: The disease-free-survival gain is driven substantially by contralateral new cancers prevented (hazard ratio 0.42) rather than by recurrence of the index cancer, and there is no survival gain to set against the bone harms. Event counts are small (165) for a ten-year strategy question.
cards.source: Goss PE et al. Extending Aromatase-Inhibitor Adjuvant Therapy to 10 Years. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(3):209-219. PMID: 27264120. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00003140 and NCT00754845, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: extension works, but the two extensions are different bargains — split stamp, Tier C
cards.summary: Extension works, but the two extensions are different bargains — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ATLAS (12,894 women; 6,846 ER-positive for efficacy) and MA.17R (1,918 women).
cards.result: Extending tamoxifen (ATLAS) bought an absolute 2.8% reduction in breast-cancer mortality over years 5–14 at the price of endometrial cancer and embolism; extending letrozole after aromatase-inhibitor therapy (MA.17R) bought a relative third fewer disease-free-survival events with no survival difference (93% vs 94%) and more bone harm. Because ATLAS's half of this shelf is a mortality claim, the whole shelf is Tier C and both stamps are PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict. Standard five-year endocrine therapy and the premenopausal suppression question live on Shelves #365 and #941; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The trials answer different extension questions (tamoxifen after tamoxifen; letrozole after aromatase-inhibitor therapy) in different menopausal populations — do not average them into a single 'ten years is better' claim.

shelves.title: Ductal carcinoma in situ: radiotherapy after lumpectomy, and tamoxifen
shelves.question: For DCIS treated with breast-conserving surgery, how much does radiotherapy cut ipsilateral recurrence in good-risk disease (RTOG 9804) — and what did the long-term NSABP B-17/B-24 programme show for radiotherapy and tamoxifen on invasive recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging,pathology,prevention & control,radiotherapy,surgery · Canada · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating/diagnostic imaging,radiotherapy,surgery · Disease Management · Disease-Free Survival · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Mammography
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Radiotherapy after lumpectomy for DCIS roughly halves invasive ipsilateral recurrence over 15 years in the NSABP programme (15-year cumulative incidence 8.9% with radiotherapy vs 19.4% with lumpectomy alone; hazard ratio 0.48), and in good-risk DCIS the RTOG 9804 trial found a seven-year local failure rate of 0.9% with radiotherapy vs 6.7% with observation (hazard ratio 0.11) — a large relative effect on a low absolute risk. Adding tamoxifen to radiotherapy reduced invasive recurrence further (hazard ratio 0.68; 15-year incidence 8.5% vs 10.0%). Neither programme showed a survival difference, and none is claimed: the 15-year breast-cancer death incidence stayed between 2.3% and 4.7% across all arms.

cards.headline: RTOG 9804 (McCormick 2015): in good-risk DCIS, radiotherapy cut seven-year local failure from 6.7% to 0.9% (HR 0.11)
cards.summary: RTOG 9804 (2015): in good-risk DCIS, radiotherapy cut seven-year local failure from 6.7% to 0.9% (HR 0.11).
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (radiotherapy vs observation after breast-conserving surgery)
cards.people: 636 women in the United States and Canada with mammographically detected, low- or intermediate-grade DCIS measuring under 2.5 cm with margins of at least 3 mm, randomised after breast-conserving surgery to radiotherapy or observation; tamoxifen use (62%) was optional. The trial was designed for 1,790 patients and closed early for slow accrual; median follow-up 7.17 years. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Two local failures occurred in the radiotherapy arm and 19 in the observation arm. At seven years the local failure rate was 0.9% (95% CI 0.0 to 2.2) with radiotherapy vs 6.7% (3.2 to 9.6) with observation (hazard ratio 0.11, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.47; P<.001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Grade 1–2 acute toxicities occurred in 76% of patients in the radiotherapy arm and 30% in the observation arm; grade 3–4 toxicities in 4.2% and 4.0%. Late radiotherapy toxicity was grade 1 in 30%, grade 2 in 4.6% and grade 3 in 0.7% of patients.
cards.watchOut: Closed early at 636 of a planned 1,790 patients, with only 21 local failures in total — the hazard ratio is dramatic but rests on few events, and the absolute benefit in this good-risk group is about six fewer failures per 100 women at seven years.
cards.source: McCormick B et al. RTOG 9804: a prospective randomized trial for good-risk ductal carcinoma in situ comparing radiotherapy with observation. J Clin Oncol. 2015;33(7):709-715. PMID: 25605856. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00003857, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: NSABP B-17/B-24 (Wapnir 2011): radiotherapy halved invasive recurrence (15-year incidence 8.9% vs 19.4%; HR 0.48) and tamoxifen added a further reduction (HR 0.68)
cards.summary: NSABP B-17/B-24 (2011): radiotherapy halved invasive recurrence (15-year incidence 8.9% vs 19.4% ; HR 0.48) and tamoxifen added a further reduction.
cards.type: Long-term outcomes analysis of two randomised trials (B-17: radiotherapy vs none; B-24: tamoxifen vs placebo, all with radiotherapy)
cards.people: Participants in two NSABP randomised trials for DCIS treated with lumpectomy: B-17 (accrual 1985–1990; n=813) randomised lumpectomy alone (n=403) vs lumpectomy plus radiotherapy (n=410); B-24 (accrual 1991–1994; n=1,799) randomised all patients to lumpectomy plus radiotherapy with placebo (n=900) or tamoxifen (n=899). Median follow-up was 207 months for B-17 and 163 months for B-24. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Of 490 ipsilateral breast tumour recurrences, 263 (53.7%) were invasive. Radiotherapy reduced invasive ipsilateral recurrence by a relative 52% (B-17; hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.69; P<.001), and radiotherapy plus tamoxifen reduced it by a relative 32% versus radiotherapy plus placebo (B-24; hazard ratio 0.68, 0.49 to 0.95; P=.025). The 15-year cumulative incidence of invasive recurrence was 19.4% for lumpectomy alone, 8.9% for lumpectomy plus radiotherapy (B-17), 10.0% for radiotherapy plus placebo and 8.5% for radiotherapy plus tamoxifen (B-24). The 15-year cumulative incidence of all contralateral breast cancers was 10.3%, 10.2%, 10.8% and 7.3% respectively. Invasive recurrence was associated with increased mortality risk (hazard ratio for death 1.75, 1.45 to 2.96), whereas DCIS recurrence was not; the 15-year cumulative incidence of breast-cancer death was 3.1% (lumpectomy alone), 4.7% (radiotherapy, B-17), 2.7% (radiotherapy plus placebo) and 2.3% (radiotherapy plus tamoxifen) — no survival advantage for any strategy, and long-term prognosis remained excellent in all arms.
cards.watchOut: A pooled long-term analysis of two trials run in the mammography era of the late 1980s and early 1990s, before modern margin and grade selection; the breast-cancer death rates do not favour radiotherapy despite the recurrence reduction, which is the central tension of DCIS treatment.
cards.source: Wapnir IL et al. Long-term outcomes of invasive ipsilateral breast tumor recurrences after lumpectomy in NSABP B-17 and B-24 randomized clinical trials for DCIS. J Natl Cancer Inst. 2011;103(6):478-488. PMID: 21398619. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trials (accrual 1985–1994).

cards.headline: Synthesis: radiotherapy and tamoxifen cut invasive recurrence; survival is excellent either way — LIKELY for the recurrence claim
cards.summary: Radiotherapy and tamoxifen cut invasive recurrence; survival is excellent either way — LIKELY for the recurrence claim.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RTOG 9804 (636 women with good-risk DCIS) and the NSABP B-17/B-24 programme (813 and 1,799 women).
cards.result: The recurrence evidence is consistent across eras and risk groups: hazard ratios of 0.11 in good-risk disease (on a 6.7% seven-year baseline risk) and 0.48 for invasive recurrence across the NSABP population (on a 19.4% 15-year baseline risk), with tamoxifen adding a relative third (hazard ratio 0.68). The decision weight therefore sits in the absolute numbers and in the absence of any survival difference, both printed on the cards. Hence LIKELY for recurrence reduction, with no mortality claim made or implied. Axillary management in invasive node-positive cancer is a different disease stage, drafted as Shelf #862; nothing from it is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the RTOG hazard ratio of 0.11 without its absolute rates (0.9% vs 6.7%) — in good-risk DCIS the relative figure flatters a small absolute gain.

shelves.title: Vulvovaginal symptoms after menopause: vaginal estradiol, moisturiser, or placebo (MsFLASH)
shelves.question: For postmenopausal vulvovaginal symptoms, do a low-dose vaginal estradiol tablet or a vaginal moisturiser actually beat a dual placebo — the MsFLASH three-arm trial whose result surprised prescribers?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Estradiol/administration & dosage · Estrogens/administration & dosage · Gels · Postmenopause · Vaginal Creams, Foams, and Jellies/administration & dosage · Vaginal Diseases/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the one large, rigorous three-arm trial (MsFLASH, 302 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe symptoms), neither low-dose vaginal estradiol (most-bothersome-symptom severity reduction −1.4) nor a vaginal moisturiser (−1.2) beat dual placebo (−1.3) over 12 weeks — P=.25 and P=.31 — and sexual-function scores improved similarly in all arms. All three groups improved substantially, which is the finding prescribers most often miss. A single trial, however rigorous, caps the null at POSSIBLE under the library's single-trial rule.

cards.headline: MsFLASH (Mitchell 2018): vaginal estradiol and vaginal moisturiser were both no better than dual placebo for vulvovaginal symptoms (reductions −1.4, −1.2 and −1.3)
cards.summary: MsFLASH (2018): vaginal estradiol and vaginal moisturiser were both no better than dual placebo for vulvovaginal symptoms over 12 weeks.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (three arms, dual-placebo controlled, 12 weeks)
cards.people: 302 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vulvovaginal itching, pain, dryness, irritation or pain with penetration, enrolled in a 12-week multicentre trial and randomised to a vaginal 10-microgram estradiol tablet (daily for two weeks, then twice weekly) plus placebo gel (n=102), placebo tablet plus vaginal moisturiser (n=100), or dual placebo (n=100). Mean age 61 (SD 4) years; 88% white, 81% sexually active. The most common most-bothersome symptom was pain with vaginal penetration (60%), then dryness (21%); 294 women (97%) provided primary-outcome data.
cards.result: Mean baseline most-bothersome-symptom severity (0–3 scale) was similar across groups (estradiol 2.4; moisturiser 2.5; placebo 2.5). Over 12 weeks all groups improved by similar amounts: estradiol −1.4 (95% CI −1.6 to −1.2), moisturiser −1.2 (−1.4 to −1.0) and placebo −1.3 (−1.5 to −1.1), with no significant difference for estradiol vs placebo (P=.25) or moisturiser vs placebo (P=.31). Mean total Female Sexual Function Index improvement was also similar (estradiol 5.4 vs placebo 4.5; P=.64; moisturiser 3.1 vs placebo; P=.17). The authors conclude that neither prescribed vaginal estradiol tablet nor over-the-counter vaginal moisturiser provides additional benefit over placebo tablet and gel in reducing postmenopausal vulvovaginal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks and symptom-severity endpoints only: the trial does not test estradiol for vaginal atrophy signs over years, for recurrent urinary tract infection (Shelf #150's question), or in women with milder or more severe symptoms than the moderate-to-severe group enrolled. The large placebo-arm improvement is a trial-context effect as much as a gel effect.
cards.source: Mitchell CM et al. Efficacy of Vaginal Estradiol or Vaginal Moisturizer vs Placebo for Treating Postmenopausal Vulvovaginal Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(5):681-690. PMID: 29554173. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02516202, from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: MsFLASH (302 postmenopausal women, three arms, dual placebo).
cards.result: This shelf has one card because one trial answers the question directly and no second trial of the same three-way comparison exists in the library. The null is unusually informative — both active arms bracket the placebo arm's improvement (−1.4, −1.2, −1.3 on a 0–3 scale) — but the single-trial ceiling keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Non-oestrogen alternatives (ospemifene, prasterone) are Shelf #945, vaginal estriol for recurrent urinary infection is Shelf #150 and vaginal laser is Shelf #608; none is re-carded here.

shelves.title: Non-oestrogen options for dyspareunia: ospemifene and prasterone
shelves.question: Do ospemifene (an oral SERM) and intravaginal prasterone (DHEA) improve dyspareunia and vulvovaginal atrophy versus placebo in postmenopausal women who avoid or cannot use oestrogen?
shelves.mesh: Atrophy · Dyspareunia/drug therapy,etiology · Placebos · Postmenopause · Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators/administration & dosage · Tamoxifen/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Vagina/drug effects,pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two non-oestrogen options each beat placebo on dyspareunia and on the tissue signs of vulvovaginal atrophy over 12 weeks. Ospemifene's pivotal trial (605 women) was significant on all co-primary endpoints including dyspareunia severity (P=0.0001), though its abstract reports significance rather than effect sizes, with hot flushes the commonest treatment-related adverse event (6.6% vs 3.6%). Prasterone's pooled three-trial data (436 treated, 260 placebo) show a 0.46-unit greater reduction in dyspareunia severity over placebo (P<0.0001). Symptom-scale benefits of modest, partly unquantified size from short trials: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Ospemifene (Portman 2013): the oral SERM beat placebo on dyspareunia severity (P=0.0001) and all tissue co-primary endpoints at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Ospemifene trial (2013): the oral SERM beat placebo on dyspareunia severity (P=0.0001) and all tissue co-primary endpoints at 12 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group phase 3 trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 605 postmenopausal women aged 40 to 80 years with vulvar and vaginal atrophy who self-reported dyspareunia as their most bothersome symptom, randomised in a multicentre phase 3 study to once-daily oral ospemifene 60 mg (n=303) or placebo (n=302) for 12 weeks; the intention-to-treat population was all 605. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Ospemifene was significantly more effective than placebo on each co-primary endpoint at 12 weeks: the percentage of parabasal cells decreased, the percentage of superficial cells increased, and vaginal pH decreased (all P<0.0001), and dyspareunia severity was significantly reduced versus placebo (P=0.0001). The abstract reports P values for these endpoints rather than the size of the dyspareunia difference, so no effect magnitude is printed on this card. At least one treatment-emergent adverse event was reported by 186 women (61.4%) on ospemifene and 154 (51.0%) on placebo; hot flushes were the most frequent treatment-related event (6.6% vs 3.6%); one participant per group discontinued for an adverse event, and investigators reported no serious adverse events related to the study drug.
cards.watchOut: A single pivotal trial whose abstract gives significance without magnitude for the symptom endpoint — the reader cannot tell from this record whether the dyspareunia gain was large or small. Twelve weeks is short for a chronic condition, and as a SERM ospemifene carries a class profile that a 605-woman trial cannot characterise.
cards.source: Portman DJ et al. Ospemifene, a novel selective estrogen receptor modulator for treating dyspareunia associated with postmenopausal vulvar and vaginal atrophy. Menopause. 2013;20(6):623-630. PMID: 23361170. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00729469, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Prasterone (Labrie 2017): pooled data from three placebo-controlled trials show dyspareunia severity reduced by 0.46 units over placebo
cards.summary: Prasterone pooled trials (2017): dyspareunia severity reduced by 0.46 units over placebo across three placebo-controlled trials.
cards.type: Combined analysis of three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (12 weeks each)
cards.people: Combined data from three independent 12-week prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies of daily intravaginal prasterone 0.50% (6.5 mg) in postmenopausal women whose most bothersome symptom of vulvovaginal atrophy was moderate-to-severe dyspareunia: 436 women treated with prasterone and 260 with placebo. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Versus placebo, prasterone produced an average 35.1% greater decrease in the percentage of parabasal cells (P<0.0001), a 7.7% increase in superficial cells (P<0.0001) and a mean 0.72-unit decrease in vaginal pH (P<0.0001). The severity score of the most bothersome symptom, dyspareunia, decreased by 0.46 units (49%) over placebo (P<0.0001), and moderate-to-severe vaginal dryness severity decreased by 0.31 units over placebo (P<0.0001). The authors report no significant drug-related side effects and a very positive evaluation of the insert's acceptability by women and of observed changes by male partners.
cards.watchOut: A sponsor-side combined analysis rather than three separately carded trials: the individual trials are not individually reported in this record, follow-up is 12 weeks, and the dyspareunia gain of 0.46 severity units is modest on its face. Prasterone is a DHEA precursor converted locally to sex steroids — 'non-oestrogen' describes the administered drug, not zero steroid activity.
cards.source: Labrie F et al. Combined data of intravaginal prasterone against vulvovaginal atrophy of menopause. Menopause. 2017;24(11):1246-1256. PMID: 28640161. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a combined analysis of three trials, and no trial accession appears in the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Drugs for hypoactive sexual desire disorder: flibanserin and bremelanotide
shelves.question: Do flibanserin (nightly, premenopausal women — pooled pivotal trials) and bremelanotide (on-demand injection, RECONNECT) improve satisfying sexual events and desire versus placebo, and at what cost in dizziness, nausea, and hypotension?
shelves.mesh: Benzimidazoles/therapeutic use · Libido/drug effects · Premenopause · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sexual Behavior · Sexual Dysfunctions, Psychological/drug therapy · Central Nervous System Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Both approved drugs beat placebo on desire and distress scores, by small amounts. Flibanserin's pooled pivotal trials (2,465 premenopausal women) found about one extra satisfying sexual event per 28 days over placebo (change 2.1 vs 1.2) and small gains on desire and distress scales, with dizziness and somnolence in at least 10% of patients. Bremelanotide's twin RECONNECT trials (1,202 in the efficacy population) found integrated gains of 0.35 points on the desire domain and −0.33 on the distress item versus placebo, with nausea, flushing and headache in at least 10%. Statistically consistent, clinically modest: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Flibanserin pooled analysis (Simon 2019): about one extra satisfying sexual event per month over placebo (change 2.1 vs 1.2 per 28 days), with dizziness and somnolence in at least 10%
cards.summary: Flibanserin pooled analysis (2019): about one extra satisfying sexual event per month over placebo (change 2.1 vs 1.2 per 28 days), with dizziness and somnolence.
cards.type: Pooled post-hoc analysis of three randomised, placebo-controlled pivotal trials (24 weeks each)
cards.people: Pooled post-hoc analysis of three pivotal 24-week randomised, placebo-controlled multicentre trials (VIOLET, DAISY, BEGONIA) of flibanserin 100 mg once daily at bedtime in premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder: 2,465 women (flibanserin n=1,227; placebo n=1,238), mean age 36 years, mean HSDD duration 56.5 months.
cards.result: The mean change from baseline to 24 weeks in satisfying sexual events over 28 days was 2.1 (SE 0.14) with flibanserin vs 1.2 (SE 0.11) with placebo (P<0.0001). Least-squares mean changes on the Female Sexual Function Index desire domain (0.9 [0.04] vs 0.6 [0.04]; P<0.0001) and the Female Sexual Distress Scale-Revised item 13 (−0.9 [0.04] vs −0.6 [0.04]; P<0.0001) were also significantly greater with flibanserin, and improvements were generally consistent across demographic and clinical subgroups. Adverse events occurring in at least 10% of patients included dizziness and somnolence; the analysis authors describe the drug as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A pooled post-hoc analysis published by the programme rather than three separately carded trials; the absolute gains are small (about 0.9 extra satisfying events per month and 0.3 scale points on desire), and the abstract's safety summary omits the hypotension and syncope concerns — especially with alcohol — that dominate flibanserin's regulatory labelling.
cards.source: Simon JA et al. Flibanserin for Premenopausal Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder: Pooled Analysis of Clinical Trials. J Womens Health (Larchmt). 2019;28(6):769-777. PMID: 30707049. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pooled analysis of three trials, and no trial accession appears in the record's databank fields.

cards.type: Two identical randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper (RECONNECT studies 301 and 302)
cards.people: Two identical phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trials of bremelanotide 1.75 mg subcutaneously, as needed, in premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder: 1,267 women randomised, 1,247 in the safety population and 1,202 in the modified intention-to-treat efficacy population; mean age 39 years, 85.6% white, 96.6% from US sites. Treatment lasted 24 weeks.
cards.result: From baseline to end of study, bremelanotide produced statistically significant increases in sexual desire on the Female Sexual Function Index desire domain versus placebo (study 301: 0.30, P<.001; study 302: 0.42, P<.001; integrated: 0.35, P<.001) and significant reductions in distress related to low desire on the Female Sexual Distress Scale item 13 (study 301: −0.37, P<.001; study 302: −0.29, P=.005; integrated: −0.33, P<.001). Patients on bremelanotide experienced more nausea, flushing and headache (each 10% or more in both studies) than on placebo; most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate. Notably, satisfying sexual events — flibanserin's headline endpoint — are not among the significant results reported in this abstract.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are fractions of a scale point, the population was overwhelmingly white and US-based, and an on-demand injection with nausea in at least a tenth of users is a different practical proposition from the scores. Hypotension and hyperpigmentation concerns from the drug's labelling are not addressed in the abstract.
cards.source: Kingsberg SA et al. Bremelanotide for the Treatment of Hypoactive Sexual Desire Disorder: Two Randomized Phase 3 Trials. Obstet Gynecol. 2019;134(5):899-908. PMID: 31599840. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02333071 (study 301) and NCT02338960 (study 302), from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: flibanserin pooled pivotal trials (2,465 women) and RECONNECT bremelanotide trials (1,202 women in the efficacy population), all in premenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder.
cards.result: Two different drugs, two different regimens (nightly oral vs on-demand injection), the same pattern: statistically robust, absolutely small improvements in desire and distress (flibanserin about one extra satisfying event a month; bremelanotide 0.35 desire-domain points), paid for with dizziness and somnolence or nausea, flushing and headache in at least 10% of users. shelves.title: Preventing recurrent bacterial vaginosis: Lactin-V and suppressive metronidazole
shelves.question: After standard treatment clears bacterial vaginosis, can recurrence be held off — by a live Lactobacillus crispatus biotherapeutic (Lactin-V) or by twice-weekly suppressive metronidazole gel?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibiosis · Gels · Incidence · Lactobacillus crispatus/isolation & purification,physiology · Metronidazole/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two single randomised trials of two different hold-off strategies each reduced recurrence while they were used. Lactin-V after metronidazole gel (228 women) cut 12-week recurrence from 45% to 30% (risk ratio 0.66, a relative figure). Twice-weekly suppressive metronidazole gel (112 randomised women) cut recurrence during suppression from 59.1% to 25.5% (relative risk 0.43), an effect that faded once therapy stopped (51.0% vs 75.0% over 28 weeks), with more vaginal candidiasis. One trial per strategy caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A 2025 trial of treating the male partner (StepUp) is fenced in the synthesis — it changes the question, and its result is strong enough that this shelf should not be read as the whole recurrence story.

cards.headline: Lactin-V (Cohen 2020): the live Lactobacillus crispatus biotherapeutic cut 12-week BV recurrence from 45% to 30% (RR 0.66)
cards.summary: Lactin-V (2020): the live Lactobacillus crispatus biotherapeutic cut 12-week BV recurrence from 45% to 30% (RR 0.66).
cards.people: 228 women aged 18 to 45 years who had been diagnosed with bacterial vaginosis and had completed a course of vaginal metronidazole gel, randomised 2:1 to vaginal Lactin-V (Lactobacillus crispatus CTV-05) or placebo for 11 weeks (152 vs 76), with follow-up through week 24; 88% of the Lactin-V group and 84% of the placebo group could be evaluated for the primary outcome. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Recurrence of bacterial vaginosis by week 12 occurred in 46 participants (30%) in the Lactin-V group and 34 (45%) in the placebo group (risk ratio after multiple imputation 0.66, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.87; P=0.01 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here, and a ratio inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, so not solid evidence on its own). The risk ratio for recurrence by week 24 was 0.73 (0.54 to 0.92). At the 12-week visit, L. crispatus CTV-05 was detected in 79% of participants in the Lactin-V group. The percentages with at least one related adverse event, and with local or systemic adverse events, did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: A single phase 2b trial of 228 women; the relative risk of 0.66 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on its own, and by week 24 a majority-path toward recurrence was already reasserting itself (risk ratio 0.73). The product is a live biotherapeutic with regulatory status that varies by country.
cards.source: Cohen CR et al. Randomized Trial of Lactin-V to Prevent Recurrence of Bacterial Vaginosis. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(20):1906-1915. PMID: 32402161. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02766023, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sobel 2006: twice-weekly suppressive metronidazole gel halved recurrence while used (25.5% vs 59.1%; RR 0.43), then the benefit faded
cards.summary: Suppressive metronidazole (2006): twice-weekly gel halved recurrence while used ( 25.5% vs 59.1% ; RR 0.43), then the benefit faded.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial of suppressive therapy (after an open-label induction course)
cards.people: Women with recurrent bacterial vaginosis: of 157 eligible women entering an initial 10-day open-label metronidazole gel course, 112 of 127 returning evaluable women (88.2%) responded clinically and were randomised to twice-weekly metronidazole vaginal gel 0.75% or placebo for 16 weeks, then followed off therapy for 12 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: During suppressive therapy, recurrent bacterial vaginosis occurred in 13 women (25.5%) on metronidazole and 26 (59.1%) on placebo (modified intention-to-treat; relative risk 0.43, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.73; P=.001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Over the entire 28-week follow-up, recurrence occurred in 26 women (51.0%) on treatment vs 33 (75%) on placebo (relative risk 0.68, 0.49 to 0.93; P=.02). The probability of remaining cured was 70% on metronidazole vs 39% on placebo during therapy, declining to 34% and 18% by week 28. Adverse effects were uncommon, but secondary vaginal candidiasis occurred significantly more often in metronidazole-treated women (P=.02).
cards.watchOut: Small (112 randomised), and it is a suppression result, not a cure result: once the gel stopped, recurrence climbed in both groups. Randomisation only of women who responded to induction also means the population is pre-selected responders.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Suppressive antibacterial therapy with 0.75% metronidazole vaginal gel to prevent recurrent bacterial vaginosis. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2006;194(5):1283-1289. PMID: 16647911. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (published 2006).

cards.headline: Synthesis: both hold-off strategies work while applied; neither is shown to cure the recurrence tendency — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Both hold-off strategies work while applied; neither is shown to cure the recurrence tendency — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lactin-V (228 women) and Sobel suppressive gel (112 randomised women).
cards.result: The two strategies converge on the same lesson: recurrence by 12–16 weeks fell from 45% to 30% (Lactin-V) and from 59.1% to 25.5% during suppression (metronidazole gel), and in both programmes recurrence resumed when treatment ended. Each strategy rests on one trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE for each. Fenced, not carded: the 2025 StepUp trial of treating the male partner as well as the woman (PMID 40043236; recurrence 35% vs 63% at 12 weeks in 150 couples completing follow-up) — a third, different strategy that postdates this shelf's question and is strong enough to deserve its own shelf rather than a card here. Expedited partner therapy for sexually transmitted infections is drafted as Shelf #536, a different question; nothing from it is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not present either relative risk (0.66; 0.43 during suppression) without its absolute rates and its time horizon — the benefit is rented, not bought.

shelves.title: Trichomoniasis in women: single-dose secnidazole, and how much metronidazole is enough
shelves.question: Does single-dose oral secnidazole cure trichomoniasis in women versus placebo — and does the older standard, metronidazole, work better as a seven-day course than as the traditional single 2 g dose (the Kissinger trial)?
shelves.mesh: Metronidazole/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Trichomonas Infections/drug therapy · Vaginosis, Bacterial · Antiprotozoal Agents/administration & dosage · Metronidazole/administration & dosage · Trichomonas Vaginitis/drug therapy · Trichomonas vaginalis/isolation & purification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Single-dose oral secnidazole cured trichomoniasis microbiologically in 92.2% of women versus 1.5% on placebo in its phase 3 trial (131 women in the modified intention-to-treat population) — a large effect from a single small trial against placebo, with no comparison against metronidazole. The older standard itself was then beaten by its longer course: in the Kissinger trial (623 HIV-uninfected, non-pregnant women), seven days of metronidazole left fewer women test-positive at four weeks than a single 2 g dose (11% vs 19%; relative risk 0.55). One trial per half, so POSSIBLE — and the practical headline is that the single-dose habit is the weaker half of this shelf.

cards.headline: Secnidazole (Muzny 2021): a single 2 g oral dose cured 92.2% of women versus 1.5% on placebo at test of cure
cards.summary: Secnidazole trial (2021): a single 2 g oral dose cured 92.2% of women versus 1.5% on placebo at test of cure.
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled delayed-treatment trial
cards.people: 147 women with trichomoniasis confirmed by positive Trichomonas vaginalis culture, enrolled at ten US sites (2019–2020) and randomised to single-dose oral secnidazole 2 g or placebo, with the opposite treatment given after the test-of-cure visit at 6–12 days; the modified intention-to-treat population was 131 women (secnidazole n=64; placebo n=67). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Microbiological cure rates were significantly higher with secnidazole than placebo in the modified intention-to-treat population (92.2% [95% CI 82.7 to 97.4] vs 1.5% [0.0 to 8.0]) and in the per-protocol population (94.9% [85.9 to 98.9] vs 1.7% [0.0 to 8.9]). Cure rates were 100% (4 of 4) in women with HIV and 95.2% (20 of 21) in women with bacterial vaginosis. Secnidazole was generally well tolerated; the most frequent treatment-emergent adverse events were vulvovaginal candidiasis and nausea (each 2.7%), and no serious treatment-emergent adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: Small (131 in the analysis population) and placebo-controlled by a delayed-treatment design: it proves secnidazole works, not that it works as well as — or better than — seven-day metronidazole, which is the comparison practice actually needs. Test of cure was at 6–12 days, so later reinfection or relapse is outside the frame.
cards.source: Muzny CA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Single Oral Dosing of Secnidazole for Trichomoniasis in Women: Results of a Phase 3, Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Delayed-Treatment Study. Clin Infect Dis. 2021;73(6):e1282-e1289. PMID: 33768237. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03935217, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Kissinger 2018: seven-day metronidazole beat the single 2 g dose — 11% vs 19% still test-positive at four weeks (RR 0.55)
cards.summary: Metronidazole dosing trial (2018): seven-day metronidazole beat the single 2 g dose — 11% vs 19% still test-positive at four weeks (RR 0.55).
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (single-dose vs seven-day metronidazole)
cards.people: 623 HIV-uninfected, non-pregnant women positive for Trichomonas vaginalis at three US sexual health clinics, randomised to a single 2 g dose of metronidazole (n=311) or 500 mg twice daily for seven days (n=312); the trial stopped early for funding limitations against a planned enrolment of 1,664. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Women in the seven-day group were less likely to be T. vaginalis positive at test of cure four weeks after completing treatment than women in the single-dose group (34 of 312 [11%] vs 58 of 311 [19%]; relative risk 0.55, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70; P<0.0001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Bacterial vaginosis status did not significantly modify the effect (P=0.17 for interaction). Self-reported adherence was 96% in the seven-day group and 99% in the single-dose group. Side-effects were similar by group; the most common was nausea (124 women [23%] overall), then headache (7%) and vomiting (4%). The authors conclude the seven-day dose should be the preferred treatment for trichomoniasis among women.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and stopped early at 623 of a planned 1,664 women; test positivity at four weeks mixes treatment failure with reinfection from untreated partners, which the trial design cannot separate. HIV-infected and pregnant women were excluded — different populations from the earlier HIV-cohort trials of the same comparison.
cards.source: Kissinger P et al. Single-dose versus 7-day-dose metronidazole for the treatment of trichomoniasis in women: an open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2018;18(11):1251-1259. PMID: 30297322. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01018095, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: Secnidazole works against placebo; for metronidazole, seven days beats one dose — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: secnidazole phase 3 (147 enrolled; 131 analysed) and Kissinger 2018 (623 women).
cards.result: The shelf's two halves answer different questions and must not be merged: secnidazole's 92.2% vs 1.5% cure is efficacy against no treatment, while Kissinger's 11% vs 19% test-positivity is the only head-to-head dosing evidence and it favours the longer course of the older drug. Whether single-dose secnidazole matches seven-day metronidazole is untested in these records. Each half rests on a single trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE. Nothing on this shelf is carded elsewhere in the library; the Kissinger citation that appears in the drafted partner-therapy shelf #536 is a guidelines reference, not this trial.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial treated partners as part of the intervention; reinfection pressure in real practice will erode both cure rates.

shelves.title: Elinzanetant for menopausal vasomotor symptoms (OASIS 1, 2 and 3)
shelves.question: Does the dual neurokinin-1/3 antagonist elinzanetant reduce the frequency and severity of menopausal hot flushes versus placebo — in the twin OASIS 1/2 trials and the longer OASIS 3?
shelves.mesh: Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Menopause/drug effects · Pyrrolidines/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Vasomotor System/drug effects,physiopathology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three double-blind phase 3 trials of the same drug and dose agree. In the twin OASIS 1 and 2 trials (about 800 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms), elinzanetant 120 mg daily reduced daily hot-flush frequency by about 3.2–3.3 more flushes than placebo at weeks 4 and 12, and reduced severity by 0.2–0.4 points, with better sleep and quality-of-life scores. OASIS 3 (628 women, 52 weeks) confirmed the week-12 frequency effect (difference −1.6 flushes per day) with no hepatotoxicity, endometrial hyperplasia or meaningful bone-density change, though treatment-related adverse events were commoner on drug (30.4% vs 14.6% — somnolence, fatigue, headache). Two-plus blinded trials with consistent effects support LIKELY.

cards.headline: OASIS 1 and 2 (Pinkerton 2024): elinzanetant cut daily hot-flush frequency by about 3.2–3.3 more than placebo at weeks 4 and 12 in both trials
cards.summary: OASIS 1 and 2 (2024): elinzanetant cut daily hot-flush frequency by about 3.2–3.3 more flushes than placebo at weeks 4 and 12 in both trials.
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one paper (26 weeks; placebo-controlled for 12 weeks)
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind phase 3 trials in postmenopausal participants aged 40 to 65 years with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms: OASIS 1 (199 randomised to elinzanetant, 197 to placebo; 77 sites in the US, Europe and Israel) and OASIS 2 (200 and 200; 77 sites in the US, Canada and Europe). Mean age 54.6 (SD 4.9) years in OASIS 1 and 54.6 (4.8) in OASIS 2; baseline frequency was 13.4–14.7 moderate-to-severe flushes per 24 hours on elinzanetant and 14.3–16.2 on placebo. Treatment was elinzanetant 120 mg once daily for 26 weeks, or placebo for 12 weeks followed by elinzanetant for 14 weeks; 78.0% and 81.0% completed the trials.
cards.result: Elinzanetant significantly reduced vasomotor symptom frequency versus placebo at week 4 (OASIS 1: difference −3.3, 95% CI −4.5 to −2.1; OASIS 2: −3.0, −4.4 to −1.7; both P<.001) and at week 12 (OASIS 1: −3.2, −4.8 to −1.6; OASIS 2: −3.2, −4.6 to −1.9; both P<.001), measured by electronic hot-flush daily diary. Severity also improved at week 4 (OASIS 1: −0.3, −0.4 to −0.2; OASIS 2: −0.2, −0.3 to −0.1) and week 12 (OASIS 1: −0.4, −0.5 to −0.3; OASIS 2: −0.3, −0.4 to −0.1; all P<.001). Elinzanetant improved sleep disturbance and menopause-related quality of life at week 12, and the safety profile was described as favourable.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled phase is only 12 weeks (after which the placebo groups switched to drug), outcomes are diary-recorded symptoms, and the trial population sought treatment for moderate-to-severe symptoms — effects in milder symptoms are untested here.
cards.source: Pinkerton JV et al. Elinzanetant for the Treatment of Vasomotor Symptoms Associated With Menopause: OASIS 1 and 2 Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2024;332(16):1343-1354. PMID: 39172446. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05042362 (OASIS 1) and NCT05099159 (OASIS 2), from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: OASIS 3 (Panay 2025): over 52 weeks, elinzanetant kept its week-12 frequency advantage (−1.6 flushes/day) with no liver, endometrial or bone signal, but more treatment-related adverse events (30.4% vs 14.6%)
cards.summary: OASIS 3 (2025): over 52 weeks, elinzanetant kept its week-12 frequency advantage ( −1.6 flushes/day ) with no liver, endometrial or bone signal.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised phase 3 trial (52 weeks)
cards.people: 628 postmenopausal women aged 40 to 65 years seeking treatment for moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms (no minimum weekly flush count required), randomised at 83 sites in North America and Europe to once-daily elinzanetant 120 mg (n=313; mean age 54.6 [SD 4.7] years) or matching placebo (n=315; mean age 54.9 [5.0] years) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: At week 12 the mean change from baseline in daily moderate-to-severe flush frequency was −5.4 (95% CI −6.3 to −4.5) with elinzanetant and −3.5 (−4.1 to −2.9) with placebo (least-squares mean difference −1.6, −2.0 to −1.1; P<.001). Descriptive analyses showed numerical advantages for elinzanetant in flush frequency and severity over 50 weeks and in sleep disturbance and menopause-related quality of life over 52 weeks, though no statistical hypotheses were defined for those endpoints. On safety, elinzanetant was not associated with hepatotoxic effects, endometrial hyperplasia, or meaningful changes in bone density or bone turnover markers. Treatment-related adverse events were more common with elinzanetant than placebo (30.4% vs 14.6%), most frequently somnolence, fatigue and headache.
cards.watchOut: Beyond week 12 the comparisons are descriptive — the trial was not powered for, and did not test, between-group differences on secondary and exploratory endpoints — and the enrolled population was broader (no minimum flush frequency) than in OASIS 1 and 2, which is part of why the week-12 difference is smaller here.
cards.source: Panay N et al. Elinzanetant for the Treatment of Vasomotor Symptoms Associated With Menopause: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2025;185(11):1319-1327. PMID: 40920404. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05030584, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Maternal RSV vaccination to protect infants (MATISSE)
shelves.question: Does bivalent RSV prefusion F vaccination in pregnancy prevent medically attended RSV lower-respiratory illness in infants through their first months — and what is the preterm-birth balance?
shelves.mesh: Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Antibodies, Viral · Communicable Diseases/therapy · Injections, Intramuscular · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections/epidemiology,prevention & control · Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccines/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal trial, MATISSE (7,358 pregnant women), met its success criterion for severe disease: vaccine efficacy against medically attended severe RSV lower-respiratory illness was 81.8% within 90 days of birth (6 vs 33 cases) and 69.4% within 180 days, while efficacy against all medically attended RSV illness at 90 days (57.1%) did not meet the statistical success criterion. The phase 2b trial showed efficient transplacental antibody transfer (ratios 1.41–2.10) without evident safety concerns. The caution on this shelf is preterm birth: MATISSE's own dedicated analysis found 5.7% vs 4.7% (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.46), concentrated in non-high-income settings, and the rival GSK maternal vaccine's phase 3 trial was stopped for a significant preterm excess (6.8% vs 4.9%; RR 1.37) and its development terminated — the signal that shaped the licensed gestational window for the Pfizer vaccine. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Older-adult RSV vaccination (Shelf #320) and infant monoclonal prophylaxis (Shelf #255) are different questions and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MATISSE 2023: maternal RSVpreF vaccination was 81.8% efficacious against severe medically attended RSV illness in infants within 90 days of birth (6 vs 33 cases)
cards.summary: MATISSE 2023: maternal RSVpreF was 81.8% efficacious against severe medically attended infant RSV illness within 90 days of birth.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (prespecified interim analysis)
cards.people: Pregnant women at 24–36 weeks' gestation in 18 countries, assigned 1:1 to a single intramuscular injection of 120 μg bivalent RSV prefusion F vaccine (3,682 received vaccine) or placebo (3,676); 3,570 and 3,558 infants, respectively, were evaluated. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Medically attended severe RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness occurred within 90 days of birth in 6 infants in the vaccine group and 33 in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy 81.8%; 99.5% CI 40.6 to 96.3), and within 180 days in 19 vs 62 cases (efficacy 69.4%; 97.58% CI 44.3 to 84.1) — relative measures from small case counts. Medically attended RSV-associated lower respiratory tract illness of any severity occurred within 90 days in 24 vs 56 infants (efficacy 57.1%; 99.5% CI 14.7 to 79.8), which did not meet the prespecified statistical success criterion. No safety signals were detected in maternal participants or in infants and toddlers up to 24 months in this report; adverse events within 1 month of injection or birth were similar (13.8% of women and 37.1% of infants on vaccine vs 13.1% and 34.5% on placebo).
cards.watchOut: An interim analysis with few severe cases (6 vs 33 drives the headline), and this primary report is not where the preterm-birth question is answered — that analysis is fenced in the synthesis (PMID 39746206) and the stopped GSK programme is carded below; do not read 'no safety signals' here as the last word on preterm birth.

cards.type: Phase 2b randomised, placebo-controlled trial (planned interim analysis)
cards.people: Pregnant women at 24–36 weeks' gestation assigned to 120 or 240 μg RSVpreF vaccine (with or without aluminium hydroxide) or placebo; this interim analysis included 406 women and 403 infants, 327 women (80.5%) receiving vaccine.

cards.headline: GSK RSVPreF3-Mat phase 3 2024: efficacious against infant RSV disease (65.5%) but stopped early for a preterm-birth excess — 6.8% vs 4.9% (relative risk 1.37) — and development was terminated
cards.summary: GSK RSVPreF3-Mat phase 3 2024: efficacious (65.5%) but stopped early for a preterm-birth excess ( 6.8% vs 4.9% , a relative measure).
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trial, enrolment stopped early for a safety signal
cards.people: 5,328 pregnant women aged 18–49 years (target ~10,000, not reached because enrolment was stopped), assigned 2:1 to RSVPreF3-Mat or placebo at 24 weeks 0 days to 34 weeks 0 days of gestation; 5,233 infants, with 3,426 (vaccine) and 1,711 (placebo) followed from birth to 6 months for efficacy.
cards.result: Any medically assessed RSV-associated lower respiratory tract disease occurred in 16 infants in the vaccine group and 24 in the placebo group (vaccine efficacy 65.5%; 95% credible interval 37.5 to 82.0), and severe disease in 8 vs 14 (efficacy 69.0%; 33.0 to 87.6) — relative measures. Preterm birth occurred in 6.8% of infants (237 of 3,494) in the vaccine group and 4.9% (86 of 1,739) in the placebo group (relative risk 1.37, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.74; P=0.01); neonatal death occurred in 0.4% vs 0.2% (RR 2.16, 0.62 to 7.56; P=0.23), an imbalance the authors attribute probably to the greater preterm percentage. No other safety signal was observed. The vaccine's development was terminated because of the preterm-birth risk.
cards.watchOut: A different manufacturer's vaccine (GSK's RSVPreF3-Mat), carded here as the class caution, not as evidence about the Pfizer product's own balance: whether the preterm signal is a class effect of prefusion-F maternal vaccination or product-specific is unresolved, and it is the reason gestational-age windows matter for the licensed Pfizer vaccine.

cards.summary: Strong protection against severe infant RSV in one pivotal trial, with a preterm-birth caution across the class — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MATISSE (7,358 women), its phase 2b predecessor (406 women) and the GSK phase 3 trial (5,328 women); MATISSE's dedicated preterm-birth analysis (PMID 39746206) is fenced here, not carded.
cards.result: Efficacy against severe infant disease is consistent across both manufacturers' trials (81.8% at 90 days in MATISSE; 69.0% against severe disease for GSK's vaccine). cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two products' safety records: the licensed Pfizer vaccine's window (vaccination later in pregnancy) exists because of the signal the GSK card documents, and MATISSE's own subgroup imbalance in non-high-income settings remains unexplained.

shelves.title: Omega-3 fatty acids in pregnancy and preterm birth (ORIP)
shelves.question: Does prenatal omega-3 long-chain fatty-acid supplementation reduce early preterm birth in an unselected obstetric population (ORIP, n≈5,500) — against the pooled signal from the earlier, smaller trials in the Cochrane review?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Supplements · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Fetal Macrosomia · Gestational Age · Incidence · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in an unselected population; POSSIBLE for the pooled earlier-trial signal. ORIP (5,486 pregnancies in the primary analysis) found early preterm delivery (before 34 weeks) in 2.2% on n-3 supplements versus 2.0% on control (adjusted relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.63; P=0.50) — no reduction, in the largest single trial. The Cochrane review (70 trials, 19,927 women) pooled a lower risk of preterm birth before 37 weeks (risk ratio 0.89, 0.81 to 0.97 — relative; high-quality evidence) and of early preterm birth before 34 weeks (RR 0.58, 0.44 to 0.77; 9 trials, 5,204 participants; high-quality evidence), alongside more prolonged gestation beyond 42 weeks (RR 1.61, 1.11 to 2.33) — a pooling dominated by smaller, often higher-risk-population trials that ORIP does not reproduce in an unselected population. Neither half is strong enough to erase the other: both are stamped POSSIBLE. (In the Cochrane abstract the comparison percentages are printed control-first; they are presented that way, and flagged, on the card.)

cards.headline: ORIP 2019: prenatal omega-3 did not reduce early preterm birth in 5,486 pregnancies — 2.2% vs 2.0% (adjusted RR 1.13)
cards.summary: ORIP 2019: prenatal omega-3 did not reduce early preterm birth in 5,486 pregnancies ( 2.2% vs 2.0% ; adjusted relative risk 1.13).
cards.people: 5,517 women (5,544 pregnancies, single or multiple fetuses) at six Australian centres, randomised to fish-oil capsules containing 900 mg of n-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids or vegetable-oil control capsules daily, from before 20 weeks of gestation to 34 weeks or delivery; 5,486 pregnancies were included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Early preterm delivery (before 34 completed weeks) occurred in 61 of 2,734 pregnancies (2.2%) in the n-3 group and 55 of 2,752 (2.0%) in the control group — not significant (adjusted relative risk 1.13, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.63; P=0.50). There were no significant differences in interventions in post-term deliveries, adverse events or other pregnancy or neonatal outcomes, except that more infants in the n-3 group were very large for gestational age (adjusted RR 1.30, 1.02 to 1.65 — relative). Percentages of serious adverse events did not differ; minor gastrointestinal disturbances were more common on n-3.
cards.watchOut: ORIP enrolled an unselected population whose early-preterm rate was only 2.0% on control — a low-risk floor that limits power for the early-preterm endpoint specifically (the confidence interval, 0.79 to 1.63, is wide). The null is firm for routine supplementation of unselected women; it is less decisive for high-risk subgroups. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Makrides M et al. A Randomized Trial of Prenatal n-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation and Preterm Delivery. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(11):1035-1045. PMID: 31509674. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12613001142729, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Middleton) 2018: pooled across 70 trials, omega-3 lowered preterm birth (RR 0.89) and early preterm birth (RR 0.58) — relative measures
cards.summary: Cochrane (Middleton) 2018: pooled across 70 trials, omega-3 lowered preterm birth (relative risk 0.89) and early preterm birth (0.58) — relative measures, printed as such.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (update of a 2006 review)
cards.people: 70 randomised trials involving 19,927 women at low, mixed or high risk of poor pregnancy outcomes, comparing omega-3 LCPUFA (supplements or food) with placebo or no omega-3; nearly half the trials included women at increased or high risk. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Preterm birth before 37 weeks was lower with omega-3 (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.97 — relative; 26 trials, 10,304 participants; high-quality evidence; the abstract prints the event percentages control-first: 13.4% versus 11.9%), as was early preterm birth before 34 weeks (RR 0.58, 0.44 to 0.77; 9 trials, 5,204 participants; high-quality evidence; percentages printed control-first: 4.6% versus 2.7%). Prolonged gestation beyond 42 weeks was probably increased (RR 1.61, 1.11 to 2.33 — relative; 5,141 participants; moderate-quality evidence; percentages printed control-first: 1.6% to 2.6% on omega-3). Low birthweight was reduced (RR 0.90, 0.82 to 0.99; high-quality evidence), perinatal death possibly reduced (RR 0.75, 0.54 to 1.03; moderate-quality evidence), and large-for-gestational-age possibly increased (RR 1.15, 0.97 to 1.36).
cards.watchOut: A pooling of many small trials, nearly half in higher-risk women, with high attrition bias in some trials — and its early-preterm estimate (RR 0.58) comes from 5,204 participants, fewer than ORIP alone randomised to the same endpoint with a null result. The abstract's percentage ordering is control-first, as flagged on this card; the risk ratios are the reliable figures. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
