shelves.title: Finding and treating postpartum haemorrhage as one bundle: E-MOTIVE
shelves.question: Does calibrated blood-loss measurement with a drape, coupled to a bundled first response, reduce severe postpartum haemorrhage, laparotomy for bleeding, or maternal death versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Pregnancy · Early Diagnosis · Oxytocics/therapeutic use · Postpartum Hemorrhage/diagnosis,therapy · Risk · Tranexamic Acid/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because maternal death from bleeding is a component of the primary composite): In one very large international cluster-randomised trial (80 hospitals, 210,132 vaginal births), early detection with a calibrated drape plus a bundled first response (massage, oxytocic, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, examination, escalation) cut the composite of severe postpartum haemorrhage, laparotomy for bleeding, or maternal death from bleeding from 4.3% to 1.6% (risk ratio 0.40, a relative figure). Detection rose from 51.1% to 93.1% and bundle use from 19.4% to 91.2%. A single trial, however large, caps a benefit claim at POSSIBLE under the library's rules.

cards.headline: E-MOTIVE (Gallos 2023): drape-plus-bundle cut the severe-haemorrhage composite from 4.3% to 1.6% (relative risk ratio 0.40)
cards.summary: E-MOTIVE (2023): drape-plus-bundle cut the severe-haemorrhage composite from 4.3% to 1.6% (risk ratio 0.40 relative).
cards.people: 210,132 patients having vaginal delivery at 80 secondary-level hospitals in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and Tanzania, randomised by hospital to the intervention or usual care. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event (severe postpartum haemorrhage [blood loss ≥1000 ml], laparotomy for bleeding, or maternal death from bleeding) occurred in 1.6% of the intervention group versus 4.3% with usual care (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.50; P<0.001 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here). Postpartum haemorrhage was detected in 93.1% versus 51.1% (rate ratio 1.58, relative), and the treatment bundle was used in 91.2% versus 19.4% (rate ratio 4.94, relative).
cards.watchOut: One trial, unblindable by nature (a care-process bundle), and the composite is dominated by severe haemorrhage rather than deaths — the maternal-death component is why this shelf is Tier C and its stamp is proposed only. The 0.40 ratio sits outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, but a single trial still caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Synthesis: measure the blood, then act as one bundle — POSSIBLE, Tier C proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: measure the blood, then act as one bundle — detection nearly doubled (51.1% to 93.1%) — POSSIBLE (Tier C: maternal death sits inside the primary composite).
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: E-MOTIVE (210,132 vaginal births, 80 hospitals, four African countries).

shelves.title: One dose of azithromycin in labour to protect the mother (A-PLUS)
shelves.question: In women planning a vaginal birth, does a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin during labour reduce maternal sepsis or death — and did it move any newborn outcome?
shelves.mesh: Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Azithromycin/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Perinatal Death/etiology,prevention & control · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Sepsis/epidemiology,mortality,prevention & control · Stillbirth/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because the primary outcome is maternal sepsis or death itself): In one very large placebo-controlled trial (29,278 women, eight low- and middle-income countries), a single 2 g oral dose of azithromycin in labour reduced maternal sepsis or death from 2.4% to 1.6% (relative risk 0.67), driven by sepsis (1.5% vs 2.3%); death itself did not differ (0.1% in both groups). The newborn composite — stillbirth or neonatal death or sepsis — did not move (10.5% vs 10.3%). A single trial caps the benefit stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: A-PLUS (Tita 2023): one 2 g dose cut maternal sepsis or death from 2.4% to 1.6% (relative risk 0.67); newborn outcomes unchanged
cards.summary: A-PLUS (2023): one 2 g dose of azithromycin in labour cut maternal sepsis or death from 2.4% to 1.6% (RR 0.67 relative); newborn outcomes unchanged.
cards.type: Multicountry, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial (stopped early at interim analysis for maternal benefit)
cards.people: 29,278 women in labour at 28 weeks' gestation or more, planning a vaginal delivery, across eight low- and middle-income countries, randomised to a single 2-g oral dose of azithromycin or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Maternal sepsis or death: 1.6% with azithromycin versus 2.4% with placebo (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.79; P<0.001 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). The difference was driven by sepsis (1.5% vs 2.3%; relative risk 0.65); death from any cause was 0.1% in both groups (relative risk 1.23, 95% CI 0.51 to 2.97). Stillbirth or neonatal death or sepsis: 10.5% vs 10.3% (relative risk 1.02, 0.95 to 1.09); neonatal sepsis 9.8% vs 9.6%; stillbirth 0.4% in both groups; neonatal death 1.5% in both groups. Azithromycin was not associated with a higher incidence of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for benefit, which can inflate effect estimates; the relative risk of 0.67 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on its own, and the mortality component on its own was null — the claim is a sepsis claim, not a survival claim. cards.headline: WHO ACTION-I (2020): dexamethasone at 26–33 weeks cut neonatal death from 23.5% to 19.6% (relative risk 0.84) in low-resource settings
cards.summary: WHO ACTION-I (2020): dexamethasone at 26–33 weeks cut neonatal death from 23.5% to 19.6% (RR 0.84 relative) in low-resource settings.
cards.type: Multicountry, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (stopped for benefit at the second interim analysis)
cards.people: 2,852 women (and their 3,070 fetuses) at risk for preterm birth at 26 weeks 0 days to 33 weeks 6 days, at 29 secondary- and tertiary-level hospitals in Bangladesh, India, Kenya, Nigeria and Pakistan, assigned to intramuscular dexamethasone or identical placebo. cards.result: Neonatal death: 278 of 1,417 infants (19.6%) with dexamethasone versus 331 of 1,406 (23.5%) with placebo (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.97; P=0.03 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). shelves.title: Ursodeoxycholic acid for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (PITCHES)
shelves.question: Does ursodeoxycholic acid improve perinatal outcomes — stillbirth, preterm birth, neonatal-unit admission — in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, or does it leave the baby outcomes it was prescribed for unchanged?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Alanine Transaminase/blood · Bile Acids and Salts/blood · Biomarkers/blood · Cholagogues and Choleretics/administration & dosage · Cholestasis, Intrahepatic/blood,drug therapy · Gestational Age
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ruled at build: the primary perinatal composite includes perinatal death, so the shelf returns for personal verdict even though its result is null and no benefit is claimed): In the single pivotal trial (605 women, 33 UK units), ursodeoxycholic acid did not reduce the composite of perinatal death, preterm delivery or neonatal-unit admission — 23% versus 27% (adjusted risk ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.15, a relative figure whose interval includes no effect). A single-trial null is stamped POSSIBLE under the library's precedent.

cards.headline: PITCHES (Chappell 2019): the perinatal composite was 23% versus 27% (relative adjusted risk ratio 0.85, CI includes 1) — no demonstrated benefit
cards.summary: PITCHES (2019): the perinatal composite was 23% vs 27% (adjusted risk ratio 0.85 relative, CI includes 1) — no demonstrated benefit of ursodeoxycholic acid.
cards.people: 605 women with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, aged 18 years or older, at 20 weeks to 40 weeks 6 days' gestation with a singleton or twin pregnancy and no known lethal fetal anomaly, at 33 hospital maternity units in England and Wales, randomised to ursodeoxycholic acid 500 mg twice daily (305) or placebo (300). cards.result: The primary composite outcome (perinatal death, preterm delivery <37 weeks, or neonatal unit admission for at least 4 hours) occurred in 74 of 322 infants (23%) in the ursodeoxycholic acid group and 85 of 318 infants (27%) in the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.15 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Two serious adverse events were reported in the ursodeoxycholic acid group and six in the placebo group; none was regarded as related to treatment. The authors conclude treatment does not reduce adverse perinatal outcomes and its routine use should be reconsidered.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for the composite, not for stillbirth alone — the rarest and most feared component — so the null is a composite null, not proof of no effect on stillbirth specifically; that component structure is also why the developer rules on this shelf personally (Tier C). shelves.title: D-mannose to prevent recurrent urinary tract infection in women
shelves.question: Does daily D-mannose reduce medically attended urinary tract infections in women with recurrent UTI versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Mannose/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Urinary Tract Infections/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In one large double-blind primary-care trial (598 women across 99 UK centres), 2 g of daily D-mannose for 6 months did not reduce medically attended urinary tract infection — 51.0% versus 55.7% (risk difference −5%, 95% CI −13% to 3%; P=.26) — and no secondary outcome differed. The authors state D-mannose should not be recommended for prophylaxis in this group. A single-trial null is stamped POSSIBLE under the library's precedent. Wording note: this shelf concerns reducing recurrent infections; it makes no diabetes-onset claim.

cards.headline: Hayward 2024: D-mannose did not reduce medically attended UTI (51.0% vs 55.7%; P=.26)
cards.summary: Hayward (2024): D-mannose did not reduce medically attended UTI ( 51.0% vs 55.7% ; P=.26).
cards.people: 598 women aged 18 years or older, living in the community, with at least 2 UTIs in the preceding 6 months or 3 in 12 months in their primary-care record, across 99 UK primary-care centres; mean (range) age 58 (18–93) years; 303 randomised to D-mannose and 295 to placebo, with primary outcome data for 583 (97.5%).
cards.result: The proportion contacting ambulatory care with a clinically suspected UTI within 6 months was 150 of 294 (51.0%) with D-mannose versus 161 of 289 (55.7%) with placebo (risk difference −5%, 95% CI −13% to 3%; P=.26). Estimates were similar in per-protocol, imputation and preplanned subgroup analyses, and there were no statistically significant differences in any secondary outcome, including symptom duration, antibiotic use, time to next medically attended UTI, and UTI-related hospital admissions.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, and its outcome is clinically suspected (medically attended) UTI rather than culture-confirmed infection — the pragmatic outcome patients act on, but a softer biological endpoint. Earlier promise came from secondary-care trials; this community test is the one that matches how the supplement is actually used.

shelves.title: Linzagolix for uterine fibroids: the PRIMROSE pair
shelves.question: Does the oral GnRH antagonist linzagolix, with or without hormonal add-back therapy, reduce heavy menstrual bleeding from uterine fibroids versus placebo — and how does the add-back choice trade bleeding control against bone density?
shelves.mesh: Carboxylic Acids · Estradiol · Leiomyoma/drug therapy · Menorrhagia/complications,etiology · Norethindrone Acetate · Pyrimidines · Receptors, LHRH/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two parallel placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (PRIMROSE 1, 511 women in the full analysis set; PRIMROSE 2, 501) each found significantly higher response rates (menstrual blood loss ≤80 ml and ≥50% reduction at 24 weeks) in every linzagolix arm than with placebo — 56.4% to 75.5% versus 35.0% in PRIMROSE 1 and 56.7% to 93.9% versus 29.4% in PRIMROSE 2. The programme's extension study found the response maintained to 52 weeks, with bone density well preserved in add-back groups and symptoms recurring in most women within weeks of stopping. Two blinded trials of the same question carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: PRIMROSE 1 & 2 (Donnez 2022): every linzagolix arm beat placebo on bleeding response at 24 weeks (up to 75.5% and 93.9% vs 35.0% and 29.4%)
cards.summary: PRIMROSE 1 & 2 (2022): every linzagolix arm beat placebo on bleeding response at 24 weeks (up to 75.5% and 93.9% vs 35.0% and 29.4%).
cards.type: Two randomised, parallel, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials reported together
cards.people: Women with uterine fibroid-associated heavy menstrual bleeding (>80 ml per cycle), randomised 1:1:1:1:1 to placebo, linzagolix 100 mg alone, 100 mg plus add-back therapy (1 mg oestradiol / 0.5 mg norethisterone acetate), 200 mg alone, or 200 mg plus add-back, for 52 weeks: PRIMROSE 1 (USA; 574 enrolled, 511 in the full analysis set) and PRIMROSE 2 (Europe and USA; 535 enrolled, 501 in the full analysis set). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Response (menstrual blood loss ≤80 ml and ≥50% reduction from baseline) at 24 weeks — PRIMROSE 1: 56.4% (100 mg), 66.4% (100 mg + add-back), 71.4% (200 mg), 75.5% (200 mg + add-back) versus 35.0% placebo. PRIMROSE 2: 56.7%, 77.2%, 77.7% and 93.9% respectively versus 29.4% placebo; all comparisons p≤0.003. The most common adverse events to 24 weeks were hot flushes — 35% (PRIMROSE 1) and 32% (PRIMROSE 2) with 200 mg linzagolix alone, versus 3–14% in all other groups.
cards.watchOut: Industry programme trials with a bleeding-volume primary endpoint, not pain, fibroid shrinkage to surgery avoidance, or quality-of-life primaries; the 200 mg-alone arm's hot-flush rate is the price of full suppression without add-back. Relugolix combination therapy lives on Shelf #247 — a different molecule — and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: PRIMROSE extension & withdrawal (2025): response held to 52 weeks; 88.8% of amenorrhoeic women bled again within 12 weeks of stopping
cards.summary: PRIMROSE extension & withdrawal (2025): response held to 52 weeks; 88.8% of amenorrhoeic women bled again within 12 weeks of stopping.
cards.type: Long-term extension and withdrawal study of two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trials
cards.people: The 1,012 women of the PRIMROSE 1 and 2 full analysis sets (women aged 18 years or older with ultrasound-confirmed fibroids and heavy menstrual bleeding ≥80 ml per cycle), followed through 52 weeks of treatment, a withdrawal phase to week 64, and bone-density assessment at week 76. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Pooled week-52 response rates: 55.0% (100 mg), 86.1% (100 mg + add-back), 76.7% (200 mg switched to 200 mg + add-back), and 89.9% (200 mg + add-back). Of women amenorrhoeic on linzagolix at week 52, 88.8% reported their first bleed or heavy bleeding between weeks 52 and 64. Hot flushes were the most common adverse event to week 52 and had returned to baseline incidence by week 64. Bone mineral density was well preserved in all groups at week 52; the lumbar-spine loss seen with 200 mg alone to week 24 recovered by week 52 after add-back was added.
cards.watchOut: An extension of the same two trials, not a third trial — counted once as programme evidence. After week 24 the placebo and 200 mg-alone groups were switched to 200 mg plus add-back, so week-52 contrasts are within-programme descriptions, not placebo comparisons.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bleeding control is real, dose- and add-back-dependent, and rented rather than bought — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: bleeding control is real, dose- and add-back-dependent, and rented rather than bought — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PRIMROSE 1 and 2 (1,012 women in the full analysis sets) and their extension/withdrawal study.
cards.result: Two blinded trials agree: linzagolix reduces heavy menstrual bleeding at both doses, with or without add-back, and the effect persists to 52 weeks on treatment. The trade-offs are equally consistent: full suppression without add-back brings hot flushes in about a third of women, add-back protects bone, and stopping brings bleeding back in most women within 12 weeks — this is continuing therapy, not a cure.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the week-52 extension percentages as placebo-controlled effects; the controlled comparison ends at week 24.

shelves.title: Chlorhexidine cord care where newborns die at home: Nepal, Pakistan, Pemba
shelves.question: Does cleansing the umbilical cord stump with chlorhexidine reduce omphalitis and neonatal death in community births — and why did the Pemba trial find no mortality effect?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Chlorhexidine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Hernia, Umbilical/classification,epidemiology,prevention & control · Incidence · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because the headline outcome is neonatal mortality itself): LIKELY for benefit in high-mortality, home-birth settings — Nepal (neonatal mortality relative risk 0.76 overall, 0.66 in infants enrolled within 24 hours) and Pakistan (relative risk 0.62) both found mortality reductions alongside large falls in omphalitis; POSSIBLE for the null in the Pemba setting — 36,911 newborns, most born in facilities, mortality 10.5 versus 11.7 per 1000 (relative risk 0.90, CI includes 1). The setting difference is the shelf's central fact, and both mortality ratios from the positive trials sit inside or at the edge of the 0.5–2.0 caution band, which is part of why this returns to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Nepal (Mullany 2006): chlorhexidine cut severe omphalitis by 75% relative; neonatal mortality 24% lower relative (0.76), 34% lower in infants enrolled within 24 h
cards.summary: Nepal (2006): chlorhexidine cut severe omphalitis by 75% relative ; neonatal mortality 24% lower relative (0.76).
cards.people: 15,123 infants in 413 communities in Sarlahi, Nepal, assigned by community to 4.0% chlorhexidine cord cleansing (4,934 infants), cleansing with soap and water (5,107), or dry cord care (5,082), with cord cleansing at home on days 1–4, 6, 8 and 10 and vital status recorded to 28 days. The abstract does not state mean age (newborns).
cards.result: Severe omphalitis was reduced by 75% (relative incidence rate ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.53; 13 infections/4,839 neonatal periods) in chlorhexidine clusters compared with dry cord care (52/4,930), and omphalitis by all three sign-based definitions was significantly reduced. Neonatal mortality was 24% lower in relative terms in the chlorhexidine group (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.04) than with dry cord care; in infants enrolled within the first 24 hours, mortality was significantly reduced by 34% in relative terms (0.66, 0.46 to 0.95). Soap and water reduced neither infection nor mortality. Absolute mortality rates are not stated in the abstract and are not printed here.
cards.watchOut: The overall mortality interval (0.55 to 1.04) crosses 1 — the significant figure is the within-24-hours subgroup — and both ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band; the shelf's LIKELY rests on two concordant trials plus the omphalitis effect, not on this trial alone. Tier C proposed.

cards.headline: Pakistan (Soofi 2012): chlorhexidine in birth kits cut neonatal mortality by 38% in relative terms (risk ratio 0.62) and omphalitis by 42% (0.58)
cards.summary: Pakistan (2012): chlorhexidine in birth kits cut neonatal mortality by 38% relative (risk ratio 0.62) and omphalitis by 42% relative.
cards.people: 9,741 liveborn infants delivered by participating traditional birth attendants in 187 clusters in Dadu, rural Sindh, Pakistan, allocated to birth kits with 4% chlorhexidine cord application (with or without handwashing promotion) or standard dry cord care promotion. The abstract does not state mean age (newborns).
cards.result: Factorial analysis: chlorhexidine application reduced omphalitis (risk ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.82; p=0.002) and neonatal mortality (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.85; p=0.003) — both relative figures; the abstract does not state the absolute mortality rates and they are not printed here. Handwashing promotion showed no evidence of an effect on omphalitis (risk ratio 0.83, 0.61 to 1.13; p=0.24) or on neonatal mortality (risk ratio 1.08, 0.79 to 1.48; p=0.62). We recorded no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Factorial design: the chlorhexidine estimate pools across the handwashing factor, which itself was null. The 0.62 mortality ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own terms; it convinces in combination with Nepal's concordant result and the omphalitis effect, not alone. Tier C proposed.

cards.headline: Pemba (Sazawal 2016): in a largely facility-birth setting, mortality was 10.5 versus 11.7 per 1000 (relative risk 0.90, CI includes 1) — no mortality effect found
cards.summary: Pemba (2016): in a largely facility-birth setting, mortality was 10.5 vs 11.7 per 1000 (RR 0.90 relative, CI includes 1).
cards.people: 36,911 newborn babies on Pemba Island, Zanzibar, Tanzania (18,015 chlorhexidine; 18,896 dry cord care), enrolled at 1–48 hours from hospital-based and community-based deliveries, with complete 28-day follow-up for 96.9% and 97.3% respectively. cards.result: Mortality to day 28 was 10.5 deaths per 1000 livebirths with chlorhexidine versus 11.7 per 1000 with dry cord care (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.09; p=0.27 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). cards.watchOut: The largest of the three trials and the null one — but its baseline mortality (~11 per 1000) was far below the Asian trials' settings, and most births were in facilities; a null where cord infection drives few deaths does not erase positive trials where it drives many. cards.summary: Synthesis: the same antiseptic, three settings, two answers — split LIKELY / POSSIBLE the null (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Nepal (15,123 infants), Pakistan (9,741 infants) and Pemba (36,911 newborns).
cards.result: Where newborns were born at home in high-mortality settings, chlorhexidine cord care reduced omphalitis sharply and neonatal mortality in relative terms by about a quarter (Nepal) and about two-fifths (Pakistan). shelves.title: Tranexamic acid to prevent blood loss at birth: TRAAP (vaginal) and TRAAP2 (caesarean)
shelves.question: Does tranexamic acid given prophylactically just after birth prevent postpartum haemorrhage — after vaginal delivery in TRAAP, and at caesarean in TRAAP2?
shelves.mesh: Antifibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Injections, Intravenous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Oxytocics/therapeutic use · Oxytocin/therapeutic use · Postpartum Hemorrhage/prevention & control
shelves.balance: Split: MAYBE (weak evidence) for vaginal birth — TRAAP's primary outcome (blood loss ≥500 ml, measured with a collector bag) narrowly missed significance (8.1% vs 9.8%; relative risk 0.83; P=0.07), with softer provider-assessed secondaries pointing the other way; POSSIBLE for caesarean birth — TRAAP2's primary outcome (calculated blood loss >1000 ml or transfusion by day 2) fell from 31.6% to 26.7% (relative adjusted risk ratio 0.84), but every clinical secondary outcome was flat, so the proven effect is on a calculated blood-loss measure, not on clinical haemorrhage outcomes. Both relative ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. Tranexamic acid as treatment of established bleeding — the mortality question — lives on Shelf #138 and is not re-opened here.

cards.headline: TRAAP (Sentilhes 2018): primary outcome narrowly missed — postpartum haemorrhage 8.1% versus 9.8% (relative risk 0.83; P=0.07)
cards.summary: TRAAP (2018): the primary outcome narrowly missed — postpartum haemorrhage 8.1% vs 9.8% (RR 0.83 relative; P=0.07).
cards.people: 4,079 women in labour with a planned vaginal delivery of a singleton live fetus at 35 or more weeks of gestation, randomised to 1 g intravenous tranexamic acid or placebo in addition to prophylactic oxytocin after delivery; 3,891 had a vaginal delivery. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Postpartum haemorrhage (blood loss ≥500 ml, measured with a collector bag) occurred in 156 of 1,921 women (8.1%) in the tranexamic acid group and 188 of 1,918 (9.8%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.01; P=0.07 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Provider-assessed clinically significant postpartum haemorrhage was lower with tranexamic acid (7.8% vs 10.4%; relative risk 0.74, 0.61 to 0.91), as was receipt of additional uterotonic agents (7.2% vs 9.7%; relative risk 0.75); other secondary outcomes did not differ significantly, and thromboembolic events in the 3 months after delivery were 0.1% versus 0.2%.
cards.watchOut: A primary-outcome miss with positive softer secondaries (one adjusted post hoc) is the classic pattern the MAYBE (weak evidence) label exists for; the 0.83 ratio is also inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band.

cards.headline: TRAAP2 (Sentilhes 2021): calculated blood loss >1000 ml or transfusion fell from 31.6% to 26.7% (relative adjusted risk ratio 0.84) — clinical secondaries did not move
cards.summary: TRAAP2 (2021): calculated blood loss >1000 ml or transfusion fell from 31.6% to 26.7% (adjusted risk ratio 0.84 relative) at caesarean birth.
cards.people: 4,551 women undergoing caesarean delivery before or during labour at 34 or more gestational weeks, randomised to a prophylactic uterotonic plus tranexamic acid 1 g or placebo; 4,431 underwent caesarean delivery and 4,153 (93.7%) had primary-outcome data. shelves.title: High-dose folic acid in pregnancy does not stop pre-eclampsia (FACT)
shelves.question: Does 4 mg daily folic acid, started after the first trimester in women at high risk, reduce pre-eclampsia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Argentina/epidemiology · Australia/epidemiology · Canada/epidemiology · Diabetes, Gestational/prevention & control · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Folic Acid/administration & dosage,supply & distribution · HELLP Syndrome/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In one large international double-blind trial (2,464 high-risk women, 70 centres, five countries), 4.0 mg/day folic acid from between 8 and 16 weeks until delivery did not reduce pre-eclampsia — 14.8% versus 13.5% (relative risk 1.10, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.34; P=0.37), a point estimate on the harm side of 1 — and no other maternal or neonatal outcome differed. A single-trial null is stamped POSSIBLE under the library's precedent. This shelf separates the vascular claim from the neural-tube-defect question: standard-dose periconception folic acid lives on Shelf #48 and is not re-litigated here.

cards.headline: FACT (Wen 2018): pre-eclampsia 14.8% versus 13.5% (relative risk 1.10; P=0.37) — high-dose folic acid did not prevent it
cards.summary: FACT (2018): pre-eclampsia 14.8% vs 13.5% (RR 1.10 relative; P=0.37) — high-dose folic acid did not prevent it.
cards.type: Randomised, phase III, double-blind, international, multicentre trial
cards.people: 2,464 pregnant women with at least one risk factor for pre-eclampsia (pre-existing hypertension, prepregnancy type 1 or 2 diabetes, twin pregnancy, previous pre-eclampsia, or body mass index ≥35) at 70 obstetrical centres in Argentina, Australia, Canada, Jamaica and the UK, randomised to four 1.0 mg folic acid tablets daily or placebo from 8 weeks to the end of week 16 of gestation until delivery; 2,301 were included in the intention-to-treat analyses. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Pre-eclampsia occurred in 169 of 1,144 women (14.8%) in the folic acid group and 156 of 1,157 (13.5%) in the placebo group (relative risk 1.10, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.34; P=0.37 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). There was no evidence of differences between the groups for any other adverse maternal or neonatal outcome. The authors conclude that supplementation with 4.0 mg/day folic acid beyond the first trimester does not prevent pre-eclampsia in women at high risk.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in high-risk women only, starting after the first trimester — it answers the high-dose vascular claim, not standard-dose periconception supplementation for neural tube defects (Shelf #48). The interval (0.90 to 1.34) excludes a large benefit but not a small one.
cards.source: Wen SW et al. Effect of high dose folic acid supplementation in pregnancy on pre-eclampsia (FACT): double blind, phase III, randomised controlled, international, multicentre trial. BMJ. 2018;362:k3478. PMID: 30209050. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01355159, ISRCTN: ISRCTN23781770.

shelves.title: Tubal flushing: oil-based vs water-based contrast at hysterosalpingography (H2Oil)
shelves.question: In infertile women undergoing HSG, does oil-based contrast vs water-based contrast increase ongoing pregnancy within 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Hysterosalpingography/methods · Infertility, Female/diagnostic imaging · Contrast Media · Pregnancy Rate · Live Birth · Female · Humans
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large multicentre randomised trial (H2Oil, 1,119 infertile women in 27 Dutch hospitals) found that hysterosalpingography with oil-based contrast produced more ongoing pregnancies within 6 months than the same procedure with water-based contrast — 39.7% versus 29.1% (rate ratio 1.37 relative, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.61; P<0.001) — and more live births (38.8% vs 28.1%; rate ratio 1.38 relative, 1.17 to 1.64; P<0.001), with low and similar adverse-event rates. A single very large trial with a hard outcome (live birth) and a precise estimate carries LIKELY; the mechanism (tubal flushing) is inseparable from the diagnostic procedure itself, which is exactly the comparison women face.

cards.headline: H2Oil 2017: oil-based contrast at HSG gave more ongoing pregnancies (39.7% vs 29.1%) and more live births than water-based contrast
cards.summary: H2Oil 2017: oil-based contrast at HSG gave more ongoing pregnancies (39.7% vs 29.1%) and more live births than water-based contrast
cards.people: 1,119 infertile women undergoing hysterosalpingography at 27 hospitals in the Netherlands, randomised to oil-based contrast (557) or water-based contrast (562), followed by expectant management or intrauterine insemination; the primary outcome (ongoing pregnancy within 6 months) was analysed in 554 women per group. The abstract does not state mean age; MeSH records the population as Adult and Young Adult women.
cards.result: Ongoing pregnancy occurred in 220 of 554 women (39.7%) in the oil group and 161 of 554 (29.1%) in the water group (rate ratio 1.37 relative, 95% confidence interval 1.16 to 1.61; P<0.001). Live births occurred in 214 of 552 (38.8%) versus 155 of 552 (28.1%) (rate ratio 1.38 relative, 1.17 to 1.64; P<0.001). Rates of adverse events were low and similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is between two versions of a procedure every participant was already having — it shows oil contrast is the better medium when HSG is done, not that HSG itself should be done for fertility treatment; couples then received expectant management or insemination, so the estimate includes those downstream paths equally in both arms.
cards.source: Dreyer K et al. Oil-Based or Water-Based Contrast for Hysterosalpingography in Infertile Women. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 28520519. Registry ID: Netherlands Trial Register NTR3270, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: when HSG is performed, oil contrast is the fertility-friendlier medium — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: when HSG is performed, oil contrast is the fertility-friendlier medium — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: H2Oil 2017 (1,119 randomised infertile women).
cards.result: An absolute gain of about 10.6 percentage points in ongoing pregnancy (39.7% vs 29.1%) and 10.7 points in live birth (38.8% vs 28.1%) within 6 months, from a one-off choice of contrast medium at a diagnostic procedure, with no added adverse events detected. shelves.title: ICSI vs conventional IVF when the male partner has normal sperm parameters
shelves.question: In couples with non-male-factor infertility, does ICSI vs conventional IVF improve live birth after the first embryo transfer?
shelves.mesh: Sperm Injections, Intracytoplasmic/methods · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Live Birth · Pregnancy Outcome · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two randomised trials, twenty years apart, agree that ICSI adds nothing when sperm parameters are normal. INVICSI (Dang 2021, 1,064 couples in Vietnam, male partner with normal total sperm count and motility) found live birth after the first embryo transfer in 35% with ICSI versus 31% with conventional IVF (absolute difference 3.4 percentage points, 95% CI -2.4 to 9.2; risk ratio 1.11 relative, 0.93 to 1.32; P=0.27), with no difference in fertilisation failure (5% vs 6%). The earlier UK trial (Bhattacharya 2001, 415 couples with non-male-factor infertility) found implantation actually higher with conventional IVF (30% vs 22%; relative risk 1.35 relative, 1.04 to 1.76) at a fraction of the laboratory time. Routine ICSI for non-male-factor infertility is an expense without a randomised benefit.

cards.headline: INVICSI 2021: ICSI did not improve live birth over conventional IVF when sperm was normal (35% vs 31%; P=0.27)
cards.summary: INVICSI 2021: ICSI did not improve live birth over conventional IVF when sperm was normal (35% vs 31%; P=0.27)
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, randomised controlled trial (two IVF centres, Vietnam)
cards.people: 1,064 couples at two IVF centres in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, randomised to ICSI (532) or conventional IVF (532); the male partner had normal total sperm count and motility by WHO 2010 criteria, couples had at most two previous IVF/ICSI attempts, used an antagonist stimulation protocol, and agreed to transfer at most two embryos. Embryologists and couples were unmasked; clinicians performing embryo transfer were unaware of allocation. Mean ages are not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Live birth after the first embryo transfer from the initiated cycle occurred in 184 of 532 couples (35%) with ICSI versus 166 of 532 (31%) with conventional IVF (absolute difference 3.4 percentage points, 95% CI -2.4 to 9.2; risk ratio 1.11 relative, 0.93 to 1.32; p=0.27). Fertilisation failure occurred in 29 couples (5%) versus 34 (6%) (absolute difference -0.9 points, -4.0 to 2.1; risk ratio 0.85 relative, 0.53 to 1.38; p=0.60). The authors conclude the results challenge the routine use of ICSI in this population.
cards.watchOut: Open-label to embryologists and couples (unavoidable for this intervention, and the outcome — live birth — is objective); a single country's practice with antagonist protocols and up to two embryos transferred, so the absolute rates travel imperfectly to single-embryo-transfer systems, though the null comparison should.
cards.source: Dang VQ et al. Lancet. 2021. PMID: 33894833. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03428919, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Bhattacharya 2001: in non-male-factor infertility, implantation was higher with conventional IVF than with ICSI (30% vs 22%)
cards.summary: Bhattacharya 2001: in non-male-factor infertility, implantation was higher with conventional IVF than with ICSI (30% vs 22%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (four UK centres)
cards.people: 415 eligible, consenting couples at four UK centres with non-male-factor infertility, randomised to IVF or ICSI (435 treatment cycles in total: 224 IVF, 211 ICSI), with usual clinical and laboratory protocols at each centre; analyses by intention to treat. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The implantation rate (gestation sacs per embryo replaced, the primary outcome) was higher in the IVF group than the ICSI group (95 of 318 [30%] versus 72 of 325 [22%]; relative risk 1.35 relative, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.76). The pregnancy rate per cycle was also higher after IVF (72 [33%] versus 53 [26%]; relative risk 1.17 relative, 0.97 to 1.35). Mean associated laboratory time was significantly shorter with IVF than with ICSI (22.9 [SD 12.1] versus 74.0 [SD 38.1] minutes).
cards.watchOut: A 2001 trial from an era of multiple-embryo transfer and different laboratory practice; its value on this shelf is directional corroboration of the 2021 trial, not its absolute rates. (The record's MeSH files the trial under 'Infertility, Male' indexing although the trial population is non-male-factor infertility as its title and abstract state; the MeSH are reproduced as the record carries them.)

cards.headline: Synthesis: ICSI for normal sperm is a null across two decades of trials — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: ICSI for normal sperm is a null across two decades of trials — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Dang 2021 (1,064 couples) and Bhattacharya 2001 (415 couples).
cards.result: Live birth 35% versus 31% (not significant) in the modern trial; implantation favouring conventional IVF in the older one; no difference in fertilisation failure where it was feared. The evidence supports reserving ICSI for male-factor indications, as both trials' authors conclude. ICSI for male-factor infertility is a different question — there the comparator logic differs — and is not what this shelf answers.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial addresses ICSI with surgically retrieved sperm, prior total fertilisation failure, or preimplantation genetic testing cycles — populations where practice reasonably differs and randomised evidence is thin.

shelves.title: Time-lapse embryo imaging/incubation vs standard care in IVF/ICSI
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF/ICSI, does time-lapse imaging (undisturbed culture ± embryo selection) vs standard incubation increase live birth?
shelves.mesh: Time-Lapse Imaging/methods · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Embryo Culture Techniques/methods · Pregnancy Rate · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large, multicentre, double-blind randomised trials — together over 3,300 couples — found no benefit from time-lapse imaging, whether used for embryo selection, for undisturbed culture, or both. TILT (Bhide 2024, 1,575 participants, three arms) found live birth in 33.7% with time-lapse selection and 36.6% with undisturbed culture alone versus 33.0% with standard care (adjusted odds ratios 1.04 relative, 97.5% CI 0.73 to 1.47, and 1.20 relative, 0.85 to 1.70). SelecTIMO (Kieslinger 2023, 1,731 couples, three arms) found 12-month cumulative ongoing pregnancy of 50.8% (time-lapse selection), 50.9% (undisturbed culture) and 49.4% (control) (P=0.85). The systems cost money and are marketed on improved results; the randomised results do not support the promise.

cards.headline: TILT 2024: time-lapse imaging did not increase live birth in IVF/ICSI (33.7% selection, 36.6% undisturbed culture, 33.0% standard care)
cards.summary: TILT 2024: time-lapse imaging did not increase live birth in IVF/ICSI (33.7% selection, 36.6% undisturbed culture, 33.0% standard care)
cards.type: Multicentre, three-parallel-group, double-blind randomised controlled trial (UK and Hong Kong)
cards.people: 1,575 participants undergoing IVF or ICSI at seven centres in the UK and Hong Kong, randomised 1:1:1 (525 per group) to a time-lapse system for undisturbed culture and embryo selection, a time-lapse system for undisturbed culture alone, or standard care without time-lapse imaging; women were aged 18-42 years, couples in their first to third treatment cycle, donor gametes excluded. Participants and trial staff were masked; embryologists were not. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Live birth rates were 33.7% (175 of 520) in the time-lapse imaging group, 36.6% (189 of 516) in the undisturbed culture group and 33.0% (172 of 522) in the standard care group. The adjusted odds ratio was 1.04 relative (97.5% CI 0.73 to 1.47) for time-lapse imaging versus control and 1.20 relative (0.85 to 1.70) for undisturbed culture versus control; absolute differences were 0.7 percentage points (-5.85 to 7.25) and 3.6 points (-3.02 to 10.22). Seventy-nine serious adverse events unrelated to the trial were reported across the groups.
cards.watchOut: The undisturbed-culture arm's point estimate (36.6% vs 33.0%) leans favourable but its interval comfortably includes no effect and harm-adjacent values; a non-significant lean in one of two comparisons is not a finding, and the trial's own interpretation is that time-lapse systems do not significantly increase live birth.
cards.source: Bhide P et al. Clinical effectiveness and safety of time-lapse imaging systems for embryo incubation and selection in in-vitro fertilisation treatment (TILT): a multicentre, three-parallel-group, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2024. PMID: 39033010. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN17792989, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SelecTIMO 2023: neither time-lapse selection nor uninterrupted culture improved ongoing pregnancy (50.8% and 50.9% vs 49.4%)
cards.summary: SelecTIMO 2023: neither time-lapse selection nor uninterrupted culture improved ongoing pregnancy (50.8% and 50.9% vs 49.4%)
cards.type: Three-armed, multicentre, double-blind randomised controlled trial (Netherlands)
cards.people: 1,731 couples undergoing IVF or ICSI at 15 fertility clinics in the Netherlands, randomised to time-lapse selection with the EEVA test plus uninterrupted culture (577), routine selection with uninterrupted culture (579), or routine selection with interrupted standard culture (575); couples and physicians were masked, embryologists and laboratory technicians could not be. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The 12-month cumulative ongoing pregnancy rate was 50.8% (293 of 577) in the time-lapse selection group, 50.9% (295 of 579) in the uninterrupted-culture group and 49.4% (284 of 575) in the control group (P=0.85). Ongoing pregnancy after fresh single embryo transfer in the good-prognosis population was 38.2% (125 of 327), 36.8% (119 of 323) and 37.8% (123 of 325) respectively (P=0.90). Ten serious adverse events were reported, none related to study procedures.
cards.watchOut: This trial's primary outcome is cumulative ongoing pregnancy rather than live birth — a near-final but not final outcome; its concordance with TILT's live-birth null, in a different country with a different time-lapse selection algorithm (EEVA), is what makes the combined null strong rather than device-specific.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large blinded trials, two countries, no live-birth or pregnancy benefit — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large blinded trials, two countries, no live-birth or pregnancy benefit — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TILT 2024 (1,575 participants) and SelecTIMO 2023 (1,731 couples) — over 3,300 randomised couples.
cards.result: The design of both trials separates the two candidate mechanisms — better selection and undisturbed culture — and both mechanisms failed independently: no arm of either trial beat standard care on live birth (TILT) or cumulative ongoing pregnancy (SelecTIMO). Time-lapse systems may have laboratory workflow value, but on the outcome couples are promised, the randomised answer is no.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate the newest AI-based selection algorithms; a future algorithm is a new claim requiring its own trial, not a reason to discount these two nulls about the systems actually tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bhide P et al. Lancet. 2024. PMID: 39033010; Kieslinger DC et al. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 37004670. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Metformin vs placebo during pregnancy in women with PCOS (PregMet programme)
shelves.question: In pregnant women with PCOS, does metformin from the first trimester to delivery vs placebo reduce late miscarriage and preterm birth?
shelves.mesh: Metformin/therapeutic use · Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/drug therapy · Pregnancy Complications/prevention & control · Abortion, Spontaneous/prevention & control · Premature Birth/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The two randomised trials do not individually show a significant benefit, and the encouraging signal lives in a post-hoc pooled analysis. PregMet2 (Løvvik 2019, 487 women) found its primary composite — late miscarriage or preterm birth — in 5% on metformin versus 10% on placebo (odds ratio 0.50 relative, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.08; P=0.08 — not significant); only the post-hoc individual-participant pooled analysis of all three programme trials reached significance (5% vs 10%; odds ratio 0.43 relative, 0.23 to 0.79; P=0.004). PregMet (Vanky 2010, 274 pregnancies) found no reduction in its composite of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes and preterm delivery (25.9% vs 24.4%; P=0.78). Neither trial reduced gestational diabetes. A real but unproven-in-trial benefit for late miscarriage/preterm birth is POSSIBLE; a claim of prevention would overstate the record. Metformin in pregnancy for glycaemia and baby size is Shelf #286's different question.

cards.headline: PregMet2 2019: metformin's primary composite was not significant in-trial (5% vs 10%; P=0.08); significance appeared only in a post-hoc pooled analysis
cards.summary: PregMet2 2019: metformin's primary composite was not significant in-trial (5% vs 10%; P=0.08); significance appeared only in a post-hoc pooled analysis
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (Norway, Sweden, Iceland)
cards.people: 487 singleton pregnant women with PCOS aged 18-45 years at 14 hospitals in Norway, Sweden and Iceland, randomised to metformin (244; 500 mg twice daily in week 1, then 1,000 mg twice daily until delivery) or placebo (243), from the late first trimester; the intention-to-treat analysis included 238 and 240 women. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The composite primary outcome of late miscarriage (week 13 to 22+6) and preterm birth (week 23 to 36+6) occurred in 12 of 238 women (5%) on metformin and 23 of 240 (10%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.50 relative, 95% CI 0.22 to 1.08; p=0.08). No secondary endpoint differed significantly, including gestational diabetes (60 of 238 [25%] versus 57 of 240 [24%]; odds ratio 1.09 relative, 0.69 to 1.66; p=0.75), and no serious adverse events were judged drug-related. In the post-hoc pooled individual-participant analysis with the two previous programme trials, late miscarriage or preterm delivery occurred in 18 of 397 women (5%) on metformin versus 40 of 399 (10%) on placebo (odds ratio 0.43 relative, 0.23 to 0.79; p=0.004).
cards.watchOut: The trial's own primary analysis missed significance (P=0.08); the P=0.004 figure comes from a post-hoc pooling decided after the data were seen — the correct reading is 'consistent with a benefit the trials were underpowered to confirm', not 'proven'. The abstract also records that an epi-analysis of the two earlier trials motivated this trial, and this trial did not confirm it on its own.

Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. 2019. PMID: 30792154. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01587378, from the record's databank fields (the abstract also names EudraCT 2011-002203-15). cards.headline: PregMet 2010: metformin did not reduce the composite of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes or preterm delivery (25.9% vs 24.4%)
cards.summary: PregMet 2010: metformin did not reduce the composite of preeclampsia, gestational diabetes or preterm delivery (25.9% vs 24.4%)
cards.people: 274 singleton pregnancies in 257 women with PCOS in the first trimester, aged 18-42 years, at 11 secondary care centres, randomised to metformin or placebo from the first trimester to delivery. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The composite primary endpoint (preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, or preterm delivery) occurred in 25.9% on metformin versus 24.4% on placebo (difference 1.5 percentage points, 95% CI -8.9 to 11.3; P=0.78). Preeclampsia was 7.4% versus 3.7% (P=0.18), preterm delivery 3.7% versus 8.2% (P=0.12) and gestational diabetes 17.6% versus 16.9% (P=0.87) — none significant, and pointing in different directions. Women on metformin gained less weight during pregnancy; there was no difference in fetal birth weight.
cards.watchOut: The preterm-delivery component leaned toward metformin (3.7% vs 8.2%) while preeclampsia leaned the other way (7.4% vs 3.7%) — both non-significant; selecting the favourable component would misrepresent a null composite, which is why this shelf grades the programme on its prespecified composites.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PregMet2 2019 (487 women) and PregMet 2010 (274 pregnancies), with PregMet2's post-hoc pooled analysis of the three-trial programme (796 women) reported on its own card.
cards.result: Prespecified analyses: PregMet2 composite 5% versus 10% (P=0.08), PregMet composite 25.9% versus 24.4% (P=0.78), gestational diabetes essentially identical in both trials. Post-hoc pooled: odds ratio 0.43 relative for late miscarriage or preterm birth. The honest summary is a possible benefit on one outcome that no individual trial has confirmed, and no benefit on gestational diabetes — metformin in PCOS pregnancy remains an unapproved indication with an open question, not an established preventive treatment.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the pooled P=0.004 without its post-hoc label; and note the wording discipline — even if confirmed, the claim would be a reduction in late miscarriage/preterm birth in PCOS pregnancy, not a general statement about metformin in pregnancy.

shelves.title: Oral dydrogesterone vs vaginal micronised progesterone for luteal-phase support in IVF (Lotus I & II)
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF, is oral dydrogesterone non-inferior to micronised vaginal progesterone for pregnancy at 12 weeks' gestation?
shelves.mesh: Dydrogesterone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Progesterone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Luteal Phase · Pregnancy Rate · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two industry-sponsored phase 3 non-inferiority trials (Lotus I, 1,031 women, blinded, versus vaginal progesterone capsules 600 mg/day; Lotus II, 1,034 women, open-label, versus 8% vaginal progesterone gel 90 mg/day) both demonstrated non-inferiority of oral dydrogesterone 30 mg/day for the primary endpoint of pregnancy with fetal heartbeat at 12 weeks — 37.6% versus 33.1% (difference 4.7 percentage points, 95% CI -1.2 to 10.6) and 38.7% versus 35.0% (adjusted difference 3.7 points, -2.3 to 9.7) — with live birth rates in the same direction (34.6% vs 29.8%; 34.4% vs 32.5%). The endpoint caveat stands: both trials were powered on the 12-week pregnancy rate, a surrogate for live birth, as both papers themselves state; the live-birth figures are consistent but were not the powered comparison.

cards.headline: Lotus I 2017: oral dydrogesterone was non-inferior to vaginal progesterone capsules for pregnancy at 12 weeks (37.6% vs 33.1%)
cards.summary: Lotus I 2017: oral dydrogesterone was non-inferior to vaginal progesterone capsules for pregnancy at 12 weeks (37.6% vs 33.1%)
cards.type: Phase III randomised controlled non-inferiority trial, blinded (38 sites, international) — Lotus I
cards.people: 1,031 premenopausal women (over 18 to under 42 years; BMI 18 to 30) with documented infertility planning IVF, at 38 sites, randomised to oral dydrogesterone 10 mg three times daily (520) or micronised vaginal progesterone 200 mg three times daily (511), from the day of oocyte retrieval until 12 weeks of gestation if pregnant; investigators, sponsor team and subjects were blinded. In the full analysis set, 497 and 477 women had an embryo transfer. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of oral dydrogesterone was demonstrated: pregnancy rates at 12 weeks of gestation (fetal heartbeat on transvaginal ultrasound) were 37.6% on dydrogesterone and 33.1% on vaginal progesterone (difference 4.7 percentage points, 95% CI -1.2 to 10.6), within the non-inferiority margin. Live birth rates were 34.6% (172 mothers, 213 newborns) versus 29.8% (142 mothers, 158 newborns) (difference 4.9 points, -0.8 to 10.7). Oral dydrogesterone was well tolerated with a safety profile similar to vaginal progesterone.
cards.watchOut: Sponsored and supported by Abbott, the dydrogesterone manufacturer, and powered on the 12-week pregnancy rate rather than live birth — the paper itself cautions that conclusions about the live-birth difference should be made with caution; the shelf's LIKELY rests on two concordant non-inferiority demonstrations, not on the live-birth point estimates.

cards.summary: Lotus II 2018: oral dydrogesterone was also non-inferior to vaginal progesterone gel (38.7% vs 35.0% at 12 weeks)
cards.type: Phase III randomised, open-label, multicentre non-inferiority trial (37 centres, 10 countries) — Lotus II
cards.people: 1,034 premenopausal women (over 18 to under 42 years) undergoing IVF at 37 centres in 10 countries, randomised 1:1 to oral dydrogesterone 30 mg daily (520) or 8% micronised vaginal progesterone gel 90 mg daily (514), from the day of oocyte retrieval until 12 weeks of gestation; the study was open-label because a placebo gel applicator was not technically feasible. cards.result: Non-inferiority was demonstrated (margin 10%): pregnancy rates at 12 weeks were 38.7% (191 of 494) on oral dydrogesterone and 35.0% (171 of 489) on vaginal gel (adjusted difference 3.7 percentage points, 95% CI -2.3 to 9.7). Live birth rates were 34.4% (170 of 494) versus 32.5% (159 of 489) (adjusted difference 1.9 points, -4.0 to 7.8). Oral dydrogesterone was well tolerated with a similar safety profile to the gel.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (unavoidable without a placebo applicator, as the authors state) and again Abbott-sponsored and powered on ongoing pregnancy rather than live birth; the fresh-cycle setting also matters — neither Lotus trial tests programmed frozen-thawed cycles, where there is no corpus luteum.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, one conclusion — the oral drug is a proven alternative for luteal support — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, one conclusion — the oral drug is a proven alternative for luteal support — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lotus I (1,031 women, blinded, capsule comparator) and Lotus II (1,034 women, open-label, gel comparator).
cards.result: Against both vaginal formulations in use, oral dydrogesterone met its non-inferiority margin on 12-week pregnancy (37.6% vs 33.1%; 38.7% vs 35.0%) with live birth rates numerically at least as high (34.6% vs 29.8%; 34.4% vs 32.5%), similar tolerability, and an oral route patients generally prefer over vaginal irritation and discharge. The claim is equivalence-class, not superiority: the point estimates lean toward dydrogesterone but the trials were designed and powered to show non-inferiority on a pregnancy endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are manufacturer-sponsored and neither was powered on live birth; independent replication would strengthen the stamp, and extrapolation to frozen-thawed programmed cycles is not licensed by these data.

shelves.title: GnRH antagonist vs long GnRH agonist protocol for ovarian stimulation in IVF
shelves.question: In women undergoing ovarian stimulation with recombinant FSH, does a ganirelix (GnRH antagonist) protocol vs a long agonist protocol give comparable pregnancy outcomes with shorter, simpler treatment?
shelves.mesh: Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/antagonists & inhibitors · Hormone Antagonists/therapeutic use · Ovulation Induction/methods · Pregnancy Rate · Triptorelin Pamoate/therapeutic use · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two large randomised trials from the ganirelix development programme show the antagonist protocol is dramatically shorter and simpler, with pregnancy rates close to — but numerically below — the long agonist protocol in both. Against long intranasal buserelin (730 women), ongoing pregnancy per attempt was 20.3% on ganirelix versus 25.7% on the agonist, with median GnRH-analogue treatment of 5 versus 26 days, less recombinant FSH (1,500 vs 1,800 IU) and less ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (2.4% vs 5.9%). Against long triptorelin (355 women), ongoing pregnancy was 31.0% versus 33.9% with an identical implantation rate (22.9%), a regimen on average 17 days shorter, and fewer local skin reactions (11.9% vs 24.1%). Neither trial was reported against a modern prespecified non-inferiority margin for pregnancy, so 'proven equivalent' overstates them; 'comparable outcomes with a much shorter, better-tolerated protocol' is POSSIBLE-to-fair — graded POSSIBLE on the pregnancy question specifically.

cards.headline: European Orgalutran Study 2000: ganirelix gave a 5-day instead of 26-day protocol, with ongoing pregnancy 20.3% vs 25.7% on long buserelin
cards.summary: European Orgalutran Study 2000: ganirelix gave a 5-day instead of 26-day protocol, with ongoing pregnancy 20.3% vs 25.7% on long buserelin
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised trial (ganirelix vs long buserelin protocol)
cards.people: 730 women undergoing ovarian stimulation with recombinant FSH, in a multicentre open-label randomised non-inferiority-designed study, randomised 2:1 to ganirelix (approximately 487) or a long protocol of intranasal buserelin (approximately 243), stratified by age, infertility type and planned IVF or ICSI. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Median duration of GnRH-analogue treatment was 5 days in the ganirelix group and 26 days in the buserelin group; median total recombinant FSH dose was 1,500 IU versus 1,800 IU, and stimulation was on average 1 day shorter with ganirelix. LH rises (at least 10 IU/L) occurred in 2.8% versus 1.3%. On the hCG day, mean follicles at least 11 mm numbered 10.7 versus 11.8 and median oestradiol was 1,190 versus 1,700 pg/mL. Mean oocytes per retrieval were 9.1 versus 10.4 and good-quality embryos 3.3 versus 3.5; fertilisation rates were equal (62.1%), the same mean number of embryos (2.2) was replaced, implantation rates were 15.7% versus 21.8%, and ongoing pregnancy rates per attempt were 20.3% versus 25.7%. Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome occurred in 2.4% versus 5.9%.
cards.watchOut: The pregnancy and implantation point estimates favour the agonist by 5-6 percentage points in this trial — the authors' 'good clinical outcome' framing rests on the totality (shorter, safer, fewer injections), not on pregnancy superiority or a reported non-inferiority interval; this card prints the numbers as the record gives them so the trade-off is visible.

cards.headline: Ganirelix vs long triptorelin 2001: ongoing pregnancy 31.0% vs 33.9%, identical implantation, 17 days shorter
cards.summary: Ganirelix vs long triptorelin 2001: ongoing pregnancy 31.0% vs 33.9%, identical implantation, 17 days shorter
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (ganirelix vs long triptorelin protocol)
cards.people: 355 women undergoing ovarian stimulation, in a multicentre randomised study, randomised 2:1 to ganirelix 0.25 mg subcutaneously (236; started on day 6 of stimulation) or triptorelin 0.1 mg in a long protocol (119; started on cycle day 21-24 of the previous cycle). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The ganirelix regimen was on average 17 days shorter (9 versus 26 days in total). The mean numbers of oocytes retrieved and of good-quality embryos (2.7 versus 2.9) were comparable. cards.watchOut: Smaller than the buserelin trial (355 women) and again without a reported non-inferiority interval for pregnancy; 'comparable' in the title is the authors' summary of point estimates that again lean slightly toward the agonist (31.0% vs 33.9%).

cards.headline: Synthesis: shorter, simpler, somewhat fewer pregnancies per attempt in the early trials — POSSIBLE for comparable outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: shorter, simpler, somewhat fewer pregnancies per attempt in the early trials — POSSIBLE for comparable outcomes
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ganirelix versus long buserelin (730 women, 2000) and ganirelix versus long triptorelin (355 women, 2001) — 1,085 randomised women.
cards.result: The consistent, undisputed gains of the antagonist protocol are process gains: about three weeks less analogue treatment, less gonadotropin, fewer local reactions, and (in the buserelin comparison) less ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (2.4% vs 5.9%). The pregnancy cost, if any, is small and unproven: ongoing pregnancy 20.3% vs 25.7% and 31.0% vs 33.9% — point estimates favouring the agonist in trials not powered or reported to exclude a modest difference. Later practice has largely adopted antagonist protocols for their safety and convenience; this shelf grades the two founding trials on what they showed.
cards.watchOut: Both trials date from 2000-2001, when transfer of two or more embryos was routine; absolute pregnancy rates do not transfer to modern single-transfer practice, and the comparison that matters now (cumulative live birth per started cycle) was not these trials' endpoint.

shelves.title: Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD vs copper IUD for emergency contraception
shelves.question: In women seeking emergency contraception who want an IUD, is the levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD non-inferior to the copper T380A IUD for pregnancy at 1 month?
shelves.mesh: Contraception, Postcoital/methods · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Intrauterine Devices, Copper · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage · Pregnancy Rate · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One randomised non-inferiority trial (Turok 2021, 711 women randomised at six Utah clinics; participants unaware of their assignment) found the levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD non-inferior to the copper T380A IUD for emergency contraception: pregnancy at 1 month was 1 in 317 (0.3%) with levonorgestrel versus 0 in 321 (0%) with copper — an absolute difference of 0.3 percentage points (95% CI -0.9 to 1.8), inside the prespecified 2.5-point non-inferiority margin, in both modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses. Adverse events prompting medical care in the first month were similar (5.2% vs 4.9%). A single large trial with a near-zero event rate in both arms and a prespecified margin carries LIKELY for the non-inferiority claim. Ongoing contraceptive use of these devices is Shelf #659's different question.

cards.headline: Turok 2021: levonorgestrel IUD was non-inferior to copper IUD for emergency contraception (pregnancy 0.3% vs 0%)
cards.summary: Turok 2021: levonorgestrel IUD was non-inferior to copper IUD for emergency contraception (pregnancy 0.3% vs 0%)
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial, participants blinded to assignment (six clinics, Utah)
cards.people: 711 women at six clinics in Utah who sought emergency contraception after at least one episode of unprotected intercourse within the previous 5 days and agreed to IUD placement, randomised 1:1 to a levonorgestrel 52-mg IUD (355) or a copper T380A IUD (356), with participants unaware of group assignments; 317 and 321 women received the interventions and provided 1-month outcome data (290 and 300 with a 1-month urine pregnancy test; survey and health-record data used when the test was unavailable). The abstract does not state mean age; MeSH records the population as Adolescent, Adult and Young Adult women.
cards.result: Pregnancy at 1 month occurred in 1 of 317 women (0.3%; 95% CI 0.01 to 1.7) in the levonorgestrel group and 0 of 321 (0%; 0 to 1.1) in the copper group; the absolute difference was 0.3 percentage points (95% CI -0.9 to 1.8) in both the modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses, meeting the prespecified 2.5-point non-inferiority margin. Adverse events resulting in participants seeking medical care in the first month occurred in 5.2% versus 4.9%.
cards.watchOut: Emergency contraception trials compare two highly effective options, so the finding is 'no meaningful difference', not 'both proven against no treatment in this trial' — the copper IUD's efficacy is the established reference. Results apply to placement within 5 days of unprotected intercourse in women who want an IUD for ongoing contraception.
cards.source: Turok DK et al. Levonorgestrel vs. Copper Intrauterine Devices for Emergency Contraception. N Engl J Med. 2021. PMID: 33503342. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02175030, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Etonogestrel implant vs low-dose levonorgestrel IUS: continuation and bleeding
shelves.question: In women aged 18–35 choosing long-acting contraception, how do the etonogestrel implant and the 13.5 mg LNG-IUS compare on 12-month discontinuation and bleeding-related discontinuation?
shelves.mesh: Intrauterine Devices, Medicated/adverse effects · Desogestrel/administration & dosage · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage · Menstruation/drug effects · Patient Satisfaction · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial (Apter 2016, 766 women aged 18-35 at 38 European centres) found the low-dose 13.5 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS 8, releasing about 8 µg/day) had a lower 12-month discontinuation rate than the etonogestrel implant — 19.6% versus 26.8% (difference -7.2 percentage points, 95% CI -13.2 to -1.2) — driven mainly by bleeding-related discontinuation (3.2% vs 11.3%) and fewer adverse-event discontinuations (14.3% vs 21.8%); satisfaction with the bleeding pattern (60.9% vs 33.6%) and preference to continue the method (70.1% vs 58.5%) also favoured the IUS. The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single open-label trial whose outcomes are continuation and satisfaction (process outcomes a woman cannot be blinded to), and the IUS studied is the low-dose 13.5 mg device, not the 52 mg system.

cards.headline: Apter 2016: 12-month discontinuation was lower with the 13.5 mg LNG-IUS than with the etonogestrel implant (19.6% vs 26.8%), driven by bleeding
cards.summary: Apter 2016: 12-month discontinuation was lower with the 13.5 mg LNG-IUS than with the etonogestrel implant (19.6% vs 26.8%), driven by bleeding
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, phase III study (38 centres, six European countries)
cards.people: 766 healthy nulliparous and parous women aged 18-35 years at 38 centres in six European countries, randomised to the levonorgestrel intrauterine system LNG-IUS 8 (13.5 mg total content, average release about 8 µg/24 h in the first year; Jaydess/Skyla) or the etonogestrel subdermal implant (68 mg). Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Twelve-month discontinuation rates were 19.6% in the LNG-IUS 8 group and 26.8% in the implant group; the -7.2 percentage point difference was statistically significant (95% CI -13.2 to -1.2). Fewer women in the LNG-IUS 8 group discontinued because of increased bleeding (3.2% vs 11.3%) or adverse events (14.3% vs 21.8%). At 12 months, more LNG-IUS 8 users were 'very/somewhat satisfied' with their bleeding pattern (60.9% vs 33.6%) and reported a preference to use their study treatment after study completion (70.1% vs 58.5%).
cards.watchOut: Continuation is partly a preference outcome measured in women who know which device they have — exactly the outcome open-label design can move; and the intrauterine device here is the low-dose 13.5 mg system, so the bleeding profile should not be assumed identical to the 52 mg levonorgestrel IUS.
cards.source: Apter D et al. A 12-month multicenter, randomized study comparing the levonorgestrel intrauterine system with the etonogestrel subdermal implant. Fertil Steril. 2016. PMID: 27016644. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01397097, from the record's databank fields (stated in the abstract). cards.headline: Synthesis: in the only head-to-head trial, the low-dose IUS kept more users at one year, on bleeding tolerability — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the only head-to-head trial, the low-dose IUS kept more users at one year, on bleeding tolerability — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Apter 2016 (766 women aged 18-35).
cards.result: Both methods are highly effective contraceptives; this shelf is about staying on them. The randomised difference is a 7.2-point lower discontinuation with the low-dose IUS at 12 months, mechanistically coherent (11.3% of implant users stopped for increased bleeding versus 3.2% of IUS users) and matched by satisfaction ratings. One trial, one device dose, one year: POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Discontinuation is not contraceptive failure: pregnancy rates are not the trial's reported primary outcome, and neither arm's efficacy is in question on this shelf — only tolerability-driven continuation.

shelves.title: Elective single-embryo transfer (eSET) vs double-embryo transfer in IVF
shelves.question: In women under 36 with at least two good-quality embryos, does an eSET strategy (fresh single transfer plus frozen single transfer if needed) vs double-embryo transfer achieve equivalent live birth with fewer multiple pregnancies?
shelves.mesh: Embryo Transfer · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Pregnancy, Multiple · Birth Rate · Cryopreservation · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One multicentre randomised equivalence trial (Thurin 2004, 661 women under 36 with at least two good-quality embryos, Scandinavia) found the elective single-embryo-transfer strategy — one fresh single transfer, then one frozen single transfer if needed — produced live-birth pregnancies in 38.8% versus 42.9% with double-embryo transfer (difference 4.1 percentage points, 95% CI -3.4 to 11.6), while multiple births collapsed from 33.1% to 0.8% (P<0.001). Two honest qualifications, both printed in the record: the trial did NOT formally demonstrate equivalence (its margin was 10 points and the interval reached 11.6), so a live-birth cost of up to about 11 points cannot be excluded; and the strategy comparison includes the frozen transfer, so this is not a fresh-transfer-only comparison. The multiple-birth effect is so large and the live-birth difference so bounded that the strategy claim carries LIKELY. Distinct from Shelf #834 (freeze-all vs fresh transfer).

cards.headline: Thurin 2004: single-embryo strategy cut multiple births from 33.1% to 0.8% with live births 38.8% vs 42.9% (equivalence not formally shown)
cards.summary: Thurin 2004: single-embryo strategy cut multiple births from 33.1% to 0.8% with live births 38.8% vs 42.9% (equivalence not formally shown)
cards.people: 661 women less than 36 years of age with at least two good-quality embryos, in a randomised multicentre trial, assigned to transfer of a single fresh embryo followed — if no live birth — by a single frozen-and-thawed embryo (330 women), or to a single transfer of two fresh embryos (331 women). Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Pregnancy resulting in at least one live birth occurred in 128 of 330 women (38.8 percent) in the single-embryo-transfer group versus 142 of 331 (42.9 percent) in the double-embryo-transfer group (difference 4.1 percentage points; 95 percent confidence interval, -3.4 to 11.6). Rates of multiple births were 0.8 percent and 33.1 percent respectively (P<0.001). The authors state these results do not demonstrate equivalence (defined as a difference of no more than 10 percentage points), but indicate that any reduction in live births with single-embryo transfer is unlikely to exceed 11.6 percentage points.
cards.watchOut: Report the record's own caution, not the folklore version: equivalence was not demonstrated, so the honest claim is 'at most a modest live-birth cost, against a near-elimination of multiple births (0.8% vs 33.1%)'. The population is young (under 36) with good-quality embryos — the group where the strategy works best.
cards.source: Thurin A et al. Elective single-embryo transfer versus double-embryo transfer in in vitro fertilization. N Engl J Med. 2004. PMID: 15575055. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the trade is a bounded possible live-birth cost for a near-elimination of twin pregnancies — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: the trade is a bounded possible live-birth cost for a near-elimination of twin pregnancies — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Thurin 2004 (661 women under 36).
cards.result: Multiple gestation is the main driver of prematurity and perinatal death after IVF; this strategy cut it from one in three deliveries to under one in a hundred while keeping cumulative live birth within 4.1 points of double transfer (with up to 11.6 points of cost not excluded). Subsequent practice worldwide moved on the strength of this trial's arithmetic; the shelf keeps the trial's own non-equivalence wording attached to the numbers.
cards.watchOut: The frozen-transfer second chance is part of the strategy; clinics comparing a single fresh transfer alone against double transfer should not quote this trial's 38.8% as the fresh-only rate.

shelves.title: Laparoscopic ovarian drilling vs gonadotropin ovulation induction in clomiphene-resistant PCOS
shelves.question: In women with clomiphene-resistant PCOS, does laparoscopic ovarian electrocautery vs ovulation induction with recombinant FSH give comparable long-term pregnancy outcomes and costs?
shelves.mesh: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/surgery,drug therapy · Electrocoagulation/methods · Ovulation Induction/methods · Live Birth · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised programme (168 women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant PCOS in the Netherlands, randomised 1998-2001) compared a strategy of laparoscopic electrocautery of the ovaries (followed by clomiphene and then gonadotrophins if anovulation persisted) against ovulation induction with recombinant FSH. At 8-12 years of follow-up, at least one live birth had occurred in 86% of the electrocautery-strategy group (71 of 83) versus 81% of the gonadotrophin group (69 of 85), and the programme's reports describe the surgical strategy as at least comparable for a first live birth, with increased chances of a second live birth, a reduced need for further ovulation induction or assisted reproduction, and significantly lower mean costs per first live birth (€11,176 versus €14,423; difference €3,247, 95% CI €650 to €5,814; P<0.05). The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single trial programme whose carded record is its long-term economic evaluation, with live-birth results reported alongside the cost analysis rather than as a powered primary comparison, in one country's practice.

cards.headline: Nahuis 2012 (trial programme long-term follow-up): electrocautery strategy gave live birth in 86% vs 81% and lower costs per first live birth over 8-12 years
cards.summary: Nahuis 2012 (trial programme long-term follow-up): electrocautery strategy gave live birth in 86% vs 81% and lower costs per first live birth over 8-12 years
cards.type: Long-term follow-up and economic evaluation of a multicentre randomised controlled trial (Netherlands)
cards.people: 168 women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant PCOS randomised between February 1998 and October 2001 in a Dutch multicentre trial to a strategy of laparoscopic electrocautery of the ovaries (followed by clomiphene citrate and gonadotrophins when anovulation persisted) or ovulation induction with gonadotrophins (recombinant FSH); the long-term economic follow-up obtained data on 159 of the 168 women (95%) at 8-12 years after randomisation. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: In total, 71 of 83 women (86%) allocated to the electrocautery strategy and 69 of 85 (81%) allocated to the gonadotrophin strategy had at least one live birth. The mean costs per first live birth after randomisation were €11,176 (95% CI €9,689 to €12,549) for the electrocautery group and €14,423 (€12,239 to €16,606) for the recombinant FSH group — significantly lower costs per first live birth with the electrocautery strategy (mean difference €3,247; 95% CI €650 to €5,814; P<0.05). The report's background states that long-term follow-up demonstrated at least comparable chances for a first live born child with the electrocautery strategy, a reduced need for ovulation induction or assisted reproduction treatment, and increased chances for a second live born child.
cards.watchOut: This carded record is the programme's economic evaluation, not its primary clinical report: the live-birth figures appear inside a cost analysis of 159 of 168 randomised women, costs are Dutch 1998-2001-era euros, and the electrocautery arm is a strategy (surgery, then drugs if needed) — not surgery alone. Multiple-pregnancy and OHSS avoidance, the strategy's classic selling points, are described in the programme's background rather than quantified in this record's abstract, so no rates are carded for them.
cards.source: Nahuis MJ et al (including Bayram N, van Wely M). Long-term follow-up of laparoscopic electrocautery of the ovaries versus ovulation induction with recombinant FSH in clomiphene citrate-resistant women with polycystic ovary syndrome: an economic evaluation. Hum Reprod. 2012. PMID: 23001778. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: one operation can substitute for months of injections, at similar baby rates and lower cost — on one programme's evidence, POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: the Dutch electrocautery-versus-gonadotrophin RCT programme (168 randomised women; 159 in the long-term economic follow-up).
cards.result: The long view favours the surgical strategy on logistics and cost (86% vs 81% ever having a live birth over 8-12 years; €3,247 less per first live birth) with no demonstrated effectiveness penalty.
