shelves.title: Transdermal testosterone for low libido in postmenopausal women
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder, does a testosterone patch (300 µg/day) vs placebo improve satisfying sexual activity and desire?
shelves.mesh: Testosterone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Libido/drug effects · Sexual Dysfunction, Physiological/drug therapy · Postmenopause · Administration, Cutaneous · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of the 300 µg/day testosterone patch found modest improvements in sexual function. APHRODITE (Davis 2008, 814 postmenopausal women NOT taking estrogen) found the 4-week frequency of satisfying sexual episodes rose by 2.1 on 300 µg/day versus 0.7 on placebo (P<0.001), with significant increases in desire and decreases in distress at both doses; the 150 µg/day dose did not beat placebo on the primary endpoint (1.2 episodes; P=0.11). The earlier surgical-menopause trial (Braunstein 2005, 447 women on oral estrogen) found the same pattern at 300 µg/day (desire +67% vs +48%, P=.05; satisfying activity +79% vs +43%, P=.049). The harms are part of the claim: unwanted hair growth was more frequent at 300 µg/day (30.0% vs 23.1% in APHRODITE), and four breast cancers were diagnosed in testosterone-treated women versus none on placebo in APHRODITE (one diagnosed within 4 months, one with symptoms predating randomisation) — long-term breast safety is unresolved, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE and the balance carries the safety signal, not just the benefit.

cards.headline: APHRODITE 2008: testosterone patch 300 µg/day modestly increased satisfying sexual episodes (+2.1 vs +0.7 per 4 weeks); 4 breast cancers on testosterone vs 0 on placebo
cards.summary: APHRODITE 2008: testosterone patch 300 µg/day modestly increased satisfying sexual episodes (+2.1 vs +0.7 per 4 weeks); 4 breast cancers on testosterone vs 0 on placebo
cards.people: 814 postmenopausal women with hypoactive sexual desire disorder not receiving estrogen therapy, randomised in a double-blind, placebo-controlled 52-week trial to a patch delivering 150 or 300 µg of testosterone per day or placebo; efficacy was measured to week 24, safety over 52 weeks, with a subgroup followed for an additional year. Mean age is not stated in the abstract; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged women.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, the increase in the 4-week frequency of satisfying sexual episodes was significantly greater with 300 µg/day than placebo (an increase of 2.1 episodes versus 0.7; P<0.001) but not with 150 µg/day (1.2 episodes; P=0.11). Both doses significantly increased desire (P<0.001 and P=0.04) and decreased distress (P<0.001 and P=0.04) versus placebo. Androgenic adverse events — primarily unwanted hair growth — were more frequent at 300 µg/day (30.0% vs 23.1%). Breast cancer was diagnosed in four women who received testosterone versus none who received placebo; one of the four was diagnosed in the first 4 months and one, in retrospect, had symptoms before randomisation. The authors conclude the improvement was modest but meaningful and that long-term effects, including on the breast, remain uncertain.
cards.watchOut: The breast-cancer imbalance (4 vs 0) is too small and too confounded (two of the four cases plausibly predated treatment effect) to be a proven harm, and too serious to omit: it is printed on this card's face, and any summary of this shelf that mentions only libido misrepresents the trial. The benefit size — about 1.4 extra satisfying episodes per 4 weeks over placebo — is the other half of the honest picture.
cards.source: Davis SR et al. Testosterone for low libido in postmenopausal women not taking estrogen. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18987368. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00131495, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Braunstein 2005: in surgically menopausal women on estrogen, the 300 µg/day patch increased desire and satisfying activity versus placebo
cards.summary: Braunstein 2005: in surgically menopausal women on estrogen, the 300 µg/day patch increased desire and satisfying activity versus placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (surgically menopausal women on oral estrogen)
cards.people: 447 women aged 24-70 years who developed distressing low sexual desire after bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and hysterectomy and were receiving oral estrogen therapy, randomised in a 24-week double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial to placebo (119) or testosterone patches of 150 µg/day (107), 300 µg/day (110) or 450 µg/day (111) twice weekly; 318 (71%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, women receiving the 300 µg/day patch had significantly greater increases from baseline in sexual desire (67% versus 48%; P=.05) and in frequency of satisfying sexual activity (79% versus 43%; P=.049). The 150 µg/day group showed no evidence of a treatment effect, and the 450 µg/day group was not statistically different from either the 300 µg/day or the placebo group. Dose-response trends were marginally significant (P=.06 for both total satisfying activity and desire). Adverse events occurred with similar frequency in the groups and no serious safety concerns were observed in 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine percent of randomised women did not complete the trial, the two positive P values sit at .05 and .049, and the population (surgical menopause on estrogen) differs from APHRODITE's (natural menopause, no estrogen) — the concordance of the 300 µg/day dose across both is reassuring, but neither trial runs long enough to address breast or cardiovascular safety.
cards.source: Braunstein GD et al. shelves.title: Bazedoxifene/conjugated estrogens (tissue-selective estrogen complex) for vasomotor symptoms (SMART)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women, does bazedoxifene 20 mg + conjugated estrogens 0.45/0.625 mg (no progestogen) vs placebo reduce hot flushes while protecting the endometrium?
shelves.mesh: Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Estrogens, Conjugated (USP)/therapeutic use · Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators/administration & dosage · Indoles/administration & dosage · Menopause · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The phase 3 SMART programme shows bazedoxifene 20 mg combined with conjugated estrogens 0.45 or 0.625 mg (no progestogen) substantially reduces hot flushes versus placebo. The dedicated vasomotor trial (SMART-2; Pinkerton 2009, 332 women with at least 7 moderate-to-severe flushes/day) found flush frequency fell 74% (0.45 mg CE) and 80% (0.625 mg CE) versus 51% on placebo by week 12, with at least 75% reduction achieved by 61% and 73% versus 27% (P<0.001). The larger 2-year SMART-1 trial (Lobo 2009, 3,397 women with an intact uterus) found the same direction — week-12 flush reductions of 51.7% to 85.7% across BZA/CE doses versus 17.1% on placebo — with improved vaginal atrophy measures, improved lipid parameters, and breast-pain and adverse-event rates similar to placebo. Two concordant blinded trials earn LIKELY for symptom relief; neither trial was powered for long-term cardiovascular, breast or endometrial outcomes, and no such claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: SMART-2 (Pinkerton 2009): BZA/CE cut hot flushes by 74-80% versus 51% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.summary: SMART-2 (Pinkerton 2009): BZA/CE cut hot flushes by 74-80% versus 51% on placebo at 12 weeks
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (SMART-2, USA)
cards.people: 332 healthy postmenopausal women aged 40-65 years with moderate to severe hot flushes (at least 7 per day or 50 per week), in a US multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, randomised to bazedoxifene 20 mg/CE 0.45 mg, BZA 20 mg/CE 0.625 mg, or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: BZA/CE significantly reduced the number and severity of hot flushes at weeks 4 and 12 (P<0.001). At week 12, hot flushes had fallen from baseline by 74% with BZA 20 mg/CE 0.45 mg (10.3 flushes at baseline versus 2.8 at week 12) and by 80% with BZA 20 mg/CE 0.625 mg (10.4 versus 2.4), compared with 51% for placebo (10.5 versus 5.4). More participants achieved at least a 75% decrease in hot flushes with BZA/CE (61% and 73%) than with placebo (27%; P<0.001). The safety profile was similar between BZA/CE and placebo, with no unexpected findings.
cards.watchOut: The placebo response is large (a 51% fall in flush frequency), as in all vasomotor trials — the drug's claim is the additional ~23-29 percentage points and the responder gap (73% vs 27% achieving at least 75% reduction), not the raw 80% figure. Twelve weeks is short for a menopause therapy, which is what the 2-year SMART-1 trial complements.

Menopause. 2009. PMID: 19546826. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. (The record's abstract identifies this trial as the Selective Estrogen Menopause and Response to Therapy 2 — SMART-2 — trial.) cards.headline: SMART-1 (Lobo 2009): in 3,397 women over 2 years, BZA/CE reduced hot flushes and improved vaginal atrophy, with placebo-like breast pain and adverse events
cards.summary: SMART-1 (Lobo 2009): in 3,397 women over 2 years, BZA/CE reduced hot flushes and improved vaginal atrophy, with placebo-like breast pain and adverse events
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 trial (SMART-1, 2 years)
cards.people: 3,397 healthy postmenopausal women aged 40-75 years with an intact uterus, in a multicentre double-blind placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 trial, taking single tablets of bazedoxifene (10, 20 or 40 mg) each combined with conjugated estrogens (0.625 or 0.45 mg), raloxifene 60 mg, or placebo daily for 2 years. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: BZA 20 mg/CE 0.625 or 0.45 mg significantly reduced the frequency and severity of hot flushes and improved measures of vaginal atrophy compared with placebo. At week 12, the daily number of hot flushes decreased by 51.7% to 85.7% with all BZA/CE doses versus 17.1% for placebo. BZA/CE improved lipid parameters and homocysteine levels, did not significantly change carbohydrate metabolism, and had only minor effects on some coagulation parameters. The incidences of breast pain and adverse events were similar between BZA/CE and placebo.
cards.watchOut: SMART-1's purpose was the broader symptom, metabolic and safety profile over 2 years, not cancer or cardiovascular endpoints — 'effects on metabolic parameters' (lipids, homocysteine) are surrogate movements and must not be read as event protection; endometrial protection rests on the programme's endometrial outcomes, which this abstract does not quantify.

shelves.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy for problematic hot flushes and night sweats (MENOS 1 & 2)
shelves.question: In menopausal women with problematic hot flushes/night sweats, does CBT (group or self-help) vs no-treatment control reduce how problematic the symptoms are?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Hot Flashes/prevention & control,therapy · Menopause · Psychotherapy, Group · Self Care · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials from the MENOS programme found that CBT — delivered in groups or as guided self-help — significantly reduced how problematic hot flushes and night sweats were rated, with effects maintained at 26 weeks. MENOS 2 (Ayers 2012, 140 women with at least 10 problematic episodes/week) found problem-rating reductions versus no-treatment control of 2.12 points (95% CI 1.36 to 2.88) for group CBT and 2.08 points (1.29 to 2.86) for self-help CBT at 6 weeks on a 1-10 scale, still significant at 26 weeks (1.33 and 1.19 points), with reduced night-sweat frequency and improved mood and quality of life. MENOS 1 (Mann 2012, 96 women after breast-cancer treatment) found group CBT reduced problem rating by 1.67 points versus usual care at 9 weeks (-2.43 to -0.91; P<0.0001), maintained at 26 weeks (-1.76), with no CBT-related adverse events. The honest framing is in both trials' design: CBT targets how problematic symptoms feel and how women manage them — the primary outcome is a problem rating, not flush counts — and participants cannot be blinded. That is the claim, and on that claim the evidence is consistent and sustained. SSRI/SNRI drugs for the same symptoms are Shelf #667.

cards.headline: MENOS 2 2012: group and self-help CBT both cut hot-flush problem ratings by about 2 points versus no treatment, sustained at 26 weeks
cards.summary: MENOS 2 2012: group and self-help CBT both cut hot-flush problem ratings by about 2 points versus no treatment, sustained at 26 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, three arms (group CBT, self-help CBT, no-treatment control)
cards.people: 140 women having 10 or more problematic hot flushes/night sweats per week for at least a month (baseline mean weekly frequency 63.15 [SD 49.24]; mean problem rating 5.87 [SD 2.28]), randomised to group CBT, guided self-help CBT, or no-treatment control; the primary outcome was the hot-flush/night-sweat problem rating (1-10) at 6 weeks. Mean age is not stated in the abstract; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged women.
cards.result: Group CBT and self-help CBT both significantly reduced problem rating at 6 weeks versus no-treatment control (adjusted mean difference 2.12, 95% CI 1.36 to 2.88, P<0.001; and 2.08, 1.29 to 2.86, P<0.001) and at 26 weeks (1.33, 0.54 to 2.13, P=0.001; and 1.19, 0.36 to 2.02, P=0.005). Both formats significantly reduced night-sweat frequency at 6 and 26 weeks. Mood and quality of life improved at 6 weeks, and emotional and physical functioning were improved for group CBT at 26 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The control is no treatment, so expectancy and attention effects are uncontrolled — unavoidable for a psychological therapy, but it means the trial measures the whole CBT package including therapist attention; and the outcome is a problem rating (how bothersome symptoms are), which is the therapy's intended target, not a reduction in objectively counted flushes.
cards.source: Ayers B et al. Effectiveness of group and self-help cognitive behavior therapy in reducing problematic menopausal hot flushes and night sweats (MENOS 2): a randomized controlled trial. Menopause. 2012. PMID: 22336748. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Gabapentin vs placebo for menopausal hot flushes
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with hot flushes, does gabapentin vs placebo reduce hot-flush frequency and severity?
shelves.mesh: Gabapentin · Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Amines/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Postmenopause · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Three small double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree that gabapentin reduces hot flushes more than placebo, but the trials are small (59, 200 and 60 women) and short (4-12 weeks). Guttuso 2003 (59 women, gabapentin 900 mg/day) found 12-week reductions of 45% in flush frequency and 54% in composite score versus 29% (P=.02) and 31% (P=.01) on placebo. Butt 2008 (200 women, 900 mg/day for 4 weeks) found hot-flush scores fell 51% versus 26% (P<0.001). Reddy 2006 (60 women) found gabapentin titrated to 2,400 mg/day reduced the composite score by 71% versus 54% on placebo (P=.004) — statistically indistinguishable from estrogen's 72% in the same trial (P=.63 between them). The harms are consistent too: dizziness, unsteadiness and drowsiness, with Reddy estimating the headache/dizziness/disorientation cluster may occur in about every fourth treated patient. Three concordant trials with one mid-sized study and surrogate symptom scores: POSSIBLE, leaning favourable. Distinct from the SSRI/SNRI shelf #667.

cards.headline: Guttuso 2003: gabapentin 900 mg/day reduced hot-flush frequency by 45% versus 29% on placebo at 12 weeks (59 women)
cards.summary: Guttuso 2003: gabapentin 900 mg/day reduced hot-flush frequency by 45% versus 29% on placebo at 12 weeks (59 women)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (with open-label extension)
cards.people: 59 postmenopausal women with seven or more hot flashes per day, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of gabapentin 900 mg/day for 12 weeks, followed by a 5-week open-label phase in which the dose could rise to 2,700 mg/day. Mean age is not stated in the abstract; MeSH records the population as Middle Aged women.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, intention-to-treat analysis showed gabapentin was associated with a 45% reduction in hot flash frequency and a 54% reduction in hot flash composite score (frequency and severity) from baseline, compared with 29% (P=.02) and 31% (P=.01) reductions for placebo. Four patients (13%) on gabapentin and one (3%) on placebo withdrew because of adverse events; 15 patients (50.0%) on gabapentin reported at least one adverse event versus 8 (27.6%) on placebo. In the open-label higher-dose phase, reductions reached 54% (frequency) and 67% (composite).
cards.watchOut: Fifty-nine women and a placebo response of 29-31% — the absolute drug advantage is roughly 16-23 percentage points of symptom reduction; the open-label dose-escalation phase is uncontrolled and its larger figures should not be quoted as trial evidence.
cards.source: Guttuso T Jr et al. Gabapentin's effects on hot flashes in postmenopausal women: a randomized controlled trial. Obstet Gynecol. 2003. PMID: 12576259. cards.headline: Butt 2008: gabapentin cut hot-flush scores by 51% versus 26% on placebo at 4 weeks (200 women)
cards.summary: Butt 2008: gabapentin cut hot-flush scores by 51% versus 26% on placebo at 4 weeks (200 women)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (community and primary care, Toronto)
cards.people: 200 women in natural menopause aged 45-65 years with at least 14 hot flashes per week, recruited across the Greater Toronto area (March 2004 to April 2006), randomised to gabapentin 300 mg three times daily or placebo for 4 weeks; 197 participants were analysed and 193 (98%) completed the study. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Hot flash scores decreased by 51% (95% CI 43% to 58%) in the gabapentin group compared with 26% (95% CI 18% to 35%) on placebo from baseline to week 4 (P<0.001). The Menopause-Specific Quality-of-Life vasomotor score decreased by 1.7 (95% CI 1.3 to 2.1; P<0.001) in the gabapentin group. Dizziness (18%), unsteadiness (14%) and drowsiness (12%) were more frequent on gabapentin at week 1, improved by week 2, and returned to baseline levels by week 4.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is the shortest useful horizon — the trial shows gabapentin works quickly, not that it keeps working or stays tolerated over the years women may take it; the early dizziness/unsteadiness signal matters for falls risk in older women even though it faded by week 4 here.

cards.people: 60 postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe hot flushes, randomised double-blind to conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg/day (20), gabapentin titrated to 2,400 mg/day (20), or placebo (20) for 12 weeks, with hot-flush diaries kept for 2 weeks before and 12 weeks after randomisation. shelves.title: Tibolone in older postmenopausal women with osteoporosis: fractures vs stroke (LIFT)
shelves.question: In older postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does tibolone 1.25 mg vs placebo reduce fractures, and at what cost in stroke and other events?
shelves.mesh: Norpregnenes/therapeutic use · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy · Spinal Fractures/prevention & control · Stroke/chemically induced · Bone Density/drug effects · Humans · Female · Aged
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — fracture reduction · LIKELY — increased stroke — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, stroke in the balance). The LIFT trial (4,538 women aged 60-85 with osteoporosis, median 34 months of treatment) found tibolone 1.25 mg daily reduced vertebral fracture (70 versus 126 cases per 1,000 person-years; relative hazard 0.55 relative, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.74; P<0.001) and nonvertebral fracture (122 versus 166 per 1,000 person-years; relative hazard 0.74 relative, 0.58 to 0.93; P=0.01), and reduced invasive breast cancer (relative hazard 0.32 relative, 0.13 to 0.80) and colon cancer (relative hazard 0.31 relative, 0.10 to 0.96). But stroke risk was increased (relative hazard 2.19 relative, 1.14 to 4.23; P=0.02) — a harm large enough that the data and safety monitoring board stopped the trial in February 2006. There were no significant differences in coronary heart disease or venous thromboembolism. In women of this age the stroke harm is the governing fact of the shelf; the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the balance turns on stroke (Tier C).

cards.headline: LIFT 2008: tibolone reduced vertebral fracture (relative hazard 0.55) and nonvertebral fracture (0.74) but increased stroke (2.19) — trial stopped early
cards.summary: LIFT 2008: tibolone reduced vertebral fracture (relative hazard 0.55) and nonvertebral fracture (0.74) but increased stroke (2.19) — trial stopped early
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (LIFT) — stopped early on a safety signal
cards.people: 4,538 women aged 60-85 years with a bone mineral density T score of -2.5 or less at hip or spine, or a T score of -2.0 or less with radiographic vertebral fracture, randomised to once-daily tibolone 1.25 mg or placebo; vertebral fracture was assessed on annual spine radiographs, and cardiovascular events and breast cancer were adjudicated by expert panels. Median treatment duration was 34 months; the trial was stopped in February 2006 on the recommendation of the data and safety monitoring board because of the stroke finding. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Vertebral fracture occurred at 70 cases per 1,000 person-years on tibolone versus 126 on placebo (relative hazard 0.55 relative, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.74; P<0.001) and nonvertebral fracture at 122 versus 166 per 1,000 person-years (relative hazard 0.74 relative, 0.58 to 0.93; P=0.01). Invasive breast cancer was reduced (relative hazard 0.32 relative, 0.13 to 0.80; P=0.02), as was colon cancer (relative hazard 0.31 relative, 0.10 to 0.96; P=0.04). Stroke was increased (relative hazard 2.19 relative, 1.14 to 4.23; P=0.02). There were no significant differences in coronary heart disease or venous thromboembolism.
cards.watchOut: All the headline effects are relative hazards; the abstract gives absolute rates per 1,000 person-years for fractures (70 vs 126; 122 vs 166) but not for stroke, so the absolute stroke excess cannot be computed from the record — the relative doubling in women aged 60-85, whose baseline stroke risk is not negligible, is the caution. Early stopping also means the fracture benefits are estimated over a median 34 months, not a full planned course.
cards.source: Cummings SR et al. The effects of tibolone in older postmenopausal women. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18703472. shelves.title: Dienogest vs placebo for endometriosis-associated pelvic pain
shelves.question: In women with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis, does dienogest 2 mg daily vs placebo reduce pelvic pain over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Endometriosis/drug therapy · Pelvic Pain/drug therapy · Progesterone Congeners/administration & dosage · Pain Measurement/methods · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Strowitzki 2010, 198 women aged 18-45 with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis and pelvic pain of at least 30 mm on a visual analogue scale, at 33 centres in Germany, Italy and Ukraine) found dienogest 2 mg daily reduced pelvic pain more than placebo over 12 weeks — mean VAS reduction 27.4 mm versus 15.1 mm, a difference of 12.3 mm in favour of dienogest (P<0.0001) — with only modest changes in rescue ibuprofen use in both groups and generally good tolerability. The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single trial, 12 weeks long, on a subjective pain-score endpoint, in three European countries. Dienogest is a progestin; the GnRH-antagonist endometriosis shelves (#246, #831) are different drugs and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Strowitzki 2010: dienogest reduced endometriosis pelvic pain by 12.3 mm more than placebo on the VAS over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Strowitzki 2010: dienogest reduced endometriosis pelvic pain by 12.3 mm more than placebo on the VAS over 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (33 centres, three European countries)
cards.people: 198 women aged 18-45 years with laparoscopically confirmed endometriosis and endometriosis-associated pelvic pain scoring at least 30 mm on a visual analogue scale, at 33 centres in Germany, Italy and Ukraine, randomised to oral dienogest 2 mg once daily or placebo for 12 weeks. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Mean reductions in VAS pain score from baseline to week 12 in the full analysis set were 27.4 mm in the dienogest group and 15.1 mm in the placebo group — a significant difference of 12.3 mm in favour of dienogest (P<0.0001). Changes in intake of supportive analgesic medication (ibuprofen) were modest in both groups. Dienogest was generally well tolerated and few adverse events were associated with therapy.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks is a short window for a chronic, fluctuating condition, and a 12.3 mm VAS advantage sits close to commonly used thresholds for a clinically important pain difference; the trial shows a real short-term effect, not durability, recurrence prevention, or fertility benefit — none of which it measured.
cards.source: Strowitzki T et al. Dienogest in the treatment of endometriosis-associated pelvic pain: a 12-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. shelves.title: Route of hysterectomy for benign disease: laparoscopic vs abdominal and vs vaginal (eVALuate)
shelves.question: In women needing hysterectomy for benign disease, how do laparoscopic, abdominal, and vaginal routes compare on major complications, pain, and recovery?
shelves.mesh: Hysterectomy/methods,adverse effects · Hysterectomy, Vaginal/methods · Laparoscopy/methods,adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Length of Stay · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The eVALuate programme ran two parallel multicentre randomised trials (1,380 women recruited; 1,346 had surgery). In the abdominal trial, laparoscopic hysterectomy caused MORE major complications than abdominal hysterectomy (11.1% versus 6.2%; P=0.02; difference 4.9 percentage points, 95% CI 0.9 to 9.1; number needed to treat to harm 20) and took longer (84 versus 50 minutes), but was less painful (VAS 3.51 versus 3.88; P=0.01), shortened hospital stay (3 versus 4 days), and gave less pain and better quality of life at six weeks. In the vaginal trial, major complications did not differ between laparoscopic and vaginal hysterectomy (9.8% versus 9.5%; P=0.92) — but that trial was underpowered and is inconclusive on complications; vaginal hysterectomy was much quicker (39 versus 72 minutes). The record's own conclusion is the balance: laparoscopy versus abdomen trades a higher major-complication rate for a faster, less painful recovery; against the vaginal route it showed no advantage and took twice as long.

cards.headline: eVALuate 2004: laparoscopic hysterectomy had more major complications than abdominal (11.1% vs 6.2%) but less pain and faster recovery; vs vaginal, no difference and slower
cards.summary: eVALuate 2004: laparoscopic hysterectomy had more major complications than abdominal (11.1% vs 6.2%) but less pain and faster recovery; vs vaginal, no difference and slower
cards.type: Two parallel multicentre randomised trials (eVALuate; UK and South Africa)
cards.people: 1,380 women needing hysterectomy for benign disease recruited at 28 UK centres and two South African centres into two parallel randomised trials (abdominal trial: laparoscopic versus abdominal hysterectomy; vaginal trial: laparoscopic versus vaginal hysterectomy); 1,346 had surgery and 937 were followed up at one year. The primary outcome was the rate of major complications. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Abdominal trial: laparoscopic hysterectomy was associated with a higher rate of major complications than abdominal hysterectomy (11.1% versus 6.2%; P=0.02; difference 4.9%, 95% confidence interval 0.9% to 9.1%), with a number needed to treat to harm of 20. Laparoscopy took longer (84 versus 50 minutes) but was less painful (visual analogue scale 3.51 versus 3.88; P=0.01) and shortened hospital stay (3 versus 4 days); at six weeks it was associated with less pain and better quality of life. Vaginal trial: no evidence of a difference in major complications between laparoscopic and vaginal hysterectomy (9.8% versus 9.5%; P=0.92; difference 0.3%, -5.2% to 5.8%; number needed to treat to harm 333); laparoscopy took longer (72 versus 39 minutes) and detected more unexpected pathology (16.4% versus 4.8%; P<0.01). The vaginal trial was underpowered.
cards.watchOut: These are 2004-era results from the laparoscopic learning-curve period — complication rates for laparoscopy in trained modern practice may differ, and the comparison should be quoted as the trial of its era that it is; and the vaginal trial's null is an underpowered null, which the authors state plainly and this card repeats.
cards.source: Garry R et al. The eVALuate study: two parallel randomised trials, one comparing laparoscopic with abdominal hysterectomy, the other comparing laparoscopic with vaginal hysterectomy. BMJ. 2004. PMID: 14711749. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: route choice is a trade, and the vaginal route was never beaten — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: route choice is a trade, and the vaginal route was never beaten — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: eVALuate 2004 (1,380 women in two parallel trials).
cards.result: Read together, the two trials support: (1) laparoscopic versus abdominal — expect about 1 extra major complication per 20 laparoscopic cases in exchange for a day less in hospital, less pain and better early quality of life; (2) laparoscopic versus vaginal — no demonstrated advantage, double the operating time. shelves.title: Systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy vs no lymphadenectomy in early endometrial cancer (ASTEC)
shelves.question: In women with endometrial cancer apparently confined to the uterus, does adding systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy to hysterectomy/BSO improve overall or recurrence-free survival?
shelves.mesh: Endometrial Neoplasms/surgery · Lymph Node Excision/methods · Hysterectomy/methods · Disease-Free Survival · Survival Analysis · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the primary claim is survival): Two randomised trials agree that adding systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy to hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy does not improve survival in early endometrial cancer. MRC ASTEC (Kitchener 2009, 1,408 women) found adjusted hazard ratios of 1.04 relative (95% CI 0.74 to 1.45) for overall survival and 1.25 relative (0.93 to 1.66) for recurrence-free survival — the unadjusted analyses leaned against lymphadenectomy (overall survival HR 1.16; recurrence-free survival HR 1.35, P=0.017). The Italian trial (Benedetti Panici 2008, 514 women) found 5-year disease-free survival of 81.0% with lymphadenectomy versus 81.7% without, and overall survival of 85.9% versus 90.0%, while lymphadenectomy found more node metastases (13.3% vs 3.2%) — better staging information — and caused significantly more early and late postoperative complications (81 versus 34 patients with complications; P=.001). More surgery, more staging information, more complications, no survival gain. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict because the outcome is survival (Tier C).

cards.headline: ASTEC 2009: pelvic lymphadenectomy did not improve overall or recurrence-free survival in early endometrial cancer (adjusted HR 1.04 and 1.25)
cards.summary: ASTEC 2009: pelvic lymphadenectomy did not improve overall or recurrence-free survival in early endometrial cancer (adjusted HR 1.04 and 1.25)
cards.type: Randomised trial (MRC ASTEC surgical trial; 85 centres, four countries)
cards.people: 1,408 women with histologically proven endometrial carcinoma thought preoperatively to be confined to the corpus, at 85 centres in four countries, randomly allocated to standard surgery (hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, peritoneal washings, palpation of para-aortic nodes; 704) or standard surgery plus systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy (704); median follow-up 37 months (IQR 24-58). Mean age is not stated in the abstract; MeSH records the population as Adult, Aged and Aged 80 and over.
cards.result: After median follow-up of 37 months, 191 women had died (88 standard surgery, 103 lymphadenectomy): hazard ratio 1.16 relative (95% CI 0.87 to 1.54; p=0.31) in favour of standard surgery, with an absolute difference in 5-year overall survival of 1% (95% CI -4 to 6). Death or recurrence occurred in 251 women (107 versus 144): hazard ratio 1.35 relative (1.06 to 1.73; p=0.017) in favour of standard surgery, an absolute 5-year recurrence-free survival difference of 6% (1 to 12). Adjusted for baseline characteristics and pathology, the hazard ratios were 1.04 relative (0.74 to 1.45; p=0.83) for overall survival and 1.25 relative (0.93 to 1.66; p=0.14) for recurrence-free survival. The authors conclude there is no evidence of benefit and that pelvic lymphadenectomy cannot be recommended as a routine therapeutic procedure outside clinical trials.
cards.watchOut: The unadjusted recurrence-free survival analysis significantly favoured NOT removing nodes (HR 1.35) — adjustment attenuated it, but nothing in either analysis leans toward a lymphadenectomy benefit; quote adjusted and unadjusted together, as this card does, rather than selecting the neutral-looking one.
cards.source: Kitchener H et al; ASTEC Study Group. Efficacy of systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy in endometrial cancer (MRC ASTEC trial): a randomised study. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19070889. cards.summary: Benedetti Panici 2008: lymphadenectomy improved staging (node metastases found in 13.3% vs 3.2%) but not survival, and caused more complications
cards.people: 514 eligible patients with preoperative FIGO stage I endometrial carcinoma, randomised from October 1996 to March 2006 to pelvic systematic lymphadenectomy (264; median 30 nodes removed, IQR 22-42) or no lymphadenectomy (250; median 0 nodes); median follow-up 49 months. cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ASTEC 2009 (1,408 women) and Benedetti Panici 2008 (514 women) — 1,922 randomised women.
cards.result: Two trials, two countries' systems, one answer: systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy in apparently uterus-confined endometrial cancer finds more positive nodes (13.3% vs 3.2%), generates more complications, and does not extend overall or recurrence-free survival (adjusted HRs 1.04 and 1.25 in the larger trial). Node information may guide adjuvant therapy decisions in individual cases, but as a routine therapeutic procedure the randomised verdict is no benefit. The stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: These trials predate sentinel-lymph-node mapping, which aims to keep the staging information at a fraction of the surgical cost; the null here is about systematic full lymphadenectomy and should not be quoted against sentinel-node biopsy, a different intervention.

shelves.title: Primary HPV testing vs cytology for cervical cancer screening (HPV FOCAL)
shelves.question: In women in an organised screening programme, does primary HPV testing vs liquid-based cytology reduce high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN3+) detected by 48 months?
shelves.mesh: Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/diagnosis,prevention & control · Papillomavirus Infections/diagnosis · Papanicolaou Test · Vaginal Smears · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial inside an organised screening programme (HPV FOCAL, Ogilvie 2018, 19,009 women aged 25-65 in Canada; 16,374 completed) found that primary HPV testing was followed by significantly less high-grade disease detected at the 48-month exit screen than cytology-based screening: CIN3+ incidence 2.3 per 1,000 versus 5.5 per 1,000 (risk ratio 0.42 relative, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69) and CIN2+ incidence 5.0 per 1,000 versus 10.6 per 1,000 (risk ratio 0.47 relative, 0.34 to 0.67). Women negative on HPV at baseline also had lower subsequent CIN3+ incidence than cytology-negative women (1.4 per 1,000; risk ratio 0.25 relative, 0.13 to 0.48). The stamp is POSSIBLE: a single (very large) trial, and the outcome is detection of CIN3+ — a surrogate for cervical cancer incidence and mortality, which the trial did not measure; fewer lesions at exit is the expected signature of earlier detection and clearance in the HPV arm, and its translation into fewer cancers requires the longer evidence this one trial does not contain.

cards.headline: HPV FOCAL 2018: primary HPV testing was followed by less CIN3+ at 48 months than cytology (2.3 vs 5.5 per 1,000; RR 0.42 relative)
cards.summary: HPV FOCAL 2018: primary HPV testing was followed by less CIN3+ at 48 months than cytology (2.3 vs 5.5 per 1,000; RR 0.42 relative)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial within an organised screening programme (Canada)
cards.people: 19,009 women aged 25-65 years in an organised cervical cancer screening programme in Canada (recruited through 224 clinicians, January 2008 to May 2012; no CIN2+ in the past 5 years, no invasive cervical cancer, no hysterectomy, no Pap test in the past 12 months, not immunosuppressed), randomised to primary HPV testing (9,552) or liquid-based cytology (9,457); mean age 45 years; 16,374 women (86.9% and 85.4%) completed the study. In the HPV arm, test-negative women returned at 48 months; in the cytology arm, negative women were re-tested at 24 months and again at 48; at the 48-month exit both groups received HPV and cytology co-testing.
cards.result: At 48 months, the CIN3+ incidence rate was 2.3 per 1,000 (95% CI 1.5 to 3.5) in the HPV group and 5.5 per 1,000 (4.2 to 7.2) in the cytology group (risk ratio 0.42 relative, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.69). The CIN2+ incidence rate was 5.0 per 1,000 (3.8 to 6.7) versus 10.6 per 1,000 (8.7 to 12.9) (risk ratio 0.47 relative, 0.34 to 0.67). Among baseline-negative women, cumulative CIN3+ incidence at 48 months was significantly lower after a negative HPV test (1.4 per 1,000; 0.8 to 2.4) than after negative cytology (risk ratio 0.25 relative, 0.13 to 0.48).
cards.watchOut: Interpretation discipline matters: the HPV arm had its prevalent lesions found and treated at baseline, so less disease at exit is the designed consequence of a more sensitive first screen — it demonstrates earlier detection and a safer negative test, not (yet) fewer cancers or deaths; and the screening intervals differed by design between arms (negative HPV → 48 months; negative cytology → 24 months), which is part of the strategy being tested.
cards.source: Ogilvie GS et al. Effect of Screening With Primary Cervical HPV Testing vs Cytology Testing on High-grade Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia at 48 Months: The HPV FOCAL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29971397. Registry ID: ISRCTN79347302, stated in the record's abstract (no databank-field registry ID). cards.summary: Synthesis: a more sensitive first screen with a safer negative — on a surrogate outcome, POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: HPV FOCAL 2018 (19,009 randomised women; 16,374 completed).
cards.result: The trial supports primary HPV testing as the more effective screening strategy on the outcome it measured: roughly half the high-grade lesions remained to be found at 48 months (CIN3+ risk ratio 0.42 relative; CIN2+ 0.47 relative), and an HPV-negative result carried about a quarter of the subsequent CIN3+ risk of a cytology-negative result (risk ratio 0.25 relative). shelves.title: Hysteroscopic morcellation vs electrosurgical resection for endometrial polyps
shelves.question: In women undergoing office hysteroscopic polypectomy, is morcellation vs bipolar electrosurgical resection faster, less painful, and more complete?
shelves.mesh: Hysteroscopy/methods · Polyps/surgery · Electrosurgery · Uterine Diseases/surgery · Single-Blind Method · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised trials agree that hysteroscopic morcellation is faster and at least as complete as electrosurgical resection for endometrial polyps. Smith 2014 (121 women, office setting, multicentre, single-blind) found morcellation quicker (median 5 minutes 28 seconds versus 10 minutes 12 seconds; P<.001), less painful (mean pain 35.9 versus 52.0 on a 100-mm scale; difference -16.1 points, 95% CI -24.7 to -7.6; P<.001) and more often complete (61 of 62, 98%, versus 49 of 59, 83%; odds ratio 12.5 relative, 95% CI 1.5 to 100.6; P=.02), with 99% of women finding office polypectomy acceptable. RESMO (Stoll 2021, 90 women, single centre, reusable morcellator) found the same direction on Bayesian analysis — shorter morcellation (6.1 vs 9 minutes) and total operating time (12.7 vs 15.6 minutes), fewer device insertions (1.5 vs 6), less fluid used and smaller fluid deficit, and better operator comfort — with no difference in pain or hospital stay. The stamp is POSSIBLE: the outcomes are procedural (time, pain, completeness), both trials are small, and RESMO's analysis is Bayesian with probability statements rather than conventional confidence intervals.

cards.headline: Smith 2014: office morcellation was quicker (5:28 vs 10:12), less painful (35.9 vs 52.0) and more complete (98% vs 83%) than electrosurgical resection
cards.summary: Smith 2014: office morcellation was quicker (5:28 vs 10:12), less painful (35.9 vs 52.0) and more complete (98% vs 83%) than electrosurgical resection
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blind, randomised controlled trial (office setting)
cards.people: 121 women randomly allocated to office hysteroscopic polyp removal by morcellation or bipolar electrosurgical resection, in a multicentre single-blind randomised trial; procedure time was measured from insertion to removal of vaginal instrumentation, and pain on a 100-mm visual analogue scale. Mean age is not stated in the abstract; MeSH records the population as Adult, Middle Aged and Aged women.
cards.result: The median time to complete the procedure was 5 minutes 28 seconds for morcellation versus 10 minutes 12 seconds for electrosurgical resection (P<.001). Polyps were completely removed in 61 of 62 women (98%) assigned to morcellation versus 49 of 59 (83%) treated with electrosurgical resection (odds ratio 12.5 relative, 95% CI 1.5 to 100.6; P=.02). Mean pain scores favoured morcellation by 16.1 points (35.9 versus 52.0; 95% CI for the difference -24.7 to -7.6; P<.001). Overall, 99% of women found office polypectomy acceptable; only one woman, in the resection group, found it unacceptable.
cards.watchOut: The completeness odds ratio (12.5 relative) has a very wide interval (1.5 to 100.6) because incomplete removals were rare — the absolute difference is 98% versus 83%, and that is the figure to quote; the trial is also from the first generation of office morcellators, and specimen handling for histology differs between techniques in ways a time-and-pain trial does not settle.
cards.source: Smith PP et al. Hysteroscopic morcellation compared with electrical resection of endometrial polyps: a randomized controlled trial. Obstet Gynecol. 2014. PMID: 24785600. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01509313, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: RESMO 2021: a reusable morcellator was quicker, used less fluid and needed fewer insertions than a resectoscope (90 women)
cards.summary: RESMO 2021: a reusable morcellator was quicker, used less fluid and needed fewer insertions than a resectoscope (90 women)
cards.type: Single-centre, randomised, prospective, single-blind trial (Strasbourg, France) — Bayesian analysis
cards.people: 90 patients presenting with a single endometrial polyp of at least 1 cm (average polyp size 13.3 mm) at a teaching hospital in Strasbourg, France, randomised to hysteroscopic morcellation (45) or standard resectoscope resection (45) in a single-blind prospective trial, with office review hysteroscopy 6-8 weeks after surgery; statistical analyses followed Bayesian methods. Mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Morcellation time was lower than resection time (6.1 versus 9 minutes; posterior probability that morcellation is faster .996), as were total operating time (12.7 versus 15.6 minutes; probability .985), number of device insertions (1.50 versus 6; probability above .999), volume of fluid used (766.9 versus 1,118.9 mL; probability .994) and fluid deficit (60.2 versus 169.8 mL; probability .989). Operator comfort (8.4 versus 7.4; probability .999) and visualisation (4 versus 3.7; probability .911) favoured morcellation. Operative complications were higher in the resection group (5 versus 0; probability .989). No differences were noted for pain assessment, length of hospitalisation, or outcome at review hysteroscopy.
cards.watchOut: One patient in the resection group died after surgery from an anaesthetic complication (anaphylactic shock complicated by pulmonary embolism), as the record reports — an anaesthetic event, not a device effect, but it belongs on the card of a trial this small. The Bayesian probability statements are not P values or confidence intervals and should not be rewritten as either; and with one polyp of at least 1 cm per patient, results do not cover multiple or very large polyps.
cards.source: Stoll F et al. Randomized Study Comparing a Reusable Morcellator with a Resectoscope in the Hysteroscopic Treatment of Uterine Polyps: The RESMO Study. J Minim Invasive Gynecol. 2021. PMID: 32681995 (journal year 2021; the record was published online in 2020). Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: Bayes Theorem · Female · Humans · Hysteroscopy · Polyps/surgery · Pregnancy · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Uterine Neoplasms

cards.headline: Synthesis: faster, gentler, at least as complete — on procedural outcomes in two small trials, POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster, gentler, at least as complete — on procedural outcomes in two small trials, POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Smith 2014 (121 women, office, multicentre) and RESMO 2021 (90 women, single centre, operating setting) — 211 women.
cards.result: Across settings, morcellation roughly halved the active procedure time, reduced pain in the office trial (35.9 vs 52.0), and removed polyps completely at least as often (98% vs 83% in the trial that reported it conventionally). Nothing here addresses recurrence, fertility or cost per completed treatment beyond the procedure itself; for the question asked — how to remove the polyp — the direction is consistent and the grade is POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Device generations and operator experience move fast in operative hysteroscopy; these 2014 and 2021 comparisons grade the techniques as trialled, and a department's own learning curve may matter more than the between-device differences shown here.

shelves.title: Planned delivery vs expectant management for late-preterm pre-eclampsia (PHOENIX)
shelves.question: In women with pre-eclampsia at 34–37 weeks, does planned delivery vs expectant management reduce maternal severe morbidity without unacceptable neonatal harm?
shelves.mesh: Pre-Eclampsia/therapy · Delivery, Obstetric/methods · Watchful Waiting · Gestational Age · Pregnancy Outcome · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, severe maternal morbidity composite): One large multicentre randomised trial (PHOENIX, 901 women in 46 UK maternity units) found planned delivery reduced the co-primary maternal outcome (maternal morbidity composite or systolic blood pressure ≥160 mm Hg) from 75% to 65% (adjusted relative risk 0.86 relative, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.94; P=0.0005). The trade-off is real and is printed on the card: the co-primary perinatal outcome (perinatal death or neonatal unit admission) was significantly HIGHER with planned delivery (42% vs 34% of infants; adjusted relative risk 1.26 relative, 1.08 to 1.47; P=0.0034) — the trial's perinatal non-inferiority hypothesis was not met — although indicators of neonatal morbidity itself were similar, and 2-year neurodevelopment scores were within the normal range in both groups (PARCA-R 89.5 vs 91.9; adjusted difference −2.4 points, −5.4 to 0.5). Planned delivery was also cost-saving in the trial's health-technology assessment. The topic file anchored this shelf to the HTA full report (PMID 36547875); the primary trial report is the Lancet 2019 paper (PMID 31472930), which is carded first here, with the HTA report and the 2-year follow-up fenced as reports of the same single trial, not as independent evidence.

cards.headline: PHOENIX 2019 (primary report): planned delivery cut the maternal morbidity/severe-hypertension composite (65% vs 75%) but raised the perinatal death/neonatal-unit-admission composite (42% vs 34%)
cards.summary: PHOENIX 2019 (primary report): planned delivery cut the maternal morbidity/severe-hypertension composite (65% vs 75%) but raised the perinatal death/neonatal-unit-admission composite (42% vs 34%)
cards.type: Parallel-group, non-masked, multicentre randomised controlled trial (46 maternity units, England and Wales)
cards.people: 901 women with late preterm pre-eclampsia at 34 to less than 37 weeks' gestation with a singleton or dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy, recruited Sept 2014 to Dec 2018: 450 allocated to planned delivery (448 women and 471 infants analysed) and 451 to expectant management (451 women and 475 infants analysed). The abstract does not state mean age or ethnic mix.
cards.result: The co-primary maternal outcome (composite of maternal morbidity or recorded systolic blood pressure of at least 160 mm Hg) occurred in 289 (65%) women with planned delivery versus 338 (75%) with expectant management (adjusted relative risk 0.86 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.79 to 0.94; P=0.0005). The co-primary perinatal outcome (composite of perinatal deaths or neonatal unit admission to infant hospital discharge) occurred in 196 (42%) infants versus 159 (34%) (adjusted relative risk 1.26 relative, 1.08 to 1.47; P=0.0034) — significantly higher with planned delivery, against the trial's non-inferiority hypothesis (margin 10 percentage points); per-protocol results were similar. There were nine serious adverse events in the planned delivery group and 12 in the expectant management group. The authors conclude planned delivery reduces maternal morbidity and severe hypertension, with more neonatal unit admissions related to prematurity but no indicators of greater neonatal morbidity.
cards.watchOut: The two co-primary outcomes point in opposite directions, and the perinatal composite is dominated by neonatal unit admissions for prematurity rather than by deaths or morbidity, which were similar. Any summary that reports only the maternal benefit — or only the admission increase — misrepresents the trial; the shelf's claim is the trade-off itself, to be settled by shared decision-making.
cards.source: Chappell LC et al. Planned early delivery or expectant management for late preterm pre-eclampsia (PHOENIX): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31472930. Registry ID: ISRCTN01879376, stated in the record's abstract and databank fields. cards.summary: PHOENIX HTA report 2023 and 2-year follow-up 2022 (same trial): development scores normal in both groups at 2 years; planned delivery cost-saving
cards.type: Full health-technology-assessment report and 2-year follow-up report of the same PHOENIX trial — counted once as evidence
cards.people: The same 901 randomised women and their infants. At 2-year follow-up, outcome data were available for 290 infants (276 women) in the planned delivery group and 256 infants (251 women) in the expectant management group — around 60% of parents returned scores, as the reports state.
cards.result: The HTA report (PMID 36547875) restates the primary results identically (maternal outcome 65% vs 75%, adjusted relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.79 to 0.94; perinatal outcome 42% vs 34%, adjusted relative risk 1.26 relative, 1.08 to 1.47) and adds that planned delivery was significantly cost-saving (−£2711, 95% CI −£4840 to −£637). The standalone follow-up paper (PMID 35362666) reports the same scores and notes the lower-than-anticipated follow-up rate limited power.
cards.watchOut: These are two further reports of one trial, not replication: the 2-year developmental reassurance rests on roughly 60% follow-up, and the cost-saving figure is a UK health-service estimate from the trial's embedded economic evaluation, not a clinical outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: planned delivery protects the mother and costs the baby unit admissions, not measurable morbidity — LIKELY, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: planned delivery protects the mother and costs the baby unit admissions, not measurable morbidity — LIKELY, Tier C
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PHOENIX (901 women, 946 infants analysed) with its HTA report and 2-year follow-up — one trial programme.
cards.result: A single large, well-run trial supports a genuine trade-off: about 10 fewer women per 100 reach the maternal morbidity/severe-hypertension composite with planned delivery (65% vs 75%), while about 8 more infants per 100 are admitted to a neonatal unit (42% vs 34%), without detected excess neonatal morbidity and with normal-range development at 2 years in both arms. shelves.title: Planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth for twin pregnancy (Twin Birth Study)
shelves.question: In women with a twin pregnancy and a cephalic first twin at 32–38 weeks, does planned caesarean vs planned vaginal birth reduce perinatal death or serious neonatal morbidity?
shelves.mesh: Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Delivery, Obstetric/methods,statistics & numerical data · Perinatal Mortality · Pregnancy, Twin · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, perinatal death inside the primary composite): One very large international randomised trial (Twin Birth Study, 2,804 women, 5,607 fetuses) found no significant difference in the composite of fetal or neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity between planned caesarean and planned vaginal delivery (2.2% vs 1.9% of fetuses/infants; odds ratio 1.16 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.74; P=0.49). A single trial, however large, caps at POSSIBLE on this library's scale. Two features qualify the null: 43.8% of the planned-vaginal group ultimately delivered by caesarean, and the trial required a cephalic first twin and centres able to offer intrapartum caesarean.

cards.headline: Twin Birth Study 2013: planned caesarean did not reduce fetal/neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity versus planned vaginal delivery (2.2% vs 1.9%)
cards.summary: Twin Birth Study 2013: planned caesarean did not reduce fetal/neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity versus planned vaginal delivery (2.2% vs 1.9%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (planned mode of delivery, intention-to-treat)
cards.people: 2,804 women between 32 weeks 0 days and 38 weeks 6 days of gestation with a twin pregnancy and the first twin in cephalic presentation: 1,398 women (2,795 fetuses) assigned to planned caesarean delivery and 1,406 women (2,812 fetuses) to planned vaginal delivery with caesarean only if indicated; elective delivery was planned between 37 weeks 5 days and 38 weeks 6 days. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (fetal or neonatal death or serious neonatal morbidity, fetus/infant as the unit of analysis) occurred in 2.2% of the planned-caesarean group and 1.9% of the planned-vaginal group (odds ratio with planned caesarean delivery 1.16 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 1.74; P=0.49). shelves.title: Antenatal betamethasone for women at risk of late preterm delivery (ALPS)
shelves.question: In singleton pregnancies at 34+0 to 36+5 weeks at high risk of late preterm delivery, does betamethasone vs placebo reduce neonatal respiratory complications?
shelves.mesh: Betamethasone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Hypoglycemia/chemically induced · Infant, Premature, Diseases/prevention & control · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, precautionary — stillbirth/neonatal death inside the primary composite; the claim itself is respiratory): One large multicentre double-blind trial (ALPS, 2,827 infants) found betamethasone reduced the primary neonatal composite (respiratory treatment in the first 72 hours, or stillbirth/neonatal death within 72 hours) from 14.4% to 11.6% (relative risk 0.80 relative, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P=0.02), with severe respiratory complications, transient tachypnoea, surfactant use and bronchopulmonary dysplasia also significantly less frequent. The price was neonatal hypoglycaemia: 24.0% vs 15.0% (relative risk 1.60 relative, 1.37 to 1.87; P<0.001). A single trial earns POSSIBLE; the long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up of steroid exposure at this gestation is not part of this record. This shelf is the late-preterm population only — early-preterm antenatal corticosteroids are a different shelf (#1132).

cards.headline: ALPS 2016: betamethasone reduced the neonatal respiratory composite (11.6% vs 14.4%) and increased neonatal hypoglycaemia (24.0% vs 15.0%)
cards.summary: ALPS 2016: betamethasone reduced the neonatal respiratory composite (11.6% vs 14.4%) and increased neonatal hypoglycaemia (24.0% vs 15.0%)
cards.people: Women with a singleton pregnancy at 34 weeks 0 days to 36 weeks 5 days of gestation at high risk for delivery during the late preterm period, assigned to two injections of betamethasone or matching placebo 24 hours apart; the primary outcome was assessed in 1,427 infants in the betamethasone group and 1,400 in the placebo group. The abstract does not state mean maternal age or ethnic mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a neonatal composite of treatment in the first 72 hours (continuous positive airway pressure or high-flow nasal cannula for at least 2 hours, supplemental oxygen with a fraction of inspired oxygen of at least 0.30 for at least 4 hours, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, or mechanical ventilation) or stillbirth or neonatal death within 72 hours — occurred in 165 of 1,427 infants (11.6%) on betamethasone versus 202 of 1,400 (14.4%) on placebo (relative risk 0.80 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.66 to 0.97; P=0.02). Severe respiratory complications, transient tachypnea of the newborn, surfactant use, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia also occurred significantly less frequently in the betamethasone group. There were no significant between-group differences in chorioamnionitis or neonatal sepsis. Neonatal hypoglycemia was more common with betamethasone (24.0% vs 15.0%; relative risk 1.60 relative, 1.37 to 1.87; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The composite is overwhelmingly respiratory treatment, not death — stillbirth/neonatal death is a component but the trial's claim is fewer babies needing respiratory support, at the cost of substantially more neonatal hypoglycaemia (an absolute increase of about 9 babies per 100). The abstract reports no long-term follow-up, so the shelf cannot speak to later neurodevelopment.
cards.source: Gyamfi-Bannerman C et al. Antenatal Betamethasone for Women at Risk for Late Preterm Delivery. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26842679. shelves.title: Nifedipine vs atosiban tocolysis for threatened preterm birth (APOSTEL III)
shelves.question: In women with threatened preterm birth at 25–34 weeks, does nifedipine vs atosiban improve perinatal outcome?
shelves.mesh: Nifedipine/administration & dosage · Calcium Channel Blockers/administration & dosage · Perinatal Mortality · Tocolytic Agents · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, perinatal death inside the composite): One multicentre open-label randomised trial (APOSTEL III, 510 women, 591 babies with outcome data) found no significant difference in the composite adverse perinatal outcome between 48 hours of oral nifedipine and intravenous atosiban (14% vs 15% of babies; relative risk 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.37). The figure that keeps this shelf honest is printed on the card: perinatal deaths were numerically more frequent with nifedipine (16 babies, 5%, vs 7, 2%; relative risk 2.20 relative, 0.91 to 5.33) — not significant, all deaths judged unlikely to be drug-related, and the trial was not powered for mortality — but the direction is against nifedipine and no summary may omit it. Maternal adverse events did not differ. A single trial caps at POSSIBLE; the authors themselves call for large placebo-controlled trials, because neither drug has beaten placebo on perinatal outcomes in a trial of this design.

cards.headline: APOSTEL III 2016: no difference in the adverse perinatal composite between nifedipine and atosiban (14% vs 15%); perinatal deaths 5% vs 2% (relative risk 2.20 relative, not significant)
cards.summary: APOSTEL III 2016: no difference in the adverse perinatal composite between nifedipine and atosiban (14% vs 15%); perinatal deaths 5% vs 2% (relative risk 2.20 relative, not significant)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised controlled trial (open-label; clinicians, assessors and women unmasked), 19 hospitals in the Netherlands and Belgium
cards.people: 510 women with threatened preterm birth at 25–34 weeks' gestation, randomly assigned to oral nifedipine (254) or intravenous atosiban (256) for 48 hours; primary outcome data were available for 248 women and 297 babies (nifedipine) and 255 women and 294 babies (atosiban). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite of adverse perinatal outcomes (perinatal mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, sepsis, intraventricular haemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, and necrotising enterocolitis) occurred in 42 babies (14%) in the nifedipine group and 45 (15%) in the atosiban group (relative risk 0.91 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.61 to 1.37). Sixteen babies (5%) died in the nifedipine group and seven (2%) in the atosiban group (relative risk 2.20 relative, 0.91 to 5.33); all deaths were deemed unlikely to be related to the study drug. Maternal adverse events did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: An unmasked trial with a mortality imbalance inside a null composite: the death difference is compatible with chance (interval 0.91 to 5.33 relative) and with a real harm, and the adjudication that deaths were 'unlikely related' was made in an open-label study. The composite null must never be quoted without the mortality line beside it.
cards.source: van Vliet EOG et al. Nifedipine versus atosiban for threatened preterm birth (APOSTEL III): a multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 26944026. shelves.title: Immersion in water during the first stage of labour
shelves.question: In low-risk women in labour, does immersion in water during the first stage vs standard care reduce use of epidural/spinal analgesia and other interventions?
shelves.mesh: Immersion · Labor Stage, First · Analgesia, Obstetrical/statistics & numerical data · Natural Childbirth · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pooled randomised evidence (Cochrane review, Cluett 2018: 15 trials, 3,663 women) finds first-stage water immersion probably has little or no effect on mode of birth or perineal trauma, but modestly reduces use of regional analgesia — from 43% to 39% of women (relative risk 0.91 relative, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99; 5 trials, 2,439 women; moderate-quality evidence) — with no evidence of increased adverse effects for woman or baby, though neonatal outcomes were imprecisely estimated. The one primary trial carded here (Cluett 2004, 99 nulliparous women with dystocia) points the same way on epidural use (47% vs 66%; relative risk 0.71 relative, 0.49 to 1.01) but is a dystocia-management trial, not a low-risk first-stage trial, and it recorded more neonatal unit admissions in the water group (6 vs 0; P=0.013) — printed on its card. Unblindable intervention, small absolute analgesia effect, and a review-level anchor cap the stamp at POSSIBLE. The Cochrane review is carded as what it is — a systematic review of the primary trials — because no single trial answers this question at scale.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2018 (15 RCTs, 3,663 women): first-stage immersion modestly reduced regional analgesia use (43% to 39%; relative risk 0.91 relative) with little or no difference in mode of birth
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018 (15 RCTs, 3,663 women): first-stage immersion modestly reduced regional analgesia use (43% to 39%; relative risk 0.91 relative) with little or no difference in mode of birth
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane) — the pooled primary-trial evidence for this question
cards.people: 15 randomised trials conducted 1990–2015 including 3,663 women: eight of first-stage immersion, two of second-stage only, four of first and second stages, and one of early versus late first-stage immersion; all in hospital labour wards, in healthy low-risk women at term with a singleton fetus. Most trial authors did not specify parity.
cards.result: For first-stage immersion versus no immersion: spontaneous vaginal birth 82% versus 83% (relative risk 1.01 relative, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.04; 6 trials, 2,559 women; moderate-quality evidence); instrumental vaginal birth 14% versus 12% (relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.70 to 1.05; low-quality); caesarean section 4% versus 5% (relative risk 1.27 relative, 0.91 to 1.79; low-quality); third- or fourth-degree tears 3% versus 3% (relative risk 1.36 relative, 0.85 to 2.18; moderate-quality). Use of regional analgesia fell from 43% to 39% (relative risk 0.91 relative, 0.83 to 0.99; 5 trials, 2,439 women; moderate-quality evidence). Perinatal deaths were not reported in the first-stage trials; neonatal unit admission (6% vs 8%; average relative risk 1.30 relative, 0.42 to 3.97; low-quality) and neonatal infection (1% vs 1%; relative risk 2.00 relative, 0.50 to 7.94; very low-quality) were imprecisely estimated. The authors conclude there is no evidence of increased adverse effects to the fetus/neonate or woman from labouring or giving birth in water, with evidence limited by clinical variability and heterogeneity and no trial in a midwifery-led setting.
cards.watchOut: A review card, labelled as such: the intervention cannot be blinded, several pooled estimates are low or very low quality, and 'no evidence of increased adverse effects' is not proof of neonatal safety — the neonatal confidence intervals are wide enough to include substantial harm or benefit.
cards.source: Cluett ER et al. Immersion in water during labour and birth. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018. PMID: 29768662. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial. cards.headline: Cluett 2004 (primary RCT, dystocia): labouring in water reduced epidural use (47% vs 66%) and augmentation, with more neonatal unit admissions (6 vs 0)
cards.summary: Cluett 2004 (primary RCT, dystocia): labouring in water reduced epidural use (47% vs 66%) and augmentation, with more neonatal unit admissions (6 vs 0)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single university teaching hospital, southern England)
cards.people: 99 nulliparous women with dystocia (cervical dilation rate under 1 cm/hour in active labour) at low risk of complications, randomised to immersion in water in a birth pool or to standard augmentation for dystocia (amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin).
cards.result: Women randomised to immersion had a lower rate of epidural analgesia than women allocated to augmentation (47% vs 66%; relative risk 0.71 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.49 to 1.01; number needed to treat for benefit 5). There was no difference in operative delivery (49% vs 50%; relative risk 0.98 relative, 0.65 to 1.47), but fewer women in the water group received augmentation (71% vs 96%; relative risk 0.74 relative, 0.59 to 0.88) or any obstetric intervention (80% vs 98%; relative risk 0.81 relative, 0.67 to 0.92). More neonates of women in the water group were admitted to the neonatal unit (6 vs 0, P=0.013), with no difference in Apgar score, infection rates, or umbilical cord pH.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a neighbouring question — water versus active augmentation for slow progress — in 99 women, not water versus standard care in unselected low-risk labour; its neonatal-admission signal (6 vs 0) is small-number fragile but is printed here because the pooled review's neonatal estimates are too imprecise to dismiss it.
cards.source: Cluett ER et al. Randomised controlled trial of labouring in water compared with standard of augmentation for management of dystocia in first stage of labour. BMJ. 2004. PMID: 14744822. shelves.title: Antenatal dietary and lifestyle intervention in overweight and obese pregnancy (LIMIT & UPBEAT)
shelves.question: In pregnant women who are overweight or obese, does structured dietary/lifestyle advice vs routine care reduce large-for-gestational-age infants or gestational diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Life Style · Diabetes, Gestational/prevention & control · Fetal Macrosomia/prevention & control · Birth Weight · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large unblinded randomised trials agree. LIMIT (Dodd 2014, 2,212 women with BMI ≥25 in South Australia) found no significant reduction in large-for-gestational-age infants (19% vs 21%; adjusted relative risk 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.07; P=0.24) and no differences in maternal pregnancy and birth outcomes; birth weight over 4,000 g was lower (15% vs 19%; relative risk 0.82 relative, 0.68 to 0.99) — a secondary outcome. UPBEAT (Poston 2015, 1,555 women with BMI ≥30 in the UK) found neither co-primary outcome moved: gestational diabetes 25% vs 26% (relative risk 0.96 relative, 0.79 to 1.16) and large-for-gestational-age infants 9% vs 8% (relative risk 1.15 relative, 0.83 to 1.59), despite improvements in dietary glycaemic load, gestational weight gain and physical activity. Advice-based programmes of this intensity do not deliver the birth outcomes they aim at — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). Neither trial was powered for, or showed, hard maternal or perinatal event benefits; the topic file's 'prevention' framing is the trials' own, and the claim tested is risk-factor modification in women without diabetes, distinct from gestational-diabetes treatment (#599).

cards.headline: LIMIT 2014: lifestyle advice did not reduce large-for-gestational-age infants (19% vs 21%; P=0.24) in overweight/obese pregnancy
cards.summary: LIMIT 2014: lifestyle advice did not reduce large-for-gestational-age infants (19% vs 21%; P=0.24) in overweight/obese pregnancy
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (three public maternity hospitals, South Australia; unblinded)
cards.people: 2,212 women with a singleton pregnancy at 10+0 to 20+0 weeks' gestation and BMI ≥25: 1,108 randomised to a comprehensive dietary and lifestyle intervention delivered by research staff and 1,104 to standard care; 2,152 women and 2,142 liveborn infants were included in the analyses. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The risk of the infant being large for gestational age (birth weight ≥90th centile) was not significantly different between groups (lifestyle advice 203/1,075, 19%, vs standard care 224/1,067, 21%; adjusted relative risk 0.90 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 1.07; P=0.24). Infants in the lifestyle group were significantly less likely to have birth weight above 4,000 g (164/1,075, 15%, vs 201/1,067, 19%; relative risk 0.82 relative, 0.68 to 0.99; number needed to treat 28, 15 to 263; P=0.04). There were no differences in maternal pregnancy and birth outcomes, including hypertension, pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes as prespecified secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The single positive finding (birth weight >4,000 g) is a secondary outcome sitting beside a null primary outcome and null maternal outcomes — it should be read as hypothesis-generating, not as the trial's verdict.
cards.source: Dodd JM et al. Antenatal lifestyle advice for women who are overweight or obese: LIMIT randomised trial. BMJ. 2014. PMID: 24513442. cards.summary: UPBEAT 2015: a behavioural intervention in obese pregnancy changed diet and weight gain but not gestational diabetes (25% vs 26%) or large-for-gestational-age infants (9% vs 8%)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (eight hospitals, inner-city UK; unblinded)
cards.people: 1,555 pregnant women older than 16 years with obesity (mean BMI 36.3 kg/m², SD 4.8), recruited at 15–18+6 weeks' gestation: 783 allocated to a behavioural intervention of eight weekly health-trainer-led sessions and 772 to standard antenatal care; 651 and 629 women respectively completed an oral glucose tolerance test. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Gestational diabetes occurred in 160 (25%) women in the intervention group versus 172 (26%) in standard care (risk ratio 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.79 to 1.16; P=0.68). Large-for-gestational-age infants (≥90th customised centile) occurred in 71 (9%) of 761 babies versus 61 (8%) of 751 (relative risk 1.15 relative, 0.83 to 1.59; P=0.40). The intervention did improve secondary measures: reduced dietary glycaemic load, gestational weight gain and maternal sum of skinfold thicknesses, and increased physical activity. Adverse events included neonatal death (three intervention vs two standard care) and fetal death in utero (six vs ten); no maternal deaths were reported, and miscarriage, major obstetric haemorrhage and small-for-gestational-age rates did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Both co-primary outcomes are null while process measures improved — the honest reading is that this intensity of advice changes behaviour modestly without changing the clinical endpoints, not that lifestyle is irrelevant to pregnancy health. Deaths are printed here as reported counts; the trial was not powered for them and no mortality claim is made on this shelf.

shelves.title: Nicotine replacement therapy for smoking cessation in pregnancy (SNAP)
shelves.question: In pregnant smokers, do nicotine patches vs placebo patches increase validated cessation by delivery without harming birth outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Nicotine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Smoking Cessation · Administration, Cutaneous · Medication Adherence · Humans · Female · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large double-blind trial (SNAP, 1,050 pregnant smokers in England) found no significant increase in validated abstinence from quit date until delivery with a 15 mg/16-hour nicotine patch added to behavioural support (9.4% vs 7.6%; odds ratio 1.26 relative, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.96), although abstinence at 1 month was higher (21.3% vs 11.7%). Rates of adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes were similar between groups. The decisive caveat is printed on the card: compliance was very low — only 7.2% of the nicotine group used patches for more than a month — so the trial tests offering patches more than it tests sustained nicotine replacement, and its safety assessment is limited by the same low exposure, as the authors state. A single trial caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: SNAP 2012: nicotine patches did not significantly raise validated abstinence at delivery (9.4% vs 7.6%); only 7.2% used patches beyond a month
cards.summary: SNAP 2012: nicotine patches did not significantly raise validated abstinence at delivery (9.4% vs 7.6%); only 7.2% used patches beyond a month
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (seven hospitals, England)
cards.people: 1,050 pregnant women aged 16 to 50 years, at 12 to 24 weeks' gestation, smoking five or more cigarettes per day, recruited from seven hospitals in England: 521 assigned to 8 weeks of active nicotine patches (15 mg per 16 hours) plus behavioural cessation support and 529 to matched placebo patches plus the same support.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in abstinence from the quit date until delivery (validated by exhaled carbon monoxide or salivary cotinine) between nicotine replacement (9.4%) and placebo (7.6%) (unadjusted odds ratio 1.26 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.82 to 1.96), although the rate was higher at 1 month with nicotine (21.3% vs 11.7%). Compliance was low: only 7.2% of women assigned to nicotine replacement and 2.8% assigned to placebo used patches for more than 1 month. Rates of adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes were similar in the two groups. The authors conclude the patch did not significantly increase abstinence until delivery or the risk of adverse outcomes, but that low compliance substantially limited the assessment of safety.
cards.watchOut: An intention-to-treat null with 93% of the active group effectively untreated after a month cannot exclude a benefit in women who actually keep patches on — and, symmetrically, its reassuring safety finding rests on very little real nicotine exposure. Both limits are the trial's own.
