shelves.title: Intermittent preventive treatment of malaria in pregnancy: dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine vs sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine
shelves.question: In pregnant women in sub-Saharan Africa with high sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance, does IPTp with dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine vs sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine reduce placental malaria and adverse birth outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Antimalarials/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Artemisinins/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Combinations · Malaria/prevention & control · Humans · Female · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in high-resistance East African settings agree that preventive dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (DP) beats sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (SP) on malaria endpoints. In Uganda (Kakuru 2016, 300 women, double-blind), histopathologically confirmed placental malaria was 50.0% on SP versus 34.1% on three-dose DP (P=0.03) and 27.1% on monthly DP (P=0.001), symptomatic malaria episodes were far fewer on DP, and the composite adverse birth outcome was lower with monthly DP (9.2%) than with SP (18.6%; P=0.05) or three-dose DP (21.3%; P=0.02). In western Kenya (Desai 2015, 1,546 women, open-label), malaria infection at delivery was 10% on SP versus 3% on preventive DP (relative risk 0.32 relative, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.56), while the screening-and-treatment DP strategy failed (13%; relative risk 1.23 relative) — only preventive DP works. Two concordant trials earn LIKELY for the malaria endpoints; the birth-outcome benefit rests mainly on one trial's composite and is stated at that strength. The primary placental endpoint is a histopathological measure, as the topic file flagged.

cards.headline: Kakuru 2016 (Uganda): placental malaria 50.0% on SP vs 34.1% (three-dose DP) and 27.1% (monthly DP); adverse birth composite lowest on monthly DP (9.2%)
cards.summary: Kakuru 2016 (Uganda): placental malaria 50.0% on SP vs 34.1% (three-dose DP) and 27.1% (monthly DP); adverse birth composite lowest on monthly DP (9.2%)
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, controlled trial (Uganda, an area of widespread sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance)
cards.people: 300 HIV-uninfected pregnant adolescents or women in Uganda, randomly assigned to sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (106), a three-dose dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine regimen (94), or a monthly dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine regimen (100). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Histopathologically confirmed placental malaria (primary outcome) was significantly higher on sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (50.0%) than on three-dose dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (34.1%, P=0.03) or monthly dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (27.1%, P=0.001). The composite adverse birth outcome was lower on monthly DP (9.2%) than on SP (18.6%, P=0.05) or three-dose DP (21.3%, P=0.02). Symptomatic malaria incidence was significantly higher on SP (41 episodes over 43.0 person-years) than on three-dose DP (12 over 38.2; P=0.001) or monthly DP (0 over 42.3; P<0.001), as was parasitaemia prevalence (40.5% vs 16.6% and 5.2%; both P<0.001). Vomiting after any dose was under 0.4% in each group and adverse events did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A 300-woman trial: the birth-outcome composite difference is one comparison among several (monthly DP also beat three-dose DP on it), and the primary endpoint is placental histopathology — a surrogate for, not a measure of, infant health. The SP resistance level in this Ugandan setting is part of the result; where SP still works, the margin would shrink.
cards.source: Kakuru A et al. Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine for the Prevention of Malaria in Pregnancy. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26962728. cards.headline: Desai 2015 (Kenya): preventive DP cut malaria infection at delivery vs SP (3% vs 10%; relative risk 0.32 relative); screening-and-treatment with DP did not (13%)
cards.summary: Desai 2015 (Kenya): preventive DP cut malaria infection at delivery vs SP (3% vs 10%; relative risk 0.32 relative); screening-and-treatment with DP did not (13%)
cards.type: Open-label, three-group, randomised controlled superiority trial (four sites, western Kenya)
cards.people: 1,546 HIV-negative pregnant women at 16 to 32 weeks' gestation in an area of high malaria transmission and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine resistance, assigned (1:1:1) to intermittent screening and treatment with dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (515), intermittent preventive treatment with dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine (516), or intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine (515); 1,368 (88%) women formed the modified intention-to-treat population for the primary endpoint.
cards.result: Malaria infection at delivery (composite of peripheral or placental parasitaemia by histology, microscopy or rapid diagnostic test) was lower with preventive DP than with preventive SP (15 [3%] of 457 vs 47 [10%] of 459 women; relative risk 0.32 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.18 to 0.56; P<0.0001), but not with screening-and-treatment DP (57 [13%] of 452; relative risk 1.23 relative, 0.86 to 1.77; P=0.26). Preventive DP was also associated with lower incidence of malaria infection during pregnancy (54.4 vs 192.0 events per 100 person-years; incidence rate ratio 0.28 relative, 0.22 to 0.36) and clinical malaria (6.1 vs 37.9 events; 0.16 relative, 0.08 to 0.33) versus SP, whereas screening-and-treatment was associated with higher incidence than SP. The 303 maternal and infant serious adverse events recorded were least frequent in the preventive-DP group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and its primary endpoint is infection at delivery rather than birth outcomes; the trial's negative screening arm is part of the evidence — replacing SP requires giving DP preventively to everyone, not testing and treating. Serious adverse events are reported as a count without a between-group significance test in the abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: preventive DP beats SP on malaria in pregnancy in high-resistance settings — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: preventive DP beats SP on malaria in pregnancy in high-resistance settings — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kakuru 2016 (300 women, Uganda) and Desai 2015 (1,546 women, Kenya).
cards.result: Monthly preventive dihydroartemisinin–piperaquine is the strongest regimen in both trials: placental malaria roughly halved versus SP in Uganda (27.1% vs 50.0%) and infection at delivery cut by about two-thirds in Kenya (3% vs 10%). The adverse-birth-outcome benefit is supported by Kakuru's composite (9.2% monthly DP vs 18.6% SP) and is not independently confirmed at that precision by Desai, whose endpoints were infection-based.
cards.watchOut: Both trials ran where SP resistance is high and transmission intense; they do not show DP is better where SP remains effective, and neither answers cost, feasibility or resistance-selection questions that a programme switch would raise.

shelves.title: Membrane sweeping at term to prevent post-term pregnancy
shelves.question: In low-risk women at term, does membrane sweeping vs no sweeping reduce post-term pregnancy and the need for formal induction?
shelves.mesh: Extraembryonic Membranes · Labor, Induced/methods · Pregnancy, Prolonged/prevention & control · Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The carded anchor is one multicentre randomised trial (de Miranda 2006, 742 low-risk Dutch women at 41 weeks): serial membrane sweeping every 48 hours reduced post-term pregnancy (≥42 weeks) from 41% to 23% (relative risk 0.57 relative, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.71; number needed to treat 6, 4 to 9), with consistent effects in nulliparous (29% vs 46%) and parous (17% vs 34%) women, similar adverse effects except more uncomplicated bleeding with sweeping, and similar other obstetric and neonatal outcomes (two perinatal deaths in each group). The wider literature of smaller sweeping trials is Cochrane-summarised in the same direction, but no pooled record was verified for this shelf, so the stamp rests on the single large trial plus that qualitative concordance: POSSIBLE. The wording on this shelf is the trial's own ('reduce post-term pregnancy'); this is an obstetric timing intervention, not a diabetes-onset claim.

cards.headline: de Miranda 2006: serial membrane sweeping from 41 weeks cut post-term pregnancy from 41% to 23% (relative risk 0.57 relative; NNT 6)
cards.summary: de Miranda 2006: serial membrane sweeping from 41 weeks cut post-term pregnancy from 41% to 23% (relative risk 0.57 relative; NNT 6)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (51 primary care midwifery practices, the Netherlands; unblinded)
cards.people: 742 low-risk pregnant women at 41 weeks of gestation, randomly assigned to serial sweeping of the membranes (every 48 hours until labour commenced, up to 42 weeks; 375 women) or no intervention (367 women). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Serial sweeping decreased the risk of post-term pregnancy (≥42 weeks) (87/375, 23%, versus 149/367, 41%; relative risk 0.57 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.46 to 0.71; number needed to treat 6, 95% CI 4 to 9). Benefits were seen in both subgroups (nulliparous: 57/198, 29%, versus 89/192, 46%; relative risk 0.62 relative, 0.48 to 0.81; parous: 30/177, 17%, versus 60/175, 34%; relative risk 0.49 relative, 0.34 to 0.73). Adverse effects were similar except uncomplicated bleeding, reported more frequently in the sweeping group. Other obstetric outcomes and indicators of neonatal morbidity were similar; there were two perinatal deaths in each group.
cards.watchOut: An unblinded mechanical intervention tested from 41 weeks in a Dutch primary-care midwifery population: the endpoint is crossing the 42-week line (and thereby avoiding formal induction pathways), not a demonstrated improvement in perinatal outcomes, which were similar and too infrequent to compare. The perinatal deaths (two per group) are printed here as counts; no mortality claim is made.

shelves.title: Immediate vs delayed pushing in the second stage with neuraxial analgesia
shelves.question: In nulliparous women receiving neuraxial analgesia, does delayed pushing vs immediate pushing at full dilatation increase spontaneous vaginal delivery?
shelves.mesh: Labor Stage, Second · Delivery, Obstetric/adverse effects,methods · Analgesia, Epidural · Parity · Humans · Female · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic multicentre trial (Cahill 2018, 2,414 nulliparous women at six US centres; stopped early for futility at 2,414 of 3,184 planned) found spontaneous vaginal delivery rates essentially identical with immediate versus delayed pushing (85.9% vs 86.5%; absolute difference −0.6 percentage points, 95% CI −3.4 to 2.1; relative risk 0.99 relative, 0.96 to 1.03). Delayed pushing lengthened the second stage overall (134.2 vs 102.4 minutes) despite shorter active pushing, and was associated with more chorioamnionitis (9.1% vs 6.7%; P=0.005) and more postpartum haemorrhage (4.0% vs 2.3%; P=0.03); the neonatal morbidity composite did not differ significantly (8.9% vs 7.3%). The topic file attributed this trial to 'Tuuli et al.' — the record's first author is Cahill AG (JAMA 2018), and the card is corrected to the record. A single very large trial with a tight interval around no difference carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null rule.

cards.headline: Cahill 2018: delayed pushing did not raise spontaneous vaginal delivery (86.5% vs 85.9%) and brought more chorioamnionitis and postpartum haemorrhage
cards.summary: Cahill 2018: delayed pushing did not raise spontaneous vaginal delivery (86.5% vs 85.9%) and brought more chorioamnionitis and postpartum haemorrhage
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised clinical trial (six US medical centres; recruitment terminated early for futility at interim analysis)
cards.people: 2,414 nulliparous women at or beyond 37 weeks' gestation admitted for spontaneous or induced labour with neuraxial analgesia (mean age 26.5 years), randomised at complete cervical dilatation to begin pushing immediately (1,200) or to wait 60 minutes (1,204); 2,404 (99.6%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Spontaneous vaginal delivery occurred in 85.9% of the immediate group versus 86.5% of the delayed group (absolute difference −0.6%, 95% CI −3.4% to 2.1%; relative risk 0.99 — a relative measure — 0.96 to 1.03). There was no significant difference in the composite neonatal morbidity outcome (7.3% immediate vs 8.9% delayed; difference −1.6%, −3.8% to 0.5%) or perineal lacerations (45.9% vs 46.4%). cards.watchOut: Early stopping was for futility on the primary outcome, which strengthens the null for delivery mode; the chorioamnionitis and haemorrhage differences are secondary outcomes among several tested and should be read as signals consistent with a longer second stage, not as independent proven harms.

shelves.title: Delayed-release doxylamine–pyridoxine for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
shelves.question: In pregnant women with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, does delayed-release doxylamine–pyridoxine vs placebo improve symptom scores?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Delayed-Action Preparations/administration & dosage · Dicyclomine · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Doxylamine/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Combinations · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gestational Age · Humans · Morning Sickness/drug therapy · Nausea/diagnosis,drug therapy · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/diagnosis,drug therapy · Pyridoxine/administration & dosage · Quality of Life · Reference Values · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/diagnosis,drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (256 pregnant women with nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, 14 days of treatment) found the delayed-release doxylamine–pyridoxine combination improved symptoms more than placebo on the pregnancy-unique quantification of emesis (PUQE) score (change −4.8±2.7 vs −3.9±2.6; P=.006) and on quality of life; after the trial, 48.9% of the treatment group versus 32.8% on placebo asked to continue the medication on compassionate use (P=.009). The between-group difference on the symptom score is modest (0.9 PUQE points), the trial is single, and the endpoint is a symptom score over 14 days — POSSIBLE. Ginger for nausea of pregnancy is Shelf #117, a different intervention.

cards.headline: Koren 2010: delayed-release doxylamine–pyridoxine improved PUQE scores more than placebo over 14 days in 256 pregnant women (−4.8 vs −3.9; P=.006)
cards.summary: Koren 2010: delayed-release doxylamine–pyridoxine improved PUQE scores more than placebo over 14 days in 256 pregnant women (−4.8 vs −3.9; P=.006)
cards.people: 256 pregnant women suffering from nausea and vomiting of pregnancy, randomised to Diclectin (delayed-release doxylamine succinate 10 mg–pyridoxine hydrochloride 10 mg; 131) or placebo (125) for 14 days, analysed by intention to treat. The abstract does not state mean age or gestational age.
cards.result: Diclectin produced a significantly larger improvement in nausea and vomiting symptoms than placebo on the pregnancy-unique quantification of emesis score (−4.8±2.7 vs −3.9±2.6; P=.006) and on quality of life. After the trial, 64 (48.9%) women receiving Diclectin asked to continue compassionate use of their medication, compared with 41 (32.8%) of placebo-treated women (P=.009). The authors conclude the delayed-release formulation is effective and well tolerated; detailed adverse-event counts are not printed in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: Both groups improved substantially (placebo −3.9 points), so the drug-attributable gain is the 0.9-point difference; the compassionate-continuation figure (48.9% vs 32.8%) is a post-trial preference measure, not a blinded endpoint. (The record's MeSH list includes 'Dicyclomine', which is not an ingredient of this combination; it is reproduced as printed in the record.)

shelves.title: Low-dose vs high-dose calcium supplementation in pregnancy (India & Tanzania trials)
shelves.question: In pregnant women in low-calcium-intake populations, is 500 mg/day calcium non-inferior to 1,500 mg/day for preventing pre-eclampsia and preterm birth?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Calcium/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects · Pre-Eclampsia/epidemiology,prevention & control · Premature Birth/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY for the pre-eclampsia non-inferiority claim · SPLIT on preterm birth (non-inferior in India, NOT non-inferior in Tanzania). Two independent randomised trials, each enrolling 11,000 nulliparous pregnant women in low-calcium-intake populations (India and Tanzania), compared 500 mg/day calcium with the WHO-recommended 1,500 mg/day. For pre-eclampsia, the low dose was non-inferior in both trials (India: cumulative incidence 3.0% vs 3.6%, relative risk 0.84 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.68 to 1.03; Tanzania: 3.0% vs 2.7%, RR 1.10 relative, 0.88 to 1.36; non-inferiority margin RR 1.54). For preterm live birth, non-inferiority (margin RR 1.16) was met in India (11.4% vs 12.8%; RR 0.89 relative, 0.80 to 0.98) but NOT in Tanzania (10.4% vs 9.7%; RR 1.07 relative, 0.95 to 1.21, which exceeded the margin). This is a dose-comparison shelf: it shows the lower dose is not unacceptably worse than the higher dose; it is not a trial of calcium versus no calcium (that question is Shelf #211).

cards.headline: India trial (Dwarkanath 2024): 500 mg calcium was non-inferior to 1,500 mg for both pre-eclampsia (3.0% vs 3.6%) and preterm birth (11.4% vs 12.8%) in 11,000 nulliparous women
cards.summary: India trial (Dwarkanath 2024): 500 mg calcium was non-inferior to 1,500 mg for both pre-eclampsia (3.0% vs 3.6%) and preterm birth (11.4% vs 12.8%) in 11,000 nulliparous women
cards.type: Randomised non-inferiority trial (one of two independent trials reported in a single paper)
cards.people: 11,000 nulliparous pregnant women in India, randomised to calcium supplementation of 500 mg daily or 1,500 mg daily. The abstract does not state mean age. (Reported jointly with the Tanzania trial in a single NEJM paper; the two trials were conducted independently.)
cards.result: The cumulative incidence of pre-eclampsia was 3.0% in the 500-mg group and 3.6% in the 1500-mg group (relative risk 0.84 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.68 to 1.03), consistent with non-inferiority of the lower dose against the prespecified margin (RR 1.54). The percentage of live births that were preterm was 11.4% in the 500-mg group and 12.8% in the 1500-mg group (RR 0.89 relative, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.98), within the non-inferiority margin of 1.16.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against a generous pre-eclampsia margin (RR 1.54) is a statement about acceptable loss, not equality: the design would have accepted a low dose up to 54% relatively worse on pre-eclampsia risk. The record's databank fields carry the ClinicalTrials.gov and CTRI identifiers; the Tanzanian registry number appears in the abstract's funding/registration line and is noted as such.

shelves.title: Induction of labour at 41 weeks vs expectant management to 42 weeks (SWEPIS & INDEX)
shelves.question: In low-risk women with uncomplicated pregnancy, does induction at 41 weeks vs expectant management with induction at 42 weeks reduce perinatal mortality and morbidity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Newborn, Diseases/epidemiology,etiology · Intention to Treat Analysis · Labor, Induced/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome/epidemiology · Stillbirth/epidemiology · Sweden/epidemiology · Term Birth · Watchful Waiting/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: perinatal mortality is central to the claim). Two large open-label randomised trials point the same way on mortality but neither is clean. SWEPIS (2,760 women, Sweden) was STOPPED EARLY because perinatal mortality was higher in the expectant group: 0 deaths with induction at 41 weeks versus 6 (five stillbirths, one early neonatal death) with expectant management to 42 weeks (P=0.03) — yet its primary composite perinatal outcome did NOT differ (2.4% vs 2.2%; relative risk 1.06 relative, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.73; P=0.90), and caesarean, instrumental delivery and major maternal morbidity did not differ. INDEX (1,801 women, Netherlands) found its adverse perinatal composite lower with induction (1.7% vs 3.1%; absolute difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 0.0) but could NOT demonstrate non-inferiority of expectant management (P=0.22 for non-inferiority); fetal deaths were 1 versus 2 and there were no neonatal deaths. A mortality signal carried by a secondary outcome in a stopped-early trial, supported directionally by a second trial's composite, earns POSSIBLE, not more. Correction on the card's face: the topic file pinned SWEPIS at PMID 34911689, a duplicate record carrying no abstract or data; the primary report (PMID 31748223, BMJ 2019) is the record carded here.

cards.headline: SWEPIS (Wennerholm 2019): stopped early — 0 perinatal deaths with induction at 41 weeks vs 6 with expectant management to 42 weeks, but the primary composite did not differ (2.4% vs 2.2%)
cards.summary: SWEPIS (Wennerholm 2019): stopped early — 0 perinatal deaths with induction at 41 weeks vs 6 with expectant management to 42 weeks, but the primary composite did not differ (2.4% vs 2.2%)
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised superiority trial — stopped early on a perinatal-mortality difference
cards.people: 2,760 women with a low-risk uncomplicated singleton pregnancy at 14 hospitals in Sweden (2016–18), randomised 1:1 via the Swedish Pregnancy Register to induction at 41 weeks (1,381) or expectant management with induction at 42 weeks (1,379). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The study was stopped early owing to a significantly higher rate of perinatal mortality in the expectant management group. The composite primary perinatal outcome (stillbirth, neonatal mortality, Apgar <7 at 5 minutes, pH <7.00 or metabolic acidosis, hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, convulsions, meconium aspiration syndrome, mechanical ventilation within 72 hours, or obstetric brachial plexus injury) did not differ: 2.4% (33/1381) induction versus 2.2% (31/1379) expectant (relative risk 1.06 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.65 to 1.73; P=0.90). No perinatal deaths occurred in the induction group, but six (five stillbirths and one early neonatal death) occurred in the expectant management group (P=0.03). The proportions of caesarean delivery, instrumental vaginal delivery, or any major maternal morbidity did not differ between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The mortality difference is a secondary outcome in a trial stopped early for that very difference — the configuration most prone to exaggerating effects — and the trial's own primary composite was null (RR 1.06). The authors themselves say the results 'should be interpreted cautiously'. The topic file's pinned record (PMID 34911689) is a duplicate of this report with an empty abstract in both PubMed and Europe PMC; the primary report is carded instead and the substitution is disclosed here.

cards.headline: INDEX (Keulen 2019): adverse perinatal composite 1.7% with induction at 41 weeks vs 3.1% expectant, but non-inferiority of expectant management could not be shown; fetal deaths 1 vs 2
cards.summary: INDEX (Keulen 2019): adverse perinatal composite 1.7% with induction at 41 weeks vs 3.1% expectant, but non-inferiority of expectant management could not be shown; fetal deaths 1 vs 2
cards.type: Open-label, randomised non-inferiority trial (of expectant management)
cards.people: 1,801 low-risk women with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy in the Netherlands (123 primary-care midwifery practices and 45 hospitals, 2012–16), randomised to induction at 41 weeks (900) or expectant management until 42 weeks (901). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (perinatal mortality and neonatal morbidity: Apgar <7 at 5 minutes, arterial pH <7.05, meconium aspiration syndrome, brachial plexus injury, intracranial haemorrhage, NICU admission) occurred in 15/900 (1.7%) in the induction group versus 28/901 (3.1%) in the expectant group (absolute risk difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −2.9 to 0.0; P=0.22 for non-inferiority — the trial could not show expectant management was non-inferior within its 2% margin). Apgar score <7 at 5 minutes: 11 (1.2%) versus 23 (2.6%) (relative risk 0.48 relative, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.98). One fetal death (0.1%) occurred in the induction group and two (0.2%) in the expectant group; no neonatal deaths occurred. NICU admission: 3 (0.3%) versus 8 (0.9%) (RR 0.38 relative, 0.10 to 1.41). Composite adverse maternal outcomes (13.6% vs 11.3%) and caesarean section rates (10.8% in both groups) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: INDEX was designed to test whether WAITING is non-inferior, and it failed to prove that — which is not the same as proving induction superior on its composite (the superiority framing belongs to SWEPIS, whose composite was null). Read together, the pair support offering induction at 41 weeks; neither licenses a claim of a proven mortality reduction at LIKELY strength.

shelves.title: Combined oral contraceptive pill for primary dysmenorrhoea
shelves.question: In women with primary dysmenorrhoea, does the combined oral contraceptive pill vs placebo or no treatment reduce menstrual pain?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Dysmenorrhea/drug therapy · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/adverse effects · Muscle Cramp · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects · Headache
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The Cochrane review (Schroll 2023; 21 RCTs, 3,723 women) found combined oral contraceptives reduce dysmenorrhoea pain versus placebo or no treatment — a moderate standardised effect (SMD −0.58, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.41; 6 RCTs, 588 women; the review rates this evidence high-quality) — and improve the chance of pain improvement (risk ratio 1.65 relative, 1.29 to 2.10; 6 RCTs, 717 women; low-quality evidence), corresponding to improvement in 37–60% of treated women versus 28% on placebo. The largest single placebo-controlled trial carded beside the review (Davis 2005, 76 adolescents) agrees: Moos Menstrual Distress Questionnaire pain score 3.1 vs 5.8 at the third cycle (P=.004). The harms are real and quantified by the review: any adverse events RR 1.31 relative (1.20 to 1.43), irregular bleeding RR 2.63 relative (2.11 to 3.28; absolute risk 39–60% vs 18% on placebo), headache RR 1.51 relative and nausea RR 1.64 relative. Pain-score outcomes, mostly older small trials, and the review's mixed certainty ratings (high for the pooled pain score, low for improvement) hold the stamp at POSSIBLE. Long-term effects were not covered by the review.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Schroll 2023) — REVIEW CARD: combined OCPs reduce dysmenorrhoea pain vs placebo (SMD −0.58) across 21 RCTs and 3,723 women, with more irregular bleeding (RR 2.63 relative)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Schroll 2023) — REVIEW CARD: combined OCPs reduce dysmenorrhoea pain vs placebo (SMD −0.58) across 21 RCTs and 3,723 women, with more irregular bleeding (RR 2.63 relative)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane) — explicitly a review card, carded beside a primary trial per library rules
cards.people: 21 randomised controlled trials including 3,723 women with primary dysmenorrhoea (diagnosed by ruling out pelvic pathology): 11 trials compared a combined OCP with placebo, 8 compared different OCP dosages, 1 compared two regimens with placebo, and 1 compared an OCP with NSAIDs. Review authors: Schroll JB, Black AY, Farquhar C, Chen I; search to 28 March 2023.
cards.result: OCP versus placebo or no treatment: pain scores favoured OCPs with a moderate reduction (standardised mean difference −0.58, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.41; I²=28%; 6 RCTs, 588 women; the review rates this high-quality evidence). Pain improvement as a dichotomous outcome: risk ratio 1.65 relative (95% CI 1.29 to 2.10; I²=69%; 6 RCTs, 717 women; low-quality evidence) — with a 28% chance of improvement on placebo or no treatment, improvement on OCPs would be 37–60%. OCPs probably increase any adverse events (RR 1.31 relative, 1.20 to 1.43; 7 RCTs, 1,025 women; moderate-quality evidence) and may increase serious adverse events (RR 1.77 relative, 0.49 to 6.43; low-quality evidence). Irregular bleeding was increased (RR 2.63 relative, 2.11 to 3.28; high-quality evidence; risk 39–60% on OCP vs 18% on placebo), as were headache (RR 1.51 relative, 1.11 to 2.04) and nausea (RR 1.64 relative, 1.17 to 2.30). Continuous OCP use may reduce pain more than the standard regimen (SMD −0.73, −1.13 to 0.34; low-quality evidence). Against NSAIDs there were insufficient data (1 RCT, 91 women). The registry identifiers in this record's databank fields belong to trials included in the review, not to the review itself.
cards.watchOut: A review card pools many small, older trials with heterogeneous pain scales (hence the SMD); the review's certainty is high for the pooled pain score but low for the improvement outcome and for serious adverse events, and long-term effects were outside its scope. Do not quote the RR 1.65 improvement figure without its low-quality rating.

shelves.title: Male-partner treatment to prevent recurrent bacterial vaginosis (StepUp)
shelves.question: In women with bacterial vaginosis whose male partners are treated concurrently (oral metronidazole plus penile clindamycin cream) versus the woman treated alone, does partner treatment reduce recurrence within 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Administration, Oral · Administration, Topical · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Clindamycin · Drug Therapy, Combination · Metronidazole · Recurrence · Secondary Prevention · Sexual Partners · Vaginosis, Bacterial · Intention to Treat Analysis · Treatment Outcome · New South Wales · Penis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label randomised trial (164 couples), stopped early by its data and safety monitoring board because woman-only treatment was inferior. Recurrence within 12 weeks occurred in 35% of women whose partners were also treated versus 63% under standard care (recurrence rate 1.6 versus 4.2 per person-year; absolute difference −2.6 per person-year, 95% CI −4.0 to −1.2; P<0.001). Early stopping for efficacy tends to inflate effect sizes, and there is no second trial, so the stamp is POSSIBLE despite the large point estimate. Flagged on its face as a two-trial-gate exception candidate — if the developer rejects the exception, this shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped. Distinct from Shelf #947 (strategies directed at the woman — Lactin-V and suppressive metronidazole): this shelf's intervention treats the male partner.

cards.headline: StepUp: recurrence 35% with partner treatment versus 63% with woman-only treatment; trial stopped early
cards.summary: StepUp: recurrence 35% with partner treatment versus 63% with woman-only treatment; trial stopped early
cards.type: Open-label, randomised, controlled trial (stopped early for efficacy)
cards.people: 164 couples in which the woman had bacterial vaginosis and was in a monogamous relationship with a male partner (81 assigned to partner treatment, 83 to control). In the partner-treatment group the woman received first-line antimicrobials and the man received oral metronidazole 400 mg plus 2% clindamycin cream to penile skin, both twice daily for 7 days. The trial was stopped after 150 couples had completed the 12-week follow-up; the modified intention-to-treat population was 69 versus 68 women. The abstract does not print mean ages.
cards.result: Recurrence of bacterial vaginosis within 12 weeks occurred in 24 of 69 women (35%) in the partner-treatment group versus 43 of 68 (63%) in the control group; recurrence rates were 1.6 versus 4.2 per person-year (absolute difference −2.6 per person-year, 95% CI −4.0 to −1.2; P<0.001). Adverse events in treated men included nausea, headache, and metallic taste.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and stopped early for benefit — both features bias toward larger apparent effects; only couples in monogamous relationships were studied, and the woman's own treatment was first-line therapy in both arms, so the card isolates the partner-treatment increment only.

shelves.title: Mediterranean-style diet in pregnancy with metabolic risk factors (ESTEEM)
shelves.question: In pregnant women with metabolic risk factors, does a Mediterranean-style diet reduce gestational diabetes and gestational weight gain versus usual antenatal care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Delphi Technique · Diabetes, Gestational · Diet, Healthy · Diet, Mediterranean · Energy Metabolism · England · Female · Gestational Weight Gain · Humans · Maternal Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Nutritional Status · Nutritive Value · Pregnancy · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: ESTEEM randomised 1,252 inner-city pregnant women with metabolic risk factors (obesity, chronic hypertension or hypertriglyceridaemia) at five UK maternity units to individualised Mediterranean-style dietary advice or usual care. Both primary composites missed significance: maternal composite (gestational diabetes or pre-eclampsia) 22.8% versus 28.6% (adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; p=0.08) and offspring composite 17.3% versus 20.9% (adjusted odds ratio 0.79, 0.58 to 1.08; p=0.14). Inside those composites, gestational diabetes alone was reduced (adjusted odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.91; p=0.01), and mothers gained less weight (6.8 versus 8.3 kg; adjusted difference −1.2 kg, p=0.03). So the honest reading is narrower than the shelf question's framing: the diet did not significantly reduce the trial's primary maternal or offspring composites, but it did reduce gestational diabetes as an individual component and modestly limited weight gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ESTEEM: primary composites not significant (maternal adjusted OR 0.76, p=0.08) — but gestational diabetes fell (OR 0.65) and weight gain was 1.2 kg less
cards.summary: ESTEEM: primary composites not significant (maternal adjusted OR 0.76, p=0.08) — but gestational diabetes fell (OR 0.65) and weight gain was 1.2 kg less
cards.people: 1,252 pregnant women with metabolic risk factors (obesity, chronic hypertension, or hypertriglyceridaemia) randomised at five maternity units in London and Birmingham — 69% were obese and 60% were of Black or Asian ethnicity — to a Mediterranean-style diet (high nuts, extra virgin olive oil, fruit, vegetables, non-refined grains, legumes and fish; low red and processed meat; no sugary drinks or fast food) with individualised advice at 18, 20 and 28 weeks, or to usual antenatal care. Primary endpoints were composite maternal (gestational diabetes or pre-eclampsia) and composite offspring (stillbirth, small for gestational age, or neonatal unit admission) outcomes.
cards.result: There was no significant reduction in the composite maternal outcome (22.8% versus 28.6%; adjusted odds ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.03; p=0.08) or the composite offspring outcome (17.3% versus 20.9%; adjusted odds ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.08; p=0.14). Gestational diabetes alone was reduced by about a third (adjusted odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.91; p=0.01), with no significant effect on other individual components; gestational weight gain was lower with the diet (mean 6.8 versus 8.3 kg; adjusted difference −1.2 kg, 95% CI −2.2 to −0.2; p=0.03). Pooling ESTEEM with a similar trial in the same report, gestational diabetes was significantly reduced overall (odds ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.84).
cards.watchOut: The gestational-diabetes result is a component of a non-significant composite — real, but a step below a positive primary endpoint, and adherence was measured by participant report rather than biomarkers. Pre-eclampsia, stillbirth and the other hard outcomes showed no significant effect; this shelf must not be read as the diet preventing them.
cards.source: Al Wattar BH et al. Mediterranean-style diet in pregnant women with metabolic risk factors (ESTEEM): A pragmatic multicentre randomised trial. PLoS Med. 2019. PMID: 31335871. shelves.title: Single-dose secnidazole for bacterial vaginosis
shelves.question: In women with bacterial vaginosis, does a single oral dose of secnidazole (1 g or 2 g granules) produce higher clinical cure rates than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antiprotozoal Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Metronidazole · Treatment Outcome · Vaginosis, Bacterial
shelves.balance: A phase 2 double-blind, dose-ranging randomised trial enrolled 215 women meeting all Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis at 24 US centres; 188 were in the modified intention-to-treat population. A single dose of secnidazole oral granules beat placebo clearly: clinical cure at 21–30 days in the intention-to-treat analysis was 65.3% with 2 g and 49.3% with 1 g versus 19.4% on placebo, and in the modified intention-to-treat analysis the 2 g dose gave clinical cure 67.7%, microbiological cure 40.3% and therapeutic cure 40.3%, versus 17.7%, 6.5% and 6.5% on placebo (all P<0.05; the authors' conclusion cites P<0.001 for both doses). Both doses were well tolerated. The proposed stamp is POSSIBLE: the placebo-controlled effect is large and dose-ordered, but this is a single phase 2 trial (THIN), cure was judged at three to four weeks, and it does not address BV recurrence, which is the harder clinical problem (covered separately on the BV recurrence shelf). This shelf is about treating an acute episode; single-dose secnidazole for trichomoniasis is a different question, covered on its own shelf.

Both doses were well tolerated.

shelves.balance: Black cohosh is among the most bought menopause supplements, and its two best trials bracket the answer. The larger and longer one, HALT (351 women aged 45–55 with at least two vasomotor symptoms a day, followed for a year), found that black cohosh alone or inside a multibotanical differed from placebo by less than one vasomotor symptom per day at 3, 6 and 12 months — while hormone therapy in the same trial differed by −4.06 symptoms per day. The smaller positive trial (Osmers; 304 patients, 12 weeks, an isopropanolic extract) reached statistical significance on the Menopause Rating Scale, but its own reported effect size was 0.03–0.05 scale units, and the benefit concentrated in women early in the climacteric. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): read together, if black cohosh does anything for hot flushes it is below what these trials could call important.

cards.headline: HALT: black cohosh (alone or in a multibotanical) differed from placebo by <1 vasomotor symptom/day over 12 months; hormone therapy differed by −4.06/day
cards.summary: HALT: black cohosh (alone or in a multibotanical) differed from placebo by <1 vasomotor symptom/day over 12 months; hormone therapy differed by −4.06/day
cards.people: 351 women aged 45–55 with ≥2 vasomotor symptoms daily (52% in menopausal transition, 48% postmenopausal), randomised for 1 year to black cohosh 160 mg/day, a multibotanical containing black cohosh, the multibotanical plus soy counselling, conjugated equine estrogen 0.625 mg (± medroxyprogesterone), or placebo.
cards.result: Vasomotor symptom frequency and intensity and the Wiklund subscale did not differ between any herbal arm and placebo at 3, 6 or 12 months (p>0.05 throughout), with one exception (multibotanical-plus-soy was worse on intensity at 12 months, p=0.016). Differences versus placebo were <1 symptom/day at every point and <0.55/day on average; hormone therapy averaged −4.06 symptoms/day (95% CI −5.93 to −2.19; p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The trial could not exclude differences smaller than 1.5 symptoms/day, and it tested extracts at set doses rather than naturopathic whole-person care — but any effect inside those bounds is small by the trial's own yardstick. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Newton KM et al.. Treatment of vasomotor symptoms of menopause with black cohosh, multibotanicals, soy, hormone therapy, or placebo: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2006. PMID: 17179056. Registry ID: NCT00169299. cards.headline: Osmers: isopropanolic black cohosh extract beat placebo on the Menopause Rating Scale (p<0.001) — with an effect size of 0.03–0.05 units
cards.summary: Osmers: isopropanolic black cohosh extract beat placebo on the Menopause Rating Scale (p<0.001) — with an effect size of 0.03–0.05 units
cards.people: 304 patients with climacteric complaints in a multicentre trial of an isopropanolic black cohosh extract (tablets corresponding to 40 mg drug daily) versus placebo for 12 weeks; primary outcome change in Menopause Rating Scale I.
cards.result: The extract was more effective than placebo (p<0.001), with efficacy depending on time from symptom onset (p=0.014) and FSH level (p=0.011); the hot-flush subscore responded most. The reported effect size was 0.03–0.05 Menopause Rating Scale units — comparable to the 0.036 units the authors cite from hormone-therapy studies. No relevant group differences in adverse events, laboratory findings or tolerability.
cards.watchOut: Statistically positive but tiny in magnitude and short; its result does not overturn HALT's year-long null on the outcome women care about — the daily symptom count. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Osmers R et al.. Efficacy and safety of isopropanolic black cohosh extract for climacteric symptoms. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2005. PMID: 15863547. Registry ID: none recorded in the PubMed record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the rigorous trial is null and the positive trial is tiny — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the rigorous trial is null and the positive trial is tiny — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Black cohosh for menopausal symptoms in HALT (351 women, 12 months) and Osmers (304 patients, 12 weeks).
cards.result: HALT: <1 symptom/day difference vs placebo at all points. Osmers: significant rating-scale difference with an effect size of 0.03–0.05 units. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

shelves.title: Iron for tired, non-anaemic women with low ferritin: fatigue fell about 19 percentage points more than placebo — benefit confined to ferritin at or below 50 µg/L
shelves.question: In non-anaemic women with unexplained fatigue and low ferritin, does oral iron reduce fatigue compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Dietary Supplements · Fatigue/blood, drug therapy · Female · Ferritins/blood · Ferrous Compounds/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Hemoglobins · Humans · Iron/administration & dosage, therapeutic use · Menstruation · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Tiredness with a normal blood count and a lowish ferritin is one of the commonest presentations in primary care, and iron is often given on instinct; two randomised trials from French and Swiss primary care test the instinct directly. Vaucher (198 non-anaemic women, ferritin <50 µg/L, haemoglobin >12.0 g/dL) found 12 weeks of oral ferrous sulfate (80 mg elemental iron daily) reduced fatigue scores by 47.7% versus 28.8% on placebo (difference −18.9 percentage points, 95% CI −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02) — with no significant effect on quality of life, depression or anxiety. Verdon (144 women, 4 weeks, same dose) found fatigue fell 29% versus 13% on placebo (p=0.004), and the subgroup analysis in both eras agrees on the boundary: benefit appears confined to women with ferritin ≤50 µg/L. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a symptomatic benefit in a defined biochemical niche — not a licence to treat tiredness with iron when ferritin is normal.

cards.headline: Fatigue fell 47.7% on iron vs 28.8% on placebo (difference −18.9 points, −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02) in 198 women with ferritin <50 µg/L
cards.summary: Fatigue fell 47.7% on iron vs 28.8% on placebo (difference −18.9 points, −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02) in 198 women with ferritin <50 µg/L
cards.people: 198 women aged 18–53 with unexplained fatigue, ferritin <50 µg/L and haemoglobin >12.0 g/dL, recruited from 44 French primary-care practices, randomised to oral ferrous sulfate 80 mg elemental iron daily (n=102) or placebo (n=96) for 12 weeks; primary outcome fatigue on the Current and Past Psychological Scale. The trial was closed-label and observer-blinded.
cards.result: Fatigue scores fell 47.7% on iron vs 28.8% on placebo (difference −18.9%, 95% CI −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02). No significant effects on quality of life (p=0.2), depression (p=0.97) or anxiety (p=0.5). Haemoglobin rose 0.32 g/dL and ferritin 11.4 µg/L versus placebo (both significant). The authors suggest checking blood markers after 6 weeks to judge efficiency.
cards.watchOut: Observer-blinded rather than fully double-blind, and the primary outcome is a subjective scale in a trial where iron's gastrointestinal effects can hint at allocation. The placebo group also improved by nearly 29% — fatigue is a high-placebo-response symptom, which is why the controlled difference, not the 47.7%, is the finding.
cards.source: Vaucher P et al.. Effect of iron supplementation on fatigue in nonanemic menstruating women with low ferritin: a randomized controlled trial. CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne. 2012. PMID: 22777991. Registry ID: EudraCT 2006-000478-56. cards.headline: Fatigue fell 29% on iron vs 13% on placebo at 4 weeks (p=0.004); benefit confined to ferritin ≤50 µg/L (n=144)
cards.summary: Fatigue fell 29% on iron vs 13% on placebo at 4 weeks (p=0.004); benefit confined to ferritin ≤50 µg/L (n=144)
cards.people: 144 women aged 18–55 with unexplained fatigue in Swiss primary care, randomised to oral ferrous sulfate 80 mg/day elemental iron (n=75) or placebo (n=69) for 4 weeks; outcome fatigue on a 10-point visual analogue scale; 136 completed.
cards.result: Fatigue fell by 1.82 of 6.37 points (29%) on iron vs 0.85 of 6.46 points (13%) on placebo (difference 0.95 points, 95% CI 0.32–1.62; p=0.004). Subgroup analysis showed only women with ferritin ≤50 µg/L improved with supplementation; about half the cohort had ferritin ≤20 µg/L.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short, and the ferritin boundary comes from subgroup analysis — but the same ≤50 µg/L boundary emerged independently in the later trial's entry criteria and results, which is what elevates it from a subgroup curiosity to the shelf's rule.
cards.source: Verdon F et al.. Iron supplementation for unexplained fatigue in non-anaemic women: double blind randomised placebo controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2003. PMID: 12763985. cards.summary: Synthesis: two primary-care trials, one ferritin boundary — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Oral iron for fatigue in non-anaemic women: Vaucher 2012 (198 women, 12 weeks) and Verdon 2003 (144 women, 4 weeks), both ferrous sulfate 80 mg/day.
cards.result: Fatigue reduction vs placebo: −18.9 percentage points (p=0.02) and 29% vs 13% (p=0.004); benefit confined to ferritin ≤50 µg/L. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The shelf's boundary is part of the claim: normal ferritin was not studied and should not be treated on this evidence. Why ferritin is low still needs its own work-up — iron treats the number and the symptom, not the cause.

shelves.title: Domperidone to boost milk supply after preterm birth: about 40 mL/day more in the one small placebo trial; most EMPOWER completers gained at least 50%
shelves.question: In mothers of preterm infants whose milk supply is low, does domperidone increase expressed breast-milk volume compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Canada · Domperidone/therapeutic use · Dopamine Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Galactogogues/therapeutic use · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Lactation/drug effects · Lactation Disorders/drug therapy · Logistic Models
shelves.balance: When mothers of very preterm infants cannot produce enough milk, domperidone is the galactagogue most often reached for, and its randomised record is one small placebo trial plus a large trial known through a secondary analysis. Da Silva randomised 20 mothers of premature newborns to domperidone or placebo for 7 days: milk production rose by 49.5 mL/day versus 8.0 mL/day on placebo (p<0.05) in the 16 analysed, with prolactin rising on domperidone and only trace drug levels in milk. The EMPOWER trial's per-protocol analysis — carded as exactly that, a secondary analysis, not the trial's primary report — found that among 83 mothers of infants ≤29 weeks who completed a 14-day course (10 mg three times daily), the proportion achieving a ≥50% rise in milk volume was high whether treatment started early (77.8%) or after a placebo fortnight (65.8%), with timing itself not significant (OR 1.96, 95% CI 0.72–5.32; p=0.19). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), flagged THIN: the direction is consistent and the mechanism (prolactin) is demonstrated, but the placebo-controlled base is 16 analysed mothers, and domperidone carries cardiac cautions that sit outside these small short trials.

cards.headline: Milk volume rose 49.5 mL/day on domperidone vs 8.0 mL/day on placebo over 7 days (p<0.05); prolactin rose, milk drug levels were trace
cards.summary: Milk volume rose 49.5 mL/day on domperidone vs 8.0 mL/day on placebo over 7 days (p<0.05); prolactin rose, milk drug levels were trace
cards.people: 20 mothers of premature newborns with low milk supply randomised to domperidone or placebo for 7 days, with daily milk-volume measurement; 16 were analysed (7 domperidone, 9 placebo). Serum prolactin was measured at baseline, day 5 and day 10; domperidone levels were assayed in milk and serum samples on day 5.
cards.result: Mean increase in milk production from day 2 to 7: 49.5 mL/day (SD 29.4) on domperidone vs 8.0 mL/day (SD 39.5) on placebo (p<0.05) — proportional increases of 44.5% and 16.6%. Prolactin was significantly higher on domperidone by day 5 and returned to baseline 3 days after the last dose. Only very small amounts of domperidone were detected in breast milk.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen analysed mothers and 7 days: this is the entire placebo-controlled foundation. Four randomised mothers contributed no analysable data, and nothing here speaks to longer use or to mothers of term infants.
cards.source: da Silva OP et al.. Effect of domperidone on milk production in mothers of premature newborns: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne. 2001. PMID: 11202662. Registry ID: none — pre-modern-registration-era trial. cards.headline: EMPOWER per-protocol analysis: 77.8% (early start) and 65.8% (later start) of completers achieved a ≥50% milk-volume rise on a 14-day course
cards.summary: EMPOWER per-protocol analysis: 77.8% (early start) and 65.8% (later start) of completers achieved a ≥50% milk-volume rise on a 14-day course
cards.type: Per-protocol secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Asztalos 2019, EMPOWER)
cards.people: 83 mothers of infants born at ≤29 weeks' gestation in the EMPOWER trial who completed a 14-day course of domperidone 10 mg three times daily — 45 treated on days 1–14 and 38 treated on days 15–28 (after the initial study period) — analysed per protocol; primary outcome the proportion achieving a 50% increase in milk volume across the course.
cards.result: Adjusted for initiation timing, the proportion achieving a ≥50% increase was 77.8% in the days 1–14 group vs 65.8% in the days 15–28 group (OR 1.96, 95% CI 0.72–5.32; p=0.19). The authors conclude completers responded irrespective of when domperidone was started, while noting potential limitations in power.
cards.watchOut: Carded as what it is: a per-protocol secondary analysis comparing early versus late starters among completers — there is no placebo arm in this comparison, so it cannot by itself show domperidone beats placebo. Its weight is corroborative (most completers gained substantially on the drug), and the placebo claim rests on da Silva.
cards.source: Asztalos EV et al.. Evaluating the Effect of a 14-Day Course of Domperidone on Breast Milk Production: A Per-Protocol Analysis from the EMPOWER Trial. Breastfeeding medicine : the official journal of the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30543461. Registry ID: NCT01512225. per-protocol secondary analysis of a randomised trial (asztalos 2019, empower) 83 mothers of infants born at ≤29 weeks' gestation in the empower trial who completed a 14-day course of domperidone 10 mg three times daily — 45 treated on days 1–14 and 38 treated on days 15–28 (after the initial study period) — analysed per protocol; primary outcome the proportion achieving a 50% increase in milk volume across the course. adjusted for initiation timing, the proportion achieving a ≥50% increase was 77.8% in the days 1–14 group vs 65.8% in the days 15–28 group (or 1.96, 95% ci 0.72–5.32; p=0.19). the authors conclude completers responded irrespective of when domperidone was started, while noting potential limitations in power. carded as what it is: a per-protocol secondary analysis comparing early versus late starters among completers — there is no placebo arm in this comparison, so it cannot by itself show domperidone beats placebo. its weight is corroborative (most completers gained substantially on the drug), and the placebo claim rests on da silva. asztalos ev et al.. evaluating the effect of a 14-day course of domperidone on breast milk production: a per-protocol analysis from the empower trial. breastfeeding medicine : the official journal of the academy of breastfeeding medicine. 2019. pmid: 30543461. registry id: nct01512225. mesh: adult · canada · domperidone/therapeutic use · dopamine antagonists/therapeutic use · female · galactogogues/therapeutic use · gestational age · humans · infant, newborn · infant, premature · lactation/drug effects · lactation disorders/drug therapy · logistic models

cards.headline: Synthesis: one tiny placebo trial plus a large trial's completer analysis — POSSIBLE (benefit), THIN
cards.summary: Synthesis: one tiny placebo trial plus a large trial's completer analysis — POSSIBLE (benefit), THIN
cards.people: Domperidone for low milk supply in mothers of preterm infants: da Silva 2001 (16 analysed, placebo-controlled) and the EMPOWER per-protocol analysis (83 completers).
cards.result: Placebo-controlled: +49.5 vs +8.0 mL/day at 7 days (p<0.05). Completers: roughly two-thirds to three-quarters achieved a ≥50% volume rise over 14 days. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Safety bounds the use: domperidone is not approved in the United States and is restricted in several countries over QT-prolongation and cardiac concerns; these small short trials in mothers of preterm infants cannot quantify that risk, and any use belongs inside local rules and lactation-specialist care.

shelves.title: Period pain: NSAIDs beat placebo, and beat aspirin and paracetamol too
shelves.question: In women and adolescents with primary dysmenorrhoea, do NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) relieve period pain compared with placebo — and how do they compare with acetaminophen (paracetamol) and aspirin?
shelves.mesh: Dysmenorrhea · Ibuprofen · Naproxen · Acetaminophen · Aspirin · Dinoprost · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Cross-Over Studies · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: NSAIDs relieve period pain better than placebo — and, at the doses tested, better than aspirin or acetaminophen (paracetamol). In a small double-blind crossover (Dawood 2007; 12 women, 10 completed), both ibuprofen 400 mg and acetaminophen 1,000 mg, each taken four times daily for 3 days of one cycle, beat placebo on pain (ibuprofen p=.002; acetaminophen p=.022), and both cut menstrual-fluid prostaglandin F2α — from 36.2 µg on placebo to 14.8 µg on ibuprofen (p=.001) and 21.4 µg on acetaminophen (p=.008). In a 32-woman crossover (Rosenwaks 1981), naproxen sodium beat both aspirin (p=.02) and placebo (p=.002), while aspirin was not superior to placebo (p=.05). In a pooled analysis of five trials in 443 women at over-the-counter doses (Milsom 2002), naproxen 400 mg beat acetaminophen and placebo within 30 minutes, and at 6 hours both naproxen doses beat acetaminophen and ibuprofen 200 mg, with similar adverse-event rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent wins across small crossovers and a 443-woman pooled analysis, held at POSSIBLE by the tiny size of the individual placebo-controlled trials.

cards.headline: Dawood 2007: in a 12-woman crossover, ibuprofen and acetaminophen both beat placebo on pain — and ibuprofen cut prostaglandin most
cards.summary: Dawood 2007: in a 12-woman crossover, ibuprofen and acetaminophen both beat placebo on pain — and ibuprofen cut prostaglandin most
cards.people: 12 women with primary dysmenorrhea randomised in a prospective, double-blind, crossover study to placebo, acetaminophen 1,000 mg orally, or ibuprofen 400 mg orally, each four times daily for 3 days of one cycle (10 patients completed); menstrual fluid was collected with preweighed super absorbent tampons and prostaglandin F2alpha (PGF2α) measured by radioimmunoassay.
cards.result: Ibuprofen (P = .002) and acetaminophen (P = .022) were both rated significantly better than placebo for pain relief. Total menstrual fluid PGF2α was 36.2 µg with placebo, 14.8 µg with ibuprofen (P = .001) and 21.4 µg with acetaminophen (P = .008); both drugs were superior to placebo for pain relief and PGF2α suppression, with ibuprofen the more potent.
cards.watchOut: Tiny and mechanistic: only 10 of 12 women completed, and the prostaglandin measurements are a mechanism marker, not a patient outcome — the card shows the drugs work and why, in very few women.
cards.source: Dawood MY et al.. Clinical efficacy and differential inhibition of menstrual fluid prostaglandin F2alpha in a randomized, double-blind, crossover treatment with placebo, acetaminophen, and ibuprofen in primary dysmenorrhea.. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2007. PMID: 17240224. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rosenwaks 1981: naproxen sodium beat aspirin and placebo; aspirin did not beat placebo
cards.summary: Rosenwaks 1981: naproxen sodium beat aspirin and placebo; aspirin did not beat placebo
cards.people: 32 women with primary dysmenorrhea in a double-blind crossover study comparing naproxen sodium with aspirin and placebo, treatment starting 1 to 5 days before the onset of menses and continuing for 3 to 5 days, with blood levels of the prostaglandin F2-alpha metabolite (PGF-M) measured before treatment and on the first day of menses.
cards.result: In affording pain relief, naproxen sodium was superior to aspirin (p = 0.02) and placebo (p = 0.002); aspirin was not superior to placebo (p = 0.05). Daily activities were less impaired during naproxen sodium treatment than during aspirin or placebo courses. Mean blood PGF-M levels fell 73.5% on naproxen sodium, fell 31.2% on aspirin, and rose 13.6% on placebo; the naproxen fall was significantly larger than with both aspirin and placebo (p = 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: A 1981 pre-registration-era crossover in 32 women, at the doses used in that study — aspirin's failure to separate from placebo (p = 0.05) is a finding about that dose and regimen, not proof aspirin can never help period pain.
cards.source: Rosenwaks Z et al.. Naproxen sodium, aspirin, and placebo in primary dysmenorrhea. Reduction of pain and blood levels of prostaglandin F2-alpha metabolite.. cards.headline: Milsom 2002: pooled across five trials and 443 women, naproxen beat acetaminophen within 30 minutes and beat acetaminophen and ibuprofen 200 mg at 6 hours
cards.summary: Milsom 2002: pooled across five trials and 443 women, naproxen beat acetaminophen within 30 minutes and beat acetaminophen and ibuprofen 200 mg at 6 hours
cards.type: Pooled analysis of five randomised trials
cards.people: 443 women with primary dysmenorrhea enrolled across five randomised trials, pooled to compare over-the-counter (nonprescription) doses: naproxen 400 mg and naproxen/naproxen sodium 200/220 mg against acetaminophen 1,000 mg, ibuprofen 200 mg, and placebo, with efficacy assessed by pain relief, relief of other dysmenorrheic symptoms, time to backup medication or remedication, and treatment preference.
cards.result: Naproxen 400 mg provided greater pain relief than acetaminophen and placebo within 30 minutes of administration (P < 0.01 and P < 0.05, respectively). Naproxen 400 mg and 200 mg provided greater pain relief than both acetaminophen (P < 0.01 and P < 0.05, respectively) and ibuprofen (P < 0.001 and P < 0.01, respectively) at 6 hours after administration. Both naproxen doses scored higher than placebo for symptom relief and drug preference (all P < 0.001). Adverse events and their frequency were similar among the treatment groups, and no serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A pooled analysis by manufacturer-era investigators rather than one new trial, and every comparison is at over-the-counter doses — the ibuprofen dose beaten at 6 hours was 200 mg, not the 400 mg prescription-style dose used in the Dawood crossover.
cards.source: Milsom I et al.. Comparison of the efficacy and safety of nonprescription doses of naproxen and naproxen sodium with ibuprofen, acetaminophen, and placebo in the treatment of primary dysmenorrhea: a pooled analysis of five studies.. Clinical Therapeutics. 2002. PMID: 12380631. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: NSAIDs beat placebo, and naproxen beat aspirin and paracetamol at the doses tested — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: NSAIDs beat placebo, and naproxen beat aspirin and paracetamol at the doses tested — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Women and adolescents with primary dysmenorrhoea across a 12-woman double-blind crossover (Dawood 2007), a 32-woman crossover (Rosenwaks 1981), and a pooled analysis of five trials in 443 women (Milsom 2002).
cards.result: Ibuprofen 400 mg and acetaminophen 1,000 mg both beat placebo on pain, with ibuprofen the stronger prostaglandin suppressor (menstrual-fluid PGF2α 14.8 vs 36.2 µg on placebo). Naproxen sodium beat aspirin (p=.02) and placebo (p=.002) while aspirin did not beat placebo (p=.05); pooled, naproxen beat acetaminophen within 30 minutes and beat acetaminophen and ibuprofen 200 mg at 6 hours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The individual placebo-controlled trials are very small and old, the largest evidence is a pooled analysis of over-the-counter doses, and nothing here compares NSAIDs with hormonal treatments or covers secondary dysmenorrhoea (pain from endometriosis or other pelvic disease).

shelves.title: Vitex (chasteberry) for PMS: one proper randomised trial of the Ze 440 extract, responders 52% versus 24% — and a long tail of uncontrolled use
shelves.question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does Vitex agnus-castus extract (the standardised preparation Ze 440) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · *Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · *Plants, Medicinal · Premenstrual Syndrome/*drug therapy/psychology · Prospective Studies · Vitex/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Vitex (chasteberry) is the standard herbal answer to premenstrual syndrome, and it rests on one genuine randomised trial. In the Schellenberg trial (170 women evaluated over three cycles), the standardised extract Ze 440 was significantly better than placebo on the main symptom outcome (p<0.001), with 52% of women responding on the extract versus 24% on placebo, and only mild adverse events. An earlier prospective series of the same extract (43 completers) found a 42.5% fall in symptom scores — consistent, but with no comparison group it cannot separate the extract from the substantial placebo response PMS trials always show. One randomised trial, a named standardised extract, a plausible effect: that is a developer-verdict shelf, and the stamp stays moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: The one randomised trial: Ze 440 beat placebo over three cycles (responders 52% versus 24%; main outcome p<0.001)
cards.summary: The one randomised trial: Ze 440 beat placebo over three cycles (responders 52% versus 24%; main outcome p<0.001)
cards.people: 170 women with premenstrual syndrome evaluated (86 on extract, 84 on placebo) in a prospective, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of Vitex agnus-castus fruit extract Ze 440 over three menstrual cycles.
cards.result: The main symptom outcome favoured Ze 440 significantly (p<0.001); 52% of women on the extract were responders versus 24% on placebo. Adverse events were mild. The tested product is the standardised extract Ze 440 — vitex products are not interchangeable, and the publication names this extract as the tested preparation.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries the benefit claim. The record's MeSH includes 'Prospective Studies' — copied verbatim, as published.

cards.headline: Uncontrolled series of the same extract: symptom scores fell 42.5% — but there was no placebo group to compare against
cards.summary: Uncontrolled series of the same extract: symptom scores fell 42.5% — but there was no placebo group to compare against
cards.type: Prospective uncontrolled series — no comparison group (Berger 2000)
cards.people: 50 women with PMS treated openly with Ze 440 (20 mg native extract daily) for three menstrual cycles; 43 completed, followed through three further untreated cycles (Berger 2000).
cards.result: Moos' Menstrual Distress Questionnaire scores fell 42.5% on treatment (p<0.001), with 20 of 43 women classed as responders (≥50% score reduction); symptoms crept back after stopping but remained 20% below baseline three cycles later. With no comparison group, this cannot show the extract caused the improvement — PMS placebo responses are large.
cards.watchOut: Supportive context only. It is carded so the shelf shows the whole record honestly: one randomised trial plus one open series, both of the same named extract, Ze 440.

shelves.title: Calcium for PMS: one large trial found a 48% symptom fall against 30% on placebo — a good result that nobody has repeated
shelves.question: In women with premenstrual syndrome, does calcium carbonate (1,200 mg/day elemental calcium) reduce premenstrual symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Calcium Carbonate/*therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Menstruation/*drug effects · Middle Aged · Premenstrual Syndrome/*drug therapy · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: Calcium for PMS is an old hypothesis — that premenstrual symptoms reflect disturbed calcium regulation — tested once, properly, at scale. In the Thys-Jacobs multicentre trial (497 women enrolled, 466 analysed), calcium carbonate supplying 1,200 mg of elemental calcium a day, taken for three menstrual cycles, reduced total symptom scores by 48% from baseline against 30% on placebo; all four symptom factors (negative affect, water retention, food cravings, pain) were significantly reduced by the third cycle, and luteal-phase scores were already significantly lower by the second cycle. Thirty percent on placebo is a reminder of how much of PMS treatment response is non-specific — but the 18-point gap over placebo in a 466-woman double-blind trial is a real result. It has simply never been repeated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large, well-run trial; a single-trial shelf for the developer's verdict.

cards.headline: Calcium carbonate 1,200 mg/day cut total PMS symptom scores 48% versus 30% on placebo over three cycles (n=466 analysed)
cards.summary: Calcium carbonate 1,200 mg/day cut total PMS symptom scores 48% versus 30% on placebo over three cycles (n=466 analysed)
cards.people: 497 women with moderate-to-severe, prospectively confirmed premenstrual syndrome enrolled at 12 US centres (466 valid for efficacy analysis), randomised double-blind to calcium carbonate (1,200 mg/day elemental calcium) or placebo for three menstrual cycles, with daily ratings of 17 core symptoms.
cards.result: By the third treatment cycle, total symptom scores had fallen 48% from baseline on calcium versus 30% on placebo; luteal-phase symptom scores were significantly lower on calcium at cycle 2 (p=0.007) and cycle 3 (p<0.001), and all four symptom factors were significantly reduced by cycle 3.
cards.watchOut: One trial, never independently replicated in nearly three decades — the gap is real but the shelf stays single-trial. Calcium is a defined supplement, so no brand question arises; the dose (1,200 mg elemental) is at the level where total dietary-plus-supplement intake deserves a thought.

shelves.title: SSRIs for premenstrual dysphoric disorder: fluoxetine and sertraline both clearly beat placebo — 62% much improved on sertraline versus 34%
shelves.question: In women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), do SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) reduce premenstrual symptoms and functional impairment compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Depression/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluoxetine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Humans · Middle Aged · Premenstrual Syndrome/*drug therapy/psychology · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder — the severe, function-wrecking end of premenstrual symptoms — is one of the clearest SSRI successes outside depression itself. In the Canadian fluoxetine trial (313 women randomised after a placebo washout), both 20 mg and 60 mg daily beat placebo on tension, irritability and dysphoria (p<0.001); 60 mg brought significantly more side effects, and the authors settled on 20 mg as the dose. In the sertraline trial (243 randomised, 200 completed), daily symptom scores fell from 64 to 44 on sertraline against 62 to 54 on placebo (p<0.001), depression ratings fell 44% versus 29% (p<0.002), and 62% of women were much or very much improved against 34% on placebo. Two drugs of the same class, two multicentre trials, the same answer. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): consistent class evidence for a disabling condition, on symptom and functioning outcomes rather than hard endpoints.

cards.headline: Fluoxetine 20 mg and 60 mg both beat placebo for premenstrual dysphoria (p<0.001); 60 mg caused more side effects
cards.summary: Fluoxetine 20 mg and 60 mg both beat placebo for premenstrual dysphoria (p<0.001); 60 mg caused more side effects
cards.people: 313 women with premenstrual dysphoria randomised in a Canadian multicentre double-blind trial (after a single-blind placebo washout) to fluoxetine 20 mg, fluoxetine 60 mg, or placebo; 180 completed.
cards.result: Both fluoxetine doses were significantly superior to placebo on the primary symptom measures — tension, irritability and dysphoria (p<0.001). The 60 mg dose caused significantly more side effects than 20 mg, and the paper endorses 20 mg as the effective, better-tolerated dose.
cards.watchOut: Completion was incomplete (180 of 313), a common weakness of this era's PMDD trials; the record's MeSH oddly includes 'Single-Blind Method' alongside 'Double-Blind Method' — copied verbatim, as published.

cards.headline: Sertraline: symptom scores fell 64→44 versus 62→54 on placebo; 62% much or very much improved versus 34%
cards.summary: Sertraline: symptom scores fell 64→44 versus 62→54 on placebo; 62% much or very much improved versus 34%
cards.people: 243 women meeting PMDD criteria randomised (200 completed) across 12 US university clinics to flexible-dose sertraline 50–150 mg/day or placebo for three cycles, after screening and a single-blind placebo cycle.
cards.result: Total daily symptom scores fell significantly more on sertraline (64±22 to 44±19) than placebo (62±22 to 54±24; p<0.001); Hamilton depression scores fell 44% versus 29% (p<0.002); end-point global ratings of much or very much improvement were 62% versus 34% (p<0.001), with functioning gains similar in size to those seen in major-depression trials.
cards.watchOut: Continuous daily dosing was the tested strategy; later luteal-phase-only dosing is a different question. Symptom-diary outcomes are subjective by nature, though the functioning measures moved with them.

shelves.title: Evening primrose oil for breast pain: two blinded trials say no — pain fell just as much on dummy oils, with a 40% placebo response
shelves.question: In women with mastalgia (breast pain), does evening primrose oil / gamolenic acid reduce breast pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · *Breast · Chronic Disease · Corn Oil/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Fatty Acids, Essential/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Female · Fish Oils/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Humans · Linoleic Acids · Oenothera biennis · Pain/*drug therapy/physiopathology · Pain Measurement · Palliative Care/standards · Plant Oils/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Linolenic Acid
shelves.balance: Evening primrose oil has been the default recommendation for cyclical breast pain for decades — and the two proper trials of its active ingredient, gamolenic acid (GLA), both say it does not work. In a 120-woman factorial trial, days with pain fell 12.3% on evening primrose oil and 13.8% on its control oil (p=0.73); fish oil, tested alongside, was likewise indistinguishable from its control. In the much larger Efamast trial (555 women), breast pain improved substantially in every group — the placebo fatty-acid groups responded at 40% — with no significant difference for GLA in any comparison, with or without antioxidant vitamins. Mastalgia improves on its own and responds strongly to reassurance and placebo; the oil adds nothing measurable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two double-blind trials, one of them large, both null.

cards.headline: Factorial trial: days with breast pain fell 12.3% on evening primrose oil versus 13.8% on its control oil (p=0.73)
cards.summary: Factorial trial: days with breast pain fell 12.3% on evening primrose oil versus 13.8% on its control oil (p=0.73)
cards.people: 120 premenopausal women with severe chronic mastalgia randomised double-blind in a 2×2 factorial trial (evening primrose oil and/or fish oil versus corn-oil controls) for 6 months; outcome was change in percentage of days with breast pain.
cards.result: Pain days fell 12.3% on evening primrose oil versus 13.8% on its control oil (p=0.73), and 15.5% on fish oil versus 10.6% on its control (p=0.28). All groups improved; neither oil beat its control. The publications do not rest the result on a named retail brand of evening primrose oil.
cards.watchOut: Severe chronic mastalgia in premenopausal women; the null for fish oil is a by-product of the factorial design and belongs to this shelf's balance, not to the fish-oil shelves.
cards.source: Blommers J et al.. Evening primrose oil and fish oil for severe chronic mastalgia: a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2002. shelves.title: Treating a urine infection with ibuprofen first: two-thirds of women never needed an antibiotic — but symptoms lasted longer and kidney infections were commoner
shelves.question: In women with uncomplicated urinary tract infection, does starting with ibuprofen (symptomatic treatment, antibiotics held in reserve) safely reduce antibiotic use compared with an immediate antibiotic?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Female · Fosfomycin/*administration & dosage · Humans · Ibuprofen/*administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Tract Infections/*drug therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Most uncomplicated urinary infections settle without antibiotics, and two German trials asked whether treating symptoms with ibuprofen first could spare antibiotics safely. The large trial (494 women) found the strategy works in the narrow sense: women on ibuprofen used significantly fewer antibiotic courses over 28 days, and two-thirds recovered with no antibiotic at all. But they paid for it — a significantly higher burden of symptoms over the first week, and more cases of pyelonephritis (kidney infection) in the ibuprofen group; four serious adverse events led to hospital referral, one possibly drug-related. The smaller pilot (80 women) had found day-4 symptom freedom at least as good on ibuprofen as on ciprofloxacin (58.3% versus 51.5%). Read together: an ibuprofen-first approach is a legitimate option for a woman with mild-to-moderate symptoms who wants to avoid antibiotics and accepts slower relief with a small risk of the infection climbing — it is not an equivalent treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for antibiotic sparing, Tier C for the harm trade-off: the developer rules personally.

cards.headline: Gágyör 2015: ibuprofen-first spared antibiotics (two-thirds needed none) but brought more symptoms and more pyelonephritis
cards.summary: Gágyör 2015: ibuprofen-first spared antibiotics (two-thirds needed none) but brought more symptoms and more pyelonephritis
cards.people: 494 women aged 18–65 with typical symptoms of uncomplicated UTI in 42 German general practices, randomised double-blind to ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 3 days or a single 3 g dose of fosfomycin (with matching placebos); antibiotics remained available for persisting, worsening or recurrent symptoms. 484 women were analysed.
cards.result: The ibuprofen group received significantly fewer antibiotic courses over days 0–28, and two-thirds of them recovered without any antibiotic. Against that, their total symptom burden over days 0–7 was significantly higher, and more of them developed pyelonephritis. Four serious adverse events led to hospital referral, one potentially related to the trial drug. Registry ID: NCT01488955 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: The authors themselves caution that the results may apply to women with mild-to-moderate symptoms rather than all uncomplicated UTI. The pyelonephritis excess is the reason this shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Gágyör I et al.. Ibuprofen versus fosfomycin for uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women: randomised controlled trial. The BMJ. 2015. PMID: 26698878. Registry ID: NCT01488955.
