cards.headline: Bleidorn 2010 pilot: day-4 symptom freedom 58.3% on ibuprofen versus 51.5% on ciprofloxacin
cards.summary: Bleidorn 2010 pilot: day-4 symptom freedom 58.3% on ibuprofen versus 51.5% on ciprofloxacin
cards.people: 80 otherwise healthy women aged 18–85 with dysuria and/or frequency and no complicating factors, randomised double-blind in 29 German practices to ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily or ciprofloxacin 250 mg twice daily for 3 days; 79 analysed.
cards.result: On day 4, 21/36 (58.3%) of the ibuprofen group were symptom-free versus 17/33 (51.5%) on ciprofloxacin, and total symptom scores were similar between groups — the pilot's purpose was a rough equivalence estimate and proof that such a trial could be run, which the later BMJ trial then did at scale. Registry ID: ISRCTN00470468 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: A pilot — small numbers, wide uncertainty — and its antibiotic comparator (ciprofloxacin) is no longer a first-line UTI drug in many guidelines. Its weight here is as the feasibility study for the 2015 trial.
cards.source: Bleidorn J et al.. Symptomatic treatment (ibuprofen) or antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) for uncomplicated urinary tract infection?--results of a randomized controlled pilot trial. shelves.title: Tranexamic acid for heavy periods: measured blood loss fell about 40–45% in two trials — a real, non-hormonal option
shelves.question: In women with heavy menstrual bleeding, does oral tranexamic acid reduce menstrual blood loss compared with placebo or hormonal treatment?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Antifibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Menorrhagia/*drug therapy · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Quality of Life · Tranexamic Acid/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Tranexamic acid is the non-hormonal tablet option for heavy periods, and it has the trial record to back the claim. In the pivotal US trial (187 women with objectively heavy loss), tranexamic acid 3.9 g/day for up to five days per cycle cut menstrual blood loss by 69.6 mL (40.4%) against 12.6 mL (8.2%) on placebo (p<0.001), meeting all three pre-specified efficacy criteria, with quality-of-life gains to match and a side-effect profile comparable to placebo. An earlier Cambridge trial, using the objective alkaline-haematin measurement, found tranexamic acid reduced loss by 45% (175 to 97 mL), while the hormonal comparator norethisterone actually increased loss by 20%; 56% of tranexamic-acid cycles normalised (under 80 mL) versus 9.5% on norethisterone. Two trials, an objective endpoint, a consistent 40–45% relative reduction in measured blood loss. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Lukes 2010: blood loss fell 69.6 mL (40.4%) on tranexamic acid versus 12.6 mL (8.2%) on placebo (p<0.001)
cards.summary: Lukes 2010: blood loss fell 69.6 mL (40.4%) on tranexamic acid versus 12.6 mL (8.2%) on placebo (p<0.001)
cards.people: Women with heavy menstrual bleeding (mean measured loss ≥80 mL/cycle) randomised double-blind to oral tranexamic acid 3.9 g/day (n=115) or placebo (n=72) for up to 5 days per cycle over six cycles.
cards.result: Mean blood-loss reduction was −69.6 mL (40.4%) on tranexamic acid versus −12.6 mL (8.2%) on placebo (p<0.001), exceeding both the 50 mL and the pre-set meaningfulness thresholds; limitations in social, leisure, physical and work activities also improved significantly (p<0.01). Gastrointestinal adverse events were comparable to placebo. Registry ID: NCT00386308 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: Tranexamic acid is a defined drug, so no product question arises. The trial excluded women with pathology needing surgery; it shows symptom relief, not treatment of any underlying cause.
cards.source: Lukes AS et al.. Tranexamic acid treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding: a randomized controlled trial. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2010. PMID: 20859150. Registry ID: NCT00386308. cards.headline: Preston 1995: tranexamic acid cut measured loss 45% (175→97 mL); norethisterone increased it 20%
cards.summary: Preston 1995: tranexamic acid cut measured loss 45% (175→97 mL); norethisterone increased it 20%
cards.people: 103 women with heavy periods recruited; the double-blind comparison covered 46 women with confirmed ovulatory menorrhagia (loss >80 mL/cycle), randomised to tranexamic acid 1 g four times daily on days 1–4 (n=25) or norethisterone (n=21) for two cycles, blood loss measured by the alkaline-haematin method.
cards.result: Tranexamic acid reduced mean loss by 45%, from 175 mL to 97 mL (95% CI for the difference 52 to 108; p<0.0001); norethisterone increased loss by 20% (173 to 208 mL). 56% of women on tranexamic acid achieved a mean loss under the 80 mL menorrhagia threshold, versus 9.5% on norethisterone. No serious adverse events in either group.
cards.watchOut: Small and old, and the placebo group's data sit behind the run-in design — but its endpoint was the objective laboratory measurement, and it points the same way as the 2010 trial.
cards.source: Preston JT et al.. Comparative study of tranexamic acid and norethisterone in the treatment of ovulatory menorrhagia. The British Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 1995. PMID: 7612535. shelves.title: Fenugreek to increase breast-milk production
shelves.question: Does fenugreek increase breast-milk production in breastfeeding mothers?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Beverages · Birth Weight · Breast Feeding · Double-Blind Method · Female · Galactogogues · Growth · Growth Disorders · Humans · Infant Nutrition Disorders · Infant, Newborn · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two trials of multi-herb blends containing fenugreek were positive (one without reporting milk volumes), while the only trial of fenugreek alone (n = 68, triple-blind) found a day-7 advantage that was gone by day 15, with no prolactin or infant-weight effect. Attribution to fenugreek itself is not established.

cards.headline: Mothers drinking a fenugreek-containing galactagogue tea produced more milk on day 3
cards.summary: Mothers drinking a fenugreek-containing galactagogue tea produced more milk on day 3
cards.people: 66 mother–infant pairs in the first week after birth; herbal tea containing fenugreek daily vs placebo tea vs no-tea control (22 per group), double-blind for the tea comparison
cards.result: Measured breast-milk volume on day 3 was significantly higher in the tea group than in both the placebo and control groups (P < 0.05; the abstract reports no volumes). Maximum infant weight loss was significantly lower in the tea group, and those infants regained their birth weight earlier (P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: The tea was a blend — fenugreek was one ingredient among several, so the effect cannot be credited to fenugreek alone. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Turkyılmaz C et al.. The effect of galactagogue herbal tea on breast milk production and short-term catch-up of birth weight in the first week of life. J Altern Complement Med. 2011. PMID: 21261516. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: A fenugreek–ginger–turmeric mixture raised milk volume 49% by week 2 and 103% by week 4 relative to baseline

cards.headline: Fenugreek alone helped at day 7 but not by day 15 in mothers of preterm babies
cards.summary: Fenugreek alone helped at day 7 but not by day 15 in mothers of preterm babies
cards.people: 68 mothers of preterm newborns (<32 weeks) in Tabriz, Iran; fenugreek 500 mg three times daily or placebo from day 5 to day 14 after delivery, triple-blind
cards.result: Milk volume was significantly higher on fenugreek at day 7 of the intervention (P = 0.017) but not at day 15 (P = 0.073). Prolactin levels did not differ (P = 0.324), nor did newborn weight gain (P = 0.172) or breastfeeding satisfaction (P = 0.484). No side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: The one trial of fenugreek alone shows an effect that appears and then fades within two weeks — the weakest pattern on this shelf. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: Something in these herbal preparations may nudge milk volume up briefly, but the two positive trials used blends, and the one trial of fenugreek alone found only a transient day-7 difference. Fenugreek for milk supply is unproven; a mother with supply problems deserves a feeding assessment first.
cards.watchOut: No trial measured infant growth as a primary outcome or followed feeding beyond the first weeks.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.

shelves.title: Continuous one-to-one support during labour
shelves.question: Does continuous one-to-one support during labour (from a doula or other dedicated companion) improve birth outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anesthesia, Epidural · Anesthesia, Obstetrical · Cesarean Section · Female · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Labor, Obstetric · Middle Aged · Obstetrics and Gynecology Department, Hospital · Oxytocin · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, Tier C — the Cochrane pooling (22 trials, 15,288 women) gives a caesarean relative risk of 0.78, and two US doula trials were strongly positive (8% vs 13–18%; 13.4% vs 25.0%), but the largest single trial — continuous support from the hospital's own nurses in 6,915 women — was exactly null. Tier C because caesarean and Apgar outcomes are hard endpoints and the effect depends on who provides the support.

cards.headline: A doula's continuous presence cut caesarean rates to 8%, vs 13% observed and 18% control
cards.summary: A doula's continuous presence cut caesarean rates to 8%, vs 13% observed and 18% control
cards.people: 412 healthy first-time mothers in labour at a Houston hospital, randomised to continuous doula support or an observed group; a further 204 women formed a control group assigned after delivery
cards.result: Caesarean delivery: 8% in the supported group, 13% in the observed group and 18% in the control group. Forceps deliveries followed the same pattern, as did epidural use for spontaneous vaginal deliveries (7.8% vs 22.6% vs 55.3%), oxytocin use, labour duration and prolonged infant hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: The control group was assembled after delivery rather than randomised alongside, so the cleanest comparison is doula 8% vs observed 13%.

cards.headline: With a partner already present, adding a doula still halved caesareans: 13.4% vs 25.0%
cards.summary: With a partner already present, adding a doula still halved caesareans: 13.4% vs 25.0%
cards.people: 420 middle-income first-time mothers in Cleveland, Ohio, all accompanied by a male partner; a doula present from soon after admission through delivery vs usual care
cards.result: Caesarean delivery: 13.4% in the doula group vs 25.0% in controls (P = 0.002). Epidural analgesia: 64.7% vs 76.0% (P = 0.008). Among women with induced labour the caesarean gap was wider still (12.5% vs 58.8%, P = 0.007). All couples with doula support rated the experience positively.
cards.watchOut: Recruited in 1988–1992 within one hospital system, and the induced-labour subgroup is small.

cards.headline: When the same support came from the hospital's own nurses, the effect vanished entirely
cards.summary: When the same support came from the hospital's own nurses, the effect vanished entirely
cards.people: 6,915 women at 13 US and Canadian hospitals with caesarean rates of at least 15%; continuous labour support by specially trained nurses vs usual care
cards.result: Caesarean delivery: 12.5% in the continuous-support group vs 12.6% in the usual-care group (P = 0.44). There were no significant differences in other maternal or neonatal events during labour, delivery or the hospital stay, nor in perceived control or depression at 6–8 weeks — though women's likes and future preferences all favoured having the support.
cards.watchOut: This is the largest trial on the shelf and it is null. The difference from the doula trials is who provides the support, and the intervention-heavy hospital culture around them.

cards.headline: Cochrane review of 22 trials: continuous support lowered caesareans by about a fifth in relative terms
cards.summary: Cochrane review of 22 trials: continuous support lowered caesareans by about a fifth in relative terms
cards.people: 22 trials, 15,288 women; continuous one-to-one intrapartum support vs usual care
cards.result: Caesarean: relative risk 0.78 (95% CI 0.67–0.91). Spontaneous vaginal birth: RR 1.08 (95% CI 1.04–1.12). Labours were 0.58 hours shorter on average; intrapartum analgesia RR 0.90; dissatisfaction RR 0.69; low five-minute Apgar score RR 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.95). Subgroup analyses suggested support was most effective when the provider was neither hospital staff nor the woman's social network, and in settings where epidural analgesia was not routinely available.
cards.watchOut: The pooled effect averages very different settings — the subgroup pattern is exactly the warning of the large nurse-support trial carded above.

cards.headline: What this means
cards.summary: What this means
cards.result: A dedicated companion who is not part of the hospital staff — a doula — reduces caesareans and interventions in most settings studied. The same hours of support delivered by the unit's own nurses in high-intervention hospitals did nothing measurable. Who supports, and the culture they work against, is the treatment.
cards.watchOut: Support cannot be blinded, and most doula trials are decades old, from eras and places with different baseline caesarean rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of the references on this shelf.

shelves.title: Cleaner cookstoves in pregnancy (HAPIN): pollution exposure fell by two-thirds, and birth weight, fetal growth and infant pneumonia did not change
shelves.question: In pregnant women who cook with biomass fuel, does switching to a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cookstove improve birth weight, fetal growth, or infant pneumonia?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Air Pollution, Indoor*/adverse effects, analysis · Biomass · Birth Weight* · Cooking*/methods · Particulate Matter*/adverse effects, analysis · Petroleum*/adverse effects, analysis · Infant, Newborn · Adolescent · Young Adult · Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a large, well-delivered randomised programme with three concordant nulls. In HAPIN, 3,200 pregnant women in Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda were randomised to LPG stoves with free fuel or continued biomass cooking; measured particulate exposure fell by about two-thirds (median PM2.5 23.9 vs 70.7 µg/m³). Birth weight differed by 19.6 g (95% CI −10.1 to 49.2; Clasen 2022, PMID: 36214599), severe infant pneumonia occurred at 5.67 vs 6.06 per 100 child-years (IRR 0.96, 98.75% CI 0.64 to 1.44; McCollum 2024, PMID: 38169488), and ultrasound fetal growth was identical (Z-scores −0.13 vs −0.12; Checkley 2024, PMID: 38614630). The three papers are one trial, not three — the shelf says so on every card. The null is scoped: intervention began in mid-pregnancy, and residual exposure stayed above clean-air targets. Tier C: a single trial programme carrying infant-outcome claims, flagged for the developer's personal verdict.

cards.headline: Clasen 2022 (HAPIN): LPG cookstoves in pregnancy — birth weight differed by 19.6 g (CI −10.1 to 49.2); the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: Clasen 2022 (HAPIN): LPG cookstoves in pregnancy — birth weight differed by 19.6 g (CI −10.1 to 49.2); the treatment made no difference
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (Clasen 2022, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: The Household Air Pollution Intervention Network (HAPIN) trial: a randomised controlled trial of 3,200 pregnant women (18 to <35 years, 9 to <20 weeks' gestation) in Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda, assigned to a free liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) cookstove with continuous fuel delivery or to continue cooking with biomass. Birth weight was measured within 24 hours of birth; 3,061 live births were analysed. Personal fine particulate (PM2.5) exposure fell substantially: median 23.9 µg/m³ in the LPG group versus 70.7 µg/m³ with biomass.
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference in birth weight was 19.6 g (95% CI −10.1 to 49.2) — a null result: despite a roughly two-thirds reduction in measured particulate exposure, babies born to women cooking with LPG weighed no more than babies in the biomass group.
cards.watchOut: A null for birth weight is not a null for every outcome of household air pollution, and exposure contrast, while large, still left the LPG group above WHO air-quality targets. The trial tested one stove-and-fuel package delivered from mid-pregnancy; earlier or longer intervention was not tested.
cards.source: Clasen TF et al. Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass for Cooking and Effects on Birth Weight. New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36214599. cards.headline: McCollum 2024 (HAPIN): severe infant pneumonia 5.67 vs 6.06 per 100 child-years (IRR 0.96) — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: McCollum 2024 (HAPIN): severe infant pneumonia 5.67 vs 6.06 per 100 child-years (IRR 0.96) — the treatment made no difference
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (McCollum 2024, New England Journal of Medicine)
cards.people: The infant-pneumonia primary-outcome report of the same HAPIN randomised trial (pregnant women 18 to 34 years in India, Guatemala, Peru and Rwanda, randomised May 2018 to September 2021 to unvented LPG stoves with fuel or continued biomass cooking); infants were followed through the first year of life with personal exposure monitoring in mothers and offspring.
cards.result: Severe pneumonia incidence in the first year of life was 5.67 per 100 child-years in the LPG group versus 6.06 per 100 child-years in the biomass group (incidence rate ratio 0.96, 98.75% CI 0.64 to 1.44; P = 0.81) — no difference.
cards.watchOut: This is the same single trial programme as the birth-weight and fetal-growth reports, not independent confirmation: HAPIN is one large trial read three ways. Severe pneumonia was uncommon enough that the interval still admits a moderate benefit or harm, but the point estimate sits on the null.
cards.source: McCollum ED et al. Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass Cooking and Severe Infant Pneumonia. New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38169488. cards.headline: Checkley 2024 (HAPIN): fetal growth on serial ultrasound — no difference in any growth measure
cards.summary: Checkley 2024 (HAPIN): fetal growth on serial ultrasound — no difference in any growth measure
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (Checkley 2024, Lancet Global Health)
cards.people: The fetal-growth report of the HAPIN open-label randomised trial (ten resource-limited settings across Guatemala, India, Peru and Rwanda): pregnant women aged 18–34 years at 9–19 weeks' gestation received an LPG stove, continuous fuel delivery and behavioural messaging, or continued biomass cooking; fetal size was measured by ultrasound at baseline, 24–28 weeks and 32–36 weeks, with 24-hour personal exposure monitoring.
cards.result: There were no differences between groups in fetal growth: estimated fetal weight and birthweight Z-scores were −0.13 in the intervention group versus −0.12 in the control group (p = 0.70), and no ultrasound growth measure separated the groups.
cards.watchOut: Ultrasound fetal biometry is a surrogate chain — growth restriction matters through birth outcomes and later health — but it agrees with the trial's directly measured nulls for birth weight and infant pneumonia. Open-label design is unavoidable for a cookstove intervention.
cards.source: Checkley W et al. Cooking with liquefied petroleum gas or biomass and fetal growth outcomes: a multi-country randomised controlled trial. Lancet Global Health. 2024. PMID: 38614630. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large, well-executed trial programme; exposure fell by two-thirds and none of the three prespecified outcome families moved — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large, well-executed trial programme; exposure fell by two-thirds and none of the three prespecified outcome families moved — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: One randomised programme (HAPIN, NCT02944682; 3,200 pregnant women, four countries) reported across three papers: birth weight (Clasen 2022), severe infant pneumonia (McCollum 2024) and ultrasound fetal growth (Checkley 2024).
cards.result: Birth weight: +19.6 g (95% CI −10.1 to 49.2). Severe infant pneumonia: IRR 0.96 (98.75% CI 0.64 to 1.44). Fetal growth: Z-scores −0.13 vs −0.12 (p = 0.70). All three are null, in a trial that achieved a large, measured exposure contrast (median PM2.5 23.9 vs 70.7 µg/m³) with monitored adherence — this is an informative null, not a failed intervention delivery.
cards.watchOut: The null applies to starting LPG in mid-pregnancy in these settings; it does not test preconception or lifelong exposure reduction, other pollutants, or non-pregnancy outcomes (the trial's maternal and older-child outcomes are reported separately and are not carded here).

shelves.title: Combined first-trimester screening for pre-eclampsia: detects about 77–82% of preterm cases versus about 41% for the risk-factor checklist — better selection, proven; delivery of the aspirin it selects for, not
shelves.question: In pregnant women, does first-trimester combined screening for preterm pre-eclampsia (maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, uterine artery Doppler, placental growth factor) select aspirin prophylaxis better than risk-factor checklists?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Algorithms · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Mass Screening/methods · Placenta Growth Factor/blood · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Pre-Eclampsia/diagnosis/prevention & control · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein-A/metabolism · Prospective Studies · Research Design · Uterine Artery/diagnostic imaging · Young Adult
shelves.balance: On accuracy, it is not close. The Fetal Medicine Foundation combined algorithm — maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, uterine artery Doppler, PAPP-A and placental growth factor at 11–13 weeks — detected 76.7% of preterm pre-eclampsia at a 10.5% screen-positive rate in ASPRE's screened population (Rolnik 2017, PMID: 28741785). In SPREE's head-to-head (Tan 2018, PMID: 29536574), the full combined test detected 82.4% of preterm pre-eclampsia versus 40.8% for the NICE risk-factor checklist at the same screen-positive rate; even the mini-combined test beat the checklist on all pre-eclampsia (42.5% versus 30.4%). Two qualifications keep this at POSSIBLE rather than higher: no trial randomises screening strategies to clinical outcomes — the benefit chain runs through the ASPRE aspirin trial (homed at shelves #151 and #412), whose 62% relative reduction in preterm pre-eclampsia applies only if the right women are actually given aspirin, and SPREE found checklist-era compliance of just 23%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: prospective accuracy studies; the linked treatment trial is homed elsewhere).

cards.headline: Rolnik 2017 (ASPRE screening performance): the combined first-trimester algorithm detected 76.7% of preterm pre-eclampsia at a 10.5% screen-positive rate — the checklist-free performance benchmark
cards.summary: Rolnik 2017 (ASPRE screening performance): the combined first-trimester algorithm detected 76.7% of preterm pre-eclampsia at a 10.5% screen-positive rate — the checklist-free performance benchmark
cards.people: Prospective multicentre screening study within the ASPRE programme: 25,797 singleton pregnancies screened at 11–13 weeks with the Fetal Medicine Foundation algorithm combining maternal factors, mean arterial pressure, uterine artery pulsatility index, PAPP-A and placental growth factor; a risk cut-off of 1 in 100 defined screen-positive. Screen-positive women were invited into the ASPRE aspirin trial, and detection rates are adjusted for aspirin's effect.
cards.result: There were 180 cases of preterm pre-eclampsia (0.7%) and 450 of term pre-eclampsia (1.7%). At the 1-in-100 cut-off, the detection rate was 76.7% (138 of 180) for preterm pre-eclampsia and 43.1% (194 of 450) for term pre-eclampsia, at a screen-positive rate of 10.5% and a false-positive rate of 9.2%. Performance matched the roughly 60,000-pregnancy development study (76.6% detection of preterm pre-eclampsia at a 10% false-positive rate). The record carries no registry ID.
cards.watchOut: Detection of preterm pre-eclampsia is the algorithm's home ground — it detects under half of term pre-eclampsia, which is the more common form. The adjustment for aspirin use in screen-positive women is modelled, not observed, and the algorithm requires a certified uterine-artery Doppler measurement, which is the implementation bottleneck in most health systems.
cards.source: Rolnik DL et al. ASPRE trial: performance of screening for preterm pre-eclampsia. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol. 2017. PMID: 28741785. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tan 2018 (SPREE): head-to-head in the same women, the combined test detected 82.4% of preterm pre-eclampsia where the NICE risk-factor checklist detected 40.8% — at the same screen-positive rate
cards.summary: Tan 2018 (SPREE): head-to-head in the same women, the combined test detected 82.4% of preterm pre-eclampsia where the NICE risk-factor checklist detected 40.8% — at the same screen-positive rate
cards.people: Prospective multicentre study in seven English NHS maternity hospitals: 16,747 singleton pregnancies screened at 11–13 weeks; the Bayes-based combined methods (maternal factors with mean arterial pressure, PAPP-A, placental growth factor and uterine artery Doppler in various combinations) were compared against screening by the NICE guideline risk-factor checklist, at the checklist's own screen-positive rate. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: Pre-eclampsia developed in 473 women (2.8%) and preterm pre-eclampsia in 142 (0.8%). The NICE method's screen-positive rate was 10.3%, with detection rates of 30.4% for all pre-eclampsia and 40.8% for preterm pre-eclampsia — and compliance with the NICE recommendation to give aspirin to high-risk women was only 23%. At the same screen-positive rate, the mini-combined test detected 42.5% of all pre-eclampsia (12.1 points above NICE, 95% CI 7.9 to 16.2), and the full combined test detected 82.4% of preterm pre-eclampsia (41.6 points above NICE, 33.2 to 49.9).
cards.watchOut: A single health system (English NHS hospitals) with research-grade measurements; the comparison fixes the screen-positive rate at the checklist's 10.3%, which flatters neither side but is a convention. The 23% compliance figure is arguably the most important number in the paper — a checklist that is not acted on detects nothing, whatever its nominal accuracy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: combined screening roughly doubles the detection of preterm pre-eclampsia over risk-factor checklists at the same screen-positive rate — and the treatment it selects for is proven, on another shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: combined screening roughly doubles the detection of preterm pre-eclampsia over risk-factor checklists at the same screen-positive rate — and the treatment it selects for is proven, on another shelf
cards.people: Two large prospective multicentre studies: ASPRE's screening-performance analysis (25,797 pregnancies) and SPREE's head-to-head against the NICE checklist (16,747 pregnancies).
cards.result: Detection of preterm pre-eclampsia: 76.7% (ASPRE, at a 10.5% screen-positive rate) and 82.4% for the full combined test in SPREE, versus 40.8% for the NICE checklist at its 10.3% screen-positive rate. Detection of all pre-eclampsia is lower for every method (30.4% NICE; 42.5% mini-combined). The point of selecting better is that the intervention works: in the ASPRE randomised trial, aspirin 150 mg daily in screen-positive women reduced preterm pre-eclampsia by 62% relative — that trial is homed at shelves #151 and #412 and is cross-referenced here, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Neither study randomises women to screening strategies with clinical outcomes — the chain is accuracy (shown here) plus treatment efficacy (shown elsewhere), and the middle link, that better selection in routine practice actually delivers the aspirin to the right women early enough, is supported by SPREE's compliance data pointing the wrong way (23%). Implementation, not accuracy, is the weak link.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rolnik DL et al. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol. 2017 (PMID: 28741785); Tan MY et al. Ultrasound Obstet Gynecol. 2018 (PMID: 29536574). ASPRE treatment trial (Rolnik DL et al. N Engl J Med. 2017, PMID: 28657417) homed at shelves #151 and #412.

shelves.title: Unexplained infertility: insemination with ovarian stimulation triples live births when the natural prognosis is poor — and adds nothing when the prognosis is intermediate
shelves.question: In couples with unexplained infertility, does intrauterine insemination with ovarian stimulation improve live birth rates over expectant management?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Clomiphene/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Fertility Agents, Female/administration & dosage · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Humans · Infertility, Female/therapy · Insemination, Artificial/methods · Letrozole · Nitriles/administration & dosage · Ovulation Induction/methods · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage · Watchful Waiting · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on the couple's prognosis for conceiving naturally, and the two direct randomised trials enrolled opposite ends of it. In couples with an unfavourable prognosis, the TUI trial (201 couples) found three cycles of intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation produced a cumulative live birth rate of 31% versus 9% with expectant management (risk ratio 3.41, 95% CI 1.71 to 6.79; P = .0003) (Farquhar CM et al., PMID: 29174128). In couples with an intermediate prognosis (30–40% predicted chance of spontaneous ongoing pregnancy within 12 months), the earlier Dutch trial (253 couples) found ongoing pregnancy in 23% after six months of IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation versus 27% with expectant management (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.1) — a large benefit excluded (Steures P et al., PMID: 16844491). The INeS trial adds the comparison couples actually face next: six cycles of IUI with ovarian hyperstimulation gave a 47% healthy-child rate, statistically non-inferior to IVF with single embryo transfer (52%), with multiple pregnancy rates of 7% per ongoing pregnancy (Bensdorp AJ et al., PMID: 25576320). The multiple-pregnancy hazard of stimulation is real but was small in these oral-agent and carefully monitored trials (two twin sets in TUI, both in the IUI arm; one triplet in Steures). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when prognosis is unfavourable) / LIKELY (no difference when prognosis is intermediate). Not Tier C: three randomised trials, two of them asking this exact question. Which stimulation drug to use with IUI is a separate question, homed at shelf #835.

cards.headline: Farquhar 2018 (TUI): in couples with an unfavourable prognosis for natural conception, three cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation tripled cumulative live births versus expectant management — 31% versus 9% (RR 3.41)
cards.summary: Farquhar 2018 (TUI): in couples with an unfavourable prognosis for natural conception, three cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation tripled cumulative live births versus expectant management — 31% versus 9% (RR 3.41)
cards.people: 201 women with unexplained infertility and an unfavourable prognosis of natural conception at two New Zealand fertility clinics, randomised to three cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation (clomiphene citrate 50–150 mg or letrozole 2.5–7.5 mg, days 2–6, clinic's choice) or three cycles of expectant management. Primary outcome: cumulative live birth rate, intention to treat. Pragmatic, open-label trial.
cards.result: Cumulative live birth was 31 of 101 (31%) in the IUI group versus 9 of 100 (9%) with expectant management (risk ratio 3.41, 95% CI 1.71 to 6.79; P = .0003) — an absolute gain of 22 percentage points. Of the 31 IUI-group live births, 23 came from IUI cycles and 8 were conceived without assistance before or between cycles. Two sets of twins were born, both in the IUI group (one from a cycle cancelled for over-response). The authors concluded IUI with ovarian stimulation is a safe and effective treatment for women with unexplained infertility and an unfavourable prognosis for natural conception.
cards.watchOut: The population is the message: these couples were selected because their predicted natural-conception chances were poor, and the expectant arm's 9% live birth rate confirms it. The result cannot be exported to couples with a reasonable natural prognosis — Steures (next card) shows what happens there. Open-label design is unavoidable for this comparison, but live birth is a hard endpoint, so bias risk is low.

cards.headline: Steures 2006: in couples with an intermediate prognosis, six months of IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation gave no more ongoing pregnancies than expectant management — 23% versus 27% (RR 0.85)
cards.summary: Steures 2006: in couples with an intermediate prognosis, six months of IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation gave no more ongoing pregnancies than expectant management — 23% versus 27% (RR 0.85)
cards.people: 253 couples with unexplained subfertility and an intermediate prognosis — a 30–40% probability of spontaneous ongoing pregnancy within 12 months — randomised in a hospital-based Dutch trial to IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation for 6 months (n = 127) or expectant management for 6 months (n = 126). Primary endpoint: ongoing pregnancy within 6 months.
cards.result: Ongoing pregnancy occurred in 29 of 127 (23%) in the IUI group and 34 of 126 (27%) with expectant management (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.1). Conception rates were nearly identical (33% vs 32%). There was one twin pregnancy in each group and one triplet pregnancy in the intervention group. The authors concluded that a large beneficial effect of IUI with hyperstimulation in this prognosis group can be excluded, and that expectant management for 6 months is justified.
cards.watchOut: An older trial using gonadotrophin-era hyperstimulation and a 6-month horizon; its null result applies to couples whose natural chances are middling, not poor. Together with TUI it makes prognosis — usually estimated with the Hunault model — the pivot of the IUI decision, which is exactly how the trials were designed and how the shelf's stamp is split.

cards.headline: Bensdorp 2015 (INeS): six cycles of IUI with ovarian hyperstimulation yielded a 47% healthy-child rate — non-inferior to IVF with single embryo transfer (52%), with a 7% multiple-pregnancy rate per ongoing pregnancy
cards.summary: Bensdorp 2015 (INeS): six cycles of IUI with ovarian hyperstimulation yielded a 47% healthy-child rate — non-inferior to IVF with single embryo transfer (52%), with a 7% multiple-pregnancy rate per ongoing pregnancy
cards.people: 602 couples with unexplained or mild male subfertility and an unfavourable prognosis for natural conception, randomised at 17 Dutch centres to IVF with single embryo transfer, IVF in a modified natural cycle, or six cycles of IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation within 12 months. Primary outcome: birth of a healthy child from a singleton pregnancy conceived within 12 months.
cards.result: A healthy child was born to 104 of 201 (52%) couples after IVF with single embryo transfer, 83 of 194 (43%) after IVF in a modified natural cycle, and 97 of 207 (47%) after IUI with controlled ovarian hyperstimulation. Relative to IUI, the risk ratios were 1.10 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.34) for IVF-SET and 0.91 (0.73 to 1.14) for IVF-MNC — both non-inferior by the pre-set margin. Multiple pregnancy rates per ongoing pregnancy were 6%, 5% and 7% respectively. Both IVF strategies were non-inferior to IUI, and IUI was by far the least invasive and cheapest route to a similar result.
cards.watchOut: INeS did not include an expectant-management arm — it positions IUI against IVF, not against waiting. It is carded here because couples choosing IUI over expectant management are implicitly also choosing it over IVF, and INeS shows that choice costs little or nothing in healthy-child rates when prognosis is unfavourable. Mild male subfertility was included alongside unexplained infertility.

cards.headline: Synthesis: IUI with stimulation works when nature's odds are poor and is an expensive placebo-cycle when they are fair — SPLIT by prognosis
cards.summary: Synthesis: IUI with stimulation works when nature's odds are poor and is an expensive placebo-cycle when they are fair — SPLIT by prognosis
cards.people: Three randomised trials: TUI (n = 201, unfavourable prognosis, IUI vs expectant), Steures (n = 253, intermediate prognosis, IUI vs expectant), and INeS (n = 602, unfavourable prognosis, IUI vs two IVF strategies).
cards.result: Versus expectant management: live birth 31% vs 9% (RR 3.41) when prognosis was unfavourable; ongoing pregnancy 23% vs 27% (RR 0.85) when prognosis was intermediate. Versus IVF: healthy child 47% with IUI, non-inferior to IVF-SET at 52%. Multiple pregnancy in the IUI arms was uncommon with oral agents and monitoring (twins in ~2% of TUI births; 7% of ongoing pregnancies in INeS). The evidence supports offering IUI with stimulation to couples with unexplained infertility whose predicted natural-conception chance is low, and supports honest waiting for couples whose chance is intermediate.
cards.watchOut: Prognosis thresholds differ between trials and clinics; the split is a faithful summary of the trials' enrolment criteria, not a precise cut-off a couple can apply to themselves without a validated prediction model. Donor insemination and IUI for other indications are different questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Farquhar CM et al. Lancet. 2018 (PMID: 29174128); Steures P et al. Lancet. 2006 (PMID: 16844491); Bensdorp AJ et al. BMJ. 2015 (PMID: 25576320).

shelves.question: In pregnant women, does screening for and treating gestational diabetes early (before 20 weeks) improve outcomes compared with standard diagnosis at 24–28 weeks?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial has asked this question. In TOBOGM, 802 women who had a risk factor for hyperglycaemia and met World Health Organization 2013 criteria for gestational diabetes before 20 weeks (mean gestation at testing 15.6 weeks) were randomised to immediate treatment or to deferred or no treatment depending on a repeat glucose-tolerance test at 24–28 weeks. Immediate treatment modestly reduced the composite of adverse neonatal outcomes — birth before 37 weeks, birth trauma, birth weight ≥ 4500 g, respiratory distress, phototherapy, stillbirth or neonatal death, or shoulder dystocia — which occurred in 24.9% versus 30.5% (adjusted risk difference −5.6 percentage points, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.2). The trial's other two primary outcomes did not move: pregnancy-related hypertension occurred in 10.6% versus 9.9%, and neonatal lean body mass was essentially identical (adjusted mean difference −0.04 kg), and there were no between-group differences in serious adverse events (Simmons D et al., PMID: 37144983). A 5.6-point absolute reduction in a broad composite, from a single trial, in women selected for having a risk factor and meeting one-step early criteria — many of whose early hyperglycaemia would not persist to 24–28 weeks — is a real but modest and not yet replicated finding. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial. The separate question of one-step versus two-step screening at the standard timepoint is homed at shelf #809.

cards.headline: Simmons 2023 (TOBOGM): immediate treatment of gestational diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks cut the adverse neonatal composite from 30.5% to 24.9% (adjusted risk difference −5.6 points) — hypertension and lean body mass unchanged
cards.summary: Simmons 2023 (TOBOGM): immediate treatment of gestational diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks cut the adverse neonatal composite from 30.5% to 24.9% (adjusted risk difference −5.6 points) — hypertension and lean body mass unchanged
cards.people: 802 women at 4 to 19 weeks 6 days of gestation who had a risk factor for hyperglycaemia and a diagnosis of gestational diabetes by World Health Organization 2013 criteria, randomised 1:1 to immediate treatment or to a control strategy of deferred or no treatment depending on a repeat oral glucose-tolerance test at 24–28 weeks. Follow-up data available for 793 women (98.9%); initial OGTT at a mean of 15.6 weeks.
cards.result: An adverse neonatal outcome event (composite of birth at < 37 weeks, birth trauma, birth weight ≥ 4500 g, respiratory distress, phototherapy, stillbirth or neonatal death, or shoulder dystocia) occurred in 94 of 378 women (24.9%) in the immediate-treatment group and 113 of 370 (30.5%) in the control group (adjusted risk difference −5.6 percentage points, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.2). Pregnancy-related hypertension occurred in 40 of 378 (10.6%) versus 37 of 372 (9.9%) (adjusted risk difference 0.7 points, 95% CI −1.6 to 2.9). Mean neonatal lean body mass was 2.86 kg versus 2.91 kg (adjusted mean difference −0.04 kg, 95% CI −0.09 to 0.02). No between-group differences in serious adverse events associated with screening and treatment.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one positive primary outcome of three, and a composite whose components range from phototherapy to stillbirth — the −5.6-point difference should not be read as 5.6 points of prevented catastrophe. Participants all had a risk factor for hyperglycaemia and met WHO 2013 (one-step) criteria applied early; the trial says nothing about screening low-risk women early, and some control-group women will have been treated from 24–28 weeks, narrowing the contrast.
cards.source: Simmons D et al. Treatment of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus Diagnosed Early in Pregnancy. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023. PMID: 37144983. Registry ID: ACTRN12616000924459. cards.headline: Synthesis: early treatment helps the baby composite modestly in the only trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), awaiting replication
cards.summary: Synthesis: early treatment helps the baby composite modestly in the only trial — POSSIBLE (benefit), awaiting replication
cards.people: One randomised trial (TOBOGM, n = 802) of immediate versus deferred treatment for gestational diabetes diagnosed before 20 weeks in women with a hyperglycaemia risk factor.
cards.result: Adverse neonatal composite 24.9% vs 30.5% (adjusted risk difference −5.6 points, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.2); pregnancy-related hypertension 10.6% vs 9.9%; neonatal lean body mass −0.04 kg (NS); no difference in serious adverse events. The direction is favourable and the intervention is standard gestational-diabetes care started earlier, so the downside is mainly the burden and labelling of treatment for women whose early hyperglycaemia might have resolved — a burden the trial did not quantify as an outcome.
cards.watchOut: A single-trial shelf: if a second trial fails to replicate, this stamp should fall. Early diagnosis also enlarges the diagnosed population (WHO 2013 one-step criteria are generous), so population-level benefit depends on how many early diagnoses represent durable dysglycaemia — unanswered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Simmons D et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 37144983).

shelves.title: Nitrous oxide in labour: used for over a century and liked by many women — but the evidence base is so poor that how much pain it relieves cannot honestly be stated
shelves.question: In women in labour, does inhaled nitrous oxide provide worthwhile pain relief compared with other options?
shelves.mesh: Analgesia, Obstetrical/methods · Anesthetics, Inhalation/administration & dosage · Apgar Score · Clinical Trials as Topic/methods · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Labor Pain/drug therapy/epidemiology · Nitrous Oxide/administration & dosage · Pain Management/methods · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): This is a shelf about the state of the evidence as much as about the gas. The definitive systematic review (Likis FE et al., PMID: 24356165) found 58 publications covering 59 study populations, of which only 2 were rated good quality, 11 fair and 46 poor. What can be said: inhaled nitrous oxide provided less effective pain relief than epidural analgesia — in studies that were predominantly poor quality; the outcomes used to assess women's satisfaction with the birth experience were so heterogeneous that no synthesis was possible; the commonest maternal effects were unpleasant tolerability effects — nausea, vomiting, dizziness and drowsiness; and Apgar scores in newborns of mothers using nitrous oxide were not significantly different from those with other methods or no analgesia. Evidence on occupational exposure harms for staff was limited. So the honest answer to 'does it provide worthwhile pain relief?' is that worthwhile relief is plausible and consistent with widespread continued use and women's reported satisfaction in individual studies, but no adequate trial quantifies the analgesic effect against placebo or modern comparators, and any shelf claiming a number would be inventing it. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C: the evidence base is dominated by poor-quality studies. Water immersion in the first stage of labour — the non-drug comparison with better trial data — is homed at shelf #1354.

cards.headline: Likis 2014 (systematic review): of 58 publications on nitrous oxide for labour pain, only 2 were good quality and 46 poor — nitrous relieved pain less than epidural, satisfaction could not be synthesised, and newborn Apgar scores did not differ
cards.summary: Likis 2014 (systematic review): of 58 publications on nitrous oxide for labour pain, only 2 were good quality and 46 poor — nitrous relieved pain less than epidural, satisfaction could not be synthesised, and newborn Apgar scores did not differ
cards.people: Systematic review of the English-language literature (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL) on nitrous oxide for management of labour pain: 58 publications representing 59 distinct study populations of women in labour intending vaginal birth, plus studies of exposed attendants/providers and of the fetus/neonate. Quality: 2 studies good, 11 fair, 46 poor.
cards.result: Inhalation of nitrous oxide provided less effective pain relief than epidural analgesia, but study quality was predominantly poor. The heterogeneous outcomes used for women's satisfaction with their birth experience and pain management made synthesis difficult. Most reported maternal adverse effects were tolerability effects — nausea, vomiting, dizziness and drowsiness. Apgar scores in newborns whose mothers used nitrous oxide were not significantly different from those whose mothers used other pain-management methods or no analgesia. Evidence about occupational harms and exposure was limited. The authors concluded that few studies of good or fair quality exist and that further research is needed on effectiveness, satisfaction and adverse effects alike.
cards.watchOut: A review whose main finding is the poverty of its own evidence base. 'Less effective than epidural' is the one comparative statement the literature supports, and even it rests on poor-quality studies; the review cannot confirm or refute the moderate analgesia that clinical experience and women's reports suggest, because the trials were never done properly. Do not quote this shelf as showing nitrous oxide 'doesn't work' — it shows the question was never adequately tested.
cards.source: Likis FE et al. Nitrous oxide for the management of labor pain: a systematic review. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 2014. PMID: 24356165. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an unquantified, probably modest analgesic with benign newborn data and nuisance side effects — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: an unquantified, probably modest analgesic with benign newborn data and nuisance side effects — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One systematic review (58 publications, 59 populations), quality-weighted: 2 good, 11 fair, 46 poor quality studies.
cards.result: Pain relief: inferior to epidural (poor-quality evidence); no reliable estimate versus placebo or no treatment. Satisfaction: reported favourably in individual studies but not synthesisable. Maternal harms: nausea, vomiting, dizziness, drowsiness — common, transient, tolerability-limiting. Newborn: no significant Apgar differences. Staff exposure: evidence limited. Nitrous oxide's self-administered, rapidly reversible character is a practical virtue no trial here measures; on trial evidence alone, the effect size a woman should expect is unknown.
cards.watchOut: This shelf grades the evidence, not the gas: MAYBE (weak evidence) means the library cannot verify the benefit, which is a different statement from 'no benefit'. Settings differ — nitrous is standard in the UK and Commonwealth and unavailable in many US units — and the shelf takes no position on provision policy.
cards.source: Synthesis of Likis FE et al. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 2014 (PMID: 24356165).

shelves.title: Episiotomy: cutting routinely prevents nothing — a selective policy leaves about 30% fewer women with severe perineal trauma, with no clear harm to mother or baby
shelves.question: Compared with selective use, does routine episiotomy prevent severe tears and pelvic-floor harm?
shelves.mesh: Apgar Score · Blood Loss, Surgical · Dyspareunia/epidemiology · *Episiotomy/adverse effects/methods/standards · Female · Humans · Pain Measurement · Parity · *Parturition · Perineum/injuries/surgery · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology · Urinary Incontinence/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The belief that a routine surgical cut prevents worse spontaneous tearing has been randomised and has failed. The Cochrane review of selective ('only if needed') versus routine episiotomy policies (12 trials, 6,177 women) found that where an unassisted vaginal birth was anticipated, a selective policy resulted in about 30% fewer women experiencing severe perineal/vaginal trauma (relative measure: risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.94; 5,375 women, 8 trials; low-certainty evidence) (Jiang H et al., PMID: 28176333). No compensating harm from selectivity appeared: blood loss differences were unclear and small (an average of 27 mL less with selective), babies with Apgar score below seven at five minutes did not differ (no events in 3,908 women), perineal infection did not clearly differ (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.82), and at six months or more there was probably little or no difference in dyspareunia (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.53) and little or no difference in urinary incontinence (risk ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.44). The one trial in women where an operative vaginal delivery was intended (175 women) was underpowered and showed no clear difference, so the instrumental-delivery setting remains genuinely open. Routine episiotomy also guarantees what it claims to prevent — perineal trauma requiring sutures — in every woman cut. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for a selective policy in unassisted vaginal birth. Not Tier C: 12 randomised trials. Antenatal perineal massage and second-stage perineal techniques are a different question, homed at shelf #837.

cards.headline: Jiang 2017 (Cochrane): selective episiotomy policies produced 30% fewer severe perineal/vaginal traumas than routine policies (RR 0.70) across 12 trials and 6,177 women — with no clear differences in infection, dyspareunia or incontinence
cards.summary: Jiang 2017 (Cochrane): selective episiotomy policies produced 30% fewer severe perineal/vaginal traumas than routine policies (RR 0.70) across 12 trials and 6,177 women — with no clear differences in infection, dyspareunia or incontinence
cards.people: Cochrane review of 12 randomised trials (6,177 women) comparing a policy of selective episiotomy ('only if needed') with routine episiotomy ('part of routine management') for vaginal birth: 11 trials in women for whom a vaginal birth was intended and 1 in women where an assisted birth was anticipated. Eight trials were in primiparous women only; settings included Argentina, the UK, Canada, Germany, Spain, Ireland, Malaysia, Pakistan, Colombia and Saudi Arabia.
cards.result: For women where an unassisted vaginal birth was anticipated, selective episiotomy may result in 30% fewer women experiencing severe perineal/vaginal trauma (relative measure: risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.94; 5,375 women; 8 RCTs; low-certainty evidence). Blood loss: an average of 27 mL less with selective, but the estimate is very uncertain (95% CI 75 mL less to 20 mL more). Apgar score < 7 at five minutes: little or no effect (four trials, no events; 3,908 women; moderate-certainty). Perineal infection: risk ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.82; low-certainty). Long-term (≥ 6 months): dyspareunia risk ratio 1.14 (95% CI 0.84 to 1.53; moderate-certainty — probably little or no difference); urinary incontinence risk ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.44; low-certainty). Genital prolapse at 3 years in one trial: risk ratio 0.30 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.41; low-certainty). Subgroup analyses by parity and by midline versus mediolateral technique found no modifying effects. The single operative-delivery trial (175 women) showed no clear difference and was underpowered.
cards.watchOut: The severe-trauma estimate is low-certainty, and 'selective' policies in the trials still cut a substantial minority of women — the comparison is restrictive versus liberal, not never versus always. The review cannot answer the operative vaginal delivery question (one small trial), where many clinicians still argue for episiotomy; that gap is stated, not filled.
cards.source: Jiang H et al. Selective versus routine use of episiotomy for vaginal birth. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28176333. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: routine episiotomy is a preventive intervention that randomised trials show causes the harm it claims to prevent — LIKELY (benefit) for selective use
cards.summary: Synthesis: routine episiotomy is a preventive intervention that randomised trials show causes the harm it claims to prevent — LIKELY (benefit) for selective use
cards.people: One Cochrane systematic review of 12 randomised policy trials, 6,177 women, in unassisted and assisted vaginal birth.
cards.result: Severe perineal/vaginal trauma: RR 0.70 (0.52–0.94) favouring selective policies in unassisted birth. No clear differences in blood loss, perineal infection, neonatal Apgar < 7, long-term dyspareunia or urinary incontinence. A routine policy additionally guarantees a sutured surgical wound to every woman delivered under it. The evidence supports episiotomy as a selective, indication-based procedure — and refutes it as routine prophylaxis.
cards.watchOut: Policy trials test the policy, not the individual cut: a selective policy still performs episiotomy when indicated, and nothing here argues against episiotomy for specific indications such as fetal compromise requiring expedited delivery.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jiang H et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28176333).

shelves.title: Where oxytocin cannot be relied on, oral misoprostol after delivery cuts postpartum haemorrhage — by about half in India and a quarter in Pakistan in community placebo-controlled trials
shelves.question: In settings where oxytocin is unavailable or unreliable, does oral misoprostol prevent postpartum haemorrhage?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Female · Home Childbirth · Humans · India · Midwifery · Misoprostol/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Oxytocics/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Postpartum Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Poverty Areas · Rural Health
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two community-based, placebo-controlled randomised trials in exactly the settings the question specifies — births at home or in low-resource communities where oxytocin's cold chain and injection requirements fail. In rural India, 1,620 women attended by auxiliary nurse midwives received oral misoprostol or placebo after delivery: acute postpartum haemorrhage (≥ 500 mL within 2 hours) fell from 12.0% to 6.4% (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.74; P < .0001) — one haemorrhage prevented for every 18 women treated — severe haemorrhage fell from 1.2% to 0.2% (relative risk 0.20, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.91), and mean blood loss fell from 262 mL to 214 mL (Derman RJ et al., PMID: 17027730). In Pakistan, 1,119 women giving birth at home received 600 micrograms of oral misoprostol or placebo from trained traditional birth attendants: haemorrhage ≥ 500 mL occurred in 16.5% versus 21.9% (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.97 — a 24% relative reduction), and a haemoglobin drop of more than 3 g/dL occurred in 5.1% versus 9.6% (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.83), with no maternal deaths in either arm (Mobeen N et al., PMID: 21176086). In both trials shivering, chills and transient fever were more common with misoprostol — the drug's signature, unpleasant but self-limiting. Neither trial compares misoprostol with oxytocin: where oxytocin is available and reliably cold-chained it remains the standard (see shelf #416 on oxytocin and heat-stable carbetocin); this shelf answers the fallback question, and the answer is yes. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit). Not Tier C: two placebo-controlled randomised trials with consistent direction.

cards.headline: Derman 2006: oral misoprostol after delivery halved acute postpartum haemorrhage in rural India — 6.4% versus 12.0% (RR 0.53), one case prevented per 18 women treated
cards.summary: Derman 2006: oral misoprostol after delivery halved acute postpartum haemorrhage in rural India — 6.4% versus 12.0% (RR 0.53), one case prevented per 18 women treated
cards.people: 1,620 women in rural India in a placebo-controlled trial (September 2002 to December 2005); 25 auxiliary nurse midwives conducted the deliveries, administered the study drug (oral misoprostol, n = 812, or placebo, n = 808) after delivery, and measured blood loss. Primary outcome: acute postpartum haemorrhage (≥ 500 mL) within 2 hours of delivery.
cards.result: Acute postpartum haemorrhage occurred in 6.4% on misoprostol versus 12.0% on placebo (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.74; P < .0001), and acute severe postpartum haemorrhage in 0.2% versus 1.2% (relative risk 0.20, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.91). One case of postpartum haemorrhage was prevented for every 18 women treated. Mean postpartum blood loss was 214.3 mL versus 262.3 mL (P < .0001). Women taking misoprostol had higher rates of transient chills and fever. The authors note the drug's low cost, ease of administration and stability make it a good option in resource-poor settings.
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not state the misoprostol dose, and this card does not supply one from outside the record — the Pakistan trial (next card) states 600 micrograms explicitly. The comparator is placebo in a setting without reliable oxytocin: the trial must not be cited as misoprostol beating, or matching, oxytocin.

cards.headline: Mobeen 2011: 600 micrograms of oral misoprostol given by trained traditional birth attendants at Pakistani home births reduced haemorrhage ≥ 500 mL from 21.9% to 16.5% (RR 0.76)
cards.summary: Mobeen 2011: 600 micrograms of oral misoprostol given by trained traditional birth attendants at Pakistani home births reduced haemorrhage ≥ 500 mL from 21.9% to 16.5% (RR 0.76)
cards.people: 1,119 women giving birth at home in Chitral, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, Pakistan, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (June 2006 to June 2008): 600 micrograms oral misoprostol (n = 534) or placebo (n = 585) administered after delivery by trained traditional birth attendants. Primary outcomes: measured blood loss ≥ 500 mL and haemoglobin drop > 2 g/dL.
cards.result: Postpartum haemorrhage (≥ 500 mL) occurred in 16.5% on misoprostol versus 21.9% on placebo (relative risk 0.76, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.97) — a 24% relative reduction. Haemoglobin drop > 2 g/dL did not differ measurably (relative risk 0.79, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.02), but a drop > 3 g/dL was significantly less common on misoprostol (5.1% vs 9.6%; relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.83). Shivering and chills were significantly more common with misoprostol. There were no maternal deaths among participants.
cards.watchOut: The smaller relative effect than in India (RR 0.76 vs 0.53) comes with a higher baseline risk (21.9% placebo haemorrhage rate) and lay-attendant administration — arguably the more generalisable result for community programmes. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness, and misoprostol quality in unregulated markets is a documented programme concern outside this trial's data.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in places where oxytocin cannot be kept cold or given by injection, a tablet after delivery prevents roughly a quarter to a half of haemorrhages — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in places where oxytocin cannot be kept cold or given by injection, a tablet after delivery prevents roughly a quarter to a half of haemorrhages — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Two community placebo-controlled randomised trials of oral misoprostol after delivery: India (n = 1,620, midwife-attended) and Pakistan (n = 1,119, traditional-birth-attendant-administered home births).
cards.result: Haemorrhage ≥ 500 mL: RR 0.53 (0.39–0.74) and RR 0.76 (0.59–0.97); severe haemorrhage RR 0.20 in the Indian trial; haemoglobin drop > 3 g/dL RR 0.53 in the Pakistani trial. Consistent direction, overlapping populations, hard measured outcomes (blood loss was measured, not estimated, in both). Harms: transient shivering, chills and fever, more frequent with misoprostol in both trials; no maternal deaths in either. The benefit is prevention versus nothing — where a uterotonic would otherwise be absent.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not position misoprostol against oxytocin or heat-stable carbetocin where those are deliverable (shelf #416) — it answers the question for settings where they are not. Prevention is also not treatment: misoprostol for established haemorrhage is a separate question with separate evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Derman RJ et al. Lancet. 2006 (PMID: 17027730); Mobeen N et al. BJOG. 2011 (PMID: 21176086).

shelves.title: Balloon tamponade for refractory postpartum haemorrhage: believed in everywhere, shown to help nowhere — and the largest trial found more surgery and death after the device was introduced
shelves.question: In women with postpartum haemorrhage not responding to uterotonics, does intrauterine balloon tamponade control bleeding and avoid hysterectomy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cluster Analysis · Condoms · Egypt · Female · Health Resources · Humans · Maternal Mortality/trends · Postpartum Hemorrhage/prevention & control/therapy · Pregnancy · Senegal · Uganda · Uterine Balloon Tamponade/instrumentation
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Balloon tamponade is standard rescue practice for haemorrhage that uterotonics fail to stop, supported by decades of enthusiastic case series — but comparative evidence, when finally gathered, did not confirm it. The largest evaluation, a stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial introducing condom-catheter uterine balloon tamponade (UBT) into 18 secondary-level hospitals in Uganda, Egypt and Senegal (60,111 deliveries), found the combined incidence of postpartum-haemorrhage-related invasive surgery or maternal death was higher after introduction than before (11.6 vs 6.7 per 10,000 deliveries; adjusted incidence rate ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.07 to 15.58) — though the device was actually used in only 55 of 1,037 diagnosed haemorrhage cases in the intervention period, so the signal may reflect detection, selection or system effects rather than device harm (Anger HA et al., PMID: 31410966). The systematic review of tamponade devices for refractory atonic haemorrhage after vaginal birth rated every included study at high risk of bias and the certainty of evidence very low to low: the one randomised comparison of a condom-catheter balloon against standard care gave unclear results for the composite of surgery or death (risk ratio 2.33, 95% CI 0.76 to 7.14) and for hysterectomy (risk ratio 4.14, 95% CI 0.48 to 35.93), and protocol-inclusion studies of Bakri and other devices were likewise unclear (Pingray V et al., PMID: 34165867). The fair summary is not that balloons harm — the data are too weak and confounded for that — but that the benefit generations of case series asserted has never been demonstrated against any comparator, and hysterectomy avoidance, the outcome that matters, is unproven. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Tier C: all comparative evidence is at high risk of bias with very low certainty.

cards.headline: Anger 2019 (stepped-wedge cluster RCT): introducing condom-catheter balloon tamponade into 18 hospitals did not improve outcomes — PPH-related surgery or maternal death rose from 6.7 to 11.6 per 10,000 deliveries (adjusted rate ratio 4.08)
cards.summary: Anger 2019 (stepped-wedge cluster RCT): introducing condom-catheter balloon tamponade into 18 hospitals did not improve outcomes — PPH-related surgery or maternal death rose from 6.7 to 11.6 per 10,000 deliveries (adjusted rate ratio 4.08)
cards.people: Stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised trial in 18 secondary-level hospitals in Uganda, Egypt and Senegal: condom-catheter uterine balloon tamponade for postpartum haemorrhage management was introduced with a half-day training and pre-packaged kits, with hospitals randomised to when introduction occurred. 28,183 deliveries in the control period and 31,928 in the intervention period (October 2016 to March 2018). Primary outcome: combined incidence of PPH-related invasive surgery and/or maternal death.
cards.result: UBT was used for 9 of 1,357 women diagnosed with PPH in the control period and 55 of 1,037 in the intervention period. PPH-related surgery or maternal death occurred in 19 women in the control period (incidence 6.7 per 10,000 deliveries) and 37 in the intervention period (11.6 per 10,000); the adjusted incidence rate ratio was 4.08 (95% CI 1.07 to 15.58). Secondary outcomes, including transfer and blood transfusion rates, were similar between periods. The authors concluded that introducing condom-catheter UBT in these settings did not improve maternal outcomes and was associated with an increase in the combined incidence of PPH-related surgery and maternal death, warranting reflection on its role.
cards.watchOut: This trial tested an introduction programme, not the device in individual refractory cases: uptake was strikingly low (55 uses among 1,037 haemorrhages), so the adverse signal cannot be a direct effect of balloons in most cases — increased recognition and recording of severe PPH, or referral-pattern changes, are plausible explanations. It nonetheless stands as the only large randomised evidence on the question, and it points the wrong way.
cards.source: Anger HA et al. cards.headline: Pingray 2021 (systematic review): every comparative study of uterine tamponade devices was at high risk of bias; effects on surgery, hysterectomy and death were unclear for every device
cards.summary: Pingray 2021 (systematic review): every comparative study of uterine tamponade devices was at high risk of bias; effects on surgery, hysterectomy and death were unclear for every device
cards.people: Systematic review (searches to January 2021) of randomised and non-randomised comparative studies of uterine tamponade devices for atonic refractory postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal birth, including the effect of including devices in institutional protocols. Outcomes: composite of surgical interventions (artery ligation, compressive sutures, hysterectomy) or maternal death, and hysterectomy.
cards.result: All included studies were at high risk of bias; certainty of evidence was very low to low. One randomised study of a condom-catheter balloon versus standard care found unclear results for the composite outcome (risk ratio 2.33, 95% CI 0.76 to 7.14) and hysterectomy (risk ratio 4.14, 95% CI 0.48 to 35.93). Of three studies of including UBT in institutional protocols, the stepped-wedge cluster trial suggested an increase in the composite outcome (risk ratio 4.08, 95% CI 1.07 to 15.58); one non-randomised Bakri-balloon study showed unclear effects (composite risk ratio 0.33, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.03; hysterectomy 0.49, 95% CI 0.04 to 5.38); and a second (Ebb or Bakri) was likewise unclear (composite 0.95, 95% CI 0.32 to 2.81; hysterectomy 1.84, 95% CI 0.44 to 7.69). The authors concluded the effect of tamponade devices for refractory PPH after vaginal delivery is unclear, as are the roles of device type and setting.
cards.watchOut: The vast case-series literature reporting 80–90% 'success' for balloons is excluded by design here — those series have no comparator, and refractory haemorrhage often stops with time, transfusion and uterotonics regardless. The review covers vaginal births and atonic haemorrhage; caesarean-delivery and non-atonic uses are outside its evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a rescue device whose benefit is asserted by series and unproven by comparison — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a rescue device whose benefit is asserted by series and unproven by comparison — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One stepped-wedge cluster-randomised introduction trial (18 hospitals, 60,111 deliveries) and one systematic review of all comparative studies of tamponade devices for refractory atonic postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal birth.
cards.result: No comparative study demonstrates that balloon tamponade reduces surgery, hysterectomy or death. Point estimates in the randomised evidence favour the control arms (composite risk/rate ratios 2.33 and 4.08) with wide intervals and high bias risk; non-randomised protocol studies straddle no-effect. The correct evidentiary statement is 'unproven', not 'disproven' — but a clinician citing tamponade as evidence-based rescue is citing case series, and this shelf says so.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE here grades a genuinely empty evidence base for a device embedded in guidelines and protocols worldwide; removing it from practice is not a conclusion this evidence can carry either, given the confounding in the one large trial. Prevention of haemorrhage — where the evidence is strong — is homed at shelves #416 and #2733.
cards.source: Synthesis of Anger HA et al. BJOG. 2019 (PMID: 31410966); Pingray V et al. BJOG. 2021 (PMID: 34165867).

shelves.title: Contraception before discharge after birth: immediate IUD or implant placement gets far more women started — but pooled continuation at 6–12 months is unproven, and immediate IUDs are expelled far more often
shelves.question: Immediately after delivery, does placing an IUD or implant increase continuation and prevent rapid repeat pregnancy versus delayed placement?
shelves.mesh: Pregnancy · Female · Humans · *Progestins · Contraception/methods · *Intrauterine Devices · Postpartum Period · Uterine Hemorrhage · Contraceptive Agents
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the strategy clearly wins on starting and is unproven on lasting. The Cochrane review of immediate versus delayed postpartum insertion (16 randomised trials; 5 implant studies with 715 participants and 11 IUD studies with 1,894) found immediate insertion probably improves initiation for implants (risk ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.98; moderate-certainty) and for IUDs (risk ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.51; moderate-certainty) — many women randomised to delayed insertion never return to get the method (Sothornwit J et al., PMID: 36302159). But pooled utilisation at 6 and 12 months was uncertain for both methods (implant use at 6 months risk ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50, very low certainty; IUD use at 6 months 1.02 and at 12 months 0.86, very low certainty), and immediate IUD insertion carried a clearly higher expulsion rate at 6 months (risk ratio 4.55, 95% CI 2.52 to 8.19). The best single trial cuts the other way on continuation: in Uganda, women randomised to immediate levonorgestrel implant insertion were using implants at 6 months at 97% versus 68% for delayed insertion (P < .001) (Averbach S et al., PMID: 28610898) — one of the trials inside the heterogeneous pooled estimate. Pregnancy prevention, the outcome that ultimately matters, is thin: one study of 1,000 women found fewer unintended pregnancies at 12 months with immediate IUD insertion (risk ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.41; low-certainty). Breastfeeding was little affected by immediate progestin-releasing methods. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit on initiation) / LIKELY (no difference demonstrated in pooled continuation; more expulsions). Not Tier C: 16 randomised trials, though several pooled outcomes are very low certainty.

cards.headline: Sothornwit 2022 (Cochrane): immediate postpartum insertion raised initiation for implants (RR 1.48) and IUDs (RR 1.27) across 16 trials — but 6- and 12-month use was uncertain, and immediate IUDs were expelled at 4.55 times the rate
cards.summary: Sothornwit 2022 (Cochrane): immediate postpartum insertion raised initiation for implants (RR 1.48) and IUDs (RR 1.27) across 16 trials — but 6- and 12-month use was uncertain, and immediate IUDs were expelled at 4.55 times the rate
cards.people: Cochrane review of 16 randomised trials comparing immediate postpartum insertion (before discharge) with delayed insertion of contraceptive implants (5 studies, 715 participants) and IUDs (11 studies, 1,894 participants), with 12 ongoing studies identified. Certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, limited by risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision.
cards.result: Implants: immediate insertion probably improves initiation (risk ratio 1.48, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.98; moderate-certainty). Utilisation at 6 months was uncertain (risk ratio 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50; very low-certainty) and at 12 months similar (0.98, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.04; very low-certainty). Immediate implant insertion was associated with more days of prolonged vaginal bleeding within six weeks and a higher rate of other adverse effects in the first six weeks (risk ratio 2.06, 95% CI 1.38 to 3.06; one study, low-certainty). IUDs: immediate insertion probably improves initiation regardless of type (risk ratio 1.27, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.51; moderate-certainty), but expulsion at 6 months was higher (risk ratio 4.55, 95% CI 2.52 to 8.19; low-certainty). IUD utilisation at 6 months (1.02, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.62) and 12 months (0.86, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.47) was uncertain. Immediate IUD insertion may reduce unintended pregnancy at 12 months (risk ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.41; one study of 1,000 participants; low-certainty). Breastfeeding rates at 6 months showed little or no difference for implants and were uncertain for progestin-releasing IUDs.
cards.watchOut: Initiation is partly an artefact of design — the delayed arm must return for a visit to start at all — but that is precisely the real-world mechanism the strategy exploits, so the initiation advantage is genuine, not a bias. The pooled continuation estimates are very low certainty with extreme heterogeneity (I² up to 98%), which is why the stamp splits rather than declaring continuation null.

cards.headline: Averbach 2017: in Uganda, women randomised to immediate postpartum implant insertion were still using implants at 6 months at 97% versus 68% for delayed insertion
cards.summary: Averbach 2017: in Uganda, women randomised to immediate postpartum implant insertion were still using implants at 6 months at 97% versus 68% for delayed insertion
cards.people: 205 women in Kampala, Uganda, who desired contraceptive implants, randomised to insertion of a two-rod levonorgestrel implant (75 mg rods) immediately after delivery (within 5 days and before discharge; n = 103) or at 6 weeks postpartum (n = 102). Primary outcome: implant utilisation at 6 months. Follow-up at 6 months was 93% complete.
cards.result: At 6 months, implant use was 97% in the immediate group versus 68% in the delayed group (P < .001), and use of any highly effective contraceptive was 98% versus 81% (P = .001). Women in the immediate group were more satisfied with the timing of placement, and 81% of the immediate group versus 63% of the delayed group said they would choose the same timing again (P = .01). There were no serious adverse events in either group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial in women who had already chosen implants — the 29-point continuation gap is driven largely by delayed-group women never receiving the method, which is the strategy working as intended in a setting where return visits are hard. It sits inside the Cochrane pooled estimate whose heterogeneity (I² = 89% for 6-month implant use) reflects how much setting matters; neither source alone should be quoted without the other.
cards.source: Averbach S et al. Immediate versus delayed postpartum use of levonorgestrel contraceptive implants: a randomized controlled trial in Uganda. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2017. PMID: 28610898. Registry ID: NCT02341027.
