cards.headline: Synthesis: offer the method before discharge — starting is proven, lasting is setting-dependent, and IUD expulsion is the price — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: offer the method before discharge — starting is proven, lasting is setting-dependent, and IUD expulsion is the price — SPLIT
cards.people: One Cochrane review of 16 randomised trials (2,609 participants across implant and IUD studies) and one well-conducted single-country implant trial (n = 205).
cards.result: Initiation: implants RR 1.48 (1.11–1.98), IUDs RR 1.27 (1.07–1.51), both moderate-certainty. Continuation: pooled 6- and 12-month use uncertain (very low certainty); best single trial shows 97% vs 68% implant use at 6 months. Unintended pregnancy at 12 months: RR 0.26 (0.17–0.41) for immediate IUD in one 1,000-woman study. Harm: IUD expulsion RR 4.55 (2.52–8.19) at 6 months; more early bleeding and minor adverse effects with immediate implants. Immediate placement is a delivery-of-care intervention whose value is converting intention into coverage before the postpartum visit that many women never attend.
cards.watchOut: Expelled IUDs are only a harm if unnoticed — programmes offering immediate postpartum IUDs need expulsion counselling and string checks, which the trials handle inconsistently. The shelf compares timing strategies for women who want a method; it is not evidence about which method to want.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sothornwit J et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022 (PMID: 36302159); Averbach S et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2017 (PMID: 28610898).

shelves.title: Vaginal oestrogen after breast cancer: no overall increase in recurrence or breast-cancer death in the large cohorts — but a recurrence signal in women taking aromatase inhibitors
shelves.question: In breast cancer survivors with genitourinary symptoms of menopause, does low-dose vaginal oestrogen increase the risk of recurrence or breast-cancer death?
shelves.mesh: Aromatase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms*/chemically induced/drug therapy/epidemiology · Cohort Studies · Denmark/epidemiology · Estrogen Replacement Therapy/adverse effects · Estrogens · Female · Hormone Replacement Therapy/adverse effects · Humans · Menopause · Receptors, Estrogen
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by the endocrine therapy a woman is taking alongside. In the Danish national cohort of 8,461 postmenopausal women treated for early oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer, vaginal oestrogen therapy (VET) was not associated with recurrence overall (adjusted relative risk 1.08, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.32) or with higher mortality (adjusted HR 0.78, 0.71 to 0.87) — but in the subgroup taking adjuvant aromatase inhibitors, recurrence was higher on VET (adjusted RR 1.39, 1.04 to 1.85), with no mortality increase (Cold S et al., PMID: 35854422). The Scottish and Welsh cohorts (49,237 women) found no higher breast-cancer-specific mortality in vaginal-oestrogen users (pooled adjusted HR 0.77, 0.63 to 0.94) (McVicker L et al., PMID: 37917089). A 2025 meta-analysis of six observational studies in women on endocrine therapy sharpened the same split: topical oestrogen during aromatase-inhibitor treatment was associated with increased recurrence (RR 2.51, 1.10 to 5.72, low-certainty evidence) but not mortality, while during tamoxifen it was associated with neither (Kastora SL et al., PMID: 39854791). No randomised trial exists and none is likely: every number here is observational, so residual confounding runs in both directions — women prescribed vaginal oestrogen may differ from non-users in symptom burden, endocrine-therapy adherence and surveillance. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (no increase in recurrence or mortality overall) / POSSIBLE (increased recurrence in women also taking aromatase inhibitors); Tier C: observational evidence only, on a harm question. Non-hormonal and non-oestrogen options for the same symptoms are homed at shelf #945.

cards.headline: Cold 2022 (Danish national cohort): vaginal oestrogen in 1,957 of 8,461 breast-cancer survivors — recurrence RR 1.08 overall, but 1.39 in women on aromatase inhibitors
cards.summary: Cold 2022 (Danish national cohort): vaginal oestrogen in 1,957 of 8,461 breast-cancer survivors — recurrence RR 1.08 overall, but 1.39 in women on aromatase inhibitors
cards.people: 8,461 postmenopausal women diagnosed 1997–2004 in Denmark with early-stage invasive oestrogen-receptor-positive non-metastatic breast cancer, who received no adjuvant treatment or 5 years of adjuvant endocrine therapy and had not used hormone therapy before diagnosis. After diagnosis, 1,957 used vaginal oestrogen therapy (VET) and 133 used systemic menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), ascertained from the national prescription registry. Median follow-up was 9.8 years for recurrence and 15.2 years for mortality.
cards.result: The adjusted relative risk of recurrence was 1.08 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.32) for VET and 1.05 (0.62 to 1.78) for MHT versus non-use. In the subgroup receiving adjuvant aromatase inhibitors, VET was associated with a higher recurrence risk (adjusted RR 1.39, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.85). Adjusted hazard ratios for overall mortality were 0.78 (0.71 to 0.87) for VET and 0.94 (0.70 to 1.26) for MHT. The authors conclude neither VET nor MHT was associated with increased recurrence or mortality overall, with the aromatase-inhibitor subgroup the exception for recurrence.
cards.watchOut: Observational prescription-registry data: women who receive vaginal oestrogen differ from non-users (more severe symptoms, possibly different endocrine-therapy adherence), and adjustment cannot remove that. The aromatase-inhibitor subgroup finding (RR 1.39) is a subgroup analysis — hypothesis-raising, not proof — and the lower overall mortality on VET (HR 0.78) almost certainly reflects healthy-user selection rather than a protective effect of oestrogen.
cards.source: Cold S et al. Systemic or Vaginal Hormone Therapy After Early Breast Cancer: A Danish Observational Cohort Study. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2022. PMID: 35854422. cards.headline: McVicker 2024 (Scotland and Wales, 49,237 women): no higher breast-cancer-specific mortality in vaginal-oestrogen users — adjusted HR 0.77
cards.summary: McVicker 2024 (Scotland and Wales, 49,237 women): no higher breast-cancer-specific mortality in vaginal-oestrogen users — adjusted HR 0.77
cards.people: 49,237 women aged 40–79 with newly diagnosed breast cancer in two population-based cohorts (Scotland, diagnoses 2010–2017; Wales, 2000–2016), followed for breast cancer-specific mortality until 2020; 5,795 breast-cancer-specific deaths occurred. Five percent used vaginal oestrogen therapy (tablets or creams) after diagnosis, ascertained from dispensing/prescription records.
cards.result: Comparing vaginal-oestrogen users with women who used no hormone replacement therapy, the pooled fully adjusted hazard ratio for breast cancer-specific mortality was 0.77 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.94) — no evidence of a higher risk. Models adjusted for confounders including cancer stage and grade, using time-dependent Cox regression.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is mortality, not recurrence — a treatment could raise recurrence without this study seeing a mortality difference within its follow-up. The HR of 0.77 below 1.0 should not be read as vaginal oestrogen preventing death; it is the signature of selection (healthier, more engaged patients get prescriptions) in observational data.
cards.source: McVicker L et al. Vaginal Estrogen Therapy Use and Survival in Females With Breast Cancer. JAMA Oncology. 2024. PMID: 37917089. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kastora 2025 (meta-analysis, 6 observational studies, 38,050 women on endocrine therapy): topical oestrogen on aromatase inhibitors — recurrence RR 2.51; on tamoxifen — no increase in recurrence or death
cards.summary: Kastora 2025 (meta-analysis, 6 observational studies, 38,050 women on endocrine therapy): topical oestrogen on aromatase inhibitors — recurrence RR 2.51; on tamoxifen — no increase in recurrence or death
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Kastora 2025)
cards.people: Six observational studies of topical (vaginal) oestrogen versus non-use in breast cancer survivors receiving adjuvant endocrine treatment (tamoxifen and/or aromatase inhibitors): 38,050 women, of whom 1,805 were exposed to topical oestrogen. Recurrence and all-cause mortality were pooled, with subgroup analyses by endocrine agent, risk of bias, node positivity, menopausal status and follow-up.
cards.result: In women on aromatase inhibitors, topical oestrogen did not increase all-cause mortality (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.69) but was associated with an increased risk of recurrence (RR 2.51, 95% CI 1.10 to 5.72; low GRADE certainty). In women on tamoxifen, topical oestrogen increased neither recurrence nor all-cause mortality. Node positivity, menopausal status and follow-up time appeared to confound the pooled estimates.
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis pools the same observational cohorts carded on this shelf (the Danish cohort among them), so it is not independent confirmation — it is a re-weighting of the same data, and its aromatase-inhibitor recurrence estimate (RR 2.51) is much larger than the Danish cohort's own subgroup estimate (1.39), driven by smaller studies. Low GRADE certainty throughout.
cards.source: Kastora SL et al. Safety of topical estrogen therapy during adjuvant endocrine treatment among patients with breast cancer: A meta-analysis based expert panel discussion. Cancer Treatment Reviews. 2025. PMID: 39854791. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: reassuring overall, one consistent exception — women on aromatase inhibitors — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: reassuring overall, one consistent exception — women on aromatase inhibitors — SPLIT
cards.people: Three observational sources: the Danish national cohort (8,461 women with ER-positive early breast cancer), the combined Scottish and Welsh cohorts (49,237 women), and a 2025 meta-analysis of six observational studies (38,050 women on endocrine therapy) that overlaps the cohorts rather than adding new patients.
cards.result: Overall, vaginal oestrogen after breast cancer has not been associated with increased recurrence (adjusted RR 1.08, 0.89–1.32) or breast-cancer mortality (adjusted HR 0.77, 0.63–0.94). The single consistent exception is concurrent aromatase-inhibitor therapy: recurrence was higher in the Danish AI subgroup (adjusted RR 1.39, 1.04–1.85) and in the meta-analysis AI stratum (RR 2.51, 1.10–5.72), with no mortality increase in either. With tamoxifen, no increase in recurrence or mortality was seen. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (no increase overall) / POSSIBLE (increased recurrence with aromatase inhibitors).
cards.watchOut: There is no randomised evidence and there will not be: randomising symptomatic survivors to oestrogen or nothing for a decade is not a trial anyone can run. The practical reading is agent-specific — the concern is real enough, and specific enough to aromatase inhibitors (which work by abolishing oestrogen, the very thing vaginal oestrogen partially restores), that guidelines route AI-treated women to non-hormonal options first; the tamoxifen and no-endocrine-therapy data are considerably more reassuring.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cold S et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2022 (PMID: 35854422); McVicker L et al. JAMA Oncology. 2024 (PMID: 37917089); Kastora SL et al. Cancer Treatment Reviews. 2025 (PMID: 39854791).

shelves.title: Myo-inositol in pregnancy: gestational diabetes roughly halved in three Italian trials — all open-label, all from one research group
shelves.question: In pregnant women at increased risk of gestational diabetes, does myo-inositol supplementation from early pregnancy prevent gestational diabetes?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy* · Diabetes, Gestational/drug therapy* · Female · Humans · Inositol/therapeutic use* · Pregnancy · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Three randomised trials, all from the same Italian research group, point the same way. In women with a parent with type 2 diabetes, myo-inositol 2 g twice daily (with folic acid) from the end of the first trimester cut gestational diabetes (GDM) from 15.3% to 6.0% (odds ratio 0.35) and reduced fetal macrosomia (D'Anna R et al., PMID: 23340885). In obese women (BMI ≥ 30), GDM fell from 33.6% to 14.0% (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68) (D'Anna R et al., PMID: 26241420). In overweight non-obese women, GDM fell from 27.4% to 11.6% (OR 0.33, 0.15 to 0.70) (Santamaria A et al., PMID: 26698911). The consistency is striking — relative reductions of about two-thirds in three different risk groups — but so is the limitation: every trial is open-label, every trial comes from one collaborating group in two Italian university hospitals, and no independent group has replicated the finding at this size. Open-label conduct matters less for a laboratory diagnosis like GDM than for symptom outcomes, but co-interventions and OGTT scheduling were not blinded. No trial was powered for neonatal or maternal clinical outcomes beyond macrosomia. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — Tier C: a single research group's open-label trials of an unregulated supplement. The records name no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: D'Anna 2013: in women with a parent with type 2 diabetes, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 15.3% to 6.0% (OR 0.35)
cards.summary: D'Anna 2013: in women with a parent with type 2 diabetes, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 15.3% to 6.0% (OR 0.35)
cards.people: 220 pregnant outpatients with a parent with type 2 diabetes, randomised from the end of the first trimester to myo-inositol 2 g plus folic acid 200 µg twice daily (n = 110) or folic acid 200 µg twice daily alone (n = 110), in a 2-year prospective, randomised, open-label, placebo-controlled study. GDM was diagnosed by IADPSG criteria; secondary outcomes included macrosomia (>4,000 g), gestational hypertension, preterm delivery, caesarean section and neonatal complications.
cards.result: GDM incidence was 6.0% on myo-inositol versus 15.3% on placebo (P = 0.04), an odds ratio of 0.35 — about a 60% relative reduction. Fetal macrosomia was significantly reduced and mean fetal weight at delivery was lower in the myo-inositol group. No other secondary outcome differed between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: participants and clinicians knew the allocation, and although GDM is a laboratory diagnosis, diet advice and testing behaviour could differ by arm. Single-centre-group evidence — the senior authors recur across all three trials on this shelf. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: D'Anna R et al. myo-Inositol supplementation and onset of gestational diabetes mellitus in pregnant women with a family history of type 2 diabetes: a prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled study. Diabetes Care. 2013. PMID: 23340885. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: D'Anna 2015: in obese pregnant women, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 33.6% to 14.0% (OR 0.34)
cards.summary: D'Anna 2015: in obese pregnant women, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 33.6% to 14.0% (OR 0.34)
cards.people: 220 pregnant women with prepregnancy BMI ≥ 30, randomised at 12–13 weeks at two Italian university hospitals to myo-inositol 2 g plus folic acid 200 µg twice daily (n = 110) or folic acid alone (n = 110), in an open-label randomised trial. Primary outcomes were GDM incidence and change in insulin resistance (HOMA) to the diagnostic OGTT.
cards.result: GDM occurred in 14.0% on myo-inositol versus 33.6% on control (P = .001; odds ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.68) — roughly a 58% relative reduction, about 20 fewer cases per 100 women treated. Insulin resistance fell more on myo-inositol (HOMA change −1.0 ± 3.1 versus +0.1 ± 1.8; P = .048).
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered for a 65% relative reduction — an optimistic target it then met almost exactly, a pattern that warrants caution. Open-label, same research group as the other trials on this shelf. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Santamaria 2016: in overweight (non-obese) pregnant women, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 27.4% to 11.6% (OR 0.33)
cards.summary: Santamaria 2016: in overweight (non-obese) pregnant women, myo-inositol cut gestational diabetes from 27.4% to 11.6% (OR 0.33)
cards.people: 220 pregnant women with prepregnancy BMI ≥ 25 and < 30, randomised at two Italian university hospitals to myo-inositol 2 g plus folic acid 200 µg twice daily (n = 110) or folic acid alone (n = 110) from the first trimester to delivery, in an open-label randomised trial. The primary outcome was GDM incidence.
cards.result: GDM occurred in 11.6% on myo-inositol versus 27.4% on control (P = 0.004), an odds ratio of 0.33 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.70) — about a 58% relative reduction, roughly 16 fewer cases per 100 women treated.
cards.watchOut: Third trial, same collaborating group, same two-hospital network, same open-label design — this is corroboration within a programme, not independent replication. No clinical outcome beyond the GDM diagnosis itself was shown to improve. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Santamaria A et al. Myo-inositol may prevent gestational diabetes onset in overweight women: a randomized, controlled trial. The Journal of Maternal-Fetal & Neonatal Medicine. 2016. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent two-thirds relative reduction in GDM across three risk groups — from one group's open-label trials — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent two-thirds relative reduction in GDM across three risk groups — from one group's open-label trials — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three open-label randomised trials totalling 660 pregnant women at increased GDM risk (family history of type 2 diabetes; obesity; overweight), all conducted by one Italian research group, all testing myo-inositol 2 g twice daily with folic acid against folic acid alone from the first trimester.
cards.result: GDM incidence fell in every trial: 6.0% vs 15.3% (family history), 14.0% vs 33.6% (obesity), 11.6% vs 27.4% (overweight) — odds ratios 0.33–0.35 in all three, absolute reductions of 9–20 cases per 100 women. Macrosomia was reduced in the family-history trial. No trial showed differences in other maternal or neonatal outcomes, and none was powered to. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The shelf's weakness is provenance, not consistency: one research group, no blinding, no independent replication, and effect sizes (~65% relative reduction) larger than almost any preventive supplement has sustained on retesting. A large blinded trial by an independent group would either promote this to LIKELY or retire it; until then the honest stamp is POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.source: Synthesis of D'Anna R et al. Diabetes Care. 2013 (PMID: 23340885); D'Anna R et al. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2015 (PMID: 26241420); Santamaria A et al. The Journal of Maternal-Fetal & Neonatal Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26698911).

shelves.title: Duloxetine for stress urinary incontinence: leakage episodes roughly halved versus a quarter on placebo — with one in four women stopping for side effects
shelves.question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, does duloxetine improve continence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · North America · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use* · Thiophenes/therapeutic use* · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/drug therapy*
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduces stress incontinence episodes by about half, against about a quarter on placebo. In the first phase 3 trial (683 North American women), median incontinence episode frequency fell 50% versus 27% (P < .001), 51% of women on duloxetine achieved at least a halving of episodes versus 34% on placebo, and quality-of-life scores improved more (11.0 vs 6.8 points) (Dmochowski RR et al., PMID: 14501737). In women with severe incontinence already scheduled for surgery, episodes fell 60% versus 27%, the responder relative risk was 4.68 (2.27 to 9.66), and 20% of duloxetine responders no longer wanted their operation (Cardozo L et al., PMID: 15339761). The Cochrane synthesis of nine trials (3,327 adults) confirmed better quality of life (weighted mean difference 5.26 points) and subjective improvement, but found no demonstrated benefit on objective pad-test cure and only a small subjective-cure effect (~3%) (Mariappan P et al., PMID: 16034945). The price is tolerability: nausea is common (usually transient), about one in three women report a treatment-related adverse effect, and in the phase 3 trial 24% stopped duloxetine for adverse events versus 4% on placebo. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — a real, moderate symptom benefit for women who can stay on the drug; it is not a cure, and objective dryness was never shown.

cards.headline: Dmochowski 2003 (phase 3, 683 women): incontinence episodes fell 50% on duloxetine vs 27% on placebo — but 24% stopped the drug for adverse events vs 4%
cards.summary: Dmochowski 2003 (phase 3, 683 women): incontinence episodes fell 50% on duloxetine vs 27% on placebo — but 24% stopped the drug for adverse events vs 4%
cards.people: 683 North American women aged 22–84 with predominant stress urinary incontinence (weekly incontinence episode frequency ≥ 7, positive cough stress and pad tests, no predominant urge symptoms), randomised after a 2-week placebo lead-in to duloxetine 40 mg twice daily (n = 344) or placebo (n = 339) for 12 weeks. Mean baseline episode frequency was 18 per week.
cards.result: Incontinence episode frequency fell by 50% on duloxetine versus 27% on placebo (P < .001); 51% of duloxetine women versus 34% on placebo achieved a 50–100% reduction. Incontinence quality-of-life scores improved more (11.0 vs 6.8; P < .001), and voiding interval lengthened more (20 vs 2 minutes; P < .001). Discontinuation for adverse events was 24% on duloxetine versus 4% on placebo (P < .001); nausea was the commonest side effect and reason for stopping (6.4%), usually mild-to-moderate and resolving within a week to a month — 74% of women who developed nausea completed the trial.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week symptom trial: it shows fewer recorded leakage episodes and better quality-of-life scores, not cure — and a quarter of women could not tolerate the drug long enough to finish 12 weeks, so the intention-to-treat benefit already nets out a substantial tolerability failure rate.
cards.source: Dmochowski RR et al. Duloxetine versus placebo for the treatment of North American women with stress urinary incontinence. The Journal of Urology. 2003. PMID: 14501737. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cardozo 2004: in 109 women with severe incontinence awaiting surgery, duloxetine cut episodes 60% vs 27% — and 1 in 5 responders no longer wanted surgery
cards.summary: Cardozo 2004: in 109 women with severe incontinence awaiting surgery, duloxetine cut episodes 60% vs 27% — and 1 in 5 responders no longer wanted surgery
cards.people: 109 women aged 33–75 with severe stress urinary incontinence (≥ 14 episodes/week, pure urodynamic stress incontinence) who already had continence surgery scheduled, randomised double-blind to placebo (n = 54) or duloxetine 80 mg/day for 4 weeks escalating to 120 mg/day for 4 weeks (n = 55).
cards.result: Incontinence episode frequency fell 60% on duloxetine versus 27% on placebo (P < .001); quality-of-life scores rose 10.6 versus 2.4 points (P = .003) and pad use fell 34.5% versus 4.8% (P = .008). Responders (≥ 50% episode reduction) were more frequent on duloxetine (relative risk 4.68, 95% CI 2.27 to 9.66; number needed to treat 2.02). At 8 weeks, 10 of 49 duloxetine women (20%) were no longer interested in surgery, versus 0 of 45 on placebo (P = .001). Side effects and discontinuations for side effects were significantly more common on duloxetine.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 109) and short (8 weeks), at doses up to 120 mg/day — higher than the 80 mg/day used in the phase 3 programme — in a selected surgical-waiting-list population. 'No longer interested in surgery' at 8 weeks is a stated preference, not evidence that surgery was avoided long-term.
cards.source: Cardozo L et al. Pharmacological treatment of women awaiting surgery for stress urinary incontinence. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2004. PMID: 15339761. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mariappan 2005 (Cochrane, 9 trials, 3,327 adults): quality of life and subjective improvement better on duloxetine; objective pad-test cure not demonstrated
cards.summary: Mariappan 2005 (Cochrane, 9 trials, 3,327 adults): quality of life and subjective improvement better on duloxetine; objective pad-test cure not demonstrated
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 9 RCTs (Mariappan 2005, Cochrane)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials involving 3,327 adults with predominantly stress urinary incontinence (some with mixed incontinence), comparing duloxetine with placebo over 3–12 weeks; three reviewers extracted data using Cochrane methods.
cards.result: Duloxetine improved quality of life more than placebo (weighted mean difference 5.26 points, 95% CI 3.84 to 6.68) and improved patients' perception of improvement; individual trials showed episode-frequency reductions of approximately 50% on duloxetine. Subjective cure favoured duloxetine with a small effect size (3%), but meta-analysis of stress pad test and 24-hour pad weight found no demonstrated objective benefit. About one in three participants on duloxetine reported treatment-related adverse effects (nausea commonest) and about one in eight stopped treatment because of them.
cards.watchOut: The review's own bottom line is narrower than the trials' headlines: subjective improvement and quality of life, yes; objectively measured dryness, not shown; and whether benefits are sustainable beyond 12 weeks was unclear — no long-term trial exists in this set.
cards.source: Mariappan P et al. Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRI) for stress urinary incontinence in adults. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2005. PMID: 16034945. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer leaks and better quality of life for women who tolerate it — LIKELY (benefit), with tolerability as the binding constraint
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer leaks and better quality of life for women who tolerate it — LIKELY (benefit), with tolerability as the binding constraint
cards.people: Nine placebo-controlled trials (3,327 adults, Cochrane) anchored by the 683-woman phase 3 trial and a 109-woman trial in severe surgical candidates; treatment durations 3–12 weeks, duloxetine 80–120 mg/day.
cards.result: Episode frequency falls by about half on duloxetine versus about a quarter on placebo; about half of treated women halve their episodes (vs a third on placebo); quality of life improves by ~5 points more than placebo. Objective cure on pad testing was not demonstrated, and roughly one in four women stopped for adverse events in the phase 3 trial (nausea leading). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for symptom reduction — not for cure.
cards.watchOut: Every trial is short and industry-era (the drug was developed for this indication); there is no head-to-head trial against pelvic-floor muscle training or surgery with long follow-up in this evidence set, and no data on whether women who respond at 12 weeks are still benefiting at a year.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dmochowski RR et al. The Journal of Urology. 2003 (PMID: 14501737); Cardozo L et al. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2004 (PMID: 15339761); Mariappan P et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2005 (PMID: 16034945).

shelves.question: In women with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, does individualised pelvic-floor muscle training improve symptoms versus lifestyle advice alone?
shelves.mesh: Ambulatory Care · Exercise Therapy/methods* · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Pelvic Floor · Pelvic Organ Prolapse/therapy* · Precision Medicine/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — on one large trial. In POPPY, 447 women with newly diagnosed symptomatic stage I–III prolapse were randomised to an individualised one-to-one pelvic-floor muscle training programme or to a prolapse lifestyle-advice leaflet alone. At 12 months, women in the training group reported fewer prolapse symptoms: the pelvic organ prolapse symptom score (POP-SS) fell by 3.77 points versus 2.09 on advice alone — an adjusted difference of 1.52 points (95% CI 0.46 to 2.59; P = .0053) (Hagen S et al., PMID: 24290404). The effect is real but modest on a symptom scale, both groups improved, and the trial measures symptoms, not anatomy: it does not show that training reverses prolapse stage or prevents eventual surgery. Adverse events were few and judged unrelated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — Tier C: a single (large, well-conducted, multicentre) trial, so the finding has no independent replication yet. Pelvic-floor training for urinary incontinence is a different question, homed elsewhere in the library.

cards.headline: Hagen 2014 (POPPY, 447 women): pelvic-floor muscle training beat a lifestyle leaflet on prolapse symptoms at 12 months — adjusted difference 1.52 POP-SS points (P = .0053)
cards.summary: Hagen 2014 (POPPY, 447 women): pelvic-floor muscle training beat a lifestyle leaflet on prolapse symptoms at 12 months — adjusted difference 1.52 POP-SS points (P = .0053)
cards.people: 447 female outpatients with newly diagnosed symptomatic stage I, II or III pelvic organ prolapse at 25 centres (UK, New Zealand, Australia), randomised to an individualised programme of pelvic-floor muscle training (n = 225) or a prolapse lifestyle advice leaflet with no muscle training (n = 222). Outcome assessors and site gynaecologists were masked; the primary endpoint was self-reported prolapse symptoms (POP-SS) at 12 months, analysed by intention to treat. Questionnaire follow-up was 84% at 6 months and 66% at 12 months.
cards.result: POP-SS fell from baseline by a mean of 3.77 points (SD 5.62) in the training group versus 2.09 (5.39) in the control group — an adjusted between-group difference of 1.52 points (95% CI 0.46 to 2.59; P = .0053) favouring training, robust to missing-data analyses. Eight adverse events and one unexpected serious adverse event, all in the intervention group, were judged unrelated to the intervention or participation.
cards.watchOut: Participants could not be blinded to an exercise programme, and the primary outcome is a self-reported symptom score — expectation effects are possible, though the leaflet control and masked assessors limit them. A third of women did not return 12-month questionnaires. The 1.52-point average difference is a group mean: it does not tell any individual woman her chance of feeling meaningfully better, and the trial does not report prolapse stage reversal or surgery avoided.
cards.source: Hagen S et al. Individualised pelvic floor muscle training in women with pelvic organ prolapse (POPPY): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24290404. Registry ID: ISRCTN35911035. cards.headline: Synthesis: symptom relief, modest on average, from the one large trial — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: symptom relief, modest on average, from the one large trial — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial of 447 women with symptomatic stage I–III prolapse, comparing individualised pelvic-floor muscle training with lifestyle advice alone over 12 months.
cards.result: Training reduced prolapse symptom scores by an additional 1.52 points (95% CI 0.46 to 2.59) over advice alone at 12 months, with no related harms. There is no replicated trial and no evidence here on anatomical stage or later surgery. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — Tier C because the shelf rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial shelf: if POPPY's result is a chance or context-specific finding, nothing else on this shelf catches it. The comparison is against a leaflet, not against pessary or surgery — the trial cannot rank training against the other main options, only establish that supervised training beats advice alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hagen S et al. The Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24290404).

shelves.title: Continuous glucose monitoring in gestational diabetes: no shown improvement in neonatal outcomes — one small trial found less excessive weight gain
shelves.question: In women with gestational diabetes, does continuous glucose monitoring improve glucose control and neonatal outcomes compared with finger-prick self-monitoring?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Chemical Analysis*/methods · Blood Glucose* · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring*/methods · Diabetes, Gestational/blood*/epidemiology* · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — no outcome benefit shown, one possible maternal benefit. The only GDM-only randomised trial (106 women) found no significant differences between continuous glucose monitoring and self-monitoring in caesarean delivery, Apgar scores, macrosomia or neonatal hypoglycaemia, and a non-significant HbA1c difference — but fewer women on CGM gained excessive weight (33.3% vs 56.4%; P = .039) (Wei Q et al., PMID: 26814139). The larger GlucoMOMS trial (300 women with type 1, type 2 or gestational diabetes on insulin) found intermittent retrospective CGM did not reduce macrosomia (31.0% vs 28.4%; relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.37) and did not improve HbA1c (Voormolen DN et al., PMID: 29603547). So the devices reveal glucose patterns without, so far, changing the outcomes those patterns predict — in GDM specifically the randomised base is one small trial plus a mixed-diabetes trial in which GDM was a minority subgroup (109 of 300). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for neonatal and obstetric outcomes / POSSIBLE (less excessive gestational weight gain); Tier C: small, indirect evidence base. CGM in type 1 diabetes in pregnancy (CONCEPTT) is a different question, homed at shelf #959.

cards.headline: Wei 2016 (106 women with GDM): CGM changed no obstetric or neonatal outcome — but excessive weight gain was less common (33.3% vs 56.4%)
cards.summary: Wei 2016 (106 women with GDM): CGM changed no obstetric or neonatal outcome — but excessive weight gain was less common (33.3% vs 56.4%)
cards.people: 106 women with gestational diabetes at 24–28 weeks, randomised to antenatal care plus a continuous glucose monitoring system (CGMS, subdivided into early and late initiation) or self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG). Outcomes included caesarean delivery, 5-minute Apgar score, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, HbA1c and gestational weight gain.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between CGMS and SMBG in caesarean delivery rate, Apgar score at 5 minutes, macrosomia or neonatal hypoglycaemia. HbA1c was lower in the CGMS group but not significantly. Excessive gestational weight gain was less frequent with CGMS (33.3% vs 56.4%; P = .039), women who started CGMS earlier gained less (P = .017), and monitoring mode was an independent factor for weight gain (adjusted OR 2.40, 95% CI 1.03 to 5.59). The authors call for a larger follow-up cohort.
cards.watchOut: Small (n = 106), single-centre, and the one positive finding — weight gain — is a secondary outcome among many tested, at P = .039: exactly the profile of a result that needs replication before it is believed. The trial used an older retrospective CGMS, not modern real-time sensors with alarms.
cards.source: Wei Q et al. Effect of a CGMS and SMBG on Maternal and Neonatal Outcomes in Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: a Randomized Controlled Trial. Scientific Reports. 2016. PMID: 26814139. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Voormolen 2018 (GlucoMOMS, 300 women): intermittent CGM in diabetic pregnancy did not reduce macrosomia (31.0% vs 28.4%; RR 1.06)
cards.summary: Voormolen 2018 (GlucoMOMS, 300 women): intermittent CGM in diabetic pregnancy did not reduce macrosomia (31.0% vs 28.4%; RR 1.06)
cards.people: 300 pregnant women in a Dutch nationwide multicentre open-label trial: type 1 diabetes (n = 109), type 2 diabetes (n = 82) or insulin-treated gestational diabetes (n = 109), randomised to intermittent retrospective CGM (5–7 days every 6 weeks) plus standard care (n = 147) or standard care alone (n = 153). Primary outcome: macrosomia (birth weight above the 90th percentile).
cards.result: Macrosomia occurred in 31.0% of the CGM group and 28.4% of the standard-care group (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.37). HbA1c levels were similar between groups. The authors conclude that, as a treatment strategy, intermittent retrospective CGM did not translate into improved pregnancy outcome.
cards.watchOut: Only 109 of the 300 women had gestational diabetes, and the GDM-specific results are not reported separately in the abstract — this card is indirect evidence for the GDM question, and it is carded as such. The CGM was intermittent and retrospective (reviewed after the fact), not the real-time monitoring now marketed for GDM.
cards.source: Voormolen DN et al. Continuous glucose monitoring during diabetic pregnancy (GlucoMOMS): A multicentre randomized controlled trial. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2018. PMID: 29603547. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: more glucose data, no better babies so far — SPLIT (no difference for outcomes / possible weight-gain benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: more glucose data, no better babies so far — SPLIT (no difference for outcomes / possible weight-gain benefit)
cards.people: Two randomised trials: one small GDM-only trial (106 women, continuous monitoring vs self-monitoring) and one larger mixed-diabetes pregnancy trial (300 women, of whom 109 had GDM; intermittent retrospective CGM vs standard care).
cards.result: Neither trial showed improvement in macrosomia, caesarean delivery, neonatal hypoglycaemia or HbA1c. The single positive signal is maternal: less excessive gestational weight gain in the small GDM trial (33.3% vs 56.4%). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for neonatal and obstetric outcomes / POSSIBLE (less excessive gestational weight gain).
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate modern real-time CGM with trend arrows and alarms, and neither tested CGM as a replacement for finger-prick monitoring in diet-treated GDM — the commonest current use case. A null result for 2011–2016 technology does not settle the question for current devices, but the burden of proof sits with the newer technology, and no GDM trial of it has yet reported better outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wei Q et al. Scientific Reports. 2016 (PMID: 26814139); Voormolen DN et al. Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism. 2018 (PMID: 29603547).

shelves.title: Emergency contraception and weight: pregnancy risk after the pills is over threefold higher in obese women — worst for levonorgestrel — while the copper IUD fails about 1 time in 1,000 at any weight
shelves.question: In women with higher body weight, do oral emergency contraceptives lose effectiveness, and does the copper IUD avoid the problem?
shelves.mesh: Contraception, Postcoital* · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined* · Female · Humans · Ireland · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage* · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Norpregnadienes/administration & dosage* · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Assessment · United States · Women's Health Services*
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pills fade with weight; the device does not. Pooling the two randomised trials of ulipristal acetate versus levonorgestrel, the risk of pregnancy after oral emergency contraception was more than threefold higher in obese women than in women with normal BMI (odds ratio 3.60, 95% CI 1.96 to 6.53), whichever pill was taken — and the increase was larger for levonorgestrel (OR 4.41, 2.05 to 9.44) than for ulipristal (OR 2.62, 0.89 to 7.00, not significant) (Glasier A et al., PMID: 21920190). The copper IUD shows no such gradient in the data available: across 42 studies and 7,034 women over 35 years, the pregnancy rate after IUD insertion for emergency contraception was 0.09% — about 1 in 1,100 — and the review identified no weight-related loss of effect (Cleland K et al., PMID: 22570193). Two cautions: the weight analysis is a pooled secondary analysis of trial data, not a trial randomised by weight, and absolute failure rates remain low for all methods (the trials' overall pregnancy rates were around 1–2%); and intercourse near ovulation raised failure risk as much as obesity did (OR 4.42) for both pills. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (effectiveness falls with weight, most for levonorgestrel) / LIKELY (copper IUD unaffected); Tier C: pooled observational analysis plus case-series review. Which pill works best head-to-head is homed at shelf #244; the 2010 Glasier trial is carded there and is not re-carded here — this shelf cards the separate 2011 pooled risk-factor analysis.

cards.headline: Glasier 2011 (pooled analysis of 2 RCTs): pregnancy after oral emergency contraception was 3.6-fold more likely in obese women — OR 4.41 for levonorgestrel, 2.62 for ulipristal
cards.summary: Glasier 2011 (pooled analysis of 2 RCTs): pregnancy after oral emergency contraception was 3.6-fold more likely in obese women — OR 4.41 for levonorgestrel, 2.62 for ulipristal
cards.type: Pooled secondary analysis of two randomised trials (Glasier 2011)
cards.people: Women enrolled in the two randomised controlled trials comparing ulipristal acetate with levonorgestrel for emergency contraception (the trials carded at shelf #244), re-analysed together to identify risk factors for emergency-contraception failure, including body mass index, cycle day of intercourse and further unprotected intercourse after treatment.
cards.result: The risk of pregnancy was more than threefold greater for obese women than for women with normal BMI (odds ratio 3.60, 95% CI 1.96 to 6.53; P < .0001), whichever pill was taken. The increase was greater for levonorgestrel (OR 4.41, 2.05 to 9.44; P = .0002) than for ulipristal acetate (OR 2.62, 0.89 to 7.00; not significant). Intercourse the day before the estimated day of ovulation carried a fourfold pregnancy risk (OR 4.42, 2.33 to 8.20), and further unprotected intercourse after taking emergency contraception also raised risk (OR 4.64, 2.22 to 8.96). The authors recommend a copper IUD for women around ovulation, and an IUD or ulipristal for women with BMI above 25.
cards.watchOut: Nobody was randomised by weight: this is an observational analysis inside trial data, with few pregnancies in the obese subgroups — hence the wide intervals, and the ulipristal estimate (2.62) is compatible with anything from no increase to a sevenfold increase. Odds ratios here describe relative failure risk; absolute pregnancy rates after either pill remained low (around 1–2% overall in the parent trials).
cards.source: Glasier A et al. Can we identify women at risk of pregnancy despite using emergency contraception? Data from randomized trials of ulipristal acetate and levonorgestrel. Contraception. 2011. PMID: 21920190. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cleland 2012 (42 studies, 7,034 women): pregnancy after an IUD for emergency contraception was 0.09% — about 1 in 1,100 insertions
cards.summary: Cleland 2012 (42 studies, 7,034 women): pregnancy after an IUD for emergency contraception was 0.09% — about 1 in 1,100 insertions
cards.people: 42 studies conducted in six countries between 1979 and 2011, covering eight IUD types (predominantly copper devices) in 7,034 women who received an IUD for emergency contraception; most insertions (74% of studies) were within 5 days of intercourse, some up to 10 or more days. Studies were included only where pregnancies were ascertained and loss to follow-up was defined.
cards.result: The pregnancy rate after IUD emergency contraception was 0.09% (excluding one outlier study) — roughly 1 pregnancy per 1,100 insertions, an order of magnitude below oral emergency contraception, with the device then continuing as ongoing contraception. The review could not analyse efficacy by delay to insertion, parity, cycle day or IUD type, and did not report a weight subgroup — no weight-related failure signal appears in this literature.
cards.watchOut: These are case series accumulated over 35 years, not randomised comparisons, and women who receive an IUD differ from pill users (they reached a clinic, accepted a procedure). 'No weight subgroup reported' is weaker than 'weight formally tested and shown irrelevant' — but with an overall failure rate of 0.09%, there is little room for a weight effect of the size seen with the pills.
cards.source: Cleland K et al. The efficacy of intrauterine devices for emergency contraception: a systematic review of 35 years of experience. Human Reproduction. 2012. PMID: 22570193. cards.headline: Synthesis: weight erodes the pills (levonorgestrel most), not the copper IUD — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: weight erodes the pills (levonorgestrel most), not the copper IUD — SPLIT
cards.people: A pooled re-analysis of the two ulipristal-versus-levonorgestrel randomised trials (pregnancy by BMI category) and a 35-year systematic review of IUD emergency contraception (42 studies, 7,034 women).
cards.result: Obesity was associated with a 3.6-fold higher odds of pregnancy after oral emergency contraception, driven mainly by levonorgestrel (OR 4.41); the ulipristal estimate was smaller and non-significant (OR 2.62). The copper IUD's pooled pregnancy rate was 0.09% with no weight signal. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (oral methods lose effectiveness with weight, levonorgestrel most) / LIKELY (copper IUD remains highly effective).
cards.watchOut: The practical consequence is about the offer, not about refusal: a heavier woman who wants a pill should still get one promptly (ulipristal preferred on these data), because a possibly-reduced pill beats no treatment — the weight data argue for offering the IUD first and being honest about relative failure rates, not for withholding oral treatment when an IUD is declined or unavailable.
cards.source: Synthesis of Glasier A et al. Contraception. 2011 (PMID: 21920190); Cleland K et al. Human Reproduction. 2012 (PMID: 22570193).

shelves.title: ROSE: a four-session interpersonal-therapy programme in pregnancy cut postpartum major depression from 20–33% to 0–4% in two small trials — in low-income women, from one research group
shelves.question: In pregnant women at high risk of postpartum depression, does a preventive interpersonal-therapy programme (ROSE) prevent postpartum depression?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Depression, Postpartum/diagnosis/prevention & control*/psychology · Female · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Life Change Events · Personality Inventory/statistics & numerical data · Pilot Projects · Postpartum Period · Pregnancy · Prenatal Care* · Psychotherapy, Group/methods* · Public Assistance* · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The programme later manualised as ROSE (Reach Out, Stand Strong: Essentials for new mothers) — four antenatal group sessions based on interpersonal psychotherapy, aimed at the role transition to motherhood and at building support — was tested in two small randomised trials in pregnant women on public assistance who had at least one risk factor for postpartum depression. In the pilot (37 women), postpartum major depression occurred in 0 of 17 women in the intervention group versus 6 of 18 (33%) on treatment as usual within 3 months of delivery (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 11282702). In the larger trial (99 women), postpartum major depressive disorder occurred in 4% on the intervention versus 20% on standard antenatal care at 3 months (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 16877662). A later adaptation for low-income women with recent intimate partner violence (54 women) did not significantly reduce major depressive episodes, PTSD or further violence, though symptom scores moved in the programme's favour (Zlotnick C et al., PMID: 21153559). The effects in the main trials are large but the samples are tiny — 2 versus 8 cases decides the larger trial — follow-up stops at 3 months, and all trials come from one research group in one population (financially disadvantaged US women). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — Tier C: small single-group trials. A secondary analysis of the 99-woman trial (Kao 2015, PMID: 26076207) reported longer breastfeeding in the ROSE group; as a repeat report of the same trial it is noted here, not carded separately.

cards.headline: Zlotnick 2001 (pilot, 37 women): postpartum major depression in 0 of 17 women after the interpersonal-therapy group vs 6 of 18 (33%) on usual care
cards.summary: Zlotnick 2001 (pilot, 37 women): postpartum major depression in 0 of 17 women after the interpersonal-therapy group vs 6 of 18 (33%) on usual care
cards.people: 37 pregnant women receiving public assistance with at least one risk factor for postpartum depression, randomised to a four-session interpersonal-therapy-oriented group intervention or treatment as usual; 35 completed the study. Postpartum major depression was assessed by structured diagnostic interview within 3 months of delivery.
cards.result: Within 3 months of giving birth, none of the 17 women in the intervention group had developed postpartum major depression, compared with 6 of 18 women (33%) in the treatment-as-usual group.
cards.watchOut: A pilot of 35 completers: six cases in one arm and zero in the other is a fragile result — two cases moving arms would erase it. The programme was not yet called ROSE in this report; the name attaches to the manualised version of this same intervention in the group's later publications.
cards.source: Zlotnick C et al. Postpartum depression in women receiving public assistance: pilot study of an interpersonal-therapy-oriented group intervention. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2001. PMID: 11282702. Registry ID: none in the record — pre-registration era. cards.summary: Zlotnick 2006 (99 women at risk): postpartum major depressive disorder in 4% after the intervention vs 20% on standard antenatal care
cards.people: 99 pregnant women on public assistance assessed to be at risk for postpartum depression, randomised to standard antenatal care plus the interpersonal-psychotherapy-based preventive intervention (the programme later named ROSE) or standard antenatal care alone. Diagnostic interviews at 3 months after delivery assessed major depressive disorder.
cards.result: Within 3 months of delivery, 2 women in the intervention condition (4%) had developed postpartum major depressive disorder, compared with 8 (20%) in the standard-care condition — an absolute difference of about 16 percentage points, roughly one case prevented for every six women treated, in this high-risk group.
cards.watchOut: The result rests on 2 versus 8 cases. Follow-up ends at 3 months postpartum, so prevention versus postponement cannot be distinguished. A secondary analysis of this same trial (Kao JC et al., PMID: 26076207) found longer breastfeeding duration in the intervention group (median 54 vs 21 days) — a repeat report of one trial, flagged as such and not carded separately on this shelf.
cards.source: Zlotnick C et al. A preventive intervention for pregnant women on public assistance at risk for postpartum depression. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2006. PMID: 16877662. cards.headline: Zlotnick 2011 (54 women with recent intimate partner violence): the adapted programme did not significantly reduce depressive episodes, PTSD or violence
cards.summary: Zlotnick 2011 (54 women with recent intimate partner violence): the adapted programme did not significantly reduce depressive episodes, PTSD or violence
cards.people: 54 low-income pregnant women with recent intimate partner violence, randomised to an interpersonally based intervention (four sessions in pregnancy plus a postpartum booster) or control, assessed during pregnancy and up to 3 months postpartum for depression, PTSD and intimate partner violence.
cards.result: The intervention did not significantly reduce the likelihood of a major depressive episode, PTSD or intimate partner violence during pregnancy or up to 3 months postpartum. Moderate effects favoured the intervention for PTSD and depression symptoms during pregnancy, and a large effect for PTSD symptoms from pregnancy to 3 months postpartum. The authors describe initial support and call for larger trials.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot, underpowered by design for episode outcomes — its null result does not refute the main trials, but it does mark the boundary of what is known: in women whose risk is driven by ongoing violence, the programme's effect on actual disorder is unproven.
cards.source: Zlotnick C et al. An interpersonally based intervention for low-income pregnant women with intimate partner violence: a pilot study. Archives of Women's Mental Health. 2011. PMID: 21153559. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: large preventive effects in two small trials in high-risk low-income women; unproven beyond them — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: large preventive effects in two small trials in high-risk low-income women; unproven beyond them — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three small randomised trials from one research group: a 37-woman pilot and a 99-woman trial of the interpersonal-therapy programme (later ROSE) in pregnant women on public assistance at risk of postpartum depression, and a 54-woman pilot of an adaptation for women with recent intimate partner violence.
cards.result: Postpartum major depression at 3 months: 0% vs 33% (pilot) and 4% vs 20% (main trial) favouring the programme; the violence-adapted version showed symptom-level benefits without significantly reducing episodes. No trial followed women beyond 3 months postpartum, and none was conducted outside low-income US populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Prevention trials in high-risk groups flatter programmes: with a 20–33% control-group event rate, even a modest true effect looks dramatic, and these samples are small enough that the true effect could be far smaller. The evidence supports offering the programme to similar high-risk women; it does not establish benefit for universal antenatal populations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zlotnick C et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2001 (PMID: 11282702); Zlotnick C et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2006 (PMID: 16877662); Zlotnick C et al. Archives of Women's Mental Health. 2011 (PMID: 21153559).

shelves.title: Self-managed medication abortion: 95–99% completed without surgery in the telemedicine and accompaniment cohorts, with serious adverse events under 1% — observational evidence only
shelves.question: Where clinic access is limited, is self-managed medication abortion with remote or accompaniment support as safe and effective as clinic-based care?
shelves.mesh: Abortifacient Agents, Nonsteroidal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Abortifacient Agents, Steroidal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Abortion, Induced/adverse effects*/methods* · Adult · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gestational Age · Humans · Internet* · Ireland · Middle Aged · Mifepristone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Misoprostol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Northern Ireland · Pregnancy · Self Report* · Telemedicine* · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two large prospective cohorts describe self-managed medication abortion with structured remote support. Through Women on Web, 1,000 women in Ireland and Northern Ireland who self-sourced mifepristone and misoprostol reported 94.7% (95% CI 93.1 to 96.0) completing abortion without surgical intervention; 0.7% received a blood transfusion, 2.6% received antibiotics, and no deaths were reported (Aiken ARA et al., PMID: 28512085). In the SAFE study — 1,051 callers to accompaniment groups in Argentina and Nigeria, supported by phone through self-management — complete abortion without surgery was reported by 99% of misoprostol-alone users and 94% of combined-regimen users, and for pregnancies under 9 weeks both regimens were non-inferior to the completion rates of clinician-managed abortion in historical clinical trials (Moseson H et al., PMID: 34801131). There is no randomised comparison and there cannot realistically be one where clinic care is legally restricted; the comparisons are against historical clinic benchmarks, outcomes are self-reported, and roughly a quarter to a third of women in these programmes are lost to follow-up — the women not heard from may fare worse. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — effectiveness and safety comparable to clinic-based care) — Tier C: observational evidence on a question where randomisation is not feasible. Telemedicine consultation inside a formal clinic service is a different model, homed at shelf #660.

cards.headline: Aiken 2017 (Women on Web, Ireland/Northern Ireland, 1,000 women): 94.7% completed self-sourced medical abortion without surgery; transfusion 0.7%; no deaths reported
cards.summary: Aiken 2017 (Women on Web, Ireland/Northern Ireland, 1,000 women): 94.7% completed self-sourced medical abortion without surgery; transfusion 0.7%; no deaths reported
cards.people: 1,000 women with follow-up data who used mifepristone and misoprostol sent by the Women on Web online telemedicine service in 2010–2012, in jurisdictions where abortion was unavailable through the formal healthcare system except in restricted circumstances. Medications were sent to 1,636 women; follow-up was obtained for 1,158 (71%), and 1,023 confirmed taking them. At request, 78% were under 7 weeks pregnant and 22% were 7–9 weeks.
cards.result: 94.7% (95% CI 93.1 to 96.0) reported ending their pregnancy without surgical intervention. Seven women (0.7%, 0.3 to 1.5) reported a blood transfusion and 26 (2.6%, 1.7 to 3.8) reported receiving antibiotics. No deaths resulting from the intervention were reported by family, friends, authorities or media. Of 93 women (9.3%) who experienced symptoms for which they were advised to seek medical attention, 95% reported seeking it; none of the five who did not seek attention reported an adverse outcome. Outcomes are self-reported.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported outcomes with 29% of women who received medications lost to follow-up: women with complications may be either more or less likely to report back, and there was no ultrasound or clinical confirmation of completion. The setting — a well-run telemedicine service with clear instructions and advice to seek care — is part of the intervention; the numbers do not describe unsupported use of pills from unregulated sources.
cards.source: Aiken ARA et al. Self reported outcomes and adverse events after medical abortion through online telemedicine: population based study in the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. BMJ. 2017. PMID: 28512085. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moseson 2022 (SAFE study, Argentina and Nigeria, 961 analysed): complete abortion without surgery in 99% (misoprostol alone) and 94% (combined regimen); non-inferior to clinic benchmarks under 9 weeks
cards.summary: Moseson 2022 (SAFE study, Argentina and Nigeria, 961 analysed): complete abortion without surgery in 99% (misoprostol alone) and 94% (combined regimen); non-inferior to clinic benchmarks under 9 weeks
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort study with historical controls (SAFE, Moseson 2022)
cards.people: 1,051 callers to two safe-abortion accompaniment groups (Argentina and Nigeria) who self-managed medication abortion with telephone accompaniment support, enrolled July 2019–April 2020; outcomes analysed for 961 participants (plus 47 reached later). Most pregnancies were under 12 weeks. Regimens: misoprostol alone (593 analysed) or mifepristone plus misoprostol (356 analysed). Baseline and 1-week and 3-week follow-up phone surveys; the comparison was a non-inferiority analysis against completion rates in historical clinical trials of the same regimens, restricted to pregnancies under 9 weeks.
cards.result: At last follow-up, 586 of 593 misoprostol-alone users (99%) and 334 of 356 combined-regimen users (94%) reported a complete abortion without surgical intervention. For pregnancies under 9 weeks, both regimens were non-inferior to clinician-managed medication abortion effectiveness in clinical settings. The study was registered (ISRCTN95769543, as given in the record).
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority claim compares this cohort with historical clinical-trial populations — different settings, eras and ascertainment — because legal restrictions prevented a concurrent clinic control group. Completion is self-reported by phone survey. The counterintuitive ordering (misoprostol alone 99% vs combined 94%) reflects who used which regimen and at what gestation, not a randomised comparison of regimens.
cards.source: Moseson H et al. Effectiveness of self-managed medication abortion with accompaniment support in Argentina and Nigeria (SAFE): a prospective, observational cohort study and non-inferiority analysis with historical controls. The Lancet Global Health. 2022. PMID: 34801131. Registry ID: ISRCTN95769543. cards.headline: Synthesis: with structured remote support, self-management completes ~95–99% of early abortions without surgery — POSSIBLE, on observational evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: with structured remote support, self-management completes ~95–99% of early abortions without surgery — POSSIBLE, on observational evidence
cards.people: Two prospective cohorts totalling about 2,000 women with outcome data: an online telemedicine service cohort in Ireland/Northern Ireland (mifepristone + misoprostol by post, self-reported outcomes) and an accompaniment-group cohort in Argentina and Nigeria (misoprostol alone or combined regimen, phone follow-up, historical-control comparison).
cards.result: Complete abortion without surgical intervention: 94.7% (telemedicine cohort) and 94–99% by regimen (accompaniment cohort, non-inferior to historical clinic benchmarks under 9 weeks). Serious adverse events were uncommon in the telemedicine cohort (transfusion 0.7%, antibiotics 2.6%, no deaths reported). No randomised or concurrent-controlled evidence exists. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit — comparably safe and effective where clinic access is limited).
cards.watchOut: Both cohorts embed the support structure — vetted medication supply, dosing instructions, symptom triage and a route into care — inside the exposure being measured. The evidence supports self-management with that support; it is silent on pills obtained without information or backup, and loss to follow-up of a quarter or more in both cohorts leaves the worst outcomes the least completely counted.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aiken ARA et al. BMJ. 2017 (PMID: 28512085); Moseson H et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2022 (PMID: 34801131).

shelves.title: A short course of furosemide after delivery speeds blood-pressure recovery in severe pre-eclampsia: day-2 systolic 142 versus 153 mm Hg in the first trial, fewer severe episodes and less add-on treatment in two more — no shortening of hospital stay
shelves.question: In women with pre-eclampsia, does a short course of furosemide after delivery improve blood-pressure control and reduce the need for other antihypertensive treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Diuresis · Diuretics/therapeutic use · Female · Furosemide/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypertension/complications/drug therapy · Postpartum Period · Pre-Eclampsia/complications/drug therapy · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for blood-pressure recovery after severe pre-eclampsia, not for milder disease. In Ascarelli 2005 (264 patients), the benefit was confined to the severe subgroup (n=70): systolic pressure on postpartum day 2 was 142 ± 13 mm Hg on furosemide 20 mg daily for 5 days versus 153 ± 19 mm Hg on no therapy (P<0.004), and antihypertensive treatment at discharge was needed by 6% versus 26% (P=0.045); patients with mild (n=169) or superimposed (n=25) pre-eclampsia gained nothing, and neither hospital stay nor delayed complications improved. Veena 2017 (108 women with severe pre-eclampsia) found additional antihypertensive drugs were required by 8.0% on furosemide plus nifedipine versus 26.0% on nifedipine alone (P=0.017). Cursino 2025 (120 women, triple-masked, placebo-controlled) found lower mean daily systolic and diastolic pressures on furosemide 40 mg daily (P<0.001), fewer severe hypertensive episodes on days 2 and 5 (P=0.04), and faster blood-pressure control (P=0.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): five days of oral furosemide after delivery accelerates blood-pressure recovery in severe pre-eclampsia.

cards.headline: Ascarelli 2005: benefit only in severe pre-eclampsia — day-2 systolic 142 versus 153 mm Hg, discharge antihypertensives 6% versus 26%; mild disease gained nothing
cards.summary: Ascarelli 2005: benefit only in severe pre-eclampsia — day-2 systolic 142 versus 153 mm Hg, discharge antihypertensives 6% versus 26%; mild disease gained nothing
cards.people: 264 patients with pre-eclampsia who, after spontaneous postpartum diuresis began and magnesium sulfate was stopped, were randomised to no therapy or oral furosemide 20 mg daily for 5 days with potassium supplementation.
cards.result: Only the severe pre-eclampsia subgroup (n=70) benefited: systolic blood pressure on postpartum day 2 was 142 ± 13 mm Hg with furosemide versus 153 ± 19 mm Hg in controls (P<0.004), with less antihypertensive therapy during hospitalisation (14% versus 26%, P=0.371) and at discharge (6% versus 26%, P=0.045). No benefit was shown in mild pre-eclampsia (n=169) or superimposed pre-eclampsia (n=25), and neither length of hospitalisation nor delayed postpartum complications was improved.
cards.watchOut: The headline result is a subgroup of 70 within a 264-patient trial, and the in-hospital treatment difference (14% versus 26%) was not itself significant — the discharge difference carries the claim.
cards.source: Ascarelli MH et al. Postpartum preeclampsia management with furosemide: a randomized clinical trial. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2005. PMID: 15625138. cards.headline: Veena 2017: additional antihypertensive drugs needed by 8.0% on furosemide plus nifedipine versus 26.0% on nifedipine alone (P=0.017)
cards.summary: Veena 2017: additional antihypertensive drugs needed by 8.0% on furosemide plus nifedipine versus 26.0% on nifedipine alone (P=0.017)
cards.people: 108 women with severe pre-eclampsia and two postpartum blood-pressure recordings ≥150/100 mm Hg within 24 hours of delivery, randomised to furosemide 20 mg once daily plus nifedipine or nifedipine alone.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in mean systolic, diastolic, or mean arterial pressures at admission. cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial with a treatment-escalation endpoint; blood-pressure trajectories themselves are reported only as non-significantly different at admission in the record, so the card rests on the add-on-treatment outcome.

cards.summary: Cursino 2025: triple-masked placebo-controlled trial — mean daily pressures lower on furosemide (P<0.001), fewer severe episodes on days 2 and 5, faster control
cards.people: 120 postpartum women with de novo pre-eclampsia with severe features or eclampsia, with adequate diuresis after magnesium sulfate, randomised to oral furosemide 40 mg daily for 5 days or placebo; 118 were analysed (58 furosemide, 60 placebo).
cards.result: Mean daily systolic and diastolic pressures were lower in the furosemide group (P<0.001), there were fewer episodes of severe hypertension on the second (P=0.04) and fifth (P=0.04) postpartum days, and the time required until blood pressure was controlled was shorter (P=0.01). cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials agree — furosemide speeds postpartum blood-pressure recovery in severe pre-eclampsia; stay and complications unmoved
cards.people: Three randomised trials of a 5-day oral furosemide course after delivery in pre-eclampsia (Ascarelli 2005, 264 patients; Veena 2017, 108; Cursino 2025, 120 analysed).
cards.result: Day-2 systolic 142 versus 153 mm Hg in severe disease (Ascarelli); add-on antihypertensives 8.0% versus 26.0% (Veena) and 6% versus 26% at discharge in severe disease (Ascarelli); lower mean daily pressures and fewer severe episodes (Cursino). shelves.title: Metformin in obese pregnancy: weight gain trimmed in two trials (4.6 versus 6.3 kg in EMPOWR) — baby's birth weight unchanged in both, preeclampsia signal in one
shelves.question: In obese pregnant women without diabetes, does metformin reduce maternal weight gain or improve pregnancy outcomes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Birth Weight · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Development · Gestational Age · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Infant, Newborn · Metformin · Obesity · Pre-Eclampsia · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Pregnancy Outcome · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for maternal weight gain, not for the baby's size. Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape of the answer. In EMPOWR (Syngelaki A et al., PMID: 26840133), 450 women with BMI over 35 without diabetes were randomised to metformin 3.0 g daily or placebo from 12–18 weeks until delivery: the primary outcome, median neonatal birth-weight z score, did not differ (0.05 versus 0.17, P=0.66), but median maternal gestational weight gain was lower on metformin (4.6 versus 6.3 kg, P<0.001) and preeclampsia was less frequent (3.0% versus 11.3%; odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.61; P=0.001), with more side effects on metformin. In GRoW (Dodd JM et al., PMID: 30528218), 514 overweight or obese women receiving dietary and lifestyle advice were randomised to metformin (up to 2,000 mg) or placebo: birthweight over 4,000 g did not differ (16% versus 14%; adjusted risk ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.65 to 1.47), weekly weight gain was slightly lower on metformin (adjusted mean difference −0.08 kg/week, P=0.007), and total weight gain and other pregnancy outcomes did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin trims gestational weight gain in obese pregnancy; a neonatal benefit was not shown in either trial, and the preeclampsia signal rests on one trial.

cards.headline: EMPOWR (Syngelaki 2016): birth-weight z score unchanged (0.05 versus 0.17, P=0.66), but weight gain 4.6 versus 6.3 kg and preeclampsia 3.0% versus 11.3% (OR 0.24)
cards.summary: EMPOWR (Syngelaki 2016): birth-weight z score unchanged (0.05 versus 0.17, P=0.66), but weight gain 4.6 versus 6.3 kg and preeclampsia 3.0% versus 11.3% (OR 0.24)
cards.people: 450 pregnant women without diabetes with BMI over 35 (225 per group), randomised to metformin 3.0 g/day or placebo from 12–18 weeks of gestation until delivery; 202 women in the metformin group and 198 in the placebo group remained after 50 consent withdrawals; primary outcome a reduction in median neonatal birth-weight z score.
cards.result: There was no significant between-group difference in the median neonatal birth-weight z score (0.05 in the metformin group versus 0.17 in the placebo group, P=0.66). Median maternal gestational weight gain was lower on metformin (4.6 kg versus 6.3 kg, P<0.001), as was the incidence of preeclampsia (3.0% versus 11.3%; odds ratio 0.24; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.61; P=0.001). The incidence of side effects was higher on metformin. There were no significant differences in gestational diabetes, large-for-gestational-age neonates, or adverse neonatal outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The preeclampsia result is a secondary outcome with few events (3.0% versus 11.3% in a trial whose primary outcome was null), the dose (3.0 g/day) is higher than routine practice, and 50 of 450 women withdrew consent — the trial was not powered to prove a preeclampsia benefit.
cards.source: Syngelaki A et al. Metformin versus Placebo in Obese Pregnant Women without Diabetes Mellitus. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 26840133. cards.headline: GRoW (Dodd 2019): birthweight >4,000 g 16% versus 14% (aRR 0.97, NS); weekly weight gain −0.08 kg on metformin; total gain and other outcomes not significantly different
cards.summary: GRoW (Dodd 2019): birthweight >4,000 g 16% versus 14% (aRR 0.97, NS); weekly weight gain −0.08 kg on metformin; total gain and other outcomes not significantly different
cards.people: 524 overweight or obese pregnant women (BMI ≥25; median 32.3) at 10–20 weeks' gestation at three Adelaide maternity units, randomised to metformin (maximum 2,000 mg/day, n=256 analysed) or placebo (n=258), all receiving an antenatal dietary and lifestyle intervention; primary outcome birthweight greater than 4,000 g.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in infants with birthweight greater than 4,000 g (40 [16%] with metformin versus 37 [14%] with placebo; adjusted risk ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.47; P=0.899). Women on metformin had lower average weekly gestational weight gain (adjusted mean difference −0.08 kg, 95% CI −0.14 to −0.02; P=0.007) and were more likely to gain below recommendations (aRR 1.46, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.94; P=0.008). Total gestational weight gain, pregnancy and birth outcomes, diet, physical activity and quality of life did not differ significantly. Side-effects (nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting) were reported by 76% on metformin and 73% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: GRoW added metformin on top of a lifestyle intervention in a broader BMI ≥25 population and used a lower maximum dose than EMPOWR — so its smaller weight effect (−0.08 kg/week, with total gain not significantly different) is the more conservative estimate, and it found no preeclampsia headline to replicate EMPOWR's.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant trials — less maternal weight gain, no change in baby size, one unreplicated preeclampsia signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant trials — less maternal weight gain, no change in baby size, one unreplicated preeclampsia signal
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling ~914 analysed women with overweight or obesity in pregnancy without diabetes (EMPOWR, BMI >35, metformin 3 g; GRoW, BMI ≥25, metformin up to 2 g plus lifestyle advice).
cards.result: Neonatal size: no difference in either trial (birth-weight z score P=0.66; birthweight >4,000 g 16% versus 14%). Maternal weight gain: lower on metformin in both (median 4.6 versus 6.3 kg in EMPOWR; −0.08 kg/week adjusted in GRoW, total gain not significant). Preeclampsia: 3.0% versus 11.3% in EMPOWR only. Gestational diabetes: no significant difference in EMPOWR. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the null neonatal primary outcomes on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was designed or powered for preeclampsia or long-term offspring outcomes, and gastrointestinal side effects are near-universal in pregnancy trials of metformin; prescribing it to non-diabetic obese pregnant women buys a modest weight-gain reduction, not a proven outcome benefit. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials carry the (narrow) claim.

shelves.title: Insulin glargine versus NPH in pregnancy: no significant difference on any maternal or neonatal outcome in 702 women — reassurance, not proof of equivalence
shelves.question: In pregnant women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, does insulin glargine achieve control comparable to NPH insulin without worse perinatal outcomes?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — glargine and NPH looked alike on every maternal and neonatal outcome measured, in the only synthesis available. The meta-analysis (Lepercq J et al., PMID: 22685467) pooled 8 studies of women with gestational or pregestational diabetes using insulin glargine (331 women) or NPH insulin (371 women), comparing maternal weight gain, HbA1c, severe hypoglycaemia, hypertension, preeclampsia and caesarean section, and neonatal congenital malformations, birth weight, macrosomia, large-for-gestational-age, NICU admission, respiratory distress, neonatal hypoglycaemia and hyperbilirubinaemia. No significant differences in efficacy or safety outcomes were found between glargine and NPH. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): comparable control and no safety signal — but the underlying studies are small and mostly non-randomised, so this is Tier C and 'no difference found' is not 'equivalence proven'.

cards.headline: Lepercq 2012 meta-analysis: 331 glargine versus 371 NPH pregnancies — no significant difference in any maternal or neonatal efficacy or safety outcome
cards.summary: Lepercq 2012 meta-analysis: 331 glargine versus 371 NPH pregnancies — no significant difference in any maternal or neonatal efficacy or safety outcome
cards.people: Eight studies (each with at least 15 women per arm) of women with gestational or pregestational diabetes treated with insulin glargine (n=331) or human NPH insulin (n=371) during pregnancy, pooled with a random-effects model for relative risks and weighted mean differences.
cards.result: No significant differences between glargine and NPH were found in maternal outcomes (weight at delivery, weight gain, first- and third-trimester HbA1c, severe hypoglycaemia, new-onset hypertension, preeclampsia, caesarean section) or neonatal outcomes (congenital malformations, gestational age at delivery, birth weight, macrosomia, large-for-gestational-age, 5-minute Apgar >7, NICU admissions, respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal hypoglycaemia, hyperbilirubinaemia).
cards.watchOut: Only 702 women across 8 mostly observational studies, assembled because glargine was being used in pregnancy without randomised trials: confidence intervals around rare outcomes such as congenital malformations are wide, so the analysis can exclude a large harm signal but cannot prove safety — and women prescribed glargine may differ systematically from those prescribed NPH.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no difference found anywhere — on a thin, largely non-randomised base
cards.summary: Synthesis: no difference found anywhere — on a thin, largely non-randomised base
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 8 comparative studies, 702 pregnant women with gestational or pregestational diabetes in total.
cards.result: Every maternal and neonatal outcome compared — glycaemic control, severe hypoglycaemia, hypertensive outcomes, delivery mode, malformations, birth weight, NICU admission and neonatal metabolic complications — showed no significant difference between glargine and NPH. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: observational-heavy evidence, personal-review tier.
cards.watchOut: A 'no difference' shelf built on 702 women should be read as reassurance against a large effect, not as a licence to prefer either insulin: the question the candidate asked — comparable control without worse perinatal outcomes — is answered 'nothing worse was found', with the emphasis on 'found'.
