shelves.title: Cabergoline roughly halves moderate-to-severe ovarian hyperstimulation in high-risk IVF patients — pooled risk ratio 0.38 in one meta-analysis, class odds ratio 0.27 in the Cochrane review — without lowering pregnancy rates
shelves.question: In women at high risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, does cabergoline prevent moderate or severe OHSS versus placebo or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/prevention & control · Administration, Oral · Aminoquinolines/therapeutic use · Bromocriptine/therapeutic use · Cabergoline · Dopamine Agonists/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Ergolines/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome/prevention & control · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reproductive Techniques, Assisted
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent syntheses of randomised trials agree. The meta-analysis restricted to cabergoline (Leitao VM et al., PMID: 24360566; 7 studies, 858 women) found moderate-to-severe OHSS risk ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.51) — a 62% relative reduction — with no signal of harm to clinical pregnancy (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.34) or oocyte yield (mean difference 1.15, 95% CI -0.76 to 3.07), though estimates for live birth (one study, 200 women) and miscarriage were imprecise. The Cochrane review of dopamine agonists (Tang H et al., PMID: 27901279; 16 trials, 2,091 high-risk women) found the class reduced moderate or severe OHSS versus placebo or no intervention with odds ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) — in absolute terms, from an expected 29% of women to between 7% and 14% — again with no difference in live birth, clinical pregnancy, multiple pregnancy or miscarriage, and cabergoline specifically beat human albumin (odds ratio 0.21, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.38). Gastrointestinal adverse effects were increased for the class, driven by quinagolide data. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): for high-risk women in assisted reproduction, cabergoline prevents a large share of moderate-to-severe OHSS without costing pregnancies — live-birth safety rests on thinner data than the OHSS benefit.

cards.headline: Leitao 2014: cabergoline RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.51) for moderate-severe OHSS across 7 studies, 858 women; clinical pregnancy RR 1.02 (0.78 to 1.34)
cards.summary: Leitao 2014: cabergoline RR 0.38 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.51) for moderate-severe OHSS across 7 studies, 858 women; clinical pregnancy RR 1.02 (0.78 to 1.34)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Leitao 2014)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials of cabergoline for OHSS prevention in women undergoing controlled ovarian stimulation for assisted reproduction (seven meta-analysed, 858 women); outcomes included moderate-severe OHSS, live birth, clinical pregnancy, oocytes retrieved and miscarriage.
cards.result: Cabergoline reduced moderate-severe OHSS: risk ratio 0.38 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.51; 7 studies, 858 women) — a 62% relative reduction. Clinical pregnancy: risk ratio 1.02 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.34; 4 studies, 561 women). Oocytes retrieved: mean difference 1.15 (95% CI -0.76 to 3.07; 5 studies, 628 women). Live birth (risk ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.48; 1 study, 200 women) and miscarriage (0.69, 0.27 to 1.76; 3 studies, 194 women) were too imprecise to distinguish harm from benefit. No study reported congenital abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: The reassuring pregnancy numbers are compatible with meaningful harm or benefit — the review is powered for OHSS, not for the outcomes patients ultimately care about. Trials used varying cabergoline doses and start times, and most enrolled women already flagged as high risk, so the relative effect may not transfer to average-risk cycles.
cards.source: Leitao VM et al. Cabergoline for the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Fertility and sterility. 2014. cards.headline: Cochrane (Tang 2016): dopamine agonists OR 0.27 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) for moderate/severe OHSS versus placebo/no treatment — absolute risk from 29% down to 7-14%; cabergoline beat albumin (OR 0.21)
cards.summary: Cochrane (Tang 2016): dopamine agonists OR 0.27 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39) for moderate/severe OHSS versus placebo/no treatment — absolute risk from 29% down to 7-14%; cabergoline beat albumin (OR 0.21)
cards.people: 16 randomised trials, 2,091 women at high risk of OHSS undergoing assisted reproduction, comparing dopamine agonists (cabergoline, quinagolide, bromocriptine) with placebo/no intervention or with co-interventions (hydroxyethyl starch, albumin, coasting, prednisolone).
cards.result: Moderate or severe OHSS, dopamine agonists versus placebo/no intervention: odds ratio 0.27 (95% CI 0.19 to 0.39; 1,022 participants, 8 studies; I2=0%; moderate-quality evidence) — from an assumed 29% risk down to 7-14%. No evidence of difference in live birth, clinical pregnancy, multiple pregnancy or miscarriage. Gastrointestinal adverse effects were increased for the class (odds ratio 4.54, 95% CI 1.49 to 13.84; mainly quinagolide data). Cabergoline versus human albumin: odds ratio 0.21 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.38; 296 participants, 3 studies) for moderate/severe OHSS; cabergoline did not differ significantly from hydroxyethyl starch, coasting or prednisolone.
cards.watchOut: The headline odds ratio pools three different dopamine agonists — cabergoline is the most studied but not the only contributor — and the review itself graded much of the evidence very low to moderate quality for poor reporting of randomisation and blinding. Absolute benefit depends entirely on the woman's baseline OHSS risk.

cards.headline: Synthesis: relative risk cut by roughly two-thirds in both syntheses, pregnancy outcomes statistically untouched — the residual uncertainty is live birth, where data are thinnest
cards.summary: Synthesis: relative risk cut by roughly two-thirds in both syntheses, pregnancy outcomes statistically untouched — the residual uncertainty is live birth, where data are thinnest
cards.people: Two systematic reviews of randomised trials in high-risk assisted-reproduction patients: cabergoline-specific meta-analysis (7 studies, 858 women) and Cochrane dopamine-agonist review (16 trials, 2,091 women).
cards.result: Moderate-to-severe OHSS: risk ratio 0.38 (0.29 to 0.51) for cabergoline; class odds ratio 0.27 (0.19 to 0.39), absolute 29% to 7-14%. Clinical pregnancy: risk ratio 1.02 (0.78 to 1.34). Live birth: one study, risk ratio 1.03 (0.71 to 1.48) — imprecise. Gastrointestinal adverse effects increased for the class. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for OHSS prevention in high-risk women.
cards.watchOut: The two reviews share most of their underlying trials, so their agreement is partly the same data counted twice; what is genuinely independent is the cabergoline-only estimate (0.38) versus the class estimate (0.27), and both exclude no effect by a wide margin. Neither review can exclude a modest effect on live birth in either direction.

shelves.title: Aspirin, heparin, or both did not raise live births in unexplained recurrent miscarriage — ALIFE: 54.5% on combination, 50.8% on aspirin, 57.0% on placebo; Cochrane agrees in low-bias studies
shelves.question: In women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, do aspirin, heparin, or both increase live births versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Habitual/blood/etiology/prevention & control · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Antiphospholipid Syndrome/complications · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Enoxaparin/therapeutic use · Female · Heparin, Low-Molecular-Weight/therapeutic use · Humans · Live Birth · Nadroparin/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Hematologic/drug therapy/etiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Thrombophilia/complications/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the biggest trial and the bias-restricted synthesis land in the same place. ALIFE (Kaandorp SP et al., PMID: 20335572) randomised 364 women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage to aspirin 80 mg plus nadroparin, aspirin alone, or placebo: live-birth rates were 54.5%, 50.8% and 57.0% respectively — the combination was 2.6 percentage points below placebo (95% CI -15.0 to 9.9) and aspirin 6.2 points below (95% CI -18.8 to 6.4); among women who became pregnant the rates were 69.1%, 61.6% and 67.0%. The Cochrane review (de Jong PG et al., PMID: 24995856; 9 studies, 1,228 women) found that two of three high-bias-risk studies claimed benefits, but in sensitivity analyses excluding them, no anticoagulant regimen improved live birth: aspirin versus placebo risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.11), low-molecular-weight heparin versus aspirin 1.08 (0.93 to 1.26), heparin plus aspirin versus no treatment 1.01 (0.87 to 1.16). The harms are real if modest: more bruising, and injection-site skin reactions in almost 40% on heparin in one study. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): in unexplained recurrent miscarriage without antiphospholipid syndrome, anticoagulants are an intervention with costs and no demonstrated live-birth benefit — this shelf does not address antiphospholipid syndrome, where the evidence and practice differ.

cards.headline: ALIFE (Kaandorp 2010): live births 54.5% (aspirin + nadroparin), 50.8% (aspirin), 57.0% (placebo) — neither regimen beat placebo
cards.summary: ALIFE (Kaandorp 2010): live births 54.5% (aspirin + nadroparin), 50.8% (aspirin), 57.0% (placebo) — neither regimen beat placebo
cards.people: 364 women aged 18-42 with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, attempting conception or under 6 weeks pregnant, randomised to aspirin 80 mg daily plus open-label subcutaneous nadroparin 2,850 IU (started once a viable pregnancy was shown), aspirin 80 mg alone, or placebo; primary outcome live-birth rate.
cards.result: Live birth: 54.5% on combination therapy, 50.8% on aspirin alone, 57.0% on placebo. Absolute differences versus placebo: combination -2.6 percentage points (95% CI -15.0 to 9.9); aspirin -6.2 points (95% CI -18.8 to 6.4) — neither significant. Among the 299 women who became pregnant: 69.1%, 61.6% and 67.0% respectively. Bruising tendency and injection-site swelling/itching were significantly more frequent in the combination group.
cards.watchOut: The nadroparin component was open-label, and the confidence intervals cannot exclude a benefit of up to about 10 points for the combination — 'no difference shown' in 364 women is not proof of zero effect. Women with antiphospholipid syndrome were not this trial's population and should not read this shelf as covering them.

cards.headline: Cochrane (de Jong 2014): apparent benefits lived in the high-bias studies — excluding them, live-birth RR 0.94 for aspirin versus placebo, 1.08 for heparin versus aspirin, 1.01 for combination versus none
cards.summary: Cochrane (de Jong 2014): apparent benefits lived in the high-bias studies — excluding them, live-birth RR 0.94 for aspirin versus placebo, 1.08 for heparin versus aspirin, 1.01 for combination versus none
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (de Jong 2014)
cards.people: Nine randomised or quasi-randomised studies, 1,228 women with at least two unexplained miscarriages, with or without inherited thrombophilia, testing aspirin, unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin or nadroparin), or combinations, against placebo, no treatment, or each other.
cards.result: Two of the three studies at high risk of bias reported benefits; in sensitivity analyses restricted to lower-bias studies, anticoagulants did not improve live birth by any comparison: aspirin versus placebo risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.11; n=256); low-molecular-weight heparin versus aspirin 1.08 (0.93 to 1.26; n=239); heparin plus aspirin versus no treatment 1.01 (0.87 to 1.16; n=322). Obstetric complications did not differ significantly. Aspirin did not increase bleeding; heparin plus aspirin increased bleeding significantly in one study, and local skin reactions to heparin injections were reported by almost 40% in the same study.
cards.watchOut: Only one low-bias study was placebo-controlled, regimens and doses varied widely, and the inherited-thrombophilia subgroup remains genuinely under-tested — the review's own conclusion is that benefit there is unproven, not disproven. The null is firmest for unexplained recurrent miscarriage as a whole.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prescribe-by-hope anticoagulation fails its trials — point estimates hover at or below placebo in every low-bias comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: prescribe-by-hope anticoagulation fails its trials — point estimates hover at or below placebo in every low-bias comparison
cards.people: ALIFE (364 women, three-arm placebo-controlled trial) within a Cochrane review of 9 studies and 1,228 women with unexplained recurrent miscarriage, with or without inherited thrombophilia.
cards.result: Live birth on anticoagulants versus control: 54.5% and 50.8% versus 57.0% (ALIFE arms versus placebo); pooled low-bias risk ratios 0.94 (aspirin), 1.08 (heparin versus aspirin), 1.01 (combination versus none) — all confidence intervals crossing 1. Harms: bruising, bleeding in one combination study, injection-site reactions in almost 40%. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for live birth in unexplained recurrent miscarriage.

shelves.title: Drospirenone contraceptive pills ease premenstrual symptoms modestly — symptom scores SMD -0.41 versus placebo in Cochrane's pooling, response 48% versus 36% in the largest trial — with more adverse effects and dropouts
shelves.question: Does a drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive improve premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/adverse effects · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Estrogens/therapeutic use · Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder · Premenstrual Syndrome/drug therapy · Progestins/therapeutic use · Androstenes
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small-to-moderate symptom benefit on low-quality evidence, bought with more side effects. The Cochrane review (Ma S et al., PMID: 37365881) pooled five randomised trials, 858 women, mostly with premenstrual dysphoric disorder: drospirenone plus ethinylestradiol improved overall premenstrual symptoms versus placebo (standardised mean difference -0.41, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.24; 2 trials, 514 women; low-quality evidence), with small improvements in productivity, social activities and relationships, but withdrawal due to adverse effects was more than three times as likely (odds ratio 3.41, 95% CI 2.01 to 5.78) and total adverse effects more than doubled (odds ratio 2.31, 95% CI 1.71 to 3.11; an assumed 28% risk on placebo becomes 40-54%). In the largest single trial (Yonkers KA et al., PMID: 16135578; 450 women, 24/4 regimen), symptom scores fell by -37.49 on drospirenone versus -29.99 on placebo (adjusted difference -7.5, 95% CI -11.2 to -3.8; p<0.001), and response (halving of symptom scores) occurred in 48% versus 36% — a number needed to treat of about 8. Placebo itself did a great deal in both records. Nothing shows benefit beyond three cycles, in milder PMS, or against other contraceptive pills. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for women with PMDD who also want contraception, drospirenone pills offer a real but modest edge over placebo, with a clear adverse-effect price.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Ma 2023): symptoms SMD -0.41 (95% CI -0.59 to -0.24) versus placebo, but withdrawal for adverse effects OR 3.41 and any adverse effect OR 2.31 — evidence rated low quality
cards.summary: Cochrane (Ma 2023): symptoms SMD -0.41 (95% CI -0.59 to -0.24) versus placebo, but withdrawal for adverse effects OR 3.41 and any adverse effect OR 2.31 — evidence rated low quality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Ma 2023)
cards.people: Five randomised trials, 858 women analysed, most diagnosed with premenstrual dysphoric disorder, comparing drospirenone-containing combined oral contraceptives with placebo (no trials against other contraceptives were found); treatment over three cycles in the placebo comparisons.
cards.result: Overall premenstrual symptoms: standardised mean difference -0.41 (95% CI -0.59 to -0.24; 2 trials, 514 women; I2=64%; low-quality evidence) favouring drospirenone. Functional impairment improved slightly (productivity mean difference -0.31, social activities -0.29, relationships -0.30). Response rate: odds ratio 1.65 (95% CI 1.13 to 2.40; 1 trial, 449 women) — from an assumed 36% on placebo to 39-58%. Withdrawal due to adverse effects: odds ratio 3.41 (95% CI 2.01 to 5.78; 4 trials, 776 women); any adverse effect: odds ratio 2.31 (95% CI 1.71 to 3.11), an assumed placebo risk of 28% becoming 40-54%. No venous thromboembolism was reported in any included study; effects on mood measured by non-PMS-specific tools were uncertain.
cards.watchOut: Cochrane graded the evidence very low to moderate quality — poor reporting, inconsistency (I2=64% on the headline outcome) and imprecision — and every trial was short (three cycles) in mostly severe PMDD, so milder PMS and longer use are extrapolations. The trials were too small to see the rare thrombotic harms that dominate drospirenone's safety debate elsewhere.
cards.source: Ma S et al. Oral contraceptives containing drospirenone for premenstrual syndrome. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2023. PMID: 37365881. cards.headline: Yonkers 2005: symptom score fell -37.49 on drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol versus -29.99 on placebo (difference -7.5; p<0.001); response 48% versus 36% (NNT about 8)
cards.summary: Yonkers 2005: symptom score fell -37.49 on drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol versus -29.99 on placebo (difference -7.5; p<0.001); response 48% versus 36% (NNT about 8)
cards.people: 450 women with premenstrual dysphoric disorder at multiple centres, randomised after two run-in cycles to drospirenone 3 mg plus ethinyl estradiol 20 micrograms in a 24/4 regimen or placebo for three treatment cycles, with daily symptom charting (Daily Record of Severity of Problems).
cards.result: Total symptom score reduction: -37.49 on drospirenone versus -29.99 on placebo (adjusted mean difference -7.5, 95% CI -11.2 to -3.8; p<0.001). Mood (-19.2 versus -15.3; difference -3.9, p=0.003), physical (-10.7 versus -8.6; difference -2.1, p<0.001) and behavioural (-7.7 versus -6.2; difference -1.5, p<0.001) subscores all favoured the active pill. Response (50% symptom-score reduction): 48% versus 36% (relative risk 1.7, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.6; p=0.015), number needed to treat 8.
cards.watchOut: The placebo response is the story inside the story — scores fell 30 points on dummy pills, so the drug's added value is the 7.5-point gap, meaningful but modest. Three cycles, industry-era trial, and no comparison with the other treatments women actually choose between (SSRIs, other pills).

shelves.title: Anti-androgens for PCOS: better than metformin for hirsutism in pooled trials, but not better than placebo — the 2023 guideline review says pills first, anti-androgens when pills can't be used
shelves.question: In polycystic ovary syndrome, do anti-androgens such as spironolactone improve hirsutism and other hyperandrogenic symptoms?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the comparator, and against placebo the case is not made. The systematic review prepared for the 2023 International PCOS Guideline (Alesi S et al., PMID: 37583655; 20 unique studies, 13 meta-analysed with 961 women, testing spironolactone, finasteride, flutamide and bicalutamide) found anti-androgens plus lifestyle beat metformin plus lifestyle for hirsutism (weighted mean difference -1.59, 95% CI -3.06 to -0.12; p=0.03) but were NOT superior to placebo plus lifestyle for hirsutism (-0.93, -3.37 to 1.51; p=0.45) or SHBG; daily dosing beat every-third-day dosing for hirsutism (-3.48, -4.58 to -2.39), and adding an anti-androgen to a combined oral contraceptive worsened lipid profiles without improving other outcomes. The reviewers' conclusion: evidence does not support anti-androgens in preference to contraceptive pills; they are an option for hirsutism when pills are contraindicated, poorly tolerated, or insufficient after six months. In the one head-to-head trial carded here (Alpañés M et al., PMID: 28912358; 46 women), a contraceptive pill plus spironolactone 100 mg beat metformin over one year on hirsutism (mean difference 4.6 points, 95% CI 2.6 to 6.7) and androgen levels, with similar cardiometabolic safety. PROPOSED SPLIT: anti-androgens outperform metformin-based care for hirsutism; superiority over placebo is unproven in this record, and they sit behind contraceptive pills in the guideline the review was written for.

cards.headline: Alesi 2023 (guideline review): hirsutism WMD -1.59 versus metformin + lifestyle (p=0.03) but -0.93 versus placebo + lifestyle (p=0.45, not significant) — 20 studies, seven at high risk of bias
cards.summary: Alesi 2023 (guideline review): hirsutism WMD -1.59 versus metformin + lifestyle (p=0.03) but -0.93 versus placebo + lifestyle (p=0.45, not significant) — 20 studies, seven at high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Alesi 2023)
cards.people: 20 unique randomised studies of oral anti-androgens (spironolactone, finasteride, flutamide, bicalutamide), alone or combined with metformin, contraceptive pills or lifestyle, in women with PCOS by Rotterdam, NIH or AE-PCOS criteria; 13 studies (961 women) pooled. Seven studies were at high risk of bias, nine moderate, four low. Studies under 6 months were excluded.
cards.result: Anti-androgens + lifestyle versus metformin + lifestyle: hirsutism weighted mean difference -1.59 (95% CI -3.06 to -0.12; p=0.03; I2=74%), with better SHBG, fasting insulin and insulin:glucose ratio. Versus placebo + lifestyle: hirsutism -0.93 (-3.37 to 1.51; p=0.45; I2=76%) and SHBG 9.72 nmol/L (-0.71 to 20.14; p=0.07) — neither significant. Daily anti-androgen dosing beat every-third-day dosing for hirsutism (-3.48, -4.58 to -2.39; p<0.0001). Anti-androgen + metformin + lifestyle lowered testosterone versus metformin + lifestyle (-0.29 nmol/L, -0.52 to -0.06) without a hirsutism difference. Adding anti-androgens to a contraceptive pill worsened lipid profiles with no other outcome gains (2 trials). The authors conclude anti-androgens should not be preferred over contraceptive pills and may be considered for hirsutism when pills are contraindicated, poorly tolerated or insufficient after at least 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is high (I2 up to 76%), a third of studies are at high risk of bias, and the placebo comparison — the one that isolates the drug's own effect — is the null one. Hirsutism scores are slow-moving and assessor-sensitive; six-month minimum study length helps but does not fix blinding weaknesses in much of this literature.
cards.source: Alesi S et al. Efficacy and safety of anti-androgens in the management of polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. EClinicalMedicine. 2023. PMID: 37583655. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Alpañés 2017: contraceptive pill + spironolactone beat metformin over 1 year — hirsutism difference 4.6 points (95% CI 2.6 to 6.7), menstrual dysfunction far less frequent (OR 0.06)
cards.summary: Alpañés 2017: contraceptive pill + spironolactone beat metformin over 1 year — hirsutism difference 4.6 points (95% CI 2.6 to 6.7), menstrual dysfunction far less frequent (OR 0.06)
cards.people: 46 women with PCOS randomised to a combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 micrograms + desogestrel 150 micrograms) plus spironolactone 100 mg daily (n=24) or metformin 850 mg twice daily (n=22) for one year, with full hormonal and metabolic assessment every 3 months, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Compared with metformin, pill + spironolactone produced larger decreases in hirsutism score (mean difference 4.6 points, 95% CI 2.6 to 6.7), total testosterone (1.1 nmol/L, 0.4 to 1.7), free testosterone (25 pmol/L, 12 to 39), androstenedione (5.5 nmol/L, 1.8 to 9.2) and DHEAS (2.7 micromol/L, 1.4 to 4.0). Menstrual dysfunction was less frequent on the combination (odds ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.23). No differences in abnormal glucose tolerance, dyslipidaemia or hypertension frequencies; no major adverse events; biochemical safety markers similar.
cards.watchOut: The winning arm contains a contraceptive pill — itself a first-line anti-androgenic treatment — so this trial cannot separate spironolactone's contribution from the pill's; it compares treatment packages, open-label, in 46 women. It supports 'pill-based anti-androgen therapy beats metformin for symptoms', not 'spironolactone alone works'.
cards.source: Alpañés M et al. Combined oral contraceptives plus spironolactone compared with metformin in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a one-year randomized clinical trial. European journal of endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28912358. Registry ID: EudraCT2008-004531-38. cards.headline: Synthesis: beats metformin, ties placebo, sits behind the pill — anti-androgens are PCOS's second-line symptom treatment on this record
cards.summary: Synthesis: beats metformin, ties placebo, sits behind the pill — anti-androgens are PCOS's second-line symptom treatment on this record
cards.people: The 2023 International Guideline systematic review (20 studies; 13 pooled, 961 women) and one 46-woman head-to-head randomised trial of pill + spironolactone versus metformin over one year.
cards.result: Hirsutism: anti-androgens + lifestyle versus metformin + lifestyle WMD -1.59 (significant); versus placebo + lifestyle -0.93 (not significant). Pill + spironolactone versus metformin: hirsutism difference 4.6 points favouring the combination. Guideline position from the review itself: contraceptive pills first; anti-androgens for hirsutism when pills are contraindicated, poorly tolerated or insufficient after 6 months. PROPOSED SPLIT by comparator, Tier C: the pivotal placebo comparison is null and the evidence base is bias-prone.
cards.watchOut: Anti-androgens in PCOS are used with contraception because of fetal anti-androgen effects — a prescribing condition, not an outcome in these records. Acne, alopecia and metabolic outcomes were secondary and thinner than the hirsutism data throughout.
cards.source: Synthesis of Alesi S et al. EClinicalMedicine. 2023 (PMID: 37583655); Alpañés M et al. European journal of endocrinology. 2017 (PMID: 28912358).

shelves.title: Levonorgestrel coil versus dienogest for adenomyosis: pain fell equally in the randomised trial — the coil controlled bleeding better (90% versus 77% lighter), dienogest scored better on quality of life; a meta-analysis leans the other way on pain
shelves.question: In adenomyosis, how do the levonorgestrel intrauterine system and dienogest compare for pain and bleeding?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — each treatment wins a different outcome, and the two records do not fully agree. In the randomised trial (Choudhury S et al., PMID: 38283750; 68 women analysed, 12 weeks), pain scores fell significantly in both groups — visual analogue scale 6.41 to 3.41 on the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) and 6.41 to 3.12 on dienogest — with no significant between-group difference; lighter menstrual bleeding was commoner on LNG-IUS (27/30, 90%, versus 17/22, 77.2%; p=0.006), while quality-of-life improvement was larger on dienogest (48.26 versus 28.76 points on the WHOQOL-BREF change; p=0.04), and neither drug caused major adverse reactions. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Akhigbe RE et al., PMID: 39032312; 6 studies, 707 women, all from Asia) leaned toward dienogest for pelvic pain (lower visual analogue scores) and uterine-volume reduction, while LNG-IUS patients had higher haemoglobin — consistent with better bleeding control — and side-effect rates (weight gain, breast tenderness, headache, insomnia, mood and skin effects) were comparable. PROPOSED SPLIT: for bleeding-dominant adenomyosis the coil has the edge; for pain-dominant disease dienogest may have it; overall the two are close substitutes, and the evidence is one small short trial plus a six-study synthesis.

cards.headline: Choudhury 2024 (RCT): pain VAS 6.41 to 3.41 (LNG-IUS) versus 6.41 to 3.12 (dienogest) at 12 weeks, no significant difference — lighter bleeding 90% versus 77.2% (p=0.006); quality-of-life gain larger on dienogest (p=0.04)
cards.summary: Choudhury 2024 (RCT): pain VAS 6.41 to 3.41 (LNG-IUS) versus 6.41 to 3.12 (dienogest) at 12 weeks, no significant difference — lighter bleeding 90% versus 77.2% (p=0.006); quality-of-life gain larger on dienogest (p=0.04)
cards.people: Women over 20 with adenomyosis-associated pain, with or without abnormal uterine bleeding, at a single Indian centre: 74 recruited, 68 analysed (34 per group reported in the trial summary; bleeding outcome reported for 30 LNG-IUS and 22 dienogest patients), randomised to levonorgestrel intrauterine system or oral dienogest for 12 weeks. Primary outcome: pain on visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Pain fell significantly within both groups (LNG-IUS 6.41 ± 1.07 to 3.41 ± 1.04; dienogest 6.41 ± 0.95 to 3.12 ± 1.40; both p<0.001 within group) with no significant difference between groups. Lighter menstrual blood loss: 27/30 (90%) on LNG-IUS versus 17/22 (77.2%) on dienogest (p=0.006). Quality-of-life (WHOQOL-BREF) improvement was more pronounced on dienogest (change 48.26 ± 44.91 versus 28.76 ± 30.47; p=0.04). No major adverse drug reactions in either group; hot flushes were reported on dienogest.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, open-label, single centre, and small — with outcome denominators (30 and 22 for bleeding) smaller than the randomised groups, suggesting dropout or missing data the abstract does not explain. Pain was self-reported by women who knew whether they had a coil or a tablet, which can move a visual analogue score.

cards.headline: Akhigbe 2024 (meta-analysis, 6 studies, 707 women): dienogest better for pelvic pain and uterine volume; LNG-IUS better for haemoglobin; side effects comparable
cards.summary: Akhigbe 2024 (meta-analysis, 6 studies, 707 women): dienogest better for pelvic pain and uterine volume; LNG-IUS better for haemoglobin; side effects comparable
cards.people: Six clinical studies, 707 women with adenomyosis (270 LNG-IUS, 354 dienogest, 83 controls), all conducted in Asia (Bangladesh, China x2, India, Japan, South Korea), comparing levonorgestrel intrauterine system with dienogest on pain, uterine volume, haemoglobin and side effects.
cards.result: Dienogest reduced pelvic pain significantly more than LNG-IUS (lower visual analogue scale scores) and reduced uterine volume significantly more. LNG-IUS patients had significantly higher haemoglobin levels than dienogest patients. Side effects — weight gain, breast tenderness/distension, headache, insomnia/sleep disorder, depression/mood disorder, skin disorder/acne, coital discomfort/reduced libido — were comparable between treatments. The authors call for well-designed randomised trials, noting only six eligible studies exist.
cards.watchOut: The six studies mix designs and are all Asian single-region data; the meta-analysis's pain conclusion (dienogest ahead) is stronger than the one randomised head-to-head trial's (no difference), which usually means the non-randomised studies are doing the pushing. Effect sizes are reported as significance, not absolute score differences, in the abstract.
cards.source: Akhigbe RE et al. Comparison of the effectiveness of levonorgestrel intrauterine system and dienogest in the management of adenomyosis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology. 2024. PMID: 39032312. cards.headline: Synthesis: a genuine toss-up decided by the dominant symptom — bleeding favours the coil, pain may favour dienogest, and neither record is strong
cards.summary: Synthesis: a genuine toss-up decided by the dominant symptom — bleeding favours the coil, pain may favour dienogest, and neither record is strong
cards.people: One open-label randomised trial (68 women, 12 weeks) and one systematic review/meta-analysis (6 studies, 707 women) directly comparing LNG-IUS with dienogest in adenomyosis.
cards.result: Pain: no significant difference in the RCT (VAS to 3.41 versus 3.12); dienogest ahead in the meta-analysis. Bleeding/haemoglobin: LNG-IUS ahead in both records (90% versus 77.2% lighter bleeding; higher haemoglobin). Quality of life: dienogest ahead in the RCT. Side effects: comparable; no major reactions. PROPOSED SPLIT by outcome, Tier C: the randomised base is one small short open-label trial.
cards.watchOut: Neither treatment is approved specifically for adenomyosis in the trial's own framing, follow-up everywhere is short, and fertility outcomes — a central concern in this condition — are absent from both records. A larger blinded-outcome trial could reorder the pain result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Choudhury S et al. Therapeutic advances in reproductive health. 2024 (PMID: 38283750); Akhigbe RE et al. European journal of obstetrics, gynecology, and reproductive biology. 2024 (PMID: 39032312).

shelves.title: Timing is the treatment: oestradiol started within 6 years of menopause slowed carotid thickening (0.0044 versus 0.0078 mm/year) in ELITE — started 10+ years out, it did nothing (0.0100 versus 0.0088)
shelves.question: Does starting oestradiol soon after menopause slow atherosclerosis progression compared with starting it late?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Administration, Oral · Atherosclerosis/prevention & control · Carotid Arteries/drug effects/pathology · Carotid Intima-Media Thickness · Coronary Artery Disease/prevention & control · Disease Progression · Drug Administration Schedule · Estradiol/administration & dosage · Estrogen Replacement Therapy · Female · Humans · Linear Models · Middle Aged · Postmenopause/drug effects · Progesterone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for early starters only, on a surrogate endpoint, in the single trial designed to test the timing hypothesis. ELITE (Hodis HN et al., PMID: 27028912) randomised 643 healthy postmenopausal women, stratified by time since menopause, to oral 17beta-estradiol 1 mg daily (plus sequential vaginal progesterone gel for women with a uterus) or placebo, with carotid intima-media thickness (CIMT) measured every 6 months over a median of 5 years. The treatment effect differed significantly by stratum (p=0.007 for interaction): in women under 6 years from menopause, CIMT progressed at 0.0044 mm/year on estradiol versus 0.0078 mm/year on placebo (p=0.008) — about a 44% relative slowing, with the absolute rates alongside; in women 10 or more years out, progression was 0.0100 on estradiol versus 0.0088 on placebo (p=0.29) — nothing. Cardiac CT measures (coronary calcium, stenosis, plaque) did not differ significantly in either stratum, and clinical cardiovascular events were not the endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): ELITE supports the timing hypothesis on arterial imaging — oestradiol slows subclinical atherosclerosis when begun early and not when begun late — but it is one trial, the endpoint is a surrogate, and the coronary CT half of its own record is null.

cards.headline: ELITE (Hodis 2016): CIMT progression 0.0044 versus 0.0078 mm/year (p=0.008) in early postmenopause; 0.0100 versus 0.0088 (p=0.29) in late postmenopause — interaction p=0.007
cards.summary: ELITE (Hodis 2016): CIMT progression 0.0044 versus 0.0078 mm/year (p=0.008) in early postmenopause; 0.0100 versus 0.0088 (p=0.29) in late postmenopause — interaction p=0.007
cards.people: 643 healthy postmenopausal women, stratified as early (<6 years since menopause) or late (≥10 years), randomised to oral 17beta-estradiol 1 mg/day or placebo, with sequential vaginal progesterone gel 45 mg (or placebo gel) for women with a uterus; CIMT every 6 months, median follow-up 5 years; coronary atherosclerosis by cardiac CT at completion.
cards.result: The estradiol effect on CIMT progression differed by timing stratum (p=0.007 for interaction). Early stratum: mean CIMT increase 0.0044 mm/year on estradiol versus 0.0078 mm/year on placebo (p=0.008) — about a 44% relative slowing, with the absolute rates alongside. Late stratum: 0.0100 versus 0.0088 mm/year (p=0.29). Cardiac CT measures of coronary artery calcium, total stenosis and plaque did not differ significantly between estradiol and placebo in either stratum.
cards.watchOut: CIMT is a surrogate whose treatment-induced changes track clinical events imperfectly — and ELITE's own coronary CT endpoints, closer to the disease that matters, were null in both strata. Participants were healthy volunteers; women 6-10 years from menopause were not studied at all, so 'early' and 'late' have an untested gap between them. One trial carries the entire timing hypothesis here.
cards.source: Hodis HN et al. Vascular Effects of Early versus Late Postmenopausal Treatment with Estradiol. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 27028912. Registry ID: NCT00114517. Coronary CT calcium, stenosis and plaque: no significant differences in either stratum. Clinical events: not assessed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for early initiation on the surrogate, Tier C: single trial, surrogate endpoint, and a cardiovascular-benefit claim of exactly the kind reserved for personal review.
cards.watchOut: This shelf must not be read as 'hormone therapy prevents heart disease when started early' — no event data exist in this record, the Women's Health Initiative's event data are a different shelf's record, and estradiol's thrombotic and breast effects sit outside ELITE's imaging endpoints entirely.

shelves.title: Sertraline after delivery cut postpartum depression recurrence from 50% to 7% — in a pilot trial of just 22 women, the only sertraline prevention trial Cochrane could find
shelves.question: In women with a previous postpartum depression, does sertraline started immediately after delivery prevent recurrence versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Depression, Postpartum/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Dizziness/chemically induced · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pilot Projects · Placebos · Pregnancy · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Secondary Prevention · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Sertraline/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a dramatic percentage gap on a handful of patients. The pilot trial (Wisner KL et al., PMID: 15229064) randomised non-depressed women with at least one previous episode of postpartum major depression to sertraline or placebo immediately after birth for 17 weeks: recurrence occurred in 1 of 14 women on sertraline (7%) versus 4 of 8 on placebo (50%), a significant difference, with time to recurrence also significantly longer on sertraline. The Cochrane review (Molyneaux E et al., PMID: 29669175) found only two eligible prevention trials in total (81 women, both from the same research group): the sertraline trial, expressed as risk ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.07) — very low quality evidence, its confidence interval just crossing 1 — and a nortriptyline trial that found nothing (postnatal depression in 23% on nortriptyline versus 24% on placebo; risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.36 to 2.59). One woman on sertraline had a hypomanic episode; dizziness and drowsiness were commoner on sertraline. No new eligible trial has appeared in over a decade. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): sertraline prophylaxis may prevent recurrence in women with previous postpartum depression — the signal is large, the denominator is 22 women, and the honest grade is weak evidence.

cards.headline: Wisner 2004 (pilot): recurrence 1/14 (7%) on sertraline versus 4/8 (50%) on placebo over 17 weeks — significant, on 22 women
cards.summary: Wisner 2004 (pilot): recurrence 1/14 (7%) on sertraline versus 4/8 (50%) on placebo over 17 weeks — significant, on 22 women
cards.people: 22 non-depressed pregnant women with at least one past episode of postpartum major depression, randomised to sertraline (n=14) or placebo (n=8) started immediately after birth for 17 weeks, assessed for 20 weeks with the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression.
cards.result: Recurrence of postpartum major depression: 1 of 14 (7%) on sertraline versus 4 of 8 (50%) on placebo — reported as a significant difference, an absolute gap of 43 percentage points on very small numbers. Time to recurrence was significantly longer in sertraline-treated women. Dizziness was among the adverse effects attributed to sertraline in the record.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial with 22 participants and five total events: moving a single recurrence between arms would erase the headline. The placebo group's 50% recurrence confirms the population was genuinely high-risk, but effect sizes from pilots this small almost always shrink — and here, no larger trial has ever tested whether this one does.
cards.source: Wisner KL et al. Prevention of postpartum depression: a pilot randomized clinical trial. The American journal of psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 15229064. cards.headline: Cochrane (Molyneaux 2018): two trials, 81 women, very low quality — sertraline RR 0.14 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.07); nortriptyline RR 0.96 (0.36 to 2.59); no new trials in over a decade
cards.summary: Cochrane (Molyneaux 2018): two trials, 81 women, very low quality — sertraline RR 0.14 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.07); nortriptyline RR 0.96 (0.36 to 2.59); no new trials in over a decade
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Molyneaux 2018)
cards.people: Two randomised trials, 81 participants total, both by the same research group, in women with a history of postnatal depression who were not currently depressed and not taking antidepressants at baseline: sertraline versus placebo, and nortriptyline versus placebo, each over the first 17 weeks postpartum.
cards.result: Sertraline: postnatal depression in 7% (1/14) versus 50% (4/8) on placebo — risk ratio 0.14 (95% CI 0.02 to 1.07), graded very low quality evidence; one woman on sertraline had a hypomanic episode, and dizziness and drowsiness were commoner on sertraline. Nortriptyline: 23% (6/26) versus 24% (6/25) on placebo — risk ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.36 to 2.59), very low quality; one woman on nortriptyline developed mania and constipation was commoner. No data were available on child development, breastfeeding, mother-infant relationship or maternal functioning. The reviewers conclude clear conclusions are not possible and note no new eligible trials in over a decade.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from one research group, so the entire world evidence on antidepressant prevention of postnatal depression is two small same-group studies. The sertraline confidence interval (0.02 to 1.07) formally includes no effect — the shelf's MAYBE (weak evidence) grade is the review's own uncertainty, carried honestly.
cards.source: Molyneaux E et al. Antidepressants for preventing postnatal depression. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 29669175. cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (molyneaux 2018) two randomised trials, 81 participants total, both by the same research group, in women with a history of postnatal depression who were not currently depressed and not taking antidepressants at baseline: sertraline versus placebo, and nortriptyline versus placebo, each over the first 17 weeks postpartum. sertraline: postnatal depression in 7% (1/14) versus 50% (4/8) on placebo — risk ratio 0.14 (95% ci 0.02 to 1.07), graded very low quality evidence; one woman on sertraline had a hypomanic episode, and dizziness and drowsiness were commoner on sertraline. nortriptyline: 23% (6/26) versus 24% (6/25) on placebo — risk ratio 0.96 (95% ci 0.36 to 2.59), very low quality; one woman on nortriptyline developed mania and constipation was commoner. no data were available on child development, breastfeeding, mother-infant relationship or maternal functioning. the reviewers conclude clear conclusions are not possible and note no new eligible trials in over a decade. both trials come from one research group, so the entire world evidence on antidepressant prevention of postnatal depression is two small same-group studies. the sertraline confidence interval (0.02 to 1.07) formally includes no effect — the shelf's maybe (weak evidence) grade is the review's own uncertainty, carried honestly. molyneaux e et al. antidepressants for preventing postnatal depression. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. pmid: 29669175. mesh: antidepressive agents/therapeutic use · depression, postpartum/prevention & control · female · humans · nortriptyline/therapeutic use · placebos/therapeutic use · randomized controlled trials as topic · sertraline/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Synthesis: the largest relative effect on this shelf rests on the smallest numbers — a promising pilot that two decades of literature never followed up
cards.summary: Synthesis: the largest relative effect on this shelf rests on the smallest numbers — a promising pilot that two decades of literature never followed up
cards.people: One pilot randomised trial of sertraline (22 women) and one of nortriptyline (51 women), both in women with previous postnatal depression, summarised by the 2018 Cochrane review (81 women total).
cards.result: Sertraline recurrence 7% versus 50% on placebo (RR 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.07). Nortriptyline 23% versus 24% (RR 0.96). Adverse effects: hypomania (one case, sertraline), mania (one case, nortriptyline), more dizziness/drowsiness and constipation respectively. No infant or breastfeeding outcome data. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for sertraline specifically, Tier C: single tiny trial.
cards.watchOut: Prevention here means women with a previous postpartum depression — the record says nothing about first-episode prevention in the general obstetric population, where baseline risk and the benefit-harm balance would be entirely different.

shelves.title: HPV vaccination after excision treatment was followed by far fewer CIN2+ recurrences — pooled risk ratio 0.43 in the BMJ meta-analysis — but almost all the evidence is observational, and the least-biased studies show less
shelves.question: Does HPV vaccination after surgical treatment (conisation) for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia reduce recurrence of HPV-related disease?
shelves.mesh: Alphapapillomavirus · Female · Human papillomavirus 16 · Humans · Papillomaviridae · Papillomavirus Infections/complications · Papillomavirus Vaccines/therapeutic use · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms/prevention & control/surgery · Vaccination · Uterine Cervical Dysplasia/pathology/prevention & control/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large association (risk ratio 0.43, below the 0.5 threshold this library asks of observational evidence) that shrinks as study quality rises, which is exactly why it is Tier C. The BMJ meta-analysis (Kechagias KS et al., PMID: 35922074; 18 studies in the meta-analyses, mostly observational) found recurrent CIN2+ risk ratio 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated women after local surgical treatment — a 57% relative reduction — and 0.26 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.43) for recurrence related to HPV16/18, over a median 36 months; evidence for CIN3, other HPV-related lesions and persistent infection was lacking or very uncertain, and GRADE confidence ranged from very low to moderate. The second meta-analysis (Eriksen DO et al., PMID: 35470865; 9 studies, 19,971 women) found the same direction with a warning label: pooling only the two randomised trials gave odds ratio 0.29 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.53) and unadjusted observational data 0.35 (0.18 to 0.67), but adjusted observational estimates were 0.54 (0.21 to 1.35) — not significant — and most studies carried serious risk of bias. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): post-treatment HPV vaccination is associated with substantially fewer CIN2+ recurrences, plausibly causally given the randomised-trial pooling, but the definitive large placebo-controlled trial does not yet exist and vaccinated women differ from unvaccinated women in ways adjustment only partly removes.

cards.headline: Kechagias 2022 (BMJ): CIN2+ recurrence RR 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated; HPV16/18-related recurrence RR 0.26 (0.16 to 0.43); GRADE very low to moderate
cards.summary: Kechagias 2022 (BMJ): CIN2+ recurrence RR 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated; HPV16/18-related recurrence RR 0.26 (0.16 to 0.43); GRADE very low to moderate
cards.people: 22 studies met inclusion (18 in meta-analyses: 12 observational, 2 randomised trials, 4 post hoc analyses of randomised trials) of HPV vaccination in individuals undergoing local surgical treatment for preinvasive genital disease; the CIN2+ analysis covered 11 studies and 19,909 participants, median follow-up 36 months.
cards.result: Recurrence of CIN2+ after local surgical treatment: risk ratio 0.43 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.60; I2=58%) in vaccinated versus unvaccinated individuals — a 57% relative reduction. For CIN2+ related to HPV16 or HPV18: risk ratio 0.26 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.43; 6 studies, 1,879 participants; I2=0%). CIN3 recurrence: risk ratio 0.28 but with a very wide interval (0.01 to 6.37). Evidence was lacking for vulvar, vaginal and anal intraepithelial neoplasia, genital warts, and persistent/incident HPV infection. GRADE confidence for the CIN2+ outcomes ranged from very low to moderate, limited by publication bias and inconsistency.
cards.watchOut: Most of the weight is observational: women who get vaccinated after treatment differ systematically (age, follow-up intensity, health behaviour) from those who do not, and vaccination timing relative to surgery varied across studies. A relative risk of 0.43 clears this library's observational floor, but confounding inflates vaccine associations in exactly this direction.
cards.source: Kechagias KS et al. Role of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination on HPV infection and recurrence of HPV related disease after local surgical treatment: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2022. PMID: 35922074. cards.headline: Eriksen 2022: randomised trials pooled OR 0.29 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.53), unadjusted observational OR 0.35 — but adjusted observational OR 0.54 (0.21 to 1.35), not significant; most studies at serious risk of bias
cards.summary: Eriksen 2022: randomised trials pooled OR 0.29 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.53), unadjusted observational OR 0.35 — but adjusted observational OR 0.54 (0.21 to 1.35), not significant; most studies at serious risk of bias
cards.people: Nine studies, 19,971 women who received prophylactic HPV vaccine after excisional treatment for histologically verified cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (2 randomised trials, 7 observational), with recurrence of CIN2+ as the primary outcome.
cards.result: Fixed-effect pooling of the two randomised trials: odds ratio 0.29 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.53) for CIN2+ recurrence. Observational studies, unadjusted (random-effects): odds ratio 0.35 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.67). Observational studies, adjusted estimates: odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.21 to 1.35) — not significant. Quality assessment found serious risk of bias in the majority of included studies. The authors conclude large, well-designed randomised placebo-controlled trials are needed before recommending post-treatment vaccination to all women.
cards.watchOut: The two 'randomised trials' in this pooling are few and small relative to the observational mass, and post hoc vaccination analyses within trials are not the same as trials randomised on post-treatment vaccination. The gap between unadjusted (0.35) and adjusted (0.54) observational estimates is the confounding problem made visible.
cards.source: Eriksen DO et al. cards.people: Two 2022 systematic reviews/meta-analyses (18 and 9 studies; about 19,900-20,000 women each, substantially overlapping study sets) of HPV vaccination after excisional treatment for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.
cards.result: CIN2+ recurrence: RR 0.43 (0.30 to 0.60) overall (Kechagias); OR 0.29 (0.16 to 0.53) in randomised trials and 0.35 unadjusted / 0.54 adjusted (non-significant) in observational data (Eriksen). HPV16/18-related recurrence: RR 0.26 (0.16 to 0.43). CIN3 and non-cervical outcomes: uncertain or lacking. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the shelf rests substantially on observational evidence.
cards.watchOut: Absolute recurrence risk after excision is modest, so even a true halving is a small absolute gain for most women — neither record gives a trustworthy absolute number to weigh against cost and the (excellent) safety record of the vaccine. Timing (before versus after surgery) and margin status may modify the effect and are unresolved here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kechagias KS et al. BMJ. 2022 (PMID: 35922074); Eriksen DO et al. Acta obstetricia et gynecologica Scandinavica. 2022 (PMID: 35470865).

shelves.title: Tamoxifen relieves mastalgia in pooled randomised trials — response risk ratio 2.04 versus placebo in the 2022 meta-analysis, 1.92 in the earlier one — with 10 mg doing what 20 mg does
shelves.question: In women with cyclical mastalgia, does tamoxifen reduce breast pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Mastodynia/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tamoxifen/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a doubled chance of pain relief versus placebo in the pooled randomised trials, in a condition with a large placebo response. The 2022 meta-analysis (Sinha MK et al., PMID: 35752405; 9 randomised trials) found oral tamoxifen beat placebo for mastalgia relief with risk ratio 2.04 (95% CI 1.49 to 2.78; p<0.001), and no significant efficacy difference between the 10 mg and 20 mg doses over 3 months (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21; p=0.18) — supporting 10 mg as the dose, typically for 3-6 months in long-standing mastalgia. An earlier meta-analysis of mastalgia treatments reached the same conclusion for tamoxifen; that record is carded at home on the danazol shelf (#3776) and is not re-carded here. Neither record is specific to strictly cyclical mastalgia — the trials enrolled mastalgia broadly — and tamoxifen's serious-harm profile (thromboembolism, endometrial effects) comes from its oncology literature, not these small pain trials, so the benefit shown here is for severe, persistent pain where that trade-off has been weighed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): tamoxifen, usually 10 mg for a few months, roughly doubles the chance of pain relief over placebo in persistent mastalgia.

cards.headline: Sinha 2022: oral tamoxifen versus placebo RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.49 to 2.78; p<0.001) for mastalgia relief across 9 RCTs; 10 mg versus 20 mg RR 1.08 (p=0.18) — no dose advantage
cards.summary: Sinha 2022: oral tamoxifen versus placebo RR 2.04 (95% CI 1.49 to 2.78; p<0.001) for mastalgia relief across 9 RCTs; 10 mg versus 20 mg RR 1.08 (p=0.18) — no dose advantage
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sinha 2022)
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials of tamoxifen (oral 10 or 20 mg daily, typically 3-6 months; a topical preparation was also noted as recently approved) in women with mastalgia, pooled for pain-relief response, dose comparison, side effects and follow-up.
cards.result: Oral tamoxifen performed better than placebo: risk ratio for relief 2.04 (95% CI 1.49 to 2.78; p<0.001). Comparing doses over 3 months, 10 mg versus 20 mg showed no significant efficacy difference (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21; p=0.18). The authors conclude oral tamoxifen is helpful in long-standing mastalgia and is safe and effective at an oral dose of 10 mg.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports response ratios without the underlying absolute response rates, and mastalgia trials are small with substantial placebo responses — a doubled relative chance of relief can still mean a modest absolute gain. 'Safe' here means within small short trials; tamoxifen's rare serious harms are not measurable at this sample size.

cards.watchOut: The candidate question specifies cyclical mastalgia; the underlying trials enrolled mastalgia broadly (cyclical and non-cyclical), so the stamp inherits that imprecision. Tamoxifen for breast pain is off-label, and its serious-harm counselling comes from outside these records — the shelf grades pain relief, not the whole prescribing decision.

shelves.title: Danazol eases breast pain more than placebo — a mean pain-score gain of about 20 points in pooled trials — but its androgenic side effects are why it is not first choice
shelves.question: In women with mastalgia, does danazol reduce breast pain versus placebo — and at what cost in side effects?
shelves.mesh: Breast Diseases/drug therapy · Bromocriptine/therapeutic use · Danazol/therapeutic use · Estrogen Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Phytotherapy · Plant Oils/therapeutic use · Primula · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators/therapeutic use · Tamoxifen/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — danazol relieves mastalgia pain versus placebo, at a real side-effect price. The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Srivastava A et al., PMID: 17509880) found a weighted mean pain-score difference of -20.23 (95% CI -28.12 to -12.34) in danazol's favour, and the small double-blind crossover trial behind it (Mansel RE et al., PMID: 6122770) found a significant, progressive fall in pain and nodularity on danazol, faster at 400 mg/day than 200 mg/day but with greater side effects at the higher dose. The same meta-analysis judged tamoxifen — not danazol — the drug of first choice because it carried the fewest side effects, so danazol's place is for severe, hormone-related breast pain when gentler options fail. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pain relief is consistent across the pooled trials, but the evidence is old and small, and tolerability limits use.

cards.headline: Srivastava 2007 meta-analysis: danazol beat placebo on pain score by -20.23 points (95% CI -28.12 to -12.34); tamoxifen, not danazol, was judged first choice on side effects
cards.summary: Srivastava 2007 meta-analysis: danazol beat placebo on pain score by -20.23 points (95% CI -28.12 to -12.34); tamoxifen, not danazol, was judged first choice on side effects
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials in English comparing bromocriptine, danazol, evening primrose oil or tamoxifen with placebo for mastalgia, pooled with RevMan; the danazol estimate rests on the small placebo-controlled trials of that era.
cards.result: Weighted mean difference in pain score favoured danazol by -20.23 (95% CI -28.12 to -12.34) and bromocriptine by -16.31 (95% CI -26.35 to -6.27); evening primrose oil did not beat placebo (-2.78, 95% CI -7.97 to 2.40). Tamoxifen achieved a relative risk of pain relief of 1.92 (95% CI 1.42-2.58) and was associated with the fewest side effects.
cards.watchOut: The pooled danazol trials are few and small, pain is a subjective score, and the abstract reports no pooled adverse-event rates for danazol — the side-effect judgement is the authors' comparative conclusion, not a quantified harm estimate on this record.

cards.headline: Mansel 1982: in 28 women, danazol progressively cut pain and nodularity versus placebo — quicker at 400 mg/day, but with greater side effects
cards.summary: Mansel 1982: in 28 women, danazol progressively cut pain and nodularity versus placebo — quicker at 400 mg/day, but with greater side effects
cards.people: 28 women with cyclical mastalgia and painful nodular benign breast disease, given danazol 200 mg/day and 400 mg/day and placebo in a double-blind crossover design, assessed subjectively and objectively.
cards.result: Danazol caused a significant and progressive decrease in breast pain and nodularity compared with placebo. Symptoms responded more quickly with 400 mg/day than with 200 mg/day, but the larger dose also caused greater side effects. The abstract reports no numerical pain scores or adverse-event counts.
cards.watchOut: Only 28 women, a crossover design from 1982, and p-value-only reporting in the abstract — this trial supports direction, not magnitude; the magnitude comes from the pooled analysis above.

shelves.title: Word catheter matches marsupialisation for Bartholin cyst or abscess: recurrence 12% versus 10% at one year — with less analgesia (33% versus 74%) and faster treatment (1 versus 4 hours)
shelves.question: For a Bartholin cyst or abscess, does Word catheter placement match marsupialisation on recurrence and healing?
shelves.mesh: Abscess/surgery · Adult · Bartholin's Glands/surgery · Catheterization/instrumentation/methods · Catheters · Cysts/surgery · Female · Gynecologic Surgical Procedures/methods · Humans · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on recurrence, the Word catheter and marsupialisation are a draw, and the catheter wins on the day itself. In the WoMan randomised trial (Kroese JA et al., PMID: 27640367), recurrence within one year was 12% after Word catheter versus 10% after marsupialisation (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.64-1.91; P=0.70), pain scores after treatment were comparable, but analgesics were used in the first 24 hours by 33% versus 74% (P<0.001) and time from diagnosis to treatment was 1 hour versus 4 hours (P=0.001). The systematic review of all eight randomised trials (Illingworth B et al., PMID: 31876985) likewise found the evidence consistent with effects in either direction (risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.41-1.40 for marsupialisation versus Word catheter approaches). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): recurrence is equivalent within the trial's precision; choose on setting, speed and patient preference, not on expected recurrence.

cards.headline: Kroese 2017 (WoMan): recurrence 12% Word catheter versus 10% marsupialisation (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.64-1.91) — analgesia 33% versus 74%, treatment at 1 versus 4 hours
cards.summary: Kroese 2017 (WoMan): recurrence 12% Word catheter versus 10% marsupialisation (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.64-1.91) — analgesia 33% versus 74%, treatment at 1 versus 4 hours
cards.people: 161 women with a symptomatic Bartholin gland cyst or abscess in 18 Dutch hospitals and one English hospital, randomised to Word catheter (n=82) or marsupialisation (n=79), August 2010 to May 2014, followed for recurrence within one year; open-label, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Recurrence occurred in 10 women (12%) allocated to Word catheter versus 8 women (10%) allocated to marsupialisation: relative risk 1.1 (95% CI 0.64-1.91; P=0.70). Pain scores after treatment were comparable. In the first 24 hours, 33% used analgesics in the Word catheter group versus 74% in the marsupialisation group (P<0.001). Time from diagnosis to treatment was 1 hour for Word catheter versus 4 hours for marsupialisation (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and sized to detect a 5-point recurrence difference it did not find — the confidence interval (0.64-1.91) still allows a meaningful advantage either way, so this is 'no difference shown', not proven exact equivalence.
cards.source: Kroese JA et al. Word catheter and marsupialisation in women with a cyst or abscess of the Bartholin gland (WoMan-trial): a randomised clinical trial. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2017. PMID: 27640367. cards.headline: Illingworth 2020 review of 8 trials (699 women): no surgical technique for Bartholin cyst or abscess is supported over another (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.41-1.40)
cards.summary: Illingworth 2020 review of 8 trials (699 women): no surgical technique for Bartholin cyst or abscess is supported over another (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.41-1.40)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials reporting data from 699 women with a symptomatic Bartholin cyst or abscess, comparing surgical interventions including marsupialisation, incision and drainage with Word catheter, silver nitrate insertion, and cavity closure; literature to April 2019.
cards.result: For recurrence, comparing marsupialisation with incision, drainage and Word catheter insertion gave a risk ratio of 0.76 (95% CI 0.41-1.40) — consistent with notable effects in either direction. Marsupialisation versus silver nitrate insertion gave RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.57-1.75), and versus cavity closure RR 0.25 (95% CI 0.01-4.89). Secondary outcomes such as haematoma, infection and persistent dyspareunia were sparsely reported.
cards.watchOut: The review pools differently specified procedures across small trials, so its wide intervals describe genuine uncertainty about every technique, not just the catheter-versus-marsupialisation pair.
cards.source: Illingworth B et al. Evaluation of treatments for Bartholin's cyst or abscess: a systematic review. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2020. PMID: 31876985. shelves.title: After endometriosis surgery, hormonal suppression cuts recurrence versus no treatment (RR 0.41 pooled) — and PRE-EMPT shows long-acting progestogen and the pill tie on pain at 3 years, both about 40% better than before surgery
shelves.question: After surgery for ovarian endometrioma, does postoperative hormonal suppression reduce recurrence versus no suppression?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Young Adult · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Endometriosis/surgery/drug therapy/complications · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Medroxyprogesterone Acetate/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Pain Measurement · Pelvic Pain/drug therapy/prevention & control/etiology · Progestins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Secondary Prevention/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — postoperative hormonal suppression reduces endometriosis recurrence compared with no suppression, and the choice between the two main strategies is a tie on pain. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Zakhari A et al., PMID: 33020832) pooled 17 studies (2,137 patients; 13 randomised trials and 4 cohorts) and found recurrence significantly lower with suppression than with expectant management or placebo (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65), with lower pain scores too (standardised mean difference -0.49, 95% CI -0.91 to -0.07). The PRE-EMPT trial (Cooper KG et al., PMID: 38749550) randomised 405 women after conservative surgery to a long-acting progestogen or the combined pill — notably, it had no untreated arm — and found pain at three years identical between strategies (adjusted mean difference -0.8, 95% CI -5.7 to 4.2; P=0.76), improved by around 40% in both groups, with fewer repeat surgical procedures on the long-acting progestogen (73 versus 97 events; hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.00). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): suppress after surgery if pregnancy is not sought immediately; pick the agent on preference and tolerability. Tier C is set because the versus-no-treatment pooling mixes randomised and cohort studies.

cards.headline: Cooper 2024 (PRE-EMPT): pain at 3 years identical on long-acting progestogen versus combined pill (-0.8, 95% CI -5.7 to 4.2), both about 40% improved — repeat surgery 73 versus 97 events
cards.summary: Cooper 2024 (PRE-EMPT): pain at 3 years identical on long-acting progestogen versus combined pill (-0.8, 95% CI -5.7 to 4.2), both about 40% improved — repeat surgery 73 versus 97 events
cards.people: 405 women of reproductive age undergoing conservative surgery for endometriosis in 34 UK hospitals, randomised to a long-acting progestogen (depot medroxyprogesterone acetate or levonorgestrel intrauterine system; n=205) or the combined oral contraceptive pill (n=200); primary outcome the pain domain of the EHP-30 at three years. Open-label, pragmatic. Registry ID: ISRCTN97865475.
cards.result: At three years there was no difference in pain scores between groups (adjusted mean difference -0.8, 95% CI -5.7 to 4.2; P=0.76); pain had improved by around 40% in both groups versus preoperative values (average 24 and 23 points). Women on a long-acting progestogen underwent fewer surgical procedures or second-line treatments (73 versus 97; hazard ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.00).
cards.watchOut: PRE-EMPT compares two suppression strategies — it has no no-treatment arm, so it cannot by itself answer 'suppression versus nothing'; that comparison comes from the meta-analysis card. Open-label with a patient-reported primary outcome.
cards.source: Cooper KG et al. Long acting progestogens versus combined oral contraceptive pill for preventing recurrence of endometriosis related pain: the PRE-EMPT pragmatic, parallel group, open label, randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Zakhari 2021 meta-analysis (17 studies, 2,137 patients): recurrence RR 0.41 (95% CI 0.26-0.65) with postoperative suppression versus expectant management or placebo
cards.summary: Zakhari 2021 meta-analysis (17 studies, 2,137 patients): recurrence RR 0.41 (95% CI 0.26-0.65) with postoperative suppression versus expectant management or placebo
cards.people: 17 studies (13 randomised trials, 4 prospective cohorts) of 2,137 premenopausal women after conservative endometriosis surgery (at least one ovary conserved) starting hormonal suppression within six weeks — combined hormonal contraceptives, progestins, levonorgestrel intrauterine system, or GnRH agonists — versus placebo or expectant management; follow-up 12-36 months, median outcome assessment 18 months.
cards.result: Postoperative hormonal suppression significantly decreased endometriosis recurrence versus expectant management or placebo (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.65; 14 studies, 1,766 patients; I²=68%), with consistent results in subgroups and in sensitivity analyses limited to randomised trials and high-quality studies. Pain scores were also lower with suppression (standardised mean difference -0.49, 95% CI -0.91 to -0.07; 7 studies, 652 patients).
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is substantial (I²=68%) and four of 17 studies are cohorts, not trials; agents and recurrence definitions vary, so 0.41 is an average across strategies, not a promise for any single drug. This mixing is why the shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Zakhari A et al. Endometriosis recurrence following post-operative hormonal suppression: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Human reproduction update. 2021. PMID: 33020832. cards.headline: Synthesis: suppression versus nothing favours suppression on recurrence; between agents, PRE-EMPT's two strategies tie on pain
cards.summary: Synthesis: suppression versus nothing favours suppression on recurrence; between agents, PRE-EMPT's two strategies tie on pain
cards.people: A 405-woman pragmatic trial of two suppression strategies (PRE-EMPT) plus a 17-study meta-analysis (2,137 women) of suppression versus placebo or expectant management after conservative endometriosis surgery.
cards.result: Recurrence with suppression versus none: RR 0.41 (95% CI 0.26-0.65). Pain at three years, long-acting progestogen versus pill: adjusted mean difference -0.8 (95% CI -5.7 to 4.2), both groups about 40% improved; repeat procedures 73 versus 97 (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.44-1.00). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for suppression after surgery, Tier C for the mixed-design versus-none base.
cards.watchOut: The candidate question was framed around endometrioma surgery; PRE-EMPT enrolled conservative endometriosis surgery more broadly, and the meta-analysis likewise — the endometrioma-only, suppression-versus-none randomised comparison remains untested in a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cooper KG et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2024 (PMID: 38749550); Zakhari A et al. Human reproduction update. 2021 (PMID: 33020832).

shelves.question: In surgery for endometrioma, does cystectomy reduce recurrence and pain compared with drainage and coagulation — and what does it cost ovarian reserve?

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for pain and recurrence, excision wins; for ovarian reserve, excision is the costlier operation, and both halves belong on the shelf. The Cochrane review (Kalra R et al., PMID: 39588841) pooled nine randomised trials (578 women): at up to two years, excision versus ablation may reduce dysmenorrhoea recurrence (odds ratio 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52; recurrence 49% after ablation versus 10-34% after excision) and dyspareunia recurrence (OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.22); at one year it may reduce endometrioma recurrence (OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.34; 37% after ablation versus 5-17% after excision) and further surgery (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.41), with little or no difference in spontaneous pregnancy (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.87). The reserve cost comes from the second meta-analysis (Paik H et al., PMID: 38509401): anti-Müllerian hormone fell by a weighted mean 1.08 after cystectomy versus 0.40 after ablation, while recurrence was higher after ablation (risk ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.12). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): cystectomy for symptom and recurrence control, chosen with open eyes about reserve — especially for bilateral cysts or women banking on future fertility.

cards.headline: Kalra 2024 Cochrane (9 RCTs, 578 women): excision may cut dysmenorrhoea recurrence (OR 0.25), endometrioma recurrence (OR 0.17) and further surgery (OR 0.16) versus ablation — low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Kalra 2024 Cochrane (9 RCTs, 578 women): excision may cut dysmenorrhoea recurrence (OR 0.25), endometrioma recurrence (OR 0.17) and further surgery (OR 0.16) versus ablation — low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Kalra 2024)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials involving 578 women of reproductive age with endometriomas at least 3 cm, presenting with pain, infertility or both, comparing laparoscopic excision (cystectomy) with laparoscopic drainage and ablation; outcomes to one and two years.
cards.result: At up to two years, excision may reduce dysmenorrhoea recurrence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52; 2 studies, 140 women; recurrence 49% after ablative surgery versus 10% to 34% after excisional surgery) and dyspareunia recurrence (OR 0.09, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.22; 58% versus 4% to 23%). At one year, excision may reduce endometrioma recurrence (OR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.34; 4 studies, 264 women; 37% versus 5% to 17%) and the need for further surgery (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.41; 32% versus 3% to 16%). Spontaneous pregnancy in the first year may differ little (OR 1.27, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.87). No study reported other surgical complications; five reported no conversions to laparotomy.
cards.watchOut: Cochrane rated the certainty low — unblinded surgical trials and small numbers — and the review reports no ovarian-reserve outcome, so the reserve half of the question rests on the second card, not this one.
cards.source: Kalra R et al. Excisional surgery versus ablative surgery for ovarian endometrioma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024. PMID: 39588841. cards.headline: Paik 2024 meta-analysis: AMH fell 1.08 after cystectomy versus 0.40 after ablation, while recurrence ran higher after ablation (RR 1.51; one-year RR 2.36)
cards.summary: Paik 2024 meta-analysis: AMH fell 1.08 after cystectomy versus 0.40 after ablation, while recurrence ran higher after ablation (RR 1.51; one-year RR 2.36)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised and prospective cohort studies (Paik 2024)
cards.people: Six randomised trials and five prospective cohort studies of women undergoing cystectomy or ablation for ovarian endometrioma, reporting anti-Müllerian hormone (the review's only reserve measure), recurrence and pregnancy; all included studies assessed as low risk of bias by the authors.
cards.result: Post- versus pre-operative AMH fell by a weighted mean difference of -1.08 (95% CI -1.34 to -0.82) after cystectomy and -0.40 (95% CI -0.61 to -0.19) after ablation; post-operative AMH was higher after ablation (WMD 0.38, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.63). Overall recurrence was higher after ablation (risk ratio 1.51, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.12) and one-year recurrence higher still (RR 2.36, 95% CI 1.30 to 4.31). Pregnancy rates were similar (OR 1.18, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.52).
cards.watchOut: AMH is a surrogate for reserve, not a pregnancy outcome — and pregnancy rates themselves did not differ; the reserve advantage of ablation was clearest after three months, in bilateral disease and with laser ablation, so technique matters within 'ablation'.
cards.source: Paik H et al. Impact of Ablation Versus Cystectomy for Endometrioma on Ovarian Reserve, Recurrence, and Pregnancy: An Updated Meta-Analysis. Reproductive sciences (Thousand Oaks, Calif.). 2024. PMID: 38509401. cards.headline: Synthesis: excision wins every symptom and recurrence endpoint; ablation preserves more AMH; pregnancy rates tie — the choice turns on which outcome the woman prioritises
cards.summary: Synthesis: excision wins every symptom and recurrence endpoint; ablation preserves more AMH; pregnancy rates tie — the choice turns on which outcome the woman prioritises
cards.people: A Cochrane review of nine randomised trials (578 women) plus a meta-analysis of six randomised trials and five cohorts reporting ovarian reserve for endometrioma surgery.
cards.result: Excision versus ablation: dysmenorrhoea recurrence OR 0.25, endometrioma recurrence OR 0.17 (37% versus 5-17% absolute), further surgery OR 0.16, pregnancy OR 1.27 (NS). AMH fall: 1.08 with cystectomy versus 0.40 with ablation. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for cystectomy on pain and recurrence, with the reserve cost on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Low-certainty randomised evidence throughout, and no trial in either review was powered for live birth — the outcome that would settle the reserve question clinically.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kalra R et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024 (PMID: 39588841); Paik H et al. Reproductive sciences (Thousand Oaks, Calif.). 2024 (PMID: 38509401).
