shelves.title: Pravastatin to prevent pre-eclampsia: three tiny trials, 213 women — pooled risk ratio 0.62 with a confidence interval (0.33–1.14) that settles nothing; safety in a 20-woman pilot looked clean
shelves.question: In women at high risk of pre-eclampsia, does pravastatin prevent pre-eclampsia versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Pilot Projects · Pravastatin/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics/therapeutic use · Pre-Eclampsia/prevention & control · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Second · Prenatal Care · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — shown so far, in far too few women to close the question. The meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (Provinciatto H et al., PMID: 38109997) pooled the entire randomised prevention literature — three trials, 213 women — and found no significant effect on pre-eclampsia incidence (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.33-1.14; P=.12), concluding that adequately powered trials are still needed. The largest contributing pilot (Costantine MM et al., PMID: 34033812) randomised just 20 women with previous early pre-eclampsia to pravastatin 20 mg or placebo from 12-16 weeks and was designed for safety and pharmacokinetics: no significant differences in adverse or serious adverse events, congenital anomalies or cord-blood chemistries, with pregnancy outcomes described as more favourable on pravastatin but not quantified in the abstract. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a biologically plausible idea with a clean early safety signal and no demonstrated prevention benefit — Tier C, because a prevention claim resting on 213 randomised women belongs in front of the developer.

cards.headline: Costantine 2021 pilot (n=20): pravastatin 20 mg from 12–16 weeks — no significant safety differences versus placebo; outcomes 'more favourable' but unquantified in the abstract
cards.summary: Costantine 2021 pilot (n=20): pravastatin 20 mg from 12–16 weeks — no significant safety differences versus placebo; outcomes 'more favourable' but unquantified in the abstract
cards.people: 20 women with singleton non-anomalous pregnancies at high risk of pre-eclampsia (previous pre-eclampsia requiring delivery before 34+6 weeks) in a multicentre, blinded, placebo-controlled pilot, randomised at 12+0 to 16+6 weeks to pravastatin 20 mg daily or placebo until delivery (10 per group completed); primary outcomes were safety and pharmacokinetics. Registry ID: NCT01717586.
cards.result: No significant differences between groups in rates of adverse or serious adverse events, congenital anomalies, or maternal and umbilical cord blood chemistries; the most common side effects were headache, heartburn and musculoskeletal pain. Pravastatin concentrations in most cord and maternal delivery samples were below the assay's limit of quantification. The abstract states pregnancy and neonatal outcomes were more favourable in the pravastatin group without printing the pre-eclampsia rates.
cards.watchOut: A 20-woman safety pilot cannot estimate a prevention effect — any pre-eclampsia difference in groups of 10 is noise; the shelf's effect estimate comes from the pooled card, and this card's declared gap is its missing outcome numbers.
cards.source: Costantine MM et al. A randomized pilot clinical trial of pravastatin versus placebo in pregnant patients at high risk of preeclampsia. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2021. PMID: 34033812. Registry ID: NCT01717586. cards.headline: Provinciatto 2024 meta-analysis (3 RCTs, 213 women): pre-eclampsia RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.33-1.14; P=.12) — no significant prevention effect
cards.summary: Provinciatto 2024 meta-analysis (3 RCTs, 213 women): pre-eclampsia RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.33-1.14; P=.12) — no significant prevention effect
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials with trial sequential analysis (Provinciatto 2024)
cards.people: Three randomised trials comprising 213 pregnant women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (106 allocated to pravastatin, any dose, started by 20 weeks) versus placebo or no treatment; literature searched to August 2023.
cards.result: There was no significant effect of pravastatin on the incidence of pre-eclampsia (risk ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.33-1.14; P=.12). The authors conclude the findings comprise only preliminary studies with a small number of subjects and that well-designed, adequately powered trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate (0.62) sits inside the zone where a real, clinically worthwhile effect and no effect are both compatible with the data — 213 women is roughly an order of magnitude too few for a pre-eclampsia prevention endpoint.
cards.source: Provinciatto H et al. The role of pravastatin in preventing preeclampsia in high-risk pregnant women: a meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis. American journal of obstetrics & gynecology MFM. 2024. PMID: 38109997. shelves.title: Adding azithromycin to standard prophylaxis at non-elective caesarean halved postoperative infection: 6.1% versus 12.0% in the 2,013-woman C/SOAP trial
shelves.question: In non-elective caesarean delivery, does adjunctive azithromycin added to standard prophylaxis reduce postoperative infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Azithromycin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cesarean Section · Endometritis/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Puerperal Infection/prevention & control · Sepsis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control · Survival Analysis · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large trial, confirmed by the pooled randomised literature. In C/SOAP (Tita AT et al., PMID: 27682034), 2,013 women having a non-elective caesarean during labour or after membrane rupture received azithromycin 500 mg or placebo on top of standard prophylaxis: the composite of endometritis, wound infection or other infection within six weeks occurred in 6.1% versus 12.0% (relative risk 0.51, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.68; P<0.001) — about a 49% relative reduction, 5.9 percentage points absolute — with endometritis 3.8% versus 6.1% and wound infection 2.4% versus 6.6%, and fewer serious maternal adverse events (1.5% versus 2.9%); the neonatal composite did not differ (14.3% versus 13.6%). The 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yang M et al., PMID: 35091057) found the same direction: endometritis relative risk 0.62 (95% CI 0.49-0.79) and wound infection 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.58). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): adjunctive azithromycin for non-elective caesarean, where membranes or labour have raised the infection risk — the trial does not speak to elective, pre-labour caesarean.

cards.headline: Tita 2016 (C/SOAP): infection composite 6.1% on azithromycin versus 12.0% on placebo (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.38-0.68); wound infection 2.4% versus 6.6%
cards.summary: Tita 2016 (C/SOAP): infection composite 6.1% on azithromycin versus 12.0% on placebo (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.38-0.68); wound infection 2.4% versus 6.6%
cards.people: 2,013 women with singleton pregnancies at 24 weeks or more undergoing non-elective caesarean delivery during labour or after membrane rupture at 14 US centres, randomised to intravenous azithromycin 500 mg (n=1,019) or placebo (n=994), all also receiving standard antibiotic prophylaxis; primary outcome a composite of endometritis, wound infection or other infection within six weeks. Registry ID: NCT01235546.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 62 women (6.1%) on azithromycin and 119 (12.0%) on placebo (relative risk 0.51, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.68; P<0.001) — a 49% relative reduction with the absolute rates printed alongside. Endometritis: 3.8% versus 6.1% (P=0.02). Wound infection: 2.4% versus 6.6% (P<0.001). Serious maternal adverse events: 1.5% versus 2.9% (P=0.03). The secondary neonatal composite (death and serious complications) did not differ: 14.3% versus 13.6% (P=0.63).
cards.watchOut: The population is non-elective caesarean in labour or after ruptured membranes — the high-infection-risk group; extrapolating the same absolute gain to elective caesarean with intact membranes is not supported by this trial. Antibiotic-resistance consequences of routine adjunctive macrolide use are not measured here.
cards.source: Tita AT et al. Adjunctive Azithromycin Prophylaxis for Cesarean Delivery. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 27682034. Registry ID: NCT01235546. cards.headline: Yang 2022 meta-analysis of RCTs: endometritis RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.49-0.79) and wound infection RR 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.58) with added azithromycin
cards.summary: Yang 2022 meta-analysis of RCTs: endometritis RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.49-0.79) and wound infection RR 0.40 (95% CI 0.27-0.58) with added azithromycin
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials and cohort studies (Yang 2022)
cards.people: Randomised trials and cohort studies of adding azithromycin to antibiotic prophylaxis at caesarean delivery, pooled separately by design; the randomised-trial pooling is the estimate carded here.
cards.result: In the randomised-trial meta-analysis, adding azithromycin significantly reduced endometritis (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.49-0.79; P<0.0001) and wound infection (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.27-0.58; P<0.00001). Cohort-study pooling pointed the same way for wound infection (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.54-0.82) and composite infection (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.66-0.96), though not significantly for endometritis (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.11-1.51). Safety could not be meta-analysed because outcome indicators differed between studies.
cards.watchOut: C/SOAP dominates the randomised evidence, so the meta-analysis is confirmation rather than independent replication; the authors themselves call for non-elective subgroup work and long-term offspring safety follow-up.

shelves.title: Remifentanil PCA beats pethidine for labour pain when an epidural is declined or unsuitable: epidural conversion 19% versus 41% in RESPITE — but an epidural itself still relieves pain better
shelves.question: For labour analgesia when an epidural is unsuitable or declined, does patient-controlled remifentanil relieve pain and satisfy mothers versus other options?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adolescent · Adult · Analgesia, Epidural/statistics & numerical data · Analgesia, Obstetrical/adverse effects/methods · Analgesia, Patient-Controlled/methods · Analgesics, Opioid/pharmacology · Female · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Labor Pain/drug therapy · Meperidine/administration & dosage/pharmacology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Satisfaction/statistics & numerical data · Piperidines/administration & dosage · Pregnancy · Remifentanil · United Kingdom/epidemiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — against pethidine, the usual fallback, remifentanil patient-controlled analgesia is clearly better; against an epidural, it is not. In RESPITE (Wilson MJA et al., PMID: 30115484), 400 women at term who requested opioid pain relief were randomised to intravenous remifentanil PCA or intramuscular pethidine: progression to epidural analgesia was 19% versus 41% (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66; p<0.0001), with no serious adverse events attributable to either drug. The earlier meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (Schnabel A et al., PMID: 22273829) found the same pattern — lower pain scores at one hour, higher satisfaction and less conversion to epidural than pethidine — while epidural analgesia decreased pain scores compared with remifentanil (P=0.003). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): when an epidural is unsuitable, declined or delayed, remifentanil PCA is the better opioid option; it is not an epidural substitute of equal strength.

cards.headline: Wilson 2018 (RESPITE): epidural conversion 19% (39/201) on remifentanil PCA versus 41% (81/199) on pethidine (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66)
cards.summary: Wilson 2018 (RESPITE): epidural conversion 19% (39/201) on remifentanil PCA versus 41% (81/199) on pethidine (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66)
cards.people: 401 women aged 16 or older, beyond 37 weeks, in labour with a singleton cephalic presentation who requested opioid pain relief, in 14 UK maternity units, randomised to intravenous remifentanil PCA (40 µg bolus on demand, 2-minute lockout; n=201) or intramuscular pethidine 100 mg every four hours (n=200, 199 analysed); open-label; primary outcome receipt of epidural analgesia after enrolment. Registry ID: ISRCTN29654603.
cards.result: Epidural conversion was 19% (39 of 201) in the remifentanil PCA group and 41% (81 of 199) in the pethidine group (risk ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66; p<0.0001) — about a 52% relative reduction, 22 percentage points absolute. There were no serious adverse events or drug reactions directly attributable to either analgesic.
cards.watchOut: Open-label by necessity (different routes), and the primary outcome is a behaviour — requesting an epidural — rather than a pain score; women who knew they had the newer drug may have persevered longer. The trial does not compare remifentanil with epidural head-to-head.
cards.source: Wilson MJA et al. Intravenous remifentanil patient-controlled analgesia versus intramuscular pethidine for pain relief in labour (RESPITE): an open-label, multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 30115484. Registry ID: ISRCTN29654603. cards.headline: Schnabel 2012 meta-analysis (12 RCTs): remifentanil beat pethidine on pain at 1 hour, satisfaction and epidural conversion — epidural beat remifentanil on pain (P=0.003)
cards.summary: Schnabel 2012 meta-analysis (12 RCTs): remifentanil beat pethidine on pain at 1 hour, satisfaction and epidural conversion — epidural beat remifentanil on pain (P=0.003)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials (2001-2011) of remifentanil PCA versus other analgesic techniques for labour pain, principally pethidine, with limited comparisons against nitrous oxide and fentanyl.
cards.result: Compared with pethidine, women on remifentanil had a lower risk of conversion to epidural analgesia (P<0.001), a lower mean pain score after one hour (P<0.001) and higher satisfaction scores (P<0.05), with a comparable degree of adverse events. Epidural analgesia decreased pain scores compared with remifentanil (P=0.003). Serious maternal or fetal adverse outcomes were not reported in these trials; the abstract gives p-values without pooled effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: P-value-only reporting in this record — direction is consistent with RESPITE but magnitudes cannot be quoted from it; and with few reported adverse events, the authors state the safety of remifentanil in labour remains an open question.
cards.source: Schnabel A et al. Remifentanil for labour analgesia: a meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. European journal of anaesthesiology. 2012. PMID: 22273829. cards.headline: Synthesis: remifentanil PCA is the stronger non-epidural opioid; the epidural remains the stronger analgesic
cards.summary: Synthesis: remifentanil PCA is the stronger non-epidural opioid; the epidural remains the stronger analgesic
cards.people: One 401-woman multicentre trial (RESPITE) plus a 12-trial meta-analysis of remifentanil PCA in labour.
cards.result: Epidural conversion 19% versus 41% versus pethidine (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.34-0.66); pooled trials agree on pain, satisfaction and conversion versus pethidine, and find epidural superior to remifentanil for pain scores. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) versus the non-epidural alternatives.

shelves.title: Tocolysis for external cephalic version splits by drug: beta-mimetics raise success, nifedipine does not (42% versus 37% on placebo), and atosiban does worse than beta-agonists (36.7% versus 45.3%)
shelves.question: For breech presentation at term, does external cephalic version with tocolysis increase cephalic presentation and vaginal birth versus version without tocolysis?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Breech Presentation/surgery · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Nifedipine/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Tocolytic Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Uterus/drug effects · Version, Fetal/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on which tocolytic. The drug class with evidence of benefit is the beta-mimetics: the systematic review (Wilcox CB et al., PMID: 21199292) records that ECV success rates are improved with betamimetic tocolytics, and found nifedipine worse than terbutaline head-to-head (pooled risk ratio 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93). Nifedipine against placebo failed in its adequately sized trial (Kok M et al., PMID: 18669722): success 42% versus 37% (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.85-1.5), caesarean delivery 51% versus 46%. Atosiban fared worse than beta-agonist controls in its meta-analysis (Riemma G et al., PMID: 33421816): success 36.7% versus 45.3% (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 0.98), though with fewer drug side effects (16.0% versus 42.9%; RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.47) and no difference in caesarean rates. PROPOSED SPLIT: tocolysis helps ECV when it is a beta-mimetic; substituting nifedipine or atosiban for convenience loses the benefit.

cards.headline: Kok 2008: nifedipine before ECV — success 42% versus 37% on placebo (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.85-1.5); caesarean 51% versus 46%
cards.summary: Kok 2008: nifedipine before ECV — success 42% versus 37% on placebo (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.85-1.5); caesarean 51% versus 46%
cards.people: 320 women (310 with outcome data) with a singleton breech fetus at 36 weeks or more, randomised to nifedipine 10 mg (two doses, 30 and 15 minutes before the version attempt) or placebo; primary outcome cephalic presentation immediately after the procedure. Registry ID: ISRCTN28715121.
cards.result: External cephalic version success was 42% on nifedipine versus 37% on placebo (relative risk 1.1, 95% CI 0.85-1.5) — no significant difference. Caesarean delivery was 51% versus 46% (RR 1.1, 95% CI 0.88-1.4). The authors conclude nifedipine did not significantly improve ECV success and its future use for this purpose should be limited to large trials.
cards.watchOut: Sized to detect a 17-point improvement from a 40% base rate — a smaller true benefit cannot be excluded, but the point estimate (5 points) is far below what the trial was built to find worthwhile.
cards.source: Kok M et al. Nifedipine as a uterine relaxant for external cephalic version: a randomized controlled trial. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2008. PMID: 18669722. Registry ID: ISRCTN28715121. cards.headline: Wilcox 2011 review: betamimetics improve ECV success; nifedipine lost to terbutaline head-to-head (pooled RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93)
cards.summary: Wilcox 2011 review: betamimetics improve ECV success; nifedipine lost to terbutaline head-to-head (pooled RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.93)
cards.people: Three randomised trials of nifedipine tocolysis for ECV in singleton term breech or transverse presentation: two versus terbutaline (n=176 combined) and one versus placebo (n=320), set against the established background that betamimetic tocolytics improve ECV success rates but cause maternal side effects.
cards.result: Nifedipine versus terbutaline: lower successful ECV rates on nifedipine, pooled risk ratio 0.67 (95% CI 0.48-0.93; P=0.016). Nifedipine versus placebo: 41.6% versus 37.2% success (P=0.43). Minor side effects were slightly higher with nifedipine than placebo, with no significant difference in adverse maternal or neonatal outcomes. The review found no evidence to support nifedipine for ECV tocolysis.
cards.watchOut: Only three nifedipine trials; the betamimetic benefit is stated as background from the wider literature rather than re-pooled here, so this card establishes the ordering (betamimetic > nifedipine ≈ placebo), not a fresh betamimetic effect size.

cards.headline: Riemma 2021 meta-analysis (4 studies, 1,534 women): atosiban success 36.7% versus 45.3% on beta-agonist controls (RR 0.78) — but side effects 16.0% versus 42.9%
cards.summary: Riemma 2021 meta-analysis (4 studies, 1,534 women): atosiban success 36.7% versus 45.3% on beta-agonist controls (RR 0.78) — but side effects 16.0% versus 42.9%
cards.people: Four studies of 1,534 women with a singleton pregnancy at 36 weeks or more scheduled for ECV, comparing atosiban tocolysis with beta-agonists or other drugs; primary outcome successful ECV.
cards.result: ECV success was significantly lower on atosiban: 36.7% versus 45.3% (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.6 to 0.98). Caesarean section (59.8% versus 52.6%; RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.98-1.38) and vaginal delivery rates did not differ significantly. Drug-related side effects were lower on atosiban: 16.0% versus 42.9% (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.47).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is an active drug class, not no tocolysis — atosiban could still beat nothing; what this shows is that it should not displace a beta-agonist where success is the goal.
cards.source: Riemma G et al. Usefulness of atosiban for tocolysis during external cephalic version: Systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: 'tocolysis' is not one intervention — beta-mimetics carry the benefit; nifedipine and atosiban do not reproduce it
cards.summary: Synthesis: 'tocolysis' is not one intervention — beta-mimetics carry the benefit; nifedipine and atosiban do not reproduce it
cards.people: A 320-woman placebo-controlled nifedipine trial, a three-trial nifedipine systematic review, and a four-study atosiban meta-analysis (1,534 women) for ECV at term.
cards.result: Nifedipine versus placebo success: 42% versus 37% (RR 1.1, NS). Nifedipine versus terbutaline: RR 0.67 for success. Atosiban versus beta-agonists: 36.7% versus 45.3% (RR 0.78). PROPOSED SPLIT by drug class.

shelves.title: Needle aspiration matches incision and drainage for breast abscess cure (RR 0.96) — and wins on healing time (about 11 days shorter), fistula (RR 0.21) and keeping breastfeeding going (interrupted breastfeeding RR 0.28)
shelves.question: In lactating women with a breast abscess, does ultrasound-guided needle aspiration match incision and drainage for cure — with better cosmetic and breastfeeding outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Abscess/surgery · Drainage/adverse effects/methods · Treatment Outcome · Bias · Fistula
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cure is a tie; everything around the cure favours the needle. The meta-analysis of nine randomised trials (Zhou F et al., PMID: 37350731; 703 patients) found no significant difference in cure rate (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.07) or recurrence (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35-1.30), but aspiration healed faster (weighted mean difference -11.02 days, 95% CI -15.14 to -6.90), caused fewer breast fistulas (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06-0.72), far less interrupted breastfeeding (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20-0.39) and higher appearance satisfaction (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03-2.21). The Cochrane review restricted to breastfeeding women (Irusen H et al., PMID: 26279276; four contributing studies, 325 women) could not pool its resolution-time data for heterogeneity (I²=97%) and found one small study favouring aspiration by 6.07 days — directionally the same, statistically fragile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspiration first for most lactational abscesses, reserving incision and drainage for large, multiloculated or aspiration-refractory collections, exactly as the meta-analysis concludes.

cards.headline: Zhou 2023 meta-analysis (9 RCTs, 703 patients): cure RR 0.96 (NS), healing 11.02 days shorter, fistula RR 0.21, interrupted breastfeeding RR 0.28 with aspiration
cards.summary: Zhou 2023 meta-analysis (9 RCTs, 703 patients): cure RR 0.96 (NS), healing 11.02 days shorter, fistula RR 0.21, interrupted breastfeeding RR 0.28 with aspiration
cards.people: Nine randomised trials, 703 patients with breast abscess, comparing needle aspiration (with or without ultrasound guidance) with traditional incision and drainage; literature to January 2022; risk of bias assessed with RoB-2 and certainty with GRADE.
cards.result: No significant difference in cure rate (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.86-1.07; p=.469) or recurrence (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35-1.30; p=.241), regardless of ultrasound guidance. Aspiration was associated with shorter healing time (weighted mean difference -11.02 days, 95% CI -15.14 to -6.90; p<.001), lower fistula incidence (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06-0.72; p=.013), lower interrupted breastfeeding (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20-0.39; p<.001) and higher appearance satisfaction (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.03-2.21; p=.035).
cards.watchOut: The pooled population mixes lactational and non-lactational abscesses; the breastfeeding outcomes come from the lactational subset. Large or multicompartment abscesses, and abscesses failing repeated aspiration, remain surgical — the authors say so themselves.

cards.headline: Irusen 2015 Cochrane (breastfeeding women; 4 studies, 325 women): resolution-time data too heterogeneous to pool (I²=97%); one study favoured aspiration by 6.07 days
cards.summary: Irusen 2015 Cochrane (breastfeeding women; 4 studies, 325 women): resolution-time data too heterogeneous to pool (I²=97%); one study favoured aspiration by 6.07 days
cards.people: Randomised trials of treatments for breast abscesses in breastfeeding women; six studies included, four contributing data from 325 women to the aspiration-versus-incision-and-drainage comparison (two further studies did not stratify lactational from non-lactational abscesses).
cards.result: Mean time to complete resolution could not be pooled: heterogeneity was substantial (I²=97%) with a clear subgroup difference by ultrasound guidance. One study found resolution favoured needle aspiration over incision and drainage (mean difference -6.07 days, 95% CI -7.81 to -4.33; n=36) but had excluded 9 of 22 women (41%) in the aspiration group — treatment failures — from that calculation. Overall risk of bias was unclear for most domains because of poor reporting.
cards.watchOut: The lactation-specific randomised base is small and poorly reported, and the one precise resolution estimate is inflated by excluding failures — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, despite the larger mixed-population meta-analysis.
cards.source: Irusen H et al. Treatments for breast abscesses in breastfeeding women. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26279276. shelves.title: Pessary self-management matches clinic care for prolapse quality of life at 18 months and at 4 years (TOPSY) — with fewer complications (16.7% versus 22.0%) and lower cost
shelves.question: In women using a vaginal pessary for prolapse, is self-management as effective as clinic-based care for symptoms and complications?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on quality of life, self-management neither improves nor worsens outcomes, and it is cheaper with fewer complications. In TOPSY (Hagen S et al., PMID: 38078194), 340 women using a pessary for prolapse were randomised to a 30-minute self-management teaching session with telephone support or to routine clinic-based care: pelvic-floor quality of life (PFIQ-7) at 18 months was 32.3 versus 32.5 (adjusted mean difference -0.03, 95% CI -9.32 to 9.25), complications were fewer with self-management (16.7% versus 22.0%; adjusted mean difference -3.83%, 95% CI -6.86% to -0.81%), and self-management cost less (incremental net benefit £564). The four-year follow-up (Bugge C et al., PMID: 40832737) found the same picture in 186 responders: PFIQ-7 32.9 versus 31.4 (adjusted mean difference 4.86, 95% CI -6.41 to 16.12), complications 17.7% versus 22.0%, and self-management still cost-effective (incremental net benefit £2,240). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): offer self-management to women who can and want to do it — the gain is convenience, cost and slightly fewer complications, not better prolapse control. Tier C is set: one trial and its own follow-up carry the shelf.

cards.headline: Hagen 2023 (TOPSY): PFIQ-7 at 18 months 32.3 self-management versus 32.5 clinic care (difference -0.03, 95% CI -9.32 to 9.25); complications 16.7% versus 22.0%
cards.summary: Hagen 2023 (TOPSY): PFIQ-7 at 18 months 32.3 self-management versus 32.5 clinic care (difference -0.03, 95% CI -9.32 to 9.25); complications 16.7% versus 22.0%
cards.people: 340 women (169 self-management, 171 clinic-based care) aged 18 or older attending pessary clinics at 21 UK centres, using a pessary (except Shelf, Gellhorn or Cube types) retained for at least two weeks; self-management was a 30-minute teaching session, leaflet, two-week follow-up call and telephone support; primary outcome pelvic-floor-specific quality of life (PFIQ-7) at 18 months. Registry ID: ISRCTN62510577. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: There was no statistically significant difference in PFIQ-7 at 18 months (mean 32.3 self-management versus 32.5 clinic care; adjusted mean difference -0.03, 95% CI -9.32 to 9.25). Self-management was less costly (incremental net benefit £564, 95% CI -£576 to £1704). A lower percentage of complications was reported with self-management (mean 16.7% versus 22.0%; adjusted mean difference -3.83%, 95% CI -6.86% to -0.81%). Self-managing women were more confident in self-management activities; 31 unrelated serious adverse events occurred (17 versus 14).
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and women with limited manual dexterity, cognitive deficit or a need for non-English teaching were excluded — the population least able to self-manage is not in this trial, so 'offer to all' overreads it.
cards.source: Hagen S et al. Clinical effectiveness of vaginal pessary self-management vs clinic-based care for pelvic organ prolapse (TOPSY): a randomised controlled superiority trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2023. PMID: 38078194. Registry ID: ISRCTN62510577. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Bugge 2025 (TOPSY 4-year follow-up): quality of life still tied (32.9 versus 31.4); self-management still cost-effective (net benefit £2,240)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Bugge 2025, TOPSY)
cards.people: 186 of the 340 TOPSY participants (55%) who responded at four years (86 of 169 self-management, 100 of 171 clinic care), followed by questionnaire for PFIQ-7, complications, prolapse symptoms and cost-effectiveness. Registry ID: ISRCTN62510577.
cards.result: No statistically significant group difference in PFIQ-7 at four years (mean 32.9 versus 31.4; adjusted mean difference 4.86, 95% CI -6.41 to 16.12). Complications were non-significantly lower with self-management (17.7% versus 22.0%). Self-management remained cost-effective at four years (incremental net benefit £2,240). One potentially related serious adverse event occurred, in the self-management group.
cards.watchOut: Only 55% responded at four years, with differential response (51% versus 58%) — the long-term tie is reassuring but rests on a self-selected subset of the original trial.

shelves.title: Soy isoflavone extracts cut hot flush frequency by about a fifth versus placebo (20.6% relative reduction) in one meta-analysis — but Cochrane pooling of the wider phytoestrogen literature found no conclusive effect
shelves.question: Do soy isoflavones reduce the frequency and severity of menopausal hot flushes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Dietary Supplements · Female · Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Humans · Isoflavones/isolation & purification/therapeutic use · Menopause · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Glycine max/chemistry · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but modest effect for extracted or synthesised soy isoflavones specifically, with a dissenting Cochrane read of the broader literature. The dedicated meta-analysis (Taku K et al., PMID: 22433977) pooled double-blind randomised trials of extracted or synthesised soybean isoflavones (median 54 mg aglycone equivalents, six weeks to 12 months) and found hot flush frequency reduced by 20.6% relative to placebo (95% CI -28.38 to -12.86; P<0.00001) and severity by 26.2% relative (95% CI -42.23 to -10.15; P=0.001), with supplements providing more than 18.8 mg of genistein more than twice as potent as lower-genistein ones — though heterogeneity was high (I²=67% for frequency, 86% for severity). The Cochrane review of all phytoestrogens (Lethaby A et al., PMID: 24323914; 43 trials, 4,364 participants) concluded there was no conclusive evidence that phytoestrogen supplements reduce flush frequency or severity, while noting high-genistein extracts consistently reduced frequency in four trials and a strong placebo effect (frequency reductions of 1% to 59% on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect, at best, about a one-fifth relative trim in flushes from a genistein-rich extract — not the abolition hormone therapy can give. No specific commercial product is named in either record, so none is named here; products on sale may differ in genistein content, safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Taku 2012 meta-analysis (17 trials pooled): flush frequency -20.6% relative (95% CI -28.38 to -12.86) and severity -26.2% relative on soy isoflavones versus placebo
cards.summary: Taku 2012 meta-analysis (17 trials pooled): flush frequency -20.6% relative (95% CI -28.38 to -12.86) and severity -26.2% relative on soy isoflavones versus placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Taku 2012)
cards.people: 19 double-blind randomised trials (17 in the meta-analyses; 13 for frequency, 9-10 for severity) of extracted or synthesised soybean isoflavones versus placebo in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, at a median dose of 54 mg aglycone equivalents for six weeks to 12 months; literature to December 2010.
cards.result: Ingestion of soy isoflavones significantly reduced hot flush frequency by 20.6% relative to placebo (95% CI -28.38 to -12.86; P<0.00001) and severity by 26.2% relative (95% CI -42.23 to -10.15; P=0.001). Supplements providing more than 18.8 mg of genistein (the median across studies) were more than twice as potent at reducing flush frequency than lower-genistein supplements. The record names no commercial product or company.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is high (I²=67% for frequency, 86% for severity), the percentages are relative reductions against a placebo response that is itself large in flush trials, and dose, form and baseline frequency all modify the effect — an average woman's gain may be one flush fewer in five.

cards.headline: Lethaby 2013 Cochrane (43 trials, 4,364 women): 'no conclusive evidence' for phytoestrogens overall — high-genistein extracts the consistent exception; placebo alone cut flushes by 1–59%
cards.summary: Lethaby 2013 Cochrane (43 trials, 4,364 women): 'no conclusive evidence' for phytoestrogens overall — high-genistein extracts the consistent exception; placebo alone cut flushes by 1–59%
cards.people: 43 randomised trials (4,364 perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, at least 12 weeks) of foods, extracts and supplements high in phytoestrogens — dietary soy, soy extracts, red clover extracts, genistein extracts and others — versus no treatment, placebo or hormone therapy; women with breast cancer were excluded.
cards.result: Most trials were too dissimilar to pool. The pooled red clover product analysis showed no significant difference in daily flush frequency versus placebo (mean difference -0.93, 95% CI -1.95 to 0.10). Four trials suggested extracts with high genistein levels (over 30 mg/day) consistently reduced flush frequency. A strong placebo effect was noted in most trials, with flush frequency falling 1% to 59% on placebo. No evidence indicated endometrial or vaginal oestrogenic stimulation or other adverse effects over up to two years. The authors' conclusion: no conclusive evidence that phytoestrogen supplements effectively reduce flush frequency or severity, though genistein concentrates merit further study.
cards.watchOut: Cochrane's net is wider than soy isoflavone extracts — it includes dietary soy and red clover — so its null headline and Taku's positive one are answers to slightly different questions; the genistein-rich extract is where the two reviews agree there may be something.

shelves.title: Hypnosis cuts hot flashes well beyond control conditions: scores fell 80% with clinician-led hypnosis versus 15% on attention control, and self-administered hypnosis beat sham (53.4% versus 40.9% score fall) in 2025
shelves.question: Does hypnosis reduce hot flush frequency and severity in postmenopausal women and breast cancer survivors versus sham or control?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Hot Flashes/therapy/psychology · Hypnosis/methods · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials from the same programme, against two different controls, point the same way. The clinician-delivered trial (Elkins GR et al., PMID: 23435026) randomised 187 postmenopausal women with at least seven flushes a day to five weekly hypnosis sessions or structured-attention control: by week 12, subjective flush frequency had fallen 74.16% versus 17.13% and flush score 80.32% versus 15.38% (both P<0.001), with physiologically monitored flushes down 56.86% versus 9.94%. The self-administered trial (Elkins G et al., PMID: 41217756) randomised 250 women (24.8% with a history of breast cancer) to six weeks of self-hypnosis audio or sham white-noise hypnosis: flush scores fell 53.4% versus 40.9% (P=.04) — a much smaller margin, because the sham was an active control carrying the full placebo and expectancy load. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): hypnosis works for hot flashes; how much of the gain survives a rigorous sham depends on delivery, and self-administration is the accessible, smaller-effect version.

cards.headline: Elkins 2025: self-administered hypnosis — flush score -53.4% versus -40.9% on sham white-noise hypnosis at 6 weeks (P=.04); 250 women, a quarter breast cancer survivors
cards.summary: Elkins 2025: self-administered hypnosis — flush score -53.4% versus -40.9% on sham white-noise hypnosis at 6 weeks (P=.04); 250 women, a quarter breast cancer survivors
cards.people: 250 postmenopausal women reporting at least four hot flashes daily or 28 weekly (mean age 55.9 years; 62 women, 24.8%, with a history of breast cancer) at two US centres, randomised to six weeks of self-administered hypnosis (cooling imagery and relaxation suggestions) or self-administered sham white-noise hypnosis designed to match placebo and expectancy components; single-blind, intention-to-treat. Registry ID: NCT03572153.
cards.result: Mean hot flash score fell from 88.7 to 41.3 in the hypnosis group (a 53.4% decrease) versus 94.6 to 55.9 in the white-noise group (a 40.9% decrease), a significantly greater improvement for hypnosis (P=.04). The hypnosis group also reported a significantly greater reduction in daily interference from hot flashes.
cards.watchOut: The sham was deliberately strong — it absorbed expectancy and ritual — so the incremental 12.5-point margin understates the total improvement women experienced, while also showing how much of self-help benefit is context; single-blind, with self-reported diaries as the outcome source.

shelves.title: Clonidine trims hot flashes by about one flush a day versus placebo (pooled mean difference -0.95) — a modest drug effect bought with dry mouth, constipation and, in the breast-cancer trial, worse sleep (41% versus 21%)
shelves.question: Does clonidine reduce menopausal hot flushes versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/therapeutic use · Amines/therapeutic use · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Clonidine/therapeutic use · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids/therapeutic use · Excitatory Amino Acid Antagonists/therapeutic use · Female · Gabapentin · Hot Flashes/drug therapy/prevention & control · Humans · Isoflavones/therapeutic use · Menopause · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Glycine max · Trifolium · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — clonidine works, a little. The JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (Nelson HD et al., PMID: 16670414) pooled four placebo-controlled clonidine trials and found daily hot flash frequency reduced by a mean 0.95 flushes versus placebo (95% CI -1.44 to -0.47) — less than the pooled effects of the antidepressants (-1.13) and gabapentin (-2.05) in the same review, and less than oestrogen. The largest single trial (Pandya KJ et al., PMID: 10819701) randomised 194 postmenopausal women with breast cancer on tamoxifen to clonidine 0.1 mg daily or placebo: flush frequency fell 37% versus 20% at four weeks and 38% versus 24% at eight weeks, but difficulty sleeping was reported by 41% on clonidine versus 21% on placebo (P=0.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but small effect — roughly one flush a day — reasonable when hormones are off the table and better-evidenced non-hormonal options do not suit, with sleep and anticholinergic-type side effects counted in.

cards.headline: Nelson 2006 meta-analysis (4 clonidine trials): daily flush frequency -0.95 versus placebo (95% CI -1.44 to -0.47) — smaller than SSRIs/SNRIs (-1.13) or gabapentin (-2.05)
cards.summary: Nelson 2006 meta-analysis (4 clonidine trials): daily flush frequency -0.95 versus placebo (95% CI -1.44 to -0.47) — smaller than SSRIs/SNRIs (-1.13) or gabapentin (-2.05)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Nelson 2006)
cards.people: 43 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of oral non-hormonal therapies for menopausal hot flashes (10 antidepressant, 10 clonidine-identified, 6 other prescribed drugs, 17 isoflavone), of which four clonidine trials reported frequency outcomes suitable for pooling.
cards.result: Daily hot flash frequency decreased versus placebo in the meta-analysis of four clonidine trials (mean difference -0.95; 95% CI -1.44 to -0.47). For comparison within the same review: SSRIs/SNRIs -1.13 (95% CI -1.70 to -0.57, seven comparisons) and gabapentin -2.05 (95% CI -2.80 to -1.30, two trials). The authors note all these effects are less than for oestrogen, most trials have methodological deficiencies, and adverse effects and cost may restrict use.
cards.watchOut: Only four of ten identified clonidine trials could be pooled, and the review is from 2006 — clonidine's evidence base has not been refreshed by a modern large trial since.
cards.source: Nelson HD et al. Nonhormonal therapies for menopausal hot flashes: systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2006. PMID: 16670414. cards.people: 194 postmenopausal women with breast cancer receiving adjuvant tamoxifen, in a US community oncology programme, randomised to oral clonidine hydrochloride 0.1 mg daily or placebo for eight weeks, with daily diaries of flush number, duration and severity; 149 women completed 12 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: The mean decrease in hot flash frequency was greater on clonidine than placebo at four weeks (37% versus 20% relative reductions; 95% CI for the difference 7% to 27%) and at eight weeks (38% versus 24%; CI for difference 3% to 27%). Difficulty sleeping was reported by 41% on clonidine versus 21% on placebo (P=0.02). cards.watchOut: A tamoxifen-induced-flush population — women with breast cancer who cannot take oestrogen — so the balance of benefit and harm here is specific to that setting; a quarter of participants did not complete follow-up.

shelves.title: Endometrial ablation beats the levonorgestrel intrauterine system on blood loss at 2 years (PBAC 14.2 versus 64.8) and surgical reintervention (10% versus 27%) — satisfaction and quality of life tie, and by 7 years hysterectomy rates converge
shelves.question: For heavy menstrual bleeding, how does endometrial ablation compare with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system on bleeding control, satisfaction and further surgery?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Contraceptive Agents, Hormonal/administration & dosage · Endometrial Ablation Techniques/methods · Female · Humans · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage · Menorrhagia/physiopathology/therapy · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life · Retreatment · Sexual Health · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ablation, on the mechanical outcomes; for the intrauterine system, on reversibility and avoiding a procedure, with satisfaction equal either way. In the MIRA randomised trial (Beelen P et al., PMID: 32795428), 270 women with heavy menstrual bleeding were allocated to a levonorgestrel intrauterine system or bipolar radiofrequency endometrial ablation: at 24 months the intrauterine system was not shown non-inferior on blood loss (Pictorial Blood Loss Assessment Chart scores 64.8 versus 14.2; difference 50.5 points, 95% CI 4.3-96.7; non-inferiority P=.87), and surgical reintervention was 27% versus 10% (relative risk 2.64, 95% CI 1.49-4.68), while satisfaction and quality of life did not differ significantly. At a mean 7.4 years (Huijs DPC et al., PMID: 38280433; 196 women), total reintervention was 40.0% versus 28.7% (RR 1.39, 95% CI 0.92-2.10), surgical reintervention remained higher after starting with the system (35.3% versus 19.1%; RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.11-3.10), but hysterectomy rates were similar (11.8% versus 18.1%; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.32-1.34) and median bleeding scores were 0.0 in the follow-up sample. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for ablation on bleeding control and durability — Tier C, because one trial and its own follow-up carry the comparison.

cards.headline: Beelen 2021 (MIRA): blood loss at 24 months PBAC 64.8 intrauterine system versus 14.2 ablation — non-inferiority not shown (P=.87); surgical reintervention 27% versus 10% (RR 2.64)

cards.people: 270 women aged 34 or older with heavy menstrual bleeding, no pregnancy wish and no intracavitary pathology, in 26 Dutch hospitals and a general-practice network, randomised to a 52-mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (n=132; the record names the product as Mirena) or bipolar radiofrequency endometrial ablation (n=138; device named as NovaSure); primary outcome blood loss (PBAC score) at 24 months. Registry ID: NL2842 (Netherlands Trial Register).
cards.result: At 24 months, mean PBAC scores were 64.8 in the intrauterine-system group and 14.2 in the ablation group (difference 50.5 points, 95% CI 4.3-96.7); non-inferiority of the system was not demonstrated (P=.87 against a 25-point margin). Surgical reintervention occurred in 34 women (27%) starting with the system versus 14 women (10%) after ablation (relative risk 2.64, 95% CI 1.49-4.68). There was no significant difference in patient satisfaction or quality of life. Both strategies produced a large decrease from baseline PBAC scores of about 616-630.
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial: women randomised to the system could cross to ablation and surgery, which is exactly what the reintervention endpoint counts — it measures the durability of starting with the coil, not the coil's effect while retained. Ablation ends fertility, so the trial's no-pregnancy-wish entry criterion is part of the answer.

cards.headline: Huijs 2024 (MIRA long-term, mean 7.4 years): surgical reintervention still higher after the system (35.3% versus 19.1%; RR 1.84) — hysterectomy similar (11.8% versus 18.1%)
cards.summary: Huijs 2024 (MIRA long-term, mean 7.4 years): surgical reintervention still higher after the system (35.3% versus 19.1%; RR 1.84) — hysterectomy similar (11.8% versus 18.1%)
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (Huijs 2024, MIRA)
cards.people: 196 of the 270 MIRA participants (94 intrauterine system, 102 ablation) completing questionnaires at a mean follow-up of 7.4 years (range 6-9 years); primary outcome cumulative reintervention after the allocated treatment strategy.
cards.result: Cumulative reintervention (medical and surgical) was 40.0% (34/85) after starting with the intrauterine system versus 28.7% (27/94) after ablation (relative risk 1.39, 95% CI 0.92-2.10). Surgical reintervention alone was significantly higher after the system (35.3% versus 19.1%; RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.11-3.10). Hysterectomy rates were similar (11.8% versus 18.1%; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.32-1.34). Most reinterventions occurred in the first 24 months; median PBAC score in the follow-up sample was 0.0, with no clinically relevant differences in quality of life, sexual function or satisfaction.
cards.watchOut: A 73% questionnaire follow-up of one trial, with denominators shifting between outcomes (85-102 per group) — the long-term picture is consistent with the two-year result but rests on the same single randomised cohort.

cards.headline: Synthesis: start with ablation for the driest, most durable result; start with the coil to keep options open — a quarter to a third will move on to surgery either way
cards.summary: Synthesis: start with ablation for the driest, most durable result; start with the coil to keep options open — a quarter to a third will move on to surgery either way
cards.people: The MIRA randomised strategy trial (270 women) at 24 months and at a mean of 7.4 years (196 respondents).
cards.result: PBAC at 24 months: 64.8 versus 14.2. Surgical reintervention: 27% versus 10% at two years; 35.3% versus 19.1% long-term. Hysterectomy long-term: 11.8% versus 18.1% (NS). cards.watchOut: Women who may want pregnancy, or who prefer to avoid theatre entirely, are outside this comparison's logic — for them the intrauterine system is not the 'losing' arm but the only applicable one.

shelves.title: Misoprostol alone aborts about 9 in 10 early pregnancies after extra doses — sublingual beats buccal at preventing continuing pregnancy (1.1% versus 5.5%), buccal causes less chills and fever
shelves.question: How effective is a misoprostol-alone regimen for early abortion, and does route (buccal versus sublingual) change success?
shelves.mesh: Abortifacient Agents, Nonsteroidal/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Abortion, Incomplete · Abortion, Induced/methods · Administration, Buccal · Administration, Sublingual · Adult · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Misoprostol/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Patient Satisfaction · Pregnancy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — misoprostol alone works, and the route changes the failure mode more than the final success rate. In the multicentre randomised trial (Sheldon WR et al., PMID: 30831103), 401 women received three doses of misoprostol 800 µg every three hours, buccal or sublingual: continuing pregnancy at first follow-up was 1.1% (2/189) sublingual versus 5.5% (11/201) buccal (p=.02), but after additional misoprostol was offered, complete abortion reached 93.7% sublingual and 92.5% buccal — statistically indistinguishable — with chills and fever reported more often sublingually. The Cochrane review of medical methods for first-trimester abortion (Zhang J et al., PMID: 35608608) places this in context: combined regimens (misoprostol with mifepristone or letrozole) may be more effective than misoprostol alone, failure may be slightly lower sublingual than vaginal (risk ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.28; low-certainty), and oral misoprostol alone may fail more than vaginal (RR 3.68, 95% CI 1.56 to 8.71). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): where mifepristone is unavailable, a three-dose misoprostol-alone regimen with a follow-up dose available succeeds in roughly 92-94% — choose sublingual to minimise continuing pregnancy, buccal to minimise fever and chills.

cards.headline: Sheldon 2019 (n=401): continuing pregnancy 1.1% sublingual versus 5.5% buccal (p=.02); final complete abortion 93.7% versus 92.5% after extra misoprostol
cards.summary: Sheldon 2019 (n=401): continuing pregnancy 1.1% sublingual versus 5.5% buccal (p=.02); final complete abortion 93.7% versus 92.5% after extra misoprostol
cards.people: 401 women seeking early abortion at six clinics in two Latin American countries, randomised to buccal (n=202) or sublingual (n=199) misoprostol 800 µg, three doses repeated every three hours; women without complete abortion at 7-14 days were offered aspiration or additional misoprostol plus seven more days. Registry ID: NCT02299401.
cards.result: Continuing pregnancy at initial follow-up occurred in 2 of 189 women (1.1%) sublingual versus 11 of 201 (5.5%) buccal (p=.02). Complete abortion before extra treatment was 87.3% sublingual and 84.6% buccal, rising with additional misoprostol to 93.7% (177/189) and 92.5% (184/199) respectively. There were no differences by gestational age. Acceptability and side effects were similar except chills and fever, reported more frequently with sublingual administration (p<.05).
cards.watchOut: One trial, in settings with clinic follow-up and aspiration backup; the headline route difference is on continuing pregnancy at first check, not on final success, which converged once extra doses were allowed.
cards.source: Sheldon WR et al. Early abortion with buccal versus sublingual misoprostol alone: a multicenter, randomized trial. Contraception. 2019. PMID: 30831103. Registry ID: NCT02299401. cards.headline: Zhang 2022 Cochrane: combined regimens may beat misoprostol alone; oral route may fail more than vaginal (RR 3.68); sublingual versus buccal failure RR 1.11 in the one direct trial
cards.summary: Zhang 2022 Cochrane: combined regimens may beat misoprostol alone; oral route may fail more than vaginal (RR 3.68); sublingual versus buccal failure RR 1.11 in the one direct trial
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Zhang 2022)
cards.people: Randomised trials comparing medical methods for abortion before 12 weeks — prostaglandins alone and combined with mifepristone, letrozole, estradiol valerate, tamoxifen or methotrexate, by various routes; literature to February 2021.
cards.result: Combined regimens may be more effective than single agents. For misoprostol alone: failure to achieve complete abortion may be higher with oral than vaginal administration (risk ratio 3.68, 95% CI 1.56 to 8.71; 2 trials, 216 women; low-certainty) and slightly reduced with sublingual versus vaginal (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.28; 5 trials, 2,705 women; low-certainty). Sublingual versus buccal failure was similar or slightly higher sublingually (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.74; 1 study, 401 women — the Sheldon trial carded above). Almost all studies were conducted with good access to emergency services.
cards.watchOut: Most route estimates are low-certainty and several rest on single small trials; the review's firmest message is comparative — misoprostol alone is the fallback where combined regimens cannot be had, not their equal.
cards.source: Zhang J et al. Medical methods for first trimester abortion. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. PMID: 35608608. shelves.title: Adding letrozole to misoprostol splits by trimester: pooled first-trimester trials show more complete abortions (RR 1.45) and faster expulsion — the one blinded second-trimester trial found no gain at all
shelves.question: Does adding letrozole to misoprostol improve complete abortion rates versus misoprostol alone?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Letrozole/administration & dosage · Misoprostol/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Abortion, Induced/methods · Abortifacient Agents, Nonsteroidal/administration & dosage · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by stage of pregnancy and by evidence quality. The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis (Miller KAR et al., PMID: 41774466) pooled 12 randomised trials (1,524 women) of letrozole pretreatment plus misoprostol versus misoprostol alone for pharmacological abortion and miscarriage management: complete abortion was higher with letrozole (risk ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.25-1.68; p<0.00001), time to abortion shorter (mean difference -5.47 hours, 95% CI -8.68 to -2.26) and haemoglobin decline smaller (mean difference +0.26 g/dL, 95% CI 0.13-0.39), with comparable side effects (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.88-1.23) — but heterogeneity was very high (I²=73% for complete abortion, 99% for time to abortion). Against that stands the cleanest single trial, in the second trimester (Lee VC et al., PMID: 22078193): 130 women randomised double-blind to letrozole 7.5 mg for three days or placebo before misoprostol had near-identical abortion rates at 24 hours (93.8% versus 90.8%) and 48 hours (98.5% versus 95.4%). PROPOSED SPLIT: a probable first-trimester gain on pooled, heterogeneous trials; no demonstrated gain in the second trimester.

cards.headline: Miller 2026 meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 1,524 women): complete abortion RR 1.45 (95% CI 1.25-1.68) with letrozole plus misoprostol — I²=73%, and 99% for the time-to-abortion gain
cards.summary: Miller 2026 meta-analysis (12 RCTs, 1,524 women): complete abortion RR 1.45 (95% CI 1.25-1.68) with letrozole plus misoprostol — I²=73%, and 99% for the time-to-abortion gain
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Miller 2026)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials, 1,524 women, comparing letrozole pretreatment combined with vaginal or oral misoprostol versus misoprostol alone for medical abortion and medical management of miscarriage; registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251165732); risk of bias by RoB2, certainty by GRADE.
cards.result: Letrozole pretreatment increased complete abortion rates (risk ratio 1.45, 95% CI 1.25-1.68; p<0.00001; I²=73%), reduced time to abortion (mean difference -5.47 hours, 95% CI -8.68 to -2.26; p=0.0008; I²=99%) and minimised haemoglobin decline (mean difference +0.26 g/dL, 95% CI 0.13-0.39; p<0.001; I²=0%). Side effects were comparable (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.88-1.23; p=0.67).
cards.watchOut: The pooling mixes induced abortion with miscarriage management and multiple letrozole regimens; with I² of 73-99%, the average effect may describe no actual regimen well. A relative risk of 1.45 for 'complete abortion' also implies low baseline completion in the contributing trials — where misoprostol alone already completes over 90%, a 45% relative gain is arithmetically impossible, so the pooled trials are not the high-completion settings.
cards.source: Miller KAR et al. Comparative effectiveness of misoprostol plus letrozole versus misoprostol alone for pharmacological abortion: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. The European journal of contraception & reproductive health care : the official journal of the European Society of Contraception. 2026. PMID: 41774466. cards.headline: Lee 2011 (second trimester, n=130, double-blind): abortion by 24 hours 93.8% letrozole versus 90.8% placebo (p=.718); by 48 hours 98.5% versus 95.4% — no benefit
cards.summary: Lee 2011 (second trimester, n=130, double-blind): abortion by 24 hours 93.8% letrozole versus 90.8% placebo (p=.718); by 48 hours 98.5% versus 95.4% — no benefit
cards.people: 130 women requesting legal termination at 12-20 weeks in a university hospital, randomised to letrozole 7.5 mg daily for three days or placebo, followed by vaginal misoprostol 400 µg every three hours up to five doses on day three.
cards.result: Abortion rates were similar: 93.8% versus 90.8% within 24 hours (p=.718) and 98.5% versus 95.4% within 48 hours (p=.496). Median induction-to-abortion interval was 9.6 versus 10.6 hours (p=.145). All side effects were comparable. The authors conclude letrozole pretreatment does not significantly improve the misoprostol-only regimen in the second trimester.
cards.watchOut: Second-trimester physiology and a three-day letrozole lead-in differ from the first-trimester regimens dominating the meta-analysis — this trial refutes the combination at 12-20 weeks, not necessarily at under 12 weeks.

shelves.title: Miscarriage management: infection is 2–3% however you manage it (MIST) — surgery completes fastest, expectant and medical care trade that for far more unplanned admissions and curettage
shelves.question: For first-trimester miscarriage, how do expectant, medical and surgical management compare on complete evacuation, infection and later pregnancy?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/therapy · Activities of Daily Living · Dilatation and Curettage/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Postpartum Hemorrhage/etiology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious/therapy · Pregnancy Outcome · Pregnancy Trimester, First · Risk Factors · Sick Leave
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for surgery, on completion; with infection a tie across all three strategies, which is what makes the choice a preference decision. In the MIST trial (Trinder J et al., PMID: 16707509), 1,200 women under 13 weeks with early fetal demise or incomplete miscarriage were randomised to expectant, medical (vaginal misoprostol, preceded by mifepristone for early fetal demise) or surgical management: confirmed infection within 14 days was 3% expectant, 2% medical and 3% surgical — no significant differences — but unplanned admissions and unplanned surgical curettage were far commoner after expectant and medical management (risk differences for unplanned curettage versus surgery: -39% and -30% respectively, in surgery's favour). The Cochrane network meta-analysis (Ghosh J et al., PMID: 34061352; 78 trials, 17,795 women) ranked every method against expectant care for complete miscarriage: suction aspiration after cervical preparation RR 2.12 (95% CI 1.41 to 3.20), dilatation and curettage 1.49, suction aspiration 1.44, mifepristone plus misoprostol 1.42 (moderate-certainty) and misoprostol alone 1.30 — all surgical methods above all medical methods, and medical above expectant. Neither record reports later-pregnancy outcomes, a declared gap for that part of the question. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): surgery for speed and certainty of completion; medical or expectant care are safe alternatives for women who accept a one-in-three-ish chance of ending up with surgery anyway.

cards.headline: Trinder 2006 (MIST, n=1,200): infection 3% expectant, 2% medical, 3% surgical — but unplanned curettage far higher without planned surgery (risk differences -39% and -30%)
cards.summary: Trinder 2006 (MIST, n=1,200): infection 3% expectant, 2% medical, 3% surgical — but unplanned curettage far higher without planned surgery (risk differences -39% and -30%)
cards.people: 1,200 women at under 13 weeks' gestation with early fetal demise or incomplete miscarriage, in early pregnancy assessment units of seven UK hospitals, randomised to expectant management (n=399), medical management (n=398; vaginal misoprostol, preceded by oral mifepristone 24-48 hours earlier for early fetal demise) or surgical evacuation (n=403); outcomes included confirmed gynaecological infection at 14 days and eight weeks, unplanned admission and unplanned surgery. Trial registration (National Research Register): N0467011677/N0467073587.
cards.result: Confirmed infection within 14 days: 3% expectant versus 3% surgical (risk difference 0.2%, 95% CI -2.2% to 2.7%) and 2% medical versus surgical (0.7%, 95% CI -1.6% to 3.1%) — no differences. Unplanned hospital admissions were significantly higher after expectant (risk difference -41%, 95% CI -47% to -36%) and medical (-10%, -15% to -6%) management than after surgery, as was unplanned surgical curettage (expectant -39%, -44% to -34%; medical -30%, -35% to -25%).
cards.watchOut: MIST's medical arm used mifepristone plus misoprostol for missed miscarriage — results do not transfer directly to misoprostol-only regimens; and MIST reports no later-pregnancy outcomes, so fertility after each strategy is unanswered by this shelf's records.

cards.headline: Ghosh 2021 Cochrane network meta-analysis (78 trials, 17,795 women): complete miscarriage versus expectant — suction aspiration with cervical preparation RR 2.12, mifepristone plus misoprostol RR 1.42, misoprostol RR 1.30
cards.summary: Ghosh 2021 Cochrane network meta-analysis (78 trials, 17,795 women): complete miscarriage versus expectant — suction aspiration with cervical preparation RR 2.12, mifepristone plus misoprostol RR 1.42, misoprostol RR 1.30
cards.people: 78 randomised trials, 17,795 women from 37 countries, with missed or incomplete miscarriage at up to 14 weeks, comparing suction aspiration (with or without cervical preparation), dilatation and curettage, mifepristone plus misoprostol, misoprostol alone, and expectant management or placebo; 59 trials (12,591 women) contributed to the complete-miscarriage network.
cards.result: Five methods were more effective than expectant management or placebo for complete miscarriage: suction aspiration after cervical preparation (risk ratio 2.12, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.20; low-certainty), dilatation and curettage (1.49, 1.26-1.75), suction aspiration (1.44, 1.29-1.62), mifepristone plus misoprostol (1.42, 1.22-1.66; moderate-certainty) and misoprostol (1.30, 1.16-1.46). All surgical methods ranked above medical methods, which ranked above expectant care. For the composite of death or serious complications, estimates were wide and compatible with a range of effects; no deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: Most component evidence is low-certainty, and relative risks against expectant care flatter surgery where expectant completion is slow — absolute completion rates vary widely by miscarriage type (missed versus incomplete), which the subgroup analyses flag.
cards.source: Ghosh J et al. Methods for managing miscarriage: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34061352. shelves.title: Antibiotics before miscarriage surgery: AIMS found pelvic infection 4.1% versus 5.3% — not significant on its pragmatic definition (P=0.09), significant on the strict one (RR 0.60); Cochrane's low-bias sensitivity analysis agrees (RR 0.57)
shelves.question: Do prophylactic antibiotics before miscarriage surgery reduce pelvic infection versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/surgery · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Africa South of the Sahara · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Developing Countries · Double-Blind Method · Doxycycline/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Metronidazole/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pakistan · Pelvic Infection/epidemiology/prevention & control · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology/prevention & control · Pregnancy · Preoperative Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the effect is probably real and modest, and the headline trial technically missed. In AIMS (Lissauer D et al., PMID: 30865795), 3,412 women and adolescents in Malawi, Pakistan, Tanzania and Uganda were randomised to a single preoperative dose of doxycycline 400 mg plus metronidazole 400 mg or placebo before miscarriage surgery: pelvic infection within 14 days was 4.1% (68/1,676) versus 5.3% (90/1,684) — risk ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; P=0.09) on the pragmatic definition adopted before unblinding, but 1.5% versus 2.6% (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.96) on the original strict definition, with no significant difference in adverse events. The 2025 Cochrane review (Ahmed SI et al., PMID: 40231786; six trials, 4,371 women) found the overall estimate equally equivocal (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.28; low-certainty) but, in the sensitivity analysis limited to low-risk-of-bias studies (3,737 women), a 43% relative reduction in uterine infection (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.86; high-certainty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single cheap preoperative dose likely prevents roughly one pelvic infection per 80-90 operations in high-baseline-risk settings; in low-risk settings the absolute gain shrinks with the baseline rate.

cards.headline: Lissauer 2019 (AIMS, n=3,412): pelvic infection 4.1% versus 5.3% (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.56-1.04; P=0.09) pragmatic — 1.5% versus 2.6% (RR 0.60) on the strict definition
cards.summary: Lissauer 2019 (AIMS, n=3,412): pelvic infection 4.1% versus 5.3% (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.56-1.04; P=0.09) pragmatic — 1.5% versus 2.6% (RR 0.60) on the strict definition
cards.people: 3,412 women and adolescents undergoing surgery to complete a spontaneous abortion in low-resource settings (Malawi, Pakistan, Tanzania, Uganda), randomised to a single preoperative oral dose of doxycycline 400 mg plus metronidazole 400 mg (n=1,705) or identical placebos (n=1,707); primary outcome pelvic infection within 14 days. Registry ID: ISRCTN97143849.
cards.result: Pelvic infection occurred in 4.1% (68 of 1,676) on antibiotics versus 5.3% (90 of 1,684) on placebo (risk ratio 0.77, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.04; P=0.09) under the pragmatic definition (two or more clinical features, or one feature plus a clinical decision to give antibiotics), which was adopted before unblinding. Under the original strict definition (two or more features), infection was 1.5% (26/1,700) versus 2.6% (44/1,704) (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.96). There were no significant between-group differences in adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The trial's answer depends on which of its two definitions you read — a pre-unblinding definition change is legitimate, but a reader is entitled to weight the non-significant primary analysis heavily; baseline infection risk in these low-resource settings is also higher than in many high-income units, inflating the absolute benefit available elsewhere.
cards.source: Lissauer D et al. A Randomized Trial of Prophylactic Antibiotics for Miscarriage Surgery. The New England journal of medicine. 2019. PMID: 30865795. Registry ID: ISRCTN97143849. cards.headline: Ahmed 2025 Cochrane (6 trials, 4,371 women): overall RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.47-1.28, low-certainty) — but RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.37-0.86, high-certainty) in low-bias studies only
cards.summary: Ahmed 2025 Cochrane (6 trials, 4,371 women): overall RR 0.78 (95% CI 0.47-1.28, low-certainty) — but RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.37-0.86, high-certainty) in low-bias studies only
cards.people: Six randomised trials, 4,371 women without signs of infection undergoing uterine evacuation for early pregnancy loss, comparing prophylactic antibiotics with placebo or no treatment; literature to October 2023.
cards.result: Prophylactic antibiotics may have little or no effect on uterine infection overall (risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.28; I²=50%; low-certainty evidence). In the sensitivity analysis limited to the three low-risk-of-bias studies (3,737 participants, 85% of the total), the effect was larger and high-certainty: a 43% relative reduction in uterine infection (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.86; I²=0%).
cards.watchOut: The overall and sensitivity estimates tell different stories, and the difference is study quality — the honest read is 'the better trials show benefit', which is also exactly the pattern publication and conduct biases can produce; AIMS dominates the low-bias set.
cards.source: Ahmed SI et al. Prophylactic antibiotics for uterine evacuation procedures to manage miscarriage. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025. PMID: 40231786. cards.headline: Synthesis: two analyses of substantially the same trials converge on a relative reduction of about 40% in the trustworthy subset — worth one cheap dose where baseline infection risk is real

cards.people: The 3,412-woman AIMS trial in four low-resource countries and the six-trial Cochrane review (4,371 women) of antibiotic prophylaxis at miscarriage surgery.
cards.result: AIMS pragmatic: RR 0.77 (P=0.09); AIMS strict: RR 0.60 (95% CI 0.37-0.96). Cochrane overall: RR 0.78; low-bias sensitivity: RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.37-0.86). Absolute AIMS rates: 4.1% versus 5.3%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

shelves.title: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose clears postpartum anaemia faster and more completely than oral iron: still anaemic at 6 weeks in 18% versus 32% in the 1,400-woman Nigerian trial (RR 0.54)
shelves.question: In postpartum anaemia, does intravenous ferric carboxymaltose restore haemoglobin faster than oral iron?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Ferrous Compounds/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Female · Ferric Compounds/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Maltose/analogs & derivatives/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Nigeria · Administration, Oral · Adult · Adolescent · Young Adult · Middle Aged · Anemia/drug therapy · Postpartum Period · Administration, Intravenous · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — intravenous ferric carboxymaltose beats oral ferrous sulphate on speed, completeness and tolerability, in trials a decade and a half apart. The IVON-PP trial (Afolabi BB et al., PMID: 41865415) randomised 1,400 Nigerian women with moderate-to-severe postpartum anaemia (haemoglobin under 100 g/L) to a single intravenous ferric carboxymaltose dose (20 mg/kg, maximum 1,000 mg) or oral ferrous sulphate twice daily for six weeks: at six weeks, 18% (115/655) versus 32% (214/662) remained anaemic (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.44-0.66; p<0.001), and adverse events were less common intravenously (8% versus 20%). The earlier US trial (Van Wyck DB et al., PMID: 17666600; 352 women, haemoglobin 10 g/dL or less) found the same pattern: a haemoglobin rise of at least 2.0 g/dL came earlier (7.0 versus 14.0 days; P<.001), a rise of at least 3.0 g/dL was commoner (86.3% versus 60.4%), and haemoglobin above 12.0 g/dL was reached by 90.5% versus 68.6%, with no serious adverse drug reactions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): where intravenous access and the drug are available, one infusion replaces six weeks of tablets that many women do not finish — the gain is largest exactly where postpartum anaemia is commonest and follow-up hardest.

cards.summary: Afolabi 2026 (IVON-PP, n=1,400): anaemia at 6 weeks 18% (115/655) on ferric carboxymaltose versus 32% (214/662) on oral ferrous sulphate (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.44-0.66); adverse events 8% versus 20%
cards.people: 1,400 postpartum women aged 15-49 with moderate-to-severe anaemia (haemoglobin under 100 g/L), recruited 6-48 hours after birth at 20 health facilities across Nigeria, randomised to a single intravenous ferric carboxymaltose dose (20 mg/kg, maximum 1,000 mg; n=701) or oral ferrous sulphate 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) twice daily until six weeks postpartum (n=699); open-label with masked laboratory staff and statistician; primary outcome anaemia (haemoglobin under 110 g/L) at six weeks, assessed in 655 and 662 women. Registry ID: ISRCTN51426226.
cards.result: At six weeks, anaemia prevalence was 18% (115 of 655) in the ferric carboxymaltose group versus 32% (214 of 662) in the ferrous sulphate group (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.44-0.66; p<0.001) — a 46% relative reduction, 14 percentage points absolute. Adverse events were less common with intravenous iron (53 women, 8%, versus 143, 20%); headache was the commonest intravenous event (2%) and dark stools the commonest oral event (11%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label — women knew they had received the one-off infusion rather than six weeks of tablets, which can itself change adherence behaviour and symptom reporting; the comparison is against real-world oral iron use, imperfect adherence included, which is precisely the pragmatic point but flatters the infusion against perfectly-taken tablets.

cards.people: 352 anaemic postpartum women (haemoglobin 10 g/dL or less) within 10 days of delivery in the United States and Mexico, randomised to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (up to 1,000 mg over 15 minutes, repeated weekly to a calculated replacement dose; 174 women, mean total dose 1,403.1 mg) or oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg three times daily for six weeks (178 women). Registry ID: NCT00396292.
cards.result: Women on ferric carboxymaltose achieved a haemoglobin rise of at least 2.0 g/dL earlier (7.0 versus 14.0 days; P<.001), were more likely to achieve a rise of at least 3.0 g/dL at any time (86.3% versus 60.4%; P<.001) and to reach haemoglobin above 12.0 g/dL (90.5% versus 68.6%; P<.001). The proportion achieving at least a 2.0 g/dL rise overall was similar (96.4% versus 94.1%; P=.443). There were no serious adverse drug reactions, and the authors report better tolerability than oral iron.
cards.watchOut: A multi-dose intravenous regimen (mean total 1,403 mg over up to three visits) — not the single-dose strategy of the later trial — and haemoglobin thresholds are surrogate outcomes; neither trial was powered for transfusion, readmission or maternal functioning endpoints.
cards.source: Van Wyck DB et al. Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose compared with oral iron in the treatment of postpartum anemia: a randomized controlled trial. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2007.
