shelves.title: CORONIS (15,935 women): none of the five caesarean technique choices — entry, exteriorisation, uterine closure layers, peritoneal closure, suture material — changed death, infection, reoperation or transfusion, at 6 weeks or at 3 years
shelves.question: Which caesarean surgical techniques — closure, suture materials, bladder flap, peritoneal closure — change infection, pain and later outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Argentina · Cesarean Section/methods/statistics & numerical data · Cesarean Section, Repeat/methods/statistics & numerical data · Chile · Female · Ghana · Humans · India · Kenya · Pakistan · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/surgery · Pregnancy Outcome · Professional Practice/statistics & numerical data · Sudan · Wound Closure Techniques/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — across every technique pair CORONIS randomised, in the short term and at three years. The main trial (CORONIS Collaborative Group; first author Abalos E et al., PMID: 23721753) randomised 15,935 women at 19 sites in seven countries in a fractional factorial design across five pairs — blunt versus sharp abdominal entry, exteriorisation versus intra-abdominal uterine repair, single- versus double-layer uterine closure, peritoneal closure versus non-closure, and chromic catgut versus polyglactin-910 — and found no significant difference in the composite of death, maternal infectious morbidity, further operations or transfusion for any pair (risk ratios 0.90 to 1.06, every confidence interval crossing 1). The three-year follow-up (Abalos E et al., PMID: 27155903; 13,153 women, 84%) likewise found no differences in hernia, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, adhesion-type symptoms or subsequent pregnancy complications, including uterine rupture (RR 3.05, 95% CI 0.32-29.29 for catgut versus polyglactin-910 — a wide interval on a rare event). One element in the question — bladder flap formation — was not among CORONIS's five randomised pairs, a declared gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): surgeons may choose these techniques on time, cost and habit; the trial gives no outcome reason to prefer one over another.

cards.headline: Abalos 2013 (CORONIS): all five technique pairs null on the primary composite — RRs 1.03, 0.96, 0.96, 1.06 and 0.90, every CI crossing 1
cards.summary: Abalos 2013 (CORONIS): all five technique pairs null on the primary composite — RRs 1.03, 0.96, 0.96, 1.06 and 0.90, every CI crossing 1
cards.type: Randomised fractional factorial trial (CORONIS Collaborative Group 2013, CORONIS)
cards.people: 15,935 women undergoing a first or second caesarean through a planned transverse incision at 19 sites in Argentina, Chile, Ghana, India, Kenya, Pakistan and Sudan, each site randomised across three of five intervention pairs (blunt versus sharp entry; uterine exteriorisation versus intra-abdominal repair; single- versus double-layer uterine closure; peritoneal closure versus non-closure; chromic catgut versus polyglactin-910); unmasked; primary outcome the composite of death, maternal infectious morbidity, further operative procedures or transfusion over one unit, to six weeks. Registry ID: ISRCTN31089967.
cards.result: No statistically significant difference within any pair for the primary outcome: blunt versus sharp entry risk ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.91-1.17); exteriorisation versus intra-abdominal repair 0.96 (0.84-1.08); single- versus double-layer closure 0.96 (0.85-1.08); peritoneal closure versus non-closure 1.06 (0.94-1.20); chromic catgut versus polyglactin-910 0.90 (0.78-1.04). Of 144 serious adverse events, 26 were possibly related to the intervention, most being known surgical complications.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked surgeons and a composite outcome dominated by infection and transfusion; the fractional factorial design estimates each pair's main effect efficiently but assumes away interactions between techniques, and bladder flap formation — asked about in the question — was not randomised here.
cards.source: Abalos E et al. Caesarean section surgical techniques (CORONIS): a fractional, factorial, unmasked, randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2013. PMID: 23721753. cards.headline: Abalos 2016 (CORONIS 3-year follow-up, 13,153 women): still no differences — hernia, infertility, adhesion symptoms, later pregnancy complications all null
cards.summary: Abalos 2016 (CORONIS 3-year follow-up, 13,153 women): still no differences — hernia, infertility, adhesion symptoms, later pregnancy complications all null
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial (CORONIS Collaborative Group 2016)
cards.people: 13,153 of the 15,935 CORONIS women (84%) followed for a mean of 3.8 years, with outcomes assessed masked to the original allocation: pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, hysterectomy, hernia, infertility, ectopic pregnancy and outcomes of subsequent pregnancies, by the same five technique pairs. Registry ID: ISRCTN31089967.
cards.result: No evidence of difference for any main comparison: abdominal hernia after blunt versus sharp entry (adjusted RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.39-1.11); child death or serious morbidity (0.99, 0.83-1.17); infertility (0.91, 0.71-1.18) or ectopic pregnancy (0.50, 0.15-1.66) after exteriorisation versus intra-abdominal repair; maternal death (0.78, 0.46-1.32) or a pregnancy-complications composite (1.20, 0.75-1.90) for single- versus double-layer closure; infertility as an adhesion-symptom proxy (0.80, 0.61-1.06) for peritoneal closure versus non-closure; and uterine rupture in a subsequent pregnancy (3.05, 0.32-29.29) for catgut versus polyglactin-910. Severe adverse outcomes were uncommon.
cards.watchOut: Not powered for modest differences in rare serious events — the uterine-rupture interval (0.32-29.29) is the honest example — so 'no evidence of difference' at three years is not proof of exact equivalence for the outcomes women fear most.

shelves.title: Probiotics prevent lactational mastitis in trials (incidence RR 0.49 pooled; one strain trial 6% versus 14%) — but the asked comparison, probiotics versus antibiotics for treating established mastitis, has no randomised trial here
shelves.question: In lactational mastitis, do probiotics reduce pain and recurrence compared with antibiotics?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Breast Feeding · Female · Humans · Lactation · Mastitis/etiology/prevention & control · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Probiotics/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for prevention, which is what the randomised evidence actually tests; the treatment-versus-antibiotics comparison in the question is a declared gap with no carded trial. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Yu Q et al., PMID: 36084006; six randomised trials) found oral probiotics during pregnancy reduced mastitis incidence (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.69; p<0.0001) and reduced milk bacterial counts in both healthy women (mean difference -0.19, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.16) and women with mastitis (-0.89, 95% CI -1.34 to -0.43). The strain-specific trial (Jiménez E et al., PMID: 34576828) randomised 328 women to Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 — the strain named in the publication; no manufacturer is named in the record — from week 35 of pregnancy to week 12 postpartum, or placebo: mastitis occurred in 9 women (6%) versus 20 (14%), hazard ratio 0.41 (95% CI 0.190-0.915; p=0.029). Neither record compares a probiotic with an antibiotic for treating established mastitis, and neither reports pain or recurrence as a treatment outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for prevention in pregnancy and lactation, Tier C: small trials, one strain carrying much of the effect, and the clinical question as asked — treatment instead of antibiotics — remains untested in the carded evidence.

cards.headline: Yu 2022 meta-analysis (6 RCTs): mastitis incidence RR 0.49 (95% CI 0.35-0.69) with oral probiotics in pregnancy; milk bacterial counts also fell in women with mastitis (MD -0.89)
cards.summary: Yu 2022 meta-analysis (6 RCTs): mastitis incidence RR 0.49 (95% CI 0.35-0.69) with oral probiotics in pregnancy; milk bacterial counts also fell in women with mastitis (MD -0.89)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yu 2022)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials of oral probiotics for preventing or treating lactational mastitis, identified from six databases and trial registries; strains and regimens varied across trials, and the record does not name a manufacturer for any product.
cards.result: Oral probiotics during pregnancy reduced the incidence of mastitis (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.69; p<0.0001). After oral probiotics, milk bacterial counts fell significantly in healthy women (mean difference -0.19, 95% CI -0.23 to -0.16; p<0.00001) and in mastitis patients (mean difference -0.89, 95% CI -1.34 to -0.43; p=0.0001). The authors conclude probiotics are beneficial to a certain extent for incidence and some symptoms, while calling for high-quality multicentre trials.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials with differing strains — a class claim built on strain-specific biology; bacterial count is a surrogate, and the review reports no pooled pain, recurrence or antibiotic-sparing outcome for established mastitis.
cards.source: Yu Q et al. The preventive and therapeutic effects of probiotics on mastitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PloS one. 2022. PMID: 36084006. cards.headline: Jiménez 2021 (PS2 trial, n=328): mastitis in 6% on Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 versus 14% on placebo (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.190-0.915)
cards.summary: Jiménez 2021 (PS2 trial, n=328): mastitis in 6% on Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 versus 14% on placebo (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.190-0.915)
cards.people: 328 women in a multicountry, multicentre trial, randomised to the probiotic strain Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 (named in the publication; no company is named in the record) or placebo, from the 35th week of pregnancy until week 12 postpartum; mastitis defined as at least two of breast pain, erythema, engorgement not relieved by breastfeeding, and temperature over 38 °C. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: The probability of remaining free of mastitis was higher in the probiotic group (p=0.022, Kaplan-Meier log-rank): nine mastitis cases (6%) versus 20 (14%), with a hazard ratio for mastitis incidence of 0.41 (95% CI 0.190-0.915; p=0.029) — the authors express this as women in the probiotic group being 58% less likely (relative) to experience mastitis. The intervention was reported as safe.
cards.watchOut: A prevention trial in unselected pregnant women — it says nothing about treating a woman who already has mastitis, and its 29 total events make the hazard ratio fragile; one strain, one product formulation, no manufacturer named in the record, so currently sold products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Jiménez E et al. Ligilactobacillus salivarius PS2 Supplementation during Pregnancy and Lactation Prevents Mastitis: A Randomised Controlled Trial. Microorganisms. 2021. PMID: 34576828. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Synthesis: prevention evidence is consistent and placebo-controlled; treatment-versus-antibiotics evidence is absent — do not let the first answer the second

shelves.title: Menopausal symptoms beyond placebo splits in two: plant-based phytoestrogens trim daily hot flashes by about 1.3, while acupuncture ties sham exactly (hot flash scores 15.36 versus 15.04)
shelves.question: Does acupuncture — or other plant-based and complementary therapies — reduce menopausal symptoms beyond placebo?
shelves.mesh: Complementary Therapies · Female · Hot Flashes/drug therapy · Humans · Menopause · Middle Aged · Phytoestrogens/therapeutic use · Phytotherapy · Plant Preparations/therapeutic use · Sweating · Vaginal Diseases/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the plant-based half shows a modest effect over placebo; the acupuncture half, tested against a proper sham, shows none. The JAMA systematic review and meta-analysis (Franco OH et al., PMID: 27327802) pooled 62 trials (6,653 women): phytoestrogens were associated with 1.31 fewer daily hot flashes than control (pooled mean difference of changes -1.31, 95% CI -2.02 to -0.61) and a small improvement in vaginal dryness score (-0.31, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.10), but no significant reduction in night sweats (-2.14, 95% CI -5.57 to 1.29); several herbal remedies, though not Chinese medicinal herbs, were associated with fewer vasomotor symptoms — with the warning that 74% of the trials were at high risk of bias in at least three quality areas. The acupuncture trial (Ee C et al., PMID: 26784863) randomised 327 women with at least seven moderate flushes daily to standardised Chinese-medicine acupuncture or non-insertive sham over eight weeks: end-of-treatment hot flash scores were 15.36 versus 15.04 (mean difference 0.33, 95% CI -1.87 to 2.52; P=0.77), with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED SPLIT: phytoestrogen supplements — a small, low-quality-evidence gain; acupuncture — no gain beyond a credible sham.

cards.headline: Franco 2016 meta-analysis (62 trials, 6,653 women): phytoestrogens -1.31 daily hot flashes (95% CI -2.02 to -0.61) and less vaginal dryness — night sweats not significantly reduced; 74% of trials high risk of bias
cards.summary: Franco 2016 meta-analysis (62 trials, 6,653 women): phytoestrogens -1.31 daily hot flashes (95% CI -2.02 to -0.61) and less vaginal dryness — night sweats not significantly reduced; 74% of trials high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Franco 2016)
cards.people: 62 randomised trials, 6,653 women, of plant-based therapies (phytoestrogens including dietary and supplemental soy isoflavones, herbal remedies, and Chinese medicinal herbs) for menopausal hot flashes, night sweats and vaginal dryness; literature to March 2016. The record names therapy classes, not commercial products or companies.
cards.result: Phytoestrogens were associated with a decrease in daily hot flashes (pooled mean difference of changes -1.31, 95% CI -2.02 to -0.61) and in vaginal dryness score (-0.31, 95% CI -0.52 to -0.10), but not in night sweats (-2.14, 95% CI -5.57 to 1.29). Soy isoflavones specifically were associated with improvement in daily hot flashes (-0.79, -1.35 to -0.23) and vaginal dryness (-0.26, -0.48 to -0.04). Several herbal remedies, but not Chinese medicinal herbs, were associated with an overall decrease in vasomotor symptom frequency. Substantial heterogeneity and suboptimal quality were present: 46 of 62 trials (74%) were at high risk of bias in three or more areas.
cards.watchOut: With three quarters of trials at high risk of bias and strong placebo responses in this field, the -1.31 average is best read as an upper bound; no product or company is named in the record, so no shelf claim attaches to any bottle on sale, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Franco OH et al. Use of Plant-Based Therapies and Menopausal Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27327802. cards.headline: Ee 2016 (n=327): acupuncture versus sham — hot flash scores 15.36 versus 15.04 at end of treatment (difference 0.33, 95% CI -1.87 to 2.52; P=0.77)
cards.summary: Ee 2016 (n=327): acupuncture versus sham — hot flash scores 15.36 versus 15.04 at end of treatment (difference 0.33, 95% CI -1.87 to 2.52; P=0.77)
cards.people: 327 women older than 40 in the late menopausal transition or postmenopause in Australia, with at least seven moderate hot flashes daily and a Chinese-medicine diagnosis of kidney yin deficiency, randomised to ten treatments over eight weeks of standardised Chinese-medicine needle acupuncture (n=163) or non-insertive sham acupuncture (n=164); participants, assessors and investigators blinded (treating acupuncturists were not). Registry ID (Australia New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry): ACTRN12611000393954.
cards.result: Mean hot flash scores at the end of treatment were 15.36 in the acupuncture group and 15.04 in the sham group (mean difference 0.33, 95% CI -1.87 to 2.52; P=0.77). No serious adverse events were reported. The authors conclude Chinese-medicine acupuncture was not superior to non-insertive sham acupuncture for moderately severe menopausal hot flashes.
cards.watchOut: One acupuncture style, one diagnostic subgroup (kidney yin deficiency), and a predominantly Caucasian sample without breast cancer or surgical menopause — the null is strong for this protocol and population, less decisive for every acupuncture variant, but the burden of proof now sits with proponents.
cards.source: Ee C et al. Acupuncture for Menopausal Hot Flashes: A Randomized Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2016. PMID: 26784863. Registry ID: ACTRN12611000393954. shelves.title: Pelvic-floor physical therapy beat overnight lidocaine for provoked vestibulodynia pain — 1.8 points better on a 0–10 scale, held at 6 months
shelves.question: In provoked vestibulodynia and vulvodynia, do medical, physical-therapy or surgical treatments reduce pain versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Anesthetics, Local/therapeutic use · Biofeedback, Psychology/methods · Coitus · Dilatation/methods · Female · Humans · Lidocaine/therapeutic use · Muscle Stretching Exercises · Musculoskeletal Manipulations/methods · Patient Satisfaction · Pelvic Floor · Physical Therapy Modalities · Psychological Distress · Sexual Dysfunction, Physiological/physiopathology/psychology · Sexual Dysfunctions, Psychological/physiopathology/psychology · Vulvodynia/physiopathology/psychology/therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for multimodal pelvic-floor physical therapy, on the one large head-to-head trial. In 212 women randomised to 10 weeks of weekly physical therapy (education, pelvic-floor exercises with biofeedback, manual therapy, dilation) or overnight 5% lidocaine ointment, pain during intercourse fell 1.8 points more on a 0–10 scale with physical therapy (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3, P<.001), the gap held at 6 months (1.8; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5), and 79% of the physical-therapy group rated themselves very much or much improved versus 39% on lidocaine. An older three-way trial (78 women) found vestibulectomy, group cognitive–behavioural therapy and biofeedback all reduced pain by 6 months, with surgery ahead on completer analysis — but 7 women assigned to surgery never had it, and there is no placebo arm anywhere in this evidence. No drug has beaten placebo in a trial carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): physical therapy is the best-supported first treatment; surgery helps selected patients in one small old trial; the drug evidence is thin.

cards.headline: Morin 2021: intercourse pain fell 1.8 points more with physical therapy than lidocaine (95% CI 1.2–2.3); 79% vs 39% much or very much improved
cards.summary: Morin 2021: intercourse pain fell 1.8 points more with physical therapy than lidocaine (95% CI 1.2–2.3); 79% vs 39% much or very much improved
cards.people: 212 women with provoked vestibulodynia recruited from the community and 4 Canadian university hospitals, randomised to weekly multimodal physical therapy sessions or overnight topical lidocaine 5% ointment for 10 weeks; 201 (95%) completed post-treatment assessment and 195 (92%) the 6-month follow-up. Outcome assessors, investigators and analysts were masked to allocation.
cards.result: Pain intensity during intercourse (0–10 numeric rating scale) improved more with physical therapy: between-group post-treatment difference 1.8 points (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3, P<.001), maintained at 6 months (1.8; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5). Physical therapy was also better on pain quality, sexual function, sexual distress and satisfaction at both time points. On the Patient Global Impression of Change, 79% of the physical-therapy group reported being very much or much improved versus 39% of the lidocaine group (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is an active first-line treatment, not placebo or usual care, and patients could not be blinded to receiving hands-on therapy — expectation effects on a pain score cannot be excluded. Lidocaine's own effect versus no treatment is not measured here.
cards.source: Morin M et al. Multimodal physical therapy versus topical lidocaine for provoked vestibulodynia: a multicenter, randomized trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2021. PMID: 32818475. Registry ID: NCT01455350. cards.headline: Bergeron 2001: vestibulectomy, group CBT and biofeedback all cut pain by 6 months — surgery ahead in completers, but 7 of its assignees never had the operation
cards.summary: Bergeron 2001: vestibulectomy, group CBT and biofeedback all cut pain by 6 months — surgery ahead in completers, but 7 of its assignees never had the operation
cards.people: 78 women with dyspareunia resulting from vulvar vestibulitis (now termed provoked vestibulodynia), randomised to 12 weeks of group cognitive–behavioural therapy, 12 weeks of surface electromyographic biofeedback, or vestibulectomy, assessed at post-treatment and 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: Completers in all three groups reported statistically significant reductions on pain measures (McGill Pain Questionnaire indices, vestibular pain index, pain during intercourse) at post-treatment and 6 months, and all groups improved on psychological adjustment and sexual function. The vestibulectomy group was significantly more successful than the other two groups on pain measures in the completer analysis; intention-to-treat analysis supported the general pattern.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-centre and 25 years old, with diagnostic labels that have since changed; seven women assigned to vestibulectomy did not undergo it, so the surgery advantage rests partly on who actually received it. No placebo or waiting-list arm.
cards.source: Bergeron S et al. A randomized comparison of group cognitive--behavioral therapy, surface electromyographic biofeedback, and vestibulectomy in the treatment of dyspareunia resulting from vulvar vestibulitis. cards.summary: Synthesis: one modern trial puts physical therapy first; everything else is small, old, or unblinded against placebo
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 290 women with provoked vestibulodynia/vulvar vestibulitis: a 212-woman multicentre trial of physical therapy versus lidocaine (10 weeks, 6-month follow-up) and a 78-woman three-way trial of vestibulectomy versus group CBT versus biofeedback (6-month follow-up).
cards.result: Physical therapy beat lidocaine by 1.8 points on a 0–10 intercourse-pain scale (95% CI 1.2 to 2.3), with 79% versus 39% much or very much improved. In the older trial all three active treatments reduced pain, surgery most in completers. No carded trial shows a drug beating placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the physical-therapy claim rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial could blind participants to hands-on or surgical treatment, and pain is self-reported — the honest ceiling for this shelf is POSSIBLE until a second physical-therapy trial replicates Morin 2021.

shelves.title: Laser for vulvar lichen sclerosus: one small trial's dual laser beat clobetasol on the clinician's score but not on symptoms — and pooled ablative-laser trials show no significant benefit
shelves.question: In vulvar lichen sclerosus, does laser treatment control disease as well as ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol)?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus · Glucocorticoids · Clobetasol/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Lasers, Solid-State/therapeutic use · Steroids/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which laser and which outcome. In the one head-to-head randomised trial (66 women), non-ablative Nd:YAG/Er:YAG dual laser (4 treatments over 4 months) lowered the objective clinical lichen sclerosus score by −2.34 points versus −0.95 on clobetasol propionate over 6 months (P<0.001), and satisfaction was higher with laser (P=0.035) — but symptom scores improved similarly in both arms with no significant difference. The 2026 meta-analysis of the different, ablative approach (fractional CO2 laser; 3 randomised trials, 151 patients) found no statistically significant benefit on symptom burden (mean difference 1.04; 95% CI −4.71 to 6.79) or disease severity (standardised mean difference −0.27; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.94). PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible objective-score edge for one dual-laser protocol in one small unblinded trial; no demonstrated benefit for ablative CO2 laser; clobetasol remains the proven standard, and this premalignant disease needs follow-up whichever treatment is used.

cards.headline: Zivanovic 2024: clinical LS score fell −2.34 on dual laser vs −0.95 on clobetasol (P<0.001) — symptom scores improved equally, satisfaction favoured laser
cards.summary: Zivanovic 2024: clinical LS score fell −2.34 on dual laser vs −0.95 on clobetasol (P<0.001) — symptom scores improved equally, satisfaction favoured laser
cards.people: 66 women with vulvar lichen sclerosus at a single Swiss tertiary referral centre, randomised 2:1 to Nd:YAG/Er:YAG dual laser (44 women; treatments at 0, 1, 2 and 4 months) or topical clobetasol propionate in decreasing doses for 6 months (22 women).
cards.result: The total objective clinical lichen sclerosus score decreased by −2.34 ± 1.20 (95% CI −2.71 to −1.98) with laser versus −0.95 ± 0.90 (95% CI −1.35 to −0.56) with steroid (P<0.001). Subjective severity (visual analogue scale) and vulvovaginal symptom questionnaire scores improved similarly in both arms without significant between-group differences. Patient satisfaction was higher in the laser arm (P=0.035). Laser treatment was reported as safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 66 women, no blinding and no sham-laser arm — the clinician-scored primary outcome is exactly the kind an unblinded assessor can move, while the patient-scored symptoms, which patients feel, did not separate. Follow-up is 6 months in a lifelong, premalignant condition.
cards.source: Zivanovic I et al. Nd:YAG/Er:YAG dual laser compared with topical steroid to treat vulvar lichen sclerosus: A randomised controlled trial. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2024. PMID: 38149520. cards.headline: Chedid 2026 meta-analysis of ablative laser: no significant benefit on symptoms (MD 1.04; 95% CI −4.71 to 6.79) or severity (SMD −0.27; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.94) across 3 RCTs
cards.summary: Chedid 2026 meta-analysis of ablative laser: no significant benefit on symptoms (MD 1.04; 95% CI −4.71 to 6.79) or severity (SMD −0.27; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.94) across 3 RCTs
cards.people: 3 randomised trials totalling 151 women with confirmed vulvar lichen sclerosus, evaluating fractional ablative CO2 laser versus sham laser, topical clobetasol propionate 0.05%, or a low-dose CO2 laser protocol, with follow-up of 18 to 32 weeks.
cards.result: Laser therapy produced a non-significant reduction in total symptom visual analogue scores (mean difference 1.04; 95% CI −4.71 to 6.79; P=0.52; I²=58%) and in lichen sclerosus severity scores (standardised mean difference −0.27; 95% CI −1.47 to 0.94; P=0.44; I²=65%). No adverse events were reported in the included trials. The authors conclude larger, adequately powered trials are needed before laser can be recommended as primary or adjunctive treatment.
cards.watchOut: This pools ablative fractional CO2 laser — a different technology from the non-ablative dual laser in the head-to-head trial — so it does not directly refute that trial; it does show the wider laser literature is small, short and null on the outcomes patients report.
cards.source: Chedid ML et al. Efficacy of ablative laser therapy for vulvar lichen sclerosus: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Lasers in medical science. 2026. shelves.title: Topical progesterone is not a clobetasol substitute in vulvar lichen sclerosus: clinician score improved 4.6→2.9 on clobetasol but only 4.6→4.5 on progesterone in the one double-blind trial
shelves.question: In vulvar lichen sclerosus, is topical progesterone as effective as clobetasol propionate?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Chronic Disease · Clobetasol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Lichen Sclerosus et Atrophicus · Ointments/therapeutic use · Pilot Projects · Progesterone/therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Vulvar Lichen Sclerosus/chemically induced/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — harm here means a worse disease outcome than standard care, not toxicity. The single double-blind randomised trial (37 premenopausal women with previously untreated, biopsy-confirmed early vulvar lichen sclerosus) compared progesterone 8% ointment with clobetasol propionate 0.05% for 12 weeks. The clinician-rated severity score improved from 4.6 to 2.9 on clobetasol but barely moved on progesterone (4.6 to 4.5); the between-group difference favoured clobetasol by 1.61 points (95% CI 0.44 to 2.77, P=0.009). Symptoms also improved more on clobetasol (score 4.7→1.9 versus 4.5→3.1; difference 1.32, 95% CI −0.25 to 2.89, P=0.095), and complete remission on biopsy was seen in 13 of 16 (81.3%) on clobetasol versus 6 of 10 (60%) on progesterone. No drug-related serious adverse event occurred in either arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): progesterone 8% is inferior to clobetasol at 12 weeks — patients swapped to it would be under-treated, on one small pilot trial.

cards.headline: Günthert 2022: clinical score 4.6→2.9 on clobetasol vs 4.6→4.5 on progesterone (difference 1.61; 95% CI 0.44–2.77; P=0.009); biopsy remission 81.3% vs 60%
cards.summary: Günthert 2022: clinical score 4.6→2.9 on clobetasol vs 4.6→4.5 on progesterone (difference 1.61; 95% CI 0.44–2.77; P=0.009); biopsy remission 81.3% vs 60%
cards.people: 37 premenopausal women with histologically confirmed, previously untreated early-onset vulvar lichen sclerosus at a single centre, randomised 1:1 to clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment (20 women) or progesterone 8% ointment (17 women) for 12 weeks; response was also assessed by end-of-treatment biopsy where available (16 clobetasol, 10 progesterone).
cards.result: Mean clinical lichen sclerosus severity score improved from 4.6 (SD 2.8) to 2.9 (SD 2.2) on clobetasol and from 4.6 (SD 2.0) to 4.5 (SD 1.7) on progesterone — a difference in favour of clobetasol of 1.61 points (95% CI 0.44 to 2.77, P=0.009). Mean symptom severity score improved from 4.7 to 1.9 on clobetasol versus 4.5 to 3.1 on progesterone (difference 1.32; 95% CI −0.25 to 2.89, P=0.095). Complete remission on biopsy: 13 of 16 (81.3%) on clobetasol versus 6 of 10 (60%) on progesterone (odds ratio in favour of clobetasol 0.35; 95% CI 0.06 to 2.06, P=0.234). No drug-related serious adverse event occurred.
cards.watchOut: A 37-woman pilot in premenopausal, early, untreated disease over 12 weeks — it cannot speak to postmenopausal women, established scarring disease, or longer courses. But the direction is consistent across clinician score, symptoms and biopsy, and the trial was double-blind.
cards.source: Gunthert AR et al. Efficacy of topical progesterone versus topical clobetasol propionate in patients with vulvar Lichen sclerosus - A double-blind randomized phase II pilot study. cards.summary: Synthesis: the only randomised test says progesterone under-treats — clobetasol stays the standard it failed to match

cards.result: Clinician severity score: 4.6→2.9 on clobetasol versus 4.6→4.5 on progesterone (difference 1.61; 95% CI 0.44 to 2.77; P=0.009). shelves.title: Intravenous calcium prevents ovarian hyperstimulation about as well as cabergoline — moderate/severe OHSS 10.6% on calcium vs 8.2% on cabergoline head-to-head, and 7% vs 23% against placebo
shelves.question: In ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome prevention, is intravenous calcium as effective as cabergoline?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cabergoline/administration & dosage · Calcium Gluconate/administration & dosage · Female · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Humans · Incidence · Infusions, Intravenous · Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Ovulation Induction/adverse effects/methods · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — yes, on the randomised record, calcium looks as effective as cabergoline, and it has its own placebo-controlled win. In the head-to-head trial (170 high-risk IVF patients), moderate or severe OHSS occurred in 8.24% on cabergoline (7 of 85) versus 10.59% on intravenous calcium gluconate (9 of 85) (P=.599; OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.14), with one severe case in each group and similar implantation, clinical and ongoing pregnancy rates. In the earlier double-blind placebo-controlled trial (200 high-risk women), calcium infusion cut overall OHSS from 23% on saline placebo to 7% (moderate 1% vs 8%; severe 0% vs 4%). Neither trial was powered to prove equivalence formally, and both come from single research groups in one region. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): calcium infusion is a credible, cheap alternative to cabergoline for OHSS prevention in high-risk cycles.

cards.headline: Fouda 2022 head-to-head: moderate/severe OHSS 8.24% on cabergoline vs 10.59% on calcium (P=.599) — pregnancy rates also similar
cards.summary: Fouda 2022 head-to-head: moderate/severe OHSS 8.24% on cabergoline vs 10.59% on calcium (P=.599) — pregnancy rates also similar
cards.people: 170 IVF patients at high risk of OHSS, stimulated with a long luteal GnRH agonist protocol, randomised 1:1 to cabergoline 0.5 mg orally daily for 8 days from the day of hCG administration, or intravenous calcium gluconate (10 mL of 10% in 200 mL saline) daily for 4 days from the day of ovum pickup.
cards.result: Six patients in the cabergoline group and eight in the calcium group developed moderate OHSS, and one patient in each group developed severe OHSS: moderate/severe OHSS incidence 8.24% versus 10.59% (P=.599; OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.269 to 2.138). Implantation rates (16.91% vs 15.84%, P=.771), clinical pregnancy rates (35.29% vs 32.94%, P=.746) and ongoing pregnancy rates (30.59% vs 28.24%, P=.736) were similar. Both treatments were reported as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Open comparison with no placebo arm and no pre-specified non-inferiority margin: 'no significant difference' in 170 patients is compatible with calcium being modestly worse (the confidence interval runs to an odds ratio of 2.14). The stimulation protocol (long agonist) is no longer the dominant high-risk protocol in many centres.
cards.source: Fouda UM et al. Cabergoline versus calcium infusion in the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: a randomised controlled study. Journal of obstetrics and gynaecology : the journal of the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 2022. PMID: 34270379. Registry ID: NCT02875587. randomised controlled trial (fouda 2022) 170 ivf patients at high risk of ohss, stimulated with a long luteal gnrh agonist protocol, randomised 1:1 to cabergoline 0.5 mg orally daily for 8 days from the day of hcg administration, or intravenous calcium gluconate (10 ml of 10% in 200 ml saline) daily for 4 days from the day of ovum pickup. six patients in the cabergoline group and eight in the calcium group developed moderate ohss, and one patient in each group developed severe ohss: moderate/severe ohss incidence 8.24% versus 10.59% (p=.599; or 0.76, 95% ci 0.269 to 2.138). implantation rates (16.91% vs 15.84%, p=.771), clinical pregnancy rates (35.29% vs 32.94%, p=.746) and ongoing pregnancy rates (30.59% vs 28.24%, p=.736) were similar. both treatments were reported as well tolerated. open comparison with no placebo arm and no pre-specified non-inferiority margin: 'no significant difference' in 170 patients is compatible with calcium being modestly worse (the confidence interval runs to an odds ratio of 2.14). the stimulation protocol (long agonist) is no longer the dominant high-risk protocol in many centres. fouda um et al. cabergoline versus calcium infusion in the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: a randomised controlled study. journal of obstetrics and gynaecology : the journal of the institute of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2022. pmid: 34270379. registry id: nct02875587. mesh: adult · cabergoline/administration & dosage · calcium gluconate/administration & dosage · female · fertilization in vitro/methods · humans · incidence · infusions, intravenous · ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · ovulation induction/adverse effects/methods · pregnancy · pregnancy rate · prospective studies · single-blind method · treatment outcome

cards.headline: El-Khayat 2015 double-blind: OHSS in 7% on calcium vs 23% on placebo — severe OHSS 0% vs 4%, moderate 1% vs 8%
cards.summary: El-Khayat 2015 double-blind: OHSS in 7% on calcium vs 23% on placebo — severe OHSS 0% vs 4%, moderate 1% vs 8%
cards.people: 200 women at risk of OHSS undergoing IVF/ICSI at a university hospital and a private IVF centre, randomised to intravenous calcium gluconate (10 mL of 10% in 100 mL saline) on the day of ovum pickup and days 1, 2 and 3 after (100 women), or 100 mL saline placebo on the same schedule (100 women).
cards.result: OHSS incidence was 7% (7 of 100) in the calcium group versus 23% (23 of 100) in the placebo group. Moderate OHSS: 1% versus 8%. Severe OHSS: 0% versus 4%. The authors report the differences as statistically significant, and pregnancy rates were not reduced by calcium infusion.
cards.watchOut: Single research group, one region, and a 23% placebo-arm OHSS rate that reflects its era and risk definition; modern antagonist protocols with agonist trigger start from a much lower baseline risk, so the absolute gain today would be smaller.
cards.source: El-Khayat W et al. Calcium infusion for the prevention of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome: a double-blind randomized controlled trial. Fertility and sterility. 2015. PMID: 25552412. cards.headline: Synthesis: calcium has both halves of the argument — a placebo win and a head-to-head draw with the standard drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: calcium has both halves of the argument — a placebo win and a head-to-head draw with the standard drug
cards.people: Two randomised trials in high-risk IVF patients: calcium versus placebo, double-blind, 200 women; calcium versus cabergoline, 170 women.
cards.result: Versus placebo: OHSS 7% versus 23% (severe 0% versus 4%). Versus cabergoline: moderate/severe OHSS 10.59% versus 8.24% (P=.599), pregnancy outcomes similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the placebo-controlled benefit rests on one trial and the head-to-head trial had no non-inferiority margin.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate widespread agonist-trigger/freeze-all practice, which has independently driven severe OHSS rates down; where those are used, the added value of either prophylactic drug is less certain.

shelves.title: Programmed intermittent epidural bolus beats continuous infusion for labour analgesia in pooled trials — less drug, less breakthrough pain, higher spontaneous delivery rate
shelves.question: For maintenance of labour epidural analgesia, does programmed intermittent epidural bolus give better analgesia and less motor block than continuous infusion?
shelves.mesh: Analgesia, Epidural · Analgesia, Obstetrical · Anesthetics, Local · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Pain Measurement · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Ropivacaine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pooled randomised trials favour programmed intermittent epidural bolus (PIEB) over continuous epidural infusion (CEI) for maintaining labour analgesia. The 2022 meta-analysis found PIEB used less ropivacaine (weighted mean difference −15.83; 95% CI −19.06 to −12.60) and less sufentanil (WMD −4.93), with fewer patients needing patient-controlled boluses (OR 0.27; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.51), less breakthrough pain (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.80), lower pain scores at 2–5 hours, a higher spontaneous vaginal delivery rate (OR 1.37; 95% CI 1.08 to 1.75), shorter first and second stages, and higher satisfaction (weighted mean difference 0.91; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.39). Within PIEB itself, the Wong 2011 randomised trial (190 women) showed a 10 mL bolus every 60 minutes used less bupivacaine per hour (median 8.8 mg) than 5 mL every 30 minutes (10.0 mg) or 2.5 mL every 15 minutes (10.4 mg) (P=0.005), with no difference in pain or satisfaction. Heterogeneity in the pooled analysis is high for several outcomes, and motor block — asked about in the question — was not consistently separated in the pooled record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): PIEB is the better-supported maintenance mode, with the widest bolus interval the most drug-sparing regimen tested.

cards.headline: Wang 2022 meta-analysis: PIEB cut breakthrough pain (OR 0.47) and PCEA demand (OR 0.27), raised spontaneous delivery (OR 1.37) and satisfaction versus CEI
cards.summary: Wang 2022 meta-analysis: PIEB cut breakthrough pain (OR 0.47) and PCEA demand (OR 0.27), raised spontaneous delivery (OR 1.37) and satisfaction versus CEI
cards.people: Randomised trials of programmed intermittent epidural bolus versus continuous epidural infusion in labouring parturients, searched to July 2021 across PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library; 19 studies reported mode of delivery, 13 reported satisfaction, and 8 reported duration of analgesia outcomes.
cards.result: PIEB was associated with lower total ropivacaine consumption (weighted mean difference −15.83; 95% CI −19.06 to −12.60; P<.00001) and sufentanil consumption (WMD −4.93), fewer patients requiring patient-controlled epidural boluses (OR 0.27; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.51), less breakthrough pain (OR 0.47; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.80; P=.005), lower pain scores at 30 minutes and at 2, 4 and 5 hours, a higher rate of normal (spontaneous vaginal) delivery (OR 1.37; 95% CI 1.08 to 1.75; P=.01), shorter first stage (WMD −10.52 minutes) and second stage (WMD −1.48 minutes), and higher satisfaction scores (WMD 0.91; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.39; P=.0003).
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is substantial for many outcomes (I² up to 100% for some), epidural solutions and bolus regimens varied across trials, and the pooled record does not give a clean pooled estimate for motor block — the outcome the shelf question names — so the motor-block advantage is asserted by the technique's rationale more than proven by this synthesis.
cards.source: Wang XX et al. Programmed intermittent epidural bolus in parturients: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35119026. cards.headline: Wong 2011: within PIEB, 10 mL hourly used the least bupivacaine (8.8 mg/h vs 10.0 and 10.4 mg/h; P=0.005) with identical pain scores and satisfaction
cards.summary: Wong 2011: within PIEB, 10 mL hourly used the least bupivacaine (8.8 mg/h vs 10.0 and 10.4 mg/h; P=0.005) with identical pain scores and satisfaction
cards.people: 190 healthy term nulliparous women in spontaneous labour with combined spinal–epidural analgesia, randomised to programmed intermittent bolus regimens of bupivacaine 0.625 mg/mL with fentanyl: 2.5 mL every 15 minutes, 5 mL every 30 minutes, or 10 mL every 60 minutes, with patient-controlled and clinician boluses available for breakthrough pain.
cards.result: Median adjusted bupivacaine consumption per hour of labour was 8.8 mg (IQR 8.0–9.7) in the 10 mL/60-minute group versus 10.0 mg (9.3–10.8) in the 5 mL/30-minute group and 10.4 mg (9.6–11.2) in the 2.5 mL/15-minute group (P=0.005). There were no differences in pain-score area under the curve, pain at delivery, patient-controlled bolus requests or use, manual boluses, time to first rescue dose, or satisfaction.
cards.watchOut: This trial compares PIEB regimens with each other, not PIEB with continuous infusion — it answers 'which bolus schedule' rather than the shelf's headline question, and its drug-sparing gradient is modest in absolute milligrams per hour.
cards.source: Wong CA et al. The effect of manipulation of the programmed intermittent bolus time interval and injection volume on total drug use for labor epidural analgesia: a randomized controlled trial. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2011. PMID: 21430035. cards.headline: Synthesis: the mode is settled in PIEB's favour by pooling, the schedule by one careful trial — motor block remains the thin spot
cards.summary: Synthesis: the mode is settled in PIEB's favour by pooling, the schedule by one careful trial — motor block remains the thin spot
cards.people: A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised PIEB-versus-CEI trials in labour (19 trials reporting delivery mode) plus a 190-woman randomised comparison of three PIEB bolus regimens.
cards.result: PIEB versus CEI: less local anaesthetic and opioid, breakthrough pain OR 0.47 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.80), spontaneous delivery OR 1.37 (95% CI 1.08 to 1.75), higher satisfaction. Within PIEB: 10 mL every 60 minutes used 8.8 mg/h bupivacaine versus 10.4 mg/h for 2.5 mL every 15 minutes (P=0.005), comfort unchanged. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: High between-trial heterogeneity and the absence of a pooled motor-block estimate keep this at POSSIBLE; individual units' pumps, solutions and staffing may not reproduce the pooled delivery-mode effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang XX et al. Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35119026); Wong CA et al. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2011 (PMID: 21430035).

shelves.title: Amnioinfusion for meconium-stained liquor: large perinatal gains only where monitoring is limited (aspiration syndrome RR 0.17, perinatal death RR 0.24) — no substantive benefit where surveillance is standard
shelves.question: In labour with meconium-stained liquor, does amnioinfusion reduce caesarean delivery and neonatal morbidity?
shelves.mesh: Amnion · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Injections · Meconium · Meconium Aspiration Syndrome/prevention & control · Obstetric Labor Complications/prevention & control · Perinatal Mortality · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sodium Chloride/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by setting, and the split is the finding. The Cochrane review (14 studies, 4,435 women with moderate or thick meconium staining) found, in settings with limited peripartum surveillance (3 studies), meconium aspiration syndrome at a relative risk of 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.52; 1,144 women) and perinatal mortality at a relative risk of 0.24 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.53; 1,151 women) with amnioinfusion, alongside fewer caesareans for fetal distress and overall. In settings with standard peripartum surveillance there was no significant reduction in meconium aspiration syndrome, perinatal death or severe morbidity, or maternal death or severe morbidity; caesareans for fetal distress (but not overall) fell, and when the reviewers excluded higher-risk-of-bias trials in a sensitivity analysis, the benefits for every outcome disappeared. The trials are too small to exclude rare serious maternal harms. PROPOSED SPLIT: amnioinfusion is a substantive intervention where fetal monitoring is limited, and an unproven one where it is standard.

cards.headline: Hofmeyr 2014 Cochrane: limited-surveillance settings — aspiration syndrome RR 0.17 (0.05–0.52), perinatal mortality RR 0.24 (0.11–0.53); standard settings — no significant primary-outcome benefit
cards.summary: Hofmeyr 2014 Cochrane: limited-surveillance settings — aspiration syndrome RR 0.17 (0.05–0.52), perinatal mortality RR 0.24 (0.11–0.53); standard settings — no significant primary-outcome benefit
cards.people: 14 randomised studies of variable quality including 4,435 women in labour with moderate or thick meconium-stained amniotic fluid, comparing amnioinfusion with no amnioinfusion, analysed separately for settings with limited facilities for peripartum surveillance (3 studies) and settings with standard surveillance.
cards.result: Limited-surveillance settings: meconium aspiration syndrome relative risk 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.52; 3 studies, 1,144 women); perinatal mortality RR 0.24 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.53; 3 studies, 1,151 women); caesarean section for fetal distress and overall caesarean section both reduced; neonatal ventilation/NICU admission reduced. Standard-surveillance settings: no significant reduction in meconium aspiration syndrome, perinatal death or severe morbidity, or maternal death or severe morbidity; caesarean for fetal distress reduced but not overall caesarean; meconium below the vocal cords and neonatal ventilation/NICU admission reduced in the initial analysis, but a sensitivity analysis excluding trials at greater risk of bias found an absence of benefit for every outcome studied.
cards.watchOut: The dramatic relative effects come from 3 studies and about 1,150 women in low-resource settings, where the benefit may reflect relief of oligohydramnios rather than meconium dilution (the reviewers state this openly); absolute event rates are not given in the record for these subgroups. Rare serious maternal adverse effects cannot be assessed from trials of this size.
cards.source: Hofmeyr GJ et al. Amnioinfusion for meconium-stained liquor in labour. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24453049. cards.headline: Synthesis: one intervention, two answers — worth doing where monitoring is scarce, unproven where it is routine
cards.summary: Synthesis: one intervention, two answers — worth doing where monitoring is scarce, unproven where it is routine
cards.people: Cochrane review of 14 randomised studies, 4,435 women in labour with moderate or thick meconium staining, pre-specified subgroup analysis by surveillance setting.
cards.result: Limited surveillance: meconium aspiration syndrome RR 0.17 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.52), perinatal mortality RR 0.24 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.53), fewer caesareans. Standard surveillance: no significant reduction in aspiration syndrome, perinatal death or severe morbidity, and no outcome benefit survived the low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the mortality claim rests on a 3-study subgroup of a systematic review.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup-by-setting findings are hypothesis-grade even when pre-specified; the honest clinical translation is about where amnioinfusion earns its place, not a universal yes or no.

shelves.title: Adding electromyographic biofeedback to pelvic floor training changed nothing at two years: incontinence severity 8.2 versus 8.5 on the ICIQ in a 600-woman trial
shelves.question: In women with urinary incontinence, does pelvic floor muscle training with electromyographic biofeedback beat pelvic floor training alone?
shelves.mesh: Electromyography/methods · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Neurofeedback/methods · Pelvic Floor/physiopathology · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence/physiopathology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the 600-woman OPAL trial, women newly presenting with stress or mixed urinary incontinence received six continence-therapist appointments over 16 weeks, with or without electromyographic biofeedback built into clinic and home training. At 24 months, self-reported incontinence severity (ICIQ-UI SF) was 8.2 (SD 5.1) with biofeedback versus 8.5 (SD 4.9) without — a mean difference of −0.09 (95% CI −0.92 to 0.75; p=0.84). Costs were similar (mean difference £121, 95% CI −£409 to £651) and quality-adjusted life years did not differ (−0.04, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.04). Forty-eight participants reported an adverse event, 23 possibly related to the interventions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine electromyographic biofeedback adds cost and kit to pelvic floor training without improving continence at two years.

cards.headline: Hagen 2020 (OPAL): ICIQ-UI SF 8.2 versus 8.5 at 24 months (difference −0.09, p=0.84); costs and QALYs also indistinguishable
cards.summary: Hagen 2020 (OPAL): ICIQ-UI SF 8.2 versus 8.5 at 24 months (difference −0.09, p=0.84); costs and QALYs also indistinguishable
cards.people: 600 women aged 18 and older newly presenting with stress or mixed urinary incontinence at 23 community and secondary care centres in Scotland and England (300 per group), each offered six continence-therapist appointments over 16 weeks: supervised PFMT plus a home programme, with electromyographic biofeedback in clinic and at home in the intervention group.
cards.result: Mean ICIQ-UI SF at 24 months was 8.2 (SD 5.1, n=225) in the biofeedback PFMT group and 8.5 (SD 4.9, n=235) with PFMT alone (mean difference −0.09, 95% CI −0.92 to 0.75; p=0.84). Costs were similar (mean difference £121, 95% CI −£409 to £651; p=0.64) and quality-adjusted life years did not differ (−0.04, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.04; p=0.28). Forty-eight participants reported an adverse event, 23 related or possibly related to the interventions.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries the shelf — but it is large, pragmatic, and followed women for two years, and its confidence interval excludes any large benefit. Attrition by 24 months (460 of 600 assessed for the primary outcome) is the main soft spot.

shelves.title: CMV hyperimmune globulin in pregnancy did not prevent congenital cytomegalovirus: 22.7% vs 19.4% in the large blinded trial stopped for futility — the earlier smaller trial was also null (30% vs 44%, p=0.13)
shelves.question: In pregnant women with primary cytomegalovirus infection, does CMV hyperimmune globulin prevent congenital CMV infection in the baby?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cytomegalovirus Infections/congenital/drug therapy/mortality/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Death/etiology/prevention & control · Fetal Diseases/prevention & control · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/therapeutic use · Incidence · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical/prevention & control · Infusions, Intravenous · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious/drug therapy · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a hopeful uncontrolled signal that two randomised trials could not confirm. An uncontrolled 2005 study had suggested transmission falling from 40% to 16%, but the phase 2 randomised trial (Revello MG et al., PMID: 24693891) found congenital infection in 30% on hyperimmune globulin versus 44% on placebo (difference 14 percentage points, 95% CI -3 to 31; p=0.13), with more obstetric adverse events on treatment (13% vs 2%). The definitive multicentre double-blind trial (Hughes BL et al., PMID: 34320288) screened 206,082 pregnant women, randomised 399 with primary CMV infection before 24 weeks to monthly hyperimmune globulin or placebo, and was stopped early for futility: the primary outcome occurred in 22.7% versus 19.4% (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.72), with point estimates for fetal/neonatal death (4.9% vs 2.6%), preterm birth and low birth weight all leaning the wrong way, none significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, the larger one blinded and futility-stopped, agree there is no demonstrated benefit to prevent.

cards.headline: Hughes 2021: primary outcome 22.7% on hyperimmune globulin vs 19.4% on placebo (RR 1.17) — trial stopped early for futility after screening 206,082 women
cards.summary: Hughes 2021: primary outcome 22.7% on hyperimmune globulin vs 19.4% on placebo (RR 1.17) — trial stopped early for futility after screening 206,082 women
cards.people: 399 pregnant women with primary CMV infection diagnosed before 24 weeks' gestation (from 206,082 screened; 712 tested positive, 399 randomised) at US centres, assigned to monthly CMV hyperimmune globulin 100 mg/kg or matching placebo until delivery. Primary outcome: congenital CMV infection, or fetal/neonatal death where CMV testing was not performed; outcome data available for 394.
cards.result: A primary outcome event occurred in 46 of 203 women (22.7%) in the hyperimmune globulin group and 37 of 191 (19.4%) in the placebo group (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.72; p=0.42). Death occurred in 4.9% versus 2.6% of fetuses/neonates (RR 1.88, 0.66 to 5.41), preterm birth in 12.2% versus 8.3% and birth weight below the 5th percentile in 10.3% versus 5.4% — all non-significant and all numerically favouring placebo. One severe allergic reaction occurred in the treatment group; headaches and shaking chills during infusion were commoner on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for futility, so the confidence interval cannot exclude a modest benefit (lower bound RR 0.80) — but the point estimate sits on the harm side of 1, and no secondary outcome leans toward benefit. Screening 206,082 women to randomise 399 also documents how rare trial-eligible primary infection is, which is why this evidence will not soon be superseded.
cards.source: Hughes BL et al. A Trial of Hyperimmune Globulin to Prevent Congenital Cytomegalovirus Infection. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 34320288. Registry ID: NCT01376778. cards.headline: Revello 2014: congenital infection 30% vs 44% (p=0.13) — a 14-point gap that was not significant, with more obstetric adverse events on treatment (13% vs 2%)
cards.summary: Revello 2014: congenital infection 30% vs 44% (p=0.13) — a 14-point gap that was not significant, with more obstetric adverse events on treatment (13% vs 2%)
cards.people: 124 pregnant women with primary CMV infection at 5 to 26 weeks' gestation, randomised within 6 weeks of presumed infection onset to hyperimmune globulin or placebo every 4 weeks until 36 weeks or detection of CMV in amniotic fluid; 123 women evaluable. Primary endpoint: congenital infection at birth or by amniocentesis.
cards.result: Congenital infection occurred in 30% (18 of 61) in the hyperimmune globulin group and 44% (27 of 62) in the placebo group — a difference of 14 percentage points (95% CI -3 to 31; p=0.13), not statistically significant. Clinical outcome of congenitally infected infants at birth was similar between groups. Obstetric adverse events were more frequent with hyperimmune globulin (13% vs 2%).
cards.watchOut: The gap looks clinically large but the trial was small: the confidence interval spans from a 3-point harm to a 31-point benefit. Read alone it invites 'promising'; read with Hughes 2021 — four times the randomised pregnancies, blinded, futility-stopped — the promising reading does not survive.
cards.source: Revello MG et al. A randomized trial of hyperimmune globulin to prevent congenital cytomegalovirus. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 24693891. Registry ID: NCT00881517. cards.headline: Synthesis: the uncontrolled 40%-to-16% story did not survive randomisation — twice
cards.summary: Synthesis: the uncontrolled 40%-to-16% story did not survive randomisation — twice
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials totalling 522 evaluable pregnant women with primary CMV infection, one Italian phase 2 trial and one large US multicentre trial stopped for futility.
cards.result: Congenital infection: 30% vs 44% (p=0.13) and a composite of infection or perinatal death 22.7% vs 19.4% (RR 1.17). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): hyperimmune globulin should not be offered to prevent congenital CMV outside a trial on current evidence.
cards.watchOut: This shelf answers the treatment question for women with diagnosed primary infection; it says nothing about CMV vaccines or hygiene counselling to prevent primary infection, which are different questions with different evidence.

shelves.title: Advance provision of emergency contraception: women used it twice as often and faster — and pregnancy rates did not fall (8% in every group of the largest trial; pooled OR 1.0)
shelves.question: Does giving women emergency contraception in advance (or direct pharmacy access) reduce unintended pregnancy rates compared with standard clinic access?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · California · Contraception Behavior/statistics & numerical data · Contraception, Postcoital/statistics & numerical data · Contraceptives, Postcoital/administration & dosage · Drug Utilization · Family Planning Services · Female · Health Services Accessibility · Humans · Pharmacies · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Pregnancy, Unplanned · Safe Sex/statistics & numerical data · Sexually Transmitted Diseases/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — to pregnancies, while clearly changing behaviour. In the largest trial (Raine TR et al., PMID: 15632336), 2,117 women aged 15–24 were randomised to pharmacy access, advance provision of three packs of levonorgestrel emergency contraception, or clinic access: advance provision nearly doubled use (37.4% vs 21.0%) yet pregnancy rates were 8% in all groups (adjusted OR for advance provision 1.10, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.84), sexually transmitted infections did not increase, and contraceptive and condom use did not deteriorate. The Cochrane review of 8 trials in 6,389 women (Polis CB et al., PMID: 17443596) found the same pattern pooled: no reduction in pregnancies at 12 months (OR 1.0, 0.78 to 1.29) despite more use (single use OR 2.52) and faster use (about 14.6 hours sooner), and no increase in unprotected intercourse or STIs. Easier access is justified on autonomy and per-episode efficacy grounds; it is not, on this record, a population pregnancy-prevention strategy, because too many episodes of unprotected intercourse still go uncovered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the pregnancy-rate claim specifically.

cards.headline: Raine 2005: advance provision doubled EC use (37.4% vs 21.0%) — pregnancies 8% in every arm, STIs and condom use unchanged
cards.summary: Raine 2005: advance provision doubled EC use (37.4% vs 21.0%) — pregnancies 8% in every arm, STIs and condom use unchanged
cards.people: 2,117 women aged 15–24 attending four California family-planning clinics, not desiring pregnancy, randomised to pharmacy access to emergency contraception, advance provision of three packs of levonorgestrel EC, or clinic access (control), with outcomes at 6 months.
cards.result: EC use: 24.2% in the pharmacy group (p=0.25 vs control) and 37.4% in the advance provision group versus 21.0% in controls (p<0.001), despite similar rates of unprotected intercourse (39.8% vs 41.0%). Only 46.7% of participants who had unprotected intercourse used EC at all. Eight percent became pregnant and 12% acquired an STI, with no significant differences: pregnancy adjusted OR 0.98 (pharmacy) and 1.10 (advance provision); STI OR 1.08 and 0.94. Contraceptive use, condom use and sexual behaviour did not differ by group.
cards.watchOut: A single-blind trial in clinic-attending young women already connected to services; the null pregnancy result reflects coverage of at-risk episodes, not per-episode efficacy of levonorgestrel, which this trial did not test. Six months is short for pregnancy outcomes, and the control condition (clinic access within an organised system) is better than access in many real settings.
cards.source: Raine TR et al. Direct access to emergency contraception through pharmacies and effect on unintended pregnancy and STIs: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 15632336. cards.headline: Cochrane 2007 (8 trials, 6,389 women): pregnancies unchanged at 12 months (OR 1.0) despite use rising (OR 2.52) and use coming ~15 hours faster
cards.summary: Cochrane 2007 (8 trials, 6,389 women): pregnancies unchanged at 12 months (OR 1.0) despite use rising (OR 2.52) and use coming ~15 hours faster
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Polis 2007, Cochrane)
cards.people: 8 randomised trials (6,389 women in the United States, China and India) comparing advance provision of emergency contraception with standard access (counselling and/or provision on request at clinic or pharmacy).
cards.result: Advance provision did not decrease pregnancy rates: OR 1.0 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.29) in studies with 12-month follow-up and OR 0.91 (0.69 to 1.19) at 6 months. It increased single use (OR 2.52, 1.72 to 3.70) and multiple use (OR 4.13, 1.77 to 9.63) and shortened time to use (weighted mean difference -14.6 hours, -16.77 to -12.4). It did not increase STIs (OR 0.99, 0.73 to 1.34), unprotected intercourse, or change contraceptive methods or condom use.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2007 and predates ulipristal and pharmacy deregulation in many countries; its behavioural safety findings have aged better than its access context. Pooling mixes advance provision with different standard-access comparators, but the pregnancy null is consistent across the included trials.
cards.source: Polis CB et al. Advance provision of emergency contraception for pregnancy prevention (full review). The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2007. PMID: 17443596. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: Pregnancy: no reduction (OR 1.0 at 12 months; 8% in all arms of the largest trial). Use: roughly doubled and ~15 hours faster. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — to pregnancy rates; the shelf is a null about a strategy, not about the drug.

shelves.title: Physician-optimised blood-pressure self-management after hypertensive pregnancy (POP-HT): 24-hour diastolic pressure 5.8 mm Hg lower at 9 months, with favourable cardiac remodelling
shelves.question: In women who have had a hypertensive pregnancy (gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia), does postpartum self-monitoring of blood pressure with physician-guided remote titration of antihypertensive medication achieve lower blood pressure at about 9 months than usual postnatal care?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · *Antihypertensive Agents/administration & dosage/pharmacology/therapeutic use · *Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cardiovascular Diseases/complications · Hypertension/drug therapy/complications · *Hypertension, Pregnancy-Induced/drug therapy · Pre-Eclampsia/prevention & control · Self-Management · Adult · *Postnatal Care/methods · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one single-centre trial with a large, coherent effect on pressure and cardiac structure. In POP-HT (220 women after hypertensive pregnancy), 24-hour diastolic blood pressure at about 8 months postpartum was 5.8 mm Hg lower with self-monitoring plus physician-optimised titration than with usual care (71.2 versus 76.6 mm Hg; difference -5.80; 95% CI -7.40 to -4.20; P < .001), and systolic pressure was 6.5 mm Hg lower (114.0 versus 120.3 mm Hg; difference -6.51; -8.80 to -4.22). The imaging substudy (187 women) found the intervention group had lower relative wall thickness (-0.06), lower left ventricular mass (-6.37 g/m²), smaller ventricular volumes and higher ejection fractions (left +2.6%, right +2.8%) at follow-up — a remodelling pattern associated with better long-term outcomes. Because the claim rests on a single trial, this shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): structured postpartum blood-pressure self-management probably achieves meaningfully lower pressure after hypertensive pregnancy; whether it prevents later hypertension or cardiovascular events is untested.

cards.headline: POP-HT (Kitt 2023): 24-hour diastolic blood pressure 5.8 mm Hg lower with the intervention (71.2 versus 76.6 mm Hg; P < .001) and systolic 6.5 mm Hg lower at about 9 months postpartum
cards.summary: POP-HT (Kitt 2023): 24-hour diastolic blood pressure 5.8 mm Hg lower with the intervention (71.2 versus 76.6 mm Hg; P < .001) and systolic 6.5 mm Hg lower at about 9 months postpartum
cards.people: 220 women after a hypertensive pregnancy (40% gestational hypertension, 60% pre-eclampsia; mean age 32.6 years) at a single UK centre, randomised to self-monitoring with physician-guided titration of antihypertensive medication (112 women) or usual postnatal outpatient care (108); 200 women (91%) were included in the primary analysis, with the primary outcome measured at a mean of 249 days postpartum.
cards.result: The 24-hour mean diastolic blood pressure was 71.2 (SD 5.6) mm Hg in the intervention group versus 76.6 (SD 5.7) mm Hg in the control group — an adjusted between-group difference of -5.80 mm Hg (95% CI -7.40 to -4.20; P < .001). The 24-hour mean systolic pressure was 114.0 (SD 7.7) versus 120.3 (SD 9.1) mm Hg — a difference of -6.51 mm Hg (95% CI -8.80 to -4.22; P < .001).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and unblinded, with a blood-pressure (not event) endpoint at 9 months; usual care in other health systems may be better or worse than the UK postnatal care compared here.

cards.type: Randomised trial imaging substudy (POP-HT — same trial as the card above)
cards.people: 187 women from POP-HT (101 intervention, 86 usual care) who underwent echocardiography at baseline and follow-up (mean 258 days postpartum), of whom 174 also had cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging at follow-up.
cards.result: Relative wall thickness by echocardiography fell by 0.06 more in the intervention group (95% CI 0.05 to 0.07 in magnitude; P < 0.001). On magnetic resonance imaging, the intervention group had lower left ventricular mass (-6.37 g/m²; 95% CI -7.99 to -4.74; P < 0.001), lower end-diastolic volume (-3.87 mL/m²; P = 0.009) and end-systolic volume (-3.25 mL/m²; P < 0.001), and higher left and right ventricular ejection fractions (+2.6%; 95% CI 1.3 to 3.9; and +2.8%; 1.4 to 4.1; both P < 0.001); diastolic function and left atrial volumes also favoured the intervention.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the postpartum months are a treatable window — one trial shows pressure and cardiac structure both improve
cards.summary: Synthesis: the postpartum months are a treatable window — one trial shows pressure and cardiac structure both improve
cards.people: Women in the first year after a pregnancy complicated by hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
cards.result: POP-HT's effects are internally consistent across measurement levels: home-monitored, physician-titrated treatment delivered about 6 mm Hg lower 24-hour pressures (diastolic -5.8, systolic -6.5) and measurably less adverse cardiac remodelling (left ventricular mass -6.37 g/m²). That coherence earns POSSIBLE despite the single-trial base; event prevention remains an extrapolation.
cards.watchOut: The intervention needs infrastructure — validated home monitors, a titration protocol and clinician oversight — so the result is about the programme, not about simply handing patients a cuff.
cards.source: Synthesis of POP-HT (PMID: 37950919) and its imaging substudy (PMID: 37950907).

shelves.title: Chlorhexidine wipes in labour: the big randomised trial found nothing (neonatal sepsis 3% versus 4%) — the striking Malawi benefit came from a before-and-after study, and the pooled randomised evidence is null
shelves.question: In women in labour in low-resource settings, does chlorhexidine cleansing of the birth canal (with wiping of the newborn) reduce neonatal sepsis and maternal postpartum infection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage · Bacteria/isolation & purification · Bacterial Infections/prevention & control · Chlorhexidine/administration & dosage · Developing Countries · Female · Humans · Infant Care · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical/prevention & control · Labor, Obstetric · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious/microbiology · Skin/microbiology · South Africa · Streptococcal Infections/prevention & control · Streptococcus agalactiae · Vagina/microbiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits cleanly by study design. The only large randomised trial (Cutland CL et al., PMID: 19846212) assigned 8,011 women in Soweto to chlorhexidine vaginal wipes in labour plus full-body chlorhexidine washes for their babies, or water wipes and foot washes: neonatal sepsis occurred in 141 (3%) of 4,072 versus 148 (4%) of 4,057 (p=0.65), and newborn group B streptococcal colonisation was identical (54% versus 55%). The famous positive result is non-randomised: in Malawi (Taha TE et al., PMID: 9253269), a phased before-and-after introduction of 0.25% chlorhexidine birth-canal cleansing was followed by neonatal sepsis admissions of 7.8 versus 17.9 per 1,000 live births, neonatal mortality of 28.6 versus 36.9 per 1,000, and postpartum infection admissions of 1.7 versus 5.1 per 1,000 deliveries — but phase comparisons absorb every other change in the hospital over those six months. The meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Bell C et al., PMID: 29739349; 11 trials, 20,101 women) found no significant difference for any maternal or neonatal colonisation or infection outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT: as tested in randomised trials, intrapartum chlorhexidine wipes do not prevent neonatal sepsis; the observational Malawi signal remains unexplained by — and unconfirmed in — randomised evidence. Tier C: the shelf's positive arm rests on a non-randomised study.

cards.headline: Cutland 2009 (Soweto RCT): neonatal sepsis 141/4,072 (3%) on chlorhexidine versus 148/4,057 (4%) on control — and GBS colonisation identical at 54% versus 55%
cards.summary: Cutland 2009 (Soweto RCT): neonatal sepsis 141/4,072 (3%) on chlorhexidine versus 148/4,057 (4%) on control — and GBS colonisation identical at 54% versus 55%
cards.people: 8,011 women (aged 12–51 years) in Soweto, South Africa, randomised 1:1 to chlorhexidine vaginal wipes or external-genitalia water wipes during active labour; their 8,129 newborns received full-body (intervention) or foot-only (control) chlorhexidine washes at birth; colonisation assessed in a 5,144-mother subset.
cards.result: Rates of neonatal sepsis did not differ: 141 (3%) of 4,072 in the chlorhexidine group versus 148 (4%) of 4,057 in the control group (p=0.6518). Newborn colonisation with group B streptococcus was 217 (54%) of 401 versus 234 (55%) of 429 (efficacy −0.05%, 95% CI −9.5 to 7.9). The authors concluded the intervention did not prevent neonatal sepsis or vertical acquisition of potentially pathogenic bacteria.
cards.watchOut: The control babies still received chlorhexidine on their feet and control mothers a water wipe, so this tests the full package against a minimal-contact comparator, not against nothing; sepsis ascertainment in a high-HIV-prevalence setting may also differ from the Malawi population in the positive study.
cards.source: Cutland CL et al. Chlorhexidine maternal-vaginal and neonate body wipes in sepsis and vertical transmission of pathogenic bacteria in South Africa: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19846212. Registry ID: NCT00136370. cards.headline: Taha 1997 (Malawi, non-randomised): after chlorhexidine cleansing began, neonatal sepsis admissions fell from 17.9 to 7.8 per 1,000 and infectious-cause mortality from 7.3 to 2.4 per 1,000
cards.summary: Taha 1997 (Malawi, non-randomised): after chlorhexidine cleansing began, neonatal sepsis admissions fell from 17.9 to 7.8 per 1,000 and infectious-cause mortality from 7.3 to 2.4 per 1,000
cards.people: 6,965 women giving birth over six months at Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital, Blantyre, Malawi (7,160 babies): two months of no intervention, three months in which the birth canal was wiped with 0.25% chlorhexidine at every vaginal examination and babies were wiped with chlorhexidine, then a final month of no intervention.
cards.result: Comparing intervention with non-intervention phases: overall neonatal admissions 16.9% versus 19.3% (p<0.01); admissions for neonatal sepsis 7.8 versus 17.9 per 1,000 live births (p<0.0002); overall neonatal mortality 28.6 versus 36.9 per 1,000 (p<0.06); mortality from infectious causes 2.4 versus 7.3 per 1,000 (p<0.005). Maternal delivery-related admissions fell (29.4 versus 40.2 per 1,000, p<0.02), as did postpartum infection admissions (1.7 versus 5.1 per 1,000, p=0.02). No adverse reactions were reported.
cards.watchOut: This is a before-and-after comparison inside one hospital: staffing, case mix, season and every other practice changed freely between phases, and the design cannot separate the chlorhexidine from the calendar. It is the hypothesis the Soweto trial then tested — and did not confirm.
cards.source: Taha TE et al. Effect of cleansing the birth canal with antiseptic solution on maternal and newborn morbidity and mortality in Malawi: clinical trial. BMJ. 1997. PMID: 9253269. cards.headline: Bell 2018 meta-analysis: 11 randomised trials, 20,101 women — no significant difference for any maternal or neonatal colonisation or infection outcome
cards.summary: Bell 2018 meta-analysis: 11 randomised trials, 20,101 women — no significant difference for any maternal or neonatal colonisation or infection outcome
cards.people: Eleven randomised controlled trials (n=20,101) of intrapartum vaginal chlorhexidine interventions (wipes, irrigation, douching) versus control, pooled with random-effects models for maternal and neonatal colonisation and infectious morbidity.
cards.result: Meta-analysis found no significant differences between intervention and control groups for any of the four outcomes examined — maternal or neonatal colonisation or infection. The reviewers noted vaginal irrigation was the preferred administration method in the included studies and that a larger multicentre trial, powered for neonatal outcomes, might still be informative.
cards.watchOut: Pooling wipes, irrigation and douching into one estimate can hide a technique that works; the review's own caveat is that the randomised base is thinner than its n suggests for the hardest outcomes, which is why the Malawi signal keeps being cited despite this null.
cards.source: Bell C et al. What is the result of vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine during labour on maternal and neonatal infections? A systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Pregnancy and Childbirth. 2018. PMID: 29739349. Registry ID: ISRCTN97143849 (as named in the record).
