shelves.title: Deworming in pregnancy: no gain in anaemia, birthweight or perinatal survival in two randomised trials — treatment looked safe for the pregnancy, but infants of albendazole-treated mothers had more eczema (HR 1.82)
shelves.question: In pregnant women in helminth-endemic settings, does anthelminthic treatment (albendazole for soil-transmitted worms, praziquantel for schistosomiasis) improve maternal anaemia, birthweight and perinatal outcomes — and is it safe for mother and baby?
shelves.mesh: Albendazole/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Anemia/parasitology · Animals · Anthelmintics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Birth Weight/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Helminthiasis/drug therapy/epidemiology · Helminths/isolation & purification · Humans · Praziquantel/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Parasitic/drug therapy/epidemiology · Regression Analysis · Treatment Outcome · Uganda/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — safe for the pregnancy, unhelpful for the outcomes it was given for, with an infant-allergy price signal. In Entebbe, Uganda (Ndibazza J et al., PMID: 20067426), 2,507 pregnant women (68% with helminths, 45% hookworm, 18% Schistosoma mansoni, 40% anaemic) were randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to single-dose albendazole and/or praziquantel or placebos, all receiving haematinics and malaria presumptive treatment. Neither drug moved the targets: maternal anaemia at delivery (35% overall) had odds ratios of 0.95 (95% CI 0.79–1.15) for albendazole and 1.00 (0.83–1.21) for praziquantel; mean birthweight differences were −0.00 kg and −0.01 kg; and there was no effect on low birthweight, perinatal mortality or congenital anomalies — the one hint was albendazole against anaemia in moderate-to-heavy hookworm infection (OR 0.45, 0.21–0.98; interaction p=0.15). The dedicated safety trial in the Philippines (Olveda RM et al., PMID: 26511959) treated 370 women infected with S. japonicum at 12–16 weeks: birthweight was 2.85 kg in both arms (β −0.002, 95% CI −0.088 to 0.083), with no significant differences in abortion, fetal death or congenital anomalies. The price signal came from the Entebbe offspring follow-up (Mpairwe H et al., PMID: 21255083): maternal albendazole was associated with more doctor-diagnosed infantile eczema (HR 1.82, 1.26–2.64) and recurrent wheeze (HR 1.58, 1.13–2.22), and praziquantel with more eczema among infants of S. mansoni-infected mothers (HR 2.65, 1.16–6.08). PROPOSED SPLIT: in low-intensity infection settings, routine deworming in pregnancy is a null for mother and newborn outcomes — reassuring on birth safety, disappointing on benefit, and not free for the infant's allergy risk. Tier C: the harm signal rests on one trial programme.

cards.headline: Ndibazza 2010 (Entebbe, 2×2 factorial): anaemia OR 0.95 for albendazole and 1.00 for praziquantel; birthweight differences −0.00 and −0.01 kg; no effect on perinatal mortality or anomalies
cards.summary: Ndibazza 2010 (Entebbe, 2×2 factorial): anaemia OR 0.95 for albendazole and 1.00 for praziquantel; birthweight differences −0.00 and −0.01 kg; no effect on perinatal mortality or anomalies
cards.people: 2,507 pregnant women in Entebbe, Uganda, randomised to single-dose albendazole or placebo and praziquantel or placebo in a 2×2 factorial design, with routine haematinics and sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine malaria treatment; at enrolment 68% had helminths, 45% hookworm, 18% Schistosoma mansoni, and 40% were anaemic (haemoglobin <11.2 g/dL).
cards.result: At delivery 35% were anaemic, with no overall effect of albendazole (OR 0.95, 95% CI 0.79–1.15) or praziquantel (OR 1.00, 0.83–1.21); a suggestion of albendazole benefit was confined to women with moderate-to-heavy hookworm (OR 0.45, 0.21–0.98; interaction p=0.15). Neither treatment affected mean birthweight (differences −0.00 kg for albendazole, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.04; −0.01 kg for praziquantel, −0.05 to 0.04), the proportion of low birthweight, perinatal mortality, or congenital anomalies.
cards.watchOut: Prevalence was high but infection intensity low, and everyone received iron/folate and malaria treatment — the trial fairly tests adding deworming to good antenatal care in such a setting, and cannot exclude benefit where worm burdens are heavy or haematinics absent.
cards.source: Ndibazza J et al. Effects of deworming during pregnancy on maternal and perinatal outcomes in Entebbe, Uganda: a randomized controlled trial. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2010. cards.headline: Olveda 2016 (Philippines): praziquantel at 12–16 weeks in S. japonicum infection — birthweight 2.85 kg in both arms; no difference in abortion, fetal death or congenital anomalies
cards.summary: Olveda 2016 (Philippines): praziquantel at 12–16 weeks in S. japonicum infection — birthweight 2.85 kg in both arms; no difference in abortion, fetal death or congenital anomalies
cards.people: 370 otherwise healthy pregnant women infected with Schistosoma japonicum in northeastern Leyte, Philippines, randomised at 12–16 weeks' gestation to over-encapsulated praziquantel (60 mg/kg in two split doses) or placebo (186 versus 184); 90% had low-intensity infections; primary outcome birthweight, with reactogenicity, 24-hour toxicology and maternal and newborn serious adverse events collected.
cards.result: Praziquantel had no significant effect on birthweight: 2.85 kg in both groups (β −0.002, 95% CI −0.088 to 0.083; p=0.962). Treatment was well tolerated, with reactogenicity similar to non-pregnant participants; severe reactions occurred in five patients in the praziquantel group and two in the placebo group (headache, fever, malaise). There were no significant differences in abortion, fetal death in utero, or congenital anomalies.
cards.watchOut: A 370-woman phase 2 trial can reassure about common harms and birthweight, not about rare congenital outcomes; and like Entebbe, it studied mostly low-intensity infection, so it speaks to the safety of treating in pregnancy rather than to treating heavy schistosomiasis, where the calculus may differ.
cards.source: Olveda RM et al. Efficacy and safety of praziquantel for the treatment of human schistosomiasis during pregnancy: a phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: Mpairwe 2011 (Entebbe offspring): infantile eczema HR 1.82 after maternal albendazole; HR 2.65 after praziquantel in S. mansoni-infected mothers; recurrent wheeze HR 1.58
cards.summary: Mpairwe 2011 (Entebbe offspring): infantile eczema HR 1.82 after maternal albendazole; HR 2.65 after praziquantel in S. mansoni-infected mothers; recurrent wheeze HR 1.58
cards.people: Infants of the 2,507 women in the Entebbe factorial trial (albendazole versus placebo and praziquantel versus placebo in pregnancy), with doctor-diagnosed infantile eczema recorded prospectively; worms had been detected in 68% of mothers before treatment.
cards.result: Doctor-diagnosed infantile eczema incidence was 10.4 per 100 infant-years. Maternal albendazole was associated with a significantly increased risk of eczema (Cox HR 1.82, 95% CI 1.26–2.64; p=0.002), an effect slightly stronger — counterintuitively — among infants whose mothers had no albendazole-susceptible worms. Praziquantel showed no overall effect but was associated with increased eczema risk among infants of mothers with Schistosoma mansoni (HR 2.65, 1.16–6.08; interaction p=0.02). Albendazole was also associated with reported recurrent wheeze (HR 1.58, 1.13–2.22; p=0.008).
cards.watchOut: A secondary outcome of one trial programme, with subgroup patterns (stronger where no susceptible worms were present) that cut both ways — consistent with a direct drug effect or with removing a protective worm exposure; either way it is a signal to weigh, not a settled harm, and it has not been replicated in an independent trial.
cards.source: Mpairwe H et al. Anthelminthic treatment during pregnancy is associated with increased risk of infantile eczema: randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial results. Pediatric Allergy and Immunology. 2011. PMID: 21255083. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the trials retire the hoped-for benefits, acquit the drugs on birth safety, and leave an infant-allergy question open
cards.summary: Synthesis: the trials retire the hoped-for benefits, acquit the drugs on birth safety, and leave an infant-allergy question open
cards.people: Two randomised trials (2,507 women in a Ugandan factorial trial of albendazole and praziquantel; 370 women in a Philippine praziquantel safety trial) plus the Ugandan trial's infant follow-up.
cards.result: Benefits: none demonstrated — anaemia ORs 0.95 and 1.00, birthweight differences of −0.00 to −0.01 kg (2.85 kg in both arms in the Philippines), no effect on perinatal mortality. Birth safety: no significant excess of abortion, fetal death or congenital anomalies in either trial. Offspring signal: eczema HR 1.82 (albendazole) and 2.65 (praziquantel in S. mansoni infection), wheeze HR 1.58 (albendazole). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C for the single-programme harm signal.
cards.watchOut: Both trials ran where infection intensity was low and antenatal haematinics were provided; they should not be read as evidence against treating clinically significant worm disease in an individual pregnant patient, which neither trial studied.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ndibazza J et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2010 (PMID: 20067426); Olveda RM et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2016 (PMID: 26511959); Mpairwe H et al. Pediatric Allergy and Immunology. 2011 (PMID: 21255083).

shelves.title: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy: untreated positive women had pyelonephritis in 2.4% versus 0.6% of negative women — but treating it changed nothing (composite 2.5% treated versus 2.9% untreated), and it was not linked to preterm birth
shelves.question: In women with uncomplicated singleton pregnancies, does screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth — the policy built on trials from over 30 years ago?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Asymptomatic Diseases · Bacteriuria/complications/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Netherlands · Nitrofurantoin/administration & dosage · Placebos · Pregnancy · Premature Birth · Prospective Studies · Pyelonephritis/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the modern reassessment. The Dutch multicentre study (Kazemier BM et al., PMID: 26255208) screened 5,132 eligible women at 16–22 weeks; in the final cohort of 4,283, 248 were asymptomatic-bacteriuria positive — 85 entered the embedded double-blind trial of nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days versus placebo, and 163 were followed untreated. The composite of pyelonephritis, preterm birth or both did not differ between untreated/placebo-positive women and bacteriuria-negative women (6 [2.9%] of 208 versus 77 [1.9%] of 4,035; adjusted OR 1.5, 95% CI 0.6–3.5), nor between nitrofurantoin-treated positive women and untreated/placebo-positive women (1 [2.5%] of 40 versus 6 [2.9%] of 208; risk difference −0.4 points, 95% CI −3.6 to 9.4). Bacteriuria was associated with pyelonephritis specifically — 5 (2.4%) of 208 untreated/placebo-positive women versus 24 (0.6%) of 4,035 negative women (adjusted OR 3.9, 1.4–11.4) — but the absolute risk was low, and bacteriuria was not associated with preterm birth. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in this low-risk population, a routine screen-and-treat policy found no measurable benefit to buy — Tier C, because the embedded randomised comparison is only 85 women and the rest is cohort evidence.

cards.headline: Kazemier 2015: composite outcome 2.5% treated versus 2.9% untreated/placebo among bacteriuria-positive women; pyelonephritis 2.4% untreated-positive versus 0.6% negative
cards.summary: Kazemier 2015: composite outcome 2.5% treated versus 2.9% untreated/placebo among bacteriuria-positive women; pyelonephritis 2.4% untreated-positive versus 0.6% negative
cards.type: Prospective cohort with embedded randomised trial (Kazemier 2015)
cards.people: Women aged 18 or older with singleton pregnancies screened at 16–22 weeks at eight hospitals and five ultrasound centres in the Netherlands: 5,621 enrolled, 5,132 eligible for screening, final cohort 4,283 after exclusions; 248 were asymptomatic-bacteriuria positive, of whom 40 were randomised to nitrofurantoin and 45 to placebo (100 mg twice daily for 5 days, double-blind), and 163 were followed without treatment.
cards.result: The proportion with pyelonephritis, preterm birth, or both did not differ between untreated or placebo-treated bacteriuria-positive women and bacteriuria-negative women (6 [2.9%] of 208 versus 77 [1.9%] of 4,035; adjusted OR 1.5, 95% CI 0.6–3.5), nor between nitrofurantoin-treated positive women and untreated or placebo-treated positive women (1 [2.5%] of 40 versus 6 [2.9%] of 208; risk difference −0.4, 95% CI −3.6 to 9.4). Untreated or placebo-treated positive women developed pyelonephritis in 5 (2.4%) of 208 cases versus 24 (0.6%) of 4,035 negative women (adjusted OR 3.9, 1.4–11.4). The authors concluded the findings question a routine screen-and-treat policy in uncomplicated singleton pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: The randomised leg randomised only 85 women — its confidence interval (−3.6 to 9.4 points) cannot exclude a worthwhile benefit, so the null leans on the cohort comparison; and this is a low-risk Dutch population with a 2.4% untreated pyelonephritis risk, not the higher-risk settings of the 1960s trials that built the policy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the association with pyelonephritis is real but small in absolute terms — and the one modern randomised test of treating it found nothing to show for treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: the association with pyelonephritis is real but small in absolute terms — and the one modern randomised test of treating it found nothing to show for treatment
cards.people: One prospective screening cohort of 4,283 pregnant women with an embedded double-blind randomised trial (85 bacteriuria-positive women, nitrofurantoin versus placebo) in the Netherlands.
cards.result: Pyelonephritis or preterm birth: 2.5% (treated positive) versus 2.9% (untreated/placebo positive) versus 1.9% (negative). Pyelonephritis alone: 2.4% in untreated positive women versus 0.6% in negative women (adjusted OR 3.9) — an absolute excess of about 1.8 cases per 100 untreated positive women, against a treatment that showed no measurable composite benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C for the small randomised leg.
cards.watchOut: This shelf addresses asymptomatic bacteriuria found on screening in uncomplicated singleton pregnancy; symptomatic urinary infection in pregnancy is a different question, and nothing here argues against treating it. The older trials underpinning guidelines were not re-carded — their populations and event rates belong to another era.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kazemier BM et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2015 (PMID: 26255208).

shelves.title: Pessary first for prolapse: surgery reported improvement a little more often (81.5% vs 76.3%) and noninferiority was not shown — but 54% crossed over to surgery and the pessary strategy cost about €1,800 less
shelves.question: In women with symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse, is starting with a pessary noninferior to surgery for patient-reported improvement at 24 months?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Pelvic Organ Prolapse/etiology/surgery/therapy · Pessaries/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Aged · Gynecologic Surgical Procedures/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — improvement is close and the pessary is cheaper, but noninferiority was not proven and most pessary users eventually had surgery. In the PEOPLE randomised trial (van der Vaart LR et al., PMID: 36538310), subjective improvement at 24 months was reported by 76.3% starting with a pessary versus 81.5% with surgery (risk difference −6.1%, 1-sided 95% CI −12.7 to ∞; P for noninferiority .16), and the per-protocol gap was wider (70.3% vs 83.3%). Crossover from pessary to surgery occurred in 54.1% of the pessary group. The alongside economic evaluation (Ben ÂJ et al., PMID: 38692718) found no significant QALY difference (−0.03, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.002) but significantly lower healthcare costs with the pessary strategy (mean difference −€1807, 95% CI −€2172 to −€1446). PROPOSED SPLIT: as a first strategy the pessary buys similar reported improvement at lower cost for the roughly half who stay with it, while surgery remains the more reliable single treatment — the trial does not support calling the two equivalent.

cards.headline: PEOPLE (van der Vaart 2022): improvement 76.3% pessary vs 81.5% surgery — noninferiority not met (P=.16); 54.1% of the pessary group crossed over to surgery
cards.summary: PEOPLE (van der Vaart 2022): improvement 76.3% pessary vs 81.5% surgery — noninferiority not met (P=.16); 54.1% of the pessary group crossed over to surgery
cards.type: Randomised noninferiority trial (van der Vaart 2022, PEOPLE)
cards.people: 440 women (mean age 64.7 years) with symptomatic stage 2 or greater pelvic organ prolapse at 21 hospitals in the Netherlands, randomised to pessary treatment (n=218) or surgery (n=222), followed for 24 months; 173 pessary and 162 surgery participants completed the trial.
cards.result: Subjective patient-reported improvement (Patient Global Impression of Improvement, much or very much better) at 24 months: 132 of 173 (76.3%) with pessary versus 132 of 162 (81.5%) with surgery (risk difference −6.1% [1-sided 95% CI, −12.7 to ∞]; P value for noninferiority, .16 — the 10-percentage-point margin was not met). Per-protocol: 70.3% versus 83.3% (risk difference −13.1%). Crossover from pessary to surgery: 118 of 218 (54.1%). Commonest adverse events: discomfort in 42.7% of pessary users versus urinary tract infection in 9% after surgery.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and an initial-strategy comparison rather than a pure device-versus-operation test: over half the pessary arm ultimately had surgery, and about a quarter of randomised women did not complete 24-month follow-up, so the intention-to-treat gap understates the per-protocol gap.
cards.source: van der Vaart LR et al. Effect of Pessary vs Surgery on Patient-Reported Improvement in Patients With Symptomatic Pelvic Organ Prolapse: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 36538310. Registry ID: NTR4883 (Netherlands Trial Register, stated in the record). cards.headline: Ben 2024 (PEOPLE economic evaluation): no QALY difference (−0.03) but healthcare costs €1,807 lower with pessary-first
cards.summary: Ben 2024 (PEOPLE economic evaluation): no QALY difference (−0.03) but healthcare costs €1,807 lower with pessary-first
cards.type: Economic evaluation alongside a randomised trial (Ben 2024, PEOPLE)
cards.people: The same 440 women randomised in the PEOPLE trial (pessary n=218, surgery n=222) in 21 Dutch hospitals, with quality-adjusted life-years from EQ-5D-3L and healthcare and societal costs over 24 months.
cards.result: Patient Global Impression of Improvement mean difference −0.05 (95% CI −0.14 to 0.03) and QALY difference −0.03 (95% CI −0.07 to 0.002), neither significant. Healthcare costs were significantly lower with pessary therapy (mean difference −€1807, 95% CI −€2172 to −€1446) and societal costs likewise (−€1850, 95% CI −€2349 to −€1341); 54.1% of the pessary group crossed over to surgery and 3.6% had recurrent surgery. The probability that pessary therapy is cost-effective was 1 at willingness-to-pay thresholds between €0 and €20,000 per QALY from both perspectives.
cards.watchOut: The cost advantage is a strategy effect in one Dutch costing setting and already absorbs the 54.1% crossover rate; it does not show the pessary itself works as well as surgery, and prices and surgical pathways differ elsewhere.
cards.source: Ben ÂJ et al. Cost-effectiveness of pessary therapy versus surgery for symptomatic pelvic organ prolapse: an economic evaluation alongside a randomised non-inferiority controlled trial. BMJ Open. 2024. PMID: 38692718. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large strategy trial — improvement close, equivalence unproven, crossover the rule, costs lower
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large strategy trial — improvement close, equivalence unproven, crossover the rule, costs lower
cards.people: One multicentre randomised noninferiority trial of 440 women with symptomatic prolapse (PEOPLE, Netherlands) comparing an initial pessary strategy with surgery over 24 months, plus its alongside economic evaluation.
cards.result: Improvement at 24 months 76.3% (pessary-first) versus 81.5% (surgery); noninferiority not demonstrated (P=.16); per-protocol 70.3% versus 83.3%; crossover to surgery 54.1%; QALYs not significantly different; healthcare costs €1,807 lower with pessary-first. PROPOSED SPLIT, as in the balance above.
cards.watchOut: Tier C is set: the shelf rests on a single trial (with its own economic re-analysis), so the developer reviews it personally. Women who most want to avoid surgery are also the least represented in the per-protocol contrast after crossover.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Vaart LR et al. JAMA. 2022 (PMID: 36538310); Ben ÂJ et al. BMJ Open. 2024 (PMID: 38692718).

shelves.title: Levonorgestrel coil for endometrial hyperplasia: every woman responded in the randomised trial (53 of 53) versus 96% on continuous oral progestogen and only 69% on cyclical oral progestogen
shelves.question: In women with endometrial hyperplasia without atypia (low or medium risk), does the levonorgestrel intrauterine system normalise the endometrium more reliably than oral progestogen — and does how the oral drug is scheduled matter?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Contraceptives, Oral, Synthetic/therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Endometrial Hyperplasia/drug therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel/therapeutic use · Medroxyprogesterone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Norway · Progestins/therapeutic use · Risk · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the coil and continuous oral therapy both work; cyclical oral therapy is the weak option. In the Norwegian multicentre randomised trial (Ørbo A et al., PMID: 24286192), histological response at 6 months was obtained in all women on the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (53 of 53), 96% on continuous oral medroxyprogesterone (46 of 48), and only 69% on cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone (36 of 52). The earlier systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Gallos ID et al., PMID: 20934679) pointed the same way: pooled regression with the intrauterine system versus oral progestogens was 92% versus 66% in complex hyperplasia and 90% versus 69% in atypical hyperplasia, with no significant difference in simple hyperplasia (96% vs 89%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for hyperplasia without atypia, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is at least as reliable as continuous oral progestogen and clearly better than cyclical oral regimens, which should not be used for this purpose.

cards.headline: Ørbo 2014: response in 53 of 53 on the coil, 46 of 48 (96%) on continuous oral medroxyprogesterone, 36 of 52 (69%) on cyclical oral therapy
cards.summary: Ørbo 2014: response in 53 of 53 on the coil, 46 of 48 (96%) on continuous oral medroxyprogesterone, 36 of 52 (69%) on cyclical oral therapy
cards.people: 170 women aged 30–70 years with low- or medium-risk endometrial hyperplasia in Norway, randomised to a levonorgestrel intrauterine system, continuous oral medroxyprogesterone 10 mg daily, or cyclical oral medroxyprogesterone 10 mg for 10 days per cycle, for 6 months; primary outcome was histological normalisation versus persisting hyperplasia.
cards.result: After 6 months, responses were obtained for all women in the intrauterine-system group (53/53, 95% CI 0.93–1.0), 96% of the continuous oral group (46/48, 95% CI 0.86–0.99), and 69% of the cyclical oral group (36/52, 95% CI 0.55–0.81); all three regimens showed significant effect overall (P<0.001), and adverse effects were relatively common with minimal differences between groups. The authors conclude cyclical progestogens are less effective and should not be used for this purpose.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, 6-month histology in low/medium-risk (non-atypical) hyperplasia from one national trial; it does not answer atypical hyperplasia or cancer prevention, where hysterectomy remains the standard comparator, and longer-term relapse after removal is outside this record.
cards.source: Ørbo A et al. Levonorgestrel-impregnated intrauterine device as treatment for endometrial hyperplasia: a national multicentre randomised trial. BJOG: An International Journal of Obstetrics & Gynaecology. 2014. PMID: 24286192. Registry ID: NCT01074892. cards.headline: Gallos 2010 meta-analysis: pooled regression favoured the coil in complex (92% vs 66%) and atypical (90% vs 69%) hyperplasia, not in simple hyperplasia
cards.summary: Gallos 2010 meta-analysis: pooled regression favoured the coil in complex (92% vs 66%) and atypical (90% vs 69%) hyperplasia, not in simple hyperplasia
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Gallos 2010)
cards.people: 24 observational studies of 1,001 women with endometrial hyperplasia treated with oral progestogens or a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system, of low methodologic quality by the review's own assessment.
cards.result: Oral progestogens achieved a lower pooled regression rate than the intrauterine system for complex hyperplasia (pooled rate 66% vs 92%; P<.01) and atypical hyperplasia (69% vs 90%; P=.03). There was no statistical difference in simple hyperplasia (89% vs 96%; P=.41).
cards.watchOut: Every pooled study was observational and rated low quality, so these rates support — but cannot substitute for — the randomised comparison; atypical-hyperplasia figures in particular come from women who declined or were unfit for surgery, a selected group.
cards.source: Gallos ID et al. Oral progestogens vs levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for endometrial hyperplasia: a systematic review and metaanalysis. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2010. PMID: 20934679. cards.summary: Synthesis: coil and continuous oral therapy both normalise the lining; cyclical oral therapy fails about a third
cards.people: One randomised trial of 170 women with low/medium-risk hyperplasia (Ørbo 2014, Norway) read with a meta-analysis of 24 observational studies totalling 1,001 women (Gallos 2010).
cards.result: Response at 6 months: intrauterine system 53/53, continuous oral 46/48 (96%), cyclical oral 36/52 (69%). Observational pooling: complex hyperplasia regression 92% (coil) versus 66% (oral); atypical 90% versus 69%; simple 96% versus 89% (not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C because the randomised base is a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Neither source follows women to cancer outcomes or post-treatment relapse; the shelf is about 6-month histological response in hyperplasia managed without hysterectomy, and atypical disease still belongs in a surgical conversation.

shelves.title: ECHO: HIV acquisition did not differ substantially between the injectable, the copper IUD and the implant — hazard ratios 1.04, 1.23 and 1.18, all non-significant, in 7,829 randomised women
shelves.question: In women at high risk of HIV who want contraception, does intramuscular depot medroxyprogesterone acetate raise HIV acquisition compared with a copper intrauterine device or a levonorgestrel implant?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Eswatini/epidemiology · Family Planning Services · Female · HIV Infections/epidemiology/etiology · Humans · Incidence · Intention to Treat Analysis · Intrauterine Devices, Copper/adverse effects · Kenya/epidemiology · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Medroxyprogesterone Acetate/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Pregnancy · South Africa/epidemiology · Young Adult · Zambia/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the randomised comparison found no substantial HIV-risk difference between the three methods. In the ECHO trial (Evidence for Contraceptive Options and HIV Outcomes (ECHO) Trial Consortium, PMID: 31204114), 7,829 women in eSwatini, Kenya, South Africa and Zambia were randomised to depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, a copper intrauterine device, or a levonorgestrel implant; 397 HIV infections occurred (incidence 3.81 per 100 woman-years). Hazard ratios for HIV acquisition were 1.04 (96% CI 0.82–1.33, p=0.72) for the injectable versus the copper device, 1.23 (0.95–1.59, p=0.097) versus the implant, and 1.18 (0.91–1.53, p=0.19) for the copper device versus the implant. All three methods were highly effective contraceptives: 255 pregnancies occurred, 71% of them after the assigned method had been discontinued. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): within this trial's precision, the long-feared injectable–HIV signal from observational data was not confirmed — the confidence intervals still allow up to roughly a 1.3- to 1.6-fold relative difference, so 'no substantial difference', not proof of exact equality, is the honest claim.

cards.headline: ECHO 2019: 397 HIV infections across 7,715 women analysed — HR 1.04 (injectable vs copper IUD), 1.23 (injectable vs implant), 1.18 (copper IUD vs implant), none significant
cards.summary: ECHO 2019: 397 HIV infections across 7,715 women analysed — HR 1.04 (injectable vs copper IUD), 1.23 (injectable vs implant), 1.18 (copper IUD vs implant), none significant
cards.type: Randomised multicentre open-label trial (ECHO Trial Consortium 2019)
cards.people: 7,829 HIV-seronegative women aged 16–35 years seeking effective contraception at 12 sites in eSwatini, Kenya, South Africa and Zambia, randomised 1:1:1 to intramuscular depot medroxyprogesterone acetate every 3 months (n=2,609), a copper intrauterine device (n=2,607), or a levonorgestrel implant (n=2,613), and asked to use the assigned method for 18 months; 7,715 women contributed to the modified intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: 397 HIV infections occurred (incidence 3.81 per 100 woman-years [95% CI 3.45–4.21]): 143 in the injectable group (4.19 per 100 woman-years), 138 with the copper device (3.94), and 116 with the implant (3.31). Hazard ratios: injectable versus copper device 1.04 (96% CI 0.82–1.33, p=0.72); injectable versus implant 1.23 (0.95–1.59, p=0.097); copper device versus implant 1.18 (0.91–1.53, p=0.19). Serious adverse events occurred in 2% (injectable), 4% (copper device) and 3% (implant); 12 women died. Pregnancies: 255 in total (61 injectable, 116 copper device, 78 implant), with 181 (71%) occurring after discontinuation of the assigned method.
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial: Tier C is set because the shelf rests on one trial and addresses a harm question. The intervals exclude a large effect but not a modest one (upper bounds 1.33–1.59), adherence to the assigned method covered 92% of woman-years rather than all of it, and the population was young African women in high-incidence settings — the group in whom the question matters most, but not every user.
cards.source: Evidence for Contraceptive Options and HIV Outcomes (ECHO) Trial Consortium. HIV incidence among women using intramuscular depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, a copper intrauterine device, or a levonorgestrel implant for contraception: a randomised, multicentre, open-label trial. The Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31204114. Registry ID: NCT02550067. cards.headline: Synthesis: the randomised answer displaced the observational fear — no substantial difference, with bounded precision
cards.summary: Synthesis: the randomised answer displaced the observational fear — no substantial difference, with bounded precision
cards.people: One randomised trial of 7,829 women (7,715 analysed) comparing three contraceptive methods head-to-head over 18 months in four African countries with high HIV incidence.
cards.result: HIV incidence 4.19 (injectable), 3.94 (copper device) and 3.31 (implant) per 100 woman-years; pairwise hazard ratios 1.04, 1.23 and 1.18, all non-significant; all methods highly effective, with most pregnancies occurring after discontinuation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C for single-trial personal review.
cards.watchOut: 'No substantial difference' is the trial's own wording and the shelf keeps it: a true relative increase of up to about 30–60% for some pairings remains inside the confidence intervals, and HIV incidence was high on every method (3.81 per 100 woman-years overall), which is an argument for integrated HIV prevention with any of them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Evidence for Contraceptive Options and HIV Outcomes (ECHO) Trial Consortium. The Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 31204114).

shelves.title: Gabapentin for vulvodynia: tampon-test pain 4.0 on gabapentin versus 4.3 on placebo (difference −0.3, P=.07) in the one double-blind crossover trial — and no tested treatment beat placebo on pain in the pooled record
shelves.question: In women with vulvodynia (provoked vestibulodynia), does extended-release gabapentin reduce pain compared with placebo — and does any tested treatment improve pain in the randomised record?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Cross-Over Studies · Delayed-Action Preparations · Diagnostic Techniques, Obstetrical and Gynecological · Double-Blind Method · Dyspareunia/drug therapy/psychology · Female · Gabapentin/administration & dosage · Humans · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Vulvodynia/drug therapy/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one rigorous trial of gabapentin missed its endpoint, and pooling the few randomised treatments shows the same pattern. In the multicentre double-blind crossover trial (Brown CS et al., PMID: 29742655), tampon-test pain was 4.0 on extended-release gabapentin (1,200–3,000 mg/day) versus 4.3 on placebo (adjusted difference −0.3, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.0; P=.07), with no benefit for intercourse pain or daily pain. The systematic review and meta-analysis of vestibulodynia treatments (Pérez-López FR et al., PMID: 31364893) found four randomised trials (n=275) across oestrogen cream, desipramine with or without lidocaine, lidocaine, laser and transcranial stimulation, and no intervention reduced dyspareunia (mean difference 0.08, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.64) or daily vestibular symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): gabapentin should not be recommended on this record, and no pooled randomised treatment has yet beaten placebo on vulvodynia pain itself.

cards.headline: Brown 2018: tampon-test pain 4.0 (gabapentin) vs 4.3 (placebo), difference −0.3 (95% CI −0.7 to 0.0), P=.07 — intercourse and daily pain also null
cards.summary: Brown 2018: tampon-test pain 4.0 (gabapentin) vs 4.3 (placebo), difference −0.3 (95% CI −0.7 to 0.0), P=.07 — intercourse and daily pain also null
cards.people: 89 women (mean age 37 years) with vulvodynia at three US academic institutions, randomised to extended-release gabapentin 1,200–3,000 mg/day or placebo in crossover phases; primary outcome was pain intensity (0–10) on the standardised tampon insertion-and-removal test in the last 7 days of each maintenance phase; the trial had 90% power to detect a 1-point difference.
cards.result: Tampon-test pain: adjusted mean 4.0 (95% CI 3.0–4.9) on gabapentin versus 4.3 (3.4–5.2) on placebo (difference −0.3, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.0; P=.07). Sexual intercourse pain: 3.9 versus 4.0 (difference −0.1, 95% CI −0.9 to 0.6; P=.76). Daily pain: 2.7 versus 2.9 (difference −0.2; P=.36). The authors conclude the data do not support recommending gabapentin alone for vulvodynia.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval excludes the 1-point benefit the trial was powered for, which makes this an informative null for a large effect — but a benefit smaller than about 0.7 points remains possible, crossover carry-over can dilute contrasts, and women with longer pain duration or not using oral contraceptives showed minimal improvement signals in subset analyses that are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Brown CS et al. Gabapentin for the Treatment of Vulvodynia: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Obstetrics & Gynecology. 2018. PMID: 29742655. Registry ID: NCT01301001. cards.headline: Pérez-López 2019: across 4 randomised trials (n=275), no treatment reduced dyspareunia (MD 0.08, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.64) or daily vestibular symptoms
cards.summary: Pérez-López 2019: across 4 randomised trials (n=275), no treatment reduced dyspareunia (MD 0.08, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.64) or daily vestibular symptoms
cards.people: Four randomised placebo- or sham-controlled trials totalling 275 women with vestibulodynia, evaluating vaginal conjugated-oestrogen cream, oral desipramine with or without topical lidocaine, topical lidocaine, laser therapy and transcranial direct current stimulation (search to December 2018).
cards.result: In traditional meta-analysis, interventions did not reduce dyspareunia (mean difference 0.08; 95% CI −0.49 to 0.64), daily vestibular symptoms (MD −0.04; 95% CI −0.31 to 0.24), or McGill Pain Questionnaire scores (MD −0.17; 95% CI −2.16 to 1.81). The Index of Sexual Satisfaction did improve (MD −5.14; 95% CI −9.52 to −0.75), and in network meta-analysis oral desipramine with or without lidocaine improved that satisfaction index versus other treatments — a satisfaction signal without a pain signal.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials of five different modalities is a thin base for a class verdict; the review predates the gabapentin trial's full influence on practice and cannot exclude benefits of treatments never randomised (including pelvic-floor physiotherapy approaches tested outside placebo-controlled designs).
cards.source: Pérez-López FR et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of treatment modalities for vestibulodynia in women. The European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care. 2019. PMID: 31364893. cards.headline: Synthesis: one powered null trial plus a null pooled record — pain relief for vulvodynia remains unproven, not disproven for every approach
cards.summary: Synthesis: one powered null trial plus a null pooled record — pain relief for vulvodynia remains unproven, not disproven for every approach
cards.people: One double-blind crossover trial of gabapentin in 89 women (Brown 2018) and a meta-analysis of four randomised vestibulodynia trials in 275 women (Pérez-López 2019).
cards.result: Gabapentin versus placebo: −0.3 points on a 0–10 tampon-test pain scale (95% CI −0.7 to 0.0). Pooled treatments versus placebo/sham: dyspareunia mean difference 0.08 (−0.49 to 0.64); daily symptoms −0.04 (−0.31 to 0.24). Sexual-satisfaction scores improved modestly in the pooled record without pain improvement. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C because the anchor claim rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: Both sources are vulnerable to the same gap: vulvodynia is heterogeneous, trials are small and short, and a treatment that helps a defined subgroup could be averaged away — the honest shelf claim is 'no demonstrated benefit', not 'nothing can work'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brown CS et al. Obstetrics & Gynecology. 2018 (PMID: 29742655); Pérez-López FR et al. The European Journal of Contraception & Reproductive Health Care. 2019 (PMID: 31364893).

shelves.title: Linzagolix for endometriosis pain: dysmenorrhoea responders 72.9% on 200 mg with add-back versus 23.5% on placebo in EDELWEISS 3 — the 75 mg dose helped periods (44.0%) but not non-menstrual pain
shelves.question: In women with moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain, does the oral GnRH antagonist linzagolix reduce dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain versus placebo — at 75 mg alone, or at 200 mg with hormonal add-back?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Endometriosis/drug therapy/complications · Double-Blind Method · Dysmenorrhea/drug therapy · Pelvic Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Adult · Estradiol/blood · Norethindrone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use/analogs & derivatives · Norethindrone Acetate · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Drug Therapy, Combination
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — linzagolix reduces endometriosis pain, with the full effect at the high dose plus add-back. In the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 trial (Donnez J et al., PMID: 38648863), responders for dysmenorrhoea at 3 months were 72.9% on linzagolix 200 mg with add-back therapy versus 23.5% on placebo (P<0.001), and for non-menstrual pelvic pain 47.3% versus 30.9% (P=0.007); the 75 mg dose without add-back improved dysmenorrhoea only (44.0% vs 23.5%, P<0.001; non-menstrual pain not significant, P=0.279). The earlier dose-ranging trial (Donnez J et al., PMID: 32505383) found the same dose pattern at 12 weeks — overall pelvic-pain responders 61.5%, 56.4% and 56.3% at 75, 100 and 200 mg versus 34.5% on placebo — with dose-dependent bone loss reaching a mean 2.6% at the spine on 200 mg without add-back. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pain relief is real and dose-graded; the 200 mg dose needs add-back to protect bone, and no trial here compares linzagolix with standard hormonal treatments.

cards.headline: EDELWEISS 3 (Donnez 2024): dysmenorrhoea responders 72.9% (200 mg + add-back) and 44.0% (75 mg) vs 23.5% placebo; non-menstrual pain responders 47.3% vs 30.9% at the high dose only
cards.summary: EDELWEISS 3 (Donnez 2024): dysmenorrhoea responders 72.9% (200 mg + add-back) and 44.0% (75 mg) vs 23.5% placebo; non-menstrual pain responders 47.3% vs 30.9% at the high dose only
cards.people: 486 women with moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, linzagolix 75 mg daily, or linzagolix 200 mg daily plus add-back therapy (estradiol 1.0 mg / norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg), treated for up to 6 months with daily electronic-diary pain scores; primary assessment at 3 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, dysmenorrhoea responders: 72.9% on 200 mg plus add-back versus 23.5% on placebo (P<0.001); 44.0% on 75 mg versus 23.5% (P<0.001). Non-menstrual pelvic pain responders: 47.3% versus 30.9% (P=0.007) at 200 mg plus add-back; the 75 mg dose did not significantly reduce non-menstrual pain (P=0.279). Dyschezia and overall pelvic pain improved significantly in both linzagolix groups; dyspareunia improvements were not significant. Hypoestrogenic effects were mild, with low hot-flush rates and bone density loss under 1% in both groups; benefits persisted at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Placebo-controlled only — the record itself notes the missing comparison with estro-progestogens or progestogens that are standard first-line care; follow-up is 6 months for a chronic disease, and the trial was funded by the drug's developers (ObsEva, with Theramex and Kissei support), with several authors holding sponsor roles disclosed in the record.
cards.source: Donnez J et al. Linzagolix therapy versus a placebo in patients with endometriosis-associated pain: a prospective, randomized, double-blind, Phase 3 study (EDELWEISS 3). Human Reproduction. 2024. PMID: 38648863. Registry ID: NCT03992846. cards.headline: Donnez 2020 (phase 2): overall pelvic-pain responders 61.5% / 56.4% / 56.3% at 75 / 100 / 200 mg vs 34.5% placebo at 12 weeks — spine bone loss up to 2.6% at 200 mg without add-back
cards.summary: Donnez 2020 (phase 2): overall pelvic-pain responders 61.5% / 56.4% / 56.3% at 75 / 100 / 200 mg vs 34.5% placebo at 12 weeks — spine bone loss up to 2.6% at 200 mg without add-back
cards.people: Women aged 18–45 years with surgically confirmed endometriosis and moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain, randomised to linzagolix 50, 75, 100 or 200 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks in a multinational double-blind trial; primary endpoint was responders (at least 30% reduction in overall pelvic pain) at 12 weeks.
cards.result: Responders for overall pelvic pain at 12 weeks: 34.5% on placebo versus 61.5% (75 mg), 56.4% (100 mg) and 56.3% (200 mg), with doses of 75 mg and above significantly better than placebo; a similar pattern held for dysmenorrhoea and non-menstrual pelvic pain, and effects were maintained or increased at 24 weeks. Estradiol suppression, amenorrhoea and quality-of-life gains were dose-dependent. Mean spine bone mineral density loss at 24 weeks was under 1% at 50 and 75 mg, rising dose-dependently to 2.6% at 200 mg (no add-back used in this trial).
cards.watchOut: A dose-finding trial with multiple dose arms and a 30%-responder endpoint; its bone-loss gradient at the unprotected 200 mg dose is exactly why the phase 3 high-dose arm added add-back therapy, so the two trials' high-dose safety pictures are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Donnez J et al. Treatment of endometriosis-associated pain with linzagolix, an oral gonadotropin-releasing hormone-antagonist: a randomized clinical trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant placebo-controlled trials, one dose lesson — full pain cover at 200 mg needs add-back; 75 mg covers dysmenorrhoea only
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant placebo-controlled trials, one dose lesson — full pain cover at 200 mg needs add-back; 75 mg covers dysmenorrhoea only
cards.people: A phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Donnez 2020) and the phase 3 EDELWEISS 3 trial of 486 women (Donnez 2024), both double-blind and placebo-controlled in moderate-to-severe endometriosis-associated pain.
cards.result: Dysmenorrhoea responders at 3 months (EDELWEISS 3): 72.9% (200 mg + add-back), 44.0% (75 mg), 23.5% (placebo). Non-menstrual pain responders: 47.3% versus 30.9% (high dose only). Phase 2 overall-pain responders at 12 weeks: 56–62% at 75–200 mg versus 34.5%. Bone loss without add-back reached 2.6% (spine, 200 mg, 24 weeks) in phase 2 and stayed under 1% with add-back in phase 3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers endometriosis pain only; the same drug's fibroid bleeding trials (PRIMROSE) are housed separately in this library. No head-to-head data against dienogest, combined pills or other GnRH antagonists exist in these records, so 'works versus placebo' must not be read as 'best in class'. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised double-blind trials carry the claim.

shelves.title: Immediate postpartum contraception and breastfeeding: milk intake and continuation were noninferior with immediate implant or coil — the price is coil expulsion in 19% versus 2%
shelves.question: In women who plan to breastfeed, does inserting a levonorgestrel intrauterine device or an etonogestrel implant immediately after delivery harm breastfeeding compared with delayed insertion or no method?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Breast Feeding · Contraceptive Agents, Female/administration & dosage · Equivalence Trials as Topic · Female · Humans · Intrauterine Device Expulsion · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel/administration & dosage · Parturition · Postpartum Period · Pregnancy · Prosthesis Implantation · Time Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — immediate insertion did not measurably harm breastfeeding in two randomised trials, but immediate coils are expelled far more often. In the noninferiority trial of immediate versus delayed levonorgestrel intrauterine device insertion (Turok DK et al., PMID: 28842126), any breastfeeding at 8 weeks was 79% with immediate insertion versus 84% with delayed insertion — noninferior within the prespecified 15% margin — and time to lactogenesis was 65.3 versus 63.6 hours; expulsions, however, were 19% versus 2% (P<.001). In the implant trial (Braga GC et al., PMID: 26209863), infants' breast-milk intake measured by deuterium dilution was essentially identical with an implant inserted within 48 hours versus no method (median 340 vs 330 mL/day after the first dose; 845 vs 785 mL/day after the second). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for breastfeeding itself, immediate long-acting contraception looks safe on this record; the trade-off to counsel is expulsion and possible unnoticed loss of contraception, not milk supply.

cards.headline: Turok 2017: breastfeeding at 8 weeks 79% (immediate IUD) vs 84% (delayed) — noninferior; lactogenesis 65.3 vs 63.6 hours; expulsion 19% vs 2%
cards.summary: Turok 2017: breastfeeding at 8 weeks 79% (immediate IUD) vs 84% (delayed) — noninferior; lactogenesis 65.3 vs 63.6 hours; expulsion 19% vs 2%
cards.people: 259 women (132 immediate, 127 delayed in the final analytic sample) aged 18–40 years at two US university centres who planned to breastfeed and wanted a levonorgestrel intrauterine device, randomised to insertion immediately after delivery or at 4–12 weeks postpartum; primary outcome was breastfeeding continuation at 8 weeks against a 15% noninferiority margin, analysed per protocol.
cards.result: Any breastfeeding at 8 weeks: 79% (95% CI 70–86%) immediate versus 84% (76–91%) delayed — the 5% difference fell within the noninferiority margin (95% CI −5.6 to 15%). Time to lactogenesis: mean 65.3 ± 25.7 hours versus 63.6 ± 21.6 hours (difference 1.7 hours, 95% CI −4.8 to 8.2), noninferior. Expulsions: 24 in the immediate group versus 2 in the delayed group (19% vs 2%, P<.001). No perforations occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: The 15% noninferiority margin is generous — the data remain compatible with up to about a 15-point lower continuation rate on the interval as printed — and 60 of 319 enrolled women were lost or excluded before the analytic sample; the expulsion gap, not lactation, is the outcome that clearly separates the strategies.
cards.source: Turok DK et al. Immediate postpartum levonorgestrel intrauterine device insertion and breast-feeding outcomes: a noninferiority randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2017. PMID: 28842126. cards.headline: Braga 2015: measured milk intake 340 vs 330 mL/day (first measure) and 845 vs 785 mL/day (second) with immediate implant versus no method — no difference
cards.summary: Braga 2015: measured milk intake 340 vs 330 mL/day (first measure) and 845 vs 785 mL/day (second) with immediate implant versus no method — no difference
cards.people: 24 postpartum women and their newborns randomised to an etonogestrel implant inserted within 48 hours of delivery (n=12) or no contraceptive method (n=12); infants' breast-milk intake over the first 6 weeks was measured objectively by the deuterium oxide dose-to-mother technique with saliva sampling.
cards.result: Median breast-milk intake was similar between groups after both deuterium doses: first dose, 340 mL/day (implant, range 240–420) versus 330 mL/day (control, 300–530), p=.54; second dose, 845 mL/day (770–980) versus 785 mL/day (680–980), p=.63. Exclusive breastfeeding rates and newborn weight were also similar over the first 6 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Only 24 mother–infant pairs: this trial can rule out a gross milk-volume effect with an objective measure, but nothing subtler; it studied the implant, whose systemic progestogen exposure differs from an intrauterine device, and followed infants for 6 weeks only.
cards.source: Braga GC et al. Immediate postpartum initiation of etonogestrel-releasing implant: A randomized controlled trial on breastfeeding impact. Contraception. 2015. PMID: 26209863. cards.headline: Synthesis: breastfeeding survives immediate insertion in both trials; expulsion is the real cost of the immediate coil
cards.summary: Synthesis: breastfeeding survives immediate insertion in both trials; expulsion is the real cost of the immediate coil
cards.people: Two randomised trials: immediate versus delayed levonorgestrel intrauterine device insertion (259 women analysed, Turok 2017) and immediate etonogestrel implant versus no method with measured milk intake (24 pairs, Braga 2015).
cards.result: Breastfeeding at 8 weeks 79% versus 84% (noninferior); lactogenesis timing essentially identical; milk intake medians within 10–60 mL/day between groups at both measures. Expulsion with immediate IUD insertion 19% versus 2%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for breastfeeding outcomes, with the expulsion harm on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for infant growth or long-duration breastfeeding endpoints, and neither compares immediate insertion against the outcome women may care about most — rapid repeat pregnancy — so this shelf answers the lactation question only. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials address the question, though one is very small.
cards.source: Synthesis of Turok DK et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2017 (PMID: 28842126); Braga GC et al. Contraception. 2015 (PMID: 26209863).

shelves.title: Ondansetron versus metoclopramide for hyperemesis gravidarum: vomiting and well-being tied at 24 hours (median 1 vs 2 episodes; well-being 9 vs 9) — ondansetron won on side effects, not on sickness
shelves.question: In women hospitalised with hyperemesis gravidarum, is ondansetron more effective than metoclopramide at controlling vomiting and nausea in the first 24 hours — and how do their side effects compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antiemetics/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Hyperemesis Gravidarum/drug therapy · Metoclopramide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Ondansetron/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for efficacy, the head-to-head trial is a tie; the separation is tolerability and price. In the double-blind randomised trial (Abas MN et al., PMID: 24807340), women with hyperemesis gravidarum received intravenous ondansetron 4 mg or metoclopramide 10 mg every 8 hours for 24 hours: median well-being scores were 9 versus 9 (P=.33), vomiting episodes 1 versus 2 (P=.38), and nausea trajectories did not differ (P=.22). Drowsiness (12.5% vs 30%; number needed to treat to benefit, 6), dry mouth (10.0% vs 23.8%; NNTB 8) and persistent ketonuria at 24 hours (12.5% vs 30%; NNTB 6) were all less frequent on ondansetron, while hospital stay was similar and metoclopramide was significantly cheaper. The JAMA systematic review of treatments for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis (McParlin C et al., PMID: 27701665) likewise found ondansetron associated with improvement across severity ranges on low-quality overall evidence, with one small trial favouring ondansetron over metoclopramide on day-4 nausea scores. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): choose between these two on side effects, availability and cost — not on expected antiemetic power.

cards.headline: Abas 2014: well-being 9 vs 9, vomiting episodes 1 vs 2, nausea no difference — but drowsiness 12.5% vs 30% and ketonuria 12.5% vs 30% favour ondansetron
cards.summary: Abas 2014: well-being 9 vs 9, vomiting episodes 1 vs 2, nausea no difference — but drowsiness 12.5% vs 30% and ketonuria 12.5% vs 30% favour ondansetron
cards.people: 160 women with hyperemesis gravidarum randomised to intravenous ondansetron 4 mg (n=80) or metoclopramide 10 mg (n=80) every 8 hours for 24 hours, with emesis diaries, 10-point well-being and nausea scales, and an adverse-effects questionnaire; analysis was intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Median well-being score 9 (range 5–10) on ondansetron versus 9 (4–10) on metoclopramide (P=.33); vomiting episodes in 24 hours 1 (0–9) versus 2 (0–23) (P=.38); nausea scores over 24 hours did not differ (P=.22). Less frequent on ondansetron: drowsiness 12.5% versus 30% (P=.01; NNTB 6), xerostomia 10.0% versus 23.8% (P<.01; NNTB 8), and persistent ketonuria at 24 hours 12.5% versus 30% (P=.01; NNTB 6). Length of hospital stay was similar; the authors note metoclopramide was significantly less expensive in their setting.
cards.watchOut: A 24-hour, single-centre comparison in hospitalised hyperemesis: it cannot speak to oral step-down therapy, refractory cases, fetal safety, or symptoms beyond the first day, and its medians hide wide ranges (vomiting episodes up to 23 in the metoclopramide arm). Tier C is set: one trial carries the head-to-head claim.
cards.source: Abas MN et al. Ondansetron compared with metoclopramide for hyperemesis gravidarum: a randomized controlled trial. Obstetrics & Gynecology. 2014. PMID: 24807340. cards.headline: McParlin 2016 (JAMA review of 78 studies): ondansetron improved symptoms across severity ranges; overall evidence quality low
cards.summary: McParlin 2016 (JAMA review of 78 studies): ondansetron improved symptoms across severity ranges; overall evidence quality low
cards.people: 78 studies (8,930 participants; 67 randomised trials and 11 nonrandomised studies) of treatments for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy and hyperemesis gravidarum, searched to June 2016 and synthesised narratively because heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis.
cards.result: Evidence from 35 low-risk-of-bias trials indicated that ginger, vitamin B6, antihistamines, metoclopramide (mild symptoms), pyridoxine-doxylamine, and ondansetron (moderate symptoms) were associated with improved symptoms versus placebo. One trial (n=83) found lower day-4 nausea scores on ondansetron than metoclopramide (mean VAS 4.1 [SD 2.9] vs 5.7 [2.3]; P=.023) but more emesis episodes (5.0 [3.1] vs 3.3 [3]; P=.013), with a better vomiting trend over 14 days (P=.042). Corticosteroids may help severe cases. The review's overall verdict: quality of evidence was low.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis, not a pooled estimate: its ondansetron-versus-metoclopramide signal comes from one 83-woman trial with internally mixed results (nausea better, episode count worse), so it supports equipoise between the two drugs rather than superiority for either.
cards.source: McParlin C et al. Treatments for Hyperemesis Gravidarum and Nausea and Vomiting in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27701665. cards.headline: Synthesis: equal sickness control, unequal side effects — the choice is tolerability and cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: equal sickness control, unequal side effects — the choice is tolerability and cost
cards.people: One double-blind head-to-head trial in 160 hospitalised women (Abas 2014) read against a 78-study systematic review of pregnancy sickness treatments (McParlin 2016).
cards.result: At 24 hours: well-being 9 versus 9; vomiting 1 versus 2 episodes; nausea trajectories equal. Side-effect gaps favouring ondansetron: drowsiness 12.5% versus 30%, dry mouth 10.0% versus 23.8%, persistent ketonuria 12.5% versus 30%. The wider review finds both drugs better than placebo for symptoms, on low-quality evidence. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for efficacy, Tier C (single head-to-head trial).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here addresses first-trimester fetal safety comparisons, which are observational questions outside these records, or treatment beyond 24 hours; women with refractory hyperemesis were not the studied population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abas MN et al. Obstetrics & Gynecology. 2014 (PMID: 24807340); McParlin C et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27701665).

shelves.title: Upright in the second stage splits by epidural: without one, fewer assisted births (RR 0.75) and episiotomies (RR 0.75) but more blood loss over 500 mL (RR 1.48); with one, upright gave fewer spontaneous births (35.2% versus 41.1%, BUMPES)
shelves.question: In women in the second stage of labour, do upright positions reduce instrumental birth and episiotomy compared with supine or lithotomy positions?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesia, Obstetrical/methods · Anesthesia, Epidural/methods · Anesthetics/administration & dosage · Apgar Score · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Labor Stage, Second/physiology · Labor, Obstetric/physiology · Long Term Adverse Effects/diagnosis/etiology/prevention & control · Obstetric Labor Complications/diagnosis/etiology/prevention & control · Parity/physiology · Patient Positioning/methods · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer reverses with epidural analgesia. Without an epidural, the Cochrane review of 30 trials in 9,015 women (Gupta JK et al., PMID: 28539008) found upright positions reduced assisted deliveries (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.66–0.86) and episiotomies (average relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61–0.92) and shortened the second stage by about 6 minutes (mean difference −6.16 minutes, 95% CI −9.74 to −2.59), at the cost of more estimated blood loss over 500 mL (relative risk 1.48, 95% CI 1.10–1.98) and a possible increase in second-degree tears (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 1.00–1.44), with no clear difference in caesarean section (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.81–1.81). With a low-dose epidural, the large BUMPES trial (PMID: 29046273) found the opposite for its primary outcome: spontaneous vaginal birth in 35.2% upright versus 41.1% lying down (adjusted risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.94). PROPOSED SPLIT: upright helps women without an epidural on instrumental birth and episiotomy while raising measured blood loss; with an epidural, lying down gave more spontaneous births.

cards.headline: Epidural and Position Trial Collaborative Group 2017 (BUMPES): spontaneous vaginal birth 35.2% upright versus 41.1% lying down (adjusted RR 0.86) in 3,093 nulliparous women with low-dose epidural
cards.summary: Epidural and Position Trial Collaborative Group 2017 (BUMPES): spontaneous vaginal birth 35.2% upright versus 41.1% lying down (adjusted RR 0.86) in 3,093 nulliparous women with low-dose epidural
cards.people: 3,093 nulliparous women aged 16 or older at term with a singleton cephalic presentation in the second stage of labour with low-dose epidural analgesia, at 41 UK hospital labour wards, allocated to an upright (n=1,556) or lying-down (n=1,537) position in the second stage.
cards.result: Spontaneous vaginal birth occurred in 35.2% (548 of 1,556) of the upright group versus 41.1% (632 of 1,537) lying down (adjusted risk ratio 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.78 to 0.94) — a 5.9% absolute increase in spontaneous vaginal birth with lying down (number needed to treat 17). No evidence of differences was found for most secondary outcomes, including instrumental vaginal delivery (adjusted risk ratio 1.08, 99% CI 0.99 to 1.18), obstetric anal sphincter injury (1.27, 0.88 to 1.84), infant Apgar score under 4 at five minutes (0.66, 0.06 to 6.88) and maternal faecal incontinence at one year (1.18, 0.61 to 2.28).
cards.watchOut: Positions could not be masked and recorded adherence was imperfect — women allocated upright did not all stay upright — so this is a policy-of-position result in epidural patients only; it says nothing about women without epidurals.
cards.source: Epidural and Position Trial Collaborative Group et al. cards.headline: Gupta 2017 (Cochrane, no epidural): assisted delivery RR 0.75 and episiotomy RR 0.75 with upright positions, second stage 6 minutes shorter — but blood loss >500 mL RR 1.48 and second-degree tears possibly up (RR 1.20)
cards.summary: Gupta 2017 (Cochrane, no epidural): assisted delivery RR 0.75 and episiotomy RR 0.75 with upright positions, second stage 6 minutes shorter — but blood loss >500 mL RR 1.48 and second-degree tears possibly up (RR 1.20)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Gupta 2017, Cochrane)
cards.people: Women in the second stage of labour without epidural anaesthesia, in 30 trials involving 9,015 women comparing any upright position (sitting, birthing stools, chairs, squatting, kneeling) with supine or lithotomy positions.
cards.result: Compared with supine positions, upright positions were associated with a reduction in assisted deliveries (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.86; 21 trials, 6,481 women), a reduction in episiotomies (average relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.92; 17 trials, 6,148 women), a shorter second stage (mean difference −6.16 minutes, 95% CI −9.74 to −2.59; 19 trials, 5,811 women), increased estimated blood loss greater than 500 mL (relative risk 1.48, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.98; 15 trials, 5,615 women), a possible increase in second-degree perineal tears (relative risk 1.20, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.44), no clear difference in caesarean section (relative risk 1.22, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.81) or in third- or fourth-degree tears (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.65), and fewer abnormal fetal heart rate patterns (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.93). Evidence quality was mostly low or very low, with high heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: The review's own warning: variable risk of bias, very low to moderate quality evidence, and heterogeneity so large (I² up to 91%) that pooled numbers are guides, not measurements. Estimated blood loss is also easier to collect — and to over-record — in upright births.
cards.source: Gupta JK et al. Position in the second stage of labour for women without epidural anaesthesia. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28539008. cards.headline: Synthesis: position is not one intervention — it is two, and the epidural decides which one a woman is getting
cards.summary: Synthesis: position is not one intervention — it is two, and the epidural decides which one a woman is getting
cards.people: One large pragmatic trial in epidural patients (BUMPES, n=3,093) and a Cochrane synthesis of 30 trials in women without epidural anaesthesia (n=9,015).
cards.result: Without epidural: assisted delivery RR 0.75, episiotomy RR 0.75, blood loss >500 mL RR 1.48. With epidural: spontaneous vaginal birth 35.2% upright versus 41.1% lying down (adjusted RR 0.86). PROPOSED SPLIT — by epidural status, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: The two halves rest on different evidence grades: BUMPES is one large modern trial; the no-epidural half is a heterogeneous pool of mostly small older trials. The split is real in the data, but the no-epidural effect sizes should not be quoted as precise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Epidural and Position Trial Collaborative Group et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2017 (PMID: 29046273); Gupta JK et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28539008).

shelves.title: Pain relief for endometrial sampling: lidocaine spray cut pain scores from 5.11 to 3.51 against placebo, and intrauterine lidocaine beat paracervical block after the procedure
shelves.question: In women having outpatient endometrial sampling, does a paracervical block or intrauterine lidocaine reduce procedural pain compared with placebo or no analgesia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage · Biopsy/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Endometrium/pathology · Female · Humans · Lidocaine/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Pain/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — local lidocaine, by spray, intrauterine infusion or added to a block, reduces sampling pain in randomised trials. Aksoy H et al. (PMID: 26471087) randomised 120 women having office endometrial biopsy to 10% lidocaine spray or placebo spray, double-blind: mean pain during the procedure was 3.51 ± 1.51 on lidocaine versus 5.11 ± 1.66 on placebo (P<.001). Cengiz H et al. (PMID: 24071820) randomised 120 women to intrauterine lidocaine or paracervical block: pain immediately after the procedure was similar (P=.079), but pain 30 minutes after was significantly lower with intrauterine lidocaine (P=.0001). Rattanachaiyanont M et al. (PMID: 16135583), in 66 women having fractional curettage under paracervical block, found adding intrauterine lidocaine lowered the median maximum pain score from 4.7 to 2.3 (P=.022) and cut the proportion with pain above 4 from 60.6% to 33.3% (number needed to treat 3.7). Paracervical block alone, tested against placebo in outpatient hysteroscopy with biopsy (live evidence at shelf #4728's Lau 1999 card), helped only at instrument insertion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lidocaine-based local anaesthesia — spray or intrauterine — reduces endometrial sampling pain; the block alone is the weakest of the tested options.

cards.headline: Aksoy 2016: pain during office endometrial biopsy 3.51 on 10% lidocaine spray versus 5.11 on placebo spray (P<.001)
cards.summary: Aksoy 2016: pain during office endometrial biopsy 3.51 on 10% lidocaine spray versus 5.11 on placebo spray (P<.001)
cards.people: 120 women undergoing office-based endometrial sampling, randomised to 10% lidocaine spray (n=60) or placebo spray (n=60) in a prospective double-blind study.
cards.result: The mean pain score during the procedure was 3.51 ± 1.51 in the lidocaine spray group and 5.11 ± 1.66 in the placebo group; lidocaine spray significantly lowered pain scores compared with placebo (P<.001). The authors describe lidocaine spray as a non-invasive, easy-to-apply and more comfortable anaesthetic method for office-based endometrial sampling.
cards.watchOut: A 1.6-point difference on a 10-point scale is real but leaves average pain in the mild-to-moderate range — spray helps, it does not numb. Single-centre trial; pain was measured during the procedure only in the figures reported in the record.
cards.source: Aksoy H et al. Effect of lidocaine spray in pain management during office-based endometrial sampling: A randomised placebo-controlled trial. Journal of obstetrics and gynaecology : the journal of the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology. 2016. PMID: 26471087. cards.headline: Cengiz 2014: intrauterine lidocaine versus paracervical block — pain equal immediately after (P=.079), lower at 30 minutes with intrauterine lidocaine (P=.0001)
cards.summary: Cengiz 2014: intrauterine lidocaine versus paracervical block — pain equal immediately after (P=.079), lower at 30 minutes with intrauterine lidocaine (P=.0001)
cards.people: 120 women undergoing endometrial biopsy, randomised to paracervical block (n=67) or intrauterine lidocaine (n=53); groups were similar in age, body mass index, gravidity, previous vaginal deliveries, menopausal status and uterine depth. Pain was measured on a visual analogue scale during and after the procedure.
cards.result: Pain scores immediately after the procedure were similar in the two groups (P=.079). Pain scores 30 minutes after the procedure were significantly lower in the intrauterine lidocaine group than in the paracervical block group (P=.0001). The authors concluded intrauterine lidocaine may be the preferred anaesthesia for endometrial biopsy, with no serious complications reported.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or no-treatment arm — this trial ranks two active techniques rather than proving either beats nothing, and the record reports P values without the underlying pain scores for this comparison, so the size of the 30-minute advantage cannot be quantified from the record.
cards.source: Cengiz H et al. Comparing the efficacy of intrauterine lidocaine and paracervical block in decreasing the pain associated with endometrial biopsy: a randomised trial. Archives of gynecology and obstetrics. 2014. PMID: 24071820. cards.headline: Rattanachaiyanont 2005: adding intrauterine lidocaine to paracervical block cut median maximum pain from 4.7 to 2.3 during fractional curettage (P=.022)
cards.summary: Rattanachaiyanont 2005: adding intrauterine lidocaine to paracervical block cut median maximum pain from 4.7 to 2.3 during fractional curettage (P=.022)
cards.people: 66 patients with abnormal uterine bleeding undergoing fractional curettage under paracervical block (10 mL 1% lidocaine), randomised to additional intrauterine 5 mL 2% lidocaine (n=33) or intrauterine saline (n=33). Primary outcome was maximum pain on a 10-cm visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Compared with saline, the lidocaine group had a significantly lower median maximum pain score (2.3 versus 4.7, P=.022) and fewer patients with a pain score above 4 (33.3% versus 60.6%, P=.026). Pain scores were lower at both the endocervical and uterine curettage steps. The number needed to treat to prevent one case with a pain score above 4 was 3.7 (95% CI 2.4–38.5). No difference in other outcomes, and no increase in adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Fractional curettage is a more invasive sampling procedure than an office Pipelle biopsy, and every woman here already had a paracervical block — the card shows intrauterine lidocaine adds benefit on top of a block, which supports, but is not identical to, the office-biopsy question.
cards.source: Rattanachaiyanont M et al. Effectiveness of intrauterine anesthesia for pain relief during fractional curettage. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2005. PMID: 16135583. cards.headline: Synthesis: lidocaine where the sampling happens beats a block around the cervix
cards.summary: Synthesis: lidocaine where the sampling happens beats a block around the cervix
cards.people: Three randomised trials of local anaesthesia for endometrial sampling or curettage (Aksoy 2016, n=120, spray versus placebo; Cengiz 2014, n=120, intrauterine versus block; Rattanachaiyanont 2005, n=66, intrauterine lidocaine added to block versus saline).
cards.result: Pain during biopsy: 3.51 versus 5.11 (spray versus placebo, P<.001). Maximum pain under block: median 2.3 versus 4.7 with intrauterine lidocaine added (P=.022); pain above 4 in 33.3% versus 60.6%. Head-to-head, intrauterine lidocaine matched the block immediately and beat it at 30 minutes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as stamped.
cards.watchOut: No trial here tested paracervical block alone against placebo for Pipelle biopsy; the block-alone evidence (Lau 1999) sits on shelf #4728 (outpatient hysteroscopy) and was weak. All trials are single-centre and modest in size.

shelves.title: Analgesia for outpatient hysteroscopy: vaginal misoprostol helped in one trial and not in another, an NSAID alone did not beat placebo, and paracervical block helped only at insertion — with more bradycardia
shelves.question: In women having outpatient hysteroscopy, which analgesia (local anaesthetic, NSAIDs, misoprostol priming) reduces pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ambulatory Care/methods · Anesthesia, Local/methods · Anesthetics, Local/pharmacology · Biopsy · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cervix Uteri · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heart Rate/drug effects · Humans · Hysteroscopy · Lidocaine/pharmacology · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Uterine Hemorrhage/diagnosis
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by technique, and the trials pull in different directions. Lau WC et al. (PMID: 10426243) randomised 100 women having outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy to paracervical block with 2% lignocaine or saline, double-blind: the block significantly reduced pain only at insertion of the hysteroscope, not at subsequent stages, and caused a higher incidence of bradycardia and hypotension. Issat T et al. (PMID: 24768981) randomised 150 women to vaginal misoprostol 400 µg, intravenous ketoprofen, or placebo: median pain scores during and immediately after hysteroscopy were significantly lower with misoprostol than with ketoprofen (P=.02) or placebo (P=.006), with no difference by 15 minutes (P=.16). Hassa H et al. (PMID: 23850898), in 158 nulliparous infertile women having vaginoscopic diagnostic hysteroscopy, found neither vaginal misoprostol nor rectal diclofenac beat placebo (median pain 4.75 and 5.01 versus 4.15 on placebo; P=.57). PROPOSED SPLIT: misoprostol priming may reduce pain in conventional outpatient hysteroscopy but showed nothing in vaginoscopic technique; NSAID alone and paracervical block have, at best, narrow and stage-specific effects.

cards.headline: Lau 1999: paracervical block reduced pain only at hysteroscope insertion — and increased bradycardia and hypotension
cards.summary: Lau 1999: paracervical block reduced pain only at hysteroscope insertion — and increased bradycardia and hypotension
cards.people: 100 women undergoing outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy for abnormal uterine bleeding, randomised to paracervical block with 10 mL of 2% lignocaine or normal saline before the procedure; pain was scored at different stages of hysteroscopy with blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, paracervical anaesthesia significantly reduced pain only at the time of insertion of the hysteroscope, but not at the subsequent stages of the procedure. Paracervical injection of lignocaine resulted in a higher incidence of bradycardia and hypotension. The authors concluded paracervical anaesthesia not only fails to reduce pain during outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy overall, but also carries a risk of inducing bradycardia and hypotension, probably from inadvertent intravascular injection.
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance by stage without the underlying pain scores, so the size of the insertion-stage benefit cannot be quantified from the record. The harm signal (bradycardia, hypotension) is part of this shelf's balance, not a footnote.
cards.source: Lau WC et al. Paracervical anaesthesia in outpatient hysteroscopy: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial. British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1999. PMID: 10426243.
