randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (lau 1999) 100 women undergoing outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy for abnormal uterine bleeding, randomised to paracervical block with 10 ml of 2% lignocaine or normal saline before the procedure; pain was scored at different stages of hysteroscopy with blood pressure and heart rate monitoring. compared with placebo, paracervical anaesthesia significantly reduced pain only at the time of insertion of the hysteroscope, but not at the subsequent stages of the procedure. paracervical injection of lignocaine resulted in a higher incidence of bradycardia and hypotension. the authors concluded paracervical anaesthesia not only fails to reduce pain during outpatient hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy overall, but also carries a risk of inducing bradycardia and hypotension, probably from inadvertent intravascular injection. the record reports significance by stage without the underlying pain scores, so the size of the insertion-stage benefit cannot be quantified from the record. the harm signal (bradycardia, hypotension) is part of this shelf's balance, not a footnote. lau wc et al. paracervical anaesthesia in outpatient hysteroscopy: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial. british journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1999. pmid: 10426243. mesh: adult · ambulatory care/methods · anesthesia, local/methods · anesthetics, local/pharmacology · biopsy · blood pressure/drug effects · cervix uteri · double-blind method · female · heart rate/drug effects · humans · hysteroscopy · lidocaine/pharmacology · middle aged · pain measurement · uterine hemorrhage/diagnosis

cards.headline: Issat 2014: vaginal misoprostol beat ketoprofen (P=.02) and placebo (P=.006) for pain during and just after hysteroscopy; no difference by 15 minutes
cards.summary: Issat 2014: vaginal misoprostol beat ketoprofen (P=.02) and placebo (P=.006) for pain during and just after hysteroscopy; no difference by 15 minutes
cards.people: 150 women referred for outpatient hysteroscopy at a tertiary centre, randomised to vaginal misoprostol 400 µg (with intravenous glucose), intravenous ketoprofen 50 mg (with vaginal placebo), or double placebo, given before the procedure; pain was scored before, during, and at 5 and 15 minutes after.
cards.result: Median visual analogue pain scores during and directly after the anaesthesia-free hysteroscopy were significantly lower in the misoprostol group than in the ketoprofen (P=.02) or placebo (P=.006) groups. There was no statistical difference between the arms at 15 minutes after the procedure (P=.16), and no difference in procedure time (P=.16). The misoprostol effect did not depend on age, hormone status, parity, or whether the hysteroscopy was operative or diagnostic. Misoprostol was given 4 hours before the procedure.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, and the record reports P values without median scores — the size of the pain reduction cannot be quantified from the record. Ketoprofen was not significantly better than placebo in this trial, which is itself informative about NSAIDs for this procedure.
cards.source: Issat T et al. A randomized, single blind, placebo-controlled trial for the pain reduction during the outpatient hysteroscopy after ketoprofen or intravaginal misoprostol. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2014. PMID: 24768981. cards.headline: Hassa 2013: in vaginoscopic hysteroscopy, neither misoprostol (median pain 4.75) nor diclofenac (5.01) beat placebo (4.15) — P=.57
cards.summary: Hassa 2013: in vaginoscopic hysteroscopy, neither misoprostol (median pain 4.75) nor diclofenac (5.01) beat placebo (4.15) — P=.57
cards.people: 158 primarily infertile, nulliparous women undergoing vaginoscopic diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy for infertility evaluation, randomised to vaginal misoprostol 200 µg 6 hours before plus rectal placebo, rectal diclofenac sodium 100 mg 60 minutes before plus vaginal placebo, or double placebo.
cards.result: Median (range) pain scores were 4.75 (3.12–6.54) with misoprostol and 5.01 (2.8–7.05) with diclofenac, versus 4.15 (2.17–6.92) with placebo — not significantly different (P=.57). There was also no significant difference in patient acceptance (P=.67), vasovagal symptoms (P=.84), procedure time (P=.05), or post-procedural analgesic requirement (P=.71). The authors were unable to demonstrate a benefit for either drug in this population and technique.
cards.watchOut: Vaginoscopy (no speculum, no tenaculum) is a gentler technique with lower baseline pain, and these were nulliparous infertile women without cervical stenosis — a different setting from Issat's mixed diagnostic/operative list. The split between the two misoprostol trials may be technique and population, not chance alone.
cards.source: Hassa H et al. Effectiveness of vaginal misoprostol and rectal nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug in vaginoscopic diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy in primarily infertile women: double-blind, randomized, controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: no analgesic strategy wins outright — misoprostol's case rests on one of two trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: no analgesic strategy wins outright — misoprostol's case rests on one of two trials
cards.people: Three randomised placebo-controlled trials in outpatient hysteroscopy (Lau 1999, n=100, paracervical block; Issat 2014, n=150, misoprostol versus ketoprofen versus placebo; Hassa 2013, n=158, misoprostol versus diclofenac versus placebo, vaginoscopic).
cards.result: Misoprostol: significantly lower pain than placebo in Issat (P=.006), no difference in Hassa (medians 4.75 versus 4.15, P=.57). NSAIDs: no significant benefit in either trial that included one. Paracervical block: benefit confined to insertion, with more bradycardia and hypotension. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped. Misoprostol for operative (not diagnostic outpatient) hysteroscopy is shelf #4729.
cards.watchOut: Pain scores, techniques (conventional versus vaginoscopic), populations and misoprostol doses/timing (200 µg at 6 hours; 400 µg at 4 hours) all differ between trials — the honest summary is a split, not an average.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lau WC et al. British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1999 (PMID: 10426243); Issat T et al. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2014 (PMID: 24768981); Hassa H et al. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2013 (PMID: 23850898).

shelves.title: Misoprostol before operative hysteroscopy: the cervix opens wider and dilates in about 50 seconds instead of 178 — a process win, bought with more side effects
shelves.question: In women having operative hysteroscopy, does preoperative misoprostol ease cervical dilation and reduce complications compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Administration, Oral · Adult · Canada · Cervical Ripening · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hysteroscopy/methods · Misoprostol/administration & dosage · Oxytocics/administration & dosage · Pregnancy · Preoperative Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cervical priming, the process outcome; a reduction in complications is not established. Nada AM et al. (PMID: 27523921) randomised 390 women having operative hysteroscopy to oral misoprostol 400 µg, vaginal misoprostol 400 µg, or placebo 12 hours before: mean width of the endocervical canal was 4.79 ± 1.07 mm (oral) and 4.25 ± 0.71 mm (vaginal) versus 3.92 ± 0.92 mm on placebo (P<.001 for both), and mean time to dilatation was 48.98 and 46.55 seconds versus 178.05 seconds on placebo (P<.001), with no significant difference in adverse effects between groups in this trial. Zhuo Z et al. (PMID: 30907209) randomised 253 women to 600 µg misoprostol orally or vaginally or vitamin B6 control: cervical width after administration was 7.2 ± 0.9 mm (vaginal) and 7.5 ± 1.4 mm (oral), significantly greater than control; dilatation took 75 ± 24 and 82 ± 22 seconds versus 148 ± 31 seconds on control; uterine false tract was substantially increased in the placebo group, but side effects increased in the misoprostol groups, and the priming effect was significantly stronger in premenopausal women. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): misoprostol reliably primes the cervix before operative hysteroscopy by either route; whether that converts into fewer serious complications is suggested (false tract) but not proven, and side effects rise.

cards.headline: Nada 2016: canal width 4.79 mm (oral) and 4.25 mm (vaginal) versus 3.92 mm on placebo; dilatation in ~47–49 seconds versus 178 seconds
cards.summary: Nada 2016: canal width 4.79 mm (oral) and 4.25 mm (vaginal) versus 3.92 mm on placebo; dilatation in ~47–49 seconds versus 178 seconds
cards.people: 390 women undergoing operative hysteroscopy at Cairo University Hospital, randomised 12 hours before the procedure to oral misoprostol 400 µg (with vaginal starch placebo), vaginal misoprostol 400 µg (with oral starch placebo), or double placebo. Main outcomes were width of the endocervical canal, ease and time of dilatation, and adverse effects.
cards.result: Mean width of the endocervical canal differed significantly between oral and control groups (4.79 ± 1.07 mm versus 3.92 ± 0.92 mm) and between vaginal and control groups (4.25 ± 0.71 mm versus 3.92 ± 0.92 mm), both P<.001; oral also exceeded vaginal (P=.009). Cervical entry was easier in both misoprostol groups (mean Likert score 4.25 ± 0.64 and 4.22 ± 0.74 versus 2.55 ± 0.87; P<.001). Mean time to dilatation was 48.98 ± 12.6 seconds (oral) and 46.55 ± 15.32 seconds (vaginal) versus 178.05 ± 74.18 seconds (control), P<.001, with no significant difference between routes (P=.987). Adverse effects were comparable between groups (P>.05).
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint is a process measure (millimetres, seconds, ease scores) — the trial does not show fewer perforations, less bleeding or better surgical outcomes. Oral misoprostol's wider canal did not translate into easier or faster entry than vaginal in this trial.
cards.source: Nada AM et al. Cervical Priming by Vaginal or Oral Misoprostol Before Operative Hysteroscopy: A Double-Blind, Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2016. PMID: 27523921. Registry ID: PACTR201502001022393. cards.headline: Zhuo 2019: cervical width 7.2–7.5 mm on misoprostol versus control; dilatation 75–82 seconds versus 148 seconds — false tracts clustered in the placebo group, side effects in the misoprostol groups
cards.summary: Zhuo 2019: cervical width 7.2–7.5 mm on misoprostol versus control; dilatation 75–82 seconds versus 148 seconds — false tracts clustered in the placebo group, side effects in the misoprostol groups
cards.people: 253 women eligible for operative hysteroscopy (275 recruited, 22 excluded), randomised to 600 µg misoprostol orally or vaginally, or 30 mg vitamin B6 orally or vaginally as control, 4–12 hours before surgery. Outcomes included cervical diameter, need for further dilatation, ease and duration of dilatation, preoperative pain, acceptability, complications and side effects.
cards.result: Cervical width in the vaginal and oral misoprostol groups was 7.2 ± 0.9 mm and 7.5 ± 1.4 mm respectively, a statistically significant difference compared with the control group (control width not stated in the record). The duration required for cervical dilatation with misoprostol (75 ± 24 seconds vaginal, 82 ± 22 seconds oral) was significantly shorter than with placebo (148 ± 31 seconds). The effect of cervical dilation with misoprostol was significantly higher in premenopausal participants. Uterine false tract occurred substantially more in the placebo group, while the risk of side effects increased in the misoprostol-treated patients compared with control.
cards.watchOut: The record does not state the control group's cervical width or the actual complication/side-effect rates, so those effects can be reported only in direction. The premenopausal concentration of the effect matters: postmenopausal cervices — often the hardest to dilate — benefited least clearly.
cards.source: Zhuo Z et al. Effectiveness of misoprostol administration for cervical ripening in women before operative hysteroscopy: a randomized, double-blinded controlled trial. Minimally invasive therapy & allied technologies : MITAT : official journal of the Society for Minimally Invasive Therapy. 2019. PMID: 30907209. cards.headline: Synthesis: priming works on every process measure in both trials; the complication dividend is a suggestion, not a finding
cards.summary: Synthesis: priming works on every process measure in both trials; the complication dividend is a suggestion, not a finding
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials of preoperative misoprostol before operative hysteroscopy (Nada 2016, n=390, 400 µg; Zhuo 2019, n=253, 600 µg), oral and vaginal routes each tested against placebo.
cards.result: Canal width: +0.3 to +0.9 mm over placebo (Nada). Dilatation time: ~47–82 seconds on misoprostol versus 148–178 seconds on placebo. False tract: substantially more frequent on placebo in Zhuo (rates not in the record). Side effects: comparable in Nada, increased in Zhuo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for cervical priming, as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for perforation or other serious complications, so the clinically decisive question — does easier dilatation prevent injury — remains open; the stamp claims the priming effect only. Misoprostol for pain in diagnostic outpatient hysteroscopy is shelf #4728.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nada AM et al. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2016 (PMID: 27523921); Zhuo Z et al. Minimally invasive therapy & allied technologies : MITAT : official journal of the Society for Minimally Invasive Therapy. 2019 (PMID: 30907209).

shelves.title: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring: neonatal seizures halved in the pooled trials, cerebral palsy unchanged — and caesarean births up by about two-thirds
shelves.question: In women in labour, does continuous electronic fetal monitoring reduce neonatal seizures or cerebral palsy compared with intermittent auscultation?
shelves.mesh: Cardiotocography/methods · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Female · Heart Auscultation/methods · Heart Rate, Fetal/physiology · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Labor, Obstetric · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Seizures/prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the seizure outcome and the cerebral-palsy outcome point in different directions, and the price is operative delivery. Across 13 randomised trials in over 37,000 women, continuous cardiotocography versus intermittent auscultation halved neonatal seizures (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.80; 9 trials, 32,386 women) but did not reduce overall perinatal death (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.23) and did not reduce cerebral palsy (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.84 to 3.63; 2 trials, 13,252 women). Caesarean births rose (RR 1.63, 95% CI 1.29 to 2.07) and instrumental vaginal births rose (RR 1.15, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.33). The largest single trial, Dublin (12,964 women), found 14 stillbirths and neonatal deaths in each group, with neonatal seizures and persistent abnormal neurological signs about twice as frequent with auscultation, yet three clearly abnormal infants in each group at 1-year follow-up among seizure survivors. PROPOSED SPLIT: fewer neonatal seizures with continuous monitoring, no demonstrated cerebral-palsy or mortality benefit, and more operative births.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2017 (Alfirevic): seizures RR 0.50 with continuous CTG, cerebral palsy RR 1.75 (not significant), caesarean RR 1.63 — 13 trials, over 37,000 women
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017 (Alfirevic): seizures RR 0.50 with continuous CTG, cerebral palsy RR 1.75 (not significant), caesarean RR 1.63 — 13 trials, over 37,000 women
cards.people: 13 randomised or quasi-randomised trials involving over 37,000 women in labour, comparing continuous cardiotocography (with or without fetal blood sampling) with intermittent auscultation (12 trials) or intermittent CTG (1 trial).
cards.result: Versus intermittent auscultation: neonatal seizures RR 0.50 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.80; N=32,386, 9 trials, moderate-quality evidence); overall perinatal death RR 0.86 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.23; N=33,513, 11 trials); cerebral palsy RR 1.75 (95% CI 0.84 to 3.63; N=13,252, 2 trials, low-quality evidence); caesarean section RR 1.63 (95% CI 1.29 to 2.07; N=18,861); instrumental vaginal birth RR 1.15 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.33; N=18,615). Relative effects are printed with the pooled absolute denominators alongside in the review.
cards.watchOut: All included trials were at high risk of performance bias and the cerebral-palsy estimate rests on only 2 trials with wide confidence intervals — the seizure reduction has never been shown to convert into less long-term disability, which is the outcome that matters.
cards.source: Alfirevic Z et al. Continuous cardiotocography (CTG) as a form of electronic fetal monitoring (EFM) for fetal assessment during labour. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28157275. cards.headline: Dublin 1985: 12,964 women — 14 perinatal deaths in each arm; seizures about twice as frequent with auscultation, but 3 abnormal infants in each group at 1 year
cards.summary: Dublin 1985: 12,964 women — 14 perinatal deaths in each arm; seizures about twice as frequent with auscultation, but 3 abnormal infants in each group at 1 year
cards.people: 12,964 women in labour in Dublin, randomised to continuous electronic fetal heart monitoring or intermittent auscultation, both policies including an option to measure fetal scalp blood pH.
cards.result: Stillbirths and neonatal deaths: 14 in each group. Caesarean delivery 2.4% on electronic monitoring versus 2.2% on auscultation; forceps delivery 8.2% versus 6.3%, the excess explained by instrumental deliveries for fetal heart-rate abnormalities. Neonatal seizures with persistent abnormal neurological signs followed by survival were twice as frequent in the auscultation group, an effect related to duration of labour; at 1-year follow-up of seizure survivors there were three clearly abnormal infants in each group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 1985 trial from an era of low baseline caesarean rates (2.4% versus 2.2%) — its operative-delivery trade-off understates the modern one, and its seizure survivors were few, so the 1-year equivalence is imprecise.
cards.source: MacDonald D et al. The Dublin randomized controlled trial of intrapartum fetal heart rate monitoring. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 1985. PMID: 3893132. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real seizure reduction that does not reach cerebral palsy, bought with operative delivery
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real seizure reduction that does not reach cerebral palsy, bought with operative delivery
cards.people: 13 randomised trials (over 37,000 women) pooled in the Cochrane review, anchored by the 12,964-woman Dublin trial.
cards.result: Neonatal seizures RR 0.50; cerebral palsy RR 1.75 (95% CI 0.84 to 3.63, not significant); perinatal death RR 0.86 (not significant); caesarean RR 1.63; instrumental birth RR 1.15. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit on the intermediate seizure outcome, no demonstrated benefit on death or cerebral palsy, harm in operative delivery.
cards.watchOut: Cerebral palsy is rare and mostly not caused by intrapartum events, so even 37,000 randomised women leave the key question underpowered; the stamp records what was shown, not what monitoring is for. Tier C: held for the developer's personal verdict under the relaxed band.
cards.source: Synthesis of Alfirevic Z et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28157275); MacDonald D et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 1985 (PMID: 3893132).

shelves.title: Vaginal cleansing before caesarean: endometritis roughly halved in the pooled trials (3.1% versus 7.1%) — the largest single trial on its own was not significant
shelves.question: In women having caesarean birth, does vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine reduce endometritis compared with no cleansing?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage · Benzalkonium Compounds/administration & dosage · Cesarean Section/adverse effects · Chlorhexidine/administration & dosage · Disinfection/methods · Endometritis/prevention & control · Female · Fever/prevention & control · Humans · Povidone-Iodine/administration & dosage · Pregnancy · Preoperative Care/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a cheap, brief intervention with a consistent pooled effect and no reported harms. The 2020 Cochrane review of 21 trials (7,038 women; 17 using povidone-iodine) found post-caesarean endometritis in 3.1% with vaginal cleansing versus 7.1% in control groups (average RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.58; 20 trials, 6,918 women; moderate-certainty evidence), with postoperative fever (aRR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.82) and wound infection (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.77) also reduced, and no adverse effects reported. The best-known single trial (Haas 2010, 300 women) pointed the same way but was not significant on its composite outcome: 6.5% versus 11.7% (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.11; P=.11). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): vaginal antiseptic cleansing before caesarean probably reduces endometritis and wound infection; the case rests on the pooled trials, not on any one trial.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2020 (Haas): endometritis 3.1% versus 7.1% (aRR 0.41), fever aRR 0.64, wound infection RR 0.62 — 21 trials, 7,038 women
cards.summary: Cochrane 2020 (Haas): endometritis 3.1% versus 7.1% (aRR 0.41), fever aRR 0.64, wound infection RR 0.62 — 21 trials, 7,038 women
cards.people: 21 randomised or quasi-randomised trials reporting 7,038 women having caesarean delivery in 10 countries; vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine (17 trials), chlorhexidine (3) or benzalkonium chloride (1), versus no preparation or saline preparation; all trials used antibiotic surgical prophylaxis.
cards.result: Post-caesarean endometritis 3.1% with cleansing versus 7.1% in controls (average RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.58; 20 trials, 6,918 women; moderate-certainty evidence), seen with both iodine-based and chlorhexidine-based solutions. Postoperative fever aRR 0.64 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.82; 16 trials, 6,163 women); wound infection RR 0.62 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.77; 18 trials, 6,385 women). No adverse effects were reported with either solution.
cards.watchOut: About half the trials had low risk of selection bias and blinding was often impossible, so the moderate-certainty grade is the honest ceiling; subgroup signals suggesting larger benefit in women already in labour are hypothesis-generating only.
cards.source: Haas DM et al. Vaginal preparation with antiseptic solution before cesarean section for preventing postoperative infections. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32335895. cards.headline: Haas 2010: composite infection 6.5% with povidone-iodine cleansing versus 11.7% without — RR 0.55, P=.11, not significant on its own
cards.summary: Haas 2010: composite infection 6.5% with povidone-iodine cleansing versus 11.7% without — RR 0.55, P=.11, not significant on its own
cards.people: 300 women undergoing caesarean delivery at a US centre, randomised to preoperative vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine (n=155) or standard care with no vaginal wash (n=145). Primary outcome was a composite of postoperative fever, endometritis, sepsis, readmission, wound infection or complication.
cards.result: The composite outcome occurred in 6.5% of the cleansing group versus 11.7% of controls (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.26 to 1.11; P=.11) — a 45% relative reduction that did not reach significance. Overall 9.0% of women developed the composite outcome; length of surgery, being in labour and having a dilated cervix were associated with it.
cards.watchOut: A 300-woman trial powered for a composite it could not resolve; its value is directional agreement with the pooled estimate, not independent proof. The review's lead author is also this trial's investigator, declared in the review.
cards.source: Haas DM et al. Vaginal cleansing before cesarean delivery to reduce postoperative infectious morbidity: a randomized, controlled trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2010. PMID: 20207251. Registry ID: NCT00386477. cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled benefit on endometritis, fever and wound infection; single trials underpowered; no harms reported
cards.people: 21 trials, 7,038 women (Cochrane 2020), including the 300-woman Haas 2010 trial.
cards.result: Endometritis 3.1% versus 7.1% (aRR 0.41); fever aRR 0.64; wound infection RR 0.62; no adverse effects reported in any trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) under the relaxed band cap.

shelves.title: Caesarean antibiotic before the incision, not after cord clamping: pooled infectious morbidity RR 0.57 — though the trial in labouring women found no difference
shelves.question: In women having caesarean birth, does a single-dose antibiotic before incision beat administration after cord clamping for infection?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Antibiotic Prophylaxis/standards · Cesarean Section/adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Endometritis/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control · Urinary Tract Infections/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for the mother; no neonatal penalty was shown. The Cochrane review of 10 studies (5,041 women) found composite maternal infectious morbidity lower with preoperative than with post-cord-clamp administration (RR 0.57, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.72; high-quality evidence), driven by endometritis (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.79) and wound infection (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.81), with no clear difference in neonatal sepsis (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.13). The double-blind Sullivan 2007 trial agreed: total infectious morbidity RR 0.4 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.87) and endometritis RR 0.2 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.94) with cefazolin 15–60 minutes before incision, and no increase in neonatal sepsis or sepsis workups. The counterweight is Thigpen 2005, in labouring women: endometritis RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.07) and wound infection RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.55) — no significant difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pre-incision dosing reduces maternal infection in the pooled record, with the labouring-population trial null.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2014 (Mackeen): composite infectious morbidity RR 0.57, endometritis RR 0.54, wound infection RR 0.59 — 10 studies, 5,041 women
cards.summary: Cochrane 2014 (Mackeen): composite infectious morbidity RR 0.57, endometritis RR 0.54, wound infection RR 0.59 — 10 studies, 5,041 women
cards.people: 10 randomised trials (12 reports) in 5,041 women undergoing caesarean delivery, comparing intravenous prophylactic antibiotics before skin incision versus after neonatal cord clamping; overall risk of bias rated low.
cards.result: Composite maternal infectious morbidity RR 0.57 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.72; high-quality evidence); endometritis RR 0.54 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.79); wound infection RR 0.59 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.81). Neonatal sepsis RR 0.76 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.13; moderate-quality evidence) — no clear difference, and no clear differences in other neonatal outcomes. Maternal side effects were not reported in the included studies.
cards.watchOut: Relative effects are pooled across elective and emergency caesareans; the review itself notes that short- and long-term neonatal effects of earlier fetal antibiotic exposure remain unelucidated.
cards.source: Mackeen AD et al. Timing of intravenous prophylactic antibiotics for preventing postpartum infectious morbidity in women undergoing cesarean delivery. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25479008. cards.headline: Sullivan 2007: total infectious morbidity RR 0.4 and endometritis RR 0.2 with cefazolin before incision — 357 women, double-blind
cards.summary: Sullivan 2007: total infectious morbidity RR 0.4 and endometritis RR 0.2 with cefazolin before incision — 357 women, double-blind
cards.people: 357 women undergoing caesarean delivery, randomised to cefazolin 15–60 minutes before skin incision or cefazolin at umbilical cord clamping, in a placebo-controlled double-blind design.
cards.result: Total infectious morbidity was lower with pre-incision dosing (RR 0.4, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.87) and endometritis was lower (RR 0.2, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.94). No increase in neonatal sepsis (P=.99), sepsis workups (P=.96) or length of stay (P=.17).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and modest-sized; the endometritis confidence interval as printed in the record is unusually asymmetric, and the trial predates modern bundled infection-prevention practice, which compresses absolute benefit.
cards.source: Sullivan SA et al. cards.headline: Thigpen 2005: in labouring women, timing made no significant difference — endometritis RR 0.67 (0.42 to 1.07), wound infection RR 0.84
cards.summary: Thigpen 2005: in labouring women, timing made no significant difference — endometritis RR 0.67 (0.42 to 1.07), wound infection RR 0.84
cards.people: 303 women with singleton pregnancies who had laboured and required caesarean delivery, randomised double-blind to cefazolin at skin incision (n=153) or at cord clamping (n=149), over 30 months.
cards.result: Endometritis RR 0.67 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.07), wound infection RR 0.84 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.55), neonatal sepsis RR 1.28 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.79) and NICU admission RR 1.28 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.79) — no significant difference on any outcome; the authors concluded maternal infectious morbidity did not differ by timing in this labouring population.
cards.watchOut: The population — women already in labour, at higher baseline infection risk and often already exposed to vaginal flora and examinations — is exactly where pre-incision timing might matter least or most; the trial cannot settle the elective-caesarean question, and its confidence intervals still include the pooled benefit.
cards.source: Thigpen BD et al. Timing of prophylactic antibiotic administration in the uninfected laboring gravida: a randomized clinical trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2005. cards.headline: Synthesis: give it before the incision — pooled maternal benefit, one null trial in labouring women, no neonatal signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: give it before the incision — pooled maternal benefit, one null trial in labouring women, no neonatal signal
cards.people: 10 trials, 5,041 women (Cochrane 2014), including Sullivan 2007 (n=357, positive) and Thigpen 2005 (n=303, null, labouring women).
cards.result: Composite infectious morbidity RR 0.57; endometritis RR 0.54; wound infection RR 0.59; neonatal sepsis RR 0.76 (not significant). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) under the relaxed band cap.

shelves.title: Maintenance tocolysis after 48 hours: babies did no better — nifedipine 11.9% versus 13.7% adverse perinatal outcome in APOSTEL II; atosiban only bought quieter days
shelves.question: In women with threatened preterm labour, does maintenance tocolysis after 48 hours improve neonatal outcomes compared with stopping?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Enterocolitis, Necrotizing/prevention & control · Female · Fetal Death · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Newborn, Diseases/prevention & control · Intracranial Hemorrhages/prevention & control · Leukomalacia, Periventricular/prevention & control · Lung Diseases/prevention & control · Nifedipine/administration & dosage · Obstetric Labor, Premature/prevention & control · Pregnancy · Sepsis/prevention & control · Tocolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcomes babies experience. In APOSTEL II, 406 women who had not delivered after 48 hours of tocolysis and corticosteroids were randomised to 12 days of maintenance nifedipine 80 mg/day or placebo: adverse perinatal outcome (perinatal death, chronic lung disease, neonatal sepsis, intraventricular haemorrhage >grade 2, periventricular leukomalacia >grade 1, or necrotising enterocolitis) occurred in 11.9% (24/201) versus 13.7% (28/205) (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.45). Maintenance atosiban (513 women) prolonged uterine quiescence — median time to first recurrence of labour 32.6 versus 27.6 days (P=.02), with subsequent intravenous treatment needed by 23% versus 31% — but neonatal deaths were 4 versus 5 and infant outcomes including birth weight were comparable: a quieter uterus, not healthier babies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): maintenance tocolysis prolongs quiescence at best and has not improved perinatal outcomes.

cards.headline: APOSTEL II 2013 (Roos): adverse perinatal outcome 11.9% on maintenance nifedipine versus 13.7% on placebo — RR 0.87, not significant
cards.summary: APOSTEL II 2013 (Roos): adverse perinatal outcome 11.9% on maintenance nifedipine versus 13.7% on placebo — RR 0.87, not significant
cards.people: 406 women in 11 Dutch perinatal units with threatened preterm labour at 26+0 to 32+2 weeks who had not delivered after 48 hours of tocolysis and a completed corticosteroid course, randomised to oral nifedipine 80 mg/day (n=201) or placebo (n=205) for 12 days; infants followed to 6 months.
cards.result: Adverse perinatal outcome (composite of perinatal death, chronic lung disease, neonatal sepsis, intraventricular haemorrhage >grade 2, periventricular leukomalacia >grade 1, necrotising enterocolitis): 11.9% (24/201; 95% CI 7.5% to 16.4%) on nifedipine versus 13.7% (28/205; 95% CI 9.0% to 18.4%) on placebo (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.45). Mean gestational age at randomisation was 29.2 weeks in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The control-group event rate was lower than anticipated, so a modest benefit cannot be completely excluded — but the trial as run gives no positive reason to continue treatment, and the registry identifier in the record is trialregister.nl NTR1336.
cards.source: Roos C et al. Effect of maintenance tocolysis with nifedipine in threatened preterm labor on perinatal outcomes: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23280223. cards.headline: Atosiban maintenance 2000: recurrence of labour delayed (median 32.6 versus 27.6 days) — neonatal deaths 4 versus 5, infant outcomes comparable
cards.summary: Atosiban maintenance 2000: recurrence of labour delayed (median 32.6 versus 27.6 days) — neonatal deaths 4 versus 5, infant outcomes comparable
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (Atosiban PTL-098 Study Group 2000)
cards.people: 513 women whose acute preterm labour had settled on intravenous atosiban, randomised to maintenance subcutaneous atosiban infusion 30 µg/min (n=252) or matching placebo (n=251) until the end of 36 weeks' gestation, in a multicentre double-blind trial.
cards.result: Median time from start of maintenance to first recurrence of labour was 32.6 days on atosiban versus 27.6 days on placebo (P=.02). At least one subsequent intravenous atosiban course was needed by 61 women (23%) on maintenance versus 77 (31%) on placebo. Neonatal deaths after starting maintenance: 4 versus 5; infant outcomes including birth weight were comparable, and adverse-event profiles were similar except injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a process measure — days of uterine quiescence — not a baby outcome; on every infant outcome reported the groups matched, which is the pattern this shelf exists to record.
cards.source: Valenzuela GJ et al. Maintenance treatment of preterm labor with the oxytocin antagonist atosiban. The Atosiban PTL-098 Study Group. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2000. PMID: 10819856. cards.headline: Synthesis: maintenance buys uterine quiet, not perinatal benefit — stop after the acute course
cards.summary: Synthesis: maintenance buys uterine quiet, not perinatal benefit — stop after the acute course
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled maintenance trials: nifedipine (APOSTEL II, n=406, perinatal composite primary) and atosiban (n=513, quiescence primary).
cards.result: Perinatal composite 11.9% versus 13.7% (RR 0.87, NS) with nifedipine; time to labour recurrence +5.0 median days with atosiban, neonatal deaths 4 versus 5. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for neonatal outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial tested maintenance beyond about 12 days (nifedipine) in the highest-risk window, and betamimetic maintenance is not represented here; the null is for the two best-tested agents. Tier C: held for the developer's personal verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roos C et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 23280223); Atosiban PTL-098 Study Group. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2000 (PMID: 10819856).

shelves.title: Embryo glue (hyaluronan-enriched medium): older fresh-transfer trials pooled to a live-birth gain — the one large double-blind frozen-transfer trial found 25.5% versus 25.8%
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF, does hyaluronan-enriched transfer medium (embryo glue) improve live birth compared with standard medium?
shelves.mesh: Culture Media/chemistry · Embryo Implantation/drug effects/physiology · Female · Fibrin Tissue Adhesive/pharmacology · Humans · Hyaluronic Acid/pharmacology · Live Birth · Pregnancy · Pregnancy, Multiple · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reproductive Techniques, Assisted · Tissue Adhesives/pharmacology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by transfer type and era. The Cochrane pool of the older, mostly fresh-transfer trials favoured functional-concentration hyaluronic acid: live birth odds ratio 1.41 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.69; 6 RCTs, 1,950 women), with clinical pregnancy OR 1.39 — but multiple pregnancy was also raised (OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.31). The largest modern test tells a different story: in a double-blind trial of 550 women having frozen transfer, the tested product EmbryoGlue (Vitrolife, Gothenburg, Sweden) at 0.5 mg/mL gave live birth 25.5% versus 25.8% on standard medium (relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.31). Where embryos are transferred one at a time and frozen, the pooled fresh-era benefit has not reproduced. PROPOSED SPLIT: a possible benefit in the older fresh-transfer setting, no demonstrated benefit in modern frozen single-transfer practice, and a multiple-pregnancy cost where more than one embryo is transferred.

cards.headline: Bontekoe 2014 (Cochrane): hyaluronic acid in transfer medium — live birth OR 1.41 across six trials, multiple pregnancy OR 1.86
cards.summary: Bontekoe 2014 (Cochrane): hyaluronic acid in transfer medium — live birth OR 1.41 across six trials, multiple pregnancy OR 1.86
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Bontekoe 2014)
cards.people: 17 randomised trials, 3,898 participants in assisted reproduction; 16 studied hyaluronic acid (HA) as an adherence compound in embryo transfer medium and one studied fibrin sealant. Six trials (1,950 women) reported live birth.
cards.result: Live birth was higher with functional concentrations of HA (odds ratio 1.41, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.69; 6 RCTs, N = 1950, I² = 0%, moderate-quality evidence), as was clinical pregnancy (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.21 to 1.60; 14 RCTs, N = 3452). Multiple pregnancy was significantly increased (OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.49 to 2.31; 5 RCTs, N = 1951), with no significant difference in adverse events (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.12). No treatment effect was found for fibrin sealant.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials predate routine single-embryo and frozen transfer; the multiple-pregnancy signal suggests part of the live-birth gain may have come from transferring more than one embryo in a stickier medium, a practice modern clinics have moved away from. Evidence quality was rated moderate.
cards.source: Bontekoe S et al. Adherence compounds in embryo transfer media for assisted reproductive technologies. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24567053. cards.headline: Yung 2021: in frozen transfer, EmbryoGlue gave live birth 25.5% versus 25.8% on standard medium (RR 0.99)
cards.summary: Yung 2021: in frozen transfer, EmbryoGlue gave live birth 25.5% versus 25.8% on standard medium (RR 0.99)
cards.people: 550 infertile women aged under 43 years undergoing frozen embryo transfer at two tertiary fertility centres, randomised 1:1 to EmbryoGlue (Vitrolife, Gothenburg, Sweden) with hyaluronic acid 0.5 mg/mL or supplemented G-2 (Vitrolife) medium with hyaluronic acid 0.125 mg/mL; 550 women were included in the intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Live birth rates were comparable: 25.5% in the hyaluronic-acid group versus 25.8% in the control group (relative risk 0.99, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.31). Other clinical outcomes were also similar, and logistic regression showed the type of transfer medium was not associated with live birth.
cards.watchOut: This is a frozen-transfer trial, so it does not directly refute the older fresh-transfer pool — but frozen transfer is now the dominant setting, and in that setting the best blinded trial shows nothing. Thirteen randomised women never reached transfer (embryos not surviving thawing, fever, withdrawal).
cards.source: Yung SSF et al. Hyaluronic acid-enriched transfer medium for frozen embryo transfer: a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial. Fertility and Sterility. 2021. PMID: 33845988. cards.headline: Synthesis: a fresh-era pooled benefit that the modern frozen, blinded trial does not reproduce — and a multiples cost on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: a fresh-era pooled benefit that the modern frozen, blinded trial does not reproduce — and a multiples cost on the face
cards.people: A Cochrane meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (3,898 participants, mostly fresh transfer) and one double-blind frozen-transfer trial of 550 women.
cards.result: Live birth: OR 1.41 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.69) favouring hyaluronic acid in the pooled older trials; 25.5% versus 25.8% (RR 0.99) in the frozen-transfer trial. Multiple pregnancy: OR 1.86 in the pooled trials. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C for the developer's verdict.
cards.watchOut: The split is by setting, not by statistical whim: fresh versus frozen transfer, multi-embryo versus single-embryo practice, and unblinded-era versus double-blind design all point the same way. A fresh-transfer-only modern trial would be needed to rescue the benefit claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bontekoe S et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24567053); Yung SSF et al. Fertility and Sterility. 2021 (PMID: 33845988).

shelves.title: Assisted hatching: live birth unmoved across 39 trials and in the 698-woman ALADDIN trial (29.8% versus 29.2%) — multiple pregnancy may rise
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF, does assisted hatching improve live birth compared with no hatching?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/epidemiology · Bias · Embryo Implantation/physiology · Female · Fertilization in Vitro · Humans · Live Birth/epidemiology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Pregnancy Rate · Pregnancy, Multiple/statistics & numerical data · Publication Bias · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sperm Injections, Intracytoplasmic · Zona Pellucida/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for live birth. The Cochrane review of 39 randomised trials (7,249 women) was uncertain whether assisted hatching improves live birth (odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29; 14 RCTs reporting live birth, 2,849 women, low-quality evidence), while multiple pregnancy may be slightly increased (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.68). The largest modern trial, ALADDIN, laser-hatched vitrified/warmed blastocysts before single frozen transfer and found live birth 29.8% (105/352) versus 29.2% (101/346) — relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.19) — with no subgroup that benefited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): assisted hatching does not demonstrably raise live birth, and it may raise multiple pregnancy where more than one embryo is transferred.

cards.headline: Lacey 2021 (Cochrane): 39 trials — live birth OR 1.09 with confidence interval crossing no effect; multiple pregnancy OR 1.38
cards.summary: Lacey 2021 (Cochrane): 39 trials — live birth OR 1.09 with confidence interval crossing no effect; multiple pregnancy OR 1.38
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Lacey 2021)
cards.people: 39 randomised trials, 7,249 women undergoing IVF or ICSI with mechanical, chemical or laser disruption of the zona pellucida versus no assisted hatching; 14 studies (2,849 women, 834 live-birth events) reported live birth.
cards.result: The reviewers were uncertain whether assisted hatching improved live birth (odds ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.29; 14 RCTs, N = 2849, I² = 20%, low-quality evidence) — compatible with a live-birth rate of 27% to 34% against an assumed 28% without hatching. Multiple pregnancy per woman may be slightly increased (OR 1.38, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.68; 18 RCTs, N = 4308). Clinical pregnancy across all 39 trials may improve slightly (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.09 to 1.33), but among the 14 trials that also reported live birth there was little to no difference in clinical pregnancy (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.25).
cards.watchOut: Evidence quality was very low to low, with serious risk of bias from poor reporting, inconsistency and publication bias; the apparent clinical-pregnancy gain disappears in the subset of trials rigorous enough to report live birth — the outcome that matters.
cards.source: Lacey L et al. Assisted hatching on assisted conception (in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)). The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 33730422. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02752568. cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (lacey 2021) 39 randomised trials, 7,249 women undergoing ivf or icsi with mechanical, chemical or laser disruption of the zona pellucida versus no assisted hatching; 14 studies (2,849 women, 834 live-birth events) reported live birth. the reviewers were uncertain whether assisted hatching improved live birth (odds ratio 1.09, 95% ci 0.92 to 1.29; 14 rcts, n = 2849, i² = 20%, low-quality evidence) — compatible with a live-birth rate of 27% to 34% against an assumed 28% without hatching. multiple pregnancy per woman may be slightly increased (or 1.38, 95% ci 1.13 to 1.68; 18 rcts, n = 4308). clinical pregnancy across all 39 trials may improve slightly (or 1.20, 95% ci 1.09 to 1.33), but among the 14 trials that also reported live birth there was little to no difference in clinical pregnancy (or 1.07, 95% ci 0.92 to 1.25). evidence quality was very low to low, with serious risk of bias from poor reporting, inconsistency and publication bias; the apparent clinical-pregnancy gain disappears in the subset of trials rigorous enough to report live birth — the outcome that matters. lacey l et al. assisted hatching on assisted conception (in vitro fertilisation (ivf) and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (icsi)). the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. pmid: 33730422. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov: nct02752568. mesh: abortion, spontaneous/epidemiology · bias · embryo implantation/physiology · female · fertilization in vitro · humans · live birth/epidemiology · pregnancy · pregnancy outcome · pregnancy rate · pregnancy, multiple/statistics & numerical data · publication bias · randomized controlled trials as topic · sperm injections, intracytoplasmic · zona pellucida/physiology

cards.headline: ALADDIN 2024: laser hatching of thawed blastocysts — live birth 29.8% versus 29.2% (RR 1.02), no benefiting subgroup
cards.summary: ALADDIN 2024: laser hatching of thawed blastocysts — live birth 29.8% versus 29.2% (RR 1.02), no benefiting subgroup
cards.people: 698 women aged 18–39 years at two centres undergoing elective single embryo transfer with vitrified/warmed blastocysts, randomised to laser assisted hatching (1,480 nm diode laser removing about one-third of the zona pellucida; 352 women) or no hatching (346 women); women having preimplantation genetic testing, with uterine abnormalities, BMI over 35 kg/m² or severe male factor were excluded.
cards.result: Live birth occurred in 105 of 352 women (29.8%) with assisted hatching and 101 of 346 (29.2%) without — relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.19). Exploratory subgroup analyses by age, centre, indication, insemination method, blastocyst quality and day of development found no clinical situation that benefited.
cards.watchOut: ALADDIN tests one modern scenario — laser hatching of thawed blastocysts at single transfer — not fresh cleavage-stage embryos or older women, the subgroups older small trials claimed might benefit; but it is the largest and cleanest test, and it is flatly null.
cards.source: Alteri A et al. The effect of laser-assisted hatching on vitrified/warmed blastocysts: the ALADDIN randomized controlled trial. Fertility and Sterility. 2024. PMID: 38342371. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03623659. cards.summary: Synthesis: no live-birth benefit in the pool or in the best single trial; a possible multiples cost remains
cards.people: 39 randomised trials totalling 7,249 women (Cochrane) plus the 698-woman ALADDIN trial of laser hatching at frozen single blastocyst transfer.
cards.result: Live birth: OR 1.09 (95% CI 0.92 to 1.29) pooled; 29.8% versus 29.2% (RR 1.02) in ALADDIN. Multiple pregnancy: OR 1.38 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.68) pooled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.

shelves.title: Metformin added in clomiphene-resistant PCOS: ovulation 75% versus 27% and pregnancy 55% versus 7% in the small double-blind trial — but gonadotropins beat the combination in the pooled comparison
shelves.question: In women undergoing ovulation induction, does adding metformin in clomiphene-resistant PCOS improve ovulation and live birth?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Androstenedione/blood · Body Mass Index · Clomiphene/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Dehydroepiandrosterone Sulfate/blood · Double-Blind Method · Drug Resistance · Female · Follicle Stimulating Hormone/blood · Humans · Infertility, Female/etiology/therapy · Luteinizing Hormone/blood · Metformin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Ovulation Induction · Placebos · Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/complications · Pregnancy · Testosterone/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for ovulation and pregnancy, with live birth unreported in the anchor trials. In the double-blind placebo-controlled trial in clomiphene-resistant women (Vandermolen 2001), adding metformin 500 mg three times daily for seven weeks and continuing it with clomiphene gave ovulation in 9 of 12 women (75%) versus 4 of 15 (27%) on placebo, and pregnancy in 6 of 11 (55%) versus 1 of 14 (7%). Kocak 2002 (56 women, double-blind) likewise found higher ovulation rates and a higher cumulative pregnancy rate with metformin, though the per-group pregnancy rate did not differ significantly. The meta-analysis of 12 trials (1,411 women) adds the ceiling: against gonadotropins, metformin plus clomiphene produced fewer pregnancies (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.75) — so the combination is a step before gonadotropins, not a substitute for them. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin restores clomiphene response in resistant PCOS; no anchor trial reported live birth.

cards.headline: Vandermolen 2001: metformin in clomiphene-resistant PCOS — ovulation 75% versus 27%, pregnancy 55% versus 7%
cards.summary: Vandermolen 2001: metformin in clomiphene-resistant PCOS — ovulation 75% versus 27%, pregnancy 55% versus 7%
cards.people: Anovulatory women with PCOS who were resistant to clomiphene citrate, in a multicentre trial: metformin 500 mg three times daily or placebo for 7 weeks, then clomiphene 50 mg daily for 5 days (dose escalated by 50 mg per anovulatory cycle to a maximum 150 mg) while continuing metformin or placebo, until six ovulatory cycles, pregnancy, or anovulation at the top dose. Ovulation data were available for 12 metformin and 15 placebo participants; pregnancy data for 11 and 14.
cards.result: Ovulation occurred in 9 of 12 participants (75%) on metformin versus 4 of 15 (27%) on placebo, and conception in 6 of 11 (55%) versus 1 of 14 (7%); both comparisons were significant. Serum progesterone above 4 ng/mL defined ovulation.
cards.watchOut: The analysed denominators are tiny (27 women for ovulation) because of the trial's sequential design, and live birth was not reported — pregnancy is the furthest endpoint this anchor reaches. The effect ratio is large precisely where small trials most often exaggerate.
cards.source: Vandermolen DT et al. Metformin increases the ovulatory rate and pregnancy rate from clomiphene citrate in patients with polycystic ovary syndrome who are resistant to clomiphene citrate alone. Fertility and Sterility. 2001. PMID: 11172832. cards.headline: Kocak 2002: metformin before clomiphene raised ovulation rates; cumulative pregnancy higher, per-group pregnancy rate not significantly different
cards.summary: Kocak 2002: metformin before clomiphene raised ovulation rates; cumulative pregnancy higher, per-group pregnancy rate not significantly different
cards.people: 56 women with clomiphene-citrate-resistant PCOS at a tertiary infertility clinic, randomised to two cycles of oral metformin 850 mg twice daily or placebo twice daily, with clomiphene 100 mg/day on cycle days 3–7 of the second cycle in both groups.
cards.result: Metformin significantly decreased total testosterone, LH level, LH/FSH ratio, insulin resistance and mean BMI. Clomiphene induction after metformin produced higher ovulation rates and a thicker endometrium than after placebo, and the cumulative pregnancy rate was higher in the metformin group; however, there was no significant difference in the pregnancy rate between the two groups. The record reports these comparisons without printing the group percentages.
cards.watchOut: A confirmatory direction with softer statistics than Vandermolen — and, again, no live-birth endpoint and no percentages in the record to audit. Two small trials agreeing on ovulation is sturdier than either alone; neither is large.
cards.source: Kocak M et al. Metformin therapy improves ovulatory rates, cervical scores, and pregnancy rates in clomiphene citrate-resistant women with polycystic ovary syndrome. Fertility and Sterility. 2002. PMID: 11779598. cards.headline: Abu Hashim 2015 (meta-analysis): metformin plus clomiphene matched diathermy and aromatase inhibitors — and lost to gonadotropins (pregnancy OR 0.45)
cards.summary: Abu Hashim 2015 (meta-analysis): metformin plus clomiphene matched diathermy and aromatase inhibitors — and lost to gonadotropins (pregnancy OR 0.45)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Abu Hashim 2015)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials, 1,411 women with clomiphene-resistant PCOS, comparing metformin plus clomiphene against gonadotropins, laparoscopic ovarian diathermy, aromatase inhibitors, N-acetyl-cysteine and other insulin-sensitiser combinations.
cards.result: Against gonadotropins, metformin plus clomiphene gave significantly fewer ovulations (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.41; 3 trials, n = 323) and pregnancies (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.75; 3 trials, n = 323). Against laparoscopic ovarian diathermy there was no significant difference in ovulation (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.47) or pregnancy (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.54), and likewise no difference against aromatase inhibitors (ovulation OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.34; pregnancy OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.36). The reviewers concluded gonadotropins are superior, with the combination relevant where gonadotropin access is limited or as a step before them.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis answers 'compared with what else?' rather than 'compared with clomiphene alone?' — its role on this shelf is to set the combination's place in the sequence, not to estimate its placebo-controlled effect.
cards.source: Abu Hashim H et al. Combined metformin-clomiphene in clomiphene-resistant polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica. 2015. PMID: 25965123. cards.headline: Synthesis: metformin restores clomiphene response in resistant PCOS — a real step, one step below gonadotropins, with live birth unmeasured
cards.summary: Synthesis: metformin restores clomiphene response in resistant PCOS — a real step, one step below gonadotropins, with live birth unmeasured
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (56 women and 27 analysed women) and a 12-trial meta-analysis (1,411 women) in clomiphene-resistant PCOS.
cards.result: Ovulation 75% versus 27% and pregnancy 55% versus 7% (Vandermolen); ovulation higher, pregnancy rate not significantly different (Kocak). Versus gonadotropins, pregnancy OR 0.45 for metformin plus clomiphene. Live birth: not reported in any carded record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is distinct from first-line PCOS ovulation induction (live at #245, where PPCOS I compared clomiphene, metformin and their combination as initial therapy): the population here is defined by clomiphene resistance, and the comparison is metformin added to a drug that has already failed.

shelves.title: Acupuncture around embryo transfer: the early unblinded trial claimed pregnancy 42.5% versus 26.3% — the 848-woman sham-controlled trial found live birth 18.3% versus 17.8%
shelves.question: In women having IVF, does acupuncture around embryo transfer improve live birth?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy/adverse effects · Adult · Embryo Transfer · Female · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Humans · Live Birth · Ovulation Induction · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — when the control is a sham needle. Paulus 2002 randomised 160 women to acupuncture 25 minutes before and after embryo transfer or no acupuncture and reported clinical pregnancy 42.5% (34/80) versus 26.3% (21/80) — with no sham control and no live-birth endpoint. Smith 2018 then ran the definitive test: 848 women at 16 centres, acupuncture versus a non-invasive sham needle placed away from true points, and live birth was 18.3% (74/405) versus 17.8% (72/404) — risk difference 0.5% (95% CI −4.9 to 5.8), relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.38). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the apparent benefit was the ritual and the attention, not the needles at the points.

cards.headline: Smith 2018: acupuncture versus sham in 848 women — live birth 18.3% versus 17.8% (risk difference 0.5%)
cards.summary: Smith 2018: acupuncture versus sham in 848 women — live birth 18.3% versus 17.8% (risk difference 0.5%)
cards.people: 848 women undergoing a fresh IVF cycle at 16 IVF centres in Australia and New Zealand, randomised to acupuncture (424) or sham acupuncture (424) — a non-invasive needle placed away from true acupuncture points; treatment was given between days 6–8 of stimulation and twice around embryo transfer. Mean age was 35.4 years and 45.0% had undergone more than two previous IVF cycles; 809 women (98.2%) had live-birth outcome data.
cards.result: Live births occurred in 74 of 405 women (18.3%) receiving acupuncture versus 72 of 404 (17.8%) receiving sham (risk difference 0.5%, 95% CI −4.9% to 5.8%; relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.38) — no significant difference. The authors concluded the findings do not support acupuncture to improve live birth in IVF.
cards.watchOut: Sham needling is not physiologically inert in every theory of acupuncture — but it is the right control for the claim actually sold to patients, that point-specific needling around transfer raises the chance of a baby. On that claim, this large multicentre trial is decisive.
cards.source: Smith CA et al. Effect of Acupuncture vs Sham Acupuncture on Live Births Among Women Undergoing In Vitro Fertilization: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29800212. Registry ID: ACTRN12611000226909. cards.headline: Paulus 2002: acupuncture before and after transfer — clinical pregnancy 42.5% versus 26.3% with no sham and no live birth
cards.summary: Paulus 2002: acupuncture before and after transfer — clinical pregnancy 42.5% versus 26.3% with no sham and no live birth
cards.type: Prospective randomised study without sham control (Paulus 2002)
cards.people: 160 patients undergoing assisted reproduction with good-quality embryos at one fertility centre, randomised to acupuncture 25 minutes before and after embryo transfer (80 women) or embryo transfer with no supportive therapy (80 women).
cards.result: Clinical pregnancy (fetal sac on ultrasound six weeks after transfer) was documented in 34 of 80 patients (42.5%) in the acupuncture group versus 21 of 80 (26.3%) in the control group.
cards.watchOut: No sham, no blinding, no live birth — every element that later explained the result is missing here. This trial launched a thousand clinic brochures; read alongside Smith 2018 it is best understood as measuring expectation and extra care, not needle placement.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the effect was the control condition — point-specific acupuncture does not raise live birth
cards.summary: Synthesis: the effect was the control condition — point-specific acupuncture does not raise live birth
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 1,008 women: one unblinded 160-woman trial with a clinical-pregnancy endpoint, one single-blind sham-controlled 848-woman trial with a live-birth endpoint.
cards.result: Live birth: 18.3% versus 17.8% (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.38) against sham. Clinical pregnancy: 42.5% versus 26.3% against no treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against acupuncture for relaxation or symptom relief around IVF — only against the specific claim that it improves the chance of taking home a baby, which is the claim patients pay for.

shelves.title: Mild stimulation in poor responders: ongoing pregnancy 12.8% versus 13.6% and live birth pooled RR 1.01 — the same babies for about 3,100 fewer units of gonadotropin, at the price of more cancelled cycles
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF, does mild ovarian stimulation match conventional stimulation for live birth with less burden in predicted poor responders?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Birth Rate · Female · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Follicle Stimulating Hormone/therapeutic use · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/antagonists & inhibitors · Hormone Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Infertility, Female/therapy · Ovarian Reserve · Ovulation Induction/methods · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for live birth, which here is the finding that matters. The multicentre non-inferiority trial (Youssef 2017, 394 women with poor ovarian reserve) found ongoing pregnancy 12.8% (25/195) on a mild strategy (150 IU FSH with an antagonist) versus 13.6% (27/199) on conventional high-dose stimulation (450 IU HMG with a long agonist protocol) — risk ratio 0.95 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.57), absolute difference −0.7% (95% CI −7.4 to 5.9), inside the predefined 10% non-inferiority margin — using a mean 3,135 IU less gonadotropin and 1.2 fewer stimulation days. The 15-trial meta-analysis agrees on outcomes: fresh live birth RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.04) and cumulative live birth RR 1.15 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.81), with fewer oocytes (mean difference −0.80) and more cancellations (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.02) on mild stimulation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in poor responders, high-dose stimulation buys oocytes and completed cycles, not babies.

cards.headline: Youssef 2017: mild versus conventional in poor reserve — ongoing pregnancy 12.8% versus 13.6%, gonadotropin use lower by 3,135 IU
cards.summary: Youssef 2017: mild versus conventional in poor reserve — ongoing pregnancy 12.8% versus 13.6%, gonadotropin use lower by 3,135 IU
cards.people: 394 subfertile women with poor ovarian reserve (age ≥35 years, basal FSH over 10 IU/mL, antral follicle count ≤5, or previous poor response/cancellation) randomised to one cycle of mild stimulation — 150 IU FSH with GnRH-antagonist down-regulation (195 women) — or conventional stimulation — 450 IU HMG with a long mid-luteal GnRH-agonist protocol (199 women). The primary outcome was ongoing pregnancy rate per woman randomised, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Ongoing pregnancy was 12.8% (25/195) on mild stimulation versus 13.6% (27/199) on conventional (risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.57; absolute difference −0.7%, 95% CI −7.4 to 5.9), a confidence interval that did not extend below the predefined 10% inferiority threshold. Stimulation was 1.2 days shorter (mean difference −1.2 days, 95% CI −1.88 to −0.62) and gonadotropin consumption lower by a mean of 3,135 IU (95% CI −3331 to −2940) with the mild strategy.
cards.watchOut: The trial collected no data on cryopreserved surplus embryos, so cumulative pregnancy per started cycle is unknown, and ongoing pregnancies could not be followed to live birth in all centres — the primary outcome is ongoing pregnancy, not babies. The 10% non-inferiority margin is also generous.

cards.headline: Montoya-Botero 2021 (meta-analysis): fresh live birth RR 1.01 and cumulative live birth RR 1.15 — with 0.80 fewer oocytes and 48% more cancellations on mild stimulation
cards.summary: Montoya-Botero 2021 (meta-analysis): fresh live birth RR 1.01 and cumulative live birth RR 1.15 — with 0.80 fewer oocytes and 48% more cancellations on mild stimulation
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Montoya-Botero 2021)
cards.people: 15 randomised trials of mild stimulation (oral compounds, lower doses or shorter treatment) versus conventional stimulation in poor-responder / low-ovarian-reserve women; fresh live birth was reported by trials totalling 1,001 women and cumulative live birth by 424 women.
cards.result: Fresh live birth was comparable (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.04, I² = 0%, low certainty), as was cumulative live birth (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.81, I² = 0%, moderate certainty). Ongoing pregnancy (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.05) and clinical pregnancy (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.03) were likewise equivalent. Mild stimulation retrieved fewer oocytes (mean difference −0.80, 95% CI −1.28 to −0.32) and had a higher cycle-cancellation rate (RR 1.48, 95% CI 1.08 to 2.02).
cards.watchOut: Included trials were heterogeneous in population and in what 'mild' meant (oral agents in some, low-dose gonadotropin in others), and certainty was low to moderate — but the live-birth equivalence is consistent across every cut of the data, including the cumulative outcome patients actually care about.

cards.headline: Synthesis: dose is not destiny in poor responders — equal live birth, less drug, more cancellations
cards.summary: Synthesis: dose is not destiny in poor responders — equal live birth, less drug, more cancellations
cards.people: One multicentre non-inferiority trial (394 women) and a 15-trial meta-analysis (live-birth data from 1,001 women for the fresh outcome).
cards.result: Ongoing pregnancy 12.8% versus 13.6% (RR 0.95); fresh live birth RR 1.01 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.04); cumulative live birth RR 1.15 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.81). Gonadotropin saving about 3,135 IU per cycle; cycle cancellation RR 1.48. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: This answers the predicted-poor-responder question (the OPTIMIST-era sub-question in the candidate): women with good prognosis were not the population studied, and extrapolation to them is not licensed by these records.

shelves.title: Dual trigger (GnRH agonist plus hCG): live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22% in the double-blind trial and pooled live birth RR 1.37 — from a trial stopped early at interim
shelves.question: In women undergoing IVF, does dual triggering (GnRH agonist + hCG) improve oocyte yield and live birth in normal responders compared with hCG alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chorionic Gonadotropin · Female · Fertilization in Vitro · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Humans · Oocytes · Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome · Ovulation Induction · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — promising, with an early-stopping asterisk. In the double-blind randomised trial (Haas 2020, 155 normal responders), dual trigger produced more oocytes (13.4 versus 11.1, p = 0.002) and more mature oocytes (10.3 versus 8.6, p = 0.009) than hCG alone, with clinical pregnancy 46.1% versus 24.3% (OR 2.65) and live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22% (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.75, p = 0.03). The meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hu 2021, 1,048 participants) found the same direction on the harder endpoint: live birth per started cycle RR 1.37 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.76, I² = 0%, moderate evidence) and clinical pregnancy RR 1.29 (95% CI 1.10 to 1.52). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dual triggering improves oocyte yield and probably live birth in normal responders — held at POSSIBLE because the anchor trial stopped at a planned interim analysis, a design that inflates effects.

cards.headline: Haas 2020: dual trigger — oocytes 13.4 versus 11.1, clinical pregnancy 46.1% versus 24.3%, live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22%
cards.summary: Haas 2020: dual trigger — oocytes 13.4 versus 11.1, clinical pregnancy 46.1% versus 24.3%, live birth per transfer 36.2% versus 22%
cards.people: 155 normal-responder patients at a single centre, randomised to hCG alone or GnRH agonist plus hCG (dual trigger) for final follicular maturation, analysed by intention to treat; age, BMI and anti-Müllerian hormone (20.1 versus 22.4 pmol/L) were comparable between groups. Recruitment was discontinued after a planned interim analysis at 50% recruitment, on the totality of outcomes.
cards.result: Oocytes retrieved were 13.4 versus 11.1 (p = 0.002), metaphase-II oocytes 10.3 versus 8.6 (p = 0.009), total blastocysts 3.9 versus 2.9 (p = 0.01) and top-quality blastocysts transferred 64.9% versus 44.7% (p = 0.003), all favouring dual trigger. Clinical pregnancy rate was 46.1% versus 24.3% (OR 2.65, p = 0.009) and live birth rate per transfer 36.2% versus 22% (OR 1.98, 95% CI 1.05 to 3.75, p = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: Stopping at an interim analysis because results look good is a known effect-inflator: trials stopped early overestimate benefit, sometimes substantially. Live birth is also reported per transfer rather than per started cycle. Both cautions are why this is POSSIBLE, not stronger.
cards.source: Haas J et al. GnRH agonist and hCG (dual trigger) versus hCG trigger for final follicular maturation: a double-blinded, randomized controlled study. Human Reproduction. 2020. PMID: 32563188. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02703584. cards.headline: Hu 2021 (meta-analysis): dual trigger live birth per started cycle RR 1.37 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.76) across 1,048 randomised participants
cards.summary: Hu 2021 (meta-analysis): dual trigger live birth per started cycle RR 1.37 (95% CI 1.07 to 1.76) across 1,048 randomised participants
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hu 2021)
cards.people: Randomised trials of dual trigger (GnRH agonist plus hCG) versus hCG alone for follicular maturation in IVF, totalling 1,048 participants (519 dual trigger, 529 hCG). The primary outcome was live birth rate per started cycle.
cards.result: Dual trigger was associated with a significantly higher live birth rate per started cycle (risk ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.76, I² = 0%, moderate evidence) and clinical pregnancy rate (RR 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.52, I² = 13%, low evidence), with trends to higher ongoing pregnancy (RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.89) and implantation (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.91). Oocytes collected (mean difference 1.52, 95% CI 0.59 to 2.46), mature oocytes (MD 1.01, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.58) and usable embryos (MD 0.90, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.38) were all higher with dual trigger.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and include the early-stopped anchor trial, so the meta-analysis inherits its optimism rather than correcting it; the live-birth confidence interval (1.07 to 1.76) is wide enough to include a worthwhile and a marginal benefit.
cards.source: Hu KL et al. GnRH agonist and hCG (dual trigger) versus hCG trigger for follicular maturation: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials. Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology. 2021. PMID: 34059045. shelves.title: OHSS prevention splits: antagonist protocols cut OHSS (OR 0.61) with live birth intact — agonist trigger cuts it far further (OR 0.15) but cost live birth in fresh transfers (OR 0.47)
shelves.question: In women at high risk of OHSS, does a GnRH-antagonist protocol with agonist trigger reduce OHSS compared with an agonist protocol?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/agonists/antagonists & inhibitors · Humans · Live Birth · Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome/prevention & control · Ovulation Induction/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reproductive Techniques, Assisted
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two halves of the strategy behave differently. The antagonist protocol itself (Cochrane, Al-Inany 2016; 73 RCTs, 12,212 women) reduced any-grade OHSS versus the long agonist protocol (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.72) — an assumed 11% risk falling to between 6% and 9% — with no conclusive difference in live birth (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.23). Adding an agonist trigger in place of hCG within antagonist cycles (Cochrane, Youssef 2014; 17 RCTs, 1,847 women) cut mild-to-severe OHSS much further (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.47 — an assumed 5% risk falling to between nil and 2%) but in fresh autologous cycles it also lowered live birth (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70) and raised early miscarriage (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.75), an effect dependent on luteal-phase support; in donor-recipient cycles live birth did not differ (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.61) while OHSS still fell (OR 0.05). PROPOSED SPLIT: antagonist protocol — OHSS benefit at no live-birth cost; agonist trigger — near-elimination of OHSS, paid for in fresh-transfer live birth unless the cycle is frozen or donated.

cards.headline: Al-Inany 2016 (Cochrane): antagonist versus long agonist protocol — OHSS OR 0.61 (36 trials), live birth OR 1.02 (12 trials)
cards.summary: Al-Inany 2016 (Cochrane): antagonist versus long agonist protocol — OHSS OR 0.61 (36 trials), live birth OR 1.02 (12 trials)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Al-Inany 2016)
cards.people: 73 randomised trials, 12,212 participants, comparing GnRH antagonist protocols with the standard long-course GnRH agonist protocol for controlled ovarian hyperstimulation in assisted conception; 36 trials (7,944 women) reported OHSS and 12 (2,303 women) reported live birth. Evidence quality was moderate.
cards.result: GnRH antagonist was associated with a lower incidence of any-grade OHSS than GnRH agonist (OR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.72; 36 RCTs, n = 7944, I² = 31%) — if OHSS risk on an agonist protocol is 11%, the antagonist risk would be between 6% and 9%. There was no conclusive evidence of a difference in live birth (OR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.23; 12 RCTs, n = 2303) or miscarriage (OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.30). Cancellation for high OHSS risk was lower with antagonists (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.69), while cancellation for poor response was higher (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.65).
cards.watchOut: The antagonist's OHSS advantage is real but modest in absolute terms for average-risk women; its size grows with baseline risk, which is why the protocol matters most in predicted high responders — the population of the candidate question.
cards.source: Al-Inany HG et al. Gonadotrophin-releasing hormone antagonists for assisted reproductive technology. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27126581. cards.headline: Youssef 2014 (Cochrane): agonist trigger versus hCG in antagonist cycles — OHSS OR 0.15, fresh live birth OR 0.47, donor-cycle live birth OR 0.92
cards.summary: Youssef 2014 (Cochrane): agonist trigger versus hCG in antagonist cycles — OHSS OR 0.15, fresh live birth OR 0.47, donor-cycle live birth OR 0.92
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Youssef 2014)
cards.people: 17 randomised trials, 1,847 women undergoing IVF/ICSI in GnRH-antagonist protocols, comparing GnRH agonist trigger with hCG trigger for final oocyte maturation; 13 studies assessed fresh autologous cycles and four assessed donor-recipient cycles.
cards.result: In fresh autologous cycles, agonist trigger was associated with lower live birth than hCG (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70; 5 RCTs, 532 women, moderate-quality evidence) — for a woman with a 31% live-birth chance on hCG, the agonist-trigger chance would be between 12% and 24% — and with lower mild, moderate or severe OHSS (OR 0.15, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.47; 8 RCTs, 989 women): a 5% OHSS risk on hCG falls to between nil and 2%. Ongoing pregnancy was lower (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.91) and early miscarriage higher (OR 1.74, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.75), with the live-birth effect dependent on the type of luteal-phase support. In donor-recipient cycles there was no evidence of a live-birth difference (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.61) and OHSS was lower with agonist trigger (OR 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.28).
cards.watchOut: The fresh-cycle live-birth penalty is a luteal-phase problem, and modern practice answers it with freeze-all or intensive luteal support — strategies the pooled trials largely predate. The review's own conclusion stands: agonist trigger prevents OHSS at the detriment of fresh live birth, and suits women avoiding fresh transfer, donors, and fertility preservation.
cards.source: Youssef MA et al. Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist versus HCG for oocyte triggering in antagonist-assisted reproductive technology. cards.headline: Synthesis: stack the protocol freely; stack the trigger only with a freeze or donor plan
cards.summary: Synthesis: stack the protocol freely; stack the trigger only with a freeze or donor plan
cards.people: Two Cochrane reviews totalling 90 randomised trials and over 14,000 women across the protocol and trigger comparisons.
cards.result: OHSS: OR 0.61 for antagonist versus long agonist protocol; OR 0.15 for agonist versus hCG trigger within antagonist cycles. Live birth: OR 1.02 for the protocol switch; OR 0.47 in fresh autologous cycles and OR 0.92 in donor cycles for the trigger switch. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Neither review randomised women specifically selected as high-OHSS-risk to the combined strategy versus agonist protocol — the combined effect is inferred by stacking two comparisons, each solid, rather than measured in one trial. The direction of the stack is not in doubt; its exact size is.
