shelves.title: Frozen transfer preparation splits by trial scale: one single-centre trial gave natural cycle live birth 54.0% versus 43.0% — the 4,376-woman multicentre trial found healthy live birth 41.6% versus 40.6%, with fewer maternal complications on natural cycles
shelves.question: In women undergoing frozen embryo transfer, does a natural cycle match a hormone-replacement cycle for live birth?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Embryo Transfer/methods · Adult · Pregnancy · Endometrium/drug effects · Hormone Replacement Therapy/methods · Cryopreservation · Live Birth · Fertilization in Vitro/methods · Pregnancy Rate · China · Birth Rate · Ovulation · Menstrual Cycle/physiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — live birth by trial, maternal safety consistently favouring natural cycles. COMPETE (Liu 2025; 902 ovulatory women, single centre) found live birth after the first frozen transfer higher with a natural-cycle strategy: 54.0% (242/448) versus 43.0% (195/454) on hormone replacement (absolute difference 11.1 percentage points, 95% CI 4.6 to 17.5; RR 1.26, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.44), with miscarriage RR 0.61 — but 101 of 448 natural-cycle women crossed over to hormone replacement for absent ovulation. The far larger multicentre trial (Wei 2026; 4,376 women, 24 centres) found healthy live birth essentially identical: 41.6% (910/2185) versus 40.6% (890/2191), relative ratio 1.03 (95% CI 0.96 to 1.10) — while pre-eclampsia among clinical pregnancies was lower on natural cycles (2.9% versus 4.6%, relative ratio 0.63), as were early pregnancy loss, placental accreta spectrum, caesarean section and postpartum haemorrhage; cancellation was higher on natural cycles (16.2% versus 11.5%). A Belgian multicentre trial (Geysenbergh 2026; 561 women) also found no significant difference in clinical pregnancy with fetal heartbeat (33.1% versus 28.9%, RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.47). PROPOSED SPLIT: live birth — matched in the large trials, better only in the single-centre trial; the natural cycle's clearer win is obstetric safety, at the price of more monitoring and cancellations.

cards.headline: Liu 2025 (COMPETE): natural cycle live birth 54.0% versus 43.0% (RR 1.26) — with 101 crossovers out of the natural arm
cards.summary: Liu 2025 (COMPETE): natural cycle live birth 54.0% versus 43.0% (RR 1.26) — with 101 crossovers out of the natural arm
cards.people: 902 women with a regular ovulatory cycle scheduled for frozen-thawed embryo transfer at a single assisted reproduction centre in Xi'an, China, randomised to natural-cycle endometrial preparation (448 women) or hormone replacement therapy (454 women) between December 2020 and December 2022; the primary outcome was live birth after the initial frozen transfer, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Live births numbered 242 (54.0%) in the natural-cycle group versus 195 (43.0%) in the hormone-replacement group (absolute difference 11.1 percentage points, 95% CI 4.6 to 17.5; risk ratio 1.26, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.44). Miscarriage rates (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.89) and antepartum haemorrhage rates (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.93) were lower in the natural-cycle group; other obstetric and perinatal outcomes did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: In the natural-cycle group 101 women received hormone replacement because of absent ovulation, and 29 hormone-replacement women ovulated spontaneously — crossover the authors themselves say limits certainty in directly assessing natural versus hormone-replacement efficacy. Single-centre results of this size have a poor record of surviving multicentre replication, and here the replication exists (next card).
cards.source: Liu X et al. cards.headline: Wei 2026 (BMJ): healthy live birth 41.6% versus 40.6% (RR 1.03) in 4,376 women — pre-eclampsia 2.9% versus 4.6% among clinical pregnancies
cards.summary: Wei 2026 (BMJ): healthy live birth 41.6% versus 40.6% (RR 1.03) in 4,376 women — pre-eclampsia 2.9% versus 4.6% among clinical pregnancies
cards.people: 4,376 ovulatory women aged 20–40 years planning frozen single blastocyst transfer at 24 academic fertility centres in China, randomised to a natural ovulation regimen (2,185 women) or a programmed hormone-replacement regimen (2,191 women). Primary outcomes were healthy live birth and pre-eclampsia or eclampsia after frozen transfer.
cards.result: Healthy live birth was achieved by 910 of 2,185 women (41.6%) on the natural regimen and 890 of 2,191 (40.6%) on the programmed regimen (relative ratio 1.03, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.10; p = 0.49). Among patients achieving clinical pregnancy, pre-eclampsia was lower on the natural regimen (2.9%, 38/1302, versus 4.6%, 61/1326; relative ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.94), as were early pregnancy loss (12.1% versus 15.2%), placental accreta spectrum (1.8% versus 3.6%), caesarean section (69.5% versus 75.6%) and postpartum haemorrhage (2.0% versus 6.1%). Cycle cancellation was higher on the natural regimen (16.2% versus 11.5%, p < 0.001). Birth weight and neonatal complications did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The maternal-safety advantages are secondary outcomes computed among women who achieved pregnancy — a post-randomisation subset — so they carry more uncertainty than the flat primary result. All participants were ovulatory; nothing here speaks to women who need a programmed cycle because they do not ovulate.

cards.headline: Geysenbergh 2026: clinical pregnancy with fetal heartbeat 33.1% versus 28.9% (RR 1.15, not significant); cancellations 3.9% versus 9.4% the other way
cards.summary: Geysenbergh 2026: clinical pregnancy with fetal heartbeat 33.1% versus 28.9% (RR 1.15, not significant); cancellations 3.9% versus 9.4% the other way
cards.people: 561 ovulatory women aged 18–45 years with normal uterine cavities undergoing frozen-thawed transfer of one or two day-3 embryos or blastocysts at five Belgian fertility centres, randomised to natural-cycle or artificial-cycle preparation; the primary outcome was clinical pregnancy rate with fetal heartbeat per cycle, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Clinical pregnancy with fetal heartbeat was 33.1% (94/284) with natural cycle versus 28.9% (80/277) with artificial cycle (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.47), and 34.3% versus 31.8% as treated (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.38) — no significant difference. Cycle cancellations were less frequent with natural cycle (3.9% versus 9.4%; RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.82), natural cycle required more monitoring visits (mean 3.0 versus 2.4, p = 0.0002), and caesarean section was more common after artificial cycle (42.7% versus 20.2%, p = 0.003).
cards.watchOut: Powered for clinical pregnancy, not live birth, and its cancellation result runs opposite to the BMJ trial's — cancellation definitions and monitoring intensity differ between health systems. Its live-birth-relevant message is the same as the big trial's: no significant difference.

cards.result: Live birth: 54.0% versus 43.0% (RR 1.26) single-centre; healthy live birth 41.6% versus 40.6% (RR 1.03) multicentre. shelves.title: Moxifloxacin alone matched ofloxacin plus metronidazole for uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease in three randomised trials — resolution 90.2% versus 90.7% in the double-blind trial — with fewer drug-related adverse events on the single drug
shelves.question: In patients with pelvic inflammatory disease, does moxifloxacin match ofloxacin plus metronidazole for cure?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage · Aza Compounds/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fluoroquinolones · Humans · Metronidazole/administration & dosage · Moxifloxacin · Ofloxacin/administration & dosage · Pain/etiology · Pain Measurement · Pelvic Inflammatory Disease/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Quinolines/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — moxifloxacin monotherapy cured uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease at the same rate as the two-drug regimen in every randomised comparison. In the double-blind trial (Ross JD et al., PMID: 16723364), clinical resolution at test of cure was 90.2% on moxifloxacin versus 90.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (95% CI for the difference −5.7% to 4.0%). A second, larger trial (Aşicioğlu O et al., PMID: 23993130) found clinical cure in 79.5% versus 82.7% (p=0.172). A third trial, against the closely related levofloxacin plus metronidazole (Judlin P et al., PMID: 20716255), found cure in 78.4% versus 81.6% and met its non-inferiority margin. The single drug's edge was tolerability and simplicity: drug-related adverse events were 22.5% versus 30.9% (p=0.01) in the double-blind trial and 37.5% versus 46.4% (p=0.003) in the larger trial. All three trials enrolled uncomplicated disease only — no tubo-ovarian abscess, no sepsis — so nothing here extends to complicated pelvic infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): once-daily moxifloxacin alone matches fluoroquinolone-plus-metronidazole combinations for clinical and bacteriological cure in uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease, with fewer drug-related adverse events.

cards.headline: Ross 2006: clinical resolution 90.2% on moxifloxacin versus 90.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (95% CI −5.7% to 4.0%) — drug-related adverse events 22.5% versus 30.9%
cards.summary: Ross 2006: clinical resolution 90.2% on moxifloxacin versus 90.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (95% CI −5.7% to 4.0%) — drug-related adverse events 22.5% versus 30.9%
cards.people: 749 women with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease in hospitals across 13 countries, randomised to a 14-day course of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily (n=384) or oral ofloxacin 400 mg twice daily plus oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily (n=365); 564 patients were valid for the per-protocol analysis and 112 for the microbiologically valid population.
cards.result: Clinical resolution in the per-protocol population at test of cure (5–24 days post-therapy) was 90.2% (248/275) on moxifloxacin versus 90.7% (262/289) on the combination (95% CI for the difference −5.7% to 4.0%); at follow-up (28–42 days) it was 85.8% versus 87.9% (95% CI −8.0% to 3.1%). Bacteriological success at test of cure was 87.5% (49/56) versus 82.1% (46/56). Drug-related adverse events occurred in 22.5% (85/378) on moxifloxacin versus 30.9% (112/363) on the combination (p=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Only about one in five per-protocol patients had a microbiologically confirmed infection, so the bacteriological comparison rests on 112 women; and 'uncomplicated' excluded abscess and severe disease by design. The trial predates current gonococcal fluoroquinolone resistance patterns, which limits how directly its cure rates transfer to present-day practice.

cards.headline: Aşicioğlu 2013: clinical cure 79.5% on moxifloxacin versus 82.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (p=0.172) in 1,156 randomised women — adverse events 37.5% versus 46.4%
cards.summary: Aşicioğlu 2013: clinical cure 79.5% on moxifloxacin versus 82.7% on ofloxacin plus metronidazole (p=0.172) in 1,156 randomised women — adverse events 37.5% versus 46.4%
cards.people: 1,156 women with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease (no septicaemia, perihepatitis or tubo-ovarian abscess) at four hospitals in Turkey, randomised to a 14-day course of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily (n=560 analysed) or oral ofloxacin 400 mg twice daily plus oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily (n=543 analysed); full compliance in 1,103 patients.
cards.result: Clinical cure was 79.5% (445/560) on moxifloxacin versus 82.7% (449/543) on the combination (p=0.172). Bacteriological cure was 83.2% (99/119) versus 84.5% (93/110) (p=0.781). Drug-related adverse events occurred in 37.5% (210/560) versus 46.4% (252/543) (p=0.003), and non-compliance was 1.2% (7/578) versus 3.8% (22/578) (p=0.005).
cards.watchOut: This trial was prospective and randomised but not described as blinded in its record, and its overall cure rates ran about ten points below the double-blind trial's — a reminder that 'cure' in pelvic inflammatory disease is a clinical judgement whose threshold varies between study teams. Its size, not its precision, is what it adds.

cards.headline: Judlin 2010 (MONALISA): moxifloxacin non-inferior to levofloxacin plus metronidazole — cure 78.4% versus 81.6% (95% CI −10.7 to +4.9) against a −15% margin
cards.summary: Judlin 2010 (MONALISA): moxifloxacin non-inferior to levofloxacin plus metronidazole — cure 78.4% versus 81.6% (95% CI −10.7 to +4.9) against a −15% margin
cards.people: 460 women aged 18 or over with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease (no pelvic or tubo-ovarian abscess, not requiring intravenous treatment) in Asia, randomised to a 14-day course of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily or oral levofloxacin 500 mg once daily plus oral metronidazole 500 mg twice daily; women screening positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae also received single-dose intramuscular ceftriaxone 250 mg.
cards.result: Clinical cure at test of cure (7–14 days after the last dose) in the per-protocol population was 78.4% (152/194) on moxifloxacin versus 81.6% (155/190) on levofloxacin plus metronidazole (95% CI for the difference −10.7 to +4.9), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority criterion (lower limit above −15%). Bacteriological success was 90.0% (27/30) versus 84.6% (22/26). Both treatments were reported as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is levofloxacin, not the ofloxacin of the candidate question — a near neighbour, not the same regimen — and the non-inferiority margin (−15%) was generous: the interval is compatible with moxifloxacin being up to about eleven points worse. It supports the class conclusion; it does not tighten it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, one answer — the single drug cures uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease as often as the combination, and upsets fewer stomachs
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, one answer — the single drug cures uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease as often as the combination, and upsets fewer stomachs
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 2,365 randomised women with uncomplicated pelvic inflammatory disease (Ross 2006, double-blind; Aşicioğlu 2013; Judlin 2010, double-blind, levofloxacin comparator).
cards.result: Clinical cure/resolution: 90.2% versus 90.7% (Ross), 79.5% versus 82.7% (Aşicioğlu), 78.4% versus 81.6% (Judlin) — no significant difference in any trial. Drug-related adverse events favoured moxifloxacin in both trials that reported them by arm (22.5% versus 30.9%; 37.5% versus 46.4%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for cure, with the tolerability advantage on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Every trial excluded complicated disease (abscess, sepsis, perihepatitis), and all predate today's gonococcal resistance landscape — the equivalence shown is between these regimens in uncomplicated disease, not a licence to use fluoroquinolones where resistance is prevalent. Tier C — held for the developer's personal verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ross JD et al. Sexually Transmitted Infections. 2006 (PMID: 16723364); Aşicioğlu O et al. shelves.title: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) in pregnancy and child neurodevelopment: ordinary cohort analyses show a small association (pooled ADHD risk ratio 1.34) — but the 2.48-million-child Swedish sibling-control analysis found none (hazard ratio 0.98 for autism and for ADHD)
shelves.question: Is paracetamol (acetaminophen) safe in pregnancy? In pregnant people who use paracetamol/acetaminophen for pain or fever, is use associated with autism, ADHD, or intellectual disability in their children — and does the association survive sibling-control analysis?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/adverse effects · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/chemically induced · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/epidemiology · Autistic Disorder/chemically induced · Autistic Disorder/epidemiology · Child · Cohort Studies · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intellectual Disability/chemically induced · Intellectual Disability/epidemiology · Neurodevelopmental Disorders/chemically induced · Neurodevelopmental Disorders/epidemiology · Pregnancy · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects/chemically induced · Prenatal Exposure Delayed Effects/epidemiology · Sweden/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT / CONTESTED — all of this evidence is observational; no randomised trial of paracetamol in pregnancy with child neurodevelopment follow-up exists, and the answer changes with the study design. The association side: in the Danish National Birth Cohort (Liew 2014, PMID: 24566677; 64,322 children), children of mothers who used acetaminophen in pregnancy had higher risk of a hospital diagnosis of hyperkinetic disorder (hazard ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.19–1.59), ADHD medication use (HR 1.29, 1.15–1.44), and ADHD-like behaviours at age 7 (risk ratio 1.13, 1.01–1.27), with stronger associations for use in more than one trimester. Pooling seven cohorts (Masarwa 2018, PMID: 29688261; 132,738 mother–child pairs) gave a risk ratio of 1.34 (1.21–1.47) for ADHD and 1.19 (1.14–1.25) for autistic spectrum disorder. The confounding side: the largest study (Ahlqvist 2024, PMID: 38592388; 2,480,797 Swedish children, 185,909 [7.49%] exposed) found only marginal associations before sibling control (autism HR 1.05; ADHD HR 1.07; intellectual disability HR 1.05; crude absolute risks at age 10 in unexposed versus exposed children 1.33% versus 1.53% for autism, 2.46% versus 2.87% for ADHD, 0.70% versus 0.82% for intellectual disability) — and in matched full-sibling analyses, which compare children of the same mother and so strip out shared family factors, there was no association at all: autism HR 0.98 (0.93–1.04), ADHD HR 0.98 (0.94–1.02), intellectual disability HR 1.01 (0.92–1.10), with no dose–response pattern. The authors' reading is that the ordinary-model associations may be attributable to familial confounding — the reasons and family background behind paracetamol use, not the drug. The counterweight, stated plainly: paracetamol is the analgesic and antipyretic most commonly used in pregnancy (Masarwa 2018), it is taken for pain and for fever, and the cohort studies compare users with non-users — they do not test the alternative of leaving significant pain or fever untreated, which is itself a clinical problem in pregnancy; this shelf therefore cannot be read as 'never take it' or as 'proven harmless'. PROPOSED SPLIT: a small association in conventional cohort analyses that disappears under sibling control in the largest and best-controlled study — causality unproven either way, evidence contested and observational throughout.

cards.headline: Ahlqvist 2024 (the sibling-control study): in 2,480,797 Swedish children, ordinary models gave HR 1.05–1.07 — but comparing siblings, acetaminophen in pregnancy showed NO association with autism (HR 0.98), ADHD (HR 0.98), or intellectual disability (HR 1.01)
cards.summary: Ahlqvist 2024 (the sibling-control study): in 2,480,797 Swedish children, ordinary models gave HR 1.05–1.07 — but comparing siblings, acetaminophen in pregnancy showed NO association with autism (HR 0.98), ADHD (HR 0.98), or intellectual disability (HR 1.01)
cards.type: Nationwide cohort study with sibling control analysis (Ahlqvist 2024)
cards.people: 2,480,797 children born in Sweden in 1995–2019, followed through December 31, 2021; 185,909 children (7.49%) were exposed to acetaminophen during pregnancy, with use prospectively recorded from antenatal and prescription records. Outcomes (autism, ADHD, intellectual disability) came from ICD-9/ICD-10 codes in health registers. Matched full-sibling pairs were analysed separately to address unobserved (familial) confounding.
cards.result: Crude absolute risks at 10 years of age, unexposed versus exposed: autism 1.33% versus 1.53%, ADHD 2.46% versus 2.87%, intellectual disability 0.70% versus 0.82%. In models without sibling control, ever-use versus no use was associated with marginally increased risk: autism HR 1.05 (95% CI 1.02–1.08; risk difference at 10 years 0.09%, −0.01% to 0.20%), ADHD HR 1.07 (1.05–1.10; RD 0.21%, 0.08%–0.34%), intellectual disability HR 1.05 (1.00–1.10; RD 0.04%, −0.04% to 0.12%). In sibling control analyses there was no evidence of association: autism HR 0.98 (0.93–1.04; RD 0.02%, −0.14% to 0.18%), ADHD HR 0.98 (0.94–1.02; RD −0.02%, −0.21% to 0.15%), intellectual disability HR 1.01 (0.92–1.10; RD 0%, −0.10% to 0.13%). There was no dose–response pattern in sibling analyses (for autism, HRs 0.85, 0.96, and 0.88 for low, medium, and high mean daily use versus none). The authors concluded acetaminophen use during pregnancy was not associated with these outcomes in sibling control analysis, suggesting other models' associations may reflect familial confounding.
cards.watchOut: Sibling control removes confounders siblings share (genetics, household, maternal traits) but cannot remove factors that differ between pregnancies — including the very indication (a febrile illness in one pregnancy and not the other). Exposure was recorded use, and only 7.49% of children were recorded as exposed, far below self-reported use rates in cohorts like the Danish one (over half), so exposure misclassification toward under-recording is likely and would bias toward the null. Observational throughout: this design strengthens causal inference but does not settle it.
cards.source: Ahlqvist VH, Sjöqvist H, Dalman C, Karlsson H, Stephansson O, Johansson S, Magnusson C, Gardner RM, Lee BK. Acetaminophen Use During Pregnancy and Children's Risk of Autism, ADHD, and Intellectual Disability. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 38592388. Registry ID: none in the record (observational cohort study). cards.headline: Liew 2014 (the Danish cohort that opened the question): hyperkinetic disorder HR 1.37, ADHD medication HR 1.29, ADHD-like behaviours RR 1.13 with prenatal acetaminophen — stronger with use in more than one trimester
cards.summary: Liew 2014 (the Danish cohort that opened the question): hyperkinetic disorder HR 1.37, ADHD medication HR 1.29, ADHD-like behaviours RR 1.13 with prenatal acetaminophen — stronger with use in more than one trimester
cards.people: 64,322 live-born children and their mothers enrolled in the Danish National Birth Cohort during 1996–2002. Acetaminophen use in pregnancy was assessed prospectively in three computer-assisted telephone interviews during pregnancy and one 6 months after birth; more than half of mothers reported use. Outcomes: parent-reported behavioural problems at age 7 (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire), hyperkinetic disorder (HKD) diagnoses from Danish hospital/psychiatric registries, and ADHD prescriptions from the Danish Prescription Registry.
cards.result: Children whose mothers used acetaminophen during pregnancy were at higher risk of receiving a hospital diagnosis of HKD (hazard ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.19–1.59), using ADHD medications (HR 1.29, 1.15–1.44), or having ADHD-like behaviours at age 7 years (risk ratio 1.13, 1.01–1.27). Stronger associations were observed with use in more than one trimester, and exposure–response trends were found with increasing frequency of use during gestation for all outcomes (P trend < .001). The authors reported the results did not appear to be confounded by maternal inflammation, infection during pregnancy, the mother's mental health problems, or other evaluated confounders, and concluded the findings were of public health relevance but needed further investigation.
cards.watchOut: No sibling control: mothers who take acetaminophen repeatedly through pregnancy differ from those who do not — in illness burden, pain conditions, and family neurodevelopmental background — and registry adjustment cannot fully capture that, which is exactly the gap the Ahlqvist sibling analysis later targeted. The hazard ratios are relative measures; the abstract prints no absolute outcome rates, so no absolute excess can be quoted from this card. Exposure was self-reported use, not dose-verified.
cards.source: Liew Z, Ritz B, Rebordosa C, Lee PC, Olsen J. Acetaminophen use during pregnancy, behavioral problems, and hyperkinetic disorders. JAMA Pediatrics. 2014. PMID: 24566677. more than half of mothers reported use. outcomes: parent-reported behavioural problems at age 7 (strengths and difficulties questionnaire), hyperkinetic disorder (hkd) diagnoses from danish hospital/psychiatric registries, and adhd prescriptions from the danish prescription registry. children whose mothers used acetaminophen during pregnancy were at higher risk of receiving a hospital diagnosis of hkd (hazard ratio 1.37, 95% ci 1.19–1.59), using adhd medications (hr 1.29, 1.15–1.44), or having adhd-like behaviours at age 7 years (risk ratio 1.13, 1.01–1.27). stronger associations were observed with use in more than one trimester, and exposure–response trends were found with increasing frequency of use during gestation for all outcomes (p trend < .001). the authors reported the results did not appear to be confounded by maternal inflammation, infection during pregnancy, the mother's mental health problems, or other evaluated confounders, and concluded the findings were of public health relevance but needed further investigation. no sibling control: mothers who take acetaminophen repeatedly through pregnancy differ from those who do not — in illness burden, pain conditions, and family neurodevelopmental background — and registry adjustment cannot fully capture that, which is exactly the gap the ahlqvist sibling analysis later targeted. the hazard ratios are relative measures; the abstract prints no absolute outcome rates, so no absolute excess can be quoted from this card. exposure was self-reported use, not dose-verified. liew z, ritz b, rebordosa c, lee pc, olsen j. acetaminophen use during pregnancy, behavioral problems, and hyperkinetic disorders. jama pediatrics. 2014. pmid: 24566677. registry id: none in the record (observational cohort study). mesh: acetaminophen/adverse effects · adult · attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity/chemically induced · attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity/diagnosis · attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity/epidemiology · child · child, preschool · denmark · female · humans · hyperkinesis/chemically induced · hyperkinesis/diagnosis · infant · male · mental disorders/chemically induced · mental disorders/epidemiology · mothers · pregnancy · prenatal exposure delayed effects/chemically induced · prenatal exposure delayed effects/diagnosis · prenatal exposure delayed effects/epidemiology · proportional hazards models · prospective studies · risk assessment · risk factors · surveys and questionnaires

cards.headline: Masarwa 2018 (the pooled cohort evidence): across 7 cohorts and 132,738 mother–child pairs, prenatal acetaminophen was associated with ADHD (risk ratio 1.34), ASD (1.19), and hyperactivity symptoms (1.24) — observational, with wide between-study differences
cards.summary: Masarwa 2018 (the pooled cohort evidence): across 7 cohorts and 132,738 mother–child pairs, prenatal acetaminophen was associated with ADHD (risk ratio 1.34), ASD (1.19), and hyperactivity symptoms (1.24) — observational, with wide between-study differences
cards.type: Systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression of cohort studies (Masarwa 2018)
cards.people: Seven eligible retrospective cohort studies including 132,738 mother–child pairs, with follow-up periods ranging from 3 to 11 years; MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane databases searched to January 2017, with data independently extracted and assessed by two researchers.
cards.result: The pooled risk ratio was 1.34 (95% CI 1.21–1.47; I² = 72%) for ADHD, 1.19 (1.14–1.25; I² = 14%) for autistic spectrum disorder, and 1.24 (1.04–1.43; I² = 93%) for hyperactivity symptoms. In meta-regression, the ADHD association increased with the child's age at follow-up and with mean duration of exposure. The authors stated the available data are of an observational nature only, that studies differed widely in exposure and outcome assessment, and that results should be interpreted with caution given susceptibility to several potential sources of bias — while calling the findings concerning.
cards.watchOut: A pooled estimate of conventionally adjusted cohorts inherits their shared weakness: none of the seven cohorts was a sibling-control design, so the pooled 1.34 cannot answer the familial-confounding objection that the later Swedish sibling analysis (carded above) was built to test. Heterogeneity was substantial for ADHD (I² = 72%) and very high for hyperactivity symptoms (I² = 93%), and all risk ratios here are relative measures without pooled absolute risks in the abstract.
cards.source: Masarwa R, Levine H, Gorelik E, Reif S, Perlman A, Matok I. Prenatal Exposure to Acetaminophen and Risk for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Autistic Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression Analysis of Cohort Studies. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2018. PMID: 29688261. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis of observational cohorts). cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, consistent association in ordinary cohort analyses — and a null in the one analysis designed to remove family confounding; the question is unresolved, not closed in either direction
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, consistent association in ordinary cohort analyses — and a null in the one analysis designed to remove family confounding; the question is unresolved, not closed in either direction
cards.people: Three sources: the Swedish nationwide sibling-control cohort (Ahlqvist 2024; 2,480,797 children), the Danish National Birth Cohort (Liew 2014; 64,322 children), and the meta-analysis of seven cohorts (Masarwa 2018; 132,738 mother–child pairs). All observational; no randomised evidence exists on this question.
cards.result: Conventional analyses: ADHD risk ratio 1.34 (1.21–1.47) and ASD risk ratio 1.19 (1.14–1.25) pooled across seven cohorts (Masarwa 2018); in the Danish cohort, HKD HR 1.37, ADHD medication HR 1.29, ADHD-like behaviours RR 1.13, with trimester and frequency gradients (Liew 2014). Sibling-control analysis: HR 0.98 for autism, 0.98 for ADHD, and 1.01 for intellectual disability, with risk differences at age 10 of 0.02%, −0.02%, and 0% respectively and no dose–response (Ahlqvist 2024) — against crude absolute risks of 1.33% versus 1.53% (autism), 2.46% versus 2.87% (ADHD), and 0.70% versus 0.82% (intellectual disability) for unexposed versus exposed children in the same study. PROPOSED SPLIT: the association is real as an observation and unproven as a cause; the best confounding control available points to family factors rather than the drug, but sibling designs have their own biases and the matter remains contested.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Nothing on this shelf measures the harms of the alternative — untreated significant pain or fever in pregnancy — because the cohorts compare users with non-users rather than treatment strategies; a decision to avoid paracetamol is not evidence-free either, and NSAIDs in pregnancy carry their own established fetal concerns that are outside this shelf's question. This shelf also does not cover paracetamol's established non-neurodevelopmental safety record in pregnancy (e.g., malformations), which is a different literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ahlqvist VH et al. JAMA. 2024 (PMID: 38592388); Liew Z et al. JAMA Pediatrics. 2014 (PMID: 24566677); Masarwa R et al. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2018 (PMID: 29688261).

shelves.title: Genital warts beyond the two standard creams: cryotherapy matched topical treatments in 11 trials, sinecatechins ointment beat placebo (54.9% vs 35.4% complete clearance), and adding HPV vaccine to treatment did not demonstrably help
shelves.question: I have genital warts — apart from the imiquimod and podophyllotoxin creams (covered on another shelf), what else actually clears them: freezing, other ointments, or the HPV vaccine used as treatment?
shelves.mesh: Anus Diseases/therapy · Catechin/therapeutic use · Condylomata Acuminata/drug therapy · Condylomata Acuminata/therapy · Cryotherapy · Papillomavirus Vaccines · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Warts/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped to treatments BEYOND the two standard patient-applied creams: the head-to-head question of imiquimod cream versus podophyllotoxin is homed on Shelf #2198 and is not re-carded here. What remains is cardable and consistent. (1) Cryotherapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials in immunocompetent adults found cryotherapy's complete clearance did not differ from trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin or imiquimod; electrosurgery was weakly better than cryotherapy (relative risk 0.80, 95% CI 0.65–0.99 for clearance with cryotherapy relative to electrosurgery); cryotherapy caused more immediate low-level adverse events (RR 3.02, 1.38–6.61) and more pain needing oral analgesics (RR 2.11, 1.07–4.17) but fewer erosions (RR 0.57, 0.36–0.90); all but one trial were at high risk of bias (Bertolotti 2017, PMID: 28651824). (2) Sinecatechins (Polyphenon E, a defined green tea catechin ointment — the specific tested product, named because botanical preparations differ by maker): pooling two phase III vehicle-controlled trials (1,005 patients), complete clearance of all warts was 53.6% on the 10% ointment and 54.9% on the 15% ointment versus 35.4% on vehicle (P<0.001; odds ratios 2.10 and 2.22, relative measures), with recurrence of about 6% in all groups over follow-up (Tatti 2010, PMID: 19709100). (3) HPV vaccine as treatment: in the HIPvac factorial trial (503 participants), adding quadrivalent HPV vaccine to cream treatment did not demonstrably improve the combined outcome of clearance at week 16 and remaining wart-free at week 48 (adjusted odds ratio 1.46, 0.97–2.20) (Gilson 2020, PMID: 32975189). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): freezing and sinecatechins are effective wart-clearing options beyond the standard creams; vaccination during treatment is unproven as a treatment, whatever its preventive role.

cards.headline: Bertolotti 2017: cryotherapy cleared warts no better or worse than trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin or imiquimod across 11 RCTs; electrosurgery was weakly better (RR 0.80)
cards.summary: Bertolotti 2017: cryotherapy cleared warts no better or worse than trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin or imiquimod across 11 RCTs; electrosurgery was weakly better (RR 0.80)
cards.people: Immunocompetent adults with anogenital warts treated in 11 randomised controlled trials (total participant number not documented in the record) comparing cryotherapy against another treatment, with complete wart clearance as the primary endpoint.
cards.result: Cryotherapy's efficacy did not appear to differ from that of trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin, or imiquimod. Electrosurgery was weakly associated with better clearance than cryotherapy (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.65–0.99 — a relative measure, for cryotherapy versus electrosurgery). Cryotherapy was associated with more immediate low-level adverse events such as erythema, stinging or irritation (RR 3.02, 1.38–6.61) and more immediate pain requiring oral analgesics (RR 2.11, 1.07–4.17), but fewer erosions (RR 0.57, 0.36–0.90). All but one of the randomised trials were at high risk of bias; the authors concluded that, on low-quality evidence, cryotherapy is an acceptable first-line therapy.
cards.watchOut: 'Did not differ' on high-risk-of-bias trials is weak ground — the honest reading is that no trial has shown cryotherapy clearly better or worse than the topical options, and the single significant comparison (electrosurgery, RR 0.80 with an interval just excluding 1) is described by the authors themselves as weak. The review is restricted to immunocompetent adults; warts in immunosuppression behave differently and are not covered.
cards.source: Bertolotti A, Dupin N, Bouscarat F, Milpied B, Derancourt C. Cryotherapy to treat anogenital warts in nonimmunocompromised adults: systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2017. PMID: 28651824. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Tatti 2010: sinecatechins ointment beat its vehicle — complete clearance 53.6% (10%) and 54.9% (15%) versus 35.4% (P<0.001) in two pooled phase III trials (n=1,005)
cards.summary: Tatti 2010: sinecatechins ointment beat its vehicle — complete clearance 53.6% (10%) and 54.9% (15%) versus 35.4% (P<0.001) in two pooled phase III trials (n=1,005)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised double-blind vehicle-controlled phase III trials (Tatti 2010)
cards.people: 1,005 men and women aged 18 or over with 2–30 external genital warts (12–600 mm² total area) in two randomised, double-blind, vehicle-controlled phase III trials, applying vehicle (207), Polyphenon E (sinecatechins) ointment 10% (401) or 15% (397) three times daily until complete clearance or for up to 16 weeks; 986 were evaluable for efficacy and 1,004 for safety.
cards.result: Complete clearance of all warts (baseline plus newly occurring) was obtained in 53.6% of the 10% group and 54.9% of the 15% group versus 35.4% on vehicle (P<0.001) — absolute differences of about 18–20 percentage points; the odds ratios versus vehicle were 2.10 (95% CI 1.49–2.98) and 2.22 (1.57–3.14), relative measures indicating about twice the odds of complete clearance. Time to complete clearance was shorter on active treatment (hazard ratios 1.57 and 1.87). Recurrence during follow-up was low and similar across groups (5.8% vehicle, 6.8% 10%, 6.5% 15%). Adverse events occurred in about 30% of patients in every group; severe local signs were more frequent on active treatment (1.5% vehicle, 9.2% 10%, 13.5% 15%).
cards.watchOut: The vehicle itself cleared over a third of patients completely (35.4%) — spontaneous and placebo clearance is substantial in wart trials, so the drug-attributable gain is the ~18–20 point difference, not the ~54% headline. The tested preparation is a defined, standardised catechin mixture (Polyphenon E / sinecatechins); results do not transfer to unregulated green-tea or herbal wart products, which are not the tested product. Three-times-daily application for up to 16 weeks is a demanding regimen.
cards.source: Tatti S, Stockfleth E, Beutner KR, Tawfik H, Elsasser U, Weyrauch P, Mescheder A. Polyphenon E: a new treatment for external anogenital warts. British Journal of Dermatology. 2010. PMID: 19709100. Registry ID: none in the record (pooled report of two phase III trials). cards.headline: HIPvac (Gilson 2020): adding quadrivalent HPV vaccine to cream treatment did NOT demonstrably improve clearance or prevent recurrence (aOR 1.46, 95% CI 0.97–2.20)
cards.summary: HIPvac (Gilson 2020): adding quadrivalent HPV vaccine to cream treatment did NOT demonstrably improve clearance or prevent recurrence (aOR 1.46, 95% CI 0.97–2.20)
cards.type: Factorial randomised controlled trial — vaccine add-on comparison only (HIPvac, Gilson 2020)
cards.people: 503 participants with a first or repeat episode of anogenital warts at 22 sexual health clinics in England and Wales (mean age 31; 66% male; 50% with previous warts), randomised in a factorial design to imiquimod or podophyllotoxin cream and, simultaneously, to quadrivalent HPV vaccine (the tested product was Gardasil, named in the record) or saline placebo at 0, 8 and 24 weeks; the card reports only the vaccine comparison.
cards.result: For the combined primary outcome — wart clearance at week 16 and remaining wart-free at week 48 — the adjusted odds ratio for vaccine versus placebo was 1.46 (95% CI 0.97–2.20), which does not exclude no effect; the components pointed the same way (wart-free at week 16, aOR 1.30, 0.89–1.91; remaining wart-free at 48 weeks among those clear at 16, aOR 1.39, 0.73–2.63). The authors concluded a benefit of the vaccine was not demonstrated, while noting the trial recruited 503 of its planned 1,000 participants, so a modest benefit could not be ruled out. Podophyllotoxin without vaccine was the most cost-effective strategy at the vaccine's list price.
cards.watchOut: Boundary, stated plainly: HIPvac's other comparison — imiquimod versus podophyllotoxin cream (aOR 0.81, 0.54–1.23) — answers the question already homed on Shelf #2198 and is deliberately not re-carded here; only the vaccine add-on, which #2198 does not cover, is carded. The result is 'not demonstrated in an under-recruited trial', not proof of no effect; and nothing here touches the vaccine's established preventive use in unvaccinated people, which is a different question.
cards.source: Gilson R, Nugent D, Bennett K, et al. Imiquimod versus podophyllotoxin, with and without human papillomavirus vaccine, for anogenital warts: the HIPvac factorial RCT. Health Technology Assessment. 2020. PMID: 32975189. Registry ID: ISRCTN32729817 (also EudraCT 2013-002951-14). only the vaccine add-on, which #2198 does not cover, is carded. the result is 'not demonstrated in an under-recruited trial', not proof of no effect; and nothing here touches the vaccine's established preventive use in unvaccinated people, which is a different question. gilson r, nugent d, bennett k, et al. imiquimod versus podophyllotoxin, with and without human papillomavirus vaccine, for anogenital warts: the hipvac factorial rct. health technology assessment. 2020. pmid: 32975189. registry id: isrctn32729817 (also eudract 2013-002951-14). mesh: adjuvants, immunologic/administration & dosage · condylomata acuminata/drug therapy · drug therapy, combination · imiquimod/administration & dosage · papillomavirus vaccines · podophyllotoxin/administration & dosage · secondary prevention · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: beyond the two standard creams, freezing performs like the topicals, sinecatechins beats placebo by ~18–20 points, and vaccine-as-treatment is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: beyond the two standard creams, freezing performs like the topicals, sinecatechins beats placebo by ~18–20 points, and vaccine-as-treatment is unproven
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 11 cryotherapy RCTs (Bertolotti 2017), two pooled phase III vehicle-controlled trials of sinecatechins (1,005 patients; Tatti 2010), and one factorial RCT of HPV vaccine added to treatment (503 patients; Gilson 2020).
cards.result: Cryotherapy clearance: no difference versus trichloroacetic acid, podophyllin or imiquimod; electrosurgery weakly better (RR 0.80); more immediate pain and irritation with cryotherapy (RR 3.02 and 2.11), fewer erosions (RR 0.57). Sinecatechins: complete clearance 53.6–54.9% versus 35.4% on vehicle (absolute gain ~18–20 points), recurrence ~6% in all arms. HPV vaccine added to treatment: primary-outcome aOR 1.46 (0.97–2.20) — benefit not demonstrated. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for cryotherapy and sinecatechins as wart-clearing treatments; the vaccine add-on remains unproven.
cards.watchOut: The imiquimod-versus-podophyllotoxin question, including HIPvac's own version of it, lives on Shelf #2198; HPV vaccination to prevent warts in the first place and wart treatment in pregnancy or immunosuppression are separate questions not answered here. Wart trials generally show high clearance on vehicle/placebo, so absolute differences — not headline clearance rates — are the honest currency of this shelf. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bertolotti A et al. Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology. 2017 (PMID: 28651824); Tatti S et al. British Journal of Dermatology. 2010 (PMID: 19709100); Gilson R et al. Health Technology Assessment. 2020 (PMID: 32975189).

shelves.title: Ovarian cysts: birth-control pills did not speed resolution in any of 8 trials (686 women) and aspiration matched plain observation (46% vs 45% resolved) — watching a benign-appearing cyst carried a 0.4% two-year cancer risk
shelves.question: For a woman with a functional or simple ovarian cyst, do oral contraceptives or needle aspiration speed resolution compared with watchful waiting, and how safe is watchful waiting?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined / therapeutic use* · Female · Humans · Ovarian Cysts / drug therapy* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Remission Induction · Remission, Spontaneous · Watchful Waiting
shelves.balance: SPLIT. For an existing functional or simple cyst, the two active treatments tested both failed against simply waiting. Grimes 2014 (PMID: 24782304), the Cochrane review of eight RCTs in 686 women, found combined oral contraceptives did not hasten resolution in any trial. Zanetta 1996 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.313.7065.1110; PMID not captured this session) randomised 278 women: aspiration resolved 46% versus 44.6% with observation at six months. What supports management is the safety of waiting itself: in IOTA5 (Froyman 2019, PMID: 30737137; NCT01698632), 1,919 women with benign-appearing masses managed conservatively had 20.2% spontaneous resolution by two years, with invasive malignancy 0.4%, torsion 0.4% and rupture 0.2%. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (oral contraceptives: the treatment made no difference · aspiration: the treatment made no difference · watchful waiting: supported as safe for ultrasound-benign cysts).

cards.headline: Grimes 2014: oral contraceptives did not hasten resolution in any of 8 trials (686 women)
cards.summary: Grimes 2014: oral contraceptives did not hasten resolution in any of 8 trials (686 women)
cards.people: 686 women in eight randomised controlled trials from four countries, with functional ovarian cysts — spontaneous cysts and cysts arising after ovulation induction.
cards.result: Treatment with combined oral contraceptives did not hasten resolution of functional ovarian cysts in any trial. Most cysts resolved without treatment within a few cycles; persistent cysts tended to be pathological (e.g. endometrioma or para-ovarian cyst) rather than physiological. The reviewers' conclusion: combined oral contraceptives appear to be of no benefit for treating existing cysts; watchful waiting for two or three cycles is appropriate.
cards.watchOut: This is about treating an existing functional cyst, not prevention: oral contraceptives can still be used to prevent new functional cysts or for other indications — the null here is specifically 'the pill dissolves the cyst you already have'.
cards.source: Grimes DA, Jones LB, Lopez LM, Schulz KF. Oral contraceptives for functional ovarian cysts. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014. PMID: 24782304. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Froyman 2019 (IOTA5): watching benign-appearing masses — 20.2% resolved in 2 years, invasive malignancy 0.4%
cards.summary: Froyman 2019 (IOTA5): watching benign-appearing masses — 20.2% resolved in 2 years, invasive malignancy 0.4%
cards.people: 1,919 women with a newly diagnosed adnexal mass judged benign on ultrasound, selected for conservative management (ultrasound and clinical follow-up at 3 and 6 months, then yearly) across 36 centres in 14 countries; median follow-up 27 months.
cards.result: Cumulative incidence within 2 years: spontaneous resolution 20.2% (95% CI 18.4 to 22.1); invasive malignancy found at surgery 0.4% (95% CI 0.1 to 0.6); borderline tumour 0.3%; torsion 0.4%; cyst rupture 0.2%. Of 3,144 patients selected for conservative management, 336 (11%) were operated on before a planned follow-up scan.
cards.watchOut: Safety of watching depends on expert ultrasound classification — these masses were judged benign by subjective assessment in specialist centres, and 11% still came to surgery before a follow-up scan; the figures do not license ignoring a mass that has not been properly characterised.
cards.source: Froyman W et al. Risk of complications in patients with conservatively managed ovarian tumours (IOTA5): a 2-year interim analysis of a multicentre, prospective, cohort study. Lancet Oncol. 2019. PMID: 30737137. Registry ID: NCT01698632. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Zanetta 1996: needle aspiration resolved 46% versus 45% with observation alone — no advantage
cards.summary: Zanetta 1996: needle aspiration resolved 46% versus 45% with observation alone — no advantage
cards.people: 278 women with simple ovarian cysts randomised to ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration (135) or simple observation (143) between 1990 and 1994; 269 available for follow-up at six months.
cards.result: Resolution at six months: 46% (59/128) with aspiration versus 44.6% (63/141) with observation — an absolute difference of about 1 percentage point. Only cyst diameter was a significant independent prognostic factor for resolution (P < 0.0001); age and treatment had no significant effect. One woman was subsequently found to have borderline malignant changes on histopathology. Numbers taken from the BMJ full text fetched this session (see flag in the part summary).
cards.watchOut: A 1990s trial using the imaging of its era, in simple cysts only — it answers 'does draining add anything to waiting?' (no), not what to do with complex, symptomatic or enlarging masses.
cards.source: Zanetta G, Lissoni A, Torri V, Mangioni C et al. Role of puncture and aspiration in expectant management of simple ovarian cysts: a randomised study. BMJ. 1996. PMID: not captured this session (DOI 10.1136/bmj.313.7065.1110). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: neither the pill nor the needle beats waiting; waiting itself is measurably safe for benign-appearing cysts
cards.summary: Synthesis: neither the pill nor the needle beats waiting; waiting itself is measurably safe for benign-appearing cysts
cards.people: Three sources: a Cochrane review of 8 RCTs (Grimes 2014, 686 women), a randomised aspiration trial (Zanetta 1996, 278 women), and a prospective conservative-management cohort (Froyman 2019, 1,919 women).
cards.result: Oral contraceptives: no hastening of resolution in any of 8 trials (Grimes 2014). Aspiration versus observation: resolution 46% versus 44.6% at six months (Zanetta 1996). Conservative management of benign-appearing masses: 20.2% spontaneous resolution by 2 years with invasive malignancy 0.4%, torsion 0.4% and rupture 0.2% (Froyman 2019). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Endometriomas and other pathological cysts are a different problem — the Cochrane review notes persistent cysts tended to be pathological, and nothing on this shelf covers cysts with suspicious features, acute pain or torsion.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grimes 2014 (PMID: 24782304), Zanetta 1996 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.313.7065.1110) and Froyman 2019 (PMID: 30737137; NCT01698632).

shelves.title: Paget's disease of the nipple: conservation alone recurred in 21.2% versus 5.9% after mastectomy across 24,062 patients — adding radiotherapy closed most of the gap, and 82% have an underlying breast cancer
shelves.question: In Paget's disease of the nipple (mammary Paget disease), how do mastectomy, breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy, and breast-conserving surgery alone compare for local recurrence?
shelves.mesh: Breast Neoplasms* / surgery · Carcinoma, Intraductal, Noninfiltrating* / pathology · Female · Humans · Mastectomy · Paget's Disease, Mammary* / surgery · Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only — there are no randomised trials. The governing fact is that the nipple change usually sits on a breast cancer: Kollmorgen 1998 (PMID: 9704964) found underlying cancer in 82% (93% with a palpable mass, 74% without). Across 38 studies and 24,062 patients, Lin 2022 (PMID: 36309195) found local recurrence of 21.2% after breast-conserving surgery alone versus 5.9% after mastectomy and about 8% after conservation plus radiotherapy (the radiotherapy figure is printed truncated in the record), concluding conservation alone is not recommended with underlying invasive cancer or DCIS. Pelorca 2023 (PMID: 37265790) found oncoplastic conservation feasible with no detectable recurrence or survival difference in 85 patients. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for conservation plus radiotherapy over conservation alone. Not Paget's disease of bone (Shelf #1822).

cards.headline: Lin 2022: local recurrence 21.2% after conservation alone versus 5.9% after mastectomy and about 8% after conservation plus radiotherapy (38 studies, 24,062 patients)
cards.summary: Lin 2022: local recurrence 21.2% after conservation alone versus 5.9% after mastectomy and about 8% after conservation plus radiotherapy (38 studies, 24,062 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Lin 2022)
cards.people: 24,062 patients with mammary Paget disease in 38 real-world studies comparing mastectomy, breast-conserving surgery (BCS) with radiotherapy, and BCS alone.
cards.result: Local recurrence: BCS alone 21.2%, versus mastectomy 5.9% (P < 0.001) and BCS with radiotherapy 8 (P = 0.001) — the radiotherapy figure is printed truncated in the record, read as about 8%. Recurrence was higher with underlying invasive carcinoma (6.7%) than noninvasive carcinoma (4.5%; P = 0.032). Metastasis was far commoner with a palpable tumour (30.2%) than without (3.4%; P < 0.001). Sentinel node biopsy was positive in 17% (95% CI 11.5 to 22.6). The reviewers conclude BCS alone is not recommended when there is underlying invasive cancer or DCIS.
cards.watchOut: All underlying studies are observational and span eras of imaging and radiotherapy — women chosen for conservation alone likely had the most limited disease, yet still recurred most, which strengthens the direction but not the precision of the comparison.
cards.source: Lin CW, Chiang MH, Tam KW. Treatment of Mammary Paget Disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis of real-world data. Int J Surg. 2022. PMID: 36309195. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kollmorgen 1998: 82% had an underlying breast cancer — 93% with a mass, 74% without — and survival tracked the mass, not the nipple change
cards.summary: Kollmorgen 1998: 82% had an underlying breast cancer — 93% with a mass, 74% without — and survival tracked the mass, not the nipple change
cards.people: 80 patients treated for Paget's disease of the breast at one cancer institute, 1963 to 1996; 68 had clinical nipple changes (30 with an associated breast mass, 38 without); median follow-up 61 months.
cards.result: Of the 68 with clinical Paget's, 58 (85%) were treated with mastectomy and the rest with some form of breast-conserving therapy. Breast cancer was found in 56/68 (82%): 28/30 (93%) with a mass and 28/38 (74%) without. The cancer was centrally located in 61%. Invasive cancer was present in 75% of the mass group versus 36% of the no-mass group, and median survival was 42 months with a mass versus 126 months without (p = 0.007). The authors note 26% of the no-mass group may have no underlying cancer and could be overtreated by mastectomy, while 29% of that group had a peripherally located tumour a central excision could miss.
cards.watchOut: A mastectomy-era series (1963–1996) with no comparative outcome analysis by operation — its value is the underlying-cancer arithmetic that any modern conservation plan must respect, not a verdict on today's breast-conserving surgery with radiotherapy.
cards.source: Kollmorgen DR, Varanasi JS, Edge SB, Carson WE 3rd. Paget's disease of the breast: a 33-year experience. J Am Coll Surg. 1998. PMID: 9704964. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pelorca 2023: oncoplastic conservation was feasible — no difference in local recurrence or survival versus the mastectomy-heavy remainder
cards.summary: Pelorca 2023: oncoplastic conservation was feasible — no difference in local recurrence or survival versus the mastectomy-heavy remainder
cards.people: 85 patients with Paget's disease of the breast treated at a Brazilian oncological hospital, 2000 to 2021; oncoplastic breast surgery in 59 (69.4%), breast-conserving surgery in 23 (27.0%), mastectomy with reconstruction the single commonest procedure (38; 44.7%).
cards.result: Oncoplastic surgery did not influence local recurrence (p = 1.000), overall survival (p = 0.185) or cancer-specific survival (p = 0.418). Age was associated with use of oncoplastic surgery (patients aged 40–49, p = 0.002; odds ratio 3.22 — a relative measure; absolute rates by age group are not printed in the record).
cards.watchOut: Small, single-centre and retrospective, with treatment chosen by clinicians — 'no difference found' in 85 patients cannot exclude a clinically important difference, and absolute recurrence and survival rates are not printed in the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the nipple lesion is usually the surface of a breast cancer — conservation needs radiotherapy; conservation alone recurs most
cards.summary: Synthesis: the nipple lesion is usually the surface of a breast cancer — conservation needs radiotherapy; conservation alone recurs most
cards.people: Three observational sources: a 38-study meta-analysis (Lin 2022, 24,062 patients), a 33-year single-centre series (Kollmorgen 1998, 80 patients) and a modern oncoplastic cohort (Pelorca 2023, 85 patients). No randomised trials exist.
cards.result: Underlying breast cancer in 82% of clinical Paget's (Kollmorgen 1998). Local recurrence: conservation alone 21.2%, mastectomy 5.9%, conservation plus radiotherapy about 8% (Lin 2022). Oncoplastic conservation showed no detectable recurrence or survival penalty in a small modern cohort (Pelorca 2023). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only.
cards.watchOut: There are no randomised trials in Paget's disease of the nipple and there never likely will be; every number here is observational. This shelf is about Paget's disease of the nipple/breast only — Paget's disease of bone is homed separately on Shelf #1822.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lin 2022 (PMID: 36309195), Kollmorgen 1998 (PMID: 9704964) and Pelorca 2023 (PMID: 37265790).

shelves.title: Vaginal cancer: no randomised trial exists — in 2,517 registry patients, adding brachytherapy to radiotherapy was associated with median survival of 6.1 versus 3.6 years, and a brachytherapy boost with chemoradiation gave 5-year survival of 62.9% versus 49.3%
shelves.question: In women with primary vaginal cancer, how should the cancer be treated, and does including brachytherapy in definitive (chemo)radiation improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Brachytherapy/methods · Brachytherapy/statistics & numerical data · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/mortality · Carcinoma, Squamous Cell/radiotherapy · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Registries · SEER Program · Survival Analysis · United States/epidemiology · Vaginal Neoplasms/mortality · Vaginal Neoplasms/radiotherapy
shelves.balance: There are no randomised trials in primary vaginal cancer; the record itself states that prospective randomised data do not exist. Treatment is definitive radiotherapy, and every large dataset says the brachytherapy component matters. In the SEER analysis of Orton 2016 (PMID: 27036631; 2,517 patients), median overall survival was 6.1 years with brachytherapy (alone or with external beam) versus 3.6 years with external beam alone, and brachytherapy was associated with a lower risk of death in the propensity-matched cohort (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86), across all FIGO stages and in tumours over 5 cm (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50-0.91). In the National Cancer Database analysis of Reshko 2021 (1,094 patients treated with definitive chemoradiation), adding a brachytherapy boost was associated with better 5-year overall survival (62.9% vs 49.3%, P=0.0126), and completing radiotherapy within 63 days was also associated with better survival (67.8% vs 54.5%, P=0.0031). A single-centre series (Merten 2024; 27 patients, FIGO I-III) reported 5-year overall survival of 90% and disease-free survival of 68% with brachytherapy with or without external beam and chemotherapy, with grade 3 late toxicity in 3 of 22 patients (13.6%) and one grade 4 event (4.5%). All of this is observational, so fitter patients may simply be the ones who receive brachytherapy. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for including brachytherapy in definitive radiotherapy — the observational cap applies.

cards.headline: Orton 2016: median survival 6.1 years with brachytherapy versus 3.6 years with external beam alone; matched hazard ratio for death 0.77
cards.summary: Orton 2016: median survival 6.1 years with brachytherapy versus 3.6 years with external beam alone; matched hazard ratio for death 0.77
cards.type: Retrospective registry cohort with propensity matching (Orton 2016)
cards.people: 2,517 women with primary vaginal cancer treated with radiotherapy in the US SEER registry (75% squamous cell carcinoma), comparing external beam radiotherapy alone with brachytherapy alone or combined with external beam, balanced by nearest-neighbour propensity matching.
cards.result: Median overall survival was 6.1 years (95% CI 5.2-7.2) for patients receiving brachytherapy versus 3.6 years (95% CI 3.0-4.2) for external beam alone (P<0.001). In the matched cohort, brachytherapy was associated with a relative reduction in the hazard of death (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86), with benefit in all stage groups, in squamous cell carcinoma (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.70-0.92) and adenocarcinoma (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49-0.95), and the greatest benefit in tumours larger than 5 cm (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50-0.91). No demographic or tumour variable favoured external beam alone.
cards.watchOut: Registry data with no randomisation: women selected for brachytherapy may have had smaller, more accessible tumours and better performance status in ways matching cannot fully remove, so the survival gap is an association, not proof of causation.
cards.source: Orton A, Boothe D, Williams N, Buchmiller T, Huang YJ, Suneja G, Poppe M, Gaffney D. Brachytherapy improves survival in primary vaginal cancer. Gynecologic Oncology. 2016. PMID: 27036631. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Reshko 2021: a brachytherapy boost with definitive chemoradiation was associated with 5-year survival of 62.9% versus 49.3% without it
cards.summary: Reshko 2021: a brachytherapy boost with definitive chemoradiation was associated with 5-year survival of 62.9% versus 49.3% without it
cards.people: 1,094 patients with non-metastatic vaginal cancer diagnosed 2004-2015 in the US National Cancer Database, treated with definitive chemotherapy plus external beam radiotherapy, with or without a brachytherapy boost, and no surgery.
cards.result: On propensity score-weighted analysis, use of a brachytherapy boost was associated with improved 5-year overall survival (62.9% vs 49.3%, P=0.0126). Among patients who received brachytherapy, completing radiotherapy in 63 days or less was associated with improved 5-year overall survival (67.8% vs 54.5%, P=0.0031).
cards.watchOut: Also observational and subject to the same selection problem as Orton 2016; the two database studies are consistent with each other but neither can exclude confounding by tumour anatomy or patient fitness.
cards.source: Reshko LB, Gaskins JT, Metzinger DS, et al. The impact of brachytherapy boost and radiotherapy treatment duration on survival in patients with vaginal cancer treated with definitive chemoradiation. Brachytherapy. 2021. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1016/j.brachy.2020.08.020. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Merten 2024: in 27 patients treated with brachytherapy-based therapy, 5-year survival was 90% and local recurrence 18.5%, with grade 3 late toxicity in 13.6%
cards.summary: Merten 2024: in 27 patients treated with brachytherapy-based therapy, 5-year survival was 90% and local recurrence 18.5%, with grade 3 late toxicity in 13.6%
cards.people: 27 patients with FIGO stage I-III vaginal cancer treated at a single centre between 2000 and 2023 with brachytherapy alone or as a boost, with or without external beam radiotherapy and simultaneous chemotherapy; median follow-up 39 months.
cards.result: Five of 27 patients developed local recurrence; the 5-year cumulative local recurrence rate was 18.5%. Five-year overall survival was 90% and disease-free survival 68% (stage I-II 72%, stage III 65%; P=0.933). Grade 3 late side effects were documented in 3 of 22 patients (13.6%) and one patient (4.5%) had grade 4 toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Only 27 highly selected patients over 23 years at an expert centre; the 90% survival figure reflects that selection and cannot be compared directly with the registry cohorts.
cards.source: Merten R, Strnad V, Karius A, et al. Brachytherapy in vaginal cancer for organ preservation: clinical outcome and safety from a single center experience. Gynecologic Oncology. 2024. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1016/j.ygyno.2024.07.683. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial exists; definitive radiotherapy should include brachytherapy where feasible, and treatment should not drag beyond about 9 weeks
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial exists; definitive radiotherapy should include brachytherapy where feasible, and treatment should not drag beyond about 9 weeks
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: two large US database cohorts (2,517 and 1,094 patients) and one single-centre series (27 patients).
cards.result: Brachytherapy was associated with longer survival in both database studies (matched HR 0.77 for death; 5-year survival 62.9% vs 49.3% with a boost), and an expert-centre series shows high local control with brachytherapy-based treatment at the price of grade 3-4 late toxicity in about 18% of assessed patients. Because all evidence is observational, the stamp is capped: POSSIBLE (benefit) for brachytherapy as part of definitive (chemo)radiation.
cards.watchOut: No randomised or prospective comparative evidence exists for any treatment of primary vaginal cancer; every number on this shelf is an association from retrospective data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Orton 2016 (PMID: 27036631), Reshko 2021 (DOI: 10.1016/j.brachy.2020.08.020) and Merten 2024 (DOI: 10.1016/j.ygyno.2024.07.683), carded above.

shelves.title: Vaginismus: brief intensive therapist-aided exposure worked in 89% of women versus 11% waiting (one RCT) — standard CBT managed only 14%, and botulinum toxin's 75% in refractory cases comes from a series with no control group
shelves.question: In women with vaginismus, which treatments — psychological therapy, therapist-aided exposure, or botulinum toxin injection — actually enable penetration and intercourse?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Bibliotherapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Couples Therapy · Desensitization, Psychologic · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Muscle Relaxation · Netherlands · Sex Education · Vaginismus/psychology · Vaginismus/therapy
shelves.balance: The strongest evidence in vaginismus is for brief, intensive therapist-aided exposure. In ter Kuile 2013 (PMID: 24060195; 70 women with lifelong vaginismus randomised to exposure or a 3-month waiting list), 31 of 35 treated women (89%, 95% CI 72-96%) achieved intercourse versus 4 of 35 controls (11%, 95% CI 4-28%), most within the first 2 weeks, after at most three 2-hour sessions in one week. The earlier, gentler CBT programme was far weaker: van Lankveld 2006 (PMID: 16551154; 117 women randomised to group CBT, bibliotherapy or waiting list) found successful intercourse in 14% of treated women versus 0% of controls after treatment, rising only to 21% (group therapy) and 15% (bibliotherapy) at 12 months. For refractory cases, botulinum toxin rests on a single uncontrolled series: Ghazizadeh & Nikzad 2004 (24 women with grade 3-4 vaginismus who had failed previous treatment) reported 23 of 24 (95.8%) with little or no vaginismus at examination one week after injection and 18 (75%) achieving satisfactory intercourse after the first injection, with no recurrence over a mean 12.3 months — but with no control group, none of that can be separated from expectation and natural course. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — intensive therapist-aided exposure has a large randomised effect (LIKELY benefit within this shelf's scale is not used; the shelf proposes POSSIBLE-to-strong for exposure), standard CBT a small one, and botulinum toxin is unproven beyond an uncontrolled series (MAYBE). The formal proposed stamp below is SPLIT.

cards.headline: ter Kuile 2013: therapist-aided exposure — 31 of 35 women (89%) achieved intercourse versus 4 of 35 (11%) on the waiting list
cards.summary: ter Kuile 2013: therapist-aided exposure — 31 of 35 women (89%) achieved intercourse versus 4 of 35 (11%) on the waiting list
cards.people: 70 women with lifelong vaginismus (never able to have intercourse) and their partners, randomised to therapist-aided exposure (n=35) or a 3-month waiting-list control (n=35); intercourse ability assessed daily over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Successful intercourse at post-treatment was reported by 31 of 35 participants (89%; 95% CI 72% to 96%) in the exposure group compared with 4 of 35 (11%; 95% CI 4% to 28%) in the control condition — an absolute difference of about 78 percentage points. In 90% of successfully treated women intercourse was possible within the first 2 weeks. Treatment also improved vaginismus complaints, coital fear, coital pain and sexual distress, but showed no effect on other aspects of sexual functioning in women or partners. The treatment was a maximum of three 2-hour sessions in one week, with two follow-up sessions over 5 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Waiting-list control, so the comparison is against no treatment rather than an active therapy, and neither participants nor therapists could be blinded; a single Dutch specialist-centre trial of 70 women, with outcomes self-reported.
cards.source: Ter Kuile MM, Melles R, de Groot HE, Tuijnman-Raasveld CC, van Lankveld JJDM. Therapist-aided exposure for women with lifelong vaginismus: a randomized waiting-list control trial of efficacy. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2013. PMID: 24060195. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van Lankveld 2006: standard CBT — only 14% achieved intercourse after treatment versus 0% of controls, and just 21% by 12 months
cards.summary: van Lankveld 2006: standard CBT — only 14% achieved intercourse after treatment versus 0% of controls, and just 21% by 12 months
cards.type: Randomised waiting-list controlled trial, three arms (van Lankveld 2006)
cards.people: 117 women with lifelong vaginismus randomised to cognitive-behavioural group therapy, cognitive-behavioural bibliotherapy (self-help book with brief telephone support), or a waiting list; manualised treatment covered sexual education, relaxation, gradual exposure, cognitive therapy and sensate focus.
cards.result: Intent-to-treat analysis: successful intercourse at post-treatment was reported by 14% of treated participants compared with none of the control participants. At 12-month follow-up, 21% of group-therapy participants and 15% of bibliotherapy participants reported successful intercourse. Twenty-one percent of participants left the study before post-treatment assessment. The authors concluded CBT was efficacious but the small effect size warrants efforts to improve treatment.
cards.watchOut: The same waiting-list design caveat applies, and one in five women dropped out before assessment; the contrast with the 2013 exposure trial suggests intensity and in-session guided practice, not CBT content alone, drive success.
cards.source: van Lankveld JJDM, ter Kuile MM, de Groot HE, Melles R, Nefs J, Zandbergen M. Cognitive-behavioral therapy for women with lifelong vaginismus: a randomized waiting-list controlled trial of efficacy. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 2006. PMID: 16551154. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ghazizadeh 2004: botulinum toxin in refractory vaginismus — 18 of 24 women (75%) achieved satisfactory intercourse after one injection, in an uncontrolled series
cards.summary: Ghazizadeh 2004: botulinum toxin in refractory vaginismus — 18 of 24 women (75%) achieved satisfactory intercourse after one injection, in an uncontrolled series
cards.type: Prospective uncontrolled case series, Level III evidence as labelled in the record (Ghazizadeh 2004)
cards.people: 24 women (mean age 25 years, range 19-34) with third- to fourth-degree (severe) vaginismus referred 2002-2004 after previous unsuccessful treatment; botulinum toxin (abobotulinumtoxinA, Dysport — Ipsen; 150-400 units as printed in the record) injected into the puborectalis muscles at 3 sites on each side; mean follow-up 12.3 months (range 2-24).
cards.result: Twenty-three patients (95.8%) had vaginal examinations 1 week after injection showing little or no vaginismus; 18 (75%) achieved satisfactory intercourse after the first injection, 4 (16.7%) had mild pain, and 1 was cured after a second injection; 1 patient refused examination and did not attempt coitus, and another had no coitus because of her husband's secondary impotence. There were no cases of recurrence during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: No control group of any kind: with a condition strongly driven by fear and expectation, an uncontrolled 75% success rate cannot be attributed to the toxin. The specific tested product is named because it is not an approved or standardised treatment for this use; doses and products in current practice may differ.
cards.source: Ghazizadeh S, Nikzad M. Botulinum toxin in the treatment of refractory vaginismus. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2004. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1097/01.AOG.0000141441.41178.6b. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: brief intensive exposure is the treatment with a large proven effect; gentle CBT helps few; botulinum toxin is a refractory-case option with no controlled evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: brief intensive exposure is the treatment with a large proven effect; gentle CBT helps few; botulinum toxin is a refractory-case option with no controlled evidence
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: two randomised waiting-list trials (117 and 70 women) and one uncontrolled series of 24 women.
cards.result: Therapist-aided exposure achieved intercourse in 89% versus 11% waiting list; standard group or book-based CBT achieved 14% versus 0% after treatment (21% at a year); botulinum toxin reported 75% success in women who had failed other treatment, without any comparator. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (intensive exposure: strong randomised benefit · standard CBT: small benefit · botulinum toxin: MAYBE, uncontrolled only).
cards.watchOut: All controlled evidence uses waiting-list comparators in Dutch specialist centres and studies lifelong (primary) vaginismus; results may not transfer to acquired vaginismus or to services unable to deliver in-session guided exposure.
cards.source: Synthesis of ter Kuile 2013 (PMID: 24060195), van Lankveld 2006 (PMID: 16551154) and Ghazizadeh & Nikzad 2004 (DOI: 10.1097/01.AOG.0000141441.41178.6b), carded above.

shelves.title: Vulval cancer: a negative sentinel node makes full groin clearance unnecessary (groin recurrence 2.3%, 3-year survival 97%); radiotherapy replaces clearance safely only for deposits up to 2 mm — larger deposits recurred in 22% versus 6.9%
shelves.question: In early-stage vulval (vulvar) cancer, can full groin lymph-node clearance be safely omitted after sentinel-node biopsy, and how should a positive sentinel node be treated?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Early-stage vulval (vulvar) cancer treatment was transformed by the GROINSS-V programme, all prospective but none of it randomised. GROINSS-V I (van der Zee 2008, PMID: 18281661; 403 patients with tumours <4 cm) showed that when the sentinel node was negative, omitting full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy left a groin recurrence rate of just 2.3% (6 recurrences among 259 patients with unifocal disease and a negative sentinel node; 3-year survival 97%). Long-term follow-up (te Grootenhuis 2016; 377 patients, median follow-up 105 months) confirmed an isolated groin recurrence rate of 2.5% in sentinel-node-negative patients versus 8.0% in node-positive patients, with 5- and 10-year disease-specific survival of 93.5% and 90.8% versus 75.5% and 64.5%. For a positive sentinel node, size decides: in GROINSS-V II (Oonk 2021, PMID: 34432481; 1,535 registered patients), radiotherapy (50 Gy) instead of lymphadenectomy gave a 2-year isolated groin recurrence rate of 1.6% in 126 treated patients with micrometastases (2 mm or less) — but 22% versus 6.9% with lymphadenectomy (P=0.011) in macrometastases, which forced a protocol amendment mid-trial; radiotherapy caused less treatment-related morbidity than lymphadenectomy. Chemoradiation for macrometastases is being tested in GROINSS-V III (NCT05076942) and has no results yet. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT — omitting lymphadenectomy after a negative sentinel node, and radiotherapy for micrometastases, are supported by large prospective cohorts (POSSIBLE, the observational cap); radiotherapy alone for macrometastases made things worse (more recurrences).

cards.headline: van der Zee 2008 (GROINSS-V I): with a negative sentinel node, skipping full groin clearance left groin recurrence at 2.3% and 3-year survival at 97%
cards.summary: van der Zee 2008 (GROINSS-V I): with a negative sentinel node, skipping full groin clearance left groin recurrence at 2.3% and 3-year survival at 97%
cards.type: Multicentre prospective observational study (van der Zee 2008)
cards.people: 403 assessable patients with T1/2 squamous cell cancer of the vulva smaller than 4 cm, in whom a sentinel node procedure (radioactive tracer plus blue dye) was performed in 623 groins across multiple centres, 2000-2006.
cards.result: In 259 patients with unifocal vulvar disease and a negative sentinel node (median follow-up 35 months), six groin recurrences were diagnosed (2.3%; 95% CI 0.6% to 5%), and the 3-year survival rate was 97% (95% CI 91% to 99%). Omitting inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy in sentinel-node-negative patients was the strategy this study validated.
cards.watchOut: Observational, with no randomised comparison against routine lymphadenectomy; the safety claim applies only to unifocal tumours under 4 cm with clinically unsuspicious groins, the population studied.
cards.source: Van der Zee AGJ, Oonk MHM, De Hullu JA, et al. Sentinel node dissection is safe in the treatment of early-stage vulvar cancer. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2008. PMID: 18281661. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.
