cards.headline: te Grootenhuis 2016 (GROINSS-V I long-term): at a median 105 months, isolated groin recurrence was 2.5% if the sentinel node was negative versus 8.0% if positive
cards.summary: te Grootenhuis 2016 (GROINSS-V I long-term): at a median 105 months, isolated groin recurrence was 2.5% if the sentinel node was negative versus 8.0% if positive
cards.people: 377 patients with unifocal squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva from the GROINSS-V I cohort, followed for a median of 105 months (range 0-179).
cards.result: Isolated groin recurrence was 2.5% in sentinel-node-negative patients and 8.0% in sentinel-node-positive patients at 5 and 10 years; all groin and distant recurrences appeared within 25 months of primary treatment. Local recurrence at 5 years was 24.6% in node-negative and 33.2% in node-positive patients (36.4% and 46.4% at 10 years; P=0.03). Disease-specific survival at 5 and 10 years was 93.5% and 90.8% in node-negative patients versus 75.5% and 64.5% in node-positive patients (P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: A follow-up of the same cohort as the van der Zee 2008 card, not independent evidence; local (vulval) recurrence was common in both groups, so a negative sentinel node protects the groin, not the vulva.
cards.source: te Grootenhuis NC, van der Zee AGJ, van Doorn HC, et al. Sentinel nodes in vulvar cancer: long-term follow-up of the GROningen INternational Study on Sentinel nodes in Vulvar cancer (GROINSS-V) I. Gynecologic Oncology. 2016. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1016/j.ygyno.2015.09.077. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Oonk 2021 (GROINSS-V II): radiotherapy instead of node clearance was safe for micrometastases (2-year groin recurrence 1.6%) but failed for macrometastases (22% vs 6.9%)
cards.summary: Oonk 2021 (GROINSS-V II): radiotherapy instead of node clearance was safe for micrometastases (2-year groin recurrence 1.6%) but failed for macrometastases (22% vs 6.9%)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre phase II single-arm treatment trial (Oonk 2021)
cards.people: 1,535 eligible patients with early-stage vulvar cancer (diameter <4 cm, no nodal involvement on imaging) registered 2005-2016, treated with local excision and sentinel node biopsy; those with a positive sentinel node were to receive inguinofemoral radiotherapy (50 Gy) instead of inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy, until a protocol amendment returned macrometastases (>2 mm) to standard lymphadenectomy.
cards.result: Among 160 patients with sentinel-node micrometastases (2 mm or less), 126 received inguinofemoral radiotherapy, with an ipsilateral isolated groin recurrence rate at 2 years of 1.6%. Among 162 patients with macrometastases, the isolated groin recurrence rate at 2 years was 22% in those who underwent radiotherapy versus 6.9% in those who underwent lymphadenectomy (P=0.011). Treatment-related morbidity after radiotherapy was less frequent than after lymphadenectomy.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and amended mid-course: the macrometastasis comparison (22% vs 6.9%) is between non-randomised groups treated in different protocol eras, though the size of the gap and the trial's own safety response make the direction hard to dismiss.
cards.source: Oonk MHM, Slomovitz B, Baldwin PJW, et al. Radiotherapy versus inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy as treatment for vulvar cancer patients with micrometastases in the sentinel node: results of GROINSS-V II. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2021. PMID: 34432481. Registry ID: NTR608/NL552 (as reported for GROINSS-V II in secondary sources this session; not in the fetched abstract). MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: sentinel-node surgery lets most women avoid full groin clearance; a positive node up to 2 mm can be treated with radiotherapy, but larger deposits still need clearance
cards.summary: Synthesis: sentinel-node surgery lets most women avoid full groin clearance; a positive node up to 2 mm can be treated with radiotherapy, but larger deposits still need clearance
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: GROINSS-V I (403 patients), its long-term follow-up (377 patients) and GROINSS-V II (1,535 registered patients).
cards.result: Negative sentinel node: groin recurrence 2.3-2.5% without lymphadenectomy, with 3-year survival 97%. Micrometastasis (2 mm or less): radiotherapy gave 1.6% groin recurrence at 2 years with less morbidity than surgery. Macrometastasis: radiotherapy alone gave 22% versus 6.9% recurrence, so lymphadenectomy remains standard while chemoradiation is tested in GROINSS-V III (NCT05076942, no results). Proposed stamp: SPLIT (de-escalation after negative node or micrometastasis: POSSIBLE (benefit) · radiotherapy alone for macrometastasis: worse than surgery).
cards.watchOut: The entire evidence base is prospective but non-randomised, from one research programme; advanced vulval cancer and chemoradiation questions are outside these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Zee 2008 (PMID: 18281661), te Grootenhuis 2016 (DOI: 10.1016/j.ygyno.2015.09.077) and Oonk 2021 (PMID: 34432481), carded above.

shelves.title: Transdermal versus oral oestrogen and venous thromboembolism (observational only): oral oestrogen carried higher VTE risk in every carded record (OR 2.5, OR 4.2, RR 1.49, HR 1.7) while transdermal oestrogen showed no detectable increase (1.2, 0.9, 1.01, 1.1)
shelves.question: Does transdermal oestrogen carry a lower risk of venous thromboembolism than oral oestrogen in postmenopausal women?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Administration, Oral · Estrogen Replacement Therapy · Female · Humans · Postmenopause · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk · Risk Factors · Venous Thromboembolism
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only. Across four carded records the direction is uniform: oral oestrogen is associated with increased venous thromboembolism (odds ratio 2.5 in the Canonico 2008 systematic review's observational meta-analysis, PMID: 18495631; odds ratio 4.2 in the ESTHER case-control study, PMID: 17309934; rate ratio 1.49 in 955,582 UK women, PMID: 20230416; hazard ratio 1.7 in the E3N cohort, PMID: 19834106), while transdermal oestrogen shows no detectable increase in any of them (odds ratios/rate ratios/hazard ratios 1.2, 0.9, 1.01 and 1.1, all with confidence intervals crossing 1). The progestogen partner modifies risk independently of route — norpregnanes carried increased risk in both ESTHER and E3N, micronised progesterone did not. No trial has randomised women by route, so this is an association, printed as observational on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: transdermal oestrogen is associated with lower venous thromboembolism risk than oral oestrogen.

cards.headline: Canonico 2008: in a systematic review of 8 observational studies and 9 randomised trials, oral oestrogen raised venous thromboembolism odds about 2.5-fold while transdermal oestrogen did not (odds ratio 1.2, confidence interval crossing 1)
cards.summary: Canonico 2008: in a systematic review of 8 observational studies and 9 randomised trials, oral oestrogen raised venous thromboembolism odds about 2.5-fold while transdermal oestrogen did not (odds ratio 1.2, confidence interval crossing 1)
cards.people: Eight observational studies and nine randomised controlled trials of hormone replacement therapy reporting venous thromboembolism, identified from Medline; total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In the observational meta-analysis, compared with non-users, the odds ratio for a first venous thromboembolism was 2.5 (95% CI 1.9 to 3.4) in current users of oral oestrogen and 1.2 (95% CI 0.9 to 1.7) in current users of transdermal oestrogen. Past users of oral oestrogen had a risk similar to never users. The oral risk was higher in the first year of treatment (odds ratio 4.0, 95% CI 2.9 to 5.7) than after more than one year (2.1, 95% CI 1.3 to 3.8). Unopposed oral oestrogen (2.2, 95% CI 1.6 to 3.0) and opposed oral oestrogen (2.6, 95% CI 2.0 to 3.2) carried similar risk. The nine randomised trials confirmed increased venous thromboembolism with oral oestrogen (2.1, 95% CI 1.4 to 3.1). Transdermal oestrogen did not seem to confer additional risk even in women with thrombogenic mutations or obesity.
cards.watchOut: The route comparison itself is observational: the randomised trials randomised hormone therapy versus control, not oral versus transdermal route, so women who receive patches may differ from women who receive tablets in ways adjustment cannot fully remove.
cards.source: Canonico M et al. Hormone replacement therapy and risk of venous thromboembolism in postmenopausal women: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2008. PMID: 18495631. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ESTHER 2007: in a French case-control study, current oral oestrogen carried an odds ratio of 4.2 for venous thromboembolism while transdermal oestrogen carried 0.9 — and the progestogen type mattered as much as the route
cards.summary: ESTHER 2007: in a French case-control study, current oral oestrogen carried an odds ratio of 4.2 for venous thromboembolism while transdermal oestrogen carried 0.9 — and the progestogen type mattered as much as the route
cards.people: 271 consecutive postmenopausal women aged 45 to 70 years with a first documented idiopathic venous thromboembolism (208 hospital cases, 63 outpatient cases) and 610 matched controls (426 hospital, 184 community), recruited in France between 1999 and 2005.
cards.result: After adjustment for potential confounders, odds ratios for venous thromboembolism in current users versus non-users were 4.2 (95% CI 1.5 to 11.6) for oral oestrogen and 0.9 (95% CI 0.4 to 2.1) for transdermal oestrogen. Micronised progesterone (odds ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.9) and pregnane derivatives (0.9, 95% CI 0.4 to 2.3) showed no significant association, whereas norpregnane derivatives were associated with a 4-fold increased risk (3.9, 95% CI 1.5 to 10.0).
cards.watchOut: A case-control study with wide confidence intervals — the oral estimate of 4.2 spans 1.5 to 11.6 — and hospital-based controls; it can show association by route, not prove that switching a given woman to a patch removes her risk.
cards.source: Canonico M et al. Hormone therapy and venous thromboembolism among postmenopausal women: impact of the route of estrogen administration and progestogens: the ESTHER study. Circulation. 2007. PMID: 17309934. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Renoux 2010: in a UK primary-care cohort of 955,582 women, transdermal oestrogen carried no increased venous thromboembolism risk (rate ratio 1.01) while oral oestrogen did (1.49)
cards.summary: Renoux 2010: in a UK primary-care cohort of 955,582 women, transdermal oestrogen carried no increased venous thromboembolism risk (rate ratio 1.01) while oral oestrogen did (1.49)
cards.people: All women aged 50 to 79 years in the UK General Practice Research Database between 1 January 1987 and 1 March 2008: a cohort of 955,582 postmenopausal women, with 23,505 incident venous thromboembolism cases matched to 231,562 controls in a nested case-control analysis.
cards.result: Relative to non-use, the rate ratio for venous thromboembolism was 1.01 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.16) for current transdermal oestrogen alone, 0.96 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.20) for transdermal oestrogen combined with a progestogen, and 0.92 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.10) for tibolone. In contrast, risk was increased with oral oestrogen (rate ratio 1.49, 95% CI 1.37 to 1.63) and oral oestrogen-progestogen (1.54, 95% CI 1.44 to 1.65), and rose with oestrogen dose. Oral risks were particularly elevated during the first year of use and disappeared 4 months after discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: Prescription-database exposure: a dispensed patch or tablet is not proof of use, and prescribers may already channel higher-risk women toward patches, which would bias the transdermal estimate toward looking safer.
cards.source: Renoux C et al. Hormone replacement therapy and the risk of venous thromboembolism: a population-based study. Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2010. PMID: 20230416. cards.headline: E3N 2010: in a French prospective cohort of 80,308 postmenopausal women followed about 10 years, oral oestrogen raised idiopathic venous thromboembolism risk (hazard ratio 1.7) while transdermal oestrogen did not (1.1)
cards.summary: E3N 2010: in a French prospective cohort of 80,308 postmenopausal women followed about 10 years, oral oestrogen raised idiopathic venous thromboembolism risk (hazard ratio 1.7) while transdermal oestrogen did not (1.1)
cards.people: 80,308 postmenopausal women in the French E3N prospective cohort (women born 1925 to 1950, followed by biennial questionnaires from 1990; average follow-up 10.1 years), among whom 549 documented idiopathic first venous thromboembolisms occurred.
cards.result: Compared with never-users, past users of hormone therapy had no increased thrombotic risk (hazard ratio 1.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.5). Oral oestrogen was associated with increased risk (hazard ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.1 to 2.8) and transdermal oestrogen was not (1.1, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.8; homogeneity P=0.01). Risk also differed by progestogen type: no significant association with progesterone (0.9, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.5), pregnanes (1.3, 95% CI 0.9 to 2.0) or nortestosterones (1.4, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.4), but norpregnanes were associated with increased risk (1.8, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.7).
cards.watchOut: Self-reported hormone use by questionnaire in a cohort of French women, many of them teachers — exposure misclassification and a healthier-than-average cohort both limit how far the exact hazard ratios travel.
cards.source: Canonico M et al. Postmenopausal hormone therapy and risk of idiopathic venous thromboembolism: results from the E3N cohort study. Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology. 2010. PMID: 19834106. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: every carded design points the same way — oral oestrogen is associated with roughly 1.5- to 2.5-fold higher venous thromboembolism risk, transdermal oestrogen with no detectable increase — but all of the route evidence is observational
cards.summary: Synthesis: every carded design points the same way — oral oestrogen is associated with roughly 1.5- to 2.5-fold higher venous thromboembolism risk, transdermal oestrogen with no detectable increase — but all of the route evidence is observational
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review (8 observational studies, 9 randomised trials of oral therapy), one case-control study (271 cases, 610 controls), one population nested case-control study (955,582 women; 23,505 cases) and one prospective cohort (80,308 women, 549 events). No randomised trial has randomised women by route of administration.
cards.result: Oral oestrogen was associated with increased venous thromboembolism in every record: odds ratio 2.5 in the review's observational meta-analysis (Canonico 2008), odds ratio 4.2 in ESTHER, rate ratio 1.49 in the UK database study (Renoux 2010) and hazard ratio 1.7 in E3N. Transdermal oestrogen showed no significant increase in any record: odds ratio 1.2 (Canonico 2008), 0.9 (ESTHER), rate ratio 1.01 (Renoux 2010) and hazard ratio 1.1 (E3N). Two records agree the progestogen partner matters: norpregnane/norpregnane-type progestogens carried increased risk in both ESTHER (odds ratio 3.9) and E3N (hazard ratio 1.8), while micronised progesterone did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Consistency across observational designs is not the same as a randomised route comparison: channelling of higher-risk women to patches, and of lower-risk women to tablets, could manufacture part of the apparent route difference in every carded study at once.
cards.source: Synthesis of Canonico M et al. BMJ. 2008 (PMID: 18495631); Canonico M et al. Circulation. 2007 (PMID: 17309934); Renoux C et al. Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis. 2010 (PMID: 20230416); Canonico M et al. Arteriosclerosis, Thrombosis, and Vascular Biology. 2010 (PMID: 19834106).

shelves.title: Opportunistic salpingectomy and ovarian cancer (observational only): associated with fewer later ovarian cancers — HR 0.65 in a Swedish nationwide cohort, no serous cancers versus 5.27 expected in British Columbia, and an approximately 80% risk reduction summarised by a 2023 systematic review
shelves.question: Does opportunistic salpingectomy at the time of other pelvic surgery reduce later ovarian cancer?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Prospective Studies · Ovarian Neoplasms · Salpingectomy · Hysterectomy · Primary Prevention
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only. A 2023 systematic review of 158 publications summarises salpingectomy as associated with an approximately 80% reduction in ovarian cancer risk, without earlier menopause (PMID: 37672283). The two population cohorts agree in direction with smaller, more precise estimates: hazard ratio 0.65 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.81) after salpingectomy in Sweden, with bilateral removal at 0.35 versus 0.71 for unilateral (PMID: 25628372); and no serous ovarian cancers among 25,889 British Columbia opportunistic-salpingectomy patients against 5.27 expected (PMID: 35138400). Follow-up in the most specific cohort is short (median 3.2 years) and no randomised evidence exists, so the association is printed as observational on the face. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: opportunistic salpingectomy is associated with fewer later ovarian cancers.

cards.headline: Kahn 2023: a systematic review of 158 publications found salpingectomy associated with an approximately 80% reduction in ovarian cancer risk, with no earlier menopause onset
cards.summary: Kahn 2023: a systematic review of 158 publications found salpingectomy associated with an approximately 80% reduction in ovarian cancer risk, with no earlier menopause onset
cards.people: 158 publications included in a systematic review of bilateral salpingectomy for ovarian cancer prevention (literature searched 4 March 2022 across PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL and 20 grey-literature sources); total participant N not documented in the record, and the review is a narrative state-of-the-science synthesis rather than a pooled meta-analysis.
cards.result: Salpingectomy has been associated with ovarian cancer risk reduction of approximately 80%. Studies demonstrated that salpingectomy was safe, cost-effective, and was not associated with an earlier age of menopause onset. With widespread implementation, salpingectomy has the potential to reduce ovarian cancer mortality in the US by an estimated 15%. The review's premise is that most ovarian cancers originate in the fimbriated end of the fallopian tube, so removing the tubes at the time of other gynaecologic or non-gynaecologic surgery (opportunistic salpingectomy) may prevent epithelial ovarian cancer in women at average risk.
cards.watchOut: The headline 'approximately 80%' is the review's summary of heterogeneous observational studies, not a pooled estimate with a confidence interval from the record — the underlying studies differ in who was operated on and what the comparison group was.
cards.source: Kahn RM et al. Salpingectomy for the Primary Prevention of Ovarian Cancer: A Systematic Review. JAMA Surgery. 2023. PMID: 37672283. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Female · Humans · Prospective Studies · Ovarian Neoplasms · Salpingectomy · Hysterectomy · Primary Prevention

cards.headline: Hanley 2022: in British Columbia, 25,889 people who had opportunistic salpingectomy developed no serous ovarian cancers, against 5.27 expected from control-group rates
cards.summary: Hanley 2022: in British Columbia, 25,889 people who had opportunistic salpingectomy developed no serous ovarian cancers, against 5.27 expected from control-group rates
cards.people: 25,889 individuals who underwent opportunistic salpingectomy (removal of both fallopian tubes at hysterectomy or instead of tubal ligation, ovaries left intact; mean age 40.2 years; median follow-up 3.2 years) and 32,080 who underwent hysterectomy alone or tubal ligation (mean age 38.2 years; median follow-up 7.3 years) in British Columbia, Canada, 2008 to 2017; people with any gynaecological cancer before or within 6 months of surgery were excluded.
cards.result: There were no serous ovarian cancers in the opportunistic salpingectomy group and 5 or fewer epithelial ovarian cancers, against age-adjusted expected numbers of 5.27 (95% CI 1.78 to 19.29) serous cancers and 8.68 (95% CI 3.36 to 26.58) epithelial cancers calculated from control-group rates. As a specificity check, age-adjusted expected versus observed numbers of breast cancers (22.1 expected vs 23 observed) and colorectal cancers (9.35 expected vs 8 observed) were not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: Median follow-up in the salpingectomy group was only 3.2 years and the expected cancer counts are small (about 5 to 9), so 'fewer than expected' rests on a handful of events; ovarian cancer latency is far longer than the follow-up here.
cards.source: Hanley GE et al. Outcomes From Opportunistic Salpingectomy for Ovarian Cancer Prevention. JAMA Network Open. 2022. PMID: 35138400. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · British Columbia · Carcinoma, Ovarian Epithelial · Female · Humans · Hysterectomy · Retrospective Studies · Salpingectomy

cards.headline: Falconer 2015: in a Swedish nationwide cohort, previous salpingectomy was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.65 for ovarian cancer — and bilateral removal with 0.35 versus 0.71 for unilateral
cards.summary: Falconer 2015: in a Swedish nationwide cohort, previous salpingectomy was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.65 for ovarian cancer — and bilateral removal with 0.35 versus 0.71 for unilateral
cards.people: Women in Sweden with previous surgery on benign indication (sterilisation, salpingectomy, hysterectomy, and hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; n = 251,465) compared with the unexposed population (n = 5,449,119), 1973 to 2009, analysed with Cox regression models.
cards.result: Ovarian cancer risk was statistically significantly lower after salpingectomy (hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.81) than in the unexposed population. Risk reductions were also seen after hysterectomy (0.79, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.88), sterilisation (0.72, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.81) and hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (0.06, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.12). Bilateral salpingectomy was associated with a lower risk than the unilateral procedure (hazard ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.73, versus 0.71, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.91) — about a 50% lower risk for bilateral compared with unilateral removal, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Registry surgery codes over 36 years: women who had any benign pelvic surgery differ from the unexposed population in parity, contraceptive history and healthcare contact, and even sterilisation and hysterectomy without tube removal showed lower risk — a pattern that warns part of the association may not be the tubes themselves.
cards.source: Falconer H et al. Ovarian cancer risk after salpingectomy: a nationwide population-based study. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2015. PMID: 25628372. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: opportunistic salpingectomy is associated with substantially fewer later ovarian cancers in every carded record — a systematic review and two population cohorts — with no randomised evidence and short follow-up in the most specific study
cards.summary: Synthesis: opportunistic salpingectomy is associated with substantially fewer later ovarian cancers in every carded record — a systematic review and two population cohorts — with no randomised evidence and short follow-up in the most specific study
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review (158 publications), one population-based retrospective cohort (25,889 opportunistic salpingectomies vs 32,080 controls) and one nationwide cohort (251,465 women with benign pelvic surgery vs 5,449,119 unexposed). All evidence is observational.
cards.result: The Swedish cohort found a hazard ratio of 0.65 for ovarian cancer after salpingectomy, with a bilateral-versus-unilateral gradient (0.35 vs 0.71) that supports a tube-specific effect (Falconer 2015). The British Columbia cohort found no serous cancers after opportunistic salpingectomy against 5.27 expected, with breast and colorectal cancers matching expectations (Hanley 2022). The systematic review summarises the literature as an approximately 80% risk reduction, with safety, cost-effectiveness and no earlier menopause onset (Kahn 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial exists and none is likely: the outcome is rare and decades away, so policy rests on observational associations whose comparison groups (women having other surgery, or no surgery) are not exchangeable.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kahn RM et al. JAMA Surgery. 2023 (PMID: 37672283); Hanley GE et al. JAMA Network Open. 2022 (PMID: 35138400); Falconer H et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2015 (PMID: 25628372).

shelves.title: Intravaginal boric acid for azole-refractory recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis (series evidence only, Ns on the face): remission in 64% and 71% of symptomatic Candida glabrata cases in one series (N = 141) and 81% of treated episodes in another (N = 60)
shelves.question: In recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis that azoles cannot control, does intravaginal boric acid achieve remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Anti-Infective Agents, Local · Antifungal Agents · Azoles · Biological Availability · Boric Acids · Candida · Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal · Case-Control Studies · Drug Resistance, Multiple, Fungal · Female · Flucytosine · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Secondary Prevention · Suppositories · Treatment Outcome · Vaginal Diseases
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — retrospective series evidence only, with every N printed on the face. The 2011 clinical evidence review (PMID: 21774671; 14 studies, mostly case series) found mycological cure rates of 40% to 100% with intravaginal boric acid and no demonstrated difference in recurrence. The two carded series are in azole-refractory Candida glabrata vaginitis: boric acid 600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks succeeded in 64% and 71% of symptomatic women at two sites (N = 141 women cultured; PMID: 14634557), and 14 days of boric acid improved or cured 21 of 26 treated episodes (81%) where azoles had responded in under 50% (N = 60 symptomatic patients; PMID: 9145739). No randomised trial in the refractory recurrent population is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — series evidence only: boric acid achieves short-term remission in a majority of azole-refractory cases in these series.

cards.headline: Iavazzo 2011: across 14 studies of intravaginal boric acid for vulvovaginal candidiasis, mycological cure rates ranged from 40% to 100%, with vaginal burning in under 10% of cases
cards.summary: Iavazzo 2011: across 14 studies of intravaginal boric acid for vulvovaginal candidiasis, mycological cure rates ranged from 40% to 100%, with vaginal burning in under 10% of cases
cards.people: 14 eligible studies identified from PubMed and Scopus (2 randomised clinical trials, 9 case series and 4 case reports) of intravaginal boric acid for vulvovaginal candidiasis, including recurrent disease and non-albicans or azole-resistant Candida; total participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: Boric acid was compared with nystatin, terconazole, flucytosine, itraconazole, clotrimazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole, buconazole and miconazole, and studied as monotherapy in 7 studies. Mycological cure rates varied from 40% to 100% in patients treated with boric acid; 4 of the 9 case series reported statistically significant outcomes for cure (mycological and clinical). None of the included studies reported statistically significant differences in recurrence rates. Adverse effects identified in 7 studies were vaginal burning sensation (under 10% of cases), watery discharge during treatment, and vaginal erythema. The authors conclude boric acid is a safe, alternative, economical option when conventional treatment fails because of non-albicans species or azole-resistant strains.
cards.watchOut: A review whose underlying evidence is mostly case series: a cure range of 40% to 100% across small heterogeneous series is a description of how variable the reports are, not an estimate of how well boric acid works.
cards.source: Iavazzo C et al. Boric acid for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: the clinical evidence. Journal of Women's Health. 2011. PMID: 21774671. Registry ID: none in the record. clinical evidence review (iavazzo 2011) 14 eligible studies identified from pubmed and scopus (2 randomised clinical trials, 9 case series and 4 case reports) of intravaginal boric acid for vulvovaginal candidiasis, including recurrent disease and non-albicans or azole-resistant candida; total participant n not documented in the record. boric acid was compared with nystatin, terconazole, flucytosine, itraconazole, clotrimazole, ketoconazole, fluconazole, buconazole and miconazole, and studied as monotherapy in 7 studies. mycological cure rates varied from 40% to 100% in patients treated with boric acid; 4 of the 9 case series reported statistically significant outcomes for cure (mycological and clinical). none of the included studies reported statistically significant differences in recurrence rates. adverse effects identified in 7 studies were vaginal burning sensation (under 10% of cases), watery discharge during treatment, and vaginal erythema. the authors conclude boric acid is a safe, alternative, economical option when conventional treatment fails because of non-albicans species or azole-resistant strains. a review whose underlying evidence is mostly case series: a cure range of 40% to 100% across small heterogeneous series is a description of how variable the reports are, not an estimate of how well boric acid works. iavazzo c et al. boric acid for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis: the clinical evidence. journal of women's health. 2011. pmid: 21774671. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, intravaginal · anti-infective agents, local · antifungal agents · azoles · biological availability · boric acids · candida · candidiasis, vulvovaginal · case-control studies · drug resistance, multiple, fungal · female · flucytosine · humans · randomized controlled trials as topic · secondary prevention · suppositories · treatment outcome · vaginal diseases

cards.headline: Sobel 2003: in 141 women with Candida glabrata vaginitis (N printed on the face), topical boric acid 600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks succeeded in 64% (Detroit) and 71% (Beer Sheba) of symptomatic women
cards.summary: Sobel 2003: in 141 women with Candida glabrata vaginitis (N printed on the face), topical boric acid 600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks succeeded in 64% (Detroit) and 71% (Beer Sheba) of symptomatic women
cards.people: 141 women with positive vaginal cultures for Candida glabrata at two sites (Wayne State University, Detroit, and Ben Gurion University, Beer Sheba), reviewed retrospectively; the boric acid regimen was assessed in 73 symptomatic women in Detroit and 38 symptomatic women in Beer Sheba. N = 141.
cards.result: The boric acid regimen (600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks) achieved clinical and mycological success in 47 of 73 symptomatic women (64%) in Detroit and 27 of 38 symptomatic women (71%) in Beer Sheba. Extending therapy from 14 to 21 days showed no advantage. Topical flucytosine cream nightly for 14 days succeeded in 27 of 30 women (90%) whose condition had failed to respond to boric acid and azole therapy. Local side effects were uncommon with both regimens.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, uncontrolled and from specialist vaginitis clinics: women referred after failing azoles are exactly the population in which any next treatment looks either heroic or hopeless depending on who was counted, and there is no untreated comparison group.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Treatment of vaginitis caused by Candida glabrata: use of topical boric acid and flucytosine. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2003. PMID: 14634557. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sobel 1997: in 60 symptomatic women with Torulopsis (Candida) glabrata vaginitis (N printed on the face), boric acid 600 mg daily for 14 days improved or cured 21 of 26 treated episodes (81%), where azoles had responded in under 50%
cards.summary: Sobel 1997: in 60 symptomatic women with Torulopsis (Candida) glabrata vaginitis (N printed on the face), boric acid 600 mg daily for 14 days improved or cured 21 of 26 treated episodes (81%), where azoles had responded in under 50%
cards.people: 80 patients whose vaginal cultures yielded Torulopsis glabrata at a vaginitis clinic between January 1989 and December 1994; 60 patients experienced 75 symptomatic episodes (40 uncomplicated infection, 20 mixed infection, most commonly with bacterial vaginosis) and are the subject of the review. N = 60 symptomatic patients; 26 episodes were treated with boric acid.
cards.result: Vaginal boric acid (600 mg/day for 14 days) produced clinical improvement or cure in 21 of 26 episodes (81%) and mycological eradication in 20 of 26 episodes (77%). One-third of the patients received maintenance therapy with boric acid. Clinical response and mycological eradication rates with topical and systemic azoles were under 50%. The response to boric acid remained high in patients with mixed T. glabrata infection. The authors conclude that, in patients for whom repeated antimycotic courses with azoles had previously failed, boric acid emerged as a promising modality.
cards.watchOut: Only 26 of 75 symptomatic episodes were treated with boric acid, and the record does not say how those episodes were chosen — selection of who got boric acid can carry the result in a series this small.
cards.source: Sobel JD et al. Treatment of Torulopsis glabrata vaginitis: retrospective review of boric acid therapy. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1997. PMID: 9145739. cards.headline: Synthesis: boric acid achieves remission in roughly two-thirds to four-fifths of azole-refractory glabrata cases in the carded series — real but weak evidence: retrospective series and a review of them, with no randomised trial in the refractory recurrent population
cards.summary: Synthesis: boric acid achieves remission in roughly two-thirds to four-fifths of azole-refractory glabrata cases in the carded series — real but weak evidence: retrospective series and a review of them, with no randomised trial in the refractory recurrent population
cards.people: The carded evidence: one clinical evidence review (14 studies: 2 randomised trials, 9 case series, 4 case reports; total N not documented in the record) and two retrospective series from specialist vaginitis clinics (N = 141 women with Candida glabrata cultures; N = 60 symptomatic patients). Every carded N is printed on the face of its card.
cards.result: In the largest series, boric acid 600 mg daily for 2 to 3 weeks succeeded clinically and mycologically in 64% (Detroit) and 71% (Beer Sheba) of symptomatic women with Candida glabrata vaginitis (Sobel 2003). In the earlier series, 14 days of boric acid improved or cured 81% of treated episodes and eradicated the organism in 77%, against under 50% response to azoles in the same clinic population (Sobel 1997). The review found mycological cure rates of 40% to 100% across studies and no demonstrated difference in recurrence rates (Iavazzo 2011). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — retrospective series evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Remission here means short-term clinical and mycological response in referred, azole-refractory cases; none of the carded records establishes durable remission or lower recurrence, and boric acid must never be taken orally or used in pregnancy — safety limits the record states only in part.
cards.source: Synthesis of Iavazzo C et al. Journal of Women's Health. 2011 (PMID: 21774671); Sobel JD et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2003 (PMID: 14634557); Sobel JD et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 1997 (PMID: 9145739).

shelves.title: Estrogen contraception in migraine with aura (observational only): the combined exposure carries the highest stroke odds (6.1, relative) — progestin-only methods are preferred, with headache evidence in their favour and their vascular safety unstudied rather than proven
shelves.question: In women with migraine with aura, is estrogen-containing contraception safe compared with progestin-only methods?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Case-Control Studies · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined · Contraceptives, Oral, Hormonal · Databases, Factual · Female · Humans · Incidence · Logistic Models · Middle Aged · Migraine with Aura · Migraine without Aura · Stroke · United States · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm for estrogen-containing methods) — observational only. The comparison this question asks for has never been run as an outcome trial, so the shelf assembles it honestly from its two sides. On the estrogen side, the signal is consistent: migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception carried the highest ischaemic-stroke odds in the largest study (odds ratio 6.1, relative, versus neither exposure; aura alone 2.7; Champaloux 2017), and the guidance systematic review found two- to fourfold stroke risks with combined pills in women with migraine across four studies (Tepper 2016). On the progestin-only side, that same review found no evidence at all on stroke — no studies — so 'safer' means 'no signal in an empty evidence base', not 'proven safe'. What progestin-only evidence exists is about headache: desogestrel reduced migraine frequency, intensity and triptan use in a prospective controlled study (Merki-Feld 2019) and over 180 days in a chart review (Merki-Feld 2015). Absolute context from the largest record: 11 strokes per 100,000 women aged 15–49 over the study window — relative risks multiply a rare outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: estrogen-containing contraception is not safe to treat as risk-neutral in migraine with aura; progestin-only methods are the preferred alternative on a harm-signal asymmetry, with their own vascular safety unstudied rather than established.

cards.headline: Champaloux 2017: migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception carried the highest stroke odds (odds ratio 6.1, relative) — above aura without contraception (2.7), and contraception added little in migraine without aura (1.8 versus 2.2 without it)
cards.summary: Champaloux 2017: migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception carried the highest stroke odds (odds ratio 6.1, relative) — above aura without contraception (2.7), and contraception added little in migraine without aura (1.8 versus 2.2 without it)
cards.people: Nested case-control study in a US nationwide healthcare claims database, 2006–2012: women aged 15–49 with first-ever ischaemic stroke (25,887 strokes in the source population; cumulative incidence 11 strokes per 100,000 females) matched to 4 controls per case by age. Migraine type and current combined hormonal contraceptive use were identified from diagnosis and pharmacy codes.
cards.result: Compared with women with neither migraine nor combined hormonal contraceptive use, the adjusted odds ratio for ischaemic stroke was highest in migraine with aura using combined hormonal contraceptives (odds ratio 6.1 [95% CI 3.1–12.1], a relative measure). Odds were also elevated for migraine with aura without contraceptive use (odds ratio 2.7 [95% CI 1.9–3.7]), migraine without aura with contraceptive use (odds ratio 1.8 [95% CI 1.1–2.9]) and migraine without aura without contraceptive use (odds ratio 2.2 [95% CI 1.9–2.7]). The authors conclude the joint effect of combined hormonal contraceptives and migraine with aura was associated with a 6-fold increased risk of ischaemic stroke compared with neither risk factor, while contraceptive use did not substantially further increase risk in migraine without aura.
cards.watchOut: Claims data: aura status from billing codes misclassifies some women, contraceptive 'use' is a filled prescription, and odds ratios are relative — the same record shows how rare the outcome is (11 strokes per 100,000 women over the study window), which is why the absolute stakes differ from the relative headline.
cards.source: Champaloux SW et al. Use of combined hormonal contraceptives among women with migraines and risk of ischemic stroke. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2017. PMID: 28034652. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tepper 2016: the systematic review behind contraceptive guidance found a two- to fourfold stroke risk with combined pills in migraine — and found no evidence at all on progestin-only methods, in studies of fair to poor quality
cards.summary: Tepper 2016: the systematic review behind contraceptive guidance found a two- to fourfold stroke risk with combined pills in migraine — and found no evidence at all on progestin-only methods, in studies of fair to poor quality
cards.people: Systematic review for contraceptive-safety guidance (PubMed to January 2016): studies of arterial thromboembolism (stroke or myocardial infarction) in women with migraine using hormonal contraception — combined methods (pills, patch, ring) and progestin-only methods (pills, injectables, implants, progestin intrauterine devices). Seven articles met inclusion criteria, all case-control studies of fair to poor quality reporting stroke outcomes for combined or unspecified oral contraceptives.
cards.result: Four studies showed that among women with migraine (not separated by subtype), combined oral contraceptive use was associated with approximately two to four times the risk of stroke compared with nonuse (relative measures). The only study examining migraine subtypes found an elevated stroke risk in migraine with aura that was similar regardless of oral contraceptive use, although those odds ratios were not reported — printed here plainly. Two further studies found increased risks with migraine and with contraceptive use independently. No evidence was found on other hormonal contraceptives — including all progestin-only methods — or on myocardial infarction. The authors conclude additional study is needed on combined and progestin-only methods across migraine subtypes.
cards.watchOut: The honest centre of this shelf: for progestin-only methods the review found an empty evidence base, so their 'safety' in migraine with aura is an absence of a signal in unstudied methods, not a measured absence of risk — and the combined-pill studies it did find were fair to poor quality.
cards.source: Tepper NK et al. Safety of hormonal contraceptives among women with migraine: A systematic review. Contraception. 2016. PMID: 27153744. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Merki-Feld 2019: the progestin-only pill desogestrel reduced migraine frequency, intensity and triptan use (all P < .001) in a prospective controlled study of women with migraine with and without aura — a headache outcome, not a stroke outcome
cards.summary: Merki-Feld 2019: the progestin-only pill desogestrel reduced migraine frequency, intensity and triptan use (all P < .001) in a prospective controlled study of women with migraine with and without aura — a headache outcome, not a stroke outcome
cards.people: Prospective non-randomised controlled trial: 150 women with migraine attending a clinic for contraceptive counselling were screened; the intervention group comprised 98 women who opted for desogestrel 75 µg daily and the control group 36 women who continued their usual contraception. Participants kept daily diaries for 90 days before and 180 days after the intervention. The study population included women with migraine with and without aura who had at least 3 migraine days per month.
cards.result: In the desogestrel group, migraine frequency (P < .001), migraine intensity (P < .001) and the number of triptans used (P < .001) all improved, already significantly after 90 days, and disability scores decreased significantly; no improvement was seen in the control group. The record reports P values without printing the underlying day counts, stated here plainly. The study measured headache outcomes only — it recorded no stroke or other vascular outcomes and was neither designed nor sized to detect them.
cards.watchOut: Women chose their group, so expectancy and selection favour the intervention; and a 134-woman headache study cannot speak to an outcome that occurs in roughly 11 per 100,000 women — it supports desogestrel for migraine burden, not as proof of vascular safety.
cards.source: Merki-Feld GS et al. Effect of desogestrel 75 µg on headache frequency and intensity in women with migraine: a prospective controlled trial. The European journal of contraception & reproductive health care : the official journal of the European Society of Contraception. 2019. PMID: 31094588. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Merki-Feld 2015: over 180 days on desogestrel, migraine days fell from 5.8 to 3.6 and triptan use from 12.3 to 7.8 in 42 women (N printed on the face) — an uncontrolled chart review
cards.summary: Merki-Feld 2015: over 180 days on desogestrel, migraine days fell from 5.8 to 3.6 and triptan use from 12.3 to 7.8 in 42 women (N printed on the face) — an uncontrolled chart review
cards.people: Retrospective chart review in a clinical setting: women with migraine who had decided to use the progestin-only pill desogestrel 75 µg for contraception, with complete routine headache diaries for 90 days before treatment and over 180 days of treatment; 42 women were analysed (25 of 42, 60%, achieved a clinically meaningful 30% reduction in pain). Starters who stopped early because of adverse events were also reported.
cards.result: Days with migraine fell from 5.8 at baseline to 3.6 after 180 days, days with any headache from 9.4 to 6.6, headache intensity from 15.7 to 10.7, days with severe headache from 5.4 to 2.4, and triptan use from 12.3 to 7.8 — all significantly reduced per the record, which reports the day counts without confidence intervals, printed here as given. MIDAS quality-of-life score and grade improved significantly, with most of the migraine-frequency reduction occurring in the first 90 days.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled, single-clinic, diary-complete cases only: women whose migraine worsened on desogestrel and stopped early are the least likely to appear in a 180-day completer analysis, so this card can support tolerability in continuers and nothing about vascular events.
cards.source: Merki-Feld GS et al. Positive effects of the progestin desogestrel 75 μg on migraine frequency and use of acute medication are sustained over a treatment period of 180 days. The journal of headache and pain. 2015. PMID: 25933634. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: estrogen-containing contraception is the method class with a consistent stroke signal in migraine with aura (odds ratio 6.1, relative, for the combined exposure); progestin-only methods have no stroke signal in the carded evidence because they have barely been studied for stroke at all — their positive evidence is about headache relief
cards.summary: Synthesis: estrogen-containing contraception is the method class with a consistent stroke signal in migraine with aura (odds ratio 6.1, relative, for the combined exposure); progestin-only methods have no stroke signal in the carded evidence because they have barely been studied for stroke at all — their positive evidence is about headache relief
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large nested case-control study (25,887 strokes in the source population), one systematic review of 7 case-control studies, and two small desogestrel studies in women with migraine (134 participants in the controlled study; 42 in the chart review — Ns printed on their faces). No randomised or cohort study in the carded set compares vascular outcomes between estrogen-containing and progestin-only methods directly; the comparison is assembled from a signal on one side and an evidence gap plus headache data on the other, and the shelf labels it that way.
cards.result: Migraine with aura plus combined hormonal contraception carried an odds ratio of 6.1 (relative) for ischaemic stroke against neither exposure, versus 2.7 (relative) for aura without contraception (Champaloux 2017), and the guidance systematic review found two- to fourfold stroke risks with combined pills in migraine while finding no evidence on progestin-only methods (Tepper 2016). Desogestrel improved migraine frequency, intensity and triptan use in both small studies (Merki-Feld 2019; Merki-Feld 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm for estrogen-containing methods) — observational only, as detailed in the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the desogestrel headache results harden into a vascular-safety claim: the correct reading is 'no stroke signal found, in evidence that largely did not look', which supports preferring progestin-only methods with aura while remaining honest that the preference rests on the estrogen side's signal plus biological plausibility, not on progestin outcome data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Champaloux SW et al. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2017 (PMID: 28034652); Tepper NK et al. Contraception. 2016 (PMID: 27153744); Merki-Feld GS et al. shelves.title: Micronized progesterone and the endometrium — split by outcome: it matched synthetic progestins against hyperplasia over 3 years in PEPI (at 200 mg for 12 days a month), but a 65,630-woman cohort associates it with more endometrial cancer than synthetic derivatives, especially beyond 5 years
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with a uterus, does micronized progesterone protect the endometrium as well as synthetic progestins?
shelves.mesh: Biopsy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Endometrial Hyperplasia · Endometrial Neoplasms · Endometrium · Estrogen Replacement Therapy · Estrogens · Female · Humans · Medroxyprogesterone Acetate · Middle Aged · Postmenopause · Progesterone · Progesterone Congeners · Progestins
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer divides by outcome and by time horizon, and the split is printed in the stamp. On the short-term histological outcome, the randomised PEPI trial found that cyclic micronized progesterone (200 mg/day for 12 days per cycle) protected the endometrium as well as either medroxyprogesterone regimen over 3 years: hyperplasia rates on all three estrogen-plus-progestogen regimens were similar to placebo, while estrogen alone produced simple hyperplasia in 27.7%, complex hyperplasia in 22.7% and atypical hyperplasia in 11.8% of women. An expert systematic review likewise concludes that oral micronized progesterone given sequentially for 12–14 days a month at 200 mg/day provides endometrial protection for up to 5 years (and that transdermal micronized progesterone does not). On the long-term cancer outcome, however, the large E3N cohort points the other way: estrogen plus micronized progesterone was associated with a higher endometrial cancer risk than never use (HR 1.80 relative), rising with duration (over 5 years HR 2.66 relative), whereas preparations containing other progesterone derivatives were not associated with increased risk (HR 0.79 relative). The cohort is observational and the doses and durations used in France may not match the PEPI regimen, but no randomised trial has followed women long enough to test the cancer outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT (short-term endometrial histology: protection comparable to synthetic progestins in a randomised trial; long-term endometrial cancer: a large cohort associates micronized progesterone — unlike synthetic derivatives — with increased risk, especially beyond 5 years).

cards.headline: PEPI 1996: over 3 years, cyclic micronized progesterone protected the endometrium as well as medroxyprogesterone — hyperplasia rates on all three combined regimens were similar to placebo, while estrogen alone caused hyperplasia in up to 27.7% of women
cards.summary: PEPI 1996: over 3 years, cyclic micronized progesterone protected the endometrium as well as medroxyprogesterone — hyperplasia rates on all three combined regimens were similar to placebo, while estrogen alone caused hyperplasia in up to 27.7% of women
cards.people: 596 postmenopausal women aged 45–64 years without contraindication to hormone therapy, randomised in a 3-year multicentre, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial to placebo, conjugated equine estrogens (CEE) 0.625 mg/day alone, CEE plus cyclic medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 10 mg/day for 12 days, CEE plus continuous MPA 2.5 mg/day, or CEE plus cyclic micronized progesterone 200 mg/day for 12 days per 28-day cycle. Endometrial histology was assessed by biopsy, curettage or hysterectomy at baseline, annually, or at unscheduled visits.
cards.result: Women assigned to estrogen alone were more likely than women on placebo to develop simple (cystic) hyperplasia (27.7% vs 0.8%), complex (adenomatous) hyperplasia (22.7% vs 0.8%) and atypical hyperplasia (11.8% vs 0%) (P < .001). Participants on any of the three estrogen-plus-progestogen regimens — including cyclic micronized progesterone — had rates of hyperplasia similar to those given placebo (P = .16). Women on estrogen alone also had more unscheduled biopsies (66.4% vs 8.4%) and curettages (17.6% vs 0.8%) than women on placebo; surgical procedure numbers were similar for placebo and the combined regimens (P = .38).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is hyperplasia over 3 years, not endometrial cancer, and the micronized progesterone regimen tested was a specific one — 200 mg/day for the first 12 days of each cycle with 0.625 mg CEE. The trial cannot speak to lower doses, fewer days per month, other estrogens, or use beyond 3 years.
cards.source: The Writing Group for the PEPI Trial. Effects of hormone replacement therapy on endometrial histology in postmenopausal women. The Postmenopausal Estrogen/Progestin Interventions (PEPI) Trial. JAMA. 1996. PMID: 8569016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fournier 2014 (E3N cohort): estrogen plus micronized progesterone was associated with increased endometrial cancer risk (HR 1.80 relative), rising to HR 2.66 beyond 5 years — while other progesterone derivatives showed no increase (HR 0.79)
cards.summary: Fournier 2014 (E3N cohort): estrogen plus micronized progesterone was associated with increased endometrial cancer risk (HR 1.80 relative), rising to HR 2.66 beyond 5 years — while other progesterone derivatives showed no increase (HR 0.79)
cards.people: 65,630 postmenopausal women in the French E3N cohort, followed from 1992 to 2008 (mean follow-up 10.8 years); 301 endometrial cancers occurred. Risks were estimated with Cox models comparing hormone therapy regimens with never use.
cards.result: Ever use of estrogen plus micronized progesterone was associated with an increased risk of endometrial cancer (hazard ratio 1.80 relative, 95% CI 1.38 to 2.34), more marked with longer use (5 years or less HR 1.39 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.97; over 5 years HR 2.66 relative, 95% CI 1.87 to 3.77). Estrogen plus dydrogesterone was not associated with risk overall (HR 1.05 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.45) but was associated with increased risk with long-term use (over 5 years HR 1.69 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 2.70). Users of preparations containing other progesterone derivatives or a norsteroid derivative were not at significantly increased risk (HR 0.79 relative, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.05, and HR 1.30 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.99, respectively). The authors conclude that micronized progesterone, and to a lesser extent dydrogesterone, at the doses used in France may not be sufficient to prevent estrogen-induced endometrial cancers. Absolute cancer rates by regimen are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Observational: women were not randomised to progestogen type, and the micronized progesterone doses and monthly durations used in France during 1992–2008 are not itemised in the record — they may often have been lower or shorter than the 200 mg for 12–14 days tested in PEPI. Confounding by prescribing pattern cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Fournier A et al. Risks of endometrial cancer associated with different hormone replacement therapies in the E3N cohort, 1992-2008. American journal of epidemiology. 2014. PMID: 25008104. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stute 2016: expert systematic review — oral micronized progesterone protects the endometrium when given sequentially 12–14 days a month at 200 mg/day for up to 5 years; transdermal micronized progesterone does not protect
cards.summary: Stute 2016: expert systematic review — oral micronized progesterone protects the endometrium when given sequentially 12–14 days a month at 200 mg/day for up to 5 years; transdermal micronized progesterone does not protect
cards.type: Systematic review with expert panel recommendations (Stute 2016)
cards.people: Systematic literature review on micronized progesterone for endometrial protection, with recommendations from an international expert panel; the record does not document a total participant N for the review.
cards.result: The panel's recommendations, as printed in the record: (1) oral micronized progesterone provides endometrial protection if applied sequentially for 12–14 days/month at 200 mg/day for up to 5 years; (2) vaginal micronized progesterone may provide endometrial protection if applied sequentially for at least 10 days/month at 4% (45 mg/day) or every other day at 100 mg/day for up to 3–5 years (off-label use); (3) transdermal micronized progesterone does not provide endometrial protection. No pooled effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: The 5-year horizon in the recommendation is a limit of the underlying evidence, not proof of safety or harm beyond it — and it sits in tension with the E3N cohort's duration gradient, in which the cancer association was strongest beyond 5 years.
cards.source: Stute P et al. The impact of micronized progesterone on the endometrium: a systematic review. Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society. 2016. PMID: 27277331. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: micronized progesterone at an adequate dose and duration (200 mg/day for 12–14 days a month) matched synthetic progestins against hyperplasia in the one randomised trial — but the only long-term cancer data associate it, unlike synthetic derivatives, with increased endometrial cancer risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: micronized progesterone at an adequate dose and duration (200 mg/day for 12–14 days a month) matched synthetic progestins against hyperplasia in the one randomised trial — but the only long-term cancer data associate it, unlike synthetic derivatives, with increased endometrial cancer risk
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of endometrial histology (596 women, 3 years), one large prospective cohort with a cancer outcome (65,630 women, 301 cancers, mean 10.8 years of follow-up), and one systematic review with expert recommendations (participant N not documented in its record). Total carded participants exceed 66,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In PEPI, cyclic micronized progesterone 200 mg/day for 12 days kept hyperplasia rates at placebo levels, as did both medroxyprogesterone regimens, while estrogen alone produced hyperplasia in 27.7% (simple), 22.7% (complex) and 11.8% (atypical) of women. In E3N, estrogen plus micronized progesterone carried an endometrial cancer hazard ratio of 1.80 relative to never use (2.66 relative beyond 5 years), while other progesterone derivatives showed no significant increase (0.79 relative). The expert review supports protection at 200 mg/day for 12–14 days a month for up to 5 years and states transdermal micronized progesterone does not protect. PROPOSED SPLIT (short-term endometrial histology: protection comparable to synthetic progestins in a randomised trial; long-term endometrial cancer: a large cohort associates micronized progesterone — unlike synthetic derivatives — with increased risk, especially beyond 5 years).
cards.watchOut: The two halves of this shelf answer different questions: a 3-year histology trial cannot refute a 10-year cancer association, and an observational cohort cannot refute a randomised histology result. Dose and days per month are the hinge — protection was demonstrated at 200 mg for 12–14 days, and the cohort's regimens are not itemised in its record.
cards.source: Synthesis of The Writing Group for the PEPI Trial. JAMA. 1996 (PMID: 8569016); Fournier A et al. American journal of epidemiology. 2014 (PMID: 25008104); Stute P et al. Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society. 2016 (PMID: 27277331).

shelves.title: Combined pill versus progestin-only pill and venous thromboembolism (observational only): combined pills raised VTE risk about 3- to 7-fold versus non-use in two large studies, while oral progestin-only pills showed no increase (relative risk 1.06, not significant)
shelves.question: Does the combined oral contraceptive pill increase venous thromboembolism risk compared with the progestin-only pill?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Androstenes · Anticoagulants · Cohort Studies · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Contraceptives, Oral · Denmark · Desogestrel · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Humans · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel · Middle Aged · Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists · Norpregnenes · Pregnancy · Time Factors · Venous Thromboembolism · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face; there is no randomised evidence for this question and the comparison is indirect. Two large observational anchors agree that combined oral contraceptives raise venous thromboembolism risk several-fold versus non-use: relative risks of 2.9 to 6.6 by progestogen in the Danish national cohort (Lidegaard 2011; absolute risk about 10 per 10,000 women-years in the higher-risk group) and an odds ratio of 5.0 in the MEGA case-control study (van Hylckama Vlieg 2009). Against the same non-user reference, the oral progestin-only pill shows no increase: the Danish cohort found no increased risk with progestogen-only pills, and a 19-study meta-analysis gives a pooled relative risk of 1.06 (95% CI 0.70–1.62) for oral progestin-only contraception (Glisic 2018) — while noting injectable progestin-only contraception did show an increase (relative risk 2.62) and is a different method. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: the combined pill increases venous thromboembolism risk compared with the (oral) progestin-only pill.

cards.headline: Lidegaard 2011: in 8,010,290 women-years, combined pills raised confirmed VTE risk 2.9- to 6.6-fold versus non-users depending on progestogen — while progestogen-only pills showed no increased risk
cards.summary: Lidegaard 2011: in 8,010,290 women-years, combined pills raised confirmed VTE risk 2.9- to 6.6-fold versus non-users depending on progestogen — while progestogen-only pills showed no increased risk
cards.people: Non-pregnant Danish women aged 15–49 with no history of thrombotic disease, followed from January 2001 to December 2009 in national registries; 4,307 first venous thromboembolic events were recorded and 4,246 included, of which 2,847 (67%) were confirmed.
cards.result: Compared with non-users of hormonal contraception, the relative risk of confirmed venous thromboembolism in users of oral contraceptives containing 30–40 µg ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel was 2.9 (95% CI 2.2 to 3.8), with desogestrel 6.6 (5.6 to 7.8), with gestodene 6.2 (5.6 to 7.0), and with drospirenone 6.4 (5.4 to 7.5) — all relative measures. The risk of confirmed venous thromboembolism was not increased with use of progestogen-only pills. The record gives an absolute risk of about 10 per 10,000 women-years for current users of the desogestrel, gestodene or drospirenone group.
cards.watchOut: This is an indirect comparison: combined pills and progestogen-only pills are each compared with non-users, not head-to-head, and women prescribed progestogen-only pills differ from combined-pill users (including by thrombosis risk factors that prompt the choice).
cards.source: Lidegaard Ø et al. Risk of venous thromboembolism from use of oral contraceptives containing different progestogens and oestrogen doses: Danish cohort study, 2001-9. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011. PMID: 22027398. Registry ID: none in the record. national registry cohort study (lidegaard 2011) non-pregnant danish women aged 15–49 with no history of thrombotic disease, followed from january 2001 to december 2009 in national registries; 4,307 first venous thromboembolic events were recorded and 4,246 included, of which 2,847 (67%) were confirmed. compared with non-users of hormonal contraception, the relative risk of confirmed venous thromboembolism in users of oral contraceptives containing 30–40 µg ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel was 2.9 (95% ci 2.2 to 3.8), with desogestrel 6.6 (5.6 to 7.8), with gestodene 6.2 (5.6 to 7.0), and with drospirenone 6.4 (5.4 to 7.5) — all relative measures. the risk of confirmed venous thromboembolism was not increased with use of progestogen-only pills. the record gives an absolute risk of about 10 per 10,000 women-years for current users of the desogestrel, gestodene or drospirenone group. this is an indirect comparison: combined pills and progestogen-only pills are each compared with non-users, not head-to-head, and women prescribed progestogen-only pills differ from combined-pill users (including by thrombosis risk factors that prompt the choice). lidegaard ø et al. risk of venous thromboembolism from use of oral contraceptives containing different progestogens and oestrogen doses: danish cohort study, 2001-9. bmj (clinical research ed.). 2011. pmid: 22027398. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · androstenes · anticoagulants · cohort studies · confounding factors, epidemiologic · contraceptives, oral · denmark · desogestrel · dose-response relationship, drug · epidemiologic methods · female · humans · intrauterine devices, medicated · levonorgestrel · middle aged · mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists · norpregnenes · pregnancy · time factors · venous thromboembolism · young adult

cards.headline: van Hylckama Vlieg 2009 (MEGA): currently available combined oral contraceptives increased venous thrombosis risk fivefold versus non-use (odds ratio 5.0, 95% CI 4.2 to 5.8), varying by progestogen type and oestrogen dose
cards.summary: van Hylckama Vlieg 2009 (MEGA): currently available combined oral contraceptives increased venous thrombosis risk fivefold versus non-use (odds ratio 5.0, 95% CI 4.2 to 5.8), varying by progestogen type and oestrogen dose
cards.type: Population-based case-control study (MEGA, van Hylckama Vlieg 2009)
cards.people: Population-based case-control study at six anticoagulation clinics in the Netherlands: 1,524 patients with a first objectively diagnosed deep venous thrombosis of the leg or pulmonary embolism and 1,760 controls, all premenopausal women under 50 who were not pregnant or recently postpartum.
cards.result: Currently available oral contraceptives increased the risk of venous thrombosis fivefold compared with non-use (odds ratio 5.0, 95% CI 4.2 to 5.8) — a relative measure. By progestogen, versus non-use: levonorgestrel 3.6 (2.9 to 4.6), gestodene 5.6 (3.7 to 8.4), desogestrel 7.3 (5.3 to 10.0), cyproterone acetate 6.8 (4.7 to 10.0), drospirenone 6.3 (2.9 to 13.7). Risk rose with oestrogen dose and was highest in the first months of use. The study did not estimate a progestin-only pill risk (users of hormone-excreting intrauterine devices or depot contraceptives were excluded).
cards.watchOut: Case-control odds ratios overstate relative risk slightly when outcomes are not rare, and — like the Danish cohort — this study anchors the combined pill against non-use, so the combined-versus-progestin-only contrast still rests on the progestin-only evidence on the next card.
cards.source: van Hylckama Vlieg A et al. The venous thrombotic risk of oral contraceptives, effects of oestrogen dose and progestogen type: results of the MEGA case-control study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2009. PMID: 19679614. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glisic 2018: across 19 observational studies, oral progestin-only contraception was not associated with venous thromboembolism (pooled relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.70–1.62) — but injectable progestin-only contraception was (relative risk 2.62)
cards.summary: Glisic 2018: across 19 observational studies, oral progestin-only contraception was not associated with venous thromboembolism (pooled relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 0.70–1.62) — but injectable progestin-only contraception was (relative risk 2.62)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Glisic 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 observational studies (seven cohort and 12 case-control) of progestin-only contraceptive (POC) use and cardiometabolic outcomes; nine studies reported venous thromboembolism risk.
cards.result: The pooled adjusted relative risk for venous thromboembolism for oral POC users versus non-users was 1.06 (95% CI 0.70–1.62) — not statistically significant, i.e. no increased risk detected. By route, injectable POC was associated with increased VTE risk (relative risk 2.62, 95% CI 1.74–3.94), while a levonorgestrel intrauterine device subgroup showed a lower risk (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.32–0.89). All measures are relative; the record reports no absolute VTE rates for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: 'Progestin-only pill' on this shelf means the oral pill: the injectable progestin-only method behaves differently in this meta-analysis, and the oral estimate's confidence interval (up to 1.62) cannot exclude a modest increase.
cards.source: Glisic M et al. Association between progestin-only contraceptive use and cardiometabolic outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. European journal of preventive cardiology. 2018. PMID: 29745237. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the combined pill carries the higher venous thromboembolism risk — combined pills are consistently associated with a 3- to 7-fold relative increase versus non-use, while the oral progestin-only pill shows no increase versus non-use; the comparison is indirect and observational throughout
cards.summary: Synthesis: the combined pill carries the higher venous thromboembolism risk — combined pills are consistently associated with a 3- to 7-fold relative increase versus non-use, while the oral progestin-only pill shows no increase versus non-use; the comparison is indirect and observational throughout
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Danish national cohort (8,010,290 women-years; 4,246 first VTE events), the Dutch MEGA case-control study (1,524 cases, 1,760 controls), and a meta-analysis of 19 observational studies of progestin-only contraception. Total carded participants run into the millions of women-years, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that every estimate is observational and the head-to-head contrast is indirect.
cards.result: Combined oral contraceptives versus non-use: relative risk 2.9 (levonorgestrel) to 6.6 (desogestrel) for confirmed VTE in Denmark (Lidegaard 2011) and odds ratio 5.0 overall in MEGA (van Hylckama Vlieg 2009), with absolute risk around 10 per 10,000 women-years in the higher-risk combined-pill group in the Danish record. Oral progestin-only contraception versus non-use: pooled relative risk 1.06 (95% CI 0.70–1.62), no increase detected (Glisic 2018); the Danish cohort likewise found no increased risk with progestogen-only pills. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: yes, the combined pill increases VTE risk compared with the progestin-only pill, on indirect observational evidence.
cards.watchOut: No randomised or head-to-head observational study of combined versus progestin-only pills is carded: prescribers channel higher-risk women toward progestin-only pills, which would bias the indirect comparison toward understating the combined pill's excess — the direction of the finding is nonetheless consistent across all three sources.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lidegaard Ø et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011 (PMID: 22027398); van Hylckama Vlieg A et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2009 (PMID: 19679614); Glisic M et al. European journal of preventive cardiology. 2018 (PMID: 29745237).

shelves.title: Intravenous iron for fatigue without anaemia: pooled evidence favours iron and the benefit concentrates at ferritin 15 ng/mL or below — but the one dedicated trial was null overall and the evidence is rated low quality
shelves.question: In adults with iron deficiency without anemia, does intravenous iron improve fatigue versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue · Female · Ferric Compounds · Ferric Oxide, Saccharated · Ferritins · Glucaric Acid · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Iron · Iron Deficiencies · Patient Selection · Placebos · Premenopause · Research Design · Sucrose
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack shelf #2458, which covers ORAL iron for fatigue in non-anaemic women with low ferritin; this shelf covers the intravenous route and the broader non-anaemic iron-deficient adult population, and does not re-card #2458's oral-iron trials. The one dedicated randomised trial (Krayenbuehl 2011; 90 non-anaemic premenopausal women, ferritin 50 ng/mL or below) missed its overall comparison — fatigue fell by 1.1 points on intravenous iron versus 0.7 on placebo at 6 weeks (P = 0.07; the treatment made no difference overall) — but in women with ferritin of 15 ng/mL or below the benefit was clear (fall of 1.8 versus 0.4 points, P = 0.005; 82% versus 47% reported improved fatigue). The abridged Cochrane synthesis of intravenous iron in non-anaemic iron deficiency (Dugan 2022; 21 trials, 3,514 participants) found fatigue improved overall (standardised mean difference 0.30 in favour of iron, as printed in the record) and peak oxygen consumption higher by 1.77 mL/kg/min, while rating the evidence low or very low quality for every outcome except fatigue. Houston 2018, pooling iron by all routes (18 trials, 1,170 patients), likewise found self-reported fatigue reduced (standardised mean difference −0.38) with no improvement in objective physical capacity. Adverse events on intravenous iron were more frequent but mild (21% versus 7% in Krayenbuehl; relative risk 1.77 for mild events in Dugan), with no difference in serious events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intravenous iron probably improves fatigue in iron deficiency without anaemia — most convincingly when ferritin is genuinely low (15 ng/mL or below) — on evidence the field itself rates low quality.

cards.headline: Krayenbuehl 2011: intravenous iron did not beat placebo on fatigue overall (P = 0.07) — but in women with ferritin 15 ng/mL or below, fatigue fell by 1.8 versus 0.4 points and 82% versus 47% improved
cards.summary: Krayenbuehl 2011: intravenous iron did not beat placebo on fatigue overall (P = 0.07) — but in women with ferritin 15 ng/mL or below, fatigue fell by 1.8 versus 0.4 points and 82% versus 47% improved
cards.people: 90 premenopausal women presenting with fatigue, serum ferritin 50 ng/mL or below and haemoglobin 120 g/L (12.0 g/dL) or above, randomised double-blind to 800 mg intravenous iron(III)-hydroxide sucrose or intravenous placebo, with fatigue and iron status assessed at baseline and at 6 and 12 weeks. Median baseline fatigue was 4.5 on a 0–10 scale.
cards.result: Fatigue decreased during the initial 6 weeks by 1.1 points in the iron group compared with 0.7 in the placebo group (P = 0.07) — the treatment made no difference on the overall comparison. In patients with baseline ferritin of 15 ng/mL or below, fatigue decreased by 1.8 in the iron group versus 0.4 in the placebo group (P = 0.005), and 82% of iron-treated compared with 47% of placebo-treated patients reported improved fatigue (P = 0.03). Drug-associated adverse events occurred in 21% of iron-treated and 7% of placebo-treated patients (P = 0.05); none was serious. The authors conclude efficacy was bound to a ferritin of 15 ng/mL or below.
cards.watchOut: The positive result is a ferritin-defined subgroup of a 90-woman trial whose headline comparison was null; treating everyone with ferritin up to 50 ng/mL on this evidence would treat many women the trial suggests do not benefit.
cards.source: Krayenbuehl PA et al. Intravenous iron for the treatment of fatigue in nonanemic, premenopausal women with low serum ferritin concentration. Blood. 2011. PMID: 21705493. Registry ID: ISRCTN78430425. cards.headline: Dugan 2022 (abridged Cochrane): across 21 trials (3,514 participants), intravenous iron improved fatigue and peak oxygen consumption versus placebo — on evidence rated low or very low quality
cards.summary: Dugan 2022 (abridged Cochrane): across 21 trials (3,514 participants), intravenous iron improved fatigue and peak oxygen consumption versus placebo — on evidence rated low or very low quality
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Dugan 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (an update and reanalysis of a Cochrane review) of 21 randomised controlled trials comprising 3,514 adults with non-anaemic iron deficiency, comparing any intravenous iron preparation with placebo; outcomes were physical performance, fatigue and quality-of-life scores, adverse effects, ferritin and haemoglobin at end of follow-up.
cards.result: Intravenous iron increased physical function measured by peak oxygen consumption (mean difference 1.77 mL/kg/min; 95% CI 0.57 to 2.97) and improved fatigue overall (standardised mean difference 0.30; 95% CI −0.52 to −0.09, as printed in the record), with no overall difference in quality of life (mean difference 0.15; 95% CI −0.01 to 0.31). Ferritin rose by a mean difference of 245.52 µg/L and haemoglobin by 4.65 g/L. Mild adverse events were more frequent on iron (relative risk 1.77; 95% CI 1.10 to 2.83; relative measure) with no difference in serious adverse events (risk difference 0). The quality of evidence was rated low and very low for all outcomes except fatigue, mainly because most studies were judged at high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: A pooled fatigue benefit across heterogeneous populations (athletes, blood donors, surgical and heart-failure patients among them) may not transfer to an unselected fatigued adult, and the reviewers themselves remain uncertain about efficacy in this population.
cards.source: Dugan C et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of intravenous iron therapy for adults with non-anaemic iron deficiency: An abridged Cochrane review.
