cards.headline: Houston 2018: iron supplementation (all routes) reduced self-reported fatigue in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults (standardised mean difference −0.38) but did not improve objective physical capacity
cards.summary: Houston 2018: iron supplementation (all routes) reduced self-reported fatigue in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults (standardised mean difference −0.38) but did not improve objective physical capacity
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Houston 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 unique randomised trials and 2 companion papers enrolling 1,170 non-anaemic iron-deficient adults (18 years or older); interventions were oral, intramuscular or intravenous iron versus placebo or active therapy (searches to October 2016). The intravenous-specific reading comes from the other two cards; this review is carded for the fatigue outcome across the whole non-anaemic population.
cards.result: Iron supplementation was associated with reduced self-reported fatigue (standardised mean difference −0.38; 95% CI −0.52 to −0.23; 4 trials, 714 participants) but was not associated with differences in objective physical capacity, including maximal oxygen consumption (standardised mean difference 0.11; 95% CI −0.15 to 0.37; 9 trials, 235 participants) or timed exercise testing. Haemoglobin rose by a mean difference of 4.01 g/L and ferritin by 9.23 µmol/L, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Subjective fatigue improving while measured exercise capacity does not is the classic signature of a partly expectation-driven effect in trials that are hard to blind perfectly; the review pools oral with intravenous iron, so it supports the fatigue claim, not the route claim.
cards.source: Houston BL et al. Efficacy of iron supplementation on fatigue and physical capacity in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials. BMJ Open. 2018. PMID: 29626044. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Fatigue · Female · Ferritins · Humans · Iron · Iron Deficiencies · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic

cards.headline: Synthesis: intravenous iron probably improves fatigue in non-anaemic iron deficiency — convincingly only at genuinely low ferritin — while objective physical capacity barely moves
cards.summary: Synthesis: intravenous iron probably improves fatigue in non-anaemic iron deficiency — convincingly only at genuinely low ferritin — while objective physical capacity barely moves
cards.people: The carded evidence: one dedicated double-blind trial (90 non-anaemic premenopausal women), one intravenous-iron-specific Cochrane-abridged synthesis (21 trials, 3,514 participants) and one all-routes synthesis (18 trials, 1,170 patients). The syntheses overlap in included trials; the dedicated trial's population (premenopausal women) is narrower than this shelf's question, which is printed here rather than smoothed over.
cards.result: Overall trial comparison null (fatigue fall 1.1 versus 0.7 points, P = 0.07), with a clear benefit at ferritin 15 ng/mL or below (1.8 versus 0.4; 82% versus 47% improved). Pooled intravenous evidence: fatigue standardised mean difference 0.30 in favour of iron and peak oxygen consumption +1.77 mL/kg/min, on low-quality evidence; all-routes evidence: fatigue standardised mean difference −0.38 with no objective-capacity gain. Mild adverse events were more common on iron; serious events were not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #2458 found oral iron also improves fatigue in non-anaemic women; nothing carded here shows the intravenous route beats the oral route for fatigue — the case for intravenous is speed and guaranteed delivery, not a proven larger effect.

shelves.title: Low-dose vaginal estrogen for vaginal dryness (partial completion of #2736): dryness relieved, systemic estradiol stays near postmenopausal levels, endometrial events extremely rare
shelves.question: Does low-dose vaginal estrogen relieve vaginal dryness without increasing systemic estrogen risks?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Atrophic Vaginitis · Estrogens · Female · Humans · Menopause · Urologic Diseases
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2736, which covers low-dose vaginal oestrogen safety in breast-cancer survivors specifically; this shelf asks the general-population question #2736 does not — dryness efficacy plus systemic risk in postmenopausal women generally. On efficacy the evidence is concordant: the systematic review behind the specialty guideline (Rahn 2014; 44 eligible studies) found vaginal estrogens improved dryness and dyspareunia versus placebo across preparations, and the pivotal randomised trial (Bachmann 2008, N = 230) found both 25 mcg and 10 mcg estradiol vaginal tablets significantly improved vaginal health and symptoms versus placebo over 12 weeks. On systemic exposure, Santen 2020's assay-critical review found systemic estradiol on low-dose products stays dose-dependent and low — roughly 4.6 to 14.8 pg/mL on the 10-mcg tablet by sensitive assays, against a proposed untreated postmenopausal range up to about 10.7 pg/mL — and Rahn 2014 found endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma extremely rare, with serum estradiol remaining within postmenopausal norms for all preparations except high-dose conjugated equine estrogen cream. The caution card is small and old: Handa 1994 (N = 20) relieved symptoms in 19 of 20 women on 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens three nights a week with no significant change in serum estrogens or endometrial thickness — but endometrial proliferation in one case. The breast-cancer-survivor population stays on #2736 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose vaginal estrogen relieves vaginal dryness, and at the low doses carded systemic estradiol stays within or near the postmenopausal range with extremely rare endometrial events — the residual uncertainty is the absence of long-term randomised safety outcomes, printed here rather than smoothed over.

cards.headline: Rahn 2014: across 44 eligible studies, vaginal estrogens improved dryness and dyspareunia versus placebo, urinary tract infection rates fell, and endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma were extremely rare
cards.summary: Rahn 2014: across 44 eligible studies, vaginal estrogens improved dryness and dyspareunia versus placebo, urinary tract infection rates fell, and endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma were extremely rare
cards.people: Systematic review (the evidence review behind clinical practice guidelines) of randomised controlled trials and prospective comparative studies of vaginal estrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause: 1,805 abstracts screened, 44 eligible studies included. Interventions covered all commercially available vaginal estrogen products; comparators included placebo, no treatment, systemic estrogen (all routes) and nonhormonal moisturizers and lubricants. Outcomes included patient-reported atrophy symptoms (vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, dysuria, urgency, frequency, recurrent urinary tract infection, incontinence), objective signs, endometrial effects, serum estradiol changes and adverse events.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, vaginal estrogens improved dryness, dyspareunia, urinary urgency, frequency, and stress and urgency urinary incontinence, and urinary tract infection rates decreased. The various estrogen preparations had similar efficacy and safety; serum estradiol levels remained within postmenopausal norms for all except high-dose conjugated equine estrogen cream. Endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma were extremely rare among those receiving vaginal estrogen. Against nonhormonal moisturizers, patients with two or more atrophy symptoms were substantially more improved on vaginal estrogen, while those with one or minor complaints had similar resolution with either. No single pooled effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: 'Extremely rare' endometrial events come from trials and comparative studies mostly far shorter than a lifetime of use, and the one preparation that pushed serum estradiol above postmenopausal norms — high-dose conjugated equine estrogen cream — is a reminder that 'vaginal' is not automatically 'low-dose'.
cards.source: Rahn DD et al. Vaginal estrogen for genitourinary syndrome of menopause: a systematic review. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2014. PMID: 25415166. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42013006656. cards.headline: Bachmann 2008: estradiol vaginal tablets 25 mcg and 10 mcg both significantly improved the composite vaginal-health score versus placebo in 230 postmenopausal women over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Bachmann 2008: estradiol vaginal tablets 25 mcg and 10 mcg both significantly improved the composite vaginal-health score versus placebo in 230 postmenopausal women over 12 weeks
cards.people: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group trial: 230 postmenopausal women received 25 mcg estradiol, 10 mcg estradiol or placebo vaginal tablets for 12 weeks; efficacy was measured by a composite score of three vaginal symptoms and grading of vaginal health, plus maturation of vaginal and urethral mucosa. Safety assessments included endometrial biopsy, adverse events, laboratory tests and physical examination; after 12 weeks all patients switched to open-label 25 mcg estradiol up to week 52. The record names the products by dose and formulation (estradiol vaginal tablets); no brand name is given in the record.
cards.result: Both 25 mcg and 10 mcg estradiol tablets showed significant (P < .001) improvement in the composite score of vaginal health versus placebo; other results with 10 mcg were not entirely consistent with those for 25 mcg. Over 12 weeks, both active treatments produced greater decreases in vaginal pH than placebo, and there were no significant differences between the 25 mcg and 10 mcg groups in maturation value or the composite symptom score; efficacy was maintained to week 52 on 25 mcg. The authors conclude both doses were effective in atrophic vaginitis, with improvements greater at 25 mcg. No exact symptom-score values are reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Twelve blinded weeks answer dryness and vaginal health, not long-term systemic safety: the endometrial biopsies and laboratory tests were safety assessments in a short trial, and the 52-week phase was open-label on the higher dose.
cards.source: Bachmann G et al. Efficacy of low-dose estradiol vaginal tablets in the treatment of atrophic vaginitis: a randomized controlled trial. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2008. PMID: 18165394. Registry ID: NCT00465192 and NCT00464971. cards.headline: Santen 2020: systemic estradiol on low-dose vaginal products is dose-dependent and low — about 4.6 to 14.8 pg/mL on the 10-mcg tablet by sensitive assays, against an untreated postmenopausal range estimated up to about 10.7 pg/mL
cards.summary: Santen 2020: systemic estradiol on low-dose vaginal products is dose-dependent and low — about 4.6 to 14.8 pg/mL on the 10-mcg tablet by sensitive assays, against an untreated postmenopausal range estimated up to about 10.7 pg/mL
cards.type: Systematic review of systemic estradiol levels (Santen 2020)
cards.people: Critical review of published systemic estradiol levels during use of low-dose vaginal estrogens (25 mcg or less estradiol, or 0.3 mg or less conjugated equine estrogens), evaluating detection method and dose; estradiol at baseline and during treatment, area under the curve and maximum concentrations were summarised by dose within assay type, and a normal untreated postmenopausal range was estimated by pooling published studies. Formulations in the record are named by dose and type (softgel capsule inserts and tablet inserts); brand names are not given in the record.
cards.result: Mean basal estradiol was 3.1 to 4.9 pg/mL by liquid or gas chromatography/mass spectrometry, ranging to 10.5 pg/mL by radioimmunoassay. By sensitive assays, systemic estradiol ran 7.1 to 9.1 pg/mL (25-mcg softgel capsule) and 16.7 to 22.7 pg/mL (25-mcg tablet); 4.6 to 7.4 pg/mL (10-mcg softgel capsule) and 6.6 to 14.8 pg/mL (10-mcg tablet); and 3.6 to 3.9 pg/mL (4-mcg softgel capsule). A mean systemic estradiol from undetectable to 10.7 pg/mL is proposed as the basal range in normal untreated postmenopausal women. Absorption may be influenced by placement higher versus lower in the vagina. The authors conclude very low systemic absorption with low/ultralow-dose products may potentially decrease any adverse events associated with higher doses. Blood levels are reported in pg/mL in the record; no mmol/L values occur.
cards.watchOut: Blood level is a surrogate: showing estradiol stays near the postmenopausal range does not by itself prove the absence of long-term systemic risk, and older radioimmunoassay numbers in the literature overstate levels compared with mass-spectrometry assays — the review's central caution.
cards.source: Santen RJ et al. Systemic estradiol levels with low-dose vaginal estrogens. Menopause. 2020. PMID: 31794498. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Handa 1994: 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens three nights a week relieved atrophic vaginitis in 19 of 20 women with no significant change in serum estrogens or endometrial thickness — but one endometrial proliferation (N = 20, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Handa 1994: 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens three nights a week relieved atrophic vaginitis in 19 of 20 women with no significant change in serum estrogens or endometrial thickness — but one endometrial proliferation (N = 20, printed on the face)
cards.people: 20 postmenopausal women with symptoms, signs and cytologic evidence of atrophic vaginitis, each treated with 0.3 mg of conjugated estrogens administered vaginally three nights per week for six months; pre- and post-treatment data were compared within each subject. Outcomes: symptoms, vaginal cytologic maturity, endometrial histology, sonographic endometrial thickness, Doppler uterine artery blood flow, and serum estrone and estradiol. N = 20.
cards.result: Satisfactory relief of symptoms occurred in 19 of 20 cases, and vaginal cellular maturation improved significantly (P < .01). There were no significant changes in endometrial thickness, uterine artery blood flow, or serum estrogen levels. Endometrial proliferation was observed in one case. The authors conclude relief can be achieved with 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens three times weekly, and that endometrial proliferation may occur at this low dose, albeit rarely.
cards.watchOut: Twenty women, no control group, 1994: the one-in-twenty proliferation is a signal to respect, not a rate to quote — and this older conjugated-estrogen regimen is not the ultralow-dose estradiol tablet evidence carded above.
cards.source: Handa VL et al. Vaginal administration of low-dose conjugated estrogens: systemic absorption and effects on the endometrium. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 1994. PMID: 8041532. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: vaginal estrogen relieves dryness (44-study review plus a 230-woman randomised trial), systemic estradiol stays within or near the postmenopausal range at low doses, and endometrial events are extremely rare — with one small-study proliferation signal kept on the face
cards.summary: Synthesis: vaginal estrogen relieves dryness (44-study review plus a 230-woman randomised trial), systemic estradiol stays within or near the postmenopausal range at low doses, and endometrial events are extremely rare — with one small-study proliferation signal kept on the face
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of 44 studies, one randomised placebo-controlled trial (N = 230), one assay-critical review of systemic estradiol levels, and one small prospective study (N = 20). Total documented participants exceed 250 on the two counting studies alone, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the smallest study's N is printed on its face.
cards.result: Vaginal estrogens improved dryness and dyspareunia versus placebo with extremely rare endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma (Rahn 2014); 10 mcg and 25 mcg estradiol tablets both beat placebo on vaginal health (P < .001; Bachmann 2008); systemic estradiol on the 10-mcg tablet ran about 4.6 to 14.8 pg/mL by sensitive assays (Santen 2020); and 0.3 mg conjugated estrogens relieved 19 of 20 women with one endometrial proliferation (Handa 1994). Safety in breast-cancer survivors stays on live shelf #2736. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — efficacy concordant, systemic exposure low at the doses carded, long-term randomised safety outcomes absent.
cards.watchOut: The safety half of this shelf rests on blood levels and short-trial endometrial assessments, not on randomised long-term outcome trials — 'without increasing systemic estrogen risks' is supported as far as exposure and rare-event data go, and no further.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rahn DD et al. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2014 (PMID: 25415166); Bachmann G et al. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2008 (PMID: 18165394); Santen RJ et al. Menopause. 2020 (PMID: 31794498); Handa VL et al. Obstetrics and Gynecology. 1994 (PMID: 8041532).

shelves.title: Embolization versus hysterectomy, long term (partial completion of #830): quality of life equal at five and ten years — one in three embolization patients eventually has the hysterectomy
shelves.question: In women with uterine fibroids, does uterine artery embolization preserve quality of life as well as hysterectomy in the long term?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Status · Humans · Hysterectomy · Leiomyoma · Menorrhagia · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Quality of Life · Retreatment · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Uterine Artery Embolization · Uterine Neoplasms
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #830, whose randomised comparison is uterine artery embolization (UAE) versus myomectomy (FEMME) with the EMMY two-year report riding along; this shelf asks the comparison #830 does not isolate — UAE versus hysterectomy over the long term. The EMMY trial followed its randomised women for a decade: at five years (van der Kooij 2010) health-related quality of life had improved significantly in both groups and remained stable with no differences between them, while 28.4% of UAE patients had undergone hysterectomy for insufficient improvement; at ten years (de Bruijn 2016) quality of life remained comparably stable with no between-group differences and comparable satisfaction (78% versus 87% at least satisfied), with 35% of the UAE group having had a secondary hysterectomy in total — meaning about two-thirds avoided hysterectomy altogether. The REST trial (Edwards 2007) found no significant difference in any SF-36 component at one year against a surgical group that was mostly hysterectomy (43 of 51), with faster recovery after embolization and 9% needing reintervention within the year; the four-trial meta-analysis (van der Kooij 2011, 515 patients) agrees: comparable mid- and long-term quality of life and equal satisfaction, at the price of a higher reintervention rate after UAE. The FEMME myomectomy comparison stays on #830 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (as good as hysterectomy for long-term quality of life): quality of life after UAE matches hysterectomy at five and ten years in the only long-term randomised record, with the trade-off — roughly one in three women eventually needs a hysterectomy — printed on the face of the stamp and every card.

cards.headline: de Bruijn 2016 (EMMY, 10 years): quality of life remained comparably stable after embolization and hysterectomy with no between-group differences — and 35% of the embolization group had eventually had a hysterectomy
cards.summary: de Bruijn 2016 (EMMY, 10 years): quality of life remained comparably stable after embolization and hysterectomy with no between-group differences — and 35% of the embolization group had eventually had a hysterectomy
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 10-year follow-up (de Bruijn 2016, EMMY)
cards.people: Ten-year follow-up of the randomised EMMY trial: 177 patients with symptomatic uterine fibroids who were eligible for hysterectomy, recruited at 28 Dutch hospitals and randomised 1:1 to uterine artery embolization or hysterectomy from 2002 through 2004; 81 embolization and 75 hysterectomy patients underwent the allocated treatment. Outcomes at ten years — reintervention rates, health-related quality of life and satisfaction, by validated questionnaires — were analysed by original assignment; questionnaires were received from 131 of 156 patients (84%), with mean follow-up 133 months.
cards.result: Ten years after treatment, five further patients had undergone secondary hysterectomy, bringing the total to 28 of 81 (35%) in the embolization group (24 of 77, 31%, after successful embolization); secondary hysterectomies were performed for persisting symptoms in all cases but one (prolapse). After the initial treatment, health-related quality of life improved significantly; after ten years, generic health-related quality of life remained stable, without differences between the groups, and urogenital and defecation distress scores decreased in both groups without significant differences. Satisfaction remained comparable: 78% of the embolization group versus 87% of the hysterectomy group declared being (very) satisfied. The authors conclude that in about two-thirds of embolization-treated patients a hysterectomy can be avoided, with comparably stable quality of life at ten years.
cards.watchOut: Quality-of-life equivalence at ten years is partly achieved by the one in three embolization patients who crossed to hysterectomy along the way — analysed by original assignment, as randomised, which is the honest comparison of strategies, not of procedures received.
cards.source: de Bruijn AM et al. Uterine artery embolization vs hysterectomy in the treatment of symptomatic uterine fibroids: 10-year outcomes from the randomized EMMY trial. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2016. PMID: 27393268. Registry ID: none in the record. questionnaires were received from 131 of 156 patients (84%), with mean follow-up 133 months. ten years after treatment, five further patients had undergone secondary hysterectomy, bringing the total to 28 of 81 (35%) in the embolization group (24 of 77, 31%, after successful embolization); secondary hysterectomies were performed for persisting symptoms in all cases but one (prolapse). after the initial treatment, health-related quality of life improved significantly; after ten years, generic health-related quality of life remained stable, without differences between the groups, and urogenital and defecation distress scores decreased in both groups without significant differences. satisfaction remained comparable: 78% of the embolization group versus 87% of the hysterectomy group declared being (very) satisfied. the authors conclude that in about two-thirds of embolization-treated patients a hysterectomy can be avoided, with comparably stable quality of life at ten years. quality-of-life equivalence at ten years is partly achieved by the one in three embolization patients who crossed to hysterectomy along the way — analysed by original assignment, as randomised, which is the honest comparison of strategies, not of procedures received. de bruijn am et al. uterine artery embolization vs hysterectomy in the treatment of symptomatic uterine fibroids: 10-year outcomes from the randomized emmy trial. american journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2016. pmid: 27393268. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · cost-benefit analysis · female · follow-up studies · health status · humans · hysterectomy · leiomyoma · menorrhagia · middle aged · patient satisfaction · quality of life · retreatment · surveys and questionnaires · treatment outcome · uterine artery embolization · uterine neoplasms

cards.headline: van der Kooij 2010 (EMMY, 5 years): quality of life improved and stayed stable with no differences between groups — while 28.4% of embolization patients had had a hysterectomy by five years
cards.summary: van der Kooij 2010 (EMMY, 5 years): quality of life improved and stayed stable with no differences between groups — while 28.4% of embolization patients had had a hysterectomy by five years
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 5-year follow-up (van der Kooij 2010, EMMY)
cards.people: Five-year follow-up of the randomised EMMY trial: patients with symptomatic uterine fibroids eligible for hysterectomy, randomised 1:1 to uterine artery embolization (n = 88) or hysterectomy (n = 89). Endpoints at five years were reintervention rates, menorrhagia, and health-related quality of life assessed by validated questionnaires.
cards.result: Five years after treatment, 23 of 81 embolization patients (28.4%) had undergone a hysterectomy because of insufficient improvement of complaints (24.7% after successful embolization). Health-related quality of life measures improved significantly and remained stable until the five-year follow-up, with no differences between the groups. Embolization had a positive effect on both urinary and defecation function. The authors conclude embolization is a well-established alternative to hysterectomy about which patients should be counselled.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, earlier timepoint as the ten-year card — the two EMMY cards are one randomised cohort read twice, not two independent trials; the independent corroboration on this shelf is REST and the meta-analysis.
cards.source: van der Kooij SM et al. Uterine artery embolization vs hysterectomy in the treatment of symptomatic uterine fibroids: 5-year outcome from the randomized EMMY trial. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2010. PMID: 20579960. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Edwards 2007 (REST): no significant difference in any SF-36 quality-of-life component at one year versus surgery (43 of 51 operations were hysterectomies) — with faster recovery and 9% needing reintervention within the year
cards.summary: Edwards 2007 (REST): no significant difference in any SF-36 quality-of-life component at one year versus surgery (43 of 51 operations were hysterectomies) — with faster recovery and 9% needing reintervention within the year
cards.people: Randomised trial (REST) comparing uterine-artery embolization with surgery in women with symptomatic uterine fibroids, randomised 2:1: 106 patients underwent embolization and 51 underwent surgery (43 hysterectomies and 8 myomectomies). The primary outcome was quality of life at one year on the Medical Outcomes Study 36-Item Short-Form General Health Survey (SF-36).
cards.result: There were no significant differences between groups in any of the eight components of the SF-36 at one year. The embolization group had a shorter median hospital stay (1 day versus 5 days, P < .001) and a shorter time before returning to work (P < .001); symptom scores at one year were better in the surgical group (P = .03). Major adverse events in the first year numbered 13 (12%) on embolization and 10 (20%) on surgery (P = .22). Ten embolization patients (9%) required repeated embolization or hysterectomy for inadequate symptom control within the year, and after the first year 14 (13%) required hospitalisation, 11 for reintervention for treatment failure. The authors conclude the faster recovery after embolization must be weighed against the need for further treatment in a minority.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is surgery, not hysterectomy alone — eight of 51 operations were myomectomies, printed here — and one year is not the long term; this card corroborates the early quality-of-life equivalence that EMMY then extends to a decade.
cards.source: Edwards RD et al. Uterine-artery embolization versus surgery for symptomatic uterine fibroids. New England Journal of Medicine. 2007. PMID: 17251532. Registry ID: ISRCTN23023665. cards.headline: van der Kooij 2011: across four randomised trials (515 patients), mid- and long-term quality of life was comparable and satisfaction equal — with a higher reintervention rate after embolization
cards.summary: van der Kooij 2011: across four randomised trials (515 patients), mid- and long-term quality of life was comparable and satisfaction equal — with a higher reintervention rate after embolization
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (van der Kooij 2011)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials comparing uterine artery embolization with hysterectomy or myomectomy in premenopausal women with heavy menstrual bleeding caused by symptomatic uterine fibroids (searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE and EMBASE, September 1995 to November 2010): four randomised trials, 515 patients in total.
cards.result: On the short term, embolization showed less blood loss, shorter hospital stay and quicker resumption of work. Mid- and long-term results showed comparable health-related quality of life and a higher reintervention rate in the embolization group, whereas both groups were equally satisfied. The authors conclude embolization has short-term advantages over surgery, and on the mid and long term the benefits were similar except for the higher reintervention rate after embolization. No pooled quality-of-life effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: The pooled comparator mixes hysterectomy and myomectomy trials and the window closes at five years — the ten-year hysterectomy-specific answer comes from the EMMY card above, not from this pool.
cards.source: van der Kooij SM et al. Uterine artery embolization versus surgery in the treatment of symptomatic fibroids: a systematic review and metaanalysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: quality of life after embolization matches hysterectomy at five and ten years in the randomised record — the price of keeping the uterus is a roughly one-in-three chance of eventually needing the hysterectomy anyway
cards.summary: Synthesis: quality of life after embolization matches hysterectomy at five and ten years in the randomised record — the price of keeping the uterus is a roughly one-in-three chance of eventually needing the hysterectomy anyway
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised cohort followed to five and ten years (EMMY; 177 randomised, 156 treated, 84% questionnaire response at ten years), one independent randomised trial against mostly-hysterectomy surgery (REST; 157 treated), and one four-trial meta-analysis (515 patients). Unique randomised participants total roughly 690 across the independent trials and the pool, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Health-related quality of life improved in both EMMY groups and remained stable and indistinguishable at five years (van der Kooij 2010) and ten years (de Bruijn 2016), with satisfaction 78% versus 87% at ten years; REST found no SF-36 difference at one year (Edwards 2007); and the meta-analysis found comparable mid- and long-term quality of life with equal satisfaction (van der Kooij 2011). Against that equivalence stand the reintervention counts: 28.4% hysterectomy by five years and 35% by ten years after embolization. The myomectomy comparison (FEMME) stays on live shelf #830. PROPOSED LIKELY (as good as hysterectomy for long-term quality of life) — with the reintervention trade-off on the face.
cards.watchOut: 'As good as hysterectomy' describes the strategy as randomised — embolization first, hysterectomy later if needed — not a promise that embolization alone resolves symptoms for every woman; women for whom avoiding any later operation matters most are the group this trade-off cuts against.
cards.source: Synthesis of de Bruijn AM et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2016 (PMID: 27393268); van der Kooij SM et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2010 (PMID: 20579960); Edwards RD et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17251532); van der Kooij SM et al. American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2011 (PMID: 21641570).

shelves.title: Vaginal progesterone for preterm birth beyond the short cervix (PARTIAL completion of live #418): pooled benefit in high-risk singletons, a null largest trial, and no benefit in twins
shelves.question: In women at risk of preterm birth, does vaginal progesterone reduce preterm delivery?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravaginal · Adult · Brain Injuries · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Death · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Pregnancy, High-Risk · Premature Birth · Progesterone · Progestins · Risk Factors · Sweden · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: SPLIT (population: pooled benefit in high-risk singletons; no benefit in the largest single trial's primary outcomes or in twins) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #418 already answers vaginal progesterone for singleton pregnancies with a short cervix (≤25 mm) at the patient level; this shelf asks the wider question — women at risk for any reason. The widest test, OPPTIMUM (1,228 women at risk through previous preterm birth, short cervix, or positive fetal fibronectin with risk factors), found no significant effect on its obstetric, neonatal or childhood primary outcomes (the treatment made no difference). The patient-level pooling of 31 trials (EPPPIC, 11,644 women) found vaginal progesterone did reduce preterm birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singleton pregnancies (relative risk 0.78), with the largest absolute gains where baseline risk is highest — the short-cervix group homed on #418. In twins, both EPPPIC (relative risk 1.01) and the dedicated PREDICT trial (15.3% vs 18.5%) found no benefit (the treatment made no difference). PROPOSED SPLIT (population): vaginal progesterone reduces early preterm birth in pooled high-risk singleton pregnancies, but the largest broad-population trial was null on its primary outcomes and there is no benefit in twin pregnancies.

cards.headline: OPPTIMUM 2016: in 1,228 women at risk of preterm birth for mixed reasons, vaginal progesterone made no difference to the obstetric, neonatal or childhood primary outcomes
cards.summary: OPPTIMUM 2016: in 1,228 women at risk of preterm birth for mixed reasons, vaginal progesterone made no difference to the obstetric, neonatal or childhood primary outcomes
cards.people: 1,228 women at risk of preterm birth because of previous spontaneous birth at ≤34 weeks, or a cervical length ≤25 mm, or a positive fetal fibronectin test combined with other clinical risk factors, randomised in a multicentre double-blind trial to vaginal progesterone 200 mg daily from 22–24 to 34 weeks (n = 618) or placebo (n = 610).
cards.result: Progesterone had no significant effect on the primary obstetric outcome, fetal death or birth before 34 weeks (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.61–1.22, after correction for multiple outcomes), or on the neonatal composite of death, brain injury or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.38–1.03), and no effect on cognitive score at 2 years (97.3 vs 97.7; difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.77 to 1.81) — the treatment made no difference on any primary outcome. Serious adverse events were similar (10% progesterone vs 11% placebo).
cards.watchOut: OPPTIMUM mixed three risk routes into one population, most recruited through previous preterm birth rather than a measured short cervix; a null average here does not erase the short-cervix subgroup evidence homed on live shelf #418 — and the pooled benefit on the next card does not erase this trial's null primaries.
cards.source: Norman JE et al. Vaginal progesterone prophylaxis for preterm birth (the OPPTIMUM study): a multicentre, randomised, double-blind trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 26921136. Registry ID: ISRCTN14568373. cards.headline: EPPPIC 2021: pooling 31 trials at the patient level, vaginal progesterone reduced preterm birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singleton pregnancies (relative risk 0.78) — but not in twins (relative risk 1.01)
cards.summary: EPPPIC 2021: pooling 31 trials at the patient level, vaginal progesterone reduced preterm birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singleton pregnancies (relative risk 0.78) — but not in twins (relative risk 1.01)
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials (EPPPIC 2021)
cards.people: Individual participant data from 31 randomised trials (11,644 women, 16,185 offspring) of vaginal progesterone, intramuscular 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate, or oral progesterone versus control in asymptomatic women at risk of preterm birth; singleton trials mostly enrolled women with previous spontaneous preterm birth or a short cervix, and multifetal trials mostly women without additional risk factors.
cards.result: In high-risk singleton pregnancies, preterm birth before 34 weeks was reduced by vaginal progesterone (nine trials, 3,769 women; relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.68–0.90), by 17-hydroxyprogesterone caproate (five trials, 3,053 women; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.68–1.01) and by oral progesterone (two trials, 181 women; RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.40–0.90), with other birth and neonatal outcomes consistently favourable but less certain; the record reports relative risks without the absolute event rates for this comparison. In twins, vaginal progesterone did not reduce preterm birth before 34 weeks (eight trials, 2,046 women; RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84–1.20) — the treatment made no difference — and analyses within subpopulations questioned efficacy in women who did not have a short cervix.
cards.watchOut: The singleton estimate pools trials dominated by previous-preterm-birth and short-cervix populations, so it cannot be read as proof of benefit for every at-risk woman; the collaboration itself notes the greatest absolute benefit falls where baseline risk — and a short cervix — is present, which is the population live shelf #418 already homes.
cards.source: EPPPIC Group et al. Evaluating Progestogens for Preventing Preterm birth International Collaborative (EPPPIC): meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomised controlled trials. Lancet (London, England). 2021. PMID: 33773630. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PREDICT 2011: in 677 twin pregnancies, vaginal progesterone did not prevent delivery before 34 weeks — 15.3% vs 18.5% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: PREDICT 2011: in 677 twin pregnancies, vaginal progesterone did not prevent delivery before 34 weeks — 15.3% vs 18.5% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 677 women with twin gestations in 17 centres in Denmark and Austria, randomised double-blind to daily vaginal micronised progesterone pessaries or identical placebo from 20–24 weeks until 34 weeks; primary outcome was delivery before 34 weeks.
cards.result: Delivery before 34 weeks occurred in 15.3% of the progesterone group and 18.5% of the placebo group (odds ratio 0.8, 95% CI 0.5–1.2) — not significant; the treatment made no difference. Maternal and neonatal complication risks were comparable, infant Ages and Stages scores at 6 and 18 months did not differ, and the authors' updated meta-analysis of twin trials gave a pooled odds ratio of 1.06 (95% CI 0.86–1.31).
cards.watchOut: PREDICT enrolled unselected twins without additional risk factors; it answers the twin question as asked, but it does not test progesterone in twins who also have a short cervix, a much smaller and separate group.
cards.source: Rode L et al. Prevention of preterm delivery in twin gestations (PREDICT): a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial on the effect of vaginal micronized progesterone. cards.headline: Synthesis: across the wider at-risk population the evidence divides by pregnancy type — pooled singleton benefit, a null largest trial, and no twin benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: across the wider at-risk population the evidence divides by pregnancy type — pooled singleton benefit, a null largest trial, and no twin benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large broad-population randomised trial (OPPTIMUM, 1,228 women), one individual-participant meta-analysis of 31 trials (EPPPIC, 11,644 women), and one dedicated twin trial (PREDICT, 677 women). Total carded participants exceed 13,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: EPPPIC's patient-level pooling found vaginal progesterone reduced preterm birth before 34 weeks in high-risk singletons (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.68–0.90), while OPPTIMUM — the largest single trial in a mixed-risk population — found no significant effect on its obstetric (OR 0.86), neonatal (OR 0.62) or childhood primary outcomes, and both EPPPIC (twins RR 1.01) and PREDICT (15.3% vs 18.5%) found no benefit in twins. The singleton short-cervix slice of this question is homed on live shelf #418 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT (population): benefit in pooled high-risk singleton pregnancies; no demonstrated benefit in the largest broad trial's primary outcomes or in twin pregnancies.
cards.watchOut: The split is the finding: quoting only the pooled singleton relative risk, or only OPPTIMUM's null, each misstates the wider-population answer this shelf was built to give.
cards.source: Synthesis of Norman JE et al. Lancet (London, England). 2016 (PMID: 26921136); EPPPIC Group et al. Lancet (London, England). 2021 (PMID: 33773630); Rode L et al. shelves.title: HPV every 5 years versus Pap every 3 years (PARTIAL completion of live #1348): the longer HPV interval protects at least as well — a negative HPV test carries less 5-year cancer risk than a negative Pap carries in 3
shelves.question: For cervical cancer screening, is primary HPV testing every 5 years as effective as Pap testing every 3 years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Colposcopy · Cytological Techniques · Early Detection of Cancer · Europe · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Incidence · Middle Aged · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Neoplasm Invasiveness · Papillomavirus Infections · Precancerous Conditions · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Uterine Cervical Neoplasms · Young Adult · Uterine Cervical Dysplasia
shelves.balance: LIKELY — on the interval question as asked. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1348 already answers whether primary HPV testing beats cytology at detecting CIN3+ by 48 months (the HPV FOCAL trial); this shelf asks the different question FOCAL cannot answer — whether stretching the HPV interval to 5 years gives up the protection that 3-yearly cytology provides. Three randomised-programme records answer it directly. Pooled across four European trials (176,464 women), HPV-based screening cut invasive cervical cancer versus cytology (rate ratio 0.60, a relative measure), and among women negative at entry the cumulative cancer incidence at 5.5 years was 8.7 per 100,000 after a negative HPV test versus 36.0 per 100,000 after negative cytology — the 5-year HPV-negative risk sitting below the 3.5-year cytology-negative risk (15.4 per 100,000). In Swedescreen's 13-year follow-up, the sensitivity of HPV testing at five years (86.40% for CIN2+) matched cytology at three years (85.94%), with cumulative CIN2+ incidence eventually identical — earlier detection, not overdiagnosis. And in POBASCAM's 14-year follow-up, HPV-negative women screened in 5-yearly rounds carried the same cancer incidence (0.09%) as cytology-negative women after fewer rounds. PROPOSED LIKELY: primary HPV testing every 5 years is at least as effective as Pap testing every 3 years at preventing invasive cervical cancer.

cards.headline: Ronco 2014: pooled across four European randomised trials (176,464 women), HPV-based screening prevented more invasive cervical cancer than cytology — and a negative HPV test protected longer than a negative Pap
cards.summary: Ronco 2014: pooled across four European randomised trials (176,464 women), HPV-based screening prevented more invasive cervical cancer than cytology — and a negative HPV test protected longer than a negative Pap
cards.type: Pooled follow-up of four randomised controlled trials (Ronco 2014)
cards.people: 176,464 women aged 20–64 randomised to HPV-based or cytology-based screening in Sweden (Swedescreen), the Netherlands (POBASCAM), England (ARTISTIC) and Italy (NTCC), followed for a median of 6.5 years (1,214,415 person-years) with 107 invasive cervical cancers identified.
cards.result: The rate ratio for invasive cervical carcinoma, HPV-based versus cytology-based screening, was 0.60 (95% CI 0.40–0.89) overall — a 40% relative reduction — with detection similar in the first 2.5 years (0.79, 95% CI 0.46–1.36) and significantly lower thereafter (0.45, 95% CI 0.25–0.81). In women with a negative entry test the rate ratio was 0.30 (95% CI 0.15–0.60), and cumulative cancer incidence in that group was 8.7 per 100,000 at 5.5 years in the HPV arm versus 36.0 per 100,000 in the cytology arm (at 3.5 years: 4.6 vs 15.4 per 100,000) — the absolute rates show a woman negative on HPV carried less risk after 5.5 years than a woman negative on cytology carried after 3.5. The authors conclude the data support HPV-based screening from age 30 with intervals extended to at least 5 years.
cards.watchOut: The four trials used different HPV assays, triage rules and background cytology intervals, and the pooled endpoint is invasive cancer over a median 6.5 years — the interval inference comes from the negative-test risk curves, not from a trial that randomised women to 5-yearly HPV versus 3-yearly Pap as such.
cards.source: Ronco G et al. Efficacy of HPV-based screening for prevention of invasive cervical cancer: follow-up of four European randomised controlled trials. Lancet (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24192252. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Elfström 2014 (Swedescreen, 13-year follow-up): HPV testing at five years matched cytology at three years for sensitivity — 86.40% vs 85.94% for CIN2+ — and cumulative CIN2+ incidence ended identical
cards.summary: Elfström 2014 (Swedescreen, 13-year follow-up): HPV testing at five years matched cytology at three years for sensitivity — 86.40% vs 85.94% for CIN2+ — and cumulative CIN2+ incidence ended identical
cards.people: 12,527 women aged 32–38 in Sweden's organised screening programme, randomised to HPV-plus-cytology double testing (n = 6,257) or cytology only with samples frozen for later HPV testing (n = 6,270), followed for 13 years.
cards.result: The longitudinal sensitivity of cytology for CIN2+ at three years (85.94%, 95% CI 76.85%–91.84%) was similar to the sensitivity of HPV testing at five years (86.40%, 95% CI 79.21%–91.37%); for CIN3+, HPV at five years gave 89.34% (95% CI 80.10%–94.58%) versus cytology at three years 92.02% (95% CI 80.59%–96.97%). The intervention arm's early excess of CIN2+ detection decreased over time: cumulative CIN3+ incidence was similar in both arms after six years and cumulative CIN2+ after 11 years, which the authors read as earlier detection rather than overdiagnosis, with the low long-term CIN3+ risk after a negative HPV test supporting five-year intervals.
cards.watchOut: The intervention arm received HPV and cytology together, so the five-year sensitivity figure is for HPV testing read out of a double-testing trial; and the cohort is one age band (32–38) in one organised programme.
cards.source: Elfström KM et al. Long term duration of protective effect for HPV negative women: follow-up of primary HPV screening randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2014. PMID: 24435414. Registry ID: NCT00479375. cards.headline: Dijkstra 2016 (POBASCAM, 14-year follow-up): after three 5-yearly rounds, HPV-negative women had the same cervical cancer incidence (0.09%) as cytology-negative women after two rounds
cards.summary: Dijkstra 2016 (POBASCAM, 14-year follow-up): after three 5-yearly rounds, HPV-negative women had the same cervical cancer incidence (0.09%) as cytology-negative women after two rounds
cards.people: 43,339 women aged 29–61 with a negative HPV and/or negative cytology test in the Dutch POBASCAM randomised trial, within an organised programme of screening rounds each five years apart, randomised to HPV-plus-cytology co-testing or cytology only and followed for 14 years.
cards.result: Cumulative cervical cancer incidence among HPV-negative women in the intervention group after three rounds was 0.09%, and CIN3+ 0.56%, versus 0.09% and 0.69% among cytology-negative women in the control group after two rounds; risk ratios were 0.97 (95% CI 0.41–2.31) for cancer and 0.82 (95% CI 0.62–1.09) for CIN3+ — no significant difference. CIN3+ incidence was 72.2% lower (95% CI 61.6%–79.9%) among HPV-negative women aged 40 or older than among younger HPV-negative women, and the authors conclude the low long-term risks support extending the interval beyond five years for women aged 40 and older, with risk stratification for HPV-positive women.
cards.watchOut: The Dutch programme's standard round is already five years, so this record tests the safety of HPV-based rounds at and beyond five years against cytology rounds — it supports the interval claim for organised programmes, and its beyond-five-years conclusion is drawn for women aged 40 and older specifically.
cards.source: Dijkstra MG et al. Safety of extending screening intervals beyond five years in cervical screening programmes with testing for high risk human papillomavirus: 14 year follow-up of population based randomised cohort in the Netherlands. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2016. PMID: 27702796. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a negative HPV test buys at least five years of protection at or below the risk a negative Pap buys in three — the 5-year HPV interval does not give up effectiveness
cards.summary: Synthesis: a negative HPV test buys at least five years of protection at or below the risk a negative Pap buys in three — the 5-year HPV interval does not give up effectiveness
cards.people: The carded evidence: a pooled follow-up of four European randomised trials (176,464 women), the 13-year Swedescreen follow-up (12,527 women) and the 14-year POBASCAM follow-up (43,339 women) — the POBASCAM and Swedescreen cohorts also contribute to the pooled record, so participants overlap between cards by design. Total unique participants exceed 175,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: HPV-based screening reduced invasive cervical cancer versus cytology overall (rate ratio 0.60, relative), and among test-negative women the 5.5-year cumulative cancer incidence after HPV (8.7 per 100,000) was a quarter of that after cytology (36.0 per 100,000). HPV sensitivity at five years matched cytology at three years (86.40% vs 85.94% for CIN2+), and HPV-negative women kept a 0.09% cancer incidence across three 5-yearly rounds. Detection of CIN3+ by 48 months — the HPV FOCAL question — is homed on live shelf #1348 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY: primary HPV testing every 5 years is at least as effective as Pap testing every 3 years.
cards.watchOut: No trial randomised the exact pair 'HPV every 5 years' versus 'Pap every 3 years' as standalone arms; the answer is assembled from cancer outcomes, negative-test risk curves and matched-interval sensitivity in organised European programmes, and intervals for HPV-positive women still need triage and earlier recall.

shelves.title: Levonorgestrel IUD versus tranexamic acid for heavy menstrual bleeding (PARTIAL completion of live #2490): the IUD cut blood loss further at 6 months (85.8% vs 60.8%) in the one small head-to-head trial
shelves.question: In women using an IUD, does the levonorgestrel IUD reduce heavy menstrual bleeding more than oral tranexamic acid?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anemia · Female · Hemostatics · Humans · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel · Menorrhagia · Middle Aged · Norethindrone · Reproductive Control Agents · Tranexamic Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the direct head-to-head rests on one small randomised trial, printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2490 already answers tranexamic acid versus placebo and versus norethisterone; this shelf asks the comparison #2490 does not make — tranexamic acid head-to-head against the levonorgestrel intrauterine system. In the one direct three-arm trial (84 women enrolled, 62 evaluated), six months of the levonorgestrel system cut measured blood loss by 85.8% against 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 53.1% on norethisterone, and it corrected anaemia more efficiently than tranexamic acid. The large pragmatic ECLIPSE trial (571 women) points the same way against usual medical treatment as a bundle — a 13.4-point advantage on the Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale at two years — but its usual-treatment arm mixed tranexamic acid with mefenamic acid, combined hormonal contraception and progesterone alone, so it cannot isolate tranexamic acid, and its advantage was no longer significant by five years (3.9 points) or at ten. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the levonorgestrel IUD probably reduces heavy menstrual bleeding more than oral tranexamic acid, on one small direct trial supported by a large pragmatic trial against mixed usual treatment.

cards.headline: Kiseli 2016: the direct head-to-head — at 6 months the levonorgestrel IUD had cut blood loss by 85.8%, against 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 53.1% on norethisterone (small trial, N on the face)
cards.summary: Kiseli 2016: the direct head-to-head — at 6 months the levonorgestrel IUD had cut blood loss by 85.8%, against 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 53.1% on norethisterone (small trial, N on the face)
cards.people: Women with idiopathic heavy menstrual bleeding randomised to norethisterone, tranexamic acid, or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for 6 months; 28 women were enrolled in each of the three groups (84 total) and the results of 62 were evaluated. Blood loss was assessed by pictorial blood loss assessment charts and haematological parameters at 1, 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: At the 6th month, menstrual blood loss had fallen by 53.1% on norethisterone, 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 85.8% on the levonorgestrel system; the levonorgestrel system was more effective than both oral treatments at decreasing blood loss, and more efficient than tranexamic acid at correcting anaemia related to menorrhagia. Satisfaction rates were comparable (70% norethisterone, 63% tranexamic acid, 77% levonorgestrel system), and quality of life in physical aspects increased significantly in the tranexamic acid and levonorgestrel groups. The record reports percentage reductions without the groups' absolute blood-loss values.
cards.watchOut: Only 62 of 84 randomised women were evaluated, the trial is single-centre and unblinded by design (a device versus tablets), and pictorial-chart percentage reductions in a small sample can overstate a device advantage — this card is why the shelf's stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Kiseli M et al. randomised controlled trial, three arms (kiseli 2016) women with idiopathic heavy menstrual bleeding randomised to norethisterone, tranexamic acid, or the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for 6 months; 28 women were enrolled in each of the three groups (84 total) and the results of 62 were evaluated. blood loss was assessed by pictorial blood loss assessment charts and haematological parameters at 1, 3 and 6 months. at the 6th month, menstrual blood loss had fallen by 53.1% on norethisterone, 60.8% on tranexamic acid and 85.8% on the levonorgestrel system; the levonorgestrel system was more effective than both oral treatments at decreasing blood loss, and more efficient than tranexamic acid at correcting anaemia related to menorrhagia. satisfaction rates were comparable (70% norethisterone, 63% tranexamic acid, 77% levonorgestrel system), and quality of life in physical aspects increased significantly in the tranexamic acid and levonorgestrel groups. the record reports percentage reductions without the groups' absolute blood-loss values. only 62 of 84 randomised women were evaluated, the trial is single-centre and unblinded by design (a device versus tablets), and pictorial-chart percentage reductions in a small sample can overstate a device advantage — this card is why the shelf's stamp is possible, not likely. kiseli m et al. comparison of therapeutic efficacies of norethisterone, tranexamic acid and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system for the treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding: a randomized controlled study. gynecologic and obstetric investigation. 2016. pmid: 26950475. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · anemia · female · hemostatics · humans · intrauterine devices, medicated · levonorgestrel · menorrhagia · middle aged · norethindrone · reproductive control agents · tranexamic acid

cards.headline: ECLIPSE 2015: in 571 primary-care women, the levonorgestrel system beat usual medical treatment by 13.4 points on the menorrhagia scale at 2 years — but usual treatment was a mix, not tranexamic acid alone, and the gap had closed by 5 years
cards.summary: ECLIPSE 2015: in 571 primary-care women, the levonorgestrel system beat usual medical treatment by 13.4 points on the menorrhagia scale at 2 years — but usual treatment was a mix, not tranexamic acid alone, and the gap had closed by 5 years
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation (ECLIPSE; Gupta 2015)
cards.people: 571 women presenting in UK primary care with heavy menstrual bleeding, randomised pragmatically to the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system or usual medical treatment — tranexamic acid, mefenamic acid, combined oestrogen–progestogen, or progesterone alone, at the clinician's usual choice; women could subsequently swap or stop treatment. Primary outcome was the patient-reported Menorrhagia Multi-Attribute Scale (MMAS) over 2 years, reassessed at 5 years.
cards.result: MMAS scores improved significantly in both groups at all time points but were significantly greater with the levonorgestrel system over 2 years (mean difference 13.4 points, 95% CI 9.9 to 16.9; P < 0.001); by 5 years the difference had shrunk and was no longer significant (3.9 points, 95% CI −0.6 to 8.3; P = 0.09). By 5 years only 47% of women still had the system in place and 15% were still taking usual medical treatment; 5-year surgery rates were low (20%) and similar in both groups, with no significant difference in serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: ECLIPSE cannot answer this shelf's exact question on its own: tranexamic acid was only one ingredient of the usual-treatment bundle and outcomes were not reported for the tranexamic-acid subgroup, so the trial supports the direction of the head-to-head result without isolating the drug.
cards.source: Gupta JK et al. A randomised controlled trial of the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system in primary care against standard treatment for menorrhagia: the ECLIPSE trial. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2015. PMID: 26507206. Registry ID: ISRCTN86566246. cards.headline: ECLIPSE at 10 years (Kai 2022): a decade on, 29.1% had surgery and quality of life had improved in both groups with no evidence of a difference between them
cards.summary: ECLIPSE at 10 years (Kai 2022): a decade on, 29.1% had surgery and quality of life had improved in both groups with no evidence of a difference between them
cards.type: Prospective 10-year follow-up cohort of a randomised trial (ECLIPSE; Kai 2022)
cards.people: 206 women from the ECLIPSE trial cohort who completed questionnaires 10 years after randomisation to the levonorgestrel system or usual medical treatments (oral tranexamic acid, mefenamic acid, combined oestrogen–progestogen, or progesterone alone); mean age 41.9 years at baseline and 53.7 years at follow-up, demographically representative of the original 571.
cards.result: Over 10 years, 60 of 206 women (29.1%) had surgery (hysterectomy 16.5%, endometrial ablation 12.6%). Between 5 and 10 years, 43.2% had ceased all medical treatment and 42.7% used the levonorgestrel system alone or in combination; 27.2% were using it at 10 years. Quality-of-life scores improved over time with no evidence of differences between the two original groups in these or other outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Only 206 of 571 trial participants responded at 10 years, treatments crossed over freely over a decade (many usual-treatment women later used the levonorgestrel system), and menopause itself ends bleeding for much of the cohort — the 10-year record speaks to long-term management, not to the head-to-head drug comparison.
cards.source: Kai J et al. Medical treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding in primary care: 10-year data from the ECLIPSE trial. The British journal of general practice : the journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners. 2022. PMID: 36376071. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the levonorgestrel IUD very likely out-reduces tranexamic acid on blood loss at 6 months — but the proof is one small direct trial plus a large trial against a treatment bundle
cards.summary: Synthesis: the levonorgestrel IUD very likely out-reduces tranexamic acid on blood loss at 6 months — but the proof is one small direct trial plus a large trial against a treatment bundle
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small three-arm randomised trial with the exact head-to-head (84 enrolled, 62 evaluated), and one large pragmatic trial programme (571 randomised; 206 respondents at 10 years) comparing the levonorgestrel system with usual medical treatment as a bundle. Total carded participants exceed 600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, but the direct-comparison evidence base is the 62 evaluated women on the first card, which is printed there.
cards.result: Blood loss fell 85.8% on the levonorgestrel system versus 60.8% on tranexamic acid at 6 months in the direct trial (Kiseli 2016); ECLIPSE found a significant 13.4-point patient-reported advantage for the system over usual medical treatment at 2 years that was no longer significant at 5 years, with low and similar surgery rates and no between-group differences at 10 years. Tranexamic acid versus placebo and versus norethisterone is homed on live shelf #2490 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the levonorgestrel IUD reduces heavy menstrual bleeding more than oral tranexamic acid.
cards.watchOut: A bigger blinded-outcome head-to-head trial of the device against tranexamic acid alone does not exist in the records fetched; women choosing between them are trading a one-off procedure with the larger measured reduction against a tablet taken only on heavy days.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kiseli M et al. Gynecologic and obstetric investigation. 2016 (PMID: 26950475); Gupta JK et al. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2015 (PMID: 26507206); Kai J et al. The British journal of general practice : the journal of the Royal College of General Practitioners. 2022 (PMID: 36376071).

shelves.title: Syphilis in pregnancy (PARTIAL completion of live #2192): penicillin prevents congenital syphilis in 98.2% of treated pregnancies, non-penicillin treatment carries threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis — and the comparison has never been randomised
shelves.question: For syphilis in pregnancy, does penicillin prevent congenital syphilis better than other antibiotics?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, U.S. · Clinical Protocols · Female · Humans · Penicillin G Benzathine · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Prospective Studies · Remission Induction · Syphilis · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (observational) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2192, which homes penicillin versus azithromycin for early syphilis in non-pregnant adults; the pregnancy question is different, because the outcome is the baby, and no randomised trial has ever compared antibiotics for syphilis in pregnancy (the Cochrane review found 26 studies and none with comparative groups). What exists is consistent observational evidence. Prospectively, CDC benzathine penicillin regimens prevented congenital syphilis in 334 of 340 treated pregnancies (98.2%), with failures concentrated in secondary syphilis (Alexander 1999). In the large Shenzhen programme cohort, non-penicillin treatment was independently associated with about threefold higher odds of congenital syphilis (adjusted OR 3.00) and about twofold higher odds of adverse pregnancy outcomes (adjusted OR 2.16) than penicillin treatment (Qin 2014). In Shanghai, congenital syphilis occurred in 12.5% of infants whose mothers completed treatment versus 50.8% with incomplete treatment (Zhu 2010). A 5-woman case series in which every infant developed congenital syphilis after maternal azithromycin exists (Zhou 2007) but is below this library's 10-person carding floor and is therefore described here, not carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): penicillin prevents congenital syphilis better than the alternatives on all the comparative evidence available; the comparison has never been randomised.

cards.headline: Alexander 1999: CDC benzathine penicillin regimens prevented congenital syphilis in 334 of 340 treated pregnancies (98.2%) — failures clustered in secondary syphilis
cards.summary: Alexander 1999: CDC benzathine penicillin regimens prevented congenital syphilis in 334 of 340 treated pregnancies (98.2%) — failures clustered in secondary syphilis
cards.people: 340 pregnant women with untreated syphilis attending prenatal clinic at Parkland Memorial Hospital, Dallas (1987–1989), staged and treated prospectively with CDC-recommended benzathine penicillin G: 2.4 million units intramuscularly for primary, secondary or early latent syphilis, and 7.2 million units over 3 weeks for late latent syphilis. (A further 108 women were diagnosed at delivery and treated postpartum.)
cards.result: Prevention of congenital syphilis succeeded in 27 of 27 women with primary syphilis, 71 of 75 with secondary syphilis, 100 of 102 with early latent syphilis and 136 of 136 with late latent syphilis — 334 of 340 overall (98.2%). The secondary-syphilis success rate differed significantly from the other stages (P = .03); two of the six fetal treatment failures were preterm stillbirths, and the single maternal treatment failure was in an HIV-infected woman.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm prospective evaluation of penicillin only: it establishes how well penicillin works, not by itself how much better it is than another antibiotic — that comparison comes from the cohort cards below.
cards.source: Alexander JM et al. Efficacy of treatment for syphilis in pregnancy. Obstetrics and gynecology. 1999. PMID: 9916946. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shenzhen programme cohort 2014: non-penicillin treatment of maternal syphilis carried threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis (aOR 3.00) versus penicillin
cards.summary: Shenzhen programme cohort 2014: non-penicillin treatment of maternal syphilis carried threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis (aOR 3.00) versus penicillin
cards.people: Pregnant women with syphilis in Shenzhen, China, within a government mother-to-child-transmission prevention programme that screened 2,441,237 pregnant women between 2002 and 2012 (screening coverage 97.2% by 2012); determinants of congenital syphilis and adverse pregnancy outcomes were analysed in a prospective cohort from 2007 to 2012.
cards.result: Non-penicillin treatment was independently associated with congenital syphilis (adjusted odds ratio 3.00) and with adverse pregnancy outcomes (adjusted OR 2.16), as were every week of delay in treatment (aOR 2.82 for congenital syphilis), higher baseline nontreponemal antibody titres (aOR 5.65) and early syphilis (aOR 23.24). Over the programme decade, congenital syphilis in Shenzhen fell from 109.3 to 9.9 cases per 100,000 live births.
cards.watchOut: Observational: women given non-penicillin treatment (often penicillin-allergic or treated late) differ from women given penicillin, and adjustment cannot remove all of that confounding — but the direction matches the pharmacology, since most alternatives cross the placenta poorly or face macrolide resistance.
cards.source: Qin JB et al. cards.headline: Shanghai cohort 2010: congenital syphilis in 12.5% of infants after complete maternal treatment versus 50.8% after incomplete treatment
cards.summary: Shanghai cohort 2010: congenital syphilis in 12.5% of infants after complete maternal treatment versus 50.8% after incomplete treatment
cards.people: 535,537 pregnant women in Shanghai, 2002–2006, among whom 1,471 maternal syphilis cases (298.7 per 100,000 live births) and 334 congenital syphilis cases (62.4 per 100,000 live births) were identified in a prospective cohort; the programme's standard treatment was benzathine penicillin.
cards.result: The congenital syphilis rate was 12.5% in infants born to mothers with complete treatment and 50.8% in infants of mothers with incomplete treatment. Fetal death (5.5% vs 30.4%), neonatal death (0.56% vs 11.0%) and major birth defects (0.46% vs 3.8%) were likewise far lower with complete treatment. Outcomes were also better with lower initial maternal RPR titres and earlier treatment initiation.
cards.watchOut: The contrast here is complete versus incomplete treatment rather than penicillin versus a named alternative drug; it shows the penicillin programme's benefit depends on the full course being given in time, and compliance was poorer in women with less education.
cards.source: Zhu L et al. Maternal and congenital syphilis in Shanghai, China, 2002 to 2006. cards.headline: Cochrane review 2001: of 26 studies scrutinised, not one compared antibiotic regimens in pregnant women — the penicillin-versus-alternatives question has never been randomised
cards.summary: Cochrane review 2001: of 26 studies scrutinised, not one compared antibiotic regimens in pregnant women — the penicillin-versus-alternatives question has never been randomised
cards.people: Systematic review of antibiotics for syphilis diagnosed during pregnancy, searching MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane registers and specialist databases to March 2001; 26 studies met criteria for detailed scrutiny.
cards.result: None of the 26 studies met the pre-determined criteria for comparative groups, and none included comparisons between randomly allocated groups of pregnant women — there were simply no eligible trials. The reviewers conclude that while there is no doubt penicillin is effective in treating syphilis in pregnancy and preventing congenital syphilis, uncertainty remains about optimal regimens, and randomised trials comparing regimens with existing recommendations are needed.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2001; it is carded because the gap it documents — no randomised comparison in pregnancy — is the reason this shelf's stamp is capped, and no later randomised comparison in pregnancy was found in this session's searches either.
cards.source: Walker GJ. Antibiotics for syphilis diagnosed during pregnancy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2001. PMID: 11686978. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: penicillin's 98.2% prevention rate, a threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis with non-penicillin treatment, and no randomised comparison anywhere — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.summary: Synthesis: penicillin's 98.2% prevention rate, a threefold adjusted odds of congenital syphilis with non-penicillin treatment, and no randomised comparison anywhere — POSSIBLE (observational)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective single-arm penicillin study (340 pregnancies), one programme cohort within 2.44 million screened pregnancies (Shenzhen), one population cohort of 535,537 pregnancies (Shanghai), and one Cochrane review (26 studies, none comparative). Total carded participants exceed 3 million screened pregnancies, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Penicillin prevented congenital syphilis in 98.2% of prospectively treated pregnancies (Alexander 1999); non-penicillin treatment carried adjusted odds of 3.00 for congenital syphilis and 2.16 for adverse pregnancy outcomes in the Shenzhen cohort; completing treatment cut congenital syphilis from 50.8% to 12.5% in Shanghai; and the Cochrane review confirms no trial has ever randomised the comparison. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): penicillin prevents congenital syphilis better than other antibiotics on all available comparative evidence. The non-pregnant early-syphilis comparison stays homed on live shelf #2192.
cards.watchOut: Every comparative number here is observational and vulnerable to confounding by allergy status and treatment timing; the honest claim is 'better on all the evidence that exists', not 'proven better in a trial'.

shelves.title: Etonogestrel implant versus the standard 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD for long-term pregnancy prevention (PARTIAL completion of live #1337): both under 1 pregnancy per 100 woman-years for years, no demonstrated difference
shelves.question: How does the etonogestrel implant compare with the levonorgestrel IUD for long-term pregnancy prevention?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Body Mass Index · Cohort Studies · Contraceptive Agents, Female · Desogestrel · Drug Implants · Female · Humans · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated · Levonorgestrel · Middle Aged · Pregnancy · Pregnancy, Unplanned · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · United States · United States Food and Drug Administration · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1337, which homes the etonogestrel implant against the low-dose 13.5 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system on discontinuation and bleeding (Apter 2016). The slice built here is different: pregnancy prevention over years of use, against the standard 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD. No trial has randomised women to implant versus 52 mg IUD and counted pregnancies as the primary outcome, so the comparison is assembled from the one head-to-head cohort and each method's own long-term record. In the head-to-head extended-use cohort, implant users had no pregnancies in 444 woman-years of use beyond the approved duration, and 52 mg IUD users had failure rates of 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years in years 6–7 (McNicholas 2017). In the Contraceptive CHOICE cohort, intrauterine devices and implants pooled failed at 0.27 per 100 participant-years versus 4.55 for pills, patch or ring (Winner 2012). The 52 mg IUD's own 7-year randomised record gives a cumulative pregnancy rate of 0.5 per 100 women (Rowe 2016), and the implant's integrated trial analysis recorded no in-treatment pregnancies in 923 women over 24,100 cycles (Graesslin 2008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: both methods prevent pregnancy at well under 1 per 100 woman-years for years; no difference between them has been demonstrated, and none could be detected without an enormous trial.

cards.headline: McNicholas 2017: head-to-head in extended use — no pregnancies in 444 woman-years on the implant; 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD failure 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years in years 6–7
cards.summary: McNicholas 2017: head-to-head in extended use — no pregnancies in 444 woman-years on the implant; 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD failure 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years in years 6–7
cards.people: Prospective cohort (Contraceptive CHOICE programme, St Louis) of women continuing their method beyond its approved duration: 291 etonogestrel implant users contributing 444.0 woman-years in years 4–5 of use, and 496 users of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device contributing 696.9 woman-years in years 6–7 of use.
cards.result: No pregnancies were documented in implant users during the 2 years beyond approved duration (failure rate 0 per 100 woman-years in year 4, one-sided 97.5% CI 0–1.48; and 0 in year 5, CI 0–2.65). Two pregnancies occurred in levonorgestrel IUD users: failure rate 0.25 per 100 woman-years in year 6 (95% CI 0.04–1.42) and 0.43 per 100 woman-years in year 7 (95% CI 0.08–2.39). Median serum etonogestrel remained above the 90 pg/mL ovulation threshold in all BMI classes through year 5.
cards.watchOut: This cohort compares the methods in different windows of use (implant years 4–5 versus IUD years 6–7) among women who had already kept their method for years — a selected, satisfied population; it shows both stay highly effective, not that one beats the other within the approved durations.
cards.source: McNicholas C et al. Prolonged use of the etonogestrel implant and levonorgestrel intrauterine device: 2 years beyond Food and Drug Administration-approved duration. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2017. PMID: 28147241. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: CHOICE 2012 (Winner): intrauterine devices and implants pooled failed at 0.27 per 100 participant-years, versus 4.55 for pills, patch or ring
cards.summary: CHOICE 2012 (Winner): intrauterine devices and implants pooled failed at 0.27 per 100 participant-years, versus 4.55 for pills, patch or ring
cards.people: 7,486 participants in the Contraceptive CHOICE Project prospective cohort (St Louis), provided reversible contraception of their choice at no cost and followed for unintended pregnancy; long-acting methods were intrauterine devices (copper and levonorgestrel) and the etonogestrel implant.
cards.result: 334 unintended pregnancies were identified. The failure rate among participants using pills, patch or ring was 4.55 per 100 participant-years, compared with 0.27 per 100 participant-years among participants using long-acting reversible contraception (adjusted hazard ratio 21.8, 95% CI 13.7 to 34.9). Rates of unintended pregnancy were similarly low among participants using depot medroxyprogesterone injection and those using an intrauterine device or implant, regardless of age, and among pill/patch/ring users under 21 the risk was almost twice that of older users.
cards.watchOut: The headline rate pools intrauterine devices and the implant together — it proves the class performance both methods share, and cannot separate implant from IUD; women chose their own method, so the comparison with pills is observational.
cards.source: Winner B et al. Effectiveness of long-acting reversible contraception. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 22621627. Registry ID: none in the record.
