cards.headline: Rowe 2016: the 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD's own 7-year record — cumulative pregnancy rate 0.5 per 100 women in a randomised trial of 1,884 users
cards.summary: Rowe 2016: the 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD's own 7-year record — cumulative pregnancy rate 0.5 per 100 women in a randomised trial of 1,884 users
cards.people: 1,884 women with interval insertion of the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine device (daily release 20 µg) in a 7-year open-label randomised comparative trial in 20 centres (11 in China), analysed with life tables; the comparator was the copper T380A IUD (1,871 women).
cards.result: The cumulative 7-year pregnancy rate with the levonorgestrel IUD was 0.5 (standard error 0.2) per 100 women, significantly lower than 2.5 (0.4) per 100 with the copper T380A. Cumulative method discontinuation at 7 years was higher with the levonorgestrel IUD (70.6 per 100) than the copper device (40.8 per 100), driven by removals for amenorrhea (26.1 per 100) and reduced bleeding (12.5 per 100).
cards.watchOut: This trial benchmarks the standard levonorgestrel IUD against copper, not against the implant; it is carded as the IUD's own long-term efficacy record, and its population was parous women, with discontinuation patterns the authors note were culturally patterned.
cards.source: Rowe P et al. Safety and efficacy in parous women of a 52-mg levonorgestrel-medicated intrauterine device: a 7-year randomized comparative study with the TCu380A. Contraception. 2016. PMID: 26916172. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Graesslin 2008: the etonogestrel implant's integrated trial record — no in-treatment pregnancies in 923 women over 24,100 cycles (tested product: Implanon)
cards.summary: Graesslin 2008: the etonogestrel implant's integrated trial record — no in-treatment pregnancies in 923 women over 24,100 cycles (tested product: Implanon)
cards.type: Integrated analysis of 11 studies plus post-marketing surveillance
cards.people: Integrated efficacy analysis of 11 international studies of the etonogestrel-releasing subdermal implant (Implanon, Organon, part of Schering-Plough — the tested product named in the publication), including 923 non-breastfeeding women exposed for 24,100 cycles, plus nine years of marketing experience (1998–2007).
cards.result: No in-treatment or pretreatment pregnancies were reported in the integrated trial analysis. Over nine years of marketing, the overall pregnancy rate was 0.049 per 100 implants sold (estimated Pearl Index 0.031 counting all reported pregnancies), and 0.010 per 100 implants sold (estimated Pearl Index 0.006) counting only contraceptive method failures. Fifty post-treatment pregnancies were reported, six within 14 days of removal, showing fertility returns quickly.
cards.watchOut: An industry-linked integrated analysis (market data were provided by the manufacturer, Organon) with no comparator; marketing-experience Pearl Indices depend on spontaneous reporting and implants sold, so they flatter the method relative to trial conditions.
cards.source: Graesslin O et al. The contraceptive efficacy of Implanon: a review of clinical trials and marketing experience. The European journal of contraception & reproductive health care : the official journal of the European Society of Contraception. 2008. PMID: 18330813. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: both methods sit well under 1 pregnancy per 100 woman-years for years of use; the only head-to-head cohort found no implant pregnancies and 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years for the IUD in extended use — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: both methods sit well under 1 pregnancy per 100 woman-years for years of use; the only head-to-head cohort found no implant pregnancies and 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years for the IUD in extended use — POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective head-to-head extended-use cohort (291 implant and 496 IUD users), one large prospective cohort pooling the methods (7,486 women), one 7-year randomised trial benchmarking the 52 mg IUD (1,884 users), and one integrated analysis of the implant's trials (923 women). Total carded participants exceed 11,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Every long-term rate carded is below 1 pregnancy per 100 woman-years: implant 0 per 100 woman-years in extended use and no in-treatment pregnancies across its integrated trials; 52 mg levonorgestrel IUD 0.5 per 100 women cumulatively over 7 years and 0.25–0.43 per 100 woman-years in years 6–7; the pooled long-acting rate in CHOICE was 0.27 per 100 participant-years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the etonogestrel implant and the standard levonorgestrel IUD are comparably effective for long-term pregnancy prevention, with no demonstrated difference — the evidence is cohort and single-method records, not a head-to-head pregnancy trial. Discontinuation and bleeding against the low-dose 13.5 mg system stay homed on live shelf #1337.
cards.watchOut: At failure rates this low, 'no demonstrated difference' is the strongest honest claim: ruling out even a twofold difference would need a trial far larger than any run, so counselling should turn on bleeding, hormones and placement preference — the ground #1337 covers for the low-dose device.

shelves.title: CBT-I in pregnancy: four randomised programmes agree — insomnia severity, sleep quality and sleep duration improve, in person and digitally
shelves.question: In pregnant women with insomnia, does cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia improve sleep versus usual care or sleep education?
shelves.mesh: Adult · California · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Patient Outcome Assessment · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications/therapy · Prenatal Care · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/therapy · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: Premise verified: CBT-I is homed for cancer (pack #5060), menopause and general digital delivery (live #437) — pregnancy was the uncovered population. Four independent randomised programmes, against four different comparators, agree. Manber 2019 (in-person, versus an active imagery control): ISI fell 15.4 to 8.0 versus 15.9 to 11.2 (P<.001, d = 0.5), remission 64% versus 52%, median time to remission 31 versus 48 days — though objective wake time did not differ. Felder 2020 (digital, versus unrestricted standard care): significantly greater insomnia improvement (d = −1.03) with secondary outcomes except sleep duration also improved, holding at follow-up. Kalmbach 2020 (digital, versus sleep education — the exact comparator named in the question): ISI −4.91 and PSQI −2.98 points, sleep 32 minutes longer, and 40 minutes longer after childbirth. Bei 2023 (scalable one-session-plus-emails programme versus attention-matched control): significant pregnancy-endpoint benefits, strongest in those with elevated baseline symptoms, with sleep benefits still present at 2 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — multiple independent concordant programmes clear the single-programme cap; depression is not claimed (effects small in one trial, absent in two).

cards.headline: Manber 2019: in-person CBT-I in pregnancy cut Insomnia Severity Index scores from 15.4 to 8.0 versus 15.9 to 11.2 on a control imagery therapy (P<.001, d = 0.5), with faster remission (median 31 vs 48 days) — 194 randomised, 179 analysed
cards.summary: Manber 2019: in-person CBT-I in pregnancy cut Insomnia Severity Index scores from 15.4 to 8.0 versus 15.9 to 11.2 on a control imagery therapy (P<.001, d = 0.5), with faster remission (median 31 vs 48 days) — 194 randomised, 179 analysed
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, in-person CBT-I (Manber 2019) — 194 randomised, 179 analysed
cards.people: Pregnant women between 18 and 32 weeks of gestation meeting diagnostic criteria for insomnia disorder (excluding major psychiatric disorders including depression, and those on non-study sleep-affecting treatments), in a randomised, unmasked, 3-site trial of cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia versus a control intervention of imagery exercises pairing distressing nighttime experiences with neutral images. 194 women were randomised, 149 completed treatment, and 179 with baseline data were analysed (89 CBT-I, 90 control). Primary outcome: Insomnia Severity Index (14–21 = moderate clinical insomnia; under 8 = no insomnia).
cards.result: Women assigned to CBT-I had significantly greater reductions in insomnia severity (scores fell from 15.4 ± 4.3 to 8.0 ± 5.2 on CBT-I versus 15.9 ± 4.4 to 11.2 ± 4.9 on control; P<.001, d = 0.5). Remission of insomnia (ISI under 8) was attained by 64% on CBT-I versus 52% on control, and remission was faster (median 31 versus 48 days, P<.001). CBT-I gave a greater reduction in self-reported but not objective total wake time, and a small but significantly greater decline in Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked (unavoidable for a behavioural therapy) with a credible active control — the control itself produced substantial improvement (to 11.2), so the incremental CBT-I effect (d = 0.5) is over and above attention/imagery effects. Objective wake time did not differ, and 48 randomised participants did not complete treatment.
cards.source: Manber R et al. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Prenatal Insomnia: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2019. PMID: 30969203. Registry ID: NCT01846585 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Felder 2020: digital CBT-I (6 weekly 20-minute sessions) improved insomnia severity more than standard care in 208 pregnant women (difference −0.36, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.23; d = −1.03), with benefits holding at follow-up
cards.summary: Felder 2020: digital CBT-I (6 weekly 20-minute sessions) improved insomnia severity more than standard care in 208 pregnant women (difference −0.36, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.23; d = −1.03), with benefits holding at follow-up
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, digital CBT-I versus standard care (Felder 2020) — N = 208
cards.people: 208 pregnant women up to 28 weeks of gestation with elevated insomnia symptom severity or insomnia caseness on self-report questionnaires (of 2,258 assessed online), randomised to digital CBT-I (n = 105) — 6 weekly sessions of about 20 minutes, delivered and assessed entirely remotely — or standard treatment (n = 103), in which non-study treatments including medication and psychotherapy were unrestricted. Outcomes at 10 weeks (post-intervention) and 18 weeks (follow-up): Insomnia Severity Index (primary), sleep efficiency and duration by diary, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale and GAD-7 anxiety.
cards.result: Digital CBT-I produced statistically significantly greater improvement in insomnia severity from baseline to post-intervention than standard treatment (time-by-group difference −0.36, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.23; chi-square 29.8; P<.001; d = −1.03), and improvements in all secondary outcomes except sleep duration were statistically significant, with a similar pattern at follow-up. Participants had a mean age of 33.6 years and mean gestational age of 17.6 weeks. The authors conclude digital CBT-I was effective, scalable, safe and acceptable for insomnia in pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is unrestricted standard care, not a matched-attention control, so part of the large effect size may reflect expectancy and engagement; the sample was predominantly white, married/cohabiting, college-educated and higher-income (per the record), which limits generalisability to the wider pregnant population.
cards.source: Felder JN et al. Efficacy of Digital Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for the Treatment of Insomnia Symptoms Among Pregnant Women: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA psychiatry. 2020. PMID: 31968068. Registry ID: NCT02805998 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Kalmbach 2020: digital CBT-I versus digital sleep education in 91 women in late pregnancy cut ISI by 4.91 points and PSQI by 2.98 points (both P<.001) and added 32 minutes of nightly sleep — with sleep 40 minutes longer than control after childbirth
cards.summary: Kalmbach 2020: digital CBT-I versus digital sleep education in 91 women in late pregnancy cut ISI by 4.91 points and PSQI by 2.98 points (both P<.001) and added 32 minutes of nightly sleep — with sleep 40 minutes longer than control after childbirth
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, digital CBT-I versus sleep education (Kalmbach 2020) — N = 91
cards.people: 91 pregnant women (mean age 29.03 years) nearing or entering the third trimester who screened positive for clinical insomnia on the Insomnia Severity Index, in a single-site RCT of internet-based digital CBT-I versus a digital sleep education control. Outcomes (ISI, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, pre-sleep cognitive arousal) were measured before and after treatment in pregnancy and six weeks after childbirth.
cards.result: From pre- to post-treatment, CBT-I patients reported ISI reductions of 4.91 points (p<0.001), PSQI reductions of 2.98 points (p<0.001) and nightly sleep duration increases of 32 minutes (p = 0.008), while sleep symptoms did not change during pregnancy in the control group. After childbirth, CBT-I patients slept 40 minutes longer per night than controls (p = 0.01) and reported better sleep maintenance. No pre- or postnatal treatment effects on depression or cognitive arousal were observed.
cards.watchOut: The smallest of the carded trials (N = 91) and single-site, with self-reported outcomes; its control (sleep education) matches the 'sleep education' comparator in the assigned question directly. The absence of a depression effect here contrasts with Manber's small depression-score benefit — depression is not a settled CBT-I outcome in pregnancy on these records.
cards.source: Kalmbach DA et al. A randomized controlled trial of digital cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia in pregnant women. Sleep medicine. 2020. PMID: 32559716. Registry ID: NCT03596879 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record). cards.headline: Bei 2023: a scalable CBT sleep programme (one telephone session plus automated emails, third trimester to 6 months postpartum) lowered insomnia severity and sleep disturbance at the pregnancy endpoint (p values 0.001 or less) and still benefited sleep at 2 years — 163 randomised
cards.summary: Bei 2023: a scalable CBT sleep programme (one telephone session plus automated emails, third trimester to 6 months postpartum) lowered insomnia severity and sleep disturbance at the pregnancy endpoint (p values 0.001 or less) and still benefited sleep at 2 years — 163 randomised
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, scalable CBT sleep intervention (Bei 2023) — N = 163
cards.people: 163 nulliparous females without severe medical or psychiatric conditions, randomised 1:1 to a cognitive behavioural sleep intervention tailored to pregnancy and postpartum (a 1-hour telephone session plus automated multimedia emails from the third trimester to 6 months postpartum) or an attention- and time-matched control, in a single-blind superiority RCT. Outcomes at gestation weeks 30 (baseline) and 35 (pregnancy endpoint) and postpartum months 1.5, 3, 6, 12 and 24: insomnia severity and sleep disturbance (primary), sleep-related impairment, depression and anxiety.
cards.result: Compared with control, CBT was associated with lower insomnia severity and sleep disturbance and lower sleep-related impairment at the pregnancy endpoint (p values 0.001 or less), and with sleep benefits at 24 months postpartum (p ranges 0.012–0.052); group differences across the first postpartum year were non-significant, and depression and anxiety differences were non-significant throughout. Participants with elevated insomnia symptoms at baseline benefited substantially more, including significantly lower insomnia symptoms through the first postpartum year. The intervention was well accepted with no reported adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Enrolled nulliparous women regardless of insomnia diagnosis — a prevention-leaning population, so effects are smaller and driven by the subgroup with elevated baseline symptoms; this card supports the programme's scalability and durability rather than adding a fourth treatment-of-insomnia estimate.
cards.source: Bei B et al. Improving perinatal sleep via a scalable cognitive behavioural intervention: findings from a randomised controlled trial from pregnancy to 2 years postpartum. Psychological medicine. 2023. PMID: 34231450. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: four independent randomised programmes agree — CBT-I improves insomnia in pregnancy whether delivered in person, digitally, or as a light-touch scalable programme, against active control, standard care and sleep education alike
cards.summary: Synthesis: four independent randomised programmes agree — CBT-I improves insomnia in pregnancy whether delivered in person, digitally, or as a light-touch scalable programme, against active control, standard care and sleep education alike
cards.people: The carded evidence: Manber 2019 (in-person CBT-I versus imagery control, 179 analysed), Felder 2020 (digital CBT-I versus standard care, 208), Kalmbach 2020 (digital CBT-I versus digital sleep education, 91), and Bei 2023 (scalable CBT versus attention-matched control, 163) — four distinct trials/programmes, total 641 analysed or randomised participants as reported on the cards. CBT-I in cancer (pack #5060), menopause and general populations (live #437) are different populations, homed elsewhere and not re-carded.
cards.result: Insomnia severity fell more with CBT-I in every trial: ISI 15.4 to 8.0 versus 15.9 to 11.2 against an active control (Manber, d = 0.5, remission 64% versus 52%, median time to remission 31 versus 48 days); a large digital effect versus standard care (Felder, d = −1.03); −4.91 ISI points and +32 minutes of sleep versus sleep education (Kalmbach); and significant pregnancy-endpoint benefits from a one-session-plus-emails programme, persisting to 2 years in those with elevated baseline symptoms (Bei). Sleep quality and duration improve; depression effects are small or absent and are not claimed. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — multiple independent concordant randomised programmes, which clears the single-programme cap.
cards.watchOut: All carded outcomes are symptom scales and diaries (objective wake time did not differ in the one trial that measured it), follow-up beyond delivery is limited except for Bei, and trial samples skew educated and higher-income — effectiveness in routine, diverse antenatal populations is the remaining gap.
cards.source: Synthesis of Manber R et al. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2019 (PMID: 30969203); Felder JN et al. JAMA psychiatry. 2020 (PMID: 31968068); Kalmbach DA et al. Sleep medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32559716); Bei B et al. Psychological medicine. 2023 (PMID: 34231450).

shelves.title: GLP-1 receptor agonists in PCOS infertility: exenatide beat metformin on pregnancy rate in one open-label trial and one meta-analysis, and liraglutide improved menstrual regularity versus placebo — but live-birth evidence is still sparse
shelves.question: In women with polycystic ovary syndrome and infertility, does a GLP-1 receptor agonist improve ovulation and pregnancy outcomes versus placebo or metformin?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Exenatide · Female · Glucose Tolerance Test · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Menstrual Cycle/drug effects · Obesity/drug therapy · Overweight/drug therapy · Peptides/therapeutic use · Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/drug therapy · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Rate · Prospective Studies · Venoms/therapeutic use · Weight Loss/drug effects · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), stamped honestly for a thin reproductive base. The pregnancy signal comes from exenatide: in Liu 2017 (176 overweight/obese women with PCOS, open-label), 12 weeks of exenatide before a 12-week metformin-only phase gave a natural pregnancy rate of 43.6% versus 18.7% after metformin alone, with more weight loss (4.29 kg vs 2.28 kg) and a higher menstrual frequency ratio (0.62 vs 0.37); the 2023 meta-analysis of 9 exenatide-versus-metformin trials (785 patients) points the same way (pregnancy relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.28 to 2.92; ovulation relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.80), though its authors call the evidence inconclusive. For liraglutide, the Frøssing programme's placebo-controlled trial (72 women, 26 weeks) improved bleeding ratio and androgen markers but reported no pregnancy outcomes. Live-birth data are sparse throughout: no carded trial uses live birth as its outcome, so this shelf answers ovulation, menstrual regularity and pregnancy rate — not live birth. Two neighbouring homes are cross-pointed, not re-carded: live shelf #245 covers letrozole, clomiphene and metformin for PCOS ovulation induction, and live shelf #2074 homes the 28-woman Salamun pilot of liraglutide added to metformin before IVF (PMID 29703793, carded there and kept out of this pack's cards under the one-home rule — this pack's question is the broader GLP-1 class question across placebo and metformin comparators, built on three free reports). Semaglutide: no randomised PCOS report with reproductive outcomes was found in this session's fetched records — only reviews and cohort reports — so no semaglutide claim is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but preliminary reproductive advantage over metformin, resting on small, mostly open-label trials.

cards.headline: Liu 2017: after 12 weeks of exenatide versus metformin, natural pregnancy in the next 12 weeks was 43.6% vs 18.7% — with more weight loss and more frequent menstruation on exenatide
cards.summary: Liu 2017: after 12 weeks of exenatide versus metformin, natural pregnancy in the next 12 weeks was 43.6% vs 18.7% — with more weight loss and more frequent menstruation on exenatide
cards.people: 176 overweight/obese women with PCOS randomised open-label to exenatide 10 micrograms twice daily (n = 88) or metformin 1000 mg twice daily (n = 88) for 12 weeks; all patients then took metformin alone for a second 12 weeks, during which natural pregnancy was tracked.
cards.result: After the first 12 weeks, exenatide beat metformin on weight loss (4.29 ± 1.29 kg vs 2.28 ± 0.55 kg, P < .001), total fat percentage (4.67% vs 1.11% reduction), insulin resistance (HOMA-IR improvement 1.30 ± 0.58 vs 0.59 ± 0.12) and menstrual frequency ratio (0.62 ± 0.12 vs 0.37 ± 0.01, P < .001). During the second 12 weeks (metformin for everyone), the natural pregnancy rate was significantly higher in the exenatide-pretreated group: 43.60% vs 18.70% (P < .05). No live-birth outcome is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo arm, and the pregnancy window followed a design in which both groups were on metformin — so the contrast is exenatide pretreatment versus metformin pretreatment, not exenatide versus nothing. Pregnancy, not live birth, is the outcome.
cards.source: Liu X et al. Efficacy of exenatide on weight loss, metabolic parameters and pregnancy in overweight/obese polycystic ovary syndrome. Clinical endocrinology. 2017. PMID: 28834553. cards.headline: Frøssing programme (Nylander 2017): liraglutide improved bleeding ratio versus placebo over 26 weeks (between-group difference 0.14) and lowered free testosterone — in 72 women, with no pregnancy outcomes reported
cards.summary: Frøssing programme (Nylander 2017): liraglutide improved bleeding ratio versus placebo over 26 weeks (between-group difference 0.14) and lowered free testosterone — in 72 women, with no pregnancy outcomes reported
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, placebo-controlled (Frøssing programme; Nylander 2017)
cards.people: 72 overweight and/or insulin-resistant women with PCOS in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, randomised 2:1 to liraglutide 1.8 mg/day or placebo for 26 weeks. Bleeding pattern, anti-Müllerian hormone, sex hormones, gonadotrophins and ovarian morphology were assessed.
cards.result: Liraglutide caused 5.2 kg (95% CI 3.0 to 7.5, P < 0.0001) more weight loss than placebo. Bleeding ratio improved more on liraglutide (0.28, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.36) than on placebo (0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.26); between-group difference 0.14 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.24, P < 0.05). Sex-hormone-binding globulin rose by 7.4 nmol/L and free testosterone fell; ovarian volume decreased by −1.6 ml versus placebo (95% CI −3.3 to 0.1). Nausea and constipation were more prevalent on liraglutide. The record reports no ovulation-rate or pregnancy outcome.
cards.watchOut: This is the ovarian-function report of a single 72-woman trial; its record carries no registry ID — the same trial's companion ectopic-fat report (Frøssing 2018) is the record that lists ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02073929. Bleeding ratio is a menstrual-regularity marker, not a direct ovulation or pregnancy measure.
cards.source: Nylander M et al. Effects of liraglutide on ovarian dysfunction in polycystic ovary syndrome: a randomized clinical trial. Reproductive biomedicine online. 2017. PMID: 28479118. cards.headline: Ye 2023 meta-analysis (9 trials, 785 patients): exenatide beat metformin on pregnancy rate (relative risk 1.93) and ovulation rate (relative risk 1.41) — authors call the evidence inconclusive
cards.summary: Ye 2023 meta-analysis (9 trials, 785 patients): exenatide beat metformin on pregnancy rate (relative risk 1.93) and ovulation rate (relative risk 1.41) — authors call the evidence inconclusive
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (Ye 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials comparing exenatide with metformin in PCOS: 785 patients in total, 385 on exenatide and 400 on metformin.
cards.result: Compared with metformin, exenatide was associated with a higher pregnancy rate (relative risk 1.93, 95% CI 1.28 to 2.92, P = 0.002) and a higher ovulation rate (relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.80, P = 0.004) — both relative measures; the record does not print pooled absolute pregnancy or ovulation rates. Body mass index fell more on exenatide (mean difference −1.72 kg/m2) and insulin resistance improved more (standardised mean difference −0.62). There was no significant difference in adverse events. The authors state that, given the moderate-to-high quality and possible bias of the included studies, the available evidence is inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and mostly from one research setting, and several overlap with the Liu programme carded above — the meta-analysis is corroboration of direction, not an independent large evidence base. Relative risks are printed without pooled absolute rates in the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: GLP-1 agonists probably improve ovulation, menstrual regularity and pregnancy rate versus metformin in PCOS — live birth remains unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: GLP-1 agonists probably improve ovulation, menstrual regularity and pregnancy rate versus metformin in PCOS — live birth remains unproven
cards.people: Women with PCOS and infertility across one open-label exenatide trial (n = 176), one placebo-controlled liraglutide trial (n = 72) and a 9-trial exenatide meta-analysis (785 patients).
cards.result: Direction is consistent — more weight loss, better menstrual regularity, higher ovulation and pregnancy rates than metformin — but every leg is small or open-label, comparators differ (metformin vs placebo), and no carded study reports live birth. The stamp is therefore POSSIBLE (benefit), not LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this shelf as evidence about live birth, miscarriage or use during pregnancy — none of the carded records answers those questions, and GLP-1 agonists were stopped before the pregnancy window in the carded trial designs.

shelves.title: Elagolix with add-back therapy for fibroid bleeding: response in 68.5% and 76.5% of women versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo in the replicate Elaris UF-1 and UF-2 trials, sustained to 12 months
shelves.question: In women with heavy menstrual bleeding due to fibroids, does elagolix with add-back therapy reduce blood loss versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bone Density/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Estradiol/therapeutic use · Estrogens/therapeutic use · Female · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone/antagonists & inhibitors · Hot Flashes/chemically induced · Humans · Hydrocarbons, Fluorinated/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Leiomyoma/complications · Menorrhagia/drug therapy,etiology · Middle Aged · Pyrimidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). The Elaris UF-1 and UF-2 trials are identical replicate double-blind phase 3 trials (790 women randomised in total) and they agree closely: elagolix 300 mg twice daily with estradiol/norethindrone acetate add-back met the primary bleeding endpoint (final-month menstrual blood loss under 80 ml and at least 50% down from baseline) in 68.5% and 76.5% of women versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo. Elagolix alone responded slightly more often (84.1% in UF-1) but at a hypoestrogenic cost the add-back exists to blunt: bone mineral density loss was attenuated with add-back, in the trials and again in UF-EXTEND, where response held at 87.9% at 12 months. Hot flushes and (in UF-1) metrorrhagia were more common on elagolix plus add-back than placebo. The adenomyosis pooled analysis shows the bleeding benefit is not limited to women without adenomyosis (77.1% vs 12.2%). This shelf is the fibroid question only: elagolix for endometriosis pain is live shelf #246, and the other fibroid GnRH-antagonist shelves are relugolix (live #247) and linzagolix (live #1136). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a large, replicated, placebo-controlled effect on measured blood loss, with bone and vasomotor costs printed on the cards.

cards.headline: Schlaff 2020 (Elaris UF-1 and UF-2): bleeding response in 68.5% and 76.5% on elagolix plus add-back versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo (P < 0.001 in both trials)
cards.summary: Schlaff 2020 (Elaris UF-1 and UF-2): bleeding response in 68.5% and 76.5% on elagolix plus add-back versus 8.7% and 10% on placebo (P < 0.001 in both trials)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trials, phase 3, replicate pair (Elaris UF-1 and UF-2; Schlaff 2020)
cards.people: Two identical double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled 6-month phase 3 trials in women with fibroid-associated heavy bleeding: 412 women in UF-1 and 378 in UF-2 underwent randomisation and were analysed. Arms were elagolix 300 mg twice daily plus add-back (estradiol 1 mg and norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg once daily), elagolix alone, or placebo.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (menstrual blood loss < 80 ml in the final month and ≥ 50% reduction from baseline) was met in UF-1 by 68.5% of 206 women on elagolix plus add-back versus 8.7% of 102 on placebo, and in UF-2 by 76.5% of 189 versus 10% of 94 (P < 0.001 for both). On elagolix alone the endpoint was met by 84.1% (UF-1) and 77% (UF-2). Hot flushes (both trials) and metrorrhagia (UF-1) occurred significantly more often with elagolix plus add-back than placebo, and the hypoestrogenic bone mineral density decreases of elagolix were attenuated by add-back therapy.
cards.watchOut: Six months of treatment only in the primary trials, in women with measured blood loss over 80 ml per cycle; the endpoint is a responder definition combining an absolute threshold and a halving of loss, not amenorrhoea. Industry-funded (AbbVie), as the record states.
cards.source: Schlaff WD et al. Elagolix for Heavy Menstrual Bleeding in Women with Uterine Fibroids. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 31971678. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02654054 and NCT02691494. cards.headline: Simon 2020 (UF-EXTEND): response sustained at 87.9% after up to 12 months of elagolix plus add-back, with smaller bone-density losses than elagolix alone
cards.summary: Simon 2020 (UF-EXTEND): response sustained at 87.9% after up to 12 months of elagolix plus add-back, with smaller bone-density losses than elagolix alone
cards.people: Phase 3 extension study: 433 women who had completed 6 months in UF-1 or UF-2 were enrolled; 218 received up to 12 months of elagolix 300 mg twice daily with add-back therapy (estradiol 1 mg/norethindrone acetate 0.5 mg once daily) in total. Mean age 42.4 years; 67.3% were Black.
cards.result: 87.9% (95% CI 83.4 to 92.3) of the elagolix-plus-add-back group met the primary endpoint (final-month blood loss < 80 ml and ≥ 50% reduction from baseline) at the end of the extension. The most frequent adverse events over up to 12 months were hot flush (6.9%), headache (5.5%), nausea (4.1%) and night sweats (3.2%). Mean bone mineral density decreases were significantly smaller with add-back than with elagolix alone (between-group difference at the lumbar spine −3.3 percentage points, 95% CI −4.1 to −2.5). The record reports no new or unexpected safety concerns with the additional 6 months.
cards.watchOut: An extension of trial completers, not a fresh randomised comparison against placebo — the 87.9% figure describes women who stayed on treatment, so it supports durability, not a new efficacy estimate. Bone loss is attenuated by add-back, not abolished.
cards.source: Simon JA et al. Elagolix Treatment for Up to 12 Months in Women With Heavy Menstrual Bleeding and Uterine Leiomyomas. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2020. PMID: 32459423. cards.headline: Muneyyirci-Delale 2021 (pooled UF-1/UF-2): in women with coexisting adenomyosis, response was 77.1% on elagolix plus add-back versus 12.2% on placebo
cards.summary: Muneyyirci-Delale 2021 (pooled UF-1/UF-2): in women with coexisting adenomyosis, response was 77.1% on elagolix plus add-back versus 12.2% on placebo
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised trials (UF-1 and UF-2 adenomyosis subset; Muneyyirci-Delale 2021)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of UF-1 and UF-2 (786 women treated); 126 women (16%) had coexisting adenomyosis diagnosed by ultrasound and/or MRI at baseline. Randomisation was 1:1:2 to placebo, elagolix 300 mg twice daily alone, or elagolix plus add-back.
cards.result: Among women with coexisting adenomyosis, 77.1% (95% CI 66.2 to 88.0) on elagolix with add-back met both primary endpoint criteria, versus 12.2% (95% CI 1.0 to 23.4) on placebo. The most frequent adverse events in the elagolix-plus-add-back adenomyosis subset were hot flushes (18.3%), nausea (11.7%) and night sweats (8.3%). The authors conclude elagolix efficacy was not adversely affected by coexisting adenomyosis.
cards.watchOut: A subset analysis (126 women) of the same two trials carded above — it answers 'does adenomyosis blunt the effect?' and is not independent efficacy evidence. Confidence intervals are wide, as the record's intervals show.
cards.source: Muneyyirci-Delale O et al. Efficacy and safety of elagolix with add-back therapy in women with uterine fibroids and coexisting adenomyosis. F&S reports. 2021. PMID: 34553161. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02654054 and NCT02691494. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.summary: Synthesis: elagolix plus add-back clearly reduces fibroid bleeding versus placebo for at least 12 months — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Premenopausal women with fibroids and heavy menstrual bleeding: 790 randomised in UF-1/UF-2, 433 entering the extension, and a 126-woman adenomyosis subset analysed separately.
cards.result: Two replicate trials show a roughly 60-percentage-point absolute advantage in bleeding response over placebo, the extension shows the response is sustained to 12 months, and add-back therapy attenuates — but does not eliminate — bone mineral density loss. shelves.title: Dexamethasone versus betamethasone before preterm birth: death or neurosensory disability at 2 years in 33% versus 32% in the 1,346-woman ASTEROID trial — no difference found, either drug is a reasonable choice
shelves.question: In women at risk of preterm birth, is antenatal dexamethasone as effective as betamethasone for newborn outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Australia/epidemiology · Betamethasone/administration & dosage · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gestational Age · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Infant Mortality/trends · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/epidemiology,prevention & control · Injections, Intramuscular · Male · New Zealand/epidemiology · Pregnancy · Premature Birth/epidemiology,prevention & control · Prenatal Care/methods · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no difference found). This is the drug-choice question, not whether antenatal steroids work — steroid-versus-placebo is answered at live shelf #1352 (betamethasone, ALPS) and live shelf #1132 (dexamethasone, WHO ACTION-I/II). Head-to-head, the one large double-blind trial, ASTEROID (1,346 women, 1,509 fetuses, Australia and New Zealand), found the primary outcome — death or neurosensory disability at 2 years — in 33% on dexamethasone and 32% on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.13, p = 0.66); the trial was not designed as a formal noninferiority study, but its interval excludes a large advantage for either drug. The Cochrane synthesis (Williams 2022; 9 dexamethasone-versus-betamethasone trials, 2,096 women and 2,319 infants) agrees: no conclusive difference in death (relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.63), little or no difference in respiratory distress syndrome (relative risk 1.06, high-certainty) or in neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up (relative risk 1.02), with a low-certainty cerebral palsy estimate (relative risk 2.50, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.39) that is compatible with both harm and no difference and keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE rather than a flat equivalence claim. ASTEROID's repeat-dose secondary analysis likewise found no difference (odds ratio 0.89). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no difference found): on current evidence either drug can be given; availability and local practice, not efficacy, should drive the choice.

cards.headline: Crowther 2019 (ASTEROID): death or neurosensory disability at 2 years in 33% on dexamethasone versus 32% on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97) — the drugs made no difference to the primary outcome
cards.summary: Crowther 2019 (ASTEROID): death or neurosensory disability at 2 years in 33% on dexamethasone versus 32% on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97) — the drugs made no difference to the primary outcome
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, multicentre (ASTEROID; Crowther 2019)
cards.people: Multicentre double-blind randomised trial at 14 maternity hospitals in Australia and New Zealand: 1,346 women at risk of preterm birth before 34 weeks (singleton or twin pregnancy), pregnant with 1,509 fetuses, randomised to two intramuscular injections 24 hours apart of dexamethasone 12 mg (n = 679 women) or betamethasone 11.4 mg (n = 667). The primary outcome was determined for 603 of 763 dexamethasone-group and 591 of 746 betamethasone-group fetuses/infants.
cards.result: Death or neurosensory disability at age 2 years (corrected for prematurity) occurred in 198 of 603 infants (33%) on dexamethasone versus 192 of 591 (32%) on betamethasone (adjusted relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.13; p = 0.66) — the choice of drug made no difference to the primary outcome. Death before age 2 years occurred in 27 (4%) versus 28 (4%). Maternal side-effects were reported by 18 of 679 women (3%) on dexamethasone and 28 of 667 (4%) on betamethasone; injection-site discomfort was less likely with dexamethasone (1% vs 3%, p = 0.02). The authors conclude either antenatal corticosteroid can be given.
cards.watchOut: Not a formal noninferiority trial — 'no difference found' with a confidence interval of 0.83 to 1.13 is not proof of exact equivalence, and the primary outcome was ascertained in 79% of fetuses. Conducted in high-income settings with preterm care available.
cards.source: Crowther CA et al. Maternal intramuscular dexamethasone versus betamethasone before preterm birth (ASTEROID): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2019. PMID: 31523039. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12608000631303 (from the record's abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty). injection-site discomfort was less likely with dexamethasone (1% vs 3%, p = 0.02). the authors conclude either antenatal corticosteroid can be given. not a formal noninferiority trial — 'no difference found' with a confidence interval of 0.83 to 1.13 is not proof of exact equivalence, and the primary outcome was ascertained in 79% of fetuses. conducted in high-income settings with preterm care available. crowther ca et al. maternal intramuscular dexamethasone versus betamethasone before preterm birth (asteroid): a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial. the lancet. child & adolescent health. 2019. pmid: 31523039. registry id: anzctr actrn12608000631303 (from the record's abstract text; cards.headline: Williams 2022 (Cochrane): across 9 head-to-head trials (2,319 infants), no conclusive difference between dexamethasone and betamethasone in death, respiratory distress syndrome or neurodevelopmental disability
cards.summary: Williams 2022 (Cochrane): across 9 head-to-head trials (2,319 infants), no conclusive difference between dexamethasone and betamethasone in death, respiratory distress syndrome or neurodevelopmental disability
cards.type: Systematic review (Cochrane; Williams 2022, Brownfoot programme update)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review update: 11 trials in total (2,494 women, 2,762 infants), of which 9 trials (2,096 women, 2,319 infants) compared dexamethasone with betamethasone, all intramuscular at a total course dose of 22.8 mg or 24 mg, in women at risk of preterm birth in high-income countries.
cards.result: Death after randomisation: relative risk 1.03 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.63; 5 trials, 2,105 infants; moderate certainty) — compatible with both appreciable benefit and harm. Respiratory distress syndrome: relative risk 1.06 (95% CI 0.91 to 1.22; high certainty) — little or no difference. Intraventricular haemorrhage: average relative risk 0.71 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.81) with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 62%; low certainty). Chronic lung disease: relative risk 0.92 (1 trial). Neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up: relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.22; moderate certainty). Cerebral palsy: relative risk 2.50 (95% CI 0.97 to 6.39; 1 trial, 1,223 children; low certainty). Maternal chorioamnionitis: relative risk 0.71 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.06; moderate certainty), not conclusive.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials are older and smaller than ASTEROID, with moderate-to-high risk of bias in several; GRADE ratings ranged from high to low certainty. The cerebral palsy point estimate is the one signal favouring betamethasone, and it is low-certainty with an interval that includes no difference.
cards.source: Williams MJ et al. Different corticosteroids and regimens for accelerating fetal lung maturation for babies at risk of preterm birth. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2022. cards.headline: Hofer 2022 (ASTEROID repeat-dose analysis): when a repeat course was given, dexamethasone versus betamethasone again made no difference to death or neurosensory disability (odds ratio 0.89)
cards.summary: Hofer 2022 (ASTEROID repeat-dose analysis): when a repeat course was given, dexamethasone versus betamethasone again made no difference to death or neurosensory disability (odds ratio 0.89)
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (ASTEROID repeat doses; Hofer 2022)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the ASTEROID trial: 168 women who remained at risk of preterm birth seven or more days after an initial course and received a repeat dose — 86 dexamethasone and 82 betamethasone — with their infants.
cards.result: Death or any neurosensory disability at age 2 years (corrected) did not differ between repeat-dose groups (odds ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.39 to 2.06, p = 0.79), and there was little to no difference in other infant, childhood and maternal adverse health outcomes. The authors conclude the results support guideline recommendations that either drug may be used for repeat doses.
cards.watchOut: Only 168 women — a small, non-randomised subset defined by who received repeat doses, with a wide confidence interval (0.39 to 2.06); it corroborates the main trial rather than standing alone.
cards.source: Hofer OJ et al. Maternal and infant morbidity following administration of repeat dexamethasone or betamethasone prior to preterm birth: A secondary analysis of the ASTEROID Trial. PloS one. 2022. PMID: 35192656. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12608000631303 (from the record's abstract text; the record's databank fields are empty). cards.summary: Synthesis: dexamethasone and betamethasone made no difference to newborn or 2-year outcomes in the head-to-head evidence — POSSIBLE (no difference found)
cards.people: Women at risk of preterm birth and their infants: 1,346 women in ASTEROID and 2,096 women across the 9 Cochrane head-to-head trials (ASTEROID included).
cards.result: Every primary comparison is null and the intervals exclude large differences for the main outcomes; residual uncertainty sits in low-certainty secondary signals (cerebral palsy) and in outcomes with few events. shelves.title: Attempting external cephalic version at term: pooled caesarean risk ratio 0.57 in two syntheses — but the Cochrane evidence is graded low to very low and the largest single trial was null
shelves.question: For breech presentation at term, does attempting external cephalic version itself (versus no attempt) increase cephalic birth and reduce caesarean delivery?
shelves.mesh: Breech Presentation · Version, Fetal/methods · Cesarean Section · Pregnancy Outcome · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Humans · Female · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — this pack is a PARTIAL completion. Pack #3783 answers which tocolytic helps version succeed (beta-mimetics help; nifedipine and atosiban do not), and live shelf #664 answers planned caesarean versus planned vaginal breech birth and the timing of version before term; neither asks whether attempting version at term beats not attempting it. On that question, the Cochrane review (Hofmeyr 2015; 8 trials, 1,308 women) found attempted version at or near term reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (average relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.61 — a relative figure), failure to achieve a vaginal cephalic birth (relative risk 0.46) and caesarean section (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.82), with no significant difference in perinatal death (relative risk 0.39, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.64) — but graded the evidence low or very low, with no blinding and suboptimal allocation in several trials. A 2020 systematic review including non-randomised studies (184,704 breech pregnancies, high-resource settings) found near-identical relative effects (caesarean relative risk 0.57; non-cephalic presentation 0.45) but also a small increase in Apgar score below 7 at 5 minutes (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.52). Against both syntheses stands the largest single trial (Kasule 1985, 640 women): no significant difference in vaginal breech delivery, caesarean rate or perinatal mortality, three perinatal deaths attributed to the procedure, and the authors' conclusion that version had no place before 36 weeks — its attempts began after 30 weeks, earlier than the at-term practice the syntheses describe. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: the direction is consistent across syntheses, but low-grade trials, one large null trial and a small neonatal signal forbid a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015 (Hofmeyr): across 8 trials and 1,308 women, attempting version at term cut non-cephalic birth (relative risk 0.42) and caesarean section (relative risk 0.57)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015 (Hofmeyr): across 8 trials and 1,308 women, attempting version at term cut non-cephalic birth (relative risk 0.42) and caesarean section (relative risk 0.57)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Hofmeyr 2015)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of external cephalic version at or near term (with or without tocolysis) versus no attempt at version in women with breech presentation: 8 studies, 1,308 women randomised (1,305 analysed for the main outcomes).
cards.result: Attempted version reduced non-cephalic presentation at birth (average relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.61), failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.62) and caesarean section (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.82) — all relative figures; the review prints no pooled absolute rates, so none are printed here. There were no significant differences in Apgar score below 7 at 1 or 5 minutes, neonatal admission, or perinatal death (relative risk 0.39, 95% CI 0.09 to 1.64). All trials had design limitations; the evidence was graded low or very low, and no trial blinded the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks from small, unblinded, low-graded trials: a relative risk of 0.57 for caesarean sounds large, but the review's own grading says the true effect could differ substantially, and complications of version could not be assessed from these trials.
cards.source: Hofmeyr GJ et al. External cephalic version for breech presentation at term. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 25828903. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review, not a single trial. cards.headline: Kasule 1985: the largest single trial (640 women) found no difference in caesarean rate or perinatal mortality — and 3 perinatal deaths were attributed to version
cards.summary: Kasule 1985: the largest single trial (640 women) found no difference in caesarean rate or perinatal mortality — and 3 perinatal deaths were attributed to version
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trial of 640 singleton breech presentations after 30 weeks' gestation: version attempted in 310 women, no attempt in 330 controls. The record prints no further demographic detail.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the attempted-version and control groups in vaginal breech delivery, caesarean section rate, or perinatal mortality and morbidity. Three perinatal deaths were directly attributable to external cephalic version. The authors concluded there is no place for external cephalic version before 36 weeks' gestation.
cards.watchOut: This trial attempted version from 30 weeks — earlier than the at-term attempts pooled in the Cochrane review — so its null result and its attributed deaths speak most directly to pre-term attempts; it does not by itself refute at-term version, but it is the largest randomised warning on the shelf.

cards.headline: Devold Pay 2020: in 184,704 breech pregnancies (randomised and non-randomised), attempted version halved caesarean risk (relative risk 0.57) but raised low 5-minute Apgar scores (relative risk 1.29)
cards.summary: Devold Pay 2020: in 184,704 breech pregnancies (randomised and non-randomised), attempted version halved caesarean risk (relative risk 0.57) but raised low 5-minute Apgar scores (relative risk 1.29)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies (Devold Pay 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review of clinical trials (randomised and non-randomised) of external cephalic version at 36 weeks or later versus no version in high-resource settings: 9 articles reporting 184,704 breech pregnancies, searched to April 2019.
cards.result: Pooled data showed attempted version reduced failure to achieve vaginal cephalic birth (relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.71), caesarean section (relative risk 0.57, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.64) and non-cephalic presentation at birth (relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.68) compared with no version — all relative figures. Attempted version was also associated with a slightly increased incidence of Apgar score below 7 at 5 minutes (relative risk 1.29, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.52). The authors note the evidence is limited by scarce high-quality research and risks of bias.
cards.watchOut: Most of the 184,704 pregnancies come from non-randomised comparisons, where women offered and accepting version differ from those who are not — confounding by indication can manufacture exactly this pattern. The randomised-only Cochrane card above is the cleaner read; this card shows the effect survives in routine-practice data, at the price of that bias.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two syntheses agree on fewer breech births and caesareans; one large early-attempt trial disagrees — POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Cochrane randomised-trials review (8 trials, 1,308 women), the largest single randomised trial (640 women, attempts from 30 weeks), and a high-resource-settings review dominated by non-randomised data (184,704 pregnancies). Tocolysis choice is homed on pack #3783 and planned-mode-of-birth on live shelf #664; neither is re-carded here.
cards.result: Attempting version at or near term, versus no attempt: non-cephalic presentation at birth relative risk 0.42–0.45 and caesarean relative risk 0.57 in both syntheses; perinatal death not significantly different in the randomised pooling (relative risk 0.39, wide interval); a small excess of low 5-minute Apgar scores in the largely non-randomised review (relative risk 1.29); and one large null trial of earlier attempts with 3 procedure-attributed deaths. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: benefit is likely in direction, uncertain in size, on low-grade evidence.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf's question with its neighbours: whether a tocolytic helps version succeed (#3783) and how a persisting breech should be delivered (#664) are separate decisions from whether to attempt version at all.

shelves.title: Drospirenone versus levonorgestrel pills and venous thromboembolism (observational, SPLIT): registries find a relative rate ratio of 1.64 for drospirenone; the EURAS cohort found 1.0
shelves.question: In women, does a drospirenone-containing combined pill carry a higher venous thromboembolism risk than a levonorgestrel-containing pill?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/adverse effects · Contraceptives, Oral, Hormonal/adverse effects · Denmark/epidemiology · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Venous Thromboembolism/chemically induced,epidemiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — observational only, graded with care. Lidegaard 2009 (Danish national cohort, 10.4 million woman-years) found a venous thromboembolism rate ratio of 1.64 for drospirenone versus levonorgestrel at the same oestrogen dose and duration (a relative figure; absolute risk 6.29 per 10,000 woman-years in current users versus 3.01 in non-users). Vinogradova 2015 (UK nested case-control, 10,562 cases) found adjusted odds ratios versus non-use of 4.12 for drospirenone versus 2.38 for levonorgestrel (relative figures). EURAS (Dinger 2007; 58,674 women, prospective) found hazard ratio 1.0 — no difference. Larivée 2017 (17 studies) found relative risks spanning 1.0–3.3, with the three highest-quality studies at 1.0–1.57. FLAG (precedent b): Lidegaard 2011 is already carded on pack #5800 (combined versus progestin-only pill — a different question) and is kept out of this shelf's cards; this shelf rests on the free reports above. Pack #5800's question is different; the progestogen-to-progestogen comparison is this shelf's slice.

cards.headline: Lidegaard 2009 (observational Danish national cohort): versus levonorgestrel pills at the same oestrogen dose and duration, drospirenone pills carried a venous thromboembolism rate ratio of 1.64 (a relative figure)
cards.summary: Lidegaard 2009 (observational Danish national cohort): versus levonorgestrel pills at the same oestrogen dose and duration, drospirenone pills carried a venous thromboembolism rate ratio of 1.64 (a relative figure)
cards.type: Observational national cohort study (Lidegaard 2009) — 10.4 million woman-years; 4,213 events
cards.people: National cohort study of Danish women aged 15–49 with no history of cardiovascular or malignant disease, 1995–2005: 10.4 million woman-years of observation, 3.3 million on oral contraceptives, with 4,213 first venous thrombotic events (2,045 in current oral contraceptive users). Rate ratios were adjusted and compared at the same oestrogen dose and length of use.
cards.result: The absolute risk of venous thrombosis was 3.01 per 10,000 woman-years in non-users and 6.29 per 10,000 woman-years in current oral contraceptive users. Compared with levonorgestrel-containing pills at the same oestrogen dose and duration of use, the rate ratio (a relative figure) was 1.64 for drospirenone (95% CI 1.27 to 2.10), 1.82 for desogestrel, 1.86 for gestodene and 0.98 for norethisterone. Progestogen-only pills and hormone-releasing intrauterine devices were not associated with increased risk.
cards.watchOut: Registry observational data: drospirenone was preferentially prescribed to women perceived at higher baseline risk (acne, weight concerns, prior side effects), and first-year users — who carry the highest risk — are unevenly distributed between products; adjustment cannot fully remove that channeling.
cards.source: Lidegaard Ø et al. Hormonal contraception and risk of venous thromboembolism: national follow-up study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2009. PMID: 19679613. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vinogradova 2015 (observational UK nested case-control): drospirenone pills carried an adjusted odds ratio of 4.12 versus non-use, against 2.38 for levonorgestrel (relative figures) — about 6 extra cases per 10,000 treated women per year on levonorgestrel, with drospirenone among the higher-risk preparations
cards.summary: Vinogradova 2015 (observational UK nested case-control): drospirenone pills carried an adjusted odds ratio of 4.12 versus non-use, against 2.38 for levonorgestrel (relative figures) — about 6 extra cases per 10,000 treated women per year on levonorgestrel, with drospirenone among the higher-risk preparations
cards.type: Observational nested case-control studies (Vinogradova 2015) — 10,562 cases across two databases
cards.people: Two nested case-control studies in UK primary-care databases (Clinical Practice Research Datalink, 618 practices; QResearch, 722 practices): 5,062 venous thromboembolism cases from CPRD and 5,500 from QResearch in women aged 15–49, each matched to up to five controls, adjusted for smoking, alcohol, ethnicity, body mass index, comorbidities and other contraceptive drugs.
cards.result: Current use of any combined oral contraceptive was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.97 versus no exposure in the previous year (relative figure). By progestogen, adjusted odds ratios (relative figures) were 4.12 for drospirenone (95% CI 3.43 to 4.96), 4.28 for desogestrel and 4.27 for cyproterone, versus 2.38 for levonorgestrel (95% CI 2.18 to 2.59) and 2.53 for norgestimate. Estimated extra cases per 10,000 treated women per year were lowest for levonorgestrel (6) and norgestimate (6) and highest for desogestrel (14) and cyproterone (14). The slate's citation of 'Vinogradova 2019' resolves to this programme's substantive BMJ report (2015), verified by title search this session.
cards.watchOut: Case-control odds ratios compare each product with non-use, so the drospirenone-versus-levonorgestrel contrast is a ratio of two relative figures, not a direct head-to-head; prescribing channeling (drospirenone offered to women with risk factors or prior intolerance) remains the main alternative explanation.
cards.source: Vinogradova Y et al. Use of combined oral contraceptives and risk of venous thromboembolism: nested case-control studies using the QResearch and CPRD databases. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2015. PMID: 26013557. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: EURAS (Dinger 2007, observational prospective cohort): venous thromboembolism hazard ratios for drospirenone versus levonorgestrel pills were 1.0 — no difference found (the products made no difference) in 58,674 women followed for 142,475 woman-years
cards.summary: EURAS (Dinger 2007, observational prospective cohort): venous thromboembolism hazard ratios for drospirenone versus levonorgestrel pills were 1.0 — no difference found (the products made no difference) in 58,674 women followed for 142,475 woman-years
cards.type: Observational prospective active-surveillance cohort, EURAS (Dinger 2007) — 58,674 women; 142,475 woman-years
cards.people: European Active Surveillance Study (EURAS): a multinational, prospective, non-interventional cohort of 58,674 new users of drospirenone-containing, levonorgestrel-containing or other progestin-containing oral contraceptives, followed with semiannual questionnaires for 142,475 woman-years of observation; loss to follow-up was 2.4%. Cardiovascular outcomes were analysed with Cox regression.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for venous thromboembolism were 1.0 for drospirenone-containing versus levonorgestrel-containing pills and 0.8 versus other oral contraceptives (upper 95% confidence limits 1.8 and 1.3) — relative figures, centred on no difference. Arterial thromboembolism hazard ratios were 0.3 in both comparisons. The authors conclude the risks of adverse cardiovascular and other serious events with a drospirenone pill are similar to those with other oral contraceptives.
cards.watchOut: EURAS was industry-sponsored surveillance with self-reported outcomes and few events — its confidence limits (up to 1.8 versus levonorgestrel) cannot exclude the increase the registry studies report; 'no difference found' here is compatible with a true relative increase of the size Lidegaard and Vinogradova describe.
cards.source: Dinger JC et al. The safety of a drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive: final results from the European Active Surveillance Study on oral contraceptives based on 142,475 women-years of observation. Contraception. 2007. PMID: 17434015. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review (Larivée 2017): across 17 observational studies the drospirenone-versus-levonorgestrel relative risk ranged from 1.0 to 3.3 (relative figures); the three highest-quality studies gave 1.0 to 1.57, and most studies carried serious or critical risk of bias
cards.summary: Systematic review (Larivée 2017): across 17 observational studies the drospirenone-versus-levonorgestrel relative risk ranged from 1.0 to 3.3 (relative figures); the three highest-quality studies gave 1.0 to 1.57, and most studies carried serious or critical risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review of observational studies (Larivée 2017) — 17 studies
cards.people: Systematic review of cohort and case-control studies comparing venous thromboembolism risk on drospirenone-containing versus levonorgestrel-containing combined oral contraceptives: 17 studies, quality-assessed with the ROBINS-I tool for prevalent-user bias, comparator choice, outcome misclassification and confounding.
cards.result: Reported relative risks of venous thromboembolism for drospirenone versus levonorgestrel ranged from 1.0 to 3.3 across studies. On ROBINS-I, 3 studies were at moderate risk of bias, 10 at serious risk and 4 at critical risk; 9 studies included prevalent users and 5 failed to account for two or more important confounders. The three highest-quality studies gave relative risks of 1.0 to 1.57, leading the authors to conclude the true risk remains unknown — the best studies suggest no or slightly increased harm, but their confidence limits do not rule out an almost doubling of risk.
cards.watchOut: A review of biased studies inherits their biases: the spread from 1.0 to 3.3 is itself the finding, and which end a reader believes depends on how much channeling and prevalent-user bias they think the adjustments removed.
cards.source: Larivée N et al. Drospirenone-containing oral contraceptive pills and the risk of venous thromboembolism: a systematic review of observational studies. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2017. PMID: 28276140. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT (observational) — large registry studies find drospirenone pills carry roughly 1.6-fold the venous thromboembolism risk of levonorgestrel pills (relative), while the prospective EURAS cohort found no difference; the best-quality studies cluster at no-to-modest increase
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT (observational) — large registry studies find drospirenone pills carry roughly 1.6-fold the venous thromboembolism risk of levonorgestrel pills (relative), while the prospective EURAS cohort found no difference; the best-quality studies cluster at no-to-modest increase
cards.people: The carded evidence is entirely observational: the Danish national cohort (Lidegaard 2009), UK nested case-control studies (Vinogradova 2015), the EURAS prospective cohort (Dinger 2007) and a bias-focused systematic review of 17 studies (Larivée 2017). FLAG — precedent (b): the Danish programme's 2011 update (Lidegaard 2011) is already carded on home pack #5800 (combined versus progestin-only pill — a different question) and is therefore kept out of this shelf's card source lines; this shelf is built on the free 2009 report and the other free programmes, with #5800 cross-pointed here in prose.
cards.result: Registry data say higher risk: rate ratio 1.64 versus levonorgestrel at matched oestrogen dose and duration (Lidegaard 2009), and adjusted odds ratios versus non-use of 4.12 (drospirenone) against 2.38 (levonorgestrel) (Vinogradova 2015), on a low absolute base (about 6 extra cases per 10,000 woman-years for levonorgestrel, more for the higher-risk preparations). EURAS found hazard ratio 1.0. The systematic review locates the disagreement in study quality: the three best studies span 1.0 to 1.57. Absolute risks remain small for both products; the dispute is over a relative difference of, at most, the size the registries report.
cards.watchOut: Observational cap applies and the split is real: no randomised comparison exists or is feasible at this event rate, prescribing channeling is documented, and the stamp must carry both halves of the split rather than a single direction.

shelves.title: IUD use, pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility (observational only): PID risk is confined to the first 20 days after insertion, and copper IUD use showed no association with tubal infertility in nulligravid women
shelves.question: In adolescents and nulliparous women, does IUD use increase pelvic inflammatory disease or later infertility versus non-use?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Female · Humans · Intrauterine Devices/adverse effects · Male · Meta-Analysis as Topic · Pelvic Inflammatory Disease/epidemiology,etiology · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no harm shown) — observational only, graded with care. Farley 1992 (WHO pooled data: 22,908 insertions, 51,399 woman-years) found pelvic inflammatory disease at 1.6 per 1,000 woman-years overall, more than six times higher in the first 20 days after insertion (9.7 vs 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years) and low and constant for up to 8 years — a pattern tied to insertion and background sexually transmitted infection risk. Hubacher 2001 (case-control, 1,895 women) found previous copper IUD use was not associated with tubal occlusion in nulligravid women (odds ratio 1.0 versus infertile controls; 0.9 versus pregnant controls), while chlamydia antibodies were associated with infertility. Hubacher 2014's review reads the wider literature the same way. Adolescent-specific data are thin in the carded set; that indirectness is stated on the face.

cards.headline: Farley 1992 (WHO pooled trial data): pelvic inflammatory disease occurred at 1.6 cases per 1,000 woman-years of IUD use overall — risk was more than 6 times higher in the first 20 days after insertion (9.7 versus 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years) and low and constant for up to 8 years thereafter
cards.summary: Farley 1992 (WHO pooled trial data): pelvic inflammatory disease occurred at 1.6 cases per 1,000 woman-years of IUD use overall — risk was more than 6 times higher in the first 20 days after insertion (9.7 versus 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years) and low and constant for up to 8 years thereafter
cards.type: Pooled analysis of WHO IUD trial data (Farley 1992) — 22,908 insertions; 51,399 woman-years
cards.people: Pooled analysis of the World Health Organisation's IUD clinical trial data: 22,908 IUD insertions with 51,399 woman-years of follow-up, examining the incidence and pattern of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) after adjustment for confounding factors.
cards.result: The overall PID rate was 1.6 cases per 1,000 woman-years of use. After adjustment, PID risk was more than six times higher during the 20 days after insertion than during later times (unadjusted rates 9.7 vs 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years); beyond that window the risk was low and constant for up to eight years of follow-up. Rates varied by geography (highest in Africa, lowest in China) and fell with age. The authors conclude PID in IUD users is most strongly related to the insertion process and to background sexually transmitted disease risk, and is an infrequent event beyond the first 20 days.
cards.watchOut: These are trial-population insertion cohorts from an earlier device era, largely in parous women — the adolescent and nulliparous population this shelf asks about is thinly represented, and PID diagnosis in the source trials was clinical, without uniform microbiological confirmation.
cards.source: Farley TM et al. Intrauterine devices and pelvic inflammatory disease: an international perspective. Lancet (London, England). 1992. PMID: 1347812. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hubacher 2001 (observational case-control): previous copper IUD use was not associated with tubal occlusion in nulligravid women — odds ratio 1.0 against infertile controls and 0.9 against pregnant controls (relative figures) — while chlamydia antibodies were associated with infertility
cards.summary: Hubacher 2001 (observational case-control): previous copper IUD use was not associated with tubal occlusion in nulligravid women — odds ratio 1.0 against infertile controls and 0.9 against pregnant controls (relative figures) — while chlamydia antibodies were associated with infertility
cards.type: Observational case-control study (Hubacher 2001) — N = 1,895 women (358 cases, 1,537 controls)
cards.people: Case-control study in Mexico, 1997–1999: 358 nulligravid women with primary infertility and documented tubal occlusion, 953 women with primary infertility without tubal occlusion (infertile controls) and 584 primigravid women (pregnant controls). Past contraceptive use, sexual history and genital infection history were collected, and blood was tested for antibodies to Chlamydia trachomatis.
cards.result: The odds ratio for tubal occlusion associated with previous copper IUD use was 1.0 (95% CI 0.6 to 1.7) against infertile controls and 0.9 (95% CI 0.5 to 1.6) against pregnant controls — no association (the exposure made no difference). Tubal infertility was not associated with duration of IUD use, reason for removal, or gynaecological problems during use. By contrast, the presence of chlamydia antibodies was associated with infertility, pointing to sexually transmitted infection — not the device — as the tubal risk.
cards.watchOut: Case-control and retrospective: recall of past contraception and selection of infertile controls can bias towards the null, and the confidence interval (up to 1.7) cannot exclude a modest increase; the study addresses copper devices in nulligravid women, not adolescents specifically and not levonorgestrel systems.

observational case-control study (hubacher 2001) — n = 1,895 women (358 cases, 1,537 controls) case-control study in mexico, 1997–1999: 358 nulligravid women with primary infertility and documented tubal occlusion, 953 women with primary infertility without tubal occlusion (infertile controls) and 584 primigravid women (pregnant controls). past contraceptive use, sexual history and genital infection history were collected, and blood was tested for antibodies to chlamydia trachomatis. the odds ratio for tubal occlusion associated with previous copper iud use was 1.0 (95% ci 0.6 to 1.7) against infertile controls and 0.9 (95% ci 0.5 to 1.6) against pregnant controls — no association (the exposure made no difference). tubal infertility was not associated with duration of iud use, reason for removal, or gynaecological problems during use. by contrast, the presence of chlamydia antibodies was associated with infertility, pointing to sexually transmitted infection — not the device — as the tubal risk. case-control and retrospective: recall of past contraception and selection of infertile controls can bias towards the null, and the confidence interval (up to 1.7) cannot exclude a modest increase; the study addresses copper devices in nulligravid women, not adolescents specifically and not levonorgestrel systems. hubacher d et al. use of copper intrauterine devices and the risk of tubal infertility among nulligravid women. the new england journal of medicine. 2001. pmid: 11529209. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · antibodies, bacterial/blood · case-control studies · chlamydia infections/complications · chlamydia trachomatis/immunology · fallopian tube diseases/etiology · female · gravidity · humans · infertility, female/epidemiology,etiology · intrauterine devices, copper/adverse effects · logistic models · odds ratio · pelvic inflammatory disease/etiology · risk factors

cards.headline: Hubacher 2014 (review): across 50 years of research, the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease with IUD use is very low, and studies linking previous IUD use to tubal infertility suggest risks lower still — with study limitations preventing firm conclusions
cards.summary: Hubacher 2014 (review): across 50 years of research, the risk of pelvic inflammatory disease with IUD use is very low, and studies linking previous IUD use to tubal infertility suggest risks lower still — with study limitations preventing firm conclusions
cards.people: Narrative review of the literature on intrauterine devices and infection over five decades, covering pelvic inflammatory disease risk and the more distant endpoint of tubal infertility, and the methodological barriers in this literature (uncertain infection diagnoses and inappropriate comparison groups for IUD users).
cards.result: The review concludes that natural-history studies of disease aetiology and observational research among IUD users suggest the risk of PID is very low, and that research linking previous IUD use to tubal infertility reveals risks that may be even lower than the risks of PID. It cautions that limitations in the studies make firm conclusions difficult and complicate the design of better studies.
cards.watchOut: A single-author narrative review is the weakest card on this shelf: it contributes the field's overall read, not new data, and its caution about firm conclusions applies to reassurance as much as to alarm.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the observational record does not show IUD use raising pelvic inflammatory disease beyond a brief post-insertion window, nor causing later tubal infertility — risk tracks sexually transmitted infection, not the device
cards.summary: Synthesis: the observational record does not show IUD use raising pelvic inflammatory disease beyond a brief post-insertion window, nor causing later tubal infertility — risk tracks sexually transmitted infection, not the device
cards.people: The carded evidence is observational and pooled-trial data: the WHO pooled analysis (22,908 insertions), the Mexican case-control study in nulligravid women (1,895 women), and a 2014 literature review. No randomised comparison of IUD versus non-use for these outcomes exists.
cards.result: PID after insertion runs at 1.6 per 1,000 woman-years overall, concentrated in the first 20 days (9.7 versus 1.4 per 1,000 woman-years later) and low and constant for up to 8 years — a pattern implicating insertion and background sexually transmitted infection risk rather than continuing device use. For the outcome women fear most, previous copper IUD use showed no association with tubal occlusion in nulligravid women (odds ratios 1.0 and 0.9), while chlamydia antibodies did associate with infertility. For adolescents specifically, the carded data are indirect — the WHO data are mostly parous adults and the infertility study is nulligravid adults — and that indirectness is printed here rather than smoothed over.
cards.watchOut: Observational cap applies to a null as much as to a harm: confidence intervals cannot exclude a modest PID or infertility effect, device types have changed since 1992, and screening for chlamydia at insertion — standard now — was not uniform in the source studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Farley TM et al. Lancet (London, England). 1992 (PMID: 1347812); Hubacher D et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11529209); Hubacher D et al. The Indian journal of medical research. 2014 (PMID: 25673543). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
