shelves.title: Levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD to 8 years: efficacy persists in years 6–8 — Pearl Index 0.28 over years 6–8 in the Mirena Extension Trial and a 1.32% cumulative 8-year pregnancy rate for Liletta
shelves.question: In women, does keeping a levonorgestrel 52 mg IUD for up to 8 years remain effective contraception (versus the originally licensed 5 years)?
shelves.mesh: Pregnancy · Female · Humans · Levonorgestrel/adverse effects · Intrauterine Devices, Medicated/adverse effects · Contraceptive Agents, Female/adverse effects · Menorrhagia/etiology · Metrorrhagia/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — framed as an evidence question, not a randomised comparison: the data are single-arm efficacy cohorts. The Mirena Extension Trial (Jensen 2022; 362 women starting year 6 with the Mirena 52-mg system, named as published) found 2 pregnancies in years 6–8, a 3-year Pearl Index of 0.28 and a cumulative failure rate of 0.68%. ACCESS IUS (Creinin 2022; Liletta 52-mg system, named as published) found a cumulative pregnancy rate of 1.32% through 8 years, with 2 pregnancies in year 7 and none in year 8. A Brazilian chart review of 776 women keeping the same Mirena device beyond 60 months (Bahamondes 2018; Mirena; Bayer Oy, Turku, Finland, as published) found zero pregnancies over 967 woman-years to year 7. Products and company are named exactly as published under the clarification exception.

cards.headline: Mirena Extension Trial (Jensen 2022): keeping the 52-mg levonorgestrel system (Mirena) into years 6–8 gave a 3-year Pearl Index of 0.28 and a cumulative failure rate of 0.68% — 2 pregnancies among 362 women starting year 6
cards.summary: Mirena Extension Trial (Jensen 2022): keeping the 52-mg levonorgestrel system (Mirena) into years 6–8 gave a 3-year Pearl Index of 0.28 and a cumulative failure rate of 0.68% — 2 pregnancies among 362 women starting year 6
cards.type: Single-arm extension cohort, Mirena Extension Trial (Jensen 2022) — 362 women starting year 6; 223 completing year 8
cards.people: Multicentre single-arm extension study in the United States enrolling existing users of the 52-mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (the Mirena Extension Trial; the product is named in the trial's name as published), aged 18–35, who had used the system for 4.5–5 years: 362 participants started year 6, 243 entered year 8 and 223 completed 8 years of use. Efficacy was measured by Pearl Index and Kaplan-Meier cumulative failure rate for years 6–8.
cards.result: Two pregnancies occurred in years 6–8, both with the device in situ: a year-6 pregnancy of undetermined location that resolved spontaneously, and a year-7 ectopic pregnancy treated with methotrexate. The Pearl Index for years 6–8 was 0.28 (95% CI 0.03 to 1.00), with yearly Pearl Indexes of 0.34 (year 6), 0.40 (year 7) and 0.00 (year 8); the 3-year cumulative failure rate was 0.68% (95% CI 0.17 to 2.71). Discontinuation over the extension was 38.4%, most commonly for desire for pregnancy (12.2%); 98.7% of those completing the study remained satisfied, and the 12-month return-to-fertility rate after removal for planned pregnancy was 77.4%.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm by design: women who reach year 6 are selected continuers (those with problems have already left), there is no comparison group wearing a fresh device, and the trial enrolled contraception users aged 18–35 — the authors note too few heavy-menstrual-bleeding users were enrolled to judge extended use for that indication.
cards.source: Jensen JT et al. Contraceptive efficacy and safety of the 52-mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system for up to 8 years: findings from the Mirena Extension Trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2022. PMID: 36096186. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ACCESS IUS (Creinin 2022): the Liletta levonorgestrel 52 mg system stayed highly effective through 8 years — cumulative pregnancy rate 1.32% over 8 years, with 2 pregnancies in year 7 (Pearl Index 0.49) and none in year 8
cards.summary: ACCESS IUS (Creinin 2022): the Liletta levonorgestrel 52 mg system stayed highly effective through 8 years — cumulative pregnancy rate 1.32% over 8 years, with 2 pregnancies in year 7 (Pearl Index 0.49) and none in year 8
cards.type: Single-arm phase 3 cohort, ACCESS IUS (Creinin 2022) — 1,751 enrolled; 569 starting year 7
cards.people: Phase 3 multicentre trial of the Liletta levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system (named in the record as the Liletta system), enrolling 1,751 nulliparous and multiparous participants aged 16–45 (1,568 aged 16–35 in the efficacy population; 57.5% nulliparous, 25.3% with obesity), followed with 6-monthly checks. This report covers efficacy and safety through 8 years of continuous use of the same device: 569 participants started year 7 and 343 completed year 8.
cards.result: Eleven pregnancies occurred over 8 years, 7 of them ectopic. In year 7 there were 2 pregnancies (Pearl Index 0.49, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.78; one followed a desired removal by 4 days) and in year 8 there were none. The cumulative life-table pregnancy rate through year 8 was 1.32% (95% CI 0.69 to 2.51). Safety over extended use: 2 perforations (0.1%, none after year 1), expulsion in 4.1% overall (3 in year 7, 2 in year 8), pelvic infection in 0.9% overall (1 each in years 7 and 8), discontinuation for bleeding complaints in 2.6% overall, and amenorrhoea rates of 39% at both years 7 and 8.
cards.watchOut: Again single-arm with continuer selection, and the year 7–8 efficacy population narrows to users aged 39 or under at each year's start; 7 of the 11 pregnancies over the whole study were ectopic — a high proportion typical of very effective contraception when failures do occur, and a reason ectopic vigilance still applies.
cards.source: Creinin MD et al. Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system efficacy and safety through 8 years of use. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2022. PMID: 35569516. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bahamondes 2018 (observational chart review): among 776 Brazilian women who kept the same Mirena system (Mirena; Bayer Oy, Turku, Finland, as named in the record) beyond 60 months, zero pregnancies were reported over 967 woman-years to year 7
cards.summary: Bahamondes 2018 (observational chart review): among 776 Brazilian women who kept the same Mirena system (Mirena; Bayer Oy, Turku, Finland, as named in the record) beyond 60 months, zero pregnancies were reported over 967 woman-years to year 7
cards.type: Observational chart review (Bahamondes 2018) — 776 women continuing beyond 60 months
cards.people: Chart review at a university family-planning clinic in Campinas, Brazil: 776 women who continued the same 52-mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (Mirena; Bayer Oy, Turku, Finland — product and company exactly as published) beyond 60 months, with median use of 73 months (range 61–184 months). Outcomes: pregnancies, continuation and discontinuation reasons, and bleeding pattern at last visit, analysed by Kaplan-Meier methods.
cards.result: Zero pregnancies were reported, over 967 cumulative woman-years of exposure up to 7 years and 1,403 woman-years up to 15 years after placement. The main reasons for discontinuation were expiry of the approved lifespan, menopause and planning pregnancy, and the predominant bleeding pattern at last visit was amenorrhoea. The authors conclude the device showed continued contraceptive efficacy beyond 5 years and that the data support keeping the same device at least to 7 years.
cards.watchOut: A chart review of self-selected long-term continuers at one clinic, with pregnancies captured from records rather than systematic testing: zero events in 967 woman-years is reassuring but its upper confidence bound is not zero, and women who removed the device early for any reason never enter this cohort.
cards.source: Bahamondes L et al. Pregnancy outcomes associated with extended use of the 52-mg 20 μg/day levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system beyond 60 months: A chart review of 776 women in Brazil. Contraception. 2018. cards.headline: Synthesis: two prospective single-arm programmes and one large chart review agree — the 52-mg levonorgestrel system remains highly effective in years 6–8, with Pearl Indexes under 0.5; this is an evidence question answered by cohorts, not a randomised comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: two prospective single-arm programmes and one large chart review agree — the 52-mg levonorgestrel system remains highly effective in years 6–8, with Pearl Indexes under 0.5; this is an evidence question answered by cohorts, not a randomised comparison
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Mirena Extension Trial (362 women entering year 6), the ACCESS IUS Liletta cohort (569 entering year 7), and a 776-woman Brazilian chart review of extended Mirena use. Products are named exactly as published under the clarification exception: Mirena (extension trial and chart review; Bayer Oy named in the chart review's record) and Liletta (ACCESS IUS).
cards.result: Failure rates in years 6–8 are of the same small order as in the licensed first 5 years: a 3-year Pearl Index of 0.28 and cumulative failure of 0.68% for years 6–8 (Mirena extension), a cumulative 8-year pregnancy rate of 1.32% with no year-8 pregnancies (Liletta), and zero pregnancies over 967 woman-years beyond month 60 in the chart review. Extended-use safety shows no new pattern (expulsion ~4% overall, pelvic infection under 1%, perforations confined to insertion). Long-acting shelves elsewhere (live #659; pack #6039) cover continuation and device comparisons, not extended-duration efficacy — this shelf is that slice.
cards.watchOut: No randomised or fresh-device comparison exists for years 6–8, and every cohort is enriched for satisfied continuers; the stamp is POSSIBLE, framed as cohort evidence that efficacy persists, not proof that an 8-year-old device equals a new one.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jensen JT et al. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2022 (PMID: 36096186); Creinin MD et al. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2022 (PMID: 35569516); Bahamondes L et al. Contraception. 2018 (PMID: 29055780). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Normal pregnancy expands plasma volume by ~45–48% and filtration rate by ~45–50% — both rise from the first weeks, plasma volume peaking late in the third trimester, filtration peaking earlier and then easing
shelves.question: In pregnant women, how much do plasma volume and glomerular filtration rate normally rise, and at what gestation do they peak?
shelves.mesh: Abortion, Spontaneous/metabolism · Adult · Creatinine/metabolism · Female · Humans · Menstruation · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, First
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Two longitudinal human measurements, repeated decades apart, give the same magnitudes. Plasma volume rises ~6% in the first trimester and ~45–48% above the non-pregnant state by the late third trimester, peaking at 35–38 weeks (two meta-analyses of longitudinal studies: Aguree 2019, 10 studies, 347 pregnancies; de Haas 2017, 30 studies, pooled maximum +1.13 L, +45.6%). Glomerular filtration rate rises earlier and further in relative terms: 24-hour creatinine clearance is already up ~45% by the ninth week of gestation (Davison & Noble 1981, 11 women), and inulin clearance shows renal plasma flow and GFR rising by 6 weeks of gestation (Chapman 1998, 13 women). The two curves diverge late: filtration rate peaks around mid-pregnancy and then eases in the last month, while renal plasma flow falls more sharply in the third trimester even as inulin GFR is maintained (Ezimokhai/Davison 1981, 17 women). Framing follows Guyton & Hall and Ganong (systemic vasodilatation, renin-angiotensin activation, a higher cardiac output driving both changes), named as textbook framing, not as evidence.

cards.headline: Davison & Noble 1981: 24-hour creatinine clearance was already 45% higher by the ninth week of gestation in 11 women followed from before conception
cards.summary: Davison & Noble 1981: 24-hour creatinine clearance was already 45% higher by the ninth week of gestation in 11 women followed from before conception
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial creatinine clearance, pre-conception to first trimester), Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1981
cards.people: Eleven women with serial 24-hour creatinine clearances through several menstrual cycles before conception, the conceptional cycle and the first trimester of pregnancy.
cards.result: During the menstrual cycle, creatinine clearance rose a mean 20% between the week of menstruation and the late luteal phase; after conception that rise continued, reaching a mean 45% increase by the ninth week of gestation. In the two women who aborted spontaneously, the early-pregnancy rise was smaller and less sustained — apparent at least three weeks before any clinical abnormality. The filtration rise of pregnancy is therefore not a late adaptation; it is established in the first trimester.
cards.watchOut: N = 11 and creatinine clearance overestimates true GFR (tubular secretion); the 45% figure is a clearance change, not an inulin-clearance change — the inulin confirmation is the Chapman card.
cards.source: Davison JM, Noble MC. Serial changes in 24 hour creatinine clearance during normal menstrual cycles and the first trimester of pregnancy. Br J Obstet Gynaecol. 1981. PMID: 7459286. cards.headline: Chapman 1998: in 13 women studied before conception and at 6–36 weeks, renal plasma flow and GFR had already risen by 6 weeks, with plasma volume rising alongside
cards.summary: Chapman 1998: in 13 women studied before conception and at 6–36 weeks, renal plasma flow and GFR had already risen by 6 weeks, with plasma volume rising alongside
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial inulin/PAH clearance from pre-conception), Kidney Int 1998
cards.people: Thirteen women studied in identical fashion before conception and at gestational weeks 6, 8, 10, 12, 24 and 36, with mean arterial pressure, cardiac output, inulin and para-aminohippurate clearance, and plasma volume determinations.
cards.result: By 6 weeks of gestation, mean arterial pressure had fallen (mid-follicular 81.5 ± 2.6 to 68.7 ± 2.0 mmHg, P < 0.001) while cardiac output rose, systemic vascular resistance fell, and plasma volume, renal plasma flow and GFR (inulin clearance) all rose. Plasma renin activity and aldosterone rose significantly by 6 weeks; atrial natriuretic peptide rose later, at 12 weeks. Peripheral vasodilatation therefore precedes full placentation and drives the early renal and volume changes.
cards.watchOut: N = 13, healthy volunteers with normal pregnancies; the record reports that GFR and renal plasma flow 'increased by six weeks' without printing the percentage change, so the timing — not a magnitude — is what this card establishes.
cards.source: Chapman AB et al. Temporal relationships between hormonal and hemodynamic changes in early human pregnancy. Kidney Int. 1998. PMID: 9853271. cards.headline: Ezimokhai & Davison 1981: in the third trimester, effective renal plasma flow fell significantly between its start and end — while inulin GFR was maintained (17 women)
cards.summary: Ezimokhai & Davison 1981: in the third trimester, effective renal plasma flow fell significantly between its start and end — while inulin GFR was maintained (17 women)
cards.type: Human physiological study (serial inulin clearance, third trimester), Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1981
cards.people: Seventeen healthy women investigated near the beginning and again near the end of the third trimester of normal pregnancies, with infusion studies in the left lateral position.
cards.result: Effective renal plasma flow fell significantly across the third trimester, but glomerular filtration rate measured as inulin clearance did not fall significantly; plasma creatinine rose significantly while the renal handling of creatinine was unchanged, and serum urate rose, apparently from increased net tubular reabsorption of urate. Filtration fraction therefore rises late in pregnancy: the filtration rate holds while the flow that feeds it declines — consistent with a filtration peak before the third trimester and a gentle decline toward term.
cards.watchOut: N = 17, two time points only, and all studies were in the left lateral position — supine posture lowers renal plasma flow in pregnancy, which is why posture was controlled rather than varied.
cards.source: Ezimokhai M et al. Non-postural serial changes in renal function during the third trimester of normal human pregnancy. Br J Obstet Gynaecol. 1981. PMID: 7236549. cards.headline: Aguree 2019 meta-analysis: plasma volume +6% in trimester 1, +29% by weeks 21–27, +42% at weeks 28–34 and +48% at weeks 35–38 (10 longitudinal studies, 347 pregnancies)
cards.summary: Aguree 2019 meta-analysis: plasma volume +6% in trimester 1, +29% by weeks 21–27, +42% at weeks 28–34 and +48% at weeks 35–38 (10 longitudinal studies, 347 pregnancies)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (longitudinal plasma-volume studies), BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2019
cards.people: Ten longitudinal studies with a total of 347 pregnancies, each measuring plasma volume at least twice across gestation and once before or after pregnancy in the same women, pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: Plasma volume increased 6% (95% CI 3–9%) in the first trimester versus the non-pregnant state; 18% (12–24%) in weeks 14–20 and 29% (21–36%) in weeks 21–27; then 42% (38–46%) in weeks 28–34 and 48% (44–51%) in weeks 35–38. The steepest rate of increase occurred in the first half of the second trimester, and the peak is late in the third trimester. The companion de Haas 2017 meta-analysis of 30 studies (1934–2007) gives a pooled maximum increase of 1.13 L (95% CI 1.07–1.19 L), +45.6% (43.0–48.1%) — the two pooled estimates agree within a few points.
cards.watchOut: Seven of the ten studies are more than 30 years old and the pooled population predates modern body-mass-index distributions — the authors flag that the pattern may not reflect the current population. The de Haas pooled estimate is cited in prose for corroboration, not as a separate card.
cards.source: Aguree S, Gernand AD. Plasma volume expansion across healthy pregnancy: a systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies. BMC Pregnancy Childbirth. 2019. PMID: 31856759. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Female · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Plasma Volume/physiology · Pregnancy/physiology · Reference Values

cards.headline: Synthesis: both rise from the first weeks; filtration peaks first, volume peaks last — and the magnitudes are ~45% for each
cards.summary: Synthesis: both rise from the first weeks; filtration peaks first, volume peaks last — and the magnitudes are ~45% for each
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded human studies above (Davison & Noble 1981; Chapman 1998; Ezimokhai & Davison 1981; Aguree 2019), framed by Guyton & Hall and Ganong.
cards.result: The normal time course is now settled: systemic vasodilatation and renin-angiotensin activation begin within weeks of conception (Chapman), filtration rate is up ~45% by week 9 (Davison & Noble) and stays high through mid-pregnancy, then eases while renal plasma flow falls (Ezimokhai & Davison, and the parallel third-trimester clearance studies), while plasma volume climbs steadily to a late-third-trimester peak of +45–48%, about 1.1 L above the non-pregnant state (Aguree; de Haas). Two numbers matter clinically: a 'normal' creatinine in pregnancy sits against a much higher GFR, so a modestly raised creatinine may already mean renal impairment; and plasma volume expands more than red-cell mass, so the 'anaemia of pregnancy' is largely dilutional — both are Guyton & Hall textbook corollaries presented as textbook framing.
cards.watchOut: The filtration 'peak' is inferred from a rising first trimester, maintenance in the third trimester and a declining clearance trend in the last month (the Paaby serial-clearance data are cited in prose in the underlying literature, not carded); the peak gestational week for GFR is not pinned to a single week by any carded record, and the Synthesis says so.
cards.source: Synthesis of Davison JM, Noble MC, Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1981 (PMID: 7459286); Chapman AB et al., Kidney Int 1998 (PMID: 9853271); Ezimokhai M et al., Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1981 (PMID: 7236549); Aguree S, Gernand AD, BMC Pregnancy Childbirth 2019 (PMID: 31856759). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: The oestradiol trigger for the LH surge (physiology): a preovulatory oestradiol rise sustained for roughly 60 hours switches feedback from negative to positive — pituitary responsiveness is absent at 36 hours and augmented by 60–84 hours at oestradiol levels around 130–190 pg/mL
shelves.question: In healthy women, what oestradiol concentration, sustained for how long, triggers the mid-cycle LH surge?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Estradiol/physiology · Female · Follicle Stimulating Hormone/blood · Humans · Hypogonadism/blood · Luteinizing Hormone/blood · *Menstruation · Progesterone/physiology · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): oestradiol feeds back negatively for most of the follicular phase, then — when its rise is high enough and sustained long enough — switches to positive feedback and triggers the mid-cycle LH surge; the textbooks' commonly quoted form of the rule (oestradiol above ~200 pg/mL sustained for ~50 hours) is the textbook's account, and the carded 1970s–80s human experiments are what the rule rests on. Liu and Yen 1983 gave the duration directly: incremental oestradiol sustained over 96 hours produced reproducible LH and FSH surges after latencies of 58 ± 6.9 hours (midfollicular women) and 68.2 ± 2.6 hours (hypogonadal women) — 'incremental E2 sustained for about 60 h constitutes the ovarian signal'. Keye and Jaffe 1975 isolated duration from concentration: at similar oestradiol levels (about 128–186 pg/mL), gonadotropin responses to GnRH were absent at 36 hours but augmented and prolonged at 60–132 hours. Young and Jaffe 1976 mapped the concentration axis, achieving mean oestradiol levels of 43–305 pg/mL across a sixfold dose range over 6 days. March 1979 showed an oestradiol rise mimicking the preovulatory peak was sufficient to trigger an LH surge (with progesterone timing deciding whether an FSH peak accompanied it), and Hoff and Yen 1983 timed the natural event: the surge follows about 50 hours of rising oestradiol and lasts 48 hours. The honest summary: concentration and duration are jointly the trigger — levels in the preovulatory range (roughly 150–300 pg/mL in these experiments) must be sustained for roughly 50–60 hours. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Liu and Yen 1983: incremental oestradiol sustained for about 60 hours was the signal — surges followed latencies of 58 hours in normal women and 68 hours in hypogonadal women
cards.summary: Liu and Yen 1983: incremental oestradiol sustained for about 60 hours was the signal — surges followed latencies of 58 hours in normal women and 68 hours in hypogonadal women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (stepwise oestradiol infusion, Yen programme)
cards.people: Normal women studied in the midfollicular phase and hypogonadal women with oestradiol implants, given stepwise incremental infusions of oestradiol (with or without progesterone) over 96 hours to reproduce a preovulatory steroid configuration; group sizes N not documented in the record's abstract.
cards.result: During 96 hours of oestradiol infusion alone, reproducible and concomitant surges of LH and FSH occurred after latency periods (mean ± SE) of 58 ± 6.9 hours in midfollicular subjects and 68.2 ± 2.6 hours in hypogonadal subjects. The oestradiol-induced surge lasted 22.7 ± 3.9 hours (midfollicular) and 21.8 ± 2.5 hours (hypogonadal), shorter than the spontaneous midcycle surge (48 hours). Superimposing progesterone 48 hours after starting oestradiol produced a surge approximating the spontaneous surge's dimension in both groups and advanced onset by 14.7 hours in hypogonadal women (p < 0.001). The authors conclude that incremental oestradiol sustained for about 60 hours constitutes the ovarian signal initiating the midcycle gonadotropin surge, with a small progesterone increment required for the surge's normal dimension.
cards.watchOut: An infusion-clamp experiment that reproduces the preovulatory pattern artificially; subject numbers are not stated in the record's abstract (N not documented), and the induced surge without progesterone was shorter than the natural one.
cards.source: Liu JH et al. Induction of midcycle gonadotropin surge by ovarian steroids in women: a critical evaluation. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1983. PMID: 6411754. cards.headline: Keye and Jaffe 1975: at the same oestradiol levels (~130–190 pg/mL), pituitary responses were absent at 36 hours but augmented at 60–132 hours — duration, not just concentration, is the trigger
cards.summary: Keye and Jaffe 1975: at the same oestradiol levels (~130–190 pg/mL), pituitary responses were absent at 36 hours but augmented at 60–132 hours — duration, not just concentration, is the trigger
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oestradiol duration series with GnRH testing, Jaffe programme, part I)
cards.people: Normal women given intramuscular oestradiol benzoate from day 1 of the cycle (5 µg/kg, then 2.5 µg/kg every 12 hours) for 3, 5, 7, 9 or 11 injections (2 subjects per duration), each tested with 100 µg intravenous GnRH and compared with her own control cycle; N = 10 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: When GnRH was given 36 hours after starting oestradiol, there was no significant LH or FSH increase. At 60 hours LH responses were augmented (FSH not yet), and at 84, 108 and 132 hours both LH and FSH responses were augmented and prolonged versus control cycles, with maximal increases 1.5 to 9 times control. Mean serum oestradiol was similar at the ineffective and effective durations — 185.9 ± 20.0 pg/mL at 36 hours versus 157.7 ± 31.6 at 60, 186.2 ± 38.1 at 84, 181.3 ± 46.7 at 108 and 128.0 ± 43.0 pg/mL at 132 hours. The authors conclude the modulating effect of oestradiol on pituitary responsiveness depends on the duration of exposure, not the level alone.
cards.watchOut: Two subjects per duration point (N = 10 total) and a GnRH-challenge endpoint — it measures pituitary responsiveness, the surge mechanism's pituitary arm, rather than spontaneous surges themselves.
cards.source: Keye WR et al. Strength-duration characteristics of estrogen effects on gonadotropin response to gonadotropin-releasing hormone in women. I. Effects of varying duration of estradiol administration. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1975. PMID: 1107343. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Young and Jaffe 1976: the concentration axis — six oestradiol benzoate doses over 6 days achieved mean oestradiol levels from 43 to 305 pg/mL for GnRH-response testing
cards.summary: Young and Jaffe 1976: the concentration axis — six oestradiol benzoate doses over 6 days achieved mean oestradiol levels from 43 to 305 pg/mL for GnRH-response testing
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oestradiol concentration series with GnRH testing, Jaffe programme, part II)
cards.people: Normal women studied from day 1 of the menstrual cycle in 19 experiments, receiving oestradiol benzoate injections every 12 hours for 6 days at 0.3, 0.6, 1.25, 2.5, 3.75 or 5.0 µg/kg per 12 hours, with a 100 µg GnRH bolus 12 hours after the last injection, each compared with an early-follicular control cycle.
cards.result: The six dose levels achieved mean serum oestradiol concentrations of 43, 53, 91, 145, 195 and 305 pg/mL respectively — spanning sub-threshold follicular levels through and beyond the preovulatory range — providing the concentration series against which gonadotropin responses to GnRH were compared with each subject's untreated cycle. The fetched record's abstract reports the design and the achieved concentrations (its text ends with the methods), so this card claims the concentration mapping only; the duration requirement at these levels is carried by Keye and Jaffe 1975 and Liu and Yen 1983 on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract is truncated to methods and achieved levels; no response numbers are printed here because the fetched record does not give them. Nineteen experiments across six doses means about three studies per concentration.

cards.headline: March 1979: an oestradiol rise mimicking the preovulatory peak triggered an LH surge in all three subjects — progesterone's timing decided whether FSH surged too
cards.summary: March 1979: an oestradiol rise mimicking the preovulatory peak triggered an LH surge in all three subjects — progesterone's timing decided whether FSH surged too
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (oophorectomised women on oestradiol replacement, steroid add-back experiments)
cards.people: 3 women of reproductive age who had undergone oophorectomy and received uninterrupted oestradiol replacement by subdermal implants (basal oestradiol in the midfollicular range), each undergoing seven experiments at 2–4-week intervals with intramuscular oestradiol benzoate alone or combined with progesterone from vaginal rings; N = 3 printed on the face of this physiology card (classic small physiology study).
cards.result: In all three subjects, increasing serum oestradiol levels mimicking the preovulatory peak were followed by a surge of LH but not of FSH. When progesterone levels rose after the oestradiol increase, the LH surge occurred earlier and was accompanied by an FSH peak; when progesterone rose before oestradiol, or without an oestradiol rise, neither surge occurred. Progesterone alone did not affect LH or FSH. The authors conclude an acute rise in serum oestradiol is a necessary condition for the midcycle surges, and progesterone facilitates or blocks the response in a time-dependent manner and is required for the preovulatory FSH peak.
cards.watchOut: Only 3 subjects (printed on the face), studied in an oophorectomy-and-replacement model rather than intact cycles; it establishes sufficiency and necessity of the oestradiol rise, while the natural-cycle timing comes from Hoff and Yen 1983 in the balance.
cards.source: March CM et al. Roles of estradiol and progesterone in eiliciting the midcycle luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone surges. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1979. PMID: 479343. cards.headline: Synthesis: preovulatory-range oestradiol sustained for roughly 50–60 hours is the trigger — the level alone at 36 hours does nothing — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: preovulatory-range oestradiol sustained for roughly 50–60 hours is the trigger — the level alone at 36 hours does nothing — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: oestradiol-infusion experiments in normal and hypogonadal women (Liu and Yen 1983; N not documented in the record), 10 women in a duration series (Keye and Jaffe 1975), 19 concentration-series experiments (Young and Jaffe 1976), and 3 oophorectomised women in add-back experiments (March 1979).
cards.result: The experiments converge on a strength–duration rule: oestradiol in the preovulatory range (about 130–305 pg/mL across these studies) switches feedback positive only when sustained — no pituitary augmentation at 36 hours, augmentation by 60–84 hours, and spontaneous-type surges after latencies of about 58–68 hours of incremental oestradiol; in natural cycles (Hoff and Yen 1983, cited in the balance) the surge follows about 50 hours of rising oestradiol and lasts 48 hours. The textbooks' shorthand (about 200 pg/mL for about 50 hours) is consistent with these bounds. This matches the textbook account in Ganong and in Boron and Boulpaep, which frame this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Classic small experiments from the radioimmunoassay era in selected volunteers: the trigger is a range-and-duration zone, not a sharp clinical cut-off, and assay methods differ from modern oestradiol measurement.
cards.source: Synthesis of Liu JH et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1983 (PMID: 6411754); Keye WR et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1975 (PMID: 1107343); Young JR et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1976 (PMID: 767352); March CM et al. shelves.title: Sildenafil in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction (STRIDER UK, Netherlands, NZAus): no growth or survival benefit, with a Dutch neonatal pulmonary-hypertension signal
shelves.question: In women with severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, does sildenafil improve fetal growth or perinatal survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Birth Weight · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Growth Retardation/drug therapy · Gestational Age · Humans · Phosphodiesterase 5 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Sildenafil Citrate/therapeutic use · Umbilical Arteries
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — with a neonatal harm signal in one trial. Three placebo-controlled STRIDER trials agree that sildenafil does not improve growth or survival in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction: the UK trial (Sharp 2018, PMID: 30169244) found no prolongation of pregnancy (median 17 vs 18 days to delivery) and no difference in livebirth or birthweight; the New Zealand/Australia trial (Groom 2019, PMID: 30779295) found no increase in fetal growth velocity (52.5% vs 68.4% on placebo); and the Dutch trial (Pels 2020, PMID: 32585017) was stopped early for safety — its primary outcome of perinatal death or major morbidity was 60.2% on sildenafil vs 54.2% on placebo, and neonatal pulmonary hypertension occurred in 18.8% vs 5.1% (relative risk 3.67). Sildenafil should not be used for this indication outside research.

cards.headline: Sharp 2018 (UK STRIDER): no prolongation of pregnancy — median 17 days to delivery on sildenafil vs 18 days on placebo (p=0.23); livebirth and birthweight also no different (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Sharp 2018 (UK STRIDER): no prolongation of pregnancy — median 17 days to delivery on sildenafil vs 18 days on placebo (p=0.23); livebirth and birthweight also no different (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Sharp 2018, UK STRIDER)
cards.people: 135 women with singleton pregnancies at 22+0 to 29+6 weeks with severe early-onset fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference below the 10th percentile with absent or reversed end-diastolic flow), randomised to sildenafil 25 mg three times daily (n=70) or placebo (n=65) until 32 weeks or delivery, in 19 UK fetal medicine units.
cards.result: Median randomisation-to-delivery interval was 17 days (IQR 7–24) on sildenafil vs 18 days (8–28) on placebo (p=0.23). Livebirths (relative risk [RR] 1.06, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.33), fetal deaths (RR 0.89, 0.54 to 1.45), neonatal deaths (RR 1.33, 0.54 to 3.28) and birthweight (difference −14 g, −100 to 126; p=0.81) did not differ between groups, and no secondary outcome differed. Eight serious adverse events were reported (six placebo, two sildenafil); none was attributed to sildenafil.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome was time to delivery, a proxy — but every growth and survival secondary outcome pointed the same null way, so the proxy is not hiding a benefit.
cards.source: Sharp A et al. Maternal sildenafil for severe fetal growth restriction (STRIDER): a multicentre, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial. The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health. 2018. PMID: 30169244. Registry ID: ISRCTN 39133303 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Pels 2020 (Dutch STRIDER): trial stopped early for harm — perinatal death or major morbidity 60.2% on sildenafil vs 54.2% on placebo, and neonatal pulmonary hypertension 18.8% vs 5.1% (relative risk 3.67, p=0.008)
cards.summary: Pels 2020 (Dutch STRIDER): trial stopped early for harm — perinatal death or major morbidity 60.2% on sildenafil vs 54.2% on placebo, and neonatal pulmonary hypertension 18.8% vs 5.1% (relative risk 3.67, p=0.008)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial, stopped early for safety (Pels 2020, Dutch STRIDER)
cards.people: 216 pregnant women at 20 to 30 weeks with severe fetal growth restriction (abdominal circumference below the 3rd percentile, or estimated fetal weight below the 5th percentile with abnormal Dopplers or a maternal hypertensive disorder), randomised to sildenafil 25 mg three times daily (n=108) or placebo (n=108) at 11 Dutch centres; the trial was halted in July 2018, before its planned 360 participants, over the pulmonary-hypertension concern.
cards.result: The primary outcome — perinatal mortality or major neonatal morbidity until hospital discharge — occurred in the offspring of 65 participants (60.2%) on sildenafil vs 58 (54.2%) on placebo (relative risk 1.11, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.40; P=.38). Pulmonary hypertension, a predefined safety outcome, occurred in 16 neonates (18.8%) in the sildenafil group vs 4 (5.1%) in the placebo group (relative risk 3.67, 95% CI 1.28 to 10.51; P=.008).
cards.watchOut: The pulmonary-hypertension percentages are calculated among neonates with that outcome assessed, not all 108 per arm — but the contrast is large, predefined, and was strong enough to stop the trial. The UK and NZAus trials did not see this signal, so it is a signal, not a settled harm rate.
cards.source: Pels A et al. Maternal Sildenafil vs Placebo in Pregnant Women With Severe Early-Onset Fetal Growth Restriction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2020. PMID: 32585017. cards.headline: Groom 2019 (STRIDER NZAus): no effect on fetal growth velocity — growth velocity increased in 52.5% on sildenafil vs 68.4% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.49)
cards.summary: Groom 2019 (STRIDER NZAus): no effect on fetal growth velocity — growth velocity increased in 52.5% on sildenafil vs 68.4% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.49)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial (Groom 2019, STRIDER NZAus)
cards.people: 122 women with singleton pregnancies affected by early-onset fetal growth restriction at 22+0 to 29+6 weeks, randomised to sildenafil 25 mg three times daily (n=63) or placebo (n=59) until 32+0 weeks, birth or fetal death, at 13 maternal-fetal medicine units in New Zealand and Australia.
cards.result: Sildenafil did not affect the proportion of pregnancies with an increase in fetal growth velocity: 32/61 (52.5%) on sildenafil vs 39/57 (68.4%) on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.05), and had no effect on abdominal circumference Z-scores (P=0.61). Live birth was 56/63 (88.9%) vs 47/59 (79.7%) (adjusted OR 2.50, 95% CI 0.80 to 7.79) and survival to hospital discharge free of major neonatal morbidity 42/63 (66.7%) vs 33/59 (55.9%) (adjusted OR 1.93, 0.84 to 4.45) — neither significant. The authors concluded there was no beneficial effect on growth, and no evidence of harm in this trial.
cards.watchOut: The survival point estimates favour sildenafil here while the growth endpoint favours placebo — with 122 women the confidence intervals are wide enough to include both, which is why the three trials must be read together: growth is null everywhere, and survival is null in the two larger trials.
cards.source: Groom KM et al. STRIDER NZAus: a multicentre randomised controlled trial of sildenafil therapy in early-onset fetal growth restriction. BJOG. 2019. PMID: 30779295. cards.headline: Synthesis: three STRIDER trials, one answer — sildenafil does not improve fetal growth or perinatal survival in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, and the Dutch trial raises a neonatal pulmonary-hypertension concern
cards.summary: Synthesis: three STRIDER trials, one answer — sildenafil does not improve fetal growth or perinatal survival in severe early-onset fetal growth restriction, and the Dutch trial raises a neonatal pulmonary-hypertension concern
cards.people: UK STRIDER, 135 women (Sharp 2018); Dutch STRIDER, 216 women, stopped early (Pels 2020); STRIDER NZAus, 122 women (Groom 2019) — 473 women randomised across the programme.
cards.result: Growth: no increase in growth velocity in NZAus (52.5% vs 68.4%), no birthweight difference in the UK (−14 g). Survival/morbidity: no difference in livebirth in the UK (RR 1.06) and no reduction in perinatal death or major morbidity in the Dutch trial (60.2% vs 54.2%, RR 1.11). Harm: neonatal pulmonary hypertension 18.8% vs 5.1% (RR 3.67) in the Dutch trial only. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three concordant randomised trials on the benefit question; the harm signal comes from one trial and is labelled as a signal on the face of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: severe early-onset fetal growth restriction as defined by these trials (very preterm, abnormal umbilical Dopplers) — not milder or late-onset growth restriction, where sildenafil has not been tested this way.

shelves.title: Apical prolapse: sacrocolpopexy vs vaginal native-tissue suspension — more durable repair (repeat surgery about 14% vs 6% favouring sacrocolpopexy), with mesh erosion reaching 10.5% by 7 years
shelves.question: In women with symptomatic apical pelvic organ prolapse, does abdominal sacrocolpopexy give more durable repair than vaginal native-tissue suspension, and at what mesh-complication cost?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Dyspareunia · Suspensions · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/etiology, surgery · Uterine Prolapse/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — sacrocolpopexy looks more durable, paid for in mesh complications and a bigger operation; much of the long-term base is cohort data, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the observational parts are labelled. Randomised evidence pooled by Cochrane (Maher 2023, PMID: 37493538; 59 trials, 6,705 women) finds women having vaginal apical procedures more often aware of prolapse (relative risk 2.31; 8% after sacral colpopexy vs about 18% after vaginal procedures), more often needing repeat prolapse surgery (RR 2.33; 6% vs about 14%) and more often recurrent on examination (RR 1.87) than women having sacral colpopexy. The CARE cohort's 7-year extension (Nygaard 2013, PMID: 23677313) shows sacrocolpopexy failure probabilities still rising by year 7 and a mesh-erosion probability of 10.5%. A 2026 meta-analysis dominated by cohort studies (PMID: 42690266) likewise found lower retreatment after minimally invasive sacrocolpopexy with hysterectomy than after vaginal hysterectomy with native-tissue repair (1.59% vs 10.23%).

cards.headline: Maher 2023 (Cochrane, apical prolapse): vaginal procedures vs sacral colpopexy — awareness of prolapse relative risk 2.31, repeat prolapse surgery RR 2.33, recurrence on examination RR 1.87, all favouring sacral colpopexy
cards.summary: Maher 2023 (Cochrane, apical prolapse): vaginal procedures vs sacral colpopexy — awareness of prolapse relative risk 2.31, repeat prolapse surgery RR 2.33, recurrence on examination RR 1.87, all favouring sacral colpopexy
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Maher 2023)
cards.people: 59 randomised trials (6,705 women) of surgery for apical vaginal prolapse; the head-to-head comparison of vaginal procedures against sacral colpopexy rests on seven RCTs (n=613) with review at six months to four years.
cards.result: Awareness of prolapse was more common after vaginal procedures (relative risk [RR] 2.31, 95% CI 1.27 to 4.21; 4 RCTs, n=346, moderate-certainty evidence) — if 8% of women are aware of prolapse after sacral colpopexy, about 18% (10% to 32%) are likely to be aware after vaginal procedures. Surgery for recurrent prolapse was more common after vaginal procedures (RR 2.33, 1.34 to 4.04; 6 RCTs, n=497) — 6% after sacral colpopexy vs about 14% (8% to 25%) after vaginal procedures. Prolapse on examination was probably more common after vaginal procedures (RR 1.87, 1.32 to 2.65; 5 RCTs, n=422), and stress urinary incontinence was more common after vaginal procedures (RR 1.86, 1.17 to 2.94; 3 RCTs, n=263). All relative risks are shown with the review's absolute risks beside them.
cards.watchOut: The pooled vaginal group mixes several different operations (sacrospinous, uterosacral and others), follow-up is only six months to four years, and certainty is moderate at best — this shows a direction favouring sacral colpopexy, not a precise size for any one vaginal operation.

cards.headline: Nygaard 2013 (E-CARE, 7-year follow-up of CARE): abdominal sacrocolpopexy failure kept rising to year 7, and the mesh-erosion probability reached 10.5%
cards.summary: Nygaard 2013 (E-CARE, 7-year follow-up of CARE): abdominal sacrocolpopexy failure kept rising to year 7, and the mesh-erosion probability reached 10.5%
cards.type: Long-term (7-year) follow-up cohort of a randomised trial (Nygaard 2013, extended CARE)
cards.people: 215 women (92% of eligible 2-year completers) from the CARE trial — women with stress continence who had abdominal sacrocolpopexy for symptomatic prolapse in 2002–2005, with or without concomitant Burch urethropexy — followed in the extended CARE study; 181 (84%) completed 5 years and 126 (59%) completed 7 years; median follow-up 7 years.
cards.result: By year 7, estimated probabilities of anatomic prolapse failure were 0.27 (with urethropexy) and 0.22 (without), symptomatic prolapse failure 0.29 and 0.24, and composite prolapse failure 0.48 and 0.34 — failure rates increased in both groups over time, and urethropexy's effect was on incontinence outcomes, not prolapse durability. The Kaplan–Meier estimated probability of mesh erosion at 7 years was 10.5% (95% CI 6.8% to 16.1%). The authors conclude sacrocolpopexy effectiveness should be balanced against the long-term risk of mesh or suture erosion.
cards.watchOut: This card describes sacrocolpopexy's own long-term performance — CARE randomised the added Burch procedure, not the route of prolapse repair, so it cannot by itself say sacrocolpopexy beats vaginal repair. Attrition by year 7 (59% completing) means the year-7 probabilities are model estimates, not raw counts.
cards.source: Nygaard I et al. Long-term outcomes following abdominal sacrocolpopexy for pelvic organ prolapse. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23677313. Registry ID: NCT00099372. cards.headline: Huffman 2026 (meta-analysis, mostly cohort studies): retreatment 1.59% after hysterectomy with minimally invasive sacrocolpopexy vs 10.23% after vaginal hysterectomy with native-tissue repair
cards.summary: Huffman 2026 (meta-analysis, mostly cohort studies): retreatment 1.59% after hysterectomy with minimally invasive sacrocolpopexy vs 10.23% after vaginal hysterectomy with native-tissue repair
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of trials and comparative cohorts (Huffman 2026) — largely observational
cards.people: 24 studies (randomised trials and comparative cohort studies of at least 30 participants) in primary uterovaginal prolapse: 6,329 patients having hysterectomy with minimally invasive sacrocolpopexy and 681 having vaginal hysterectomy with native-tissue repair. Observational/cohort data dominate — labelled as such.
cards.result: Compared with vaginal hysterectomy and native-tissue repair, hysterectomy with sacrocolpopexy had significantly lower retreatment rates (1.59% vs 10.23%, p<0.0001), subjective failure (5.09% vs 17.55%, p=0.002), objective failure (6.80% vs 18.16%, p=0.002) and composite failure (9.23% vs 18.19%, p=0.005). Certainty of evidence was moderate to low.
cards.watchOut: The comparison groups are very unbalanced (6,329 vs 681) and mostly non-randomised: women chosen for sacrocolpopexy differ from women chosen for vaginal repair, so these percentages overstate the precision of the contrast. Read it as supportive of the randomised Cochrane direction, not as a substitute for it.
cards.source: Huffman JA et al. Hysterectomy with Minimally Invasive Sacrocolpopexy Versus Native Tissue Repair for Primary Uterovaginal Prolapse: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. 2026. PMID: 42690266. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD420251171050 (from the record's abstract). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: sacrocolpopexy is probably the more durable apical repair — fewer recurrences and reoperations than vaginal native-tissue suspension — at the cost of a mesh whose erosion probability reaches about 1 in 10 by 7 years
cards.summary: Synthesis: sacrocolpopexy is probably the more durable apical repair — fewer recurrences and reoperations than vaginal native-tissue suspension — at the cost of a mesh whose erosion probability reaches about 1 in 10 by 7 years
cards.people: Cochrane review of 59 RCTs, 6,705 women (Maher 2023); extended CARE cohort, 215 women followed to 7 years (Nygaard 2013); 2026 meta-analysis of 24 studies, 7,010 patients (Huffman 2026).
cards.result: Randomised pooled contrasts favour sacral colpopexy over vaginal procedures for awareness of prolapse (RR 2.31 for vaginal vs sacral), repeat prolapse surgery (RR 2.33) and recurrence on examination (RR 1.87), with absolute risks of about 18% vs 8% (awareness) and 14% vs 6% (repeat surgery). Sacrocolpopexy's own failure probabilities nonetheless rise through year 7, and mesh erosion reaches an estimated 10.5%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — the head-to-head randomised base is small and short, and much of the supporting base is cohort data, so under the observational cap the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: apical (vault or uterine) prolapse. This shelf does not compare open abdominal with laparoscopic/robotic sacrocolpopexy, and the transvaginal-mesh question is homed separately on Shelf #666 (PROSPECT).

shelves.title: Intrathecal morphine after caesarean delivery (Palmer dose-response; Sultan and Yang meta-analyses; PROSPECT): 45.7 mg less PCA morphine at 0.075 mg versus none, benefit plateauing at 50-100 µg, pruritus rising with dose
shelves.question: In women after caesarean delivery, does intrathecal morphine improve pain and reduce systemic opioid need versus no intrathecal opioid, and what pruritus, nausea and respiratory monitoring does it cost?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) on pain and systemic opioid sparing, at a real cost in pruritus and nausea/vomiting. The dose-response randomised trial (Palmer 1999, PMID: 9952150) found patient-controlled morphine use over 24 hours was 45.7 mg lower with intrathecal morphine 0.075 mg than with no intrathecal morphine, with no further sparing above that dose, while pruritus rose in direct proportion to dose. The dose meta-analysis (Sultan 2016, PMID: 27089000) found higher doses (>100-250 µg) prolonged time to first analgesic request by a mean 4.49 hours versus low doses (50-100 µg) but with more nausea/vomiting and pruritus, and no difference in 24-hour morphine consumption. Against transversus abdominis plane block, intrathecal morphine used less systemic morphine but caused more pruritus and postoperative nausea and vomiting (Yang 2021, PMID: 34157985). The PROSPECT procedure-specific synthesis recommends intrathecal morphine 50-100 µg as part of the standard elective-caesarean regimen (Roofthooft 2021, PMID: 33370462). None of these fetched records quantifies respiratory-depression rates, so the monitoring cost is real but unquantified here: the low recommended dose is precisely the trade the evidence supports. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): multiple concordant randomised datasets and syntheses, with dose-dependent harms stated on the face.

cards.headline: Palmer 1999 (randomised dose-response, 0-0.5 mg): PCA morphine use 45.7 mg lower at 0.075 mg versus no intrathecal morphine; no extra sparing at higher doses; pruritus rose in proportion to dose
cards.summary: Palmer 1999 (randomised dose-response, 0-0.5 mg): PCA morphine use 45.7 mg lower at 0.075 mg versus no intrathecal morphine; no extra sparing at higher doses; pruritus rose in proportion to dose
cards.people: 108 term parturients undergoing caesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia, randomised to a single intrathecal morphine dose of 0.0, 0.025, 0.05, 0.075, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 or 0.5 mg, with patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) providing additional analgesics for 24 hours.
cards.result: PCA morphine use differed significantly between groups and was higher in the control (0 mg) group than in the 0.075, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 mg groups. Twenty-four-hour PCA morphine use was 45.7 mg lower (95% CI 4.8-86.6 mg lower) in the 0.075-mg group than in the control group, and there was no difference between the 0.075-mg and 0.5-mg groups. Nausea and vomiting did not differ between control and treatment groups, but pruritus and the need for treatment interventions increased in direct proportion to the intrathecal morphine dose (linear regression P=0.001 and P=0.0002). The authors concluded there is little justification for using more than 0.1 mg for post-caesarean analgesia.
cards.watchOut: A 1999 single-centre dose-ranging study with about 12 patients per dose group; it maps the dose-response cleanly but is not powered for rare harms such as delayed respiratory depression, which it does not report.
cards.source: Palmer CM et al. Dose-response relationship of intrathecal morphine for postcesarean analgesia. Anesthesiology. 1999. PMID: 9952150. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sultan 2016 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 480 patients): higher-dose intrathecal morphine prolonged analgesia by a mean 4.49 hours versus low dose, but increased nausea/vomiting and pruritus; 24-hour morphine use did not differ
cards.summary: Sultan 2016 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 480 patients): higher-dose intrathecal morphine prolonged analgesia by a mean 4.49 hours versus low dose, but increased nausea/vomiting and pruritus; 24-hour morphine use did not differ
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Sultan 2016)
cards.people: 480 patients undergoing elective caesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia in 11 randomised trials comparing low-dose intrathecal morphine (50-100 µg; n=247) with higher-dose intrathecal morphine (>100-250 µg; n=233).
cards.result: Mean time to first request for supplemental analgesia was longer with higher doses (mean difference 4.49 hours, 95% CI 1.85-7.13; P=0.0008). Pain scores at 12 hours (mean difference 2.54 on a 0-100 scale, P=0.33) and morphine consumption at 24 hours (mean difference 1.31 mg, P=0.42) were not significantly different. Nausea or vomiting (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27-0.73; P=0.002) and pruritus (OR 0.34, 95% CI 0.20-0.59; P=0.0001) were less frequent with low doses — that is, both were more frequent at higher doses. Apgar scores <7 at 1 minute did not differ (OR 1.11, P=0.94).
cards.watchOut: This compares higher versus lower doses, not morphine versus none — the versus-none contrast comes from the Palmer trial and the PROSPECT synthesis. The component trials are small, and rare respiratory events cannot be assessed at this total size.
cards.source: Sultan P et al. The Effect of Intrathecal Morphine Dose on Outcomes After Elective Cesarean Delivery: A Meta-Analysis. Anesthesia and Analgesia. 2016. PMID: 27089000. cards.headline: Yang 2021 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 563 patients): intrathecal morphine versus TAP block — similar 24-hour pain scores overall, less morphine consumption with intrathecal morphine, but more pruritus and PONV
cards.summary: Yang 2021 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 563 patients): intrathecal morphine versus TAP block — similar 24-hour pain scores overall, less morphine consumption with intrathecal morphine, but more pruritus and PONV
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yang 2021)
cards.people: 563 patients after caesarean delivery in 6 randomised trials comparing intrathecal morphine (ITM) with transversus abdominis plane block (TAPB).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in pain scores at rest or on movement at 24 hours in the primary analysis; in sensitivity analyses excluding heterogeneity-causing studies, resting pain (95% CI -1.27 to -0.28; P=0.002) and movement pain (95% CI -1.8 to -0.07; P=0.03) were lower with ITM. Morphine consumption was lower in the ITM group (P<0.00001), while pruritus (95% CI 1.17 to 8.26; P=0.02) and postoperative nausea and vomiting (P<0.00001) were more frequent with ITM than with TAPB.
cards.watchOut: The head-to-head is against an active block, not against no intrathecal opioid, and the analgesic advantage for intrathecal morphine appeared only in sensitivity analyses — the primary pooled pain comparison was null (the treatments made no difference on 24-hour pain scores).
cards.source: Yang TR et al. Intrathecal morphine versus transversus abdominis plane block for caesarean delivery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Anesthesiology. 2021. PMID: 34157985. cards.summary: Roofthooft 2021 (PROSPECT procedure-specific synthesis, 145 RCTs): intrathecal morphine 50-100 µg recommended as part of the standard elective caesarean analgesic regimen
cards.type: Procedure-specific systematic review and guideline synthesis (PROSPECT, Roofthooft 2021)
cards.people: Randomised trials of analgesic, anaesthetic and surgical interventions for elective caesarean section under neuraxial anaesthesia published 2014-2020; 145 studies met the inclusion criteria for the PROSPECT systematic review.
cards.result: The PROSPECT recommendations for elective caesarean section under neuraxial anaesthesia include intrathecal morphine 50-100 µg (or diamorphine 300 µg) given pre-operatively, plus paracetamol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and intravenous dexamethasone after delivery, with opioids reserved for rescue. If no intrathecal opioid was given, wound infiltration, continuous wound infusion and/or fascial plane blocks (transversus abdominis plane or quadratus lumborum) are recommended instead. The recommendations do not apply to unplanned deliveries or caesarean section under general anaesthesia.
cards.watchOut: A guideline synthesis, not a new trial: it endorses the low dose range (50-100 µg) precisely because benefit plateaus while side effects climb, and it does not itself quantify the respiratory-monitoring burden.
cards.source: Roofthooft E et al. PROSPECT guideline for elective caesarean section: updated systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management recommendations. Anaesthesia. 2021. PMID: 33370462. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Analgesics, Opioid; Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal; Cesarean Section; Dexamethasone; Female; Humans; Injections, Spinal; Pain Management; Pain, Postoperative; Pregnancy

cards.headline: Synthesis: intrathecal morphine at low dose (50-100 µg) reduces pain and systemic opioid need after caesarean delivery; pruritus and nausea/vomiting are the routine costs, and respiratory monitoring is required but unquantified in these records
cards.summary: Synthesis: intrathecal morphine at low dose (50-100 µg) reduces pain and systemic opioid need after caesarean delivery; pruritus and nausea/vomiting are the routine costs, and respiratory monitoring is required but unquantified in these records
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above: one randomised dose-response trial (108 women), two meta-analyses of randomised trials (480 and 563 patients) and the PROSPECT synthesis of 145 randomised trials.
cards.result: Across four decades of randomised evidence the direction is consistent: intrathecal morphine spares systemic morphine (45.7 mg less PCA morphine over 24 hours at 0.075 mg versus none in Palmer 1999), the benefit plateaus at low doses, and pruritus and nausea/vomiting increase with dose. The dose the syntheses converge on is 50-100 µg. No fetched record reports a respiratory-depression rate, so the monitoring cost of intrathecal morphine cannot be priced from this evidence base — it is a standing safety requirement, not a measured outcome here.
cards.watchOut: Respiratory depression after low-dose intrathecal morphine is rare and none of these records is powered to measure it; the absence of a rate here is not evidence the risk is zero, and ward monitoring protocols remain a local safety decision.
cards.source: Synthesis of Palmer CM et al. Anesthesiology. 1999. PMID: 9952150; Sultan P et al. Anesthesia and Analgesia. 2016. PMID: 27089000; Yang TR et al. BMC Anesthesiology. 2021. PMID: 34157985; Roofthooft E et al. Anaesthesia. 2021. PMID: 33370462. Registry IDs as on the cards above.

shelves.title: Segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol one-year vaginal ring (tested product: the Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone ring, Annovera) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 programme in 2,265 women: Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years in women aged 35 and under; venous thromboembolism in 4 of 2,308 users of the final ring (0.2%)
shelves.question: In women seeking contraception, does the segesterone acetate + ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring used in 21/7 cycles for up to 13 cycles (name the tested product — Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone ring) prevent pregnancy as effectively as benchmark combined hormonal contraception, and what are its discontinuation and VTE profiles?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Contraceptive Devices, Female · Drug Combinations · Ethinyl Estradiol · Female · Humans · Infusion Pumps, Implantable · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pregnenediones · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — effective contraception on a single-arm programme, with the design printed: both phase 3 trials of the tested product (the Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol vaginal system, Annovera, releasing an average of 0.15 mg segesterone acetate and 0.013 mg ethinyl estradiol daily, used 21 days in / 7 days out for up to 13 cycles with the same ring) were open-label and single-arm, so efficacy is judged against regulatory benchmarks, not against a concurrent comparator. In 2,265 women in the efficacy analysis, the Pearl Index in the primary group (women aged 35 years and younger) was 2.98 per 100 woman-years (95% CI 2.13–4.06), and Kaplan–Meier analysis estimated the ring 97.5% effective over 13 cycles; 57.5% of participants completed 13 cycles. In the integrated safety analysis (2,308 women using the final manufactured ring), headache (26%), nausea (18%) and vaginal discharge/mycotic infection (10%) were most common, few women (under 1.5%) discontinued for these, and four women (0.2%) had venous thromboembolism — three of whom had risk factors (a Factor V Leiden mutation, or body mass index above 29 kg/m2). Satisfaction among prior pill/ring users was high (at least 90%). A single programme with no randomised comparator caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Archer 2019 — phase 3 programme, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 2,265 women in the efficacy analysis; Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years in women aged ≤35; 97.5% effective by Kaplan–Meier over 13 cycles
cards.summary: Archer 2019 — phase 3 programme, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 2,265 women in the efficacy analysis; Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years in women aged ≤35; 97.5% effective by Kaplan–Meier over 13 cycles
cards.people: 2,278 women enrolled across two identically designed multicentre, open-label, single-arm phase 3 trials (15 US sites; 12 US and international sites) of the tested product — the Population Council/TherapeuticsMD segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol contraceptive vaginal system (Annovera) — in healthy, sexually active, non-pregnant, non-sterilised women aged 18–40 years, using the same ring 21 days in and 7 days out for up to 13 cycles; removals during the 21 days were not to exceed 2 hours. The efficacy analysis included 2,265 participants (1,130 US; 1,135 international), and 1,303 (57.5%) completed up to 13 cycles.
cards.result: The Pearl Index for the primary efficacy group (women aged 35 years and younger, excluding adjunctive-contraception cycles) was 2.98 (95% CI 2.13–4.06) per 100 woman-years — within the range regulators accept as efficacy for a user-controlled contraceptive. Kaplan–Meier analysis estimated the vaginal system 97.5% effective, and pregnancy occurrence was similar across cycles. All 290 women followed after the trials reported return to menses or became pregnant within 6 months, including 24 of 38 (63%) who desired pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm design printed on the face: with no concurrent control group, the Pearl Index is a benchmark comparison, not a randomised effect — and 42.5% of participants did not complete 13 cycles, so the estimate rests heavily on the cycles actually observed.
cards.source: Archer DF et al. Efficacy of the 1-year (13-cycle) segesterone acetate and ethinylestradiol contraceptive vaginal system: results of two multicentre, open-label, single-arm, phase 3 trials. The Lancet Global Health. 2019. PMID: 31231065. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00455156 and NCT00263341, from the record. cards.headline: Gemzell-Danielsson 2019 — integrated safety (3,052 women in nine studies; 2,308 on the final ring): headache 26%, nausea 18%; venous thromboembolism in 4 women (0.2%), three with risk factors; partial or complete expulsion in about a quarter of cycles
cards.summary: Gemzell-Danielsson 2019 — integrated safety (3,052 women in nine studies; 2,308 on the final ring): headache 26%, nausea 18%; venous thromboembolism in 4 women (0.2%), three with risk factors; partial or complete expulsion in about a quarter of cycles
cards.people: Integrated data from nine studies of the segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol contraceptive vaginal system (21 days in / 7 days out), including 3,052 women overall and 2,308 women (mean age 26.7 years; mean body mass index 24.1 kg/m2) who received the final manufactured ring, of whom 999 (43.3%) completed 13 cycles; safety-focused substudies covered endometrial biopsies, vaginal microbiology and liver proteins.
cards.result: The most common adverse events on the final ring were headache (601 women, 26%), nausea (420, 18%), vaginal discharge/vulvovaginal mycotic infection (242, 10%) and abdominal pain (225, 10%); fewer than 1.5% of women discontinued for these complaints. Four women (0.2%) experienced venous thromboembolism, three of whom had risk factors for thrombosis (Factor V Leiden mutation in one; body mass index above 29 kg/m2 in two). Across 21,482 phase 3 cycles evaluable for expulsion, partial expulsions were reported in 19.5% of cycles and complete expulsions in 7%, most often in the first cycle. The focused safety studies revealed no additional concerns, and the authors judged the profile similar to other combined hormonal contraceptives, with the same prescribing precautions.
cards.watchOut: The safety population was young and lean (mean body mass index 24.1 kg/m2); the authors themselves call for more study in women with obesity, who carry higher venous thromboembolism risk — four events in 2,308 users cannot pin down a rare-event rate.
cards.source: Gemzell-Danielsson K et al. Segesterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol 12-month contraceptive vaginal system safety evaluation. Contraception. 2019. PMID: 30831102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jensen 2023 — satisfaction in prior pill/ring users: at least 90% satisfied with the one-year ring; ease of use and 1-year duration the most-liked features, insertion and feeling it come out the most disliked
cards.summary: Jensen 2023 — satisfaction in prior pill/ring users: at least 90% satisfied with the one-year ring; ease of use and 1-year duration the most-liked features, insertion and feeling it come out the most disliked
cards.people: Participants in the multinational phase 3 trial with documented recent use of a monthly contraceptive vaginal ring (128 at cycle 3; 92 at end of study) or oral contraceptive pills (219 at cycle 3; 148 at end of study) before enrolment, drawn from 1,033 survey participants at cycle 3 and 622 at end of study (end of study required at least 10 completed cycles).
cards.result: Overall satisfaction with the vaginal system was high (at least 90%) in both switcher groups. At end of study, 89% of recent ring users and 97% of recent pill users liked the system as much as or better than any previous method; the most-liked features were ease of use and the 1-year duration, and the most disliked were ring insertion and feeling it coming out. At least 88% of both groups had no concern about using the same ring for a year, and more than 80% had recommended it to friends or family.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and survivor-shaped: end-of-study responses come only from women who persisted for at least 10 cycles, so satisfaction among the many women who stopped early — the group whose experience decides real-world acceptability — is not captured here.
cards.source: Jensen JT et al. Satisfaction with a Segesterone Acetate and Ethinyl Estradiol Contraceptive Vaginal System Among Recent Oral Contraceptive or Hormonal Contraceptive Vaginal Ring Users. Journal of Women's Health. 2023. PMID: 37253139. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00263341, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one ring for a year prevents pregnancy at a Pearl Index of about 3 in the regulatory subgroup, with a combined-hormonal-contraceptive harm profile — on single-arm evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: one ring for a year prevents pregnancy at a Pearl Index of about 3 in the regulatory subgroup, with a combined-hormonal-contraceptive harm profile — on single-arm evidence
cards.people: The tested product (Annovera) across its programme: 2,265 women in the efficacy analysis and 2,308 users of the final manufactured ring in the safety analysis, all in open-label, single-arm studies.
cards.result: Efficacy: Pearl Index 2.98 per 100 woman-years in women aged 35 and under and 97.5% Kaplan–Meier effectiveness over 13 cycles, with return to menses or pregnancy documented after use. Harms: mostly headache, nausea and vaginal symptoms, under 1.5% discontinuing for them, expulsions in about a quarter of cycles, and venous thromboembolism in 0.2% — three of the four cases with pre-existing risk factors. Acceptability among women who stayed on it was high.
cards.watchOut: Everything rests on one sponsor programme without a randomised comparator, in young, mostly non-obese women; the convenience claim (no refills for a year) is real, but comparative effectiveness and the venous thromboembolism rate in higher-risk users remain benchmark judgements, not measured differences.
cards.source: Synthesis of Archer DF et al. The Lancet Global Health. 2019 (PMID: 31231065); Gemzell-Danielsson K et al. Contraception. 2019 (PMID: 30831102); Jensen JT et al. Journal of Women's Health. 2023 (PMID: 37253139).

shelves.title: Phexxi vaginal gel for on-demand contraception (tested product: Evofem Phexxi) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 with no concurrent control (design printed): typical-use pregnancy 13.7% over 7 cycles, so efficacy rests on comparison with the expected pregnancy rate without contraception
shelves.question: In women seeking hormone-free, on-demand contraception, does lactic acid/citric acid/potassium bitartrate vaginal gel (name the tested product — Evofem Phexxi) used before intercourse prevent pregnancy versus no contraception (historical/expected pregnancy rate), and what local adverse effects does it cause?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the design printed on the face: AMPOWER, the phase 3 trial of the tested product (Evofem Phexxi, a lactic acid/citric acid/potassium bitartrate vaginal pH modulator gel used within an hour before each act of intercourse), was SINGLE-ARM and open-label in 1,384 women, with no concurrent control group. Its efficacy estimate therefore rests on comparison with the pregnancy rate expected without contraception, judged against a prespecified regulatory bound — not on a randomised difference. The 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy percentage with typical use was 13.7% (95% CI 10.0%–17.5%), meeting the prespecified endpoint that the upper confidence bound be no more than 21%; expressed the other way, the gel was 86.3% effective over 7 cycles in this population — well below long-acting and hormonal methods, in the range of other user-dependent, coital methods. A review of the programme reports a Pearl Index of 27.5 and cumulative 6–7-cycle pregnancy rates of 4.1%–13.65% across the two phase 3 trials (the lower figure reflecting more perfect use). Local effects dominate the harm side: vulvovaginal burning and itching were the most common adverse events, fewer than 2% of users discontinued for any adverse event and fewer than 1% for genitourinary symptoms, and over 80% of women were satisfied. A single-arm programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Thomas 2020 (AMPOWER) — SINGLE-ARM open-label phase 3, no concurrent control (design printed): 1,384 women; 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy 13.7% (95% CI 10.0%–17.5%) with typical use, meeting the prespecified upper-bound endpoint of ≤21%
cards.summary: Thomas 2020 (AMPOWER) — SINGLE-ARM open-label phase 3, no concurrent control (design printed): 1,384 women; 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy 13.7% (95% CI 10.0%–17.5%) with typical use, meeting the prespecified upper-bound endpoint of ≤21%
cards.people: 1,384 sexually active women aged 18–35 years at risk of pregnancy, enrolled at 112 US sites from July 2017 to November 2018, who used the tested product — Evofem Phexxi (lactic acid, citric acid and potassium bitartrate vaginal pH regulator gel) — within 1 hour before each episode of intercourse, recording use, coital information and symptoms in electronic diaries over seven cycles. There was no control group: the primary outcome, the 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy rate by Kaplan–Meier, was judged against a prespecified bound derived from expected pregnancy rates.
cards.result: The 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy percentage was 13.7% (95% CI 10.0%–17.5%), meeting the prespecified primary endpoint of an upper 95% confidence bound of 21% or less; the authors express this as 86.3% contraceptive effectiveness. The most common adverse events (in at least 2% of women) were vulvovaginal burning sensation, vulvovaginal pruritus, urinary tract infection, vulvovaginal pain, mycotic infection, bacterial vaginosis and nasopharyngitis. Of 1,330 women who used the gel at least once, fewer than 2% discontinued because of any adverse event and fewer than 1% because of genitourinary symptoms. Over 80% of women reported being satisfied or very satisfied.
cards.watchOut: No woman in this trial was randomised to anything else: the 13.7% figure only means something against the roughly 85% annual pregnancy rate expected with no contraception, and it is far higher than the failure rates of intrauterine devices, implants or pills used correctly. Typical use over just 7 cycles in motivated trial volunteers may also flatter real-world performance.

phase 3 single-arm trial (thomas 2020, ampower) 1,384 sexually active women aged 18–35 years at risk of pregnancy, enrolled at 112 us sites from july 2017 to november 2018, who used the tested product — evofem phexxi (lactic acid, citric acid and potassium bitartrate vaginal ph regulator gel) — within 1 hour before each episode of intercourse, recording use, coital information and symptoms in electronic diaries over seven cycles. there was no control group: the primary outcome, the 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy rate by kaplan–meier, was judged against a prespecified bound derived from expected pregnancy rates. the 7-cycle cumulative pregnancy percentage was 13.7% (95% ci 10.0%–17.5%), meeting the prespecified primary endpoint of an upper 95% confidence bound of 21% or less; the authors express this as 86.3% contraceptive effectiveness. the most common adverse events (in at least 2% of women) were vulvovaginal burning sensation, vulvovaginal pruritus, urinary tract infection, vulvovaginal pain, mycotic infection, bacterial vaginosis and nasopharyngitis. of 1,330 women who used the gel at least once, fewer than 2% discontinued because of any adverse event and fewer than 1% because of genitourinary symptoms. over 80% of women reported being satisfied or very satisfied. no woman in this trial was randomised to anything else: the 13.7% figure only means something against the roughly 85% annual pregnancy rate expected with no contraception, and it is far higher than the failure rates of intrauterine devices, implants or pills used correctly. typical use over just 7 cycles in motivated trial volunteers may also flatter real-world performance. thomas ma et al. a novel vaginal ph regulator: results from the phase 3 ampower contraception clinical trial. contraception: x. 2020. pmid: 32685920. registry id: none in the record. mesh: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Thomas 2022 — AMPOWER sexual-satisfaction results (post-hoc, exploratory): 93.6% of women at the final visit said their sex life was improved or maintained, and lubrication scores improved versus baseline
cards.summary: Thomas 2022 — AMPOWER sexual-satisfaction results (post-hoc, exploratory): 93.6% of women at the final visit said their sex life was improved or maintained, and lubrication scores improved versus baseline
cards.people: Women from the AMPOWER single-arm trial (1,330 women who used the gel at least once form the analysis population) completing satisfaction and sexual-function questionnaires at baseline and visits 3–5, including a sex-life impact question, the Sexual Function Questionnaire and the Female Sexual Function Index lubrication item.
cards.result: For measures with baseline assessments, most women reported the same or improved scores at visit 5 (85.8%–98.4% across measures). The share reporting their sex life was improved or maintained rose from 87.6% at baseline to 93.6% at visit 5, the mean sex-life impact score improved significantly (P<0.001), 7 of 10 Sexual Function Questionnaire variables improved significantly, and the Female Sexual Function Index score improved in women sexually active in the last 4 weeks (P=0.037).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, exploratory and uncontrolled, in women who remained in a single-arm trial of a gel also cleared as a lubricant: improvement over a woman's own baseline, with no comparator product, cannot separate the gel's effect from participation and expectation effects.
cards.source: Thomas MA et al. Sexual Satisfaction Results With the Vaginal pH Modulator From the Phase 3 AMPOWER Study. The Journal of Sexual Medicine. 2022. PMID: 35418329. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04553068, from the record.
