cards.headline: Su & Vincent 2022 — review of the programme: two phase 3 trials; cumulative 6–7-cycle pregnancy rates 4.1%–13.65% and Pearl Index 27.5 across the reporting; gel judged safe with minimal systemic effects
cards.summary: Su & Vincent 2022 — review of the programme: two phase 3 trials; cumulative 6–7-cycle pregnancy rates 4.1%–13.65% and Pearl Index 27.5 across the reporting; gel judged safe with minimal systemic effects
cards.people: A review compiling the published preclinical and clinical evidence for the tested product (Phexxi vaginal pH modulator gel), identifying two phase 3 trials on the registry and summarising their efficacy and safety reporting, including the AMPOWER typical-use result and a lower cumulative pregnancy figure reflecting more adherent use.
cards.result: Across the two phase 3 trials, the cumulative 6–7-cycle pregnancy rate ranged from 4.1% to 13.65%, with a Pearl Index of 27.5 per 100 woman-years. The reviewers judged the gel safe, with minimal side effects — local symptoms predominating, consistent with a non-systemic, surfactant-free product — and noted microbicidal effects suggesting possible sexually transmitted infection prevention, which was under phase 3 evaluation for chlamydia and gonorrhoea at the time and is not an established benefit.
cards.watchOut: The 4.1% end of the range and the 13.7% AMPOWER typical-use figure describe different use patterns and analysis populations; quoting the low end alone overstates what typical users experienced. A Pearl Index of 27.5 places the gel among the least effective prescription contraceptives per year of use — its value is being hormone-free and on-demand, not maximal efficacy.
cards.source: Su S, Vincent KL. Lactic acid, citric acid, and potassium bitartrate non-hormonal prescription vaginal pH modulator (VPM) gel for the prevention of pregnancy. Expert Review of Clinical Pharmacology. 2022. PMID: 35802958. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a hormone-free, on-demand gel that prevents most expected pregnancies — 13.7% pregnant over 7 cycles of typical use in its only large trial, judged against no-treatment expectations because the trial had no control arm
cards.summary: Synthesis: a hormone-free, on-demand gel that prevents most expected pregnancies — 13.7% pregnant over 7 cycles of typical use in its only large trial, judged against no-treatment expectations because the trial had no control arm
cards.people: One large single-arm phase 3 trial (1,384 women, 7 cycles) plus a second phase 3 trial summarised in review, and post-hoc satisfaction analyses of the same population.
cards.result: Benefit: typical-use pregnancy of 13.7% over 7 cycles where most women using nothing would be expected to conceive over a comparable period — real contraception, at the effectiveness level of other coital, user-dependent methods. Harms: predominantly local burning and itching, with under 2% discontinuing for adverse events, and high reported satisfaction including sexual-satisfaction measures. There is no randomised or head-to-head evidence against any other method.
cards.watchOut: Counselling should carry both halves: the design (single-arm, benchmark-judged) and the number (about 1 in 7 typical users pregnant within 7 cycles). Women for whom pregnancy prevention is critical have far more effective options; this product's place is for those who prioritise hormone-free, on-demand use and accept that trade-off.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thomas MA et al. Contraception: X. 2020 (PMID: 32685920); Thomas MA et al. The Journal of Sexual Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35418329); Su S, Vincent KL. Expert Review of Clinical Pharmacology. 2022 (PMID: 35802958).

shelves.title: PlGF-based testing for suspected preterm pre-eclampsia: an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio of 38 or lower rules out pre-eclampsia within a week with 99.3% negative predictive value; revealing the result halved time to diagnosis (1.9 vs 4.1 days), but REPEAT testing (PARROT-2) made no difference to perinatal outcomes
shelves.question: In women presenting with suspected preterm pre-eclampsia, does revealing a PlGF-based test result (PlGF alone or sFlt-1/PlGF ratio) to clinicians shorten time to diagnosis and improve maternal/perinatal outcomes versus concealed testing/usual care — and how accurately does the test rule out pre-eclampsia within 1–2 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Biomarkers/blood · Female · Humans · Placenta Growth Factor · Pre-Eclampsia/blood/diagnosis · Predictive Value of Tests · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Proteins/blood · Prospective Studies · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity · Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor-1/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for a single revealed test as a diagnostic strategy; repeat testing is a null. Accuracy first (accuracy figures stated as accuracy): in PROGNOSIS (Zeisler 2016; 500-woman development cohort plus 550-woman validation cohort), an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio of 38 or lower had a negative predictive value of 99.3% (95% CI 97.9–99.9) for absence of pre-eclampsia within 1 week, with 80.0% sensitivity and 78.3% specificity; a ratio above 38 had a positive predictive value of only 36.7% for pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks — the test rules out far better than it rules in. Strategy next (strategy outcomes stated as outcomes): in PARROT (Duhig 2019; stepped-wedge cluster trial, 1,023 women), revealing the PlGF result with a management algorithm cut median time to diagnosis from 4.1 to 1.9 days (time ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.15–0.87) and severe maternal adverse outcomes were less frequent (4% versus 5%; adjusted odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.11–0.96), with no difference in perinatal adverse outcomes (15% versus 14%) or gestation at delivery. In PARROT-2 (Duhig/Hurrell 2024; 1,252 women), REVEALED REPEAT testing made no difference: the perinatal composite (stillbirth, early neonatal death or neonatal-unit admission) occurred in 31.2% versus 27.8% (p=0.18; the treatment made no difference), and routine repeat testing was not recommended. One positive strategy trial plus one null repeat-testing trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Zeisler 2016 (PROGNOSIS) — accuracy: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio ≤38 had a 99.3% negative predictive value for no pre-eclampsia within 1 week; a ratio above 38 predicted pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks with only 36.7% positive predictive value
cards.summary: Zeisler 2016 (PROGNOSIS) — accuracy: sFlt-1/PlGF ratio ≤38 had a 99.3% negative predictive value for no pre-eclampsia within 1 week; a ratio above 38 predicted pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks with only 36.7% positive predictive value
cards.people: Women with singleton pregnancies and suspected pre-eclampsia at 24 weeks 0 days to 36 weeks 6 days of gestation in a prospective multicentre observational study: a development cohort of 500 women, in which the ratio cutoff of 38 was derived, and a validation cohort of a further 550 women.
cards.result: In the validation cohort, an sFlt-1/PlGF ratio of 38 or lower had a negative predictive value of 99.3% (95% CI 97.9 to 99.9) for the absence of pre-eclampsia in the subsequent week, with 80.0% sensitivity (95% CI 51.9 to 95.7) and 78.3% specificity (95% CI 74.6 to 81.7). A ratio above 38 had a positive predictive value of 36.7% (95% CI 28.4 to 45.7) for a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks, with 66.2% sensitivity and 83.1% specificity. These are accuracy figures: the test is a strong rule-out and a weak rule-in.
cards.watchOut: Negative predictive value depends on how common pre-eclampsia is in the tested population — in these suspected-case cohorts about 99 of 100 women below the cutoff stayed free of pre-eclampsia for a week; the same cutoff performs differently where prevalence differs, and a high ratio alone diagnoses nothing (roughly 2 of 3 women above it did not develop pre-eclampsia within 4 weeks). The study was funded by the test's manufacturer, Roche Diagnostics.
cards.source: Zeisler H et al. Predictive Value of the sFlt-1:PlGF Ratio in Women with Suspected Preeclampsia. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26735990. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Duhig 2019 (PARROT) — strategy: revealing PlGF results cut median time to diagnosis from 4.1 to 1.9 days and severe maternal adverse outcomes were 4% versus 5% (adjusted OR 0.32); perinatal outcomes did not differ (15% vs 14%)
cards.summary: Duhig 2019 (PARROT) — strategy: revealing PlGF results cut median time to diagnosis from 4.1 to 1.9 days and severe maternal adverse outcomes were 4% versus 5% (adjusted OR 0.32); perinatal outcomes did not differ (15% vs 14%)
cards.people: 1,023 eligible women aged 18 years and older presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia between 20 weeks 0 days and 36 weeks 6 days of gestation with a live singleton fetus, in 11 UK maternity units (3,000–9,000 deliveries per year each); 573 women were analysed in the revealed-testing periods and 446 in the concealed-testing (usual care) periods, in a pragmatic stepped-wedge cluster-randomised design in which PlGF was measured in everyone but only revealed in the intervention phase, alongside a clinical management algorithm.
cards.result: Median time from presentation to documented pre-eclampsia diagnosis was 1.9 days with revealed testing versus 4.1 days with concealed testing (time ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.15–0.87; p=0.027). Severe maternal adverse outcomes occurred in 22 of 573 women (4%) in the revealed group versus 24 of 447 (5%) in the concealed group (adjusted odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.11–0.96; p=0.043) — an odds ratio, a relative measure, on small absolute numbers. There was no evidence of a difference in perinatal adverse outcomes (15% versus 14%) or in gestation at delivery (36.6 versus 36.8 weeks).
cards.watchOut: The maternal-outcome signal rests on 46 events in a cluster trial whose primary outcome was time to diagnosis — a process outcome that revealing a test almost mechanically improves; the perinatal outcomes women and babies ultimately care about did not differ, and the stepped-wedge design is vulnerable to calendar-time trends.
cards.source: Duhig KE et al. Placental growth factor testing to assess women with suspected pre-eclampsia: a multicentre, pragmatic, stepped-wedge cluster-randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2019. PMID: 30948284. Registry ID: ISRCTN 16842031, from the record. cards.headline: Hurrell 2024 (PARROT-2) — REPEAT testing NULL: revealed repeat PlGF testing did not improve the perinatal composite (31.2% vs 27.8%; p=0.18) (the treatment made no difference); routine repeat testing not recommended
cards.summary: Hurrell 2024 (PARROT-2) — REPEAT testing NULL: revealed repeat PlGF testing did not improve the perinatal composite (31.2% vs 27.8%; p=0.18) (the treatment made no difference); routine repeat testing not recommended
cards.people: 1,252 pregnant women aged 18 years and older with suspected preterm pre-eclampsia between 22 weeks 0 days and 35 weeks 6 days of gestation, in 22 maternity units across England, Scotland and Wales, randomly assigned to revealed repeat PlGF-based testing (625 women, using a management algorithm and nationally recommended thresholds) or concealed repeat testing with usual care (627 women). The primary outcome was a perinatal composite of stillbirth, early neonatal death or neonatal unit admission.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary perinatal composite outcome: 195 of 625 women (31.2%) in the revealed repeat-testing group versus 174 of 626 (27.8%) in the concealed group (p=0.18; the treatment made no difference), with per-protocol results similar. Serious adverse events were few (four versus six) and all deemed unrelated to the intervention. The authors concluded that universal, routine repeat PlGF-based testing of everyone with suspected pre-eclampsia is not recommended in a high-income setting with a low prevalence of adverse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: PARROT-2 tests repeat testing, not the first test: its null does not erase PARROT's faster-diagnosis result, but it does close the door on the natural 'test again later' extension — and its point estimate, if anything, favoured the concealed group, underlining that more testing is not automatically better care.
cards.source: Hurrell A et al. Repeat placental growth factor-based testing in women with suspected preterm pre-eclampsia (PARROT-2): a multicentre, parallel-group, superiority, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. 2024. cards.headline: Synthesis: test once and reveal — a strong rule-out (NPV 99.3%) and a faster, possibly safer diagnostic pathway; test repeatedly — no benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: test once and reveal — a strong rule-out (NPV 99.3%) and a faster, possibly safer diagnostic pathway; test repeatedly — no benefit
cards.people: The evidence chain: a 1,050-woman accuracy study (PROGNOSIS), a 1,023-woman cluster-randomised strategy trial of revealed versus concealed testing (PARROT), and a 1,252-woman randomised trial of revealed versus concealed repeat testing (PARROT-2), all in women with suspected preterm pre-eclampsia.
cards.result: Accuracy and strategy answer different questions and are kept separate on this shelf. Accuracy: a ratio at or below 38 makes pre-eclampsia within a week very unlikely (99.3% negative predictive value), while a high ratio is a weak predictor (36.7% positive predictive value over 4 weeks). Strategy: revealing a first PlGF result with an algorithm halved time to diagnosis and was associated with fewer severe maternal adverse outcomes, without perinatal benefit; revealing repeat results changed nothing (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Adoption arguments often merge the accuracy headline with outcome claims the trials did not show: no trial here demonstrated fewer perinatal deaths or admissions from testing, and the maternal-outcome signal comes from one cluster trial with 46 events. The supported claim is narrower — faster, better-targeted assessment after a single test.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zeisler H et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26735990); Duhig KE et al. The Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 30948284); Hurrell A et al. The Lancet. 2024 (PMID: 38342128).

shelves.title: Drospirenone-only pill 4 mg 24/4 (tested product: Exeltis drospirenone-only pill, Slynd) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 trials: Pearl Index 0.51 in Europe (n=713) and 4.0 in the US trial (n=953 in the primary analysis; 2.9 for confirmed pregnancies at clean sites); no venous thromboembolism in either trial
shelves.question: In women seeking progestin-only contraception, does drospirenone 4 mg in a 24/4 regimen (name the tested product — Exeltis drospirenone-only pill) prevent pregnancy versus benchmark progestin-only pills, with what bleeding pattern and VTE signal?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a distinct product from the combined drospirenone pills carded elsewhere in the library: this is the oestrogen-free drospirenone 4 mg pill taken 24 days on and 4 days off (tested product: the Exeltis drospirenone-only pill, marketed as Slynd). Both phase 3 trials were single-arm and non-comparative, so efficacy is benchmark-judged. In Europe (Archer 2015; 713 women, 7,638 cycles), the overall Pearl Index was 0.51 (95% CI 0.11–1.49); pooled with its sister European study (Palacios 2019; 1,571 women, 14,329 cycles), the overall Pearl Index was 0.73 (95% CI 0.31–1.43). In the US trial (Kimble 2020; 1,006 women dosed, only 35.0% completing), the Pearl Index in non-breastfeeding women aged 35 and under was 4.0 (95% CI 2.3–6.4) counting all 17 pregnancies, and 2.9 (95% CI 1.5–5.1) for confirmed pregnancies at sites without protocol violations — a reminder that the US figure was dragged by unconfirmed pregnancies and two excluded sites. Bleeding improved over time: in Europe, any bleeding fell from 72.7% of women in cycle 1 to 32.1% by cycle 13, and unscheduled bleeding from 49.1% to 22.8%. No venous thromboembolism was reported in either programme and hyperkalemia was rare (0.5% in the US trial; one case in the pooled European studies). Single-arm evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Archer 2015 — European phase 3, SINGLE-ARM non-comparative (design printed): 713 women, 7,638 cycles; overall Pearl Index 0.51; no deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or hyperkalemia
cards.summary: Archer 2015 — European phase 3, SINGLE-ARM non-comparative (design printed): 713 women, 7,638 cycles; overall Pearl Index 0.51; no deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or hyperkalemia
cards.people: 713 healthy women at risk of pregnancy, aged 18 to 45 years, at 41 European sites, taking the tested product — drospirenone 4.0 mg daily for 24 days followed by placebo for 4 days (DRSP 4 mg 24/4, Exeltis, Spain, as named in the report; marketed as Slynd) — for thirteen 28-day cycles, in a prospective multicentre non-comparative study whose primary endpoint was the overall Pearl Index.
cards.result: The overall Pearl Index was 0.51 (95% CI 0.1053–1.4922). Bleeding settled with use: the proportion of women with any bleeding fell from 72.7% in cycle 1 to 40% in cycle 6 and 32.1% in cycle 13, and unscheduled bleeding fell from 49.1% to 27.8% to 22.8% over the same cycles; prolonged bleeding fell from 6.5% (cycles 2–4) to 4.2% (cycles 11–13). There were no reports of deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism or hyperkalemia, no relevant changes in laboratory values, weight, body mass index, blood pressure or heart rate, and over 82% of women rated acceptability excellent or good.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm: a Pearl Index of 0.51 is a benchmark figure from motivated European trial volunteers, not a measured advantage over desogestrel or norethindrone progestin-only pills, and 713 women cannot exclude a rare venous thromboembolism risk — 'none seen' is not 'none exists'.
cards.source: Archer DF et al. Drospirenone-only oral contraceptive: results from a multicenter noncomparative trial of efficacy, safety and tolerability. Contraception. 2015. PMID: 26232513. Registry ID: EudraCT 2010-021787-15, from the record. cards.headline: Kimble 2020 — US phase 3, SINGLE-ARM (design printed): 1,006 women dosed, only 35.0% completed; Pearl Index 4.0 in the primary analysis (17 pregnancies) and 2.9 for confirmed pregnancies at sites without protocol violations; no venous thromboembolism; hyperkalemia 0.5%
cards.summary: Kimble 2020 — US phase 3, SINGLE-ARM (design printed): 1,006 women dosed, only 35.0% completed; Pearl Index 4.0 in the primary analysis (17 pregnancies) and 2.9 for confirmed pregnancies at sites without protocol violations; no venous thromboembolism; hyperkalemia 0.5%
cards.people: 1,006 sexually active US women who received at least one dose of drospirenone 4 mg in a 24/4 regimen for up to thirteen 28-day cycles in a prospective, open-label, single-arm multicentre phase 3 trial; 352 women (35.0%) completed and 654 (65.0%) discontinued early. Most participants (92.2%) were aged 35 or under and one third had a body mass index of at least 30 kg/m2. The primary analysis covered 953 non-breastfeeding women aged 35 and under.
cards.result: There were 17 pregnancies in the primary population (Pearl Index 4.0, 95% CI 2.3–6.4), of which three were unconfirmed and two came from sites excluded from the main analysis for major breaches of FDA regulations; the Pearl Index was 2.9 (95% CI 1.5–5.1) for confirmed pregnancies among 915 women at sites with no protocol violations. Nearly all treatment-emergent adverse events (95.4%) were mild or moderate. No venous thromboembolism was reported and hyperkalemia frequency was 0.5%. Women entering with blood pressure at least 130/85 mmHg had a mean fall of 8.5/4.9 mmHg by the exit visit (n=119). Satisfaction was high among those who remained.
cards.watchOut: A 65% discontinuation rate and excluded sites make the US estimate fragile in both directions — and the gap between the European 0.51 and US 4.0 Pearl Indices is a lesson in how population, adherence and site conduct, not pharmacology alone, set real-world pill effectiveness.
cards.source: Kimble T et al. A 1-year prospective, open-label, single-arm, multicenter, phase 3 trial of the contraceptive efficacy and safety of the oral progestin-only pill drospirenone 4 mg using a 24/4-day regimen. cards.headline: Palacios 2019 — pooled European phase 3 programme: 1,571 women, 14,329 cycles; overall Pearl Index 0.73 (95% CI 0.31–1.43), method-failure Pearl Index reported separately; no deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, one case of hyperkalemia
cards.summary: Palacios 2019 — pooled European phase 3 programme: 1,571 women, 14,329 cycles; overall Pearl Index 0.73 (95% CI 0.31–1.43), method-failure Pearl Index reported separately; no deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, one case of hyperkalemia
cards.people: Pooled analysis of two prospective multicentre European phase 3 studies of the drospirenone-only 4 mg 24/4 pill in healthy women aged 18–45 years: study 1 (713 women, 13 cycles, 7,638 exposure cycles — the Archer 2015 trial) and study 2 (858 women, 9 cycles, 6,691 exposure cycles), totalling 1,571 women and 14,329 exposure cycles.
cards.result: The pooled overall Pearl Index was 0.7258 (95% CI 0.3133–1.4301), with a separate method-failure Pearl Index counting pregnancies in perfect-medication cycles. No single case of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism was reported, and only one case of hyperkalemia. Laboratory parameters, body mass index, body weight, heart rate and blood pressure showed no statistically significant changes on treatment.
cards.watchOut: Pooling two single-arm studies from one sponsor programme doubles the cycles, not the design strength: there is still no comparator, and the venous thromboembolism reassurance rests on the absence of events in about 1,600 relatively young, healthy women.
cards.source: Palacios S et al. Multicenter, phase III trials on the contraceptive efficacy, tolerability and safety of a new drospirenone-only pill. Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica. 2019. PMID: 31321765. Registry ID: EudraCT 2010-021787-15 and 2011-002396-42, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an oestrogen-free drospirenone pill with combined-pill-level Pearl Indices in Europe, a weaker US figure, settling bleeding, and no VTE seen — all without a comparator
cards.summary: Synthesis: an oestrogen-free drospirenone pill with combined-pill-level Pearl Indices in Europe, a weaker US figure, settling bleeding, and no VTE seen — all without a comparator
cards.people: The Exeltis drospirenone-only 4 mg 24/4 programme: 713 women in the European efficacy trial, 858 in its European sister study and 1,006 dosed in the US trial — all single-arm.
cards.result: Efficacy by benchmark: Pearl Indices of 0.51 (Europe), 0.73 (pooled Europe) and 4.0 (US primary analysis; 2.9 on the confirmed, clean-site analysis). Bleeding: frequent early, settling to about a third of women bleeding in a late cycle and about 23% unscheduled. Safety: no venous thromboembolism anywhere in the programme, hyperkalemia rare (one European case; 0.5% in the US), and no adverse metabolic or blood-pressure signal — the profile that makes an oestrogen-free pill attractive for women who cannot or will not take oestrogen.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge this shelf with the combined drospirenone-pill shelves (PMDD, acne, VTE comparisons): those are oestrogen-containing products with a different risk question. And the absence of VTE in trials is not proof of VTE safety at population scale — that question belongs to post-marketing data.
cards.source: Synthesis of Archer DF et al. Contraception. 2015 (PMID: 26232513); Kimble T et al. Contraception: X. 2020 (PMID: 32550535); Palacios S et al. Acta Obstetricia et Gynecologica Scandinavica. 2019 (PMID: 31321765).

shelves.title: Estetrol/drospirenone combined pill (tested product: Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill, Nextstellis) — SINGLE-ARM phase 3 programme: Pearl Index 0.47 in Europe/Russia and 2.65 in North America (pooled 1.52); one treatment-related venous thromboembolism in the European trial, none in North America
shelves.question: In women seeking combined oral contraception, does estetrol 15 mg + drospirenone 3 mg (name the tested product — Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill) prevent pregnancy versus benchmark combined pills, and what are its bleeding, metabolic and VTE profiles?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Contraceptives, Oral, Combined/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Estetrol/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Europe · Female · Humans · Metrorrhagia · Middle Aged · Russia · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the first combined pill built on estetrol (E4), a native oestrogen, paired with drospirenone 3 mg in a 24/4 regimen (tested product: the Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill, marketed as Nextstellis). Both E4 FREEDOM phase 3 trials were open-label and single-arm, so Pearl Indices are benchmark judgements, printed per trial as reported: 0.47 per 100 woman-years (95% CI 0.15–1.11) in Europe/Russia (Gemzell-Danielsson 2022; 1,553 women treated, primary group aged 18–35) and 2.65 (95% CI 1.73–3.88) in North America (Creinin 2021; 1,864 enrolled, 1,674 aged 16–35), with a pooled Pearl Index of 1.52 (95% CI 1.04–2.16) and a 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate of 1.28% across 3,027 participants (Jensen 2022). Bleeding was predictable: scheduled bleeding in about 83–94% of cycles depending on trial and cycle, with unscheduled bleeding/spotting falling over time. In the pooled safety analysis (Chen 2022; 3,417 users), 28.7% had a treatment-related adverse event — bleeding complaints (9.5%), breast pain (4.0%), acne (3.3%) and mood disturbance (3.2%) the most frequent — 8.0% discontinued for treatment-related events, and three treatment-related serious events included one venous thromboembolism; the European trial reported one treatment-related lower-extremity venous thromboembolism and the North American trial none. No clinically relevant changes in weight, blood pressure or laboratory parameters (including lipids, glucose and potassium) were found. Whether E4's hoped-for lower thrombosis risk is real is unproven — the trials were not powered for it and the authors call for large phase 4 studies — so a single single-arm programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Gemzell-Danielsson 2022 — Europe/Russia phase 3, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 1,553 women treated; Pearl Index 0.47 per 100 woman-years (method-failure 0.29); one treatment-related venous thromboembolism
cards.summary: Gemzell-Danielsson 2022 — Europe/Russia phase 3, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 1,553 women treated; Pearl Index 0.47 per 100 woman-years (method-failure 0.29); one treatment-related venous thromboembolism
cards.people: 1,553 sexually active women aged 18–50 years (1,353 of them aged 18–35) with regular menstrual cycles and body mass index up to 35 kg/m2, at 69 sites in Europe and Russia, taking the tested product — estetrol 15 mg/drospirenone 3 mg (Mithra/Gedeon Richter estetrol pill, Nextstellis) — in a 24 active / 4 placebo regimen for up to 13 cycles, recording intake, bleeding and intercourse in daily diaries.
cards.result: The Pearl Index for women aged 18–35 was 0.47 pregnancies per 100 woman-years (95% CI 0.15–1.11), and the method-failure Pearl Index was 0.29 (95% CI 0.06–0.83). Scheduled bleeding or spotting occurred in 91.9%–94.4% of women over cycles 1 to 12, lasting a median of 4–5 days per cycle, and unscheduled bleeding/spotting episodes fell from 23.5% in cycle 1 to under 16% from cycle 6 onwards. The most common adverse events were headache (7.7%), metrorrhagia (5.5%), vaginal haemorrhage (4.8%) and acne (4.2%). One treatment-related serious adverse event was reported — a lower-extremity venous thromboembolism — and 141 women (9.1%) discontinued because of treatment-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and in a leaner European/Russian population: the 0.47 Pearl Index is the programme's best figure and should not be quoted without the North American 2.65 beside it; one venous thromboembolism in 1,553 users neither confirms nor refutes the lower-thrombosis hope for estetrol.
cards.source: Gemzell-Danielsson K et al. Estetrol-Drospirenone combination oral contraceptive: a clinical study of contraceptive efficacy, bleeding pattern and safety in Europe and Russia. BJOG. 2022. PMID: 34245666. Registry ID: none in the record. phase 3 single-arm trial (gemzell-danielsson 2022) 1,553 sexually active women aged 18–50 years (1,353 of them aged 18–35) with regular menstrual cycles and body mass index up to 35 kg/m2, at 69 sites in europe and russia, taking the tested product — estetrol 15 mg/drospirenone 3 mg (mithra/gedeon richter estetrol pill, nextstellis) — in a 24 active / 4 placebo regimen for up to 13 cycles, recording intake, bleeding and intercourse in daily diaries. the pearl index for women aged 18–35 was 0.47 pregnancies per 100 woman-years (95% ci 0.15–1.11), and the method-failure pearl index was 0.29 (95% ci 0.06–0.83). scheduled bleeding or spotting occurred in 91.9%–94.4% of women over cycles 1 to 12, lasting a median of 4–5 days per cycle, and unscheduled bleeding/spotting episodes fell from 23.5% in cycle 1 to under 16% from cycle 6 onwards. the most common adverse events were headache (7.7%), metrorrhagia (5.5%), vaginal haemorrhage (4.8%) and acne (4.2%). one treatment-related serious adverse event was reported — a lower-extremity venous thromboembolism — and 141 women (9.1%) discontinued because of treatment-related adverse events. single-arm and in a leaner european/russian population: the 0.47 pearl index is the programme's best figure and should not be quoted without the north american 2.65 beside it; one venous thromboembolism in 1,553 users neither confirms nor refutes the lower-thrombosis hope for estetrol. gemzell-danielsson k et al. estetrol-drospirenone combination oral contraceptive: a clinical study of contraceptive efficacy, bleeding pattern and safety in europe and russia. bjog. 2022. pmid: 34245666. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · contraceptives, oral, combined/administration & dosage/adverse effects · estetrol/administration & dosage/adverse effects · europe · female · humans · metrorrhagia · middle aged · russia · young adult

cards.headline: Creinin 2021 — North American phase 3, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 1,864 women enrolled; Pearl Index 2.65 (method-failure 1.43) in women 16–35; no thromboembolic events
cards.summary: Creinin 2021 — North American phase 3, SINGLE-ARM open-label (design printed): 1,864 women enrolled; Pearl Index 2.65 (method-failure 1.43) in women 16–35; no thromboembolic events
cards.people: 1,864 women aged 16 to 50 years with body mass index up to 35 kg/m2 enrolled in a multicentre, open-label, 13-cycle North American phase 3 trial of estetrol 15 mg/drospirenone 3 mg in a 24-active/4-placebo regimen, with daily diaries of pill use and bleeding; efficacy was assessed in the 1,674 women aged 16 to 35 years.
cards.result: Women aged 16 to 35 had a Pearl Index of 2.65 (95% CI 1.73–3.88), a method-failure Pearl Index of 1.43 (95% CI 0.7–2.39) and a 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate of 2.1%. Scheduled bleeding occurred in 82.9%–87.0% of women per cycle with a median duration of 4.5 days; unscheduled bleeding fell from 30.3% in cycle 1 to about 15.5%–19.2% in later cycles. The most frequent adverse events were headache (5.0%) and metrorrhagia (4.6%); 132 women (7.1%) discontinued early for an adverse event, most commonly metrorrhagia (0.9%) and menorrhagia (0.8%). No thromboembolic events occurred.
cards.watchOut: The fivefold gap between the North American (2.65) and European/Russian (0.47) Pearl Indices — in the same programme, with the same pill — is the strongest reminder on this shelf that Pearl Indices measure populations and adherence as much as pharmacology.
cards.source: Creinin MD et al. Estetrol-drospirenone combination oral contraceptive: North American phase 3 efficacy and safety results. Contraception. 2021. PMID: 34000251. cards.headline: Jensen 2022 — pooled efficacy (3,027 participants): Pearl Index 1.52 and 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate 1.28%; failure risk rose with prior pregnancy, younger age and taking under 99% of expected pills
cards.summary: Jensen 2022 — pooled efficacy (3,027 participants): Pearl Index 1.52 and 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate 1.28%; failure risk rose with prior pregnancy, younger age and taking under 99% of expected pills
cards.people: Pooled at-risk-cycle efficacy data from the two pivotal phase 3 trials (United States/Canada and Europe/Russia) of estetrol 15 mg/drospirenone 3 mg in a 24/4 regimen: 3,027 participants aged 16 to 35 years, of whom 451 (14.9%) had a body mass index of at least 30 kg/m2.
cards.result: The pooled Pearl Index was 1.52 (95% CI 1.04–2.16) and the 13-cycle life-table pregnancy rate was 1.28% (95% CI 0.83%–1.73%). By body mass index, the unadjusted Pearl Index was 1.14 below 25 kg/m2, 2.19 at 25–29.9 kg/m2 and 2.27 at 30 kg/m2 or above; by age it was 1.61 at 16–25 years and 1.43 at 26–35 years. In multivariable analysis, prior pregnancy (hazard ratio 3.61), Black race (hazard ratio 4.61), age 16–25 (hazard ratio 2.37) and compliance below 99% of expected pills (hazard ratio 4.21) were associated with conception — hazard ratios are relative measures.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup Pearl Indices from single-arm trials describe who conceived in these studies, not biological effect modification; the compliance finding (hazard ratio 4.21) is the actionable one, and it is about pill-taking, not about the oestrogen.
cards.source: Jensen JT et al. Pooled efficacy results of estetrol/drospirenone combined oral contraception phase 3 trials. Contraception. 2022. PMID: 35921870. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2022 — pooled safety (3,417 users): 28.7% had a treatment-related adverse event; discontinuation for treatment-related events 8.0%; three treatment-related serious events including one venous thromboembolism; no clinically relevant metabolic changes
cards.summary: Chen 2022 — pooled safety (3,417 users): 28.7% had a treatment-related adverse event; discontinuation for treatment-related events 8.0%; three treatment-related serious events including one venous thromboembolism; no clinically relevant metabolic changes
cards.people: Pooled data from the two multicentre open-label phase 3 trials: 3,725 participants enrolled and 3,417 who took at least one dose of estetrol 15 mg/drospirenone 3 mg with a follow-up assessment, analysed for adverse events, vital signs and laboratory parameters including lipids, glucose, glycated hemoglobin and potassium.
cards.result: Of 3,417 users, 1,786 (52.3%) reported at least one adverse event and 981 (28.7%) at least one treatment-related event — most frequently bleeding complaints (323, 9.5%), breast pain or tenderness (136, 4.0%), acne (113, 3.3%) and mood disturbance (111, 3.2%); most events were mild or moderate and arose in cycles 1–3. Discontinuation for treatment-related events occurred in 272 participants (8.0%), only bleeding complaints (2.8%) and mood disturbance (1.1%) exceeding 1%. Three participants had serious events investigators considered treatment-related: one venous thromboembolism, one worsening of depression and one ectopic pregnancy. No clinically relevant changes in weight, blood pressure, heart rate or laboratory parameters were found.
cards.watchOut: Three thousand users cannot measure a venous thromboembolism rate that matters at population scale (combined-pill VTE is counted per 10,000 woman-years): the pooled safety set shows tolerability, not comparative thrombosis safety versus ethinylestradiol pills — the authors state post-marketing studies are needed for exactly that.
cards.source: Chen MJ et al. Tolerability and safety of the estetrol/drospirenone combined oral contraceptive: Pooled analysis of two multicenter, open-label phase 3 trials. Contraception. 2022. PMID: 36257374. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an effective native-oestrogen pill on benchmark evidence — Pearl Indices 0.47 to 2.65 by region, predictable bleeding, ordinary combined-pill tolerability, and an unproven thrombosis advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: an effective native-oestrogen pill on benchmark evidence — Pearl Indices 0.47 to 2.65 by region, predictable bleeding, ordinary combined-pill tolerability, and an unproven thrombosis advantage
cards.people: The E4 FREEDOM programme: 1,553 women treated in Europe/Russia, 1,864 enrolled in North America, 3,027 in the pooled efficacy analysis and 3,417 in the pooled safety analysis — all open-label and single-arm.
cards.result: Efficacy sits within the combined-pill range in both regions, bleeding is scheduled and predictable for most users, discontinuation for adverse events is about 7–9%, metabolic parameters were unmoved, and one treatment-related venous thromboembolism occurred among 3,417 pooled users. Nothing in the programme compares estetrol/drospirenone with an ethinylestradiol pill, so every comparative claim — especially lower thrombosis risk — remains a hypothesis awaiting phase 4 and population data, as the trialists themselves state.
cards.watchOut: Estetrol's 'natural oestrogen' framing invites an assumption of safety the evidence has not yet earned; this shelf credits the pill with the contraception it demonstrated and leaves the thrombosis question explicitly open.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gemzell-Danielsson K et al. BJOG. 2022 (PMID: 34245666); Creinin MD et al. Contraception. 2021 (PMID: 34000251); Jensen JT et al. Contraception. 2022 (PMID: 35921870); Chen MJ et al. Contraception. 2022 (PMID: 36257374).

shelves.title: Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily for stress urinary incontinence in women: median episode frequency fell ~50–54% in relative terms versus 29–41% on placebo across three trials — but 17–22% stopped for adverse events, mostly nausea; licensed for this indication in Europe, not the US
shelves.question: In women with stress urinary incontinence, does duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduce incontinence-episode frequency versus placebo, and at what nausea/discontinuation cost?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Nausea/chemically induced · Neurotransmitter Uptake Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Quality of Life · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Thiophenes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three concordant double-blind placebo-controlled trials (1,505 women carded) agree. Duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduced incontinence-episode frequency by a median of 50% (van Kerrebroeck 2004, Europe/Canada, n=494) and 54% (Millard 2004, four continents, n=458) in relative terms, versus 29% and 40% respectively on placebo; the earlier dose-ranging trial (Norton 2002, n=553) showed a dose-dependent relative decrease of 54–64% across 20–80 mg/day versus 41% on placebo. These are relative (percentage) reductions in diary episode counts — entry frequencies were ≥7 episodes/week and mean baseline was 18.4/week in Millard — not absolute episode counts or dryness rates. The cost sits beside the benefit: discontinuation for adverse events was 22% versus 5% (van Kerrebroeck) and 17.2% versus 1.7% (Millard), with nausea the commonest reason; in Norton it rose dose-dependently to 15% at 80 mg/day versus 5%. Quality of life improved in parallel in most analyses, though van Kerrebroeck's prespecified I-QOL co-primary analysis was formally negative because of early discontinuers' carried-forward scores. Duloxetine is licensed for this indication in Europe, not in the US — say so plainly, because a US reader cannot be prescribed it for incontinence.

cards.headline: Norton 2002 (n=553, dose-ranging): median incontinence-episode frequency fell 54% on duloxetine 20 mg/day, 59% on 40 mg/day and 64% on 80 mg/day, versus 41% on placebo (relative decreases)
cards.summary: Norton 2002 (n=553, dose-ranging): median incontinence-episode frequency fell 54% on duloxetine 20 mg/day, 59% on 40 mg/day and 64% on 80 mg/day, versus 41% on placebo (relative decreases)
cards.people: 553 women aged 18–65 years with a predominant symptom of stress urinary incontinence, randomised to placebo (n=138) or duloxetine 20 mg/day (n=138), 40 mg/day (n=137) or 80 mg/day (n=140, given as 40 mg twice daily) for 12 weeks; incontinence episode frequency (IEF) was recorded in a real-time diary. A subgroup of 163 women had severe incontinence (≥14 episodes/week).
cards.result: Median IEF decreased by 54% on 20 mg/day (P=.06 vs placebo), 59% on 40 mg/day (P=.002) and 64% on 80 mg/day (P<.001), versus 41% on placebo — these are relative (percentage) decreases in episode counts, not absolute episode numbers. At 80 mg/day, 67% of women had a ≥50% reduction in IEF (P=.001 vs placebo). In the severe subgroup, IEF fell 49%–64% on duloxetine versus 30% on placebo. Patient Global Impression of Improvement and Incontinence Quality of Life scores improved in parallel, and voiding intervals lengthened dose-dependently. Discontinuation for adverse events rose with dose: 5% on placebo versus 9%, 12% and 15% at 20, 40 and 80 mg/day (P=.04); nausea was the commonest reason, and no reported adverse event was considered clinically severe.
cards.watchOut: This is the dose-ranging trial, not the licensed-dose confirmatory trial: the 40 mg twice-daily regimen is its top (80 mg/day) arm. The placebo group's 41% median relative decrease is large, so the drug's added relative benefit over placebo is roughly 13–23 percentage points of episode frequency, and the trial predates trial registration, so no registry ID is in the record.
cards.source: Norton PA et al. Duloxetine versus placebo in the treatment of stress urinary incontinence. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2002. PMID: 12114886. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van Kerrebroeck 2004 (n=494, Europe/Canada): median episode frequency fell 50% on duloxetine 40 mg twice daily versus 29% on placebo (P=0.002) — but 22% versus 5% stopped for adverse events
cards.summary: van Kerrebroeck 2004 (n=494, Europe/Canada): median episode frequency fell 50% on duloxetine 40 mg twice daily versus 29% on placebo (P=0.002) — but 22% versus 5% stopped for adverse events
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (van Kerrebroeck 2004)
cards.people: 494 women aged 24–83 years at 46 centres in seven European countries and Canada, with predominant stress urinary incontinence (weekly IEF ≥7, positive cough stress test and stress pad test, bladder capacity ≥400 mL), randomised after a 2-week placebo lead-in to duloxetine 40 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks. Co-primary outcomes were percentage decrease in IEF and change in Incontinence Quality of Life (I-QOL) total score.
cards.result: Median IEF decreased 50% on duloxetine versus 29% on placebo (P=0.002) — a relative decrease; in the more severely incontinent subgroup (≥14 episodes/week) the decreases were 56% versus 27% (P<0.001). The primary I-QOL analysis did not reach significance, because scores carried forward from women who stopped duloxetine very early for adverse events were low; I-QOL increases were significantly greater on duloxetine at each of the 4-, 8- and 12-week visits. Discontinuation for adverse events was 22% on duloxetine versus 5% on placebo (P<0.001), with nausea the commonest reason (5.3%); nausea was mild to moderate, not progressive, and transient.
cards.watchOut: The headline efficacy and the headline cost come from the same women: about one in five stopped the drug within 12 weeks, mostly for nausea, and the quality-of-life co-primary endpoint was formally negative on its prespecified analysis even though visit-by-visit scores favoured duloxetine.
cards.source: van Kerrebroeck P et al. Duloxetine versus placebo in the treatment of European and Canadian women with stress urinary incontinence. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2004. PMID: 14961887. Registry ID: none in the record. in the more severely incontinent subgroup (≥14 episodes/week) the decreases were 56% versus 27% (p<0.001). the primary i-qol analysis did not reach significance, because scores carried forward from women who stopped duloxetine very early for adverse events were low; i-qol increases were significantly greater on duloxetine at each of the 4-, 8- and 12-week visits. discontinuation for adverse events was 22% on duloxetine versus 5% on placebo (p<0.001), with nausea the commonest reason (5.3%); nausea was mild to moderate, not progressive, and transient. the headline efficacy and the headline cost come from the same women: about one in five stopped the drug within 12 weeks, mostly for nausea, and the quality-of-life co-primary endpoint was formally negative on its prespecified analysis even though visit-by-visit scores favoured duloxetine. van kerrebroeck p et al. duloxetine versus placebo in the treatment of european and canadian women with stress urinary incontinence. bjog : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2004. pmid: 14961887. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · blood pressure/drug effects · double-blind method · duloxetine hydrochloride · female · heart rate/drug effects · humans · middle aged · quality of life · selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · thiophenes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · treatment outcome · urinary incontinence, stress/drug therapy,physiopathology

cards.headline: Millard 2004 (n=458, four continents): median episode frequency fell 54% on duloxetine versus 40% on placebo (P=0.05); discontinuation for adverse events 17.2% versus 1.7%
cards.summary: Millard 2004 (n=458, four continents): median episode frequency fell 54% on duloxetine versus 40% on placebo (P=0.05); discontinuation for adverse events 17.2% versus 1.7%
cards.people: 458 women aged 27–79 years in Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Finland, Poland, South Africa and Spain, with predominantly stress urinary incontinence identified by a validated clinical algorithm, randomised to duloxetine 40 mg twice daily (n=227) or placebo (n=231) for 12 weeks. Mean baseline IEF was 18.4 episodes/week; 55% had a baseline IEF ≥14/week.
cards.result: Median IEF fell 54% on duloxetine versus 40% on placebo (P=0.05) — again a relative decrease, from a mean baseline of about 18 episodes a week. I-QOL scores rose 10.3 versus 6.4 points (P=0.007), and voiding intervals increased 20.4 versus 8.5 minutes more (P<0.001). The placebo response was 10.7–12.5 percentage points higher than in the North American and European phase 3 trials, which the authors attribute to more participants being naïve to incontinence management. Discontinuation for adverse events was 17.2% on duloxetine versus 1.7% on placebo (P<0.001); nausea was the commonest adverse event and the commonest reason for stopping (3.1%), was mild or moderate in 81% of cases, resolved within 7 days in 60% and within 1 month in 86% of women who continued, and 88% of women who had nausea completed the trial.
cards.watchOut: The between-group difference in relative episode reduction is the smallest of the three trials (14 percentage points, P=0.05) because the placebo response was unusually large — the result is consistent in direction with the other trials but closest to the line.
cards.source: Millard RJ et al. Duloxetine vs placebo in the treatment of stress urinary incontinence: a four-continent randomized clinical trial. BJU international. 2004. PMID: 14764128. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three concordant trials, a real but modest relative gain, and a one-in-five early discontinuation cost — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three concordant trials, a real but modest relative gain, and a one-in-five early discontinuation cost — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded randomised trials (1,505 women in total across North America-adjacent, European/Canadian and four-continent populations). A fourth large North American phase 3 trial of the same regimen exists in the programme but is not carded here because its record is already homed elsewhere in the library's carded set; the three carded trials are sufficient and concordant.
cards.result: Across three double-blind placebo-controlled trials, duloxetine 40 mg twice daily reduced incontinence-episode frequency by a median of about 50–54% in relative terms, versus 29–41% on placebo, with quality-of-life gains in the two trials whose analyses reached significance. Against that, 17–22% of women on duloxetine stopped within 12 weeks for adverse events (versus 2–5% on placebo), nausea being the dominant cause. Duloxetine is licensed for stress urinary incontinence in Europe but not in the United States — that licensing asymmetry is part of this shelf's answer.
cards.watchOut: All efficacy figures are relative (percentage) reductions in episode counts from diaries; no carded trial reports a cure or dryness rate, and 12 weeks is the horizon of every trial — long-term persistence on a drug one in five women stop early is untested here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Norton PA et al. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2002 (PMID: 12114886); van Kerrebroeck P et al. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2004 (PMID: 14961887); Millard RJ et al. BJU international. 2004 (PMID: 14764128).

shelves.title: Lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day for postmenopausal osteoporosis (PEARL, n=8,556): vertebral fractures down 42% relative (13.1 vs 22.4 per 1,000 person-years) and non-vertebral down 24% relative — venous thromboembolism roughly doubled in relative terms (2.9 vs 1.4 per 1,000 person-years)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduce vertebral and non-vertebral fractures versus placebo over 5 years, and what are its VTE and endometrial profiles?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Breast Neoplasms/epidemiology,prevention & control · Coronary Disease/epidemiology,prevention & control · Female · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology,prevention & control · Humans · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/complications,drug therapy · Pyrrolidines/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Receptors, Estrogen/analysis · Risk · Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology,prevention & control · Stroke/epidemiology,prevention & control · Tetrahydronaphthalenes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Venous Thromboembolism/chemically induced,epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large trial programme (PEARL, 8,556 women, 5 years) is the entire evidence base, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduced vertebral fractures by 42% in relative terms (hazard ratio 0.58; absolute rates 13.1 versus 22.4 per 1,000 person-years) and non-vertebral fractures by 24% in relative terms (HR 0.76; 18.7 versus 24.5 per 1,000 person-years) — it is the one SERM whose pivotal trial showed a non-vertebral fracture reduction. The VTE cost must be read both ways: roughly doubled in relative terms (HR 2.06 at 0.5 mg; HR 2.67 at 0.25 mg), which in absolute terms is 2.9 versus 1.4 events per 1,000 person-years. Breast cancer fell in relative terms in a 49-event analysis (total breast cancer HR 0.21), and 5-year gynaecological follow-up found endometrial cancer in 2 women on 0.5 mg versus 3 on placebo, with more polyps, bleeding and endometrial thickening on the drug. Premise note: the slate attributed PEARL's fracture report to a 2009 Gennari paper; no such primary record was found on PubMed this session — the definitive fracture report is Cummings et al., N Engl J Med 2010, and that is what is carded.

cards.headline: PEARL — Cummings 2010 (n=8,556, 5 years): lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day cut vertebral fractures by 42% relative (13.1 vs 22.4 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.58) and non-vertebral fractures by 24% relative (18.7 vs 24.5; HR 0.76) — VTE roughly doubled in relative terms (HR 2.06; 2.9 vs 1.4 per 1,000 person-years)
cards.summary: PEARL — Cummings 2010 (n=8,556, 5 years): lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day cut vertebral fractures by 42% relative (13.1 vs 22.4 per 1,000 person-years; HR 0.58) and non-vertebral fractures by 24% relative (18.7 vs 24.5; HR 0.76) — VTE roughly doubled in relative terms (HR 2.06; 2.9 vs 1.4 per 1,000 person-years)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Cummings 2010, PEARL)
cards.people: 8,556 postmenopausal women aged 59–80 years with a bone mineral density T score of −2.5 or less at the femoral neck or spine, randomised to lasofoxifene 0.25 mg/day, lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day, or placebo for 5 years. Primary endpoints were vertebral fractures, estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer and non-vertebral fractures.
cards.result: At 0.5 mg/day versus placebo: vertebral fracture 13.1 versus 22.4 cases per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.47–0.70 — a 42% relative reduction, and an absolute difference of 9.3 fewer cases per 1,000 person-years); non-vertebral fracture 18.7 versus 24.5 per 1,000 person-years (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.91 — a 24% relative reduction, 5.8 fewer per 1,000 person-years). ER-positive breast cancer, coronary heart disease events and stroke were also less frequent (HRs 0.19, 0.68 and 0.64). The harm: venous thromboembolic events were roughly doubled in relative terms at 0.5 mg (2.9 versus 1.4 per 1,000 person-years; HR 2.06, 95% CI 1.17–3.60 — an absolute excess of 1.5 per 1,000 person-years) and higher still in relative terms at 0.25 mg (3.8 per 1,000 person-years; HR 2.67). Endometrial cancer occurred in 2 women on 0.5 mg, 2 on 0.25 mg and 3 on placebo. Death rates per 1,000 person-years were 5.7 (0.5 mg), 7.0 (0.25 mg) and 5.1 (placebo).
cards.watchOut: One trial carries every number on this shelf: PEARL is a single large programme, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite its size. The fracture and VTE figures are hazard ratios (relative measures) — the absolute rates beside them are the honest scale: about 9 fewer vertebral fractures but about 1.5 extra VTE events per 1,000 woman-years at the 0.5 mg dose.
cards.source: Cummings SR et al. Lasofoxifene in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20181970. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00141323, from the record. cards.headline: PEARL breast-cancer analysis — LaCroix 2010: total breast cancer reduced by 79% relative (HR 0.21) and ER-positive invasive breast cancer by 83% relative (HR 0.17) at 0.5 mg/day — on 49 confirmed cases in total
cards.summary: PEARL breast-cancer analysis — LaCroix 2010: total breast cancer reduced by 79% relative (HR 0.21) and ER-positive invasive breast cancer by 83% relative (HR 0.17) at 0.5 mg/day — on 49 confirmed cases in total
cards.type: Prespecified trial analysis with nested case-control study (LaCroix 2010, PEARL)
cards.people: The same 8,556 PEARL participants, with normal mammograms at entry; breast cancer was confirmed in 49 women over 5 years. A nested case-control study (49 cases, 156 controls) examined whether baseline estradiol and sex hormone-binding globulin modified the effect.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduced total breast cancer (invasive plus ductal carcinoma in situ) by 79% in relative terms (HR 0.21, 95% CI 0.08–0.55) and ER-positive invasive breast cancer by 83% in relative terms (HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.05–0.57). Effects on total breast cancer were similar across Gail scores but markedly stronger in women with baseline estradiol above the median (odds ratio 0.11) than below it (odds ratio 0.78; P for interaction = .04).
cards.watchOut: Forty-nine events is a small base for an 83% relative reduction — the confidence interval (0.05–0.57) is wide, and breast cancer was not the question this shelf was built to answer; it is carded because it is part of PEARL's benefit–harm balance, not as a prevention claim.
cards.source: LaCroix AZ et al. Breast cancer incidence in the randomized PEARL trial of lasofoxifene in postmenopausal osteoporotic women. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2010. cards.headline: PEARL gynaecological outcomes — Goldstein 2011 (5 years): endometrial cancer 2 versus 3 women (0.5 mg vs placebo), hyperplasia 2 versus 0, polyps 5.5% versus 3.3%, vaginal bleeding 2.6% versus 1.3%
cards.summary: PEARL gynaecological outcomes — Goldstein 2011 (5 years): endometrial cancer 2 versus 3 women (0.5 mg vs placebo), hyperplasia 2 versus 0, polyps 5.5% versus 3.3%, vaginal bleeding 2.6% versus 1.3%
cards.people: The 8,556 PEARL women followed for 5 years on lasofoxifene 0.25 mg/day, 0.5 mg/day or placebo, with gynaecological outcomes including endometrial cancer, hyperplasia, polyps, bleeding and endometrial thickness.
cards.result: Endometrial cancer was confirmed in two women in each lasofoxifene group and three on placebo; endometrial hyperplasia occurred in three women on 0.25 mg, two on 0.5 mg and none on placebo. Vaginal bleeding occurred in 2.6% on 0.5 mg and 2.2% on 0.25 mg versus 1.3% on placebo. Endometrial thickness increased slightly on lasofoxifene (least-squares mean change +1.43 mm at 0.5 mg and +1.19 mm at 0.25 mg versus −0.72 mm on placebo). Endometrial polyps were found in 5.5% (0.5 mg), 8.8% (0.25 mg) and 3.3% (placebo). Surgery for pelvic organ prolapse was similar at 0.5 mg versus placebo (1.6% vs 1.2%). The authors conclude the endometrial changes were benign and did not increase endometrial cancer or hyperplasia risk.
cards.watchOut: Absolute endometrial cancer counts are tiny and equal across arms, but hyperplasia and polyps lean the other way and endometrial thickness rose — the fair reading is 'no cancer signal in 5 years, with benign endometrial stimulation', not 'no endometrial effect'. This record carries no registry ID of its own; PEARL's registration (NCT00141323) is in the Cummings 2010 record.
cards.source: Goldstein SR et al. Postmenopausal Evaluation and Risk Reduction With Lasofoxifene (PEARL) trial: 5-year gynecological outcomes. Menopause (New York, N.Y.). 2011. PMID: 20689465. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large trial — fractures and breast cancer down in relative terms, VTE up — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large trial — fractures and breast cancer down in relative terms, VTE up — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Synthesis of three reports of the single PEARL trial (8,556 women, 5 years).
cards.result: PEARL is the whole evidence base: lasofoxifene 0.5 mg/day reduced vertebral fractures by 42% relative and non-vertebral fractures by 24% relative (absolute differences 9.3 and 5.8 fewer per 1,000 person-years), reduced breast cancer in a 49-event analysis, and roughly doubled venous thromboembolism in relative terms (absolute excess ~1.5 per 1,000 person-years), with benign endometrial changes and no endometrial-cancer excess. A single programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: No second trial, no head-to-head against raloxifene or bisphosphonates, and no fracture data beyond 5 years exist in the carded record; lasofoxifene's regulatory and commercial history means PEARL is unlikely ever to be replicated, so this balance is final as it stands.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cummings SR et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20181970); LaCroix AZ et al. Journal of the National Cancer Institute. 2010 (PMID: 21051656); Goldstein SR et al. Menopause (New York, N.Y.). 2011 (PMID: 20689465).

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — KNDy neurons and neurokinin B in the menopausal hot flush: post-mortem NKB neurons hypertrophied (194% of premenopausal size, 15-fold more numerous), neurokinin B infusion provoked flushes in 8 of 10 women versus 0 on vehicle, and the thermoneutral zone was ~0.0 °C in symptomatic women versus 0.4 °C in symptom-free women
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women, does hypertrophy of hypothalamic KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin) neurons and increased neurokinin B signalling narrow the thermoneutral zone so that small core-temperature rises trigger hot flushes — and does neurokinin B infusion provoke flush-like episodes in young women?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Cell Count · Female · Gene Expression Regulation · Humans · Hypertrophy · Hypothalamus/metabolism,pathology · Menopause/metabolism · Middle Aged · Neurokinin B/genetics · Neurons/metabolism,physiology · RNA, Messenger/metabolism · Receptors, Estrogen/genetics · Substance P/genetics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): hypothalamic KNDy neurons — co-expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin B (NKB) and dynorphin — link estrogen feedback to thermoregulatory circuitry, and NKB signalling is the pathway blocked by the NK3-antagonist treatment shelves this pack partners. The carded primary human data form a complete chain. Post-mortem: infundibular neurons containing NKB mRNA hypertrophied after menopause (cross-sectional area 194% of premenopausal values; NKB-labelled neurons 15-fold more numerous; increased gene expression — Rance & Young 1991, n=3 versus n=3, printed plainly), and stereology shows the nucleus loses no neurons with age while soma volume rises 40% (Abel & Rance 2000) — hypertrophy, not degeneration. Provocation: intravenous NKB induced flushes in 8 of 10 healthy women versus 0 of 10 on vehicle, with flush-typical heart-rate and skin-temperature rises (Jayasena 2015). Downstream: symptomatic postmenopausal women had a thermoneutral zone of ~0.0 °C versus 0.4 °C in symptom-free women, so small core-temperature rises trigger a flush (Freedman & Krell 1999, n=20). No animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only as textbook framing.

cards.headline: Rance & Young 1991: in post-mortem hypothalami, infundibular neurons containing neurokinin B mRNA were hypertrophied after menopause (cross-sectional area 194% of premenopausal values), NKB-labelled neurons were 15-fold more numerous, and NKB gene expression was increased (n=3 postmenopausal vs n=3 premenopausal in the comparison study, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Rance & Young 1991: in post-mortem hypothalami, infundibular neurons containing neurokinin B mRNA were hypertrophied after menopause (cross-sectional area 194% of premenopausal values), NKB-labelled neurons were 15-fold more numerous, and NKB gene expression was increased (n=3 postmenopausal vs n=3 premenopausal in the comparison study, printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human post-mortem in-situ hybridisation study (Rance & Young 1991)
cards.people: Hypothalami of postmenopausal women (n=3 in the first study) and, in the comparison study, premenopausal (n=3) versus postmenopausal (n=3) women; neuronal cross-sectional areas, cell densities and autoradiographic grain densities were measured for neurons labelled with cDNA probes for neurokinin B (NKB), substance P (SP) and ten other peptide/receptor mRNAs. Sub-10 samples, printed plainly per the labelling rule.
cards.result: Neurons labelled with the NKB and substance P probes matched the previously described hypertrophied, estrogen-receptor-mRNA-containing neurons in size, morphology and distribution; neurons labelled with the other probes were smaller, sparser or differently located. Mean cross-sectional areas of postmenopausal infundibular neurons containing NKB and SP mRNAs rose to 194% and 176% of premenopausal values respectively; grain densities (gene expression per neuron) were significantly increased for both; and the numbers of labelled neurons per tissue rose 6-fold (SP) and 15-fold (NKB) after menopause. The authors propose these neurons participate in the hypothalamic circuitry of estrogen negative feedback in humans.
cards.watchOut: Three brains per group is the entire comparison — the effect sizes are large and the direction has been corroborated (see the stereology card), but every number here rests on n=3 versus n=3 post-mortem tissue, with all the selection limits that implies. This study predates the discovery of kisspeptin, so it identifies the NKB/SP neurons; their identity as KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin) neurons is the later textbook framing, not a measurement in this paper.
cards.source: Rance NE et al. Hypertrophy and increased gene expression of neurons containing neurokinin-B and substance-P messenger ribonucleic acids in the hypothalami of postmenopausal women. Endocrinology. 1991. PMID: 1708331. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Abel & Rance 2000: unbiased stereology found no loss of infundibular neurons in older women (520,000 ± 42,000 young versus 505,000 ± 51,000 older) while mean neuronal soma volume rose 40% — hypertrophy without degeneration
cards.summary: Abel & Rance 2000: unbiased stereology found no loss of infundibular neurons in older women (520,000 ± 42,000 young versus 505,000 ± 51,000 older) while mean neuronal soma volume rose 40% — hypertrophy without degeneration
cards.type: Primary human post-mortem stereology study (Abel & Rance 2000)
cards.people: Hypothalamic infundibular (arcuate) nucleus of young (premenopausal) and older (postmenopausal) women, compared with unbiased stereologic methods; the fetched record does not state the group sizes, so this card prints N not documented for its groups.
cards.result: Total infundibular neuron number did not differ significantly between young (520,000 ± 42,000, mean ± SEM) and older women (505,000 ± 51,000). Mean neuronal soma volume was increased by 40% in older women (1,860 ± 180 µm³ versus 2,610 ± 230 µm³; P<0.05). The authors conclude neuronal hypertrophy in older women is not accompanied by degeneration of the infundibular nucleus, and that loss of menstrual cyclicity cannot be explained by loss of neurons in this hypothalamic control centre. Their summary of the field restates that hypertrophy of neurons expressing substance P and neurokinin B gene transcripts, with increased tachykinin gene expression, accompanies ageing in women.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record, and stereology of the whole nucleus cannot isolate the KNDy subpopulation — its role here is to rule out the competing explanation (neuron death) for the postmenopausal changes the 1991 study described.
cards.source: Abel TW et al. Stereologic study of the hypothalamic infundibular nucleus in young and older women. The Journal of comparative neurology. 2000. PMID: 10931489. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jayasena 2015: intravenous neurokinin B provoked hot flushes in 8 of 10 healthy young women versus 0 of 10 on vehicle (P=0.0007), with the heart-rate and skin-temperature rises of a menopausal flush (N=10, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Jayasena 2015: intravenous neurokinin B provoked hot flushes in 8 of 10 healthy young women versus 0 of 10 on vehicle (P=0.0007), with the heart-rate and skin-temperature rises of a menopausal flush (N=10, printed plainly)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover provocation study (Jayasena 2015)
cards.people: 10 healthy women in a temperature- and humidity-controlled research unit, receiving 30-minute intravenous infusions of neurokinin B and vehicle in random order, with symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure, sweating and skin temperature compared double-blind. N=10 printed plainly.
cards.result: Eight of ten participants experienced flushing during neurokinin B infusion and none during vehicle infusion (P=0.0007). During flush episodes, heart rate rose significantly (P=0.0106 versus pre-symptoms) and skin temperature rose on both skin-probe (P=0.0258) and thermal-imaging (P=0.0491) measurement — the physiological signature of a menopausal hot flush. The authors conclude neurokinin B administration can cause hot flushes in women, and that whether blocking neurokinin B signalling inhibits menopausal flushes requires further study.
cards.watchOut: Provocation in 10 young, premenopausal women shows NKB is sufficient to trigger a flush-like episode; it does not by itself prove endogenous NKB drives spontaneous menopausal flushes — that inference rests on combining this study with the post-mortem hypertrophy data and the narrowed-thermoneutral-zone work carded here.
cards.source: Jayasena CN et al. Neurokinin B administration induces hot flushes in women. Scientific reports. 2015. PMID: 25683060. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Freedman & Krell 1999: the thermoneutral (interthreshold) zone was ~0.0 °C in 12 postmenopausal women with hot flashes versus 0.4 °C in 8 without (rectal temperature; P<.005) — small core-temperature rises cross the sweating threshold and trigger a flush
cards.summary: Freedman & Krell 1999: the thermoneutral (interthreshold) zone was ~0.0 °C in 12 postmenopausal women with hot flashes versus 0.4 °C in 8 without (rectal temperature; P<.005) — small core-temperature rises cross the sweating threshold and trigger a flush
cards.type: Primary human thermoregulation laboratory study (Freedman & Krell 1999)
cards.people: 12 postmenopausal women with hot-flash symptoms and 8 without, studied over three sessions (sweating threshold by body heating, shivering threshold by body cooling, sweating threshold replicated with exercise), with core temperature measured by rectal probe, ingested telemetry pill and a weighted mean body temperature.
cards.result: Women with symptoms had significantly smaller interthreshold zones by every measure: rectal temperature 0.0 ± 0.06 °C versus 0.4 ± 0.18 °C (P<.005); telemetry pill 0.0 ± 0.11 °C versus 0.4 ± 0.18 °C (P<.005); mean body temperature 0.8 ± 0.09 °C versus 1.5 ± 0.20 °C (P<.0006). Sweat rates were higher in symptomatic women (0.06 versus 0.03 mg·cm⁻²·min⁻¹; P<.05). During exercise, all symptomatic women and no symptom-free women had hot flashes. The authors conclude most menopausal hot flashes are preceded by small core-temperature elevations, and may be triggered when those elevations act within a reduced thermoneutral zone.
cards.watchOut: Twenty women in one laboratory, and the zone is inferred from threshold testing rather than observed during spontaneous flushes — but it supplies the downstream half of the mechanism (why a small temperature rise triggers a full flush response) that the KNDy/NKB cards supply the upstream half for.
cards.source: Freedman RR et al. Reduced thermoregulatory null zone in postmenopausal women with hot flashes. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 1999. PMID: 10411797. cards.headline: Synthesis: post-mortem KNDy-neuron hypertrophy with increased NKB expression, NKB provocation of flushes, and a narrowed thermoneutral zone converge — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: post-mortem KNDy-neuron hypertrophy with increased NKB expression, NKB provocation of flushes, and a narrowed thermoneutral zone converge — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded primary human studies. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): the hypothalamic KNDy neurons of the infundibular/arcuate nucleus — co-expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin — sit in the circuitry linking estrogen feedback to thermoregulation, and neurokinin B signalling through its receptor is the pathway the menopause treatment shelves (fezolinetant, elinzanetant) block; those shelves assert this mechanism, and this pack is their physiology partner.
cards.result: The human chain is complete at each link: after menopause the infundibular NKB neurons hypertrophy and express more NKB (Rance & Young 1991), without any loss of infundibular neurons to explain the change away (Abel & Rance 2000); infusing NKB into healthy women provokes flush episodes with the objective signature of a menopausal flush (Jayasena 2015, 8/10 versus 0/10); and symptomatic postmenopausal women have a thermoneutral zone narrowed to ~0.0 °C, so small core-temperature rises trigger sweating and flushing (Freedman & Krell 1999). No animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only in the textbook framing. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Every link rests on small human samples (n=3 per group post-mortem; n=10 provocation; n=20 thermoregulation) — the stamp reflects concordance across four independent methods and subsequent textbook settlement, not sample size, and the individual Ns are printed on each card's face.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rance NE et al. Endocrinology. 1991 (PMID: 1708331); Abel TW et al. The Journal of comparative neurology. 2000 (PMID: 10931489); Jayasena CN et al. synthesis synthesis of the four carded primary human studies. textbook framing (ganong's review of medical physiology; boron & boulpaep medical physiology): the hypothalamic kndy neurons of the infundibular/arcuate nucleus — co-expressing kisspeptin, neurokinin b and dynorphin — sit in the circuitry linking estrogen feedback to thermoregulation, and neurokinin b signalling through its receptor is the pathway the menopause treatment shelves (fezolinetant, elinzanetant) block; those shelves assert this mechanism, and this pack is their physiology partner. the human chain is complete at each link: after menopause the infundibular nkb neurons hypertrophy and express more nkb (rance & young 1991), without any loss of infundibular neurons to explain the change away (abel & rance 2000); infusing nkb into healthy women provokes flush episodes with the objective signature of a menopausal flush (jayasena 2015, 8/10 versus 0/10); and symptomatic postmenopausal women have a thermoneutral zone narrowed to ~0.0 °c, so small core-temperature rises trigger sweating and flushing (freedman & krell 1999). no animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only in the textbook framing. physiology — established. every link rests on small human samples (n=3 per group post-mortem; n=10 provocation; n=20 thermoregulation) — the stamp reflects concordance across four independent methods and subsequent textbook settlement, not sample size, and the individual ns are printed on each card's face. synthesis of rance ne et al. endocrinology. 1991 (pmid: 1708331); abel tw et al. the journal of comparative neurology. 2000 (pmid: 10931489); jayasena cn et al. scientific reports. 2015 (pmid: 25683060); freedman rr et al. american journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 1999 (pmid: 10411797).

shelves.title: Low-dose paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg for menopausal hot flushes: two phase 3 trials met their frequency endpoints, severity separation was partial, and pooled analyses showed fewer night-time awakenings with no weight or sexual-function cost
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, does paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg at bedtime, versus placebo, reduce hot-flush frequency and severity?
mesh: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors / administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). This shelf answers the specific product question — paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg once daily at bedtime (the Noven Pharmaceuticals programme, per a fetched review record, PMID 24601805; the brand name does not appear in the fetched trial records) — and is not interchangeable with antidepressant-dose paroxetine hydrochloride or with the controlled-release paroxetine 12.5–25 mg carded, with escitalopram, on live shelf #667, which this shelf cross-points and does not duplicate: the Stearns 2003 trial homed there is deliberately not re-carded here. The two phase 3 trials (1,184 women randomised) both significantly reduced weekly vasomotor-symptom frequency at weeks 4 and 12; severity separation was complete in the 24-week study but partial in the 12-week study (the week-12 severity endpoint was the one primary endpoint missed), and the trials' abstract reports p-values rather than absolute flush counts, so the size of the benefit cannot be stated from these records — the class context from #667 is a modest absolute gain over a large placebo response. Pooled analyses of the same two trials found fewer night-time awakenings attributed to flushes (39% vs 28% reduction at week 4, percentages as reported) and about 15 extra minutes of sleep, with no weight gain or sexual-function deterioration versus placebo. Paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg remains the only FDA-approved non-hormonal drug for vasomotor symptoms (per the fetched records); SSRI-class cautions apply, including the CYP2D6 interaction that makes paroxetine a poor choice alongside tamoxifen — a caution from class pharmacology, flagged here because the trial populations were not breast-cancer populations. Neighbouring homes: fezolinetant live #250, elinzanetant live #949, gabapentin pack #1343, oxybutynin pack #2802.

cards.headline: Two phase 3 trials (Simon 2013): paroxetine 7.5 mg significantly reduced weekly flush frequency at weeks 4 and 12 in both studies; severity endpoints were met fully in the 24-week study but only partly in the 12-week study
cards.summary: Two phase 3 trials (Simon 2013): paroxetine 7.5 mg significantly reduced weekly flush frequency at weeks 4 and 12 in both studies; severity endpoints were met fully in the 24-week study but only partly in the 12-week study
cards.type: Two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported in one publication (Simon 2013)
cards.people: Postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms randomised 1:1 to paroxetine mesylate 7.5 mg (n=591) or placebo (n=593) once daily in two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 studies of 12 and 24 weeks. The four primary endpoints were mean changes in frequency and severity of moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms at weeks 4 and 12, with persistence of benefit at week 24 as an additional endpoint. Registered as NCT01101841 and NCT01361308.
cards.result: All primary endpoints were met in the 24-week study; three of four were met in the 12-week study. Frequency fell significantly more on paroxetine in both studies at week 4 (p<0.0001 for both) and week 12 (p=0.0090, 12-week study; p=0.0001, 24-week study). Severity fell significantly more at week 4 in the 12-week study (p=0.0048) and at weeks 4 (p=0.0452) and 12 (p=0.0114) in the 24-week study; persistence of benefit was demonstrated at week 24. Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild or moderate, with no clinically significant laboratory or vital-sign changes and no short-term discontinuation symptoms reported after stopping. The abstract reports p-values without absolute flush-frequency changes, so no magnitudes are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A programme that reports significance without absolute numbers in its abstract asks to be trusted rather than checked: the missed week-12 severity endpoint in the shorter study is visible, but the actual flushes-per-week gained over placebo is not in this record — for absolute magnitudes in this drug class, see the escitalopram and paroxetine-CR trials on live shelf #667. Both trials come from one sponsor programme.
