cards.headline: Pooled sleep analysis (Pinkerton 2015): night-time awakenings from flushes fell 39% vs 28% at week 4 and sleep duration rose by 31 vs 16 minutes — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials
cards.summary: Pooled sleep analysis (Pinkerton 2015): night-time awakenings from flushes fell 39% vs 28% at week 4 and sleep duration rose by 31 vs 16 minutes — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised trials (Pinkerton 2015) — explicitly labelled pooled report
cards.people: The same two phase 3 trials pooled for weeks 1–12 (paroxetine 7.5 mg n=591; placebo n=593), in postmenopausal women with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms who reported a mean of 3.6 night-time awakenings attributed to vasomotor symptoms at baseline; sleep was a predefined prospective assessment (awakenings, sleep-onset latency, sleep duration, sleep-related adverse events). Registered as NCT01101841 and NCT01361308 — the same trials as the first card.
cards.result: Awakenings attributed to vasomotor symptoms were significantly reduced within 4 weeks (39% reduction on paroxetine vs 28% on placebo; p=0.0049 — percentage reductions as reported) and the reduction was sustained through 12 or 24 weeks. Sleep duration increased more on paroxetine at week 4 (+31 vs +16 minutes; p=0.0075). There were no significant between-group differences in sleep-onset latency or in sleep-related adverse events such as sedation.
cards.watchOut: A pooled secondary analysis adds outcomes, not patients: the sleep benefit is a genuine, prospectively assessed plus of the same 1,184 women, worth roughly 15 extra minutes of sleep and about one fewer awakening in nine versus placebo at week 4 — worthwhile to women woken nightly, and not a hypnotic effect (latency unchanged, no sedation signal).

cards.headline: Pooled weight and sexual-function analysis (Portman 2014): no clinically meaningful weight gain or sexual-function deterioration on paroxetine 7.5 mg vs placebo — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials
cards.summary: Pooled weight and sexual-function analysis (Portman 2014): no clinically meaningful weight gain or sexual-function deterioration on paroxetine 7.5 mg vs placebo — explicitly labelled pooled report of the same two trials
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two randomised trials (Portman 2014) — explicitly labelled pooled report
cards.people: Pooled efficacy (n=1,174) and safety (n=1,175) populations of the same two phase 3 trials: postmenopausal women aged ≥40 with moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, median baseline weight ~75 kg and BMI ~28 kg/m², with ~58% reporting sexual dysfunction at baseline. Outcomes were weight and BMI change, Arizona Sexual Experiences Scale scores, a hot-flush interference sexuality subscore, and related adverse events. Registered as NCT01101841 and NCT01361308.
cards.result: No clinically meaningful or statistically significant changes in weight or sexual-function measures occurred in the paroxetine group; small statistically significant weight and BMI increases appeared in the placebo group at week 4 only. There was no between-group difference in the proportion gaining ≥7% of body weight at weeks 4, 12 or 24, and adverse events suggestive of sexual dysfunction were low and similar in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Reassuring on the two harms patients most fear from an SSRI at antidepressant doses — but 12–24 weeks at 7.5 mg in trial volunteers does not price longer use, and a null on weight and sexual function says nothing about the class cautions that do apply at this dose, notably CYP2D6 inhibition (tamoxifen) and discontinuation effects with longer exposure, which are outside these records.

shelves.title: Fractional CO2 laser for genitourinary syndrome of menopause: sham-controlled trials show no benefit over sham (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with vaginal symptoms of genitourinary syndrome of menopause, does fractional CO2 laser therapy, versus sham laser, improve symptom severity at 12 months?
shelves.balance: This is a heavily marketed, usually cash-pay intervention, and the sham-controlled evidence is the crux: it is null. In the LIGHT trial in breast-cancer survivors on aromatase inhibitors, sexual function improved in both arms with no difference between laser and sham at 6 months, and the trial's 12-month report was likewise null on every outcome. A small US sham-controlled trial found 64% improved on laser vs 67% on sham. A pilot in gynaecologic cancer survivors found no difference in vaginal symptoms, with a preliminary sexual-function signal in 18 women that the larger trials do not confirm. The largest sham-controlled trial of this question (Sydney, 85 women, 12 months) is already carded elsewhere in this library and was also null on symptom severity; it is cross-pointed here in prose and is not re-carded. The US FDA issued a safety communication in 2018 warning against energy-based devices marketed for 'vaginal rejuvenation' outside cleared indications. Product naming: the abstracts of the carded trials do not name a specific commercial laser system, so no system can be named on this shelf's face; results should not be assumed to transfer between systems, and no system-specific claim is made. Uncontrolled case series reporting large improvements exist, but they cannot separate laser effect from the contextual improvement the sham arms demonstrate.

cards.headline: LIGHT (Mension 2023): CO2 laser vs sham in breast-cancer survivors on aromatase inhibitors — no difference in sexual function at 6 months
cards.summary: LIGHT (Mension 2023): CO2 laser vs sham in breast-cancer survivors on aromatase inhibitors — no difference in sexual function at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (LIGHT), JAMA Network Open 2023
cards.people: 84 women deemed eligible, 72 randomised and analysed (mean age 52.6 years): survivors of breast cancer using aromatase inhibitors with genitourinary syndrome of menopause, at a tertiary hospital in Spain. Five monthly sessions of fractional CO2 laser (35) or sham laser (37); all patients also used first-line nonhormonal therapy (moisturisers and vaginal vibrator stimulation). Primary outcome: Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) at 6 months.
cards.result: FSFI improved in both groups (laser 14.8 to 20.0 points; sham 15.6 to 23.5 points) with no significant between-group difference in improvement (5.2 vs 7.9 points; P=.15). No differences in dyspareunia, Vaginal Health Index, body image, quality of life, vaginal pH, maturation index, epithelial thickness or elasticity. Tolerance was worse with real laser (Likert 3.3 vs 4.1; P=.007); no differences in complications or serum estradiol.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received first-line nonhormonal therapy, so the within-group improvements cannot be credited to the laser — the sham arm improved at least as much. The population (aromatase-inhibitor users) has more severe GSM than the general postmenopausal population.
cards.source: Mension E et al. Effect of Fractional Carbon Dioxide vs Sham Laser on Sexual Function in Survivors of Breast Cancer Receiving Aromatase Inhibitors for Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause: The LIGHT Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: LIGHT 12-month report (Anglès-Acedo 2026) — second, explicitly labelled report of the same LIGHT trial: still no difference at 12 months
cards.summary: LIGHT 12-month report (Anglès-Acedo 2026) — second, explicitly labelled report of the same LIGHT trial: still no difference at 12 months
cards.type: Secondary analysis / 12-month report of the LIGHT randomised sham-controlled trial, JAMA Network Open 2026
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the same LIGHT trial (PMID 36763359): 84 randomised breast-cancer survivors with GSM and dyspareunia receiving aromatase inhibitors in Spain; 67 completed 12-month follow-up (laser 32, sham 35). Five monthly sessions of fractional CO2 laser or sham, plus first-line nonhormonal therapy.
cards.result: No difference between laser and sham in FSFI change at 12 months (difference −0.69 points [95% CI −3.58 to 2.20]; P=.64), nor in any secondary outcome. Across both groups combined, FSFI, dyspareunia, body image, Vaginal Health Index, pH and maturation index all improved from baseline — improvements the authors attribute to first-line therapy adherence, trial participation or contextual factors rather than laser efficacy. No severe adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of one trial, not independent evidence — it is carded as an explicitly labelled companion report because the 12-month horizon is the shelf question's horizon. It adds follow-up duration, not a second trial.

cards.headline: Cruff & Khandwala 2021: fractional CO2 laser vs sham for GSM dyspareunia — 64% improved on laser vs 67% on sham
cards.summary: Cruff & Khandwala 2021: fractional CO2 laser vs sham for GSM dyspareunia — 64% improved on laser vs 67% on sham
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, Journal of Sexual Medicine 2021
cards.people: 30 menopausal women randomised to fractional CO2 laser (14) or sham (16); three treatments 6 weeks apart; primary endpoint a 2-stage improvement in GSM-related dyspareunia at 6 months.
cards.result: No difference in the proportion improved (64% laser vs 67% sham; P=1.000). Both arms improved within-group on Vaginal Health Index and visual analogue scales, with no between-group differences, and similar findings on sexual-function questionnaires. No adverse events in either arm.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=30) and underpowered, as its authors state — its value is directional agreement with the larger null trials, and its sham arm again shows the size of the contextual/placebo improvement.
cards.source: Cruff J, Khandwala S. A Double-Blind Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial to Evaluate the Efficacy of Fractional Carbon Dioxide Laser Therapy on Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause. J Sex Med. 2021. PMID 33757774. cards.headline: Quick 2021 pilot: CO2 laser vs sham in gynaecologic cancer survivors — no difference in vaginal symptoms; a preliminary sexual-function signal in 18 women
cards.summary: Quick 2021 pilot: CO2 laser vs sham in gynaecologic cancer survivors — no difference in vaginal symptoms; a preliminary sexual-function signal in 18 women
cards.people: 18 women with gynaecologic cancers and dyspareunia and/or vaginal dryness, randomised to fractional CO2 laser (10) or sham (8) in a multi-institutional pilot trial; primary aim the proportion with symptom improvement on the Vaginal Assessment Scale.
cards.result: No difference in change in median Vaginal Assessment Scale score. Change in median total FSFI favoured treatment (Δ 6.5 vs −0.3; p=0.02); urinary symptom change did not differ significantly (p=0.17). No serious adverse events reported.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility pilot of 18 women: the FSFI signal is hypothesis-generating only and is not confirmed by the larger LIGHT trial in a comparable survivor population. Single-blind design.
cards.source: Quick AM et al. Pilot study of fractional CO2 laser therapy for genitourinary syndrome of menopause in gynecologic cancer survivors. Maturitas. 2021. PMID 33358206 · NCT03372720. cards.headline: Synthesis: the sham-controlled record is concordantly null — improvement happens, but sham produces it too
cards.summary: Synthesis: the sham-controlled record is concordantly null — improvement happens, but sham produces it too
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: LIGHT (72 analysed; 84 randomised with 12-month report), Cruff (30) and Quick (18) — three sham-controlled trials, all null on their symptom primaries.
cards.result: No carded sham-controlled trial shows fractional CO2 laser beating sham on symptom severity or sexual function. Within-group improvements are consistent and sometimes large — and occur equally with sham, which is why uncontrolled series overstate this treatment. Stamp: NO BENEFIT DEMONSTRATED (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The largest sham-controlled trial (Sydney, n=85, 12-month symptom severity) is homed elsewhere in the library and is deliberately not re-carded here; its null result is concordant and is described in the balance in prose only.
cards.source: Synthesis of PMIDs 36763359, 42879157 (two labelled reports of the LIGHT trial), 33757774, 33358206 — this pack's own cards.

shelves.title: Lactation (physiology): mothers feed ~11 times a day and a feed transfers ~76 g of milk; suckling releases oxytocin in discrete pulses (about 2 per 20 minutes, fewer under stress) that eject milk, while prolactin rises with suckling early on and its basal level falls across established lactation — and milk secretion is insulated from short-term glucose and insulin swings
shelves.question: In lactating humans, how much milk is produced and how is ejection controlled — 24-hour milk production volumes by test-weighing/isotope methods, the frequency and amplitude of oxytocin pulses with suckling on frequent-sampling studies, and prolactin's permissive time course across established lactation?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong — lactation sections): milk secretion is prolactin-permitted and supply follows removal, while milk ejection is a neuroendocrine reflex — suckling triggers pulsatile oxytocin release, oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells, milk is ejected. The carded human studies quantify each limb. Production: in 71 exclusively breastfeeding mothers test-weighing every feed for 24–26 hours, infants fed 11 ± 3 times a day and took 76.0 ± 12.6 g per feed, about two-thirds of the milk available in the breast — and feed frequency did not predict 24-hour production (Kent 2006). Ejection: suckling-induced oxytocin release is pulsatile with discrete short pulses — 2.25 ± 0.71 pulses per 20 minutes of nursing at rest, falling to ~1.1–1.3 under mental-arithmetic or noise stress, with no change in prolactin rise or milk yield in that session (Ueda 1994; N = 22). Hormone time course: basal oxytocin and prolactin were higher on day 4 than at 3–4 months, both rose with suckling throughout, basal prolactin fell within 24 hours of weaning, and prolactin at 3–4 months — not oxytocin — correlated with how much longer breastfeeding continued; milk yield correlated with neither hormone's level (Uvnäs-Moberg 1990; N = 55). Secretion is metabolically insulated: 20 hours of fasting and 4 hours of clamped hyperinsulinaemia did not change milk volume or lactose secretion, and doubling plasma glucose raised milk glucose threefold without raising lactose synthesis (Neville 1993) — consistent with local, removal-driven control (the autocrine limb the textbooks describe; the Wilde programme's primary work is in ruminants and is presented here only as that textbook framing, never as a card). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Kent 2006: exclusively breastfed infants fed 11 ± 3 times in 24 hours and took 76.0 ± 12.6 g per feed — 67% of the milk available in the breast — and feed frequency did not predict 24-hour production (N = 71)
cards.summary: Kent 2006: exclusively breastfed infants fed 11 ± 3 times in 24 hours and took 76.0 ± 12.6 g per feed — 67% of the milk available in the breast — and feed frequency did not predict 24-hour production (N = 71)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (24-hour test-weighing, Hartmann programme)
cards.people: 71 mothers of infants aged 1–6 months, exclusively breastfeeding on demand, who test-weighed their infants before and after every breastfeeding from each breast for 24–26 hours and collected small milk samples at each weighing (Hartmann programme).
cards.result: Infants breastfed 11 ± 3 times in 24 hours (range 6–18). A breastfeeding transferred 76.0 ± 12.6 g (range 0–240 g), which was 67.3 ± 7.8% (range 0–100%) of the volume available in the breast at the start of that feed. Left and right breasts rarely produced the same volume; the amount taken depended on which breast, pairing, time of day and night feeding, and night feeds made an important contribution to total intake. Milk fat content was 41.1 ± 7.8 g/L (range 22.3–61.6) and was independent of feeding frequency. There was no relationship between the number of breastfeedings per day and the mothers' 24-hour milk production — production is a property of the breast and its emptying, not of the feed count.
cards.watchOut: The record prints per-feed volumes and feed frequency, not a single pooled 24-hour total; multiplying them here would be arithmetic on means of correlated measures, so the shelf reports the printed quantities and the record's own conclusion about 24-hour production.
cards.source: Kent JC et al. Volume and frequency of breastfeedings and fat content of breast milk throughout the day. Pediatrics. 2006. PMID: 16510619. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Breast Feeding · Dietary Fats/analysis · Feeding Behavior · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lactation · Milk, Human/chemistry

cards.headline: Ueda 1994: suckling released oxytocin in discrete pulses — 2.25 ± 0.71 per 20 minutes of nursing — and psychological stress cut the pulse frequency roughly in half without changing prolactin or milk yield (N = 22)
cards.summary: Ueda 1994: suckling released oxytocin in discrete pulses — 2.25 ± 0.71 per 20 minutes of nursing — and psychological stress cut the pulse frequency roughly in half without changing prolactin or milk yield (N = 22)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (frequent-sampling oxytocin pulses during suckling)
cards.people: 22 puerperal women nursing their infants, with blood sampled at 2-minute intervals (collected to minimise oxytocinase degradation, extracted, radioimmunoassay) during suckling under three conditions: control, stress by mental calculation, and stress by noise. The record classifies the study as a randomised clinical trial of the stress conditions.
cards.result: Suckling-induced oxytocin release was pulsatile, with discrete, short pulses. Pulse frequency per 20-minute suckling period was 2.25 ± 0.71 in the control group versus 1.28 ± 0.76 under mental calculation and 1.14 ± 0.38 under noise — significantly lower in both stress groups. There were no differences among the groups in the prolactin increase during nursing or in milk yield. The authors conclude the let-down reflex is centrally modulated and that psychological relaxation is necessary for an adequate let-down response.
cards.watchOut: Early-puerperium women and a single nursing session per condition: the pulse counts are the ejection reflex's signature, but pulse amplitude in absolute concentration units is not printed in the record and is not claimed here.
cards.source: Ueda T et al. Influence of psychological stress on suckling-induced pulsatile oxytocin release. Obstetrics and gynecology. 1994. PMID: 8041543. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Uvnäs-Moberg 1990: basal prolactin and oxytocin were higher on day 4 than at 3–4 months, both rose with suckling throughout lactation, basal prolactin fell within 24 hours of weaning — and milk yield correlated with neither hormone (N = 55)
cards.summary: Uvnäs-Moberg 1990: basal prolactin and oxytocin were higher on day 4 than at 3–4 months, both rose with suckling throughout lactation, basal prolactin fell within 24 hours of weaning — and milk yield correlated with neither hormone (N = 55)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (suckling hormone profiles, early versus established lactation)
cards.people: 55 primiparous women, each giving 18 blood samples in connection with breastfeeding on day 4 postpartum and again after 3–4 months, with oxytocin and prolactin measured by radioimmunoassay and profiles correlated with lactation performance and duration.
cards.result: Basal levels of both hormones were significantly higher 4 days postpartum than 3–4 months later and after weaning, and basal prolactin fell significantly within 24 hours of weaning. Oxytocin and prolactin both rose in response to breastfeeding throughout the lactation period; the suckling-induced prolactin release (but not oxytocin) was related to basal levels, and each woman's oxytocin level was individually characteristic across time points. Milk yield did not correlate with oxytocin or prolactin levels, but prolactin levels at 3–4 months correlated with the remaining duration of breastfeeding, and mothers still exclusively breastfeeding at 3–4 months had significantly higher oxytocin and prolactin than those giving supplements — prolactin's role reads as permissive and time-keeping rather than dose-driving yield.
cards.watchOut: Correlations across a lactation course, in primiparous women: the prolactin–duration link is associational, and the absence of a yield correlation is itself the physiological point — circulating hormone level is not the throttle on volume.
cards.source: Uvnäs-Moberg K et al. Oxytocin and prolactin levels in breast-feeding women. Correlation with milk yield and duration of breast-feeding. Acta obstetricia et gynecologica Scandinavica. 1990. PMID: 2244461. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Neville 1993: 20 hours of fasting and 4 hours of clamped high insulin did not change milk volume or lactose secretion; doubling plasma glucose tripled milk glucose but did not raise lactose synthesis (N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Neville 1993: 20 hours of fasting and 4 hours of clamped high insulin did not change milk volume or lactose secretion; doubling plasma glucose tripled milk glucose but did not raise lactose synthesis (N not documented in the record)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (glucose-clamp and fasting manipulations of milk secretion, Neville programme)
cards.people: Exclusively and partially breast-feeding women studied with glucose-clamp methodology — 20-hour fasting, 4 hours of raised plasma insulin at maintained fasting glucose, and 4–6 hours of plasma glucose held at twice fasting levels; a partially breastfeeding subgroup produced no more than 200 ml of milk per day. The record does not print the number of women studied (N not documented).
cards.result: Twenty hours of fasting had no discernible effect on milk output or macronutrient composition. Four hours of increased plasma insulin at fasting glucose had no effect on milk volume, milk glucose, total fat or lactose secretion rate. Glucose at twice fasting levels produced a threefold increase in milk glucose concentration but no significant effect on the rate of lactose synthesis; in the low-producing partial breastfeeders the same hyperglycaemia raised milk glucose more than fourfold without significantly increasing milk secretion rate. The authors conclude human milk production is isolated from the homeostatic mechanisms regulating glucose metabolism elsewhere, partly because the lactose synthetase system has a Km for glucose below the concentration available in the Golgi compartment.
cards.watchOut: Short (hours-long) metabolic manipulations and an unprinted N: the card establishes insulation from acute glucose/insulin swings, not from chronic undernutrition, and its N is labelled 'not documented' on the face as the labelling rule requires.
cards.source: Neville MC et al. Effects of fasting, elevated plasma glucose and plasma insulin concentrations on milk secretion in women. The Journal of endocrinology. 1993. PMID: 8254289. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: production is removal-driven and metabolically insulated (~11 feeds/day, ~76 g a feed, two-thirds of what the breast holds), ejection is a pulsatile oxytocin reflex that stress can halve, and prolactin permits rather than meters supply — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: production is removal-driven and metabolically insulated (~11 feeds/day, ~76 g a feed, two-thirds of what the breast holds), ejection is a pulsatile oxytocin reflex that stress can halve, and prolactin permits rather than meters supply — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: 71 mothers by 24-hour test-weighing, 22 puerperal women by 2-minute oxytocin sampling, 55 primiparous women followed from day 4 to 3–4 months, and a clamp-study cohort whose record does not print its N.
cards.result: The three control limbs separate cleanly in the human data. Volume: a feed removes about two-thirds of available milk, feeds average 76 g about 11 times a day including at night, and 24-hour production does not track feed count. Ejection: oxytocin arrives in discrete pulses (~2.25 per 20 minutes of suckling), and acute psychological stress roughly halves pulse frequency in the same session without changing prolactin or yield. Permission and time course: prolactin and oxytocin basals are high on day 4 and lower by 3–4 months, suckling still raises both, basal prolactin collapses within a day of weaning, and prolactin level predicts breastfeeding duration while predicting yield not at all. Metabolic insulation: fasting, insulin and doubled glucose move milk glucose but not milk volume or lactose secretion over hours. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Ganong) adds the local autocrine control limb; its primary programme (Wilde) is animal work and is framing here, not evidence. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Test-weighing measures milk transferred to the infant, the standard human proxy for production; isotope (deuterium) dilution studies are the other accepted method and none is carded, so cross-method totals should not be mixed with these figures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kent JC et al. Pediatrics. 2006 (PMID: 16510619); Ueda T et al. Obstet Gynecol. 1994 (PMID: 8041543); Uvnäs-Moberg K et al. Acta Obstet Gynecol Scand. 1990 (PMID: 2244461); Neville MC et al. J Endocrinol. 1993 (PMID: 8254289). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Ganong (lactation) — framing, not evidence cards.

shelves.title: Radiofrequency ablation for uterine fibroids (Sonata / Acessa): symptom relief on a single-arm base
shelves.question: In premenopausal women with symptomatic uterine fibroids who wish to avoid hysterectomy, does ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation (transcervical or laparoscopic), versus myomectomy, hysterectomy or expectant care, reduce fibroid volume and symptom severity, and at what reintervention rate?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Leiomyoma/surgery · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Quality of Life · Radiofrequency Ablation/methods · Treatment Outcome · Uterine Neoplasms/surgery
shelves.balance: Radiofrequency ablation shrinks fibroids and relieves symptoms in every series that reports it — the AAGL Practice Committee's 2025 review (30 studies) pools fibroid-volume reductions of 46.0% at 3 months and 65.4% at 12 months, with bleeding and quality-of-life scores improved throughout. The two pivotal programmes agree: SONATA (transcervical Sonata system, Gynesonics; n=147) halved symptom severity (55 to 24 at 2 years, 22 at 3) with reintervention of 5.5% at 2 years and 9.2% at 3; HALT (laparoscopic Acessa; n=135) showed the same pattern with 11% repeat intervention at 36 months. The discipline is in the design column: 26 of the 30 reviewed studies are single-group, the few RCTs are unblinded, and post-RFA hysterectomy across the literature ranges from 1.0% to 24.1% as follow-up lengthens. The devices are named separately (clarification exception) because the routes differ — transcervical and incisionless (Sonata) versus laparoscopic (Acessa ProVu, Hologic). Fertility data are insufficient, per the AAGL committee itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: AAGL systematic review 2025 (30 studies, 49 articles, 3 RCTs): fibroid volume fell 46.0% at 3 months and 65.4% at 12 months after RFA; post-RFA hysterectomy rates ranged 1.0% to 24.1% across variable follow-up
cards.summary: AAGL systematic review 2025 (30 studies, 49 articles, 3 RCTs): fibroid volume fell 46.0% at 3 months and 65.4% at 12 months after RFA; post-RFA hysterectomy rates ranged 1.0% to 24.1% across variable follow-up
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (AAGL Practice Committee) — 30 studies in 49 articles
cards.people: Published peer-reviewed studies of radiofrequency ablation for symptomatic uterine fibroids (3 randomised trials, 1 nonrandomised comparative study, 26 single-group studies, plus TRUST study publications), in demographically diverse but clinically heterogeneous populations, mostly excluding patients who desired future fertility.
cards.result: Across studies, RFA was associated with fibroid volume reduction of 46.0% (11 studies) at 3 months and 65.4% (10 studies) at 12 months. All studies reported decreased abnormal, heavy or prolonged menstrual bleeding. Pooled Uterine Fibroid Symptom quality-of-life scores improved substantially (53.4 points; 19 studies) and Symptom Severity Scores fell (trough 12.8 at 12 months; 11 studies). Return to work and normal activities was mostly within 2 weeks; unplanned hospitalisations were infrequent. Post-RFA hysterectomy ranged from 2 of 205 (1.0%) to 15 of 62 (24.1%) over follow-up from 45 days to 74 months. The committee notes a paucity of comparative studies, RCTs limited by lack of blinding, and reproductive data insufficient for interpretation.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six of 30 studies are single-group: pre-post improvements in symptom scores are what such designs produce even for mediocre treatments, and the hysterectomy range (1.0% to 24.1%) shows how much follow-up length and case mix move the durability answer. This review is the map of the evidence, not a substitute for the missing comparative trials.
cards.source: Chen I et al. Radiofrequency ablation for the treatment of uterine fibroids: a systematic review and meta-analysis by the AAGL Practice Committee. J Minim Invasive Gynecol. 2025. cards.headline: SONATA pivotal trial (transcervical Sonata system, N = 147): symptom severity fell from 55 to 24 at 2 years and 22 at 3 years; surgical reintervention for heavy bleeding 5.5% at 2 years and 9.2% at 3 years — single-arm
cards.summary: SONATA pivotal trial (transcervical Sonata system, N = 147): symptom severity fell from 55 to 24 at 2 years and 22 at 3 years; surgical reintervention for heavy bleeding 5.5% at 2 years and 9.2% at 3 years — single-arm
cards.type: Prospective multicentre single-arm pivotal trial with 2- and 3-year reports — N = 147
cards.people: 147 premenopausal women with symptomatic uterine fibroids (up to 10 clinically relevant fibroids, each 1-5 cm) treated as outpatients with sonography-guided transcervical fibroid ablation using the Sonata system (Gynesonics, Inc., Redwood City, CA, USA); 125 (85%) returned for 2-year follow-up.
cards.result: At 2 years: mean symptom severity score fell from 55 (+/-19) to 24 (+/-18) (p<0.001), health-related quality of life rose from 40 to 83, treatment satisfaction was 94%, and surgical reintervention for heavy menstrual bleeding had been performed in 5.5%. At 3 years: symptom severity 22 (+/-21), quality of life 83, satisfaction 94%, and reintervention rates of 9.2% (binomial) / 8.2% (Kaplan-Meier); no late complications occurred. One singleton pregnancy with a normal peripartum outcome was reported by 2 years.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm and unblinded, in women selected for fibroid size and number, with 15% lost by 2 years: the symptom-score falls are large but the design cannot separate device effect from expectancy, regression to the mean and natural history. One pregnancy is an anecdote, not fertility evidence — the trial largely excluded women seeking fertility, and the AAGL review (card above) calls the reproductive data insufficient.

cards.headline: SONATA 3-year report (same pivotal cohort, N = 147): benefits exceeded the minimal clinically important difference at every visit; work impairment due to fibroids fell from 51% to 12%
cards.summary: SONATA 3-year report (same pivotal cohort, N = 147): benefits exceeded the minimal clinically important difference at every visit; work impairment due to fibroids fell from 51% to 12%
cards.type: Prospective single-arm trial 3-year report (same programme as the card above) — N = 147 enrolled
cards.people: The same 147 premenopausal women treated with the Sonata system, assessed over 3 years for reintervention, symptom severity and quality-of-life subscales, EuroQol, treatment satisfaction, work impairment and pregnancy outcomes.
cards.result: At 3 years, 88% reported reduced fibroid symptoms; work absenteeism due to fibroid symptoms fell from 2.9% to 1.4%, work impairment from 51% to 12% and activity impairment from 58% to 14% (all p<0.001); EQ-5D rose from 0.72 to 0.88. Treatment benefit on symptom severity, quality of life and EQ-5D exceeded the minimal clinically important difference at every follow-up visit.
cards.watchOut: A second report of the same cohort, carded separately because it carries the 3-year durability and work outcomes — it is not independent evidence, and attrition plus the absence of any comparator still cap what the programme can claim. Durability beyond 3 years rests on the heterogeneous follow-up in the AAGL review, where hysterectomy after RFA reached 24.1% in one series.

cards.headline: HALT trial (laparoscopic Acessa radiofrequency ablation, N = 135 treated): symptom severity fell 32.6 points by 36 months and cumulative repeat intervention was 11% — prospective single-arm follow-up
cards.summary: HALT trial (laparoscopic Acessa radiofrequency ablation, N = 135 treated): symptom severity fell 32.6 points by 36 months and cumulative repeat intervention was 11% — prospective single-arm follow-up
cards.type: Prospective multicentre single-arm trial follow-up — N = 135 treated, 104 with 36-month data
cards.people: 135 premenopausal women (mean age 42.5 years) with symptomatic myomas and objectively confirmed heavy menstrual bleeding (160-500 mL) treated with outpatient laparoscopic ultrasound-guided radiofrequency volumetric thermal ablation (the Acessa route), followed prospectively for 36 months; 104 participants had 36-month data.
cards.result: Mean symptom severity fell by 32.6 points from baseline (60.2) at 36 months (95% CI -37.5 to -27.8; p<.001), with all quality-of-life subscores significantly improved and EuroQOL-5D health state rising from 71.0 to 86.2. The cumulative repeat intervention rate at 36 months was 11% (14 of 135).
cards.watchOut: Single-arm again, with 31 of 135 women missing from the 36-month analysis — if women who did poorly were likelier to leave or seek surgery elsewhere, the sustained-benefit picture flatters the device. The laparoscopic Acessa route (Hologic) is a different procedure from transcervical Sonata — general anaesthesia and abdominal entry versus none — and the two programmes' results are not pooled on this shelf.
cards.source: Berman JM et al. Three-year outcome of the Halt trial: a prospective analysis of radiofrequency volumetric thermal ablation of myomas. J Minim Invasive Gynecol. 2014. PMID: 24613404. Registry ID: NCT01563783 and NCT01750008, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent large symptom improvements and low short-term reintervention, on an almost entirely single-arm base — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent large symptom improvements and low short-term reintervention, on an almost entirely single-arm base — POSSIBLE
cards.people: 30 studies in the AAGL review (only 3 randomised, mostly unblinded and comparative-poor), anchored by two single-arm pivotal programmes: SONATA transcervical (Sonata system, Gynesonics; N = 147) and HALT laparoscopic (Acessa; N = 135 treated).
cards.result: Fibroid volume fell about 46% at 3 months and 65% at 12 months across studies; symptom severity roughly halved in both pivotal programmes and stayed down at 3 years; reintervention was 5.5% (SONATA, 2 years), 9.2% (SONATA, 3 years) and 11% (HALT, 3 years), while post-RFA hysterectomy across the wider literature ranged from 1.0% to 24.1% with longer and variable follow-up. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the direction and size of symptom benefit are consistent, but with almost no blinded comparative evidence against myomectomy, hysterectomy or expectant care, the stamp cannot rise on pre-post data alone.
cards.watchOut: The two devices are different access routes and are named separately throughout (clarification exception): Sonata (Gynesonics) is transcervical and incisionless; Acessa ProVu (Hologic) is laparoscopic. Fertility after RFA is essentially unstudied — most studies excluded women desiring fertility — so this shelf must not be used to counsel on pregnancy chances.

shelves.title: Normal pregnancy raises cardiac output by about half: the serial echocardiography record
shelves.question: In healthy pregnant women, how much do cardiac output, stroke volume, systemic vascular resistance and plasma volume change across gestation, when do they peak, and how fast do they normalise postpartum?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cardiac Output* · Echocardiography · Echocardiography, Doppler · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Myocardial Contraction · Pregnancy/physiology · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: Framed by the standard maternal-physiology account in Cunningham's obstetrics and the Guyton & Hall / Ganong tradition: cardiac output rises early and substantially, systemic vascular resistance falls in the first half of pregnancy, and plasma volume expands by roughly 40–50% against a smaller rise in red-cell mass (the physiological 'anaemia of pregnancy') — the plasma-volume and red-cell figures are presented here as the textbook's account, because no record fetched this session measured them directly. The primary human record fetched agrees on the cardiac side: in 13 women measured from before conception, cardiac output rose from 4.88 L/min to a maximum of 7.21 L/min at 32 weeks (about a 48% rise), significant by 5 weeks after the last menstrual period, with total peripheral resistance falling over the first 20 weeks. Labour adds large transient surges, and values return to prelabour levels within 24 hours of delivery in the labour study. Pre-eclampsia haemodynamics are a different, pathological question and are not covered here.

cards.headline: Robson 1989: cardiac output rose from 4.88 L/min before conception to 7.21 L/min at 32 weeks in 13 women measured serially (N = 13, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Robson 1989: cardiac output rose from 4.88 L/min before conception to 7.21 L/min at 32 weeks in 13 women measured serially (N = 13, printed plainly)
cards.people: 13 women studied on two occasions before conception and then at monthly intervals throughout pregnancy, with cardiac output measured by Doppler and cross-sectional echocardiography at the aortic, pulmonary and mitral valves (classic small serial study — N = 13).
cards.result: Cardiac output increased from a mean of 4.88 L/min before conception to a maximum of 7.21 L/min at 32 weeks — a rise of about 48% — and the increase was already significant by 5 weeks after the last menstrual period. Heart rate and left ventricular performance rose in the first trimester, heart rate rose further in the second, and derived total peripheral vascular resistance fell during the first 20 weeks.
cards.watchOut: N = 13 — a classic small study, labelled as such. Doppler echocardiographic cardiac output is an estimate, and the 'peak at 32 weeks' describes this cohort's monthly measurements, not a universal peak week.
cards.source: Robson SC et al. Serial study of factors influencing changes in cardiac output during human pregnancy. The American journal of physiology. 1989. PMID: 2705548. cards.headline: Twin pregnancy (Robson 1989): cardiac output was already 7.63 L/min at 20 weeks in 10 women with twins and fell to 5.07 L/min after delivery (N = 10, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Twin pregnancy (Robson 1989): cardiac output was already 7.63 L/min at 20 weeks in 10 women with twins and fell to 5.07 L/min after delivery (N = 10, printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human serial echocardiography study (Robson 1989, twin cohort)
cards.people: 10 women with twin pregnancies studied at 20, 24, 28, 32 and 36 weeks and at 6 months after delivery, compared with the 13 women with singleton pregnancies from the companion study (N = 10 twins).
cards.result: Mean Doppler cardiac output was 7.63 L/min at 20 weeks of twin pregnancy, showed no significant change during the remainder of pregnancy, and fell to 5.07 L/min after delivery. The increase was significantly greater than in singleton pregnancy, because of a relatively greater increase in heart rate; left atrial dimension increased more, while left ventricular dimensions, wall thickness and function changed comparably.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 — very small, labelled plainly. Twins exaggerate the singleton adaptation; do not read twin values across to singleton pregnancy.
cards.source: Robson SC et al. Hemodynamic changes during twin pregnancy. A Doppler and M-mode echocardiographic study. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 1989. PMID: 2589450. cards.headline: Robson 1987 (labour): cardiac output rose from 6.99 L/min before labour to 10.57 L/min during contractions late in the first stage, and all values were back to prelabour levels by 24 hours after delivery (N = 15)
cards.summary: Robson 1987 (labour): cardiac output rose from 6.99 L/min before labour to 10.57 L/min during contractions late in the first stage, and all values were back to prelabour levels by 24 hours after delivery (N = 15)
cards.type: Primary human serial study of labour (Robson 1987)
cards.people: 15 women studied serially during the first stage of labour and at 1 and 24 hours after delivery, with cardiac output measured by Doppler and cross-sectional echocardiography at the pulmonary valve (N = 15).
cards.result: Basal cardiac output (between contractions) rose from a prelabour mean of 6.99 L/min to 7.88 L/min at ≥8 cm dilatation, through stroke volume; during contractions it rose further, to 10.57 L/min at ≥8 cm, through both stroke volume and heart rate. One hour after delivery heart rate and cardiac output had returned to prelabour values, though mean arterial pressure and stroke volume remained raised; by 24 hours all haemodynamic variables had returned to prelabour values.
cards.watchOut: N = 15, labelled plainly, and a labour study — its postpartum normalisation (complete by 24 hours for the variables measured) is faster than the weeks-long resolution of the structural changes of pregnancy described in textbooks; the two timescales describe different variables.

cards.headline: Synthesis: output up by roughly half by the early third trimester, resistance down early, labour surges on top — textbook-settled physiology
cards.summary: Synthesis: output up by roughly half by the early third trimester, resistance down early, labour surges on top — textbook-settled physiology
cards.people: Four primary human serial-measurement studies (Ns 13, 10, 15 and one with N not documented) plus the textbook framing named in the balance.
cards.result: Cardiac output 4.88 → 7.21 L/min by 32 weeks (singleton, N = 13); twin output 7.63 L/min at 20 weeks falling to 5.07 L/min after delivery (N = 10); labour contraction peaks of 10.57 L/min with full return to prelabour values by 24 hours postpartum (N = 15). Plasma-volume expansion of ~40–50% is the textbook's account (Cunningham's; Guyton & Hall tradition), not a value measured in the records fetched. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The classic serial studies are small (N = 10–15) — normal for invasive-era physiology and labelled on every card. Modern larger cohorts refine the time course but do not overturn the direction or approximate size of the changes.

shelves.title: The luteal phase resets the thermostat upward: sweating and vasodilation thresholds rise by about half a degree
shelves.question: In healthy women, how do resting core temperature and the thresholds for sweating and cutaneous vasodilation shift between the follicular and luteal phases, and by how much (~0.3–0.5 °C)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Arm/blood supply · Body Temperature · Body Temperature Regulation* · Circadian Rhythm* · Esophagus/physiology · Female · Follicular Phase · Humans · Luteal Phase · Menstrual Cycle* · Physical Exertion · Regional Blood Flow · Skin/blood supply · Sweating* · Vasodilation
shelves.balance: Framed by Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep on progesterone's thermogenic effect: after ovulation the regulated core temperature sits higher, and the thresholds at which sweating, cutaneous vasodilation and shivering begin all shift upward together — a resetting of the set point, not a failure of the effectors, whose slopes above threshold are essentially unchanged. The primary record fetched is concordant: resting oesophageal temperature averaged 0.3 °C higher in the luteal phase in Stephenson & Kolka's exercise study (4 women), and 0.59 °C higher at night in Hessemer & Brück's 10 women, whose shivering, sweating and vasodilation thresholds were all raised by an average of 0.47 °C in the luteal phase. Effect sizes are small and method-sensitive — threshold values depend on the temperature site and the mean-body-temperature weighting used — so this shelf gives the range (~0.3–0.6 °C), not a single point value.

cards.headline: Stephenson & Kolka 1985: resting core temperature 0.3 °C higher in the luteal phase, and sweating/vasodilation thresholds shifted up with phase and time of day (N = 4, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Stephenson & Kolka 1985: resting core temperature 0.3 °C higher in the luteal phase, and sweating/vasodilation thresholds shifted up with phase and time of day (N = 4, printed plainly)
cards.people: 4 women exercised at 60% of peak oxygen uptake in 35 °C heat for 30 minutes at 04:00 and 16:00 in the follicular and luteal phases, with oesophageal temperature, arm sweating rate and forearm blood flow measured (classic small study — N = 4).
cards.result: At rest, oesophageal temperature averaged 0.3 °C higher in the luteal than the follicular phase at both times of day, and about 0.4 °C higher at 16:00 than at 04:00 in both phases. Slopes of the forearm-blood-flow and sweating relationships against oesophageal temperature did not differ between conditions — the thresholds moved, the gains did not. Thresholds in the follicular phase at 04:00 averaged 36.44 °C for sweating and 36.80 °C for vasodilation; in the luteal phase at 16:00 they averaged 37.46 °C and 37.53 °C respectively.
cards.watchOut: N = 4 — a classic very small study, labelled plainly; its threshold values combine menstrual-phase and circadian effects (the two comparisons are separated in the result above), and absolute threshold temperatures are method-specific.
cards.source: Stephenson LA et al. Menstrual cycle phase and time of day alter reference signal controlling arm blood flow and sweating. The American journal of physiology. 1985. PMID: 4025576. cards.headline: Hessemer & Brück 1985 (night studies): core temperatures 0.59 °C higher and all autonomic thresholds raised by 0.47 °C in the luteal phase (N = 10)
cards.summary: Hessemer & Brück 1985 (night studies): core temperatures 0.59 °C higher and all autonomic thresholds raised by 0.47 °C in the luteal phase (N = 10)
cards.people: 10 women studied with external cold and heat exposures between 03:00 and 04:30, when the luteal–follicular core-temperature difference is maximal, in mid-luteal phase (serum progesterone 46.0 nmol/L) and early follicular phase (0.9 nmol/L) (N = 10).
cards.result: At neutral ambient temperature, oesophageal, tympanic, rectal and mean skin temperatures averaged 0.59 °C higher in the luteal phase. Thresholds for shivering, chest sweating and cutaneous vasodilation were increased in the luteal phase by an average of 0.47 °C, however temperature was referenced. Above-threshold sweat rate and heat clearances were also enhanced in the luteal phase, and resting metabolic rate, arm blood flow and heart rate were higher (by 5.0%, 1.1 mL/100 mL/min and 4.6 beats/min).
cards.watchOut: N = 10, labelled plainly. Night-time measurements maximise the phase difference; daytime differences are smaller. The pattern (all thresholds moving together) supports a set-point resetting rather than separate effector changes.
cards.source: Hessemer V et al. Influence of menstrual cycle on shivering, skin blood flow, and sweating responses measured at night. Journal of applied physiology (Bethesda, Md. : 1985). 1985. cards.headline: Inoue 2005: rectal and mean body temperatures higher in the luteal phase during passive heating, and the mean-body-temperature thresholds for vasodilation and sweat onset were phase-shifted (N = 10 women)
cards.summary: Inoue 2005: rectal and mean body temperatures higher in the luteal phase during passive heating, and the mean-body-temperature thresholds for vasodilation and sweat onset were phase-shifted (N = 10 women)
cards.people: 10 young women (and 6 young men as comparators) heated passively by leg immersion in 42 °C water for 60 minutes, women tested in both mid-follicular and mid-luteal phases confirmed by hormone assay (N = 10 women).
cards.result: Rectal and mean body temperatures of women in the luteal phase were significantly greater than in the follicular phase and than men's, before and during heating. Local sweat rates did not change between phases at any site, while cutaneous blood flow on the back was greater in the luteal phase. The authors conclude the menstrual cycle modified the mean-body-temperature threshold for vasodilation and sweat onset in women, so the sex difference in threshold was more marked in the luteal phase.
cards.watchOut: N = 10 women, labelled plainly. This study reports thresholds qualitatively (phase-shifted) rather than with a single pooled degree figure — one reason this shelf presents a range across methods rather than one number.
cards.source: Inoue Y et al. Sex- and menstrual cycle-related differences in sweating and cutaneous blood flow in response to passive heat exposure. European journal of applied physiology. 2005. shelves.title: Hot flushes are triggered by small core-temperature rises: the sweating threshold is lowered in symptomatic women
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women, is the hot flush triggered by small elevations of core temperature acting on a narrowed thermoneutral zone — and how wide is that zone in symptomatic versus asymptomatic women?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Body Temperature · Body Temperature Regulation* · Estradiol/blood · Female · Hot Flashes/blood,physiopathology · Humans · Menopause/blood,physiology · Menstrual Cycle/blood,physiology · Middle Aged · Progesterone/blood · Skin Temperature · Sweating
shelves.balance: Framed by Ganong / Boron & Boulpaep on the thermoneutral (interthreshold) zone, and by the Freedman laboratory programme this shelf is built from: in symptomatic postmenopausal women the sweating threshold is lowered, so small elevations of core temperature — of the size produced by ordinary activity, a warm room or the circadian rise — trigger the full heat-loss response experienced as a flush. The classic laboratory comparison that measured the zone's width directly (symptomatic women's zone near 0.0 °C by rectal temperature versus about 0.4 °C in asymptomatic women) is homed elsewhere in this library and is cross-pointed here in prose, not carded: its finding is stated as that programme's account. The free primary record fetched this session supports the mechanism at every step it measures: most flushes were preceded by core-temperature elevations on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, and symptomatic women had significantly lower sweating thresholds and higher maximum sweat rates than asymptomatic and cycling women in the controlled-laboratory comparison. The further claim that central sympathetic (noradrenergic) activation narrows the zone is thinner — supported indirectly, including an association of flush bother with higher baseline plasma noradrenaline in a stress-protocol cohort — and is labelled accordingly. This mechanism is the frame the neurokinin-antagonist treatment shelves in the library presuppose.

cards.headline: Freedman 1995: on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, the majority of hot flushes were preceded by elevations in core temperature (N = 16, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Freedman 1995: on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, the majority of hot flushes were preceded by elevations in core temperature (N = 16, printed plainly)
cards.people: 10 symptomatic and 6 asymptomatic postmenopausal women with 24-hour ambulatory monitoring of sternal skin conductance (to detect flushes), ambient and skin temperature, and core temperature by ingested radiotelemetry pill (N = 16).
cards.result: Cosinor analysis showed a circadian rhythm of hot flushes (P<0.02) peaking at about 18:25. Core temperatures of symptomatic women were lower than those of asymptomatic women from 00:00–04:00 and at 15:00 and 22:00 (P<.05). The majority of hot flushes were preceded by elevations in core temperature — the observation behind the trigger hypothesis.
cards.watchOut: N = 16 (10 symptomatic, 6 asymptomatic) — small, labelled plainly. 'Preceded by' is a temporal association on monitoring, not proof that the rise alone is sufficient to trigger every flush.
cards.source: Freedman RR et al. Core body temperature and circadian rhythm of hot flashes in menopausal women. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1995. PMID: 7629229. cards.headline: Freedman & Subramanian 2005: symptomatic women had significantly lower sweating thresholds and higher maximum sweat rates than all other women studied
cards.summary: Freedman & Subramanian 2005: symptomatic women had significantly lower sweating thresholds and higher maximum sweat rates than all other women studied
cards.people: 12 symptomatic and 10 asymptomatic postmenopausal women and 12 eumenorrheic (cycling) women recorded in a temperature- and humidity-controlled laboratory under thermoneutral and warm conditions, with core temperature by ingested radiotelemetry pill and sweat rate by capacitance hygrometer (N = 34 total).
cards.result: Symptomatic women had significantly lower sweating thresholds and higher maximum sweat rates compared with all other women. These results could not be explained by differences in estrogen, progesterone or body mass index. The authors conclude postmenopausal women with hot flushes are uniquely characterised by low sweating thresholds and high sweat rates, relative to asymptomatic and cycling women.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (12/10/12), labelled plainly. The record reports the threshold difference as significant without a single pooled degree value in its abstract — this shelf therefore does not attach a precise degree figure to this study; the zone-width figures in the balance are the earlier programme study's account, cross-pointed in prose.
cards.source: Freedman RR et al. Effects of symptomatic status and the menstrual cycle on hot flash-related thermoregulatory parameters. Menopause (New York, N.Y.). 2005. PMID: 15772562. cards.headline: Gordon 2016: hot-flush bother was associated with higher baseline plasma noradrenaline and a sympathetic-activation profile under stress (N = 186)
cards.summary: Gordon 2016: hot-flush bother was associated with higher baseline plasma noradrenaline and a sympathetic-activation profile under stress (N = 186)
cards.people: 186 women in the menopausal transition or early postmenopause (age 45–60) who underwent a standardised psychosocial stress battery (speech and mental arithmetic) with cardiovascular, neuroendocrine and inflammatory measurements; vasomotor symptom bother was self-reported on the Greene Climacteric Scale (N = 186).
cards.result: In adjusted analyses, hot-flush bother was associated with lower cardiac index and stroke volume index, higher vascular resistance index and interleukin-6, tended to be associated with higher cortisol, and was associated with higher baseline levels of plasma noradrenaline. The authors characterise the profile as increased hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal and central sympathetic activation, inflammation and vasoconstriction.
cards.watchOut: This is the thinner sympathetic limb, labelled as such: an observational association with self-reported bother (not laboratory-provoked flushes), in a stress protocol — it supports, but does not establish, the claim that central noradrenergic activation narrows the thermoneutral zone.
cards.source: Gordon JL et al. Cardiovascular, hemodynamic, neuroendocrine, and inflammatory markers in women with and without vasomotor symptoms. Menopause (New York, N.Y.). 2016. PMID: 27465715. shelves.title: The normal endometrial cycle: ~12 mm thick at ovulation on ultrasound, histologic dating far less precise than the classic criteria claimed, and measured loss over 80 mL in only a third of women complaining of heavy periods
shelves.question: In healthy ovulatory women, how does the endometrium change across the cycle (thickness, glandular and stromal histology by cycle day), what mechanism triggers shedding (progesterone withdrawal, spiral-artery vasoconstriction, tissue breakdown), and how much blood is actually lost in a normal cycle when measured objectively?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Endometrium/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging,growth & development · Female · Humans · Menstrual Cycle/physiology · Ovulation/physiology · Ultrasonography · Vagina
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the cycle pattern and the progesterone-withdrawal mechanism, framed by the standard reproductive-physiology textbook account (Cunningham's / Ganong tradition): oestrogen drives proliferative growth, ovulation switches the gland to progesterone-driven secretion, and progesterone withdrawal at the end of an infertile cycle triggers spiral-artery vasoconstriction, ischaemia and tissue breakdown — the shedding mechanism is presented here as the textbook's account, because the classic experimental observations behind it could not be carded from verifiable records this session (see the Synthesis card's refusals). What the fetched primary record does quantify: on serial transvaginal ultrasound in 23 healthy volunteers the endometrium reaches a mean 12 mm (both layers) at ovulation and then plateaus (Bakos 1993); MRI in 6 women shows endometrial area rising linearly through the follicular phase with the rate dropping after ovulation (Haynor 1986; N = 6, printed plainly). The classic histologic dating criteria are much less precise than originally claimed — in 130 fertile women they could not reliably distinguish any specific cycle day (Murray 2004). For measured loss, the distribution is method-bound (alkaline haematin): among 226 women referred complaining of heavy periods, only 34% actually measured over 80 mL (Warner 2004) — the >80 mL line is a statistical tail definition, and the population mean of roughly 30-40 mL often quoted from the classic Swedish population study is the textbook's account, since that study's record could not be verified this session.

cards.headline: Bakos 1993: serial ultrasound in 23 healthy volunteers — one thin line after menstruation, a triple-line pattern before ovulation, mean thickness 12 mm at ovulation, then a plateau
cards.summary: Bakos 1993: serial ultrasound in 23 healthy volunteers — one thin line after menstruation, a triple-line pattern before ovulation, mean thickness 12 mm at ovulation, then a plateau
cards.type: Primary human serial transvaginal ultrasound study
cards.people: 23 healthy volunteers followed with repeated transvaginal ultrasound through spontaneous ovulatory cycles, with serial serum oestradiol, progesterone and LH; the day of the LH peak was designated day 0 (N = 23).
cards.result: From menstruation to day -7 only one thin echogenic line was seen. From days -6 to -1 the pattern changed to three thin lines with increasingly hypoechogenic texture between them, tracking rising oestradiol and endometrial thickness. At ovulation the hypoechogenic texture was maximal and mean endometrial thickness (both layers) was 12 mm. From day +1 the lines blurred and echogenicity rose; from day +7 to menstruation the endometrium was generally hyperechogenic, and luteal-phase growth plateaued.
cards.watchOut: N = 23 volunteers in a descriptive study: the 12 mm ovulatory mean describes this cohort's spontaneous cycles and technique, not a diagnostic cut-off for any individual cycle.
cards.source: Bakos O et al. Transvaginal sonographic evaluation of endometrial growth and texture in spontaneous ovulatory cycles--a descriptive study. Human reproduction (Oxford, England). 1993. PMID: 8345066. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Haynor 1986: twice-weekly MRI in 6 women — endometrial area rose linearly through the follicular phase and the rate fell after ovulation (N = 6, printed plainly)
cards.summary: Haynor 1986: twice-weekly MRI in 6 women — endometrial area rose linearly through the follicular phase and the rate fell after ovulation (N = 6, printed plainly)
cards.type: Primary human serial MRI study (classic small study)
cards.people: 6 healthy women imaged sagittally by MRI twice a week through one full menstrual cycle, with parallel endocrine and ultrasound studies to fix the day of ovulation (N = 6 — a classic small study, labelled plainly).
cards.result: Consistent changes in thickness and intensity of the endometrium and myometrium were seen in all subjects. Both myometrial thickness and endometrial area increased linearly during the follicular (preovulatory) phase, and the rate of increase dropped significantly during the luteal phase. Two myometrial layers were distinguishable, with the best contrast in the first half of the cycle.
cards.watchOut: N = 6 — very small, labelled plainly per the physiology labelling rule. A 1986 imaging study: it establishes the direction and timing of change, not modern absolute thickness values.

cards.headline: Murray 2004: in 130 fertile women, classic histologic endometrial dating could not reliably distinguish any specific secretory-phase day
cards.summary: Murray 2004: in 130 fertile women, classic histologic endometrial dating could not reliably distinguish any specific secretory-phase day
cards.type: Primary human randomised observational study of endometrial dating accuracy
cards.people: 130 healthy, regularly cycling fertile volunteers aged 18 to 35 years, randomised to endometrial sampling 1 to 14 days after the midcycle urinary LH surge, with serum oestradiol and progesterone measured and three gynaecologic histopathologists scoring 32 histologic features blinded.
cards.result: The traditional histologic dating criteria were much less temporally distinct and discriminating than originally described, because of considerable intersubject, intrasubject and interobserver variability. Neither the traditional criteria nor any combination of the best-performing features could reliably distinguish any specific cycle day or narrow interval of days. The authors conclude histologic dating lacks the accuracy and precision to diagnose luteal-phase deficiency or guide management of reproductive failure.
cards.watchOut: This card measures the dating method, not the underlying biology: the secretory transformation itself is real and ESTABLISHED — what failed is day-level histologic precision. Biopsies came from fertile volunteers, so the variability shown is a best-case estimate.
cards.source: Murray MJ et al. A critical analysis of the accuracy, reproducibility, and clinical utility of histologic endometrial dating in fertile women. Fertility and sterility. 2004. PMID: 15136099. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Warner 2004: of 226 women referred for heavy periods who had loss measured, only 34% actually exceeded 80 mL
cards.summary: Warner 2004: of 226 women referred for heavy periods who had loss measured, only 34% actually exceeded 80 mL
cards.type: Primary human measured menstrual blood loss survey with follow-up
cards.people: 952 menstrual-complaint referrals at three hospital gynaecology clinics in Glasgow and Edinburgh, including 226 women with putatively heavy periods who consented to objective measurement of their blood loss.
cards.result: Only 34% (95% CI 28%-40%) of the women complaining of heavy periods had a measured loss over 80 mL, though measured volume did track subjective heaviness. A logistic model combining ferritin status, clots and changing rate during full flow predicted a loss over 80 mL correctly for 76% of women (n=161; sensitivity 60%, specificity 86%). Diagnosis and treatment appeared unrelated to the measured volume.
cards.watchOut: A referred, complaining population — not a healthy-population distribution: it shows how complaint and measured loss diverge, and it cannot by itself give the normal mean loss. The companion analysis by the same group found the 80 mL criterion itself of limited clinical usefulness, since the groups just either side of 80 mL were virtually indistinguishable.
cards.source: Warner PE et al. Menorrhagia I: measured blood loss, clinical features, and outcome in women with heavy periods: a survey with follow-up data. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2004. PMID: 15167821. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: growth, secretion and withdrawal shedding are ESTABLISHED; two classic anchors were refused as unverifiable this session
cards.summary: Synthesis: growth, secretion and withdrawal shedding are ESTABLISHED; two classic anchors were refused as unverifiable this session
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bakos 1993 (23 healthy volunteers), Haynor 1986 (6 women, N printed plainly), Murray 2004 (130 fertile women) and Warner 2004 (226 women with measured loss).
cards.result: The fetched record establishes the measurable shape of the normal cycle: proliferative growth to about 12 mm at ovulation with a luteal plateau, secretory histology that is real but not day-precise, and objectively measured loss in which the >80 mL 'abnormal' line captures only a minority even of women complaining of heaviness. The progesterone-withdrawal / spiral-artery vasoconstriction shedding mechanism is carried in the balance as the textbook's account (Cunningham's / standard reproductive physiology), consistent with everything carded here. REFUSALS, reported per the physiology build rules: the classic Swedish population study of menstrual blood loss (Hallberg and colleagues, 1966) and the classic endometrial-dating reports (Noyes and colleagues) were NOT carded, because their PubMed records fetched this session carry empty abstracts and their numbers could not be verified from the record — the often-quoted population mean loss of roughly 30-40 mL therefore appears only as the textbook's account in the balance, not as a carded measurement. The classic endometrial-transplant vasoconstriction observations (Markee) likewise could not be verified from a fetched record and were not carded.
cards.watchOut: Keep this shelf on normal physiology: treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding (tranexamic acid, hormonal and procedural shelves) is homed elsewhere and cross-pointed in prose only, not imported here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bakos O et al. Hum Reprod. 1993. PMID: 8345066; Haynor DR et al. Radiology. 1986. PMID: 3532190; Murray MJ et al. Fertil Steril. 2004. PMID: 15136099; Warner PE et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2004. PMID: 15167821. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Follicular waves: two or three waves of follicle development in every natural cycle
shelves.question: In healthy women, what does serial ultrasound show about ovarian follicular development across a natural menstrual cycle — how many follicular waves occur per cycle, when is the dominant follicle selected, and how fast does it grow to ovulation?
shelves.mesh: Ovarian Follicle/diagnostic imaging,physiology · Menstrual Cycle/physiology · Ovulation/physiology · Ultrasonography · Follicular Phase/physiology · Humans · Female
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of the ovarian cycle — FSH-driven antral recruitment, selection of a dominant follicle, and the LH surge — the serial-ultrasound literature has replaced the textbook's single-cohort picture with a wave model, and the primary human data are concordant. In 50 healthy women scanned daily for one interovulatory interval, 68% showed two waves of follicle development and 32% showed three; no woman showed a single wave. A 39-woman cohort from the same programme confirmed the two/three-wave split and linked three-wave cycles to higher systemic inflammation (C-reactive protein). A 56-woman comparison then characterised the ovulatory follicle itself against luteinised unruptured follicles: selection (deviation) timing, growth rates and final diameters differ measurably between follicles that rupture and those that luteinise unruptured, with matching endocrine differences. All three cohorts come from one research programme (Baerwald, Pierson and colleagues), which is stated plainly; within that programme the wave model is consistent and is now the textbook framing. Exact day-by-day growth rates in mm/day live in the studies' tables; where a fetched record does not print a number, this shelf does not invent one.

cards.headline: Baerwald 2003: in 50 healthy women scanned daily, 68% had two follicular waves and 32% had three — none had one
cards.summary: Baerwald 2003: in 50 healthy women scanned daily, 68% had two follicular waves and 32% had three — none had one
cards.people: 50 healthy women of reproductive age (19–43 years) with regular menstrual cycles and no medication interfering with reproductive function, undergoing daily transvaginal ultrasonography for one interovulatory interval, tracking diameter and number of follicles ≥5 mm.
cards.result: Sixty-eight percent of women exhibited two waves of follicle development during the interovulatory interval and 32% exhibited three waves. A wave was characterised by an increase and subsequent decrease in the number of follicles ≥5 mm, occurring in association with growth of at least two follicles to ≥6 mm. A day effect and a day-by-wave interaction were detected in the mean diameter of the largest three follicles and in the number of follicles ≥5 mm. The authors conclude folliculogenesis in women occurs in a wave-like fashion — a new model of ovarian function during the menstrual cycle.
cards.watchOut: One interovulatory interval per woman in one academic cohort: the two/three-wave proportions describe that sample, and wave number in the same woman across successive cycles is not established by this study.

cards.headline: Clancy 2013: in 39 healthy women, the two/three-wave split held — and three-wave cycles ran with higher C-reactive protein
cards.summary: Clancy 2013: in 39 healthy women, the two/three-wave split held — and three-wave cycles ran with higher C-reactive protein
cards.type: Serial-ultrasound cohort with serial endocrine/inflammatory sampling
cards.people: 39 healthy women undergoing daily transvaginal ultrasound for one interovulatory interval (a cohort drawn from the same research programme), with serum collected every 3 days for C-reactive protein (CRP) measurement: 25 women with two waves and 14 with three waves.
cards.result: Women with three waves had higher average log CRP concentrations over the interval (−0.43 ± 0.35) than women with two waves (−0.82 ± 0.47), a statistically significant difference as reported. Average log CRP was also greater in women with three major waves (0.30 ± 0.31) than with one (−0.71 ± 0.55) or two (−0.91 ± 0.47) major waves. The excess CRP in three-wave women was localised to the follicular, not the luteal, phase. The authors interpret more waves as more tissue remodelling, with correspondingly greater local and systemic inflammation.
cards.watchOut: An association study, not a mechanism: CRP differences do not show inflammation causes extra waves (the authors argue the reverse direction), and the cohort overlaps the founding programme's volunteer base.
cards.source: Clancy KBH, Baerwald AR, Pierson RA. Systemic inflammation is associated with ovarian follicular dynamics during the human menstrual cycle. PLoS One. 2013. PMID: 23717660. cards.headline: Bashir 2018: in 56 healthy women, ovulatory follicles were selected, grew and peaked differently from luteinised unruptured follicles
cards.summary: Bashir 2018: in 56 healthy women, ovulatory follicles were selected, grew and peaked differently from luteinised unruptured follicles
cards.type: Retrospective observational serial-ultrasound and endocrine study
cards.people: 56 healthy women of reproductive age (19–41 years) with regular menstrual cycles, undergoing daily transvaginal ultrasonography for one interovulatory interval (all follicles >2 mm measured) with blood sampling every 3 days for FSH, LH, estradiol and progesterone; cycles ending in an ovulatory follicle were compared with cycles developing a luteinised unruptured follicle (LUF).
cards.result: The interval from emergence to deviation (follicle selection) was shorter for LUFs than for ovulatory follicles, but the intervals from emergence to maximum diameter and from deviation to maximum diameter were longer for LUFs. Deviation in LUFs occurred at a larger diameter, LUFs grew to larger maximum diameters (P < 0.0001), and LUFs grew faster both from emergence to deviation and from deviation to maximum diameter. Endocrine profiles differed in parallel: LUFs were associated with lower systemic LH at emergence and maximum diameter, lower FSH and higher progesterone at deviation/maximum respectively, and estradiol higher at deviation but lower at maximum diameter.
cards.watchOut: A retrospective analysis with 3-day hormone sampling, which cannot capture acute endocrine changes; the record reports the direction and significance of growth differences rather than a single mm/day growth rate, so none is claimed here.
cards.source: Bashir ST et al. Follicle growth and endocrine dynamics in women with spontaneous luteinized unruptured follicles versus ovulation. Hum Reprod. 2018. PMID: 29659847. Registry ID: NCT01389141 (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: the cycle is waves, not a single cohort — selection is deviation, and fate is visible in growth pattern
cards.summary: Synthesis: the cycle is waves, not a single cohort — selection is deviation, and fate is visible in growth pattern
cards.people: Three primary human serial-ultrasound cohorts (50, 39 and 56 healthy women, each followed daily for one interovulatory interval), all from the Baerwald–Pierson research programme. Framing follows Guyton & Hall's and Ganong's accounts of FSH recruitment, dominant-follicle selection and ovulation, updated by the wave model, as textbook context, not as an evidence card. Cross-points: estradiol triggering of the LH surge and GnRH pulse-frequency physiology are shelved separately.
cards.result: Every woman studied developed either two (about two-thirds) or three (about one-third) waves of antral follicle development per interovulatory interval; the final wave is the ovulatory one. Selection appears on ultrasound as deviation — one follicle continuing to grow while its cohort stalls — and the growth pattern thereafter distinguishes follicles destined to rupture from those that luteinise unruptured (the latter deviating later and larger, growing faster and reaching larger diameters). Wave number also tracks a systemic signal, with three-wave cycles showing higher follicular-phase CRP.
cards.watchOut: The entire primary base comes from one research group and one volunteer population, with one interval per woman; independent replication and cycle-to-cycle stability within women remain thinner than the within-programme consistency. No anchor in this pack was refused: every carded record had a verifiable abstract this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Anti-Müllerian hormone by age in healthy women: peak at ~24.5 years, then a non-linear fall to menopause
shelves.question: In healthy women, how does serum anti-Müllerian hormone fall with age from adolescence to menopause — the population centile curves and validated decline models — and how much do assay generation and ethnicity shift the values?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Mullerian Hormone/blood · Age Factors · Reference Values · Nomograms · Menopause/blood · Female
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — framed by Ganong (female reproductive endocrinology) and Guyton & Hall ch. 83, and resting on concordant population data: in 1,015 naturally fertile women AMH fell non-linearly with age; a validated model built on a combined n = 3,260 peaks at age 24.5 years and then declines to menopause, with age alone explaining 34% of the variation; and external validation in 15,834 US women confirmed the quadratic decline model (earlier models overestimated AMH by about 11% relative to the nomogram — a relative difference, printed beside the model it describes). The shape — rise to a mid-20s peak, then a long fall — is settled; the exact centile a woman sits on is assay- and population-dependent, so values are carded per cohort and no single number is presented as universal. Cross-point: the follicular-wave imaging dynamics shelf (Slate 8 row S8-4-35's build) describes the ovarian process AMH indexes — a different measurement, not carded here.

cards.headline: Tehrani 2014: in 1,015 naturally fertile women from a general-population cohort, serum AMH fell non-linearly with age, and age-specific centiles (5th–95th) were published as a nomogram
cards.summary: Tehrani 2014: in 1,015 naturally fertile women from a general-population cohort, serum AMH fell non-linearly with age, and age-specific centiles (5th–95th) were published as a nomogram
cards.type: Human population cohort (age-specific AMH centiles), Climacteric 2014
cards.people: 1,015 naturally fertile women aged 18–50 years with regular menstrual cycles, selected directly from the Tehran Lipid and Glucose Study general-population cohort (mean age 36.7 years, mean BMI 27.0 kg/m²); centiles were estimated with an exponential-normal 3-parameter model, and the analysis was repeated including 141 women aged 40–50 who met all criteria except having entered natural menopause after age 40.
cards.result: A non-linear decline of serum AMH concentration with age was observed, and age-specific AMH levels for the 5th, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th and 95th percentiles were calculated; the centile pattern was reproduced after including the 141 older women. The record's abstract does not reproduce the individual centile values, so none are printed here — the verified content is the cohort, the non-linear shape and the existence of the full centile nomogram.
cards.watchOut: A single population (Iranian, naturally fertile, regular cycles): centiles from women selected for proven fertility and regular menstruation may sit above those of an unselected clinic population, and the assay generation used is part of the value — centiles are not portable across assays without checking.
cards.source: Tehrani FR et al. Age-specific serum anti-Müllerian hormone levels: estimates from a large population-based sample. Climacteric. 2014. PMID: 24716733. Registry ID: none in the record.
