cards.headline: Kelsey 2011: the validated AMH model (combined n = 3,260) peaks at age 24.5 years, then declines to menopause — age alone explains 34% of the variation
cards.summary: Kelsey 2011: the validated AMH model (combined n = 3,260) peaks at age 24.5 years, then declines to menopause — age alone explains 34% of the variation
cards.type: Human modelling study of published + own AMH data (conception to menopause), PLoS One 2011
cards.people: A model built by searching the published literature for AMH concentrations in healthy pre-menopausal females and combining them with the authors' own data (combined n = 3,260), generating and robustly validating a model of AMH concentration from conception to menopause.
cards.result: AMH peaks at age 24.5 years, followed by a decline to the menopause; the model also shows a neonatal peak and a potential pre-pubertal peak. Age alone accounted for 34% of the variation in AMH — so two-thirds of the spread between women of the same age is not age. After the early-adulthood transition, AMH reflects the progressive loss of the non-growing follicle pool.
cards.watchOut: A model of pooled published data across assays and populations: it fixes the shape and the peak age, but its normative values inherit the assay mix of the source studies, and the wide residual variation (66% not explained by age) is the honest headline — a single AMH value locates a woman only loosely on her age curve.
cards.source: Kelsey TW et al. A validated model of serum anti-müllerian hormone from conception to menopause. PLoS One. 2011. PMID: 21789206. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nelson 2011: external validation in 15,834 US women confirmed the quadratic AMH–age nomogram — other decline models overestimated AMH by about 11% relative to it
cards.summary: Nelson 2011: external validation in 15,834 US women confirmed the quadratic AMH–age nomogram — other decline models overestimated AMH by about 11% relative to it
cards.type: Human external-validation cohort (AMH nomogram), Reprod Biomed Online 2011
cards.people: 15,834 US women in a population study of infertility patients (named as published — an infertility-patient cohort, not healthy volunteers), used to externally validate a quadratic model-based AMH–age nomogram against linear, bi-linear, decay-curve, power and quadratic alternatives, with bootstrapping of 1,000 datasets.
cards.result: All previously investigated models tended to overestimate AMH by approximately 11% versus the published nomogram (a relative difference), indicating some between-population heterogeneity; bootstrapping indicated the quadratic model provided the best fit, confirming the choice of model in the AMH–age nomogram, which the authors conclude can be used with confidence for interpreting AMH in clinical populations.
cards.watchOut: The validation population is infertility patients, whose AMH distribution is not a healthy-population distribution; the card is used for what it verifies — the model's shape and fit — not as a source of healthy centiles. The ~11% overestimation by rival models is a relative, model-to-model difference, not a change in any woman's hormone level.

cards.headline: Synthesis: AMH rises to a peak at about age 24.5 years and then falls non-linearly to menopause; age explains only about a third of the variation
cards.summary: Synthesis: AMH rises to a peak at about age 24.5 years and then falls non-linearly to menopause; age explains only about a third of the variation
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human records (the 1,015-woman fertile population cohort, the validated conception-to-menopause model on a combined n = 3,260, and the 15,834-woman external validation), framed by Ganong and Guyton & Hall ch. 83 on female reproductive endocrinology.
cards.result: The three records agree on the physiology: AMH is low in childhood with neonatal and possible pre-pubertal peaks, reaches its maximum at about 24.5 years, and then declines non-linearly to menopause, tracking the shrinking non-growing follicle pool. Population centile nomograms exist (Tehrani) and the quadratic decline model is externally validated (Nelson), but age explains only 34% of the variation (Kelsey), and assay generation and population shift values — so an AMH result is read against an age centile from a named assay and population, never against a single universal number.
cards.watchOut: Ethnicity and assay-generation effects are asserted in the row's question and are consistent with the between-population heterogeneity the validation found, but no carded record here quantifies an ethnicity-specific shift — none is printed as a number on this shelf.

shelves.title: Normal ovarian volume by age: decade means fall from 6.6 cm³ under 30 years to 1.8 cm³ at ≥70 (13,963 women, 58,673 observations), with upper limits of 20 cm³ premenopausal and 10 cm³ postmenopausal; by years since menopause, volume falls from 8.6 cm³ in the first year to 2.2 cm³ after 15 years
shelves.question: In healthy women, what is the normal ovarian volume by age and menopausal status — the decade means from the twenties to the seventies, the postmenopausal nomogram by years since menopause, and the upper limits of normal before and after menopause (20 cm³ and 10 cm³) — and how do ultrasound and MRI values compare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aging/physiology · Anthropometry · Body Height · Body Weight · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Ovary/anatomy & histology,diagnostic imaging · Postmenopause · Premenopause · Reference Values · Ultrasonography · Ovarian Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging · Prospective Studies · Ultrasonography/methods · Aged, 80 and over · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Ovarian Follicle/anatomy & histology · Ovary/anatomy & histology · Child · Endometrium/diagnostic imaging · Pelvis/diagnostic imaging · Sensitivity and Specificity · Uterus/diagnostic imaging
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED, per modality and per partition. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, reproductive sections) is brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. The lead dataset is one programme's cohort and is labelled as such wherever carded: the University of Kentucky Ovarian Cancer Screening Program (Pavlik 2000; 13,963 women aged 25–91, 58,673 transvaginal-sonography observations) gives decade means of 6.6 cm³ (<30 years), 6.1 (30–39), 4.8 (40–49), 2.6 (50–59), 2.1 (60–69) and 1.8 (≥70), premenopausal 4.9 vs postmenopausal 2.2 cm³, and upper limits of normal of 20 cm³ premenopausal and 10 cm³ postmenopausal. A self-selected screening population, not a general-population sample — stated on its card. The postmenopausal nomogram (Tepper 1995; 311 women) partitions by years since menopause instead: 8.6 ± 2.3 cm³ in the first menopausal year falling curvilinearly to 2.2 ± 1.4 cm³ more than 15 years after menopause. Its first-year mean (8.6) sits far above the screening cohort's 50–59 decade mean (2.6) because the partitions differ — the two series may not be spliced into one curve, and the partition prints on every card. On MRI (Hauth 2006; 100 women), mean volume rose with age to a peak at 31–40 years and fell thereafter, with no significant difference between menstrual-cycle phases. The 2022 systematic review (Mathis; 33 studies, 1970–2020) is carded as the synthesis of this same literature, not as a fourth dataset: normal ovarian-volume distributions are narrow, with small postmenopausal volumes. This shelf gives size norms only — ovarian-volume screening accuracy for cancer is a different question and is not rowed here.

cards.headline: Screening-programme cohort (Pavlik 2000 — one programme's cohort, labelled): 13,963 women, 58,673 observations — mean volume 6.6 cm³ under 30 years falling by decade to 1.8 cm³ at ≥70; premenopausal 4.9 vs postmenopausal 2.2 cm³; upper limits of normal 20 cm³ and 10 cm³
cards.summary: Screening-programme cohort (Pavlik 2000 — one programme's cohort, labelled): 13,963 women, 58,673 observations — mean volume 6.6 cm³ under 30 years falling by decade to 1.8 cm³ at ≥70; premenopausal 4.9 vs postmenopausal 2.2 cm³; upper limits of normal 20 cm³ and 10 cm³
cards.type: Transvaginal-sonography reference study in a single screening programme's cohort (13,963 women, 58,673 observations) — programme-labelled
cards.people: 13,963 women aged 25–91 undergoing annual transvaginal sonography as part of the University of Kentucky Ovarian Cancer Screening Program — a self-selected screening-programme population, not a general-population sample, printed here on the face wherever this dataset is carded. Each ovary was measured in three dimensions and volume calculated by the prolate ellipsoid formula (L × H × W × 0.523), yielding 58,673 observations.
cards.result: Mean ovarian volume was 6.6 ± 0.19 cm(3) in women under 30 years of age; 6.1 ± 0.06 at 30–39; 4.8 ± 0.03 at 40–49; 2.6 ± 0.01 at 50–59; 2.1 ± 0.01 at 60–69; and 1.8 ± 0.08 at ≥70 — a statistically significant decrease with each decade from age 30 to 70. Mean volume was 4.9 ± 0.03 cm(3) in premenopausal women and 2.2 ± 0.01 cm(3) in postmenopausal women (P < 0.001). The upper limit of normal for ovarian volume is 20 cm(3) in premenopausal women and 10 cm(3) in postmenopausal women. Exogenous oestrogen use was associated with significantly reduced volume at ages 40–59 but not ≥60; volume was unrelated to weight but greater in tall women (>68 in.) than short women (<58 in.).
cards.watchOut: Programme-labelled and self-selected: women who enrol in annual ovarian screening are not a population sample, and repeated observations per woman mean the 58,673 figure is observations, not women. The 20 / 10 cm³ upper limits come from this one programme and print with that provenance.

cards.headline: Postmenopausal nomogram (Tepper 1995): 311 healthy postmenopausal women — volume falls curvilinearly from 8.6 ± 2.3 cm³ in the first menopausal year to 2.2 ± 1.4 cm³ more than 15 years after menopause
cards.summary: Postmenopausal nomogram (Tepper 1995): 311 healthy postmenopausal women — volume falls curvilinearly from 8.6 ± 2.3 cm³ in the first menopausal year to 2.2 ± 1.4 cm³ more than 15 years after menopause
cards.type: Prospective transvaginal-ultrasound nomogram study in healthy postmenopausal women (311 women), partitioned by years since menopause
cards.people: 311 healthy postmenopausal women (menopausal age from 1 to more than 15 years) examined prospectively by transvaginal ultrasonography; each ovary measured in three dimensions and volume calculated for every menopausal year to build a size nomogram for menopausal age.
cards.result: Curvilinear relationships were found between ovarian volume and menopausal age: volume decreased progressively from 8.6 ± 2.3 cm3 in the first menopausal year to 2.2 ± 1.4 cm3 after more than 15 years after the menopause. The authors present these data as a comprehensive characterisation of normal ovarian volumes related to postmenopausal age, intended to assist sonographic diagnosis of abnormal ovarian size.
cards.watchOut: Partition warning, load-bearing: this series is indexed by years since menopause, the Kentucky series by age decade — the first-year mean (8.6 cm³) and the 50–59 decade mean (2.6 cm³) describe differently partitioned populations and must never be spliced into one curve or quoted against each other.

cards.summary: MRI reference study (Hauth 2006): 100 healthy women — mean ovarian volume rose with age to a peak at 31–40 years and fell thereafter; no significant difference between menstrual-cycle phases
cards.type: MRI reference-values study in healthy women (100 women) — modality-specific card
cards.people: 100 healthy women undergoing pelvic MRI; ovarian volume, largest-follicle volume and diameter, and follicle number determined by menstrual-cycle phase and age.
cards.result: The mean volume of the ovaries significantly increased with age, reached its peak between 31 and 40 years, and subsequently decreased. The mean volume of the largest ovarian follicles also increased with age to a peak at 41–50 years. The highest mean numbers of ovarian follicles were found at 20–40 years. Comparing the first and second phases of the menstrual cycle, no significant differences were found for ovarian or largest-follicle volumes or follicle number. The authors conclude MRI normal values can aid early identification of ovarian pathology.
cards.watchOut: MRI values are carded per modality and never merged with the ultrasound series. The fetched abstract reports the age pattern qualitatively without printing the numeric means, so this card claims no MRI number — the quantitative norms rest on the two ultrasound datasets.

cards.headline: Systematic review (Mathis 2022) — synthesis of the same literature, not a fourth dataset: 33 studies (1970–2020) — normal ovarian-volume distributions are narrow, with small postmenopausal volumes; no consensus exists on an endometrial-thickness cut-off in asymptomatic postmenopausal women
cards.summary: Systematic review (Mathis 2022) — synthesis of the same literature, not a fourth dataset: 33 studies (1970–2020) — normal ovarian-volume distributions are narrow, with small postmenopausal volumes; no consensus exists on an endometrial-thickness cut-off in asymptomatic postmenopausal women
cards.type: Systematic review of female-pelvis ultrasound reference values (33 studies) — synthesis card, not an independent dataset
cards.people: Systematic review of published reference values for the female pelvis in healthy subjects (transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound, literature 1970–2020, with cross-checking of reference lists): 33 studies included and analysed, applying 95% reference intervals with 90% confidence intervals as the standard for reference values. Carded as the synthesis of the same literature carded above — explicitly not counted as an independent dataset.
cards.result: Transvaginal ultrasound has higher sensitivity and specificity than transabdominal ultrasound for imaging the uterus and adnexa. Normal uterine length is about 50–80 mm in fertile age. There is no consensus about the cut-off value for endometrial thickness in asymptomatic postmenopausal women, while a measurement >5 mm with postmenopausal bleeding is suspect and requires further examination. The distribution of normal ovarian volumes is narrow, with small volumes in postmenopausal women. The authors conclude normative values for the internal genital organs are sufficiently validated, while further research is required on their role in routine practice and in sonographic screening.
cards.watchOut: A review of the same literature cannot corroborate the datasets it summarises — it is carded for its consensus statement only. Its endometrial limb (no consensus cut-off; no verified primary dataset) is a below-floor question recorded in the slate's Audit B, not built here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ovarian volume falls steeply with age and menopause on every dataset — decade means 6.6 → 1.8 cm³ (ultrasound, screening cohort), a postmenopausal fall from 8.6 cm³ in year one to 2.2 cm³ after 15 years (nomogram partition), an MRI peak at 31–40 years — with upper limits of 20 cm³ (premenopausal) and 10 cm³ (postmenopausal) from the one large programme

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: the Kentucky screening-programme cohort (13,963 women, 58,673 observations; programme-labelled), the postmenopausal nomogram cohort (311 women), the MRI cohort (100 women), and a systematic review of 33 studies carded as synthesis only — three independent populations, not four. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall frame reproductive physiology briefly; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. Cross-points: anti-Müllerian hormone centiles (pack #7170) are a blood test, not a volume; serial follicular development (pack #7075) is a cycle-mechanism question.
cards.result: Print each series with its modality and its partition: age decade (Kentucky), years since menopause (nomogram) and MRI age pattern are three different organisations of the same biology, and splicing them manufactures contradictions (8.6 vs 2.6 cm³) that are partition artefacts. What is consistent everywhere: volume peaks by the thirties at the latest, falls every decade thereafter, and is small after menopause — the quantitative spine of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Portable bladder scanner vs catheterisation: accuracy is setting-dependent — systematic underestimation postpartum (median 42.7 mL, worse at BMI ≥30), fluid- and volume-dependent errors in critical care, prolapse-stage effects, and r = 0.89 for the named BladderScan BVI 9400 after hysterectomy
shelves.question: How accurate is a portable bladder scanner (and bedside bladder ultrasound) against catheterised volume — the reference standard — for measuring bladder / post-void residual volume in postpartum women, critically ill adults with low urine output, women with pelvic organ prolapse, and postoperative gynaecological patients, and in which settings (obesity, ascites / abdominal fluid, advanced prolapse, very low or very high volumes) does its error grow?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Pregnancy · Adult · Urinary Bladder · Prospective Studies · Postpartum Period · Parturition · Obesity
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — setting-dependent accuracy, with no pooled bias figure, because the direction of bias differs by population. Postpartum, the scanner systematically underestimated catheterised volume (median difference 42.7 mL; underestimation in 82.9% of 70 women) and was significantly less accurate at BMI ≥30. In 73 critically ill adults with low urine output, mean bias was near zero overall (−1.3 mL for 2D ultrasound, +3.3 mL for bladder scanning vs catheter), but abdominal fluid (present in 28%) degraded scanner decisions at low volumes while scanning outperformed horizontal ultrasound at catheter volumes ≥300 mL. In 70 women with stage ≥II prolapse, mean PVR differences were small and non-significant (5.94 mL initial, 1.37 mL final), but stage III/IV prolapse increased scanner error. Postoperatively after radical hysterectomy, the named tested device (BladderScan BVI 9400) correlated r = 0.89 with catheter volume and gave 90.0% overall accuracy for the re-catheterisation decision at the 100 mL cut-off. Patient N (70–73 per study) prints, not paired-measurement counts alone. This is a measurement-accuracy shelf: no card claims scanner-guided catheterisation policies improve outcomes.

cards.headline: Postpartum cohort (Zheng 2023, N = 70 after vaginal delivery): median scanner–catheter difference 42.7 mL (P<0.001) with the scanner underestimating true volume in 82.9% of patients, and accuracy significantly worse at BMI ≥30 (P = 0.001)
cards.summary: Postpartum cohort (Zheng 2023, N = 70 after vaginal delivery): median scanner–catheter difference 42.7 mL (P<0.001) with the scanner underestimating true volume in 82.9% of patients, and accuracy significantly worse at BMI ≥30 (P = 0.001)
cards.type: Prospective cohort, bladder scanner vs catheterisation in postpartum women (N = 70)
cards.people: 70 women older than 18 years after term vaginal delivery (61.4% nulliparous; median age 34 years; median BMI 30.5), each with three sequential bladder-scanner measurements followed by transurethral catheterisation as the reference standard.
cards.result: The median difference between bladder scanner and catheterised volume was 42.7 mL (P<0.001), with the scanner underestimating the true volume 82.9% of the time. The scanner was less accurate in patients with a body mass index ≥30 (P = 0.001). The authors judged the 42.7 mL median difference small enough for clinical use while noting the scanner is less accurate than catheterised volume and deteriorates in obesity.
cards.watchOut: The bias here is systematic underestimation — the opposite direction from a 'near-zero bias' reading, and specific to the postpartum setting. Do not carry this 42.7 mL figure, or its direction, into the ICU, prolapse or postoperative populations on the cards below.
cards.source: Zheng et al. Accuracy of Bladder Scanner in Measuring Bladder Volumes in Postpartum Women. Urogynecology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2023. PMID: 37607312. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Critical-care study (Schallom 2020, N = 73 with low urine output): bias −1.3 mL for 2D ultrasound vs catheter and +3.3 mL for bladder scanning vs catheter overall — but with abdominal fluid (present in 28%) and catheter volume <150 mL, not-catheterising decisions were accurate 97–100% on ultrasound vs 86–89% on scanning (P = .02), while at catheter volumes ≥300 mL scanning decisions were accurate 94–100% vs 50–56% for horizontal ultrasound (P = .001)
cards.summary: Critical-care study (Schallom 2020, N = 73 with low urine output): bias −1.3 mL for 2D ultrasound vs catheter and +3.3 mL for bladder scanning vs catheter overall — but with abdominal fluid (present in 28%) and catheter volume <150 mL, not-catheterising decisions were accurate 97–100% on ultrasound vs 86–89% on scanning (P = .02), while at catheter volumes ≥300 mL scanning decisions were accurate 94–100% vs 50–56% for horizontal ultrasound (P = .001)
cards.type: Prospective correlational study, bladder scanning and 2D ultrasound vs catheterisation in critically ill adults (N = 73)
cards.people: 73 adult critical care patients with low urine output receiving haemodialysis or unable to void; bladder volumes measured independently by a physician and an advanced practice registered nurse using 2-dimensional ultrasound, by an advanced practice registered nurse and a bedside nurse using bladder scanning, and by urinary catheterisation. Mean (SD) catheter volume was 171.7 (269.7) mL, range 0–1100 mL; abdominal fluid was observed in 28% of patients.
cards.result: Overall bias was −1.3 mL for ultrasound vs catheterisation and +3.3 mL for bladder scanning vs catheterisation. In patients with abdominal fluid and catheter volume below 150 mL, decisions not to catheterise were accurate more often when based on ultrasound (97–100%) than on bladder scanning (86–89%; P = .02). At catheter volumes of 300 mL or more, decisions to catheterise were accurate more often when based on bladder scanning (94–100%) than on horizontal ultrasound (50–56%; P = .001). The authors concluded both methods can measure bladder volume accurately, with abdominal fluid a confounding factor limiting bladder-scanning accuracy.
cards.watchOut: The near-zero mean biases conceal the volume- and fluid-dependence that is this card's content: scanning is the weaker method exactly where abdominal fluid meets low volumes, and the stronger method at volumes ≥300 mL. Mean bias alone must never be quoted from this study.
cards.source: Schallom et al. Accuracy of Measuring Bladder Volumes With Ultrasound and Bladder Scanning. prospective correlational study, bladder scanning and 2d ultrasound vs catheterisation in critically ill adults (n = 73) 73 adult critical care patients with low urine output receiving haemodialysis or unable to void; bladder volumes measured independently by a physician and an advanced practice registered nurse using 2-dimensional ultrasound, by an advanced practice registered nurse and a bedside nurse using bladder scanning, and by urinary catheterisation. mean (sd) catheter volume was 171.7 (269.7) ml, range 0–1100 ml; abdominal fluid was observed in 28% of patients. overall bias was −1.3 ml for ultrasound vs catheterisation and +3.3 ml for bladder scanning vs catheterisation. in patients with abdominal fluid and catheter volume below 150 ml, decisions not to catheterise were accurate more often when based on ultrasound (97–100%) than on bladder scanning (86–89%; p = .02). at catheter volumes of 300 ml or more, decisions to catheterise were accurate more often when based on bladder scanning (94–100%) than on horizontal ultrasound (50–56%; p = .001). the authors concluded both methods can measure bladder volume accurately, with abdominal fluid a confounding factor limiting bladder-scanning accuracy. the near-zero mean biases conceal the volume- and fluid-dependence that is this card's content: scanning is the weaker method exactly where abdominal fluid meets low volumes, and the stronger method at volumes ≥300 ml. mean bias alone must never be quoted from this study. schallom et al. accuracy of measuring bladder volumes with ultrasound and bladder scanning. american journal of critical care : an official publication, american association of critical-care nurses. 2020. pmid: 33130866. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acute kidney injury · adult · humans · prospective studies · ultrasonography · urinary bladder · urinary catheterization

cards.headline: Prolapse cohort (Theisen 2019, N = 70 with stage ≥II pelvic organ prolapse): scanner–catheter post-void residual mean differences 5.94 mL (initial, 95% CI −3.8 to 15.7) and 1.37 mL (final, 95% CI −10.9 to 13.6), both non-significant — but stage III/IV prolapse was associated with increased scanner error (P = 0.03), and scanner maximum-capacity measurements ran 21.3 mL below catheterised values
cards.summary: Prolapse cohort (Theisen 2019, N = 70 with stage ≥II pelvic organ prolapse): scanner–catheter post-void residual mean differences 5.94 mL (initial, 95% CI −3.8 to 15.7) and 1.37 mL (final, 95% CI −10.9 to 13.6), both non-significant — but stage III/IV prolapse was associated with increased scanner error (P = 0.03), and scanner maximum-capacity measurements ran 21.3 mL below catheterised values
cards.type: Prospective accuracy study, portable bladder scanner vs catheterisation in women with pelvic organ prolapse (N = 70)
cards.people: 70 women with stage II or greater pelvic organ prolapse undergoing complex urodynamic studies, with post-void residual measured by urethral catheterisation before and after filling cystometry and a corresponding portable bladder-scanner measurement for each catheterised value.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between catheter and bladder-scanner post-void residual at the initial (mean difference 5.94 mL; 95% CI −3.8 to 15.7) or final (mean difference 1.37 mL; 95% CI −10.9 to 13.6) measurements. Maximum bladder capacity by scanner was significantly smaller than by catheter (mean difference −21.3 mL; 95% CI −40.3 to −2.3). Stage III/IV prolapse was associated with increased bladder scanner error (P = 0.03). The authors concluded the portable scanner accurately measures post-void residual in prolapse patients, with the stage III/IV caveat considered when choosing candidates.
cards.watchOut: Accurate on average for post-void residual is not accurate for maximum bladder capacity (−21.3 mL) and not equally accurate in advanced prolapse — the stage III/IV error association (P = 0.03) prints with the headline agreement, not beneath it.
cards.source: Theisen et al. The Accuracy of Portable Ultrasound Bladder Scanner Measurements of Postvoid Residual Volume in Women With Pelvic Organ Prolapse. Female pelvic medicine & reconstructive surgery. 2019. PMID: 29424755. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Postoperative study with the named tested device (Thanagumtorn 2016 — BladderScan BVI 9400, per the product-naming rule; N = 70 postoperative radical-hysterectomy patients, 140 paired measurements): scan–catheter correlation r = 0.89 (P<0.001), and at the <100 mL catheter-volume cut-off the scan gave specificity 91.0%, NPV 93.1% and 90.0% overall accuracy for the re-catheterisation decision
cards.summary: Postoperative study with the named tested device (Thanagumtorn 2016 — BladderScan BVI 9400, per the product-naming rule; N = 70 postoperative radical-hysterectomy patients, 140 paired measurements): scan–catheter correlation r = 0.89 (P<0.001), and at the <100 mL catheter-volume cut-off the scan gave specificity 91.0%, NPV 93.1% and 90.0% overall accuracy for the re-catheterisation decision
cards.type: Prospective accuracy study, BladderScan BVI 9400 vs catheterisation after radical hysterectomy (N = 70 patients, 140 paired measurements; tested device named)
cards.people: 70 postoperative radical hysterectomy patients (140 paired measurements across repeated voids after Foley catheter removal), with post-void residual measured promptly after voiding using the BladderScan BVI 9400 (Verathon) and immediately afterwards by urethral catheterisation. Patient N is 70; the 140 figure is paired measurements, not patients.
cards.result: Scan and catheter volumes correlated at r = 0.89 (P<0.001). Using scan volume to predict a catheter volume below 100 mL gave specificity 91.0% and negative predictive value 93.1%; when a catheter volume above 100 mL was the cut-off for re-catheterisation, scan volume returned 90.0% accuracy. Repeating the scan in patients whose first scan was below 100 mL yielded 97.2% specificity and 100% NPV for predicting catheter volume below 100 mL. Measurement differences were not related to age, BMI, parity, co-existing illness, incision type or duration of indwelling catheter in this population.
cards.watchOut: The device is named because the publication names it — these figures belong to the BladderScan BVI 9400 in postoperative radical-hysterectomy patients and are not a class claim for all scanners or all settings. The BMI finding here (no relation to error) differs from the postpartum cohort's — population-specific, and printed as such.
cards.source: Thanagumtorn et al. Accuracy of Post-Void Residual Urine Volume Measurement Using an Ultrasound Bladder Scanner among Postoperative Radical Hysterectomy Patients. Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand = Chotmaihet thangphaet. 2016. PMID: 29952185. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: bladder-scanner accuracy against catheterisation is real but setting-dependent — systematic underestimation postpartum (median 42.7 mL, 82.9% of women; worse at BMI ≥30), near-zero mean bias in critical care that conceals fluid- and volume-dependent decision errors, small non-significant mean PVR differences in prolapse with error rising at stage III/IV, and r = 0.89 with 90.0% decision accuracy for the named BladderScan BVI 9400 after radical hysterectomy; no pooled bias figure is printed because the direction of bias differs by population
cards.summary: Synthesis: bladder-scanner accuracy against catheterisation is real but setting-dependent — systematic underestimation postpartum (median 42.7 mL, 82.9% of women; worse at BMI ≥30), near-zero mean bias in critical care that conceals fluid- and volume-dependent decision errors, small non-significant mean PVR differences in prolapse with error rising at stage III/IV, and r = 0.89 with 90.0% decision accuracy for the named BladderScan BVI 9400 after radical hysterectomy; no pooled bias figure is printed because the direction of bias differs by population
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: postpartum cohort (N = 70 women), critical-care study (N = 73 adults), prolapse cohort (N = 70 women) and postoperative radical-hysterectomy study (N = 70 patients, 140 paired measurements) — patient numbers, not measurement counts, are the denominators throughout.
cards.result: The error modifiers — BMI ≥30, abdominal fluid, stage III/IV prolapse, and very low or very high volumes — are the usable content of this shelf. No card addresses whether scanner-guided catheterisation policies improve infection, retention or length-of-stay outcomes; that intervention question is uncarded here. This shelf also supplies no normative post-void residual values — it is a device-accuracy question only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Antral follicle count age nomograms (PHYS, 4 datasets, all fertility-clinic populations): decline ≈0.4–0.8 follicles/year with published age centiles — not norms for unselected women
shelves.question: Across a woman's reproductive life, how does the antral follicle count (the number of 2–10 mm follicles visible on transvaginal ultrasound in the early follicular phase) decline with age in normally cycling and fertility-clinic populations — what annual rate of decline and what age-specific centiles (5th to 95th, or 3rd to 97th) do the four nomogram datasets report, and how does the decline differ between women attending fertility services and women with regular cycles? (PHYSIOLOGY: every dataset is a fertility-clinic or subfertile population — flagged on the face; textbook framing only, the shelf rests on these datasets.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aging/physiology · Cell Count/standards · Cross-Sectional Studies · Diagnostic Techniques, Obstetrical and Gynecological/standards · Down-Regulation · Female · Health · Humans · Middle Aged · Nomograms · Ovarian Follicle/cytology/diagnostic imaging · Reference Values · Reproduction/physiology · Ultrasonography · Young Adult · Adolescent · Cell Count/methods/standards · Cohort Studies · Infertility, Female/diagnosis/etiology/pathology · Ovarian Follicle/cytology/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Polycystic Ovary Syndrome/complications/pathology · Practice Guidelines as Topic · Retrospective Studies · Anti-Mullerian Hormone/blood · Infertility, Female/blood · Ovarian Follicle · Ovarian Reserve/physiology · Social Factors · China/ethnology · Infertility, Female/pathology · Ovarian Follicle/pathology · Singapore
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Four nomogram datasets, and every one is a fertility-clinic or subfertile population (the nearest to a general sample, La Marca 2011, mixes infertile women with oocyte donors) — no figure on this shelf may be presented as a norm for unselected women, and the population prints on every figure. The decline is consistent in direction and roughly linear: median −0.4 follicles/year in 362 regularly cycling women (5th–95th centiles per year of age, 24–50); a biphasic decline in 1,866 infertile McGill patients without polycystic ovaries (3rd–97th percentiles; the polycystic-ovary exclusion is this dataset's, unspecified in others); −0.6 to −0.8/year under 45 in 2,495 Arabian Peninsula fertility-centre women (median AFC 11 overall); and −0.79/year in 1,009 subfertile Singaporean Chinese women (LMS nomograms). Counting technique (2D vs 3D ultrasound, follicle diameter band) is not standardised across the four datasets and no centile is merged across them. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age-decline rate and centile method in regularly cycling / clinic populations; PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING for transport to unselected populations.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 4 (La Marca 2011, Fertility and Sterility — 362 women with regular menstrual cycles analysed, of 415 recruited; infertile women and oocyte donors): antral follicle count declined linearly with age, the median count declined by 0.4 follicles per year, and the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th centiles were calculated for each year of age from 24 to 50
cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 4 (La Marca 2011, Fertility and Sterility — 362 women with regular menstrual cycles analysed, of 415 recruited; infertile women and oocyte donors): antral follicle count declined linearly with age, the median count declined by 0.4 follicles per year, and the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th centiles were calculated for each year of age from 24 to 50
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — AFC age nomogram, regularly cycling women (dataset 1 of 4)
cards.people: 362 premenopausal women with regular menstrual cycles (infertile women and oocyte donors) at a university hospital, with antral follicle count (2–10 mm follicles) measured by transvaginal ultrasound. The nearest dataset to a general sample on this shelf — and it still mixes infertile women with oocyte donors, which prints on every figure.
cards.result: The analysis showed a linear decline in antral follicle count with age; for every year increase in age, the median AFC decreases by 0.4. The AFC corresponding to the 5th, 25th, 50th, 75th and 95th centiles for each age have been calculated, providing a nomogram of normal and interquartile values age by age throughout the reproductive period.
cards.watchOut: Fertility-clinic/donor population, not unselected women: these centiles may not be presented as norms for unselected women. Cross-sectional, not longitudinal — the 'decline' is an age gradient across women, not a within-woman trajectory.
cards.source: La Marca A et al. Age-specific nomogram for the decline in antral follicle count throughout the reproductive period. Fertility and sterility. 2011. PMID: 20797717. cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 4 (Almog 2011, Fertility and Sterility — 1,866 infertile patients without polycystic ovaries at McGill): the count declined with age in a biphasic pattern, with percentiles from the 3rd to the 97th reported per year of age
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 4 (Almog 2011, Fertility and Sterility — 1,866 infertile patients without polycystic ovaries at McGill): the count declined with age in a biphasic pattern, with percentiles from the 3rd to the 97th reported per year of age
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — AFC age normogram, infertile population without polycystic ovaries (dataset 2 of 4)
cards.people: 1,866 infertile patients at a university teaching centre, retrospectively analysed, with baseline transvaginal ultrasound between days 2 and 4 of the menstrual cycle; women with polycystic ovaries were excluded — the exclusion prints, as the row directs.
cards.result: The age-related normogram for the 3rd, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th and 97th percentile of antral follicle count showed a biphasic mode of decline with two different rates of loss: a steep-slope phase and a moderate-slope phase. In the low percentiles (3rd, 10th, 25th) the high-loss phase preceded the slow-loss phase, whereas in the high percentiles (75th, 90th, 97th) the opposite was found. The authors note future validation with longitudinal data is still needed.
cards.watchOut: Infertile population with polycystic ovaries excluded — one dataset's exclusion, unspecified in others; no centile may be merged across the four datasets, whose counting technique (2D vs 3D ultrasound, diameter band) is not standardised.
cards.source: Almog B et al. Age-related normogram for antral follicle count: McGill reference guide. Fertility and sterility. 2011. PMID: 20869703. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 4 (Melado 2021, Frontiers in Endocrinology — 2,495 women attending fertility centres in the Arabian Peninsula): median antral follicle count was 11 overall; counts declined with age (−0.6 to −0.8 per year under age 45, as published) and 10th–90th centile charts were produced
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 4 (Melado 2021, Frontiers in Endocrinology — 2,495 women attending fertility centres in the Arabian Peninsula): median antral follicle count was 11 overall; counts declined with age (−0.6 to −0.8 per year under age 45, as published) and 10th–90th centile charts were produced
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — AFC age values, Arabian Peninsula fertility-centre population (dataset 3 of 4)
cards.people: 2,495 women aged 19–50, native to the Arabian Peninsula, whose AMH and antral follicle count were measured as part of fertility assessment at tertiary-care fertility centres; median age 34.81 years. A fertility-centre population — printed on the figure.
cards.result: Median AFC was 11 overall. For women under 45 years old, the decrease in AFC was between −0.6 and −0.8 per year, as published. Age-specific values and nomograms were calculated by 1-year and 5-year intervals. AMH and AFC were significantly lower in the niqab group than the hijab group (P = 0.04 for AFC), as published — a sociocultural association reported by the authors, printed as such and not as a biological mechanism.
cards.watchOut: Fertility-centre population only. This dataset's AMH limb belongs to the built AMH-centile territory (pack #7170) and is not carded here — only its AFC limb anchors this shelf.

cards.summary: Dataset 4 of 4 (Loy 2017, PLoS One — 1,009 subfertile ethnic-Chinese women in Singapore): the count declined by 0.79 follicles per year (95% CI −0.93 to −0.64 for the per-year estimate, as published) and LMS-method age-specific nomograms (3rd to 97th centiles) were constructed
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — AFC age nomogram, subfertile Chinese women in Singapore (dataset 4 of 4)
cards.people: 1,009 ethnic-Chinese women aged 26–44 whose AFC and AMH were measured as part of subfertility screening at KK Women's and Children's Hospital, Singapore (December 2010 to November 2014). A subfertile population — printed on the figure.
cards.result: On average, AFC decreased by 0.79 follicle (95% CI −0.93 to −0.64) per year of age. Age-related AFC nomograms for the 3rd, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th and 97th percentiles were produced by the lambda-mu-sigma method and showed an approximately linear pattern, inversely correlated with age, regardless of percentile; there were large inter-individual variations up to about age 40. The authors note future validation with longitudinal data is required.
cards.watchOut: Subfertile population; cross-sectional LMS nomogram, not a longitudinal trajectory. This dataset's AMH limb is not carded here (AMH centiles are pack #7170's territory).

cards.headline: Synthesis: across four fertility-clinic or regularly-cycling datasets (N = 362 + 1,866 + 2,495 + 1,009), antral follicle count declines approximately linearly with age at 0.4–0.8 follicles per year — 0.4/year in regularly cycling women, a biphasic pattern in infertile women without polycystic ovaries, −0.6 to −0.8/year in Arabian Peninsula fertility-centre women, and 0.79/year in subfertile Singaporean Chinese women — with age-specific centiles (5th–95th or 3rd–97th) published by each dataset and never merged across datasets

cards.people: All datasets carded on this shelf: La Marca 2011, Almog 2011, Melado 2021 and Loy 2017 — every one a fertility-clinic, subfertile or donor-mixed population. Distinct from pack #7075 (serial follicular development across a natural cycle — a dynamic, within-cycle question) and pack #7170 (AMH centiles — a different analyte).
cards.result: PHYSIOLOGY framing only — no intervention stamp applies. The established limb is the age-decline rate and centile method in regularly cycling / clinic populations; transport of these centiles to unselected women is EMERGING, because no dataset sampled unselected women.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
